CNN, MS NOW and Politico prevail against White House — for now
A federal judge ruled late Tuesday that President Trump cannot ban news organizations from covering him at the White House because he does not like the nature of their coverage - at least, not until the matter goes to a formal trial.
U.S. District Court Judge Timothy J. Kelly found that Trump's decision to bar more than 70 journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico violated their fundamental free speech in two separate ways as well as their due process rights. Both rights are enshrined in the Bill of Rights to the U.S. Constitution.
The news organizations sued last month after the Trump administration denied them access. The judge granted a temporary restraining order to CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Sept. 24.
Kelly pointed repeatedly to Trump's own public statements and social media posts to construct his conclusion that Trump was not responding to national security concerns. Instead, he wrote, Trump sought to pressure news outlets to cover him more favorably by stripping them of press credentials to gain access to the White House.
"President Trump's own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before," Kelly wrote in the opinion.
He later continued, "[T]he ban threatens to cut off all Plaintiffs' access to the White House press area -- a space open to many of their competitors -- thereby restricting their ability to observe happenings there firsthand, immediately report on those activities, and try to engage with government officials."
Theodore J. Boutrous, the noted First Amendment attorney representing the three U.S. news outlets, had argued in court last week that Trump was the best witness his clients could offer for their case - because the president was so blatant about not liking the tenor of their coverage. Late Tuesday, after the release of Kelly's ruling, he hailed the judge's words.
"When the President issued his 'ban on the free press,' he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment," Boutrous said in a statement shared with NPR.
"Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn't like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers," Boutrous wrote. "The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound."
The White House did not immediately return NPR's requests for comment. Nor did the president speak publicly about the ruling in the first hours after the ruling was released.
Kelly, a Trump appointee, turned aside the U.S. Justice Department's arguments invoking national security concerns and the objections the White House took with their reporting. Trump has said coverage is framed in a way to drag him down and make his Democratic critics look good.
The judge also rejected the department's claims that the court should not weigh in on such matters. Kelly had ruled against the Trump administration during the president's first term in office on a related matter involving efforts to bar then CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta. And Kelly pointed to other precedents that he said must guide his conclusions, even as the Justice Department argued in court they were wrongly decided.
Even so, Kelly took pains to note that he did not utterly dismiss those as valid governmental concerns.
"No one should interpret the Court's decision to suggest that President Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded," Kelly wrote, "or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed."
Even so, Kelly found that the White House's actions to put the president's words into practice had caused a kind of irreparable harm. Trump was not required to admit the reporters to the White House. Once they were credentialed to do so, under earlier court rulings, those credentials could not be stripped away simply because the president or other administration officials do not like their coverage.
The Justice Department invoked national security only in court filings days after the White House acted against the reporters. And the news outlets were neither given fair warning of what was ahead nor a means to object ahead of time. The White House communications office sent letters expressing concern over accuracy and what it said were national security disclosures days later and gave the journalists several days to respond and appeal.
Kelly wrote that the Justice Department's presentation was inadequate to make a compelling case. And he said that after-the-fact notification did not constitute an adequate process to be warned about consequences and to appeal the punishment.
"It is not hard to conclude that President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him," Kelly wrote. And that, he wrote, represents a form of unlawful retaliation.
The ruling did not, however, address the question of the administration's periodic refusal since the ban to permit CNN's journalists into smaller spaces where the full press corps cannot fit simultaneously, such as Air Force One or the Oval Office.
That has made it impossible for CNN to serve as the designated representative of the video pool.
The pool - made up of CNN and four competitors (ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC) - share costs and logistical obligations to capture video of Trump at every public appearance, even in tightly held locations.
Even after Kelly earlier issued a temporary restraining order compelling the administration to allow the reporters back into the White House, the order was observed unevenly. CNN was periodically blocked by the administration from representing the pool either generally or in tight spaces. In one recent instance, CNN was blocked from accompanying Trump aboard Air Force One on a trip to Tennessee.
The three major U.S. news organizations sued shortly after reporters for the outlets reported their credentials, which give them daily access to the White House, were confiscated.
The administration has waged a multi-front battle against the press, including an early review of the broadcast licenses for ABC's local TV stations that could lead to them being revoked. It also forced news outlets out from the Pentagon when they did not agree to withhold any reports that had not been authorized for release ahead of time. The administration has launched investigations of all major networks — including NPR — except Fox, which is controlled by Rupert Murdoch, the president's ally, and successfully pressured the Republican leaders of Congress to pull back all federal funds for public media.
Last week, the Department of Justice said it was investigating five major television networks - CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News, alleging that they have broken antitrust laws when they decided to stick together after the president banned CNN.
As a private citizen, Trump has sued the New York Times, CNN, the Des Moines Register, the BBC, and Wall Street Journal (also owned by Murdoch). ABC settled a Trump lawsuit ahead of his return to office and CBS settled days before its corporate owner received the green light from Trump's pick as the nation's chief broadcast regulator to sell itself to its new owners, allies of the president.

Israel returns stolen Greek artefacts in landmark handover
It is the first such repatriation between the two countries

A ceremony at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens has marked the handover of 22 ancient artefacts, returned by Israel after their illegal removal from Greece.
Culture Minister Lina Mendoni received the objects from the Israel Antiquities Authority and from Amir Ganor, director of its theft prevention division, on Tuesday.
The return comes as Athens intensifies an international repatriation campaign, which has an ultimate goal of securing the return of sculptures taken from the Acropolis.
“It is the first time that Israel has returned antiquities to Greece, marking the starting point of closer cooperation between the two countries for the protection of cultural heritage,” Ms Mendoni said.
“Every return of a cultural object to its place of origin has a broader symbolic and moral dimension.”
The recovered collection spans centuries, with the objects provisionally dated to between about 700 B.C. and 320 B.C.
Among them is a small bronze statuette of a woman. The rest is pottery: slender oil flasks, two-handled amphorae and drinking cups.
The vessels are decorated with mythological scenes and geometric motifs.
The handover forms part of a wider Greek effort to broaden bilateral cultural ties as it pursues the return of the Parthenon Marbles.
The 2,500-year-old sculptures, also known as the Elgin Marbles, were removed from the Acropolis in the early 19th century by agents of Thomas Bruce, the 7th Earl of Elgin.
They are now displayed at the British Museum in London.
Greece's current conservative government has built closer energy and defence ties with Israel in recent years.
In August, Israel signed a €3 billion (about £2.5 billion) deal to build an air defence system in Greece, dubbed Achilles Shield.
That agreement was described as the largest defence deal between the two countries.
Officials from both countries did not disclose on Tuesday how the artefacts came to light in Israel, nor the circumstances of their illegal removal from Greece.
In previous cases, antiquities returned from private collections abroad have often been traced to illicit excavations.
Pninat Yanay, the Israeli ambassador to Greece, said the items were recovered during an “investigation by the Israeli authorities into the illegal antiquities trade”.

Young Malaysians’ US$1.3bn short-term credit spree sparks warning over bad debt
Consumers aged 30 and below drove a third of ‘buy now, pay later’ purchases, prompting caution over ‘excessive’ borrowing
The ministry said it had recorded 65.9 million “buy now, pay later” (BNPL) purchases among younger consumers in the first six months of 2026 – equivalent to more than one in three, or 37.9 per cent, of total purchases nationwide.
As of June 30, the outstanding BNPL financing balance among this age group stood at 2.4 billion ringgit, it said. Some 96.8 million ringgit, or 4 per cent of the outstanding balance, was classified as non-performing or unpaid.
The ministry said that industry regulator the Consumer Credit Commission strictly required BNPL providers to conduct creditworthiness checks and affordability assessments before extending lines of credit to young customers.

Police in Germany seize robot after teen girl is allegedly groped
Investigators probe whether machine was controlled in real time as two teens face scrutiny for live-streaming incident
German authorities opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment after a robot controlled by two young men touched the buttocks of a 16-year-old girl and made thrusting movements toward her, police said.
Police in the western city of Cologne responded after the incident overnight Saturday to Sunday in which the robot’s suspected 16-year-old owner and a 19-year-old companion were said to have filmed the alleged assault.
They were said to have streamed the incident and commentated on it online.
Cologne police spokesman Christoph Bermel said the two male teenagers have not been charged but are considered suspects, and investigators were examining whether the robot’s movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time.

Welcome to Chief Complaint, a new STAT+ column from Frances Mei Hardin, M.D. A former ear, nose, and throat surgeon, she writes about the many challenges facing those who practice medicine in a time of great change.
In some clinical settings, resident physicians have to ask for permission to use the restroom. You read that correctly: Many of these people are approaching or in their 30s, they all have M.D.s and other graduate degrees, and they are still requesting permission to accommodate basic tasks in Maslow’s hierarchy, such as leaving to grab a bite of food or drink, or use the restroom.
And when the beginning of training is marked by infantilizing treatment, even as their responsibility for patient lives quickly grows, it can often lead to something plaguing medicine: learned helplessness, a psychological state wherein a person stops trying to change an unfavorable or unsavory situation because they believe that they have no control over the outcome, even when they do.

Washington, Oct 14: Facing criticism over the diesel deal with Russia, US President Donald Trump said the fuel from Moscow’s refineries was meant to stabilise the global market, which has been hit by high prices.
On October 9, Trump announced that Russia would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”
To facilitate the shipments, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary licence easing sanctions on Russian diesel shipments to global markets until April 7, 2027.
The move came ahead of November congressional midterms in the US, as diesel prices surged amid supply disruptions caused by the Iran war.
“That's a diesel deal. Not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us,” Trump told reporters here on Tuesday, amid a growing chorus against the surprise deal he announced last week after talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Republicans and Democrats hit out at the deal, which Trump announced three weeks after the US Congress authorised him to impose sweeping sanctions on Russia and slapped tariffs on its key trading partners, including China and India.
“That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices. And when you knock out diesel refineries, that’s not a great thing. But they are not releasing it to us. They are releasing it to the entire world,” Trump said.
On Tuesday, a bipartisan group of US senators wrote to Trump, terming the Russia deal a “gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies”.
“The deal you struck with President Vladimir Putin on October 9 will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans,” the senators said.
The letter was signed by Democrats Richard Blumenthal, Chris Coons, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, Jeanne Shaheen and Sheldon Whitehouse and Republicans Alan Armstrong, Susan Collins, John Cornyn, Mitch McConnell, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis.
"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded," the letter said.
Senators said they recognised the need to lower energy costs for Americans, but asserted that allowing Russian diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans.
The deal “only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians,” they said.
“It will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea,” the senators said.
Last month, Congress passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump swiftly signed into law.
“Both chambers passed the legislation with resounding, bipartisan votes, clearly demonstrating our intent and granting you the authorities to broker a just and fair peace,” the senators said.
They said these authorities require the president to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, particularly China, thereby enhancing the US negotiating position to bring a swift end to this ruinous conflict.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

IIIT Ranchi director sent on leave amid stir after student's suicide
It comes a day after the ministry of education instituted a three-member panel to look into issues related to the institution and the students' demands.
In an administrative crackdown following prolonged student protests at the Indian Institute of Information Technology, Ranchi (IIIT-Ranchi) after the alleged suicide of a first-year student on Saturday night, the Union ministry of education sent the institute's Director, Rajiv Srivastava, on a 30-day leave with immediate effect, people aware of the development said on Wednesday.
The development comes a day after the ministry instituted a three-member panel to look into issues related to the institution and the students' demands.
To resolve the administrative deadlock, Prof. V. M. S. R. Murthy, the current Director of IIEST Shibpur, has been given the additional charge as the Officiating Director of IIIT Ranchi.
Prof. Murthy will head the institution for one month or until further orders.
IIIT Registrar in charge, Munuren Samson Champia, confirmed both developments.
"The director has proceeded on 30 days' leave as a probe is being done into the complaint against him. V. M. S. R. Murthy has been appointed as officiating director," he said without elaborating details.
Protesting students halt stir
A protesting IIIT student said they have temporarily halted their strike following the administrative action.
"Strike has now ended after the director was shunted for 30 days," the student said.
An insider sharing an administrative order said that following the director's 30-day removal, the institute administration has also cancelled the recent recruitment process for various non-teaching posts, which had been mired in controversy.
According to an official notice issued by the Registrar in-charge, a copy of which is available with Hindustan Times, the recruitment process stands cancelled with immediate effect due to unavoidable administrative circumstances.
The administration confirmed that the application fees paid by candidates will be fully refunded. The official link and necessary instructions for claiming the refund will be uploaded shortly to the institute’s official website.

Helen Branswell, a renowned infectious disease reporter who earned the respect of experts and public health officials around the world with her accessible, prescient dispatches on scourges from influenza to polio and Ebola to Covid-19, becoming a vital source of information for the public during the most chaotic of times, died Tuesday at age 69.
The cause was complications from cancer, said her sister, Brenda Branswell.
Branswell, a longtime reporter at the Canadian Press, joined STAT at its founding in 2015, working out of the Boston headquarters before returning home to Canada last year to be closer to family in Ottawa.
“Throughout her career, Helen demonstrated an unwavering commitment to evidence, science, and truth, helping the public understand some of the most complex and consequential health challenges of our time,” Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director-general of the World Health Organization, wrote in an email. “At a moment when misinformation competes with facts, her reporting was a trusted source of clarity, honesty, and insight.”
Among the awards Branswell received were the Victor Cohn Prize for Excellence in Medical Science Reporting and the George Polk Award for Public Service, which cited her “relentless coverage of all aspects of the [Covid] pandemic that became must reading for the medical community and the general public” — stories that, the judges wrote, were “almost uniformly timely and astute.” She was also a Pulitzer Prize finalist with two colleagues for their early Covid stories, and received an honorary degree from Ottawa’s Carleton University.
Not bad for someone whose career was, as she put it in a 2020 interview, “really a fluke.”
Branswell, who was born in Sherbrooke, Quebec, started freelancing for a small newspaper in Eastern Canada after graduating from New Brunswick’s St. Thomas University with a degree in English literature, thinking that writing was one skill she had. She eventually worked her way to the Canadian Press, covering politics, sports, and a bit of everything else.
Her introduction to the beat that she would fall in love with came about by happenstance. She was working in Toronto for the Canadian Press during the city’s 2003 SARS outbreak, and coverage of viruses and other pathogens turned out to be a natural fit. She had a background in breaking news that many health and science journalists didn’t. She also found herself taking to the often complex scientific issues she was learning about — like transmission rates and case trajectories — that other breaking news reporters were struggling to understand. She became a medical reporter at the CP.
“She loved her work,” Brenda Branswell said. “She loved science and medical writing. She thought her job was a gift. She found it so interesting.”
Over the years, at the CP and then at STAT, she gained a loyal following for chronicling the twists and turns of influenza, the grinding campaign to eradicate polio, and the development of vaccines for a host of pathogens. Her beat was inherently unpredictable. With little notice, a new outbreak could go from smoldering to explosive, or a virus only a coterie of experts cared about — think Zika — could become a global crisis.
But it was her ahead-of-the-curve insights on Covid — in the early days of what would become the pandemic and throughout the emergency — that hundreds of thousands of people began turning to her for, on STAT’s site and on social media.
Branswell was not alarmist — she rightly thought the recent cruise ship hantavirus outbreak, though serious, didn’t merit the outsized reaction it seemed to be getting — but she was clear-eyed about the threat that the SARS-CoV-2 virus could pose even before scientists had sequenced it.
“Hopefully this is nothing out of the ordinary. But a @ProMED_mail posting about ‘unexplained pneumonias’ in China is giving me #SARS flashbacks,” she famously tweeted on Dec. 31, 2019. “Not liking the look of this,” she added a few days later.
Thanks to Branswell’s leading coverage, the New York Times wrote in late March 2020 that STAT “was early to a story that would dominate the news,” in an article in which a Harvard University expert referred to Branswell as “a godlike figure to people who are infectious-disease epidemiologists.”
Throughout the pandemic, she saw around corners, and her coverage showed it. She wrote in May 2020 that Covid vaccines were more likely to be strongly protective against severe outcomes than to put a stop to transmission — something the world only caught onto a year later when faced with that reality. She described in August 2020 how the upcoming winter “could be Dickensianly bleak,” previewing a season during which 3,000 Americans a day were dying from Covid.
“I always found her writing just so scientifically sound,” said Jeanne Marrazzo, a former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and now the CEO of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “It was very sophisticated, yet accessible and clear.”
When Marrazzo and her team at NIAID were considering which reporter to speak with for one of her first interviews after taking over as director in 2023, Branswell’s name came up immediately. “I trusted her, and I knew she would ask the right questions.”
Branswell cared deeply about ensuring her stories captured the complexity of the science she was writing about and the sometimes competing viewpoints experts would advance about emerging research. She was also a bit obsessive. On Monday afternoon, from the hospital, she shared in STAT’s Slack new data about uptake of the maternal RSV vaccine.
“A terrible loss for all of us, for everyone who cares about health and medicine,” STAT co-founder and owner John W. Henry wrote in a note to staff on Tuesday. “She was someone we all leaned on for so many years on so many important issues. Beyond that she was a wonderful person.”
At first impression, Branswell could come across as intense, even, by her own admission, a bit gruff. But in fact, there was no bigger cheerleader for STAT and its staff. She celebrated other reporters’ stories and recognition even as she was quick to remind colleagues she despised the reply-all email chains that typically accompanied such successes. When she worked in Boston, she also frequently brought in treats she baked, whether banana bread or — ever the proud Canadian — maple butter tarts.
“She had a big heart and she looked out for people and she did kind things for people, but she did them quietly,” Brenda Branswell said. “She was never seeking any attention or glory for her good deeds.”
Branswell is survived by her five siblings and eight nieces and nephews, whom she proudly doted on.
From 2010 to 2011, Branswell participated in a Nieman Fellowship in Global Health Reporting at Harvard, where she focused on polio eradication. She was also a CDC Knight fellow in 2004, when she embedded at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for three months.
In the newsroom, if you walked by Branswell’s computer screen, you’d likely see her highlighting and adding notes in the margins to the latest scientific paper she was reading. But you might also spot her catching up on the latest hubbub with the British royal family. (She had done a stint in London with the Canadian Press.)
She also wasn’t above office gossip — scouring for news within STAT’s newsroom as well as beyond it.
“She always asked the one question nobody else asked, and it just happened to be the most important one,” said Michael Osterholm, the director of the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy.
Many of the public health officials Branswell wrote about — sometimes critically — also deeply respected her. Maria Van Kerkhove, a top WHO official, said Branswell was out for more than a snappy quote — but rather information that she knew would be useful for the public to understand.
“Helen was someone I spent hours and hours and hours on the phone with over the years,” Van Kerkhove said. “I always wanted to have a conversation with Helen. No matter what the topic was, no matter how complex it was, she always asked the most thoughtful questions, and followed up with an even more thoughtful question.”
“She was also pretty kickass, and no nonsense,” she added.
Indeed, Branswell wasn’t afraid to call out public health officials on perceived lapses. In one memorable interview in April 2020, she pressed then-CDC Director Robert Redfield why the agency hadn’t held a briefing in a month, as would have been the case in any other serious disease outbreak.
“You’re invisible now, sir. Your agency is invisible,” Branswell told Redfield.
Other reporters recognized Branswell’s prowess on the beat. As Meg Tirrell, a longtime health reporter now at CNN (and formerly the host of a STAT podcast), tweeted in April 2021, “When @HelenBranswell gets called on in FDA/CDC #covid19 pressers I literally get a mental picture of Babe Ruth striding up to home plate.”
Lawrence Altman, a longtime New York Times reporter who covered the health of presidents and political leaders, had never heard of Branswell until some long-ago press briefing. He said he doesn’t remember the exact occasion but he remembers being struck by the quality of her questions. After it happened a few times, Altman called the Canadian Press and asked to speak to Branswell, starting up what became a friendship.
“She was the best reporter on infectious diseases that I know,” Altman said.
In August, Branswell was named as this year’s recipient of the Kovler Prize for Trust in Life Science Journalism, awarded by the Foundation for the National Institutes of Health, which cited her “exceptional ability to clearly convey complex and often urgent science topics for the public.”
The prize came with a $25,000 honorarium, which Branswell told STAT Executive Editor Rick Berke she wanted to contribute to a fellowship that was named in honor of veteran science journalist Sharon Begley, who died of cancer in 2021 and was a friend of Branswell’s at STAT. The fellowship is intended for early-career U.S. journalists from racial and ethnic groups underrepresented in the profession.
Before the work-at-home period of the pandemic, Branswell and Begley sat next to each other in the Boston newsroom, the doyennes of STAT, and of science journalism. Reporters and editors alike regularly sought their advice on how to cover a certain story, the history of a certain therapeutic approach, or just their general wisdom.
As one STAT reporter put it Tuesday, it was a comforting thought that they might be back at their desks together again.

One dead and several hurt after rollercoaster incident at Six Flags
- Published
Warning: This article contains some graphic details
One person has died and several others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the state of Georgia.
The Cobb County Police Department said it was investigating the fatality at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24km) from Atlanta, according to the BBC's news partner CBS News.
Police did not specify which ride was involved, but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, with riders being helped off by workers.
Six Flags Over Georgia said it was "deeply saddened" by the incident and later announced it was temporarily closing nine rides across the US and Canada out of precaution.
Officials have not said how the person died, or how the other riders were injured. The BBC has contacted local police and fire authorities, as well as park officials.
The identity of the person who died has also not been disclosed.
Witnesses told local media they saw a man ejected from the ride - an account of events that the BBC has not verified.
Local outlet 11 Alive quoted a witness saying the man had come loose from his seat and had then struck the rollercoaster and some of his fellow riders before falling onto the roof of a nearby haunted house attraction.
The incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion, the witness added.
A husband and wife, who were on the ride, also told 11 Alive that the man fell from the ride and was struck by it. They said workers at the park had checked their safety harnesses before the ride set off.
"We were having a great time and to just screaming 'Oh my God, what is happening?'," the woman said.
Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she was in line to ride Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a girl covered in blood.
Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off".
Brittany Landry, who believes she saw the man ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears.
"I broke because we were just on there," Landry said.
A park spokesperson said in a statement that its team and local authorities had responded immediately and that they were co-operating on an investigation into the incident.
Mableton Mayor Michael Owens said the city's public safety director was co-ordinating with local police and park security on the situation.
The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.
Six Flags is the largest amusement park operator in North America, with 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.
The death in Georgia comes just weeks after one of Six Flags' parks in southern California announced it would close the popular X2 roller coaster after more than 100 people alleged brain injuries from the ride.
Six Flags said that ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire the attraction because it was "the right thing to do".

Priya cannot remember a time when her mother was not busy. Apart from her work, there were always social engagements to attend, friends to visit or new books to read. But something changed after retirement.
“She seemed to lose some of her sparkle. She became a little inward and moody at times, as though an inertia had taken over. Her outings became less frequent. She no longer went shopping, as everything could be home-delivered. The fact that my father preferred to stay at home further reduced her opportunities to socialise. This transition from a busy, active person to a listless and diffident individual was quite shocking and sad,” she says.
When she opened up to her friends about this, Priya discovered that they had similar stories to share. Parents who had once led full, active lives were now confined to the quiet routines of home. They had not lost their zest for life, but age had caught up with them, sapping their energy and enthusiasm to get out and about.
“Then it struck us that, in a few years, this could be our lives too. Why should we allow the years to steal all the colours from our lives?” says Dimple Mohan, who runs a consultancy service in the city.
Five women
And so, Young at Heart (YaH) was born — a dream that took wings when five women entrepreneurs and working professionals in Thiruvananthapuram came together to explore how they could help their parents rediscover the joy of living and embrace ageing with enthusiasm.
Envisioned as a platform for senior citizens and those in their 50s, YaH hopes to bring people together to rediscover life’s little pleasures — new friendships, new learning experiences, evenings out, and a little fun and frolic. Growing older, the founders believe, should never mean compromising on emotional happiness and mental well-being.
“We all have successful careers, active social lives and wide networks of friends. But living with our parents, we have seen how their personalities and attitudes towards life change as they grow older, even when they are financially secure and have no major worries,” says Ms. Mohan, who is one of YaH’s founder.
“It made us think that, regardless of age, we should be able to embrace life with gusto and live it to the fullest in the company of good friends. YaH is an initiative to help senior citizens and people in their 50s connect, forge friendships, share interests and build a community that helps everyone lead more fulfilling lives. Many have the money and time, but are hesitant to venture out on their own,” she adds
On October 16
A formal launch event of YaH, featuring music and entertainment, is planned in the capital on October 16. The event will also offer participants an opportunity to meet and get to know one another.
YaH plans to organise regular entertainment and recreational activities, while creating opportunities for like-minded people to discover, share and nurture their talents. Events will be tailored to the interests, hobbies and leisure preferences of those who have registered with the initiative.
The group has also identified areas such as diet and nutrition, physical fitness, digital literacy and financial planning as important components of healthy, active ageing.
“We had several women register with us and we asked them what has been on their bucket list. One wants to learn to speak English fluently so she can converse with her grandchildren abroad. Another has always wanted to design dresses, while someone else simply wants to travel — something she could never manage while working. We hope to facilitate the fulfilment of some of these dreams,” says actor Manju Pillai, who is spearheading the initiative along with Devi Mohan, Sankari Unnithan and Maya Menon.
Younger volunteers
In time, YaH hopes to involve younger volunteers, building bridges between generations. They could take senior citizens to the beach or the movies, or simply spend an afternoon playing chess.
As age-related frailties set in, many older people find themselves increasingly disconnected from the world around them. The resulting isolation can take a toll on their emotional health and leave them vulnerable to depression.
Young at Heart hopes to address this often-overlooked need for socialisation and companionship first and help them embrace life, wholeheartedly.

A spokesperson for Joint Task Force-District of Columbia said it was "addressing" the instance the photos and videos showed, supporting Snopes' conclusion they were authentic. Snopes independently verified the location the photos and videos showed.
There was no evidence to suggest the National Guard members seen in the video had been assigned to guard the ballot drop box or otherwise intimidate voters. The joint task force spokesperson said the service members were "standing near," not guarding, the drop box.
It remained unclear why the National Guard members were at the Foggy Bottom-GWU Metro station on Oct. 8. National Guard troops have been patrolling Washington, D.C., since August 2025.
On Oct. 8, videos and images (archived, archived) circulated online that social media users claimed showed National Guard members illegally guarding a ballot drop box in Washington, D.C.
The footage spread less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
For example, one Facebook page that shared an image of three National Guard members standing around a ballot drop box wrote, "This is not what democracy is supposed to look like in America. And it isn't just wrong. It may be against the law."
Images and videos of the National Guard members standing around the ballot drop box also circulated on X (archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the images and videos.
Claims about the images and videos were a mixture of true, false and undetermined elements.
A spokesperson for Joint Task Force-D.C., the military command unit that coordinates National Guard troops in Washington, told Snopes via email that it was "aware" of photos and videos of National Guard members standing near a ballot box, supporting Snopes' conclusion that the imagery was authentic, meaning not digitally altered or generated using artificial intelligence.
However, there is no evidence that the National Guard members seen in the imagery were patrolling or guarding the ballot drop box. The Joint Task Force D.C. spokesperson said:
Maintaining public trust is a top priority, and JTF-DC service members are directed not to monitor or secure polling locations. JTF-DC is actively addressing this specific instance and remains fully committed to conducting its missions professionally, lawfully, and with respect for the public's constitutional rights.
The spokesperson did not elaborate on why, if not to guard the ballot drop box, the National Guard members were standing by it. The reason for their presence remains unclear.
The Washington Post reported on Oct. 9, citing two anonymous National Guard officials, that the Guard members seen in photos and videos were part of "a larger group that had paused as part of a patrol but were not specifically guarding the box." Snopes contacted the National Guard to independently verify this statement but had not heard back at the time of this writing.
We also contacted the Washington, D.C., Board of Elections, which the Post reported had requested "limitations" on National Guard members standing near ballot drop boxes and voting locations, to ask whether it had received confirmation of why the Guard members were at the ballot drop box and await a reply.
U.S. federal law criminalizes deploying federal troops or armed federal law enforcement agents to "any place where a general or special election is held." Voter intimidation, which federal law defines as "interfering with the right of such other person to vote or to vote as he may choose," also is illegal.
There's no evidence that the troops seen in the photos and videos from Washington were illegally deployed to the ballot box in question to guard it or intimidate voters. JTF-DC has been coordinating National Guard troops in the U.S. capital since Aug. 11, 2025, at the behest of President Donald Trump.
Snopes verified the location of the ballot drop box that appeared in videos and photos using Google Maps imagery as outside the Foggy Bottom-GWU Metro station.
The video that circulated showed the ballot box next to a statue of the former President George Washington on the 800 block of 23rd Street Northwest. A street sign that indicated the intersection of 23rd Street Northwest and I Street Northwest appeared at the beginning of the video.
Images of the National Guard members on X and Facebook showed at least one of the same National Guard members from the video and the statue of Washington.
Bryan Randolph, a lawyer who goes by BrynoDC on social media, said he recorded the footage of the National Guard members at the ballot box on Oct. 8.
For further reading, Snopes has reported on numerous claims connected to the 2026 elections.

The story so far:
Chief Justice of India Surya Kant declined a request made by Opposition leaders for an audience to discuss allegations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s conduct during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process, alongside detentions of peaceful protestors and lockdown of arterial Delhi.
The refusal was anchored in the ethos of maintaining a neutral distance from the political thicket. The CJI’s letter emphasised that the judiciary cannot blur constitutional lines.
The representations to Chief Justice of Surya Kant
On October 10, the Leaders of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha, Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi, respectively, wrote to the Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant. It marked a rare and historic instance of the Opposition directly engaging the highest judicial office of the country to complain against another constitutional authority, the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC).
The brief request, submitted on a joint letterhead, stated that the two leaders wished to submit a memorandum to the Chief Justice concerning the CEC and the Election Commission of India. Sent hours after the brutal police crackdown on citizens demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar, the representation said the arbitrary arrest of students, closure of Metro stations, cancellation of trains, and barricading of roads created an “atmosphere of siege in the city of Delhi”.
Mr. Gandhi followed up with a second, detailed representation to Chief Justice Kant on October 11. He underscored the Supreme Court’s role as the guardian of the Constitution and the fundamental right of every citizen to vote. Writing in his capacity as the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha on behalf of crores of voters anxious about the integrity of the electoral rolls, Mr. Gandhi pointed out that he was also a member of the Selection Committee constituted under Section 7 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. He underscored that he had recorded a formal note of dissent on the procedure followed for selecting CEC Kumar during a committee meeting on February 17, 2025.
The representation accused the CEC was an arbitrary and unilateral exercise of power during the SIR. He asked the CJI to treat the representation as a letter petition in public interest.
He urged the CJI to direct a complete disclosure of SIR records with the Election Commission of India and the setting up of an independent committee headed by a retired Supreme Court judge to review decisions and audit voter deletions made during SIR to safeguard free and fair elections. He sought an interim suspension of the SIR process itself.
Chief Justice Kant’s response
On October 12, the Chief Justice responded to the October 10 request for a meeting, while omitting any direct reference to Mr. Gandhi’s subsequent October 11 representation.
Addressing both Mr. Kharge and Mr. Gandhi and declining their request for an appointment on October 12 between 4 p.m. and 5 p.m. to submit a memorandum, the CJI noted that the issues regarding the CEC, the arbitrary arrests, Metro closure and train cancellations, etc, were already sub judice before the court.
The CJI said that, “therefore, convening a meeting to discuss pending cases would wholly contravene the principle of Separation of Powers, an intrinsic facet of the basic structure doctrine of the Constitution of India, and would be incompatible with the established ethics and judicial propriety”.
The two-page response also reminded the leaders that the constitutional framework did not vest the Supreme Court with administrative powers to “deal with the issues highlighted in your letter”. But the CJI said the Supreme Court was duty-bound, on the judicial side to consider the gravamen of issues affecting the citizens of India.
The top judge reiterated in his reply to the Opposition leaders the court’s commitment to preserve and protect the fundamental rights of every citizen of India. Chief Justice Kant said citizens were “entitled to seek enforcement of such rights at all hours through the procedure known in law”.
Chief Justice Kant advised the two leaders in his response that it would be “more appropriate on your part to invoke the judicial powers of the Supreme Court of India, instead of submitting a memorandum on the administrative side”.
The CJI informed that petitions raising parallel issues were listed for hearing on October 13. He said the leader, acting on legal advice, could file their petition on October 12. The CJI observed that the leaders could file their petition on October 12 based on legal advice, assuring that “any such petition shall be heard at the earliest possible opportunity, in accordance with law”. A writ petition was subsequently filed by Mr. Gandhi alongside 12 other Opposition leaders, which was successfully registered, numbered, and is primed for a judicial hearing.
The law behind the CJI’s refusal
At the heart of the CJI’s response lie three factors — the doctrine of separation of powers, sub judice rules and judicial propriety, and the Bangalore Principles.
ALSO WATCH Opposition leaders file Supreme Court petition over SIR row after massive protest in delhi
As Chief Justice Kant’s response said, the separation of powers, which divides governance among the three distinct organs of the legislature, the executive, and the judiciary, was an unalterable part of the basic structure of the Constitution. The court functions as an impartial arbiter with a clear mandate to adjudicate disputes impartially, apply laws, and review executive or legislative actions only through established judicial proceedings. The judiciary did not hold executive or administrative oversight to unilaterally intervene in government policy or governance demands.
A parallel out-of-court meeting between the Chief Justice, who also happens to lead the Bench hearing the CEC-related cases and Opposition leaders, belies fair play and bypasses procedural fairness. Entertaining political factions on a one-to-one basis outside the court room compromises judicial impartiality and creates an impression of bias. Disputes must be settled in the open court, transparently, in proceedings in which opposing parties get an equal say in accordance with the principles of natural justice.
The Bangalore Principles of Judicial Conduct puts in place ethical benchmarks for judges, which include that they must avoid any act of impropriety which would compromise the public’s perception of judicial neutrality.
Some instances which drew public ire
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s 2024 visit to the residence of then Chief Justice of India, Justice Dhananjay Chandrachud, to perform pooja during Ganesh Chaturthi drew public criticism over perceptions of the executive and judiciary cosying up. Historical precedents of serving judges expressing admiration for political figures include Justice P.N. Bhagwati sending a congratulatory letter to Indira Gandhi upon her return to power, and Justice M.R. Shah reportedly describing Prime Minister Modi as a “model and a hero”. Similarly, former Supreme Court judge Arun Mishra had sparked controversy by publicly describing Prime Minister Modi as a “versatile genius” and an “internationally acclaimed visionary who can think global and act locally”.
On a separate occasion, Prime Minister Modi visited the Supreme Court premises at the invitation of then-CJI Ranjan Gogoi on the sidelines of a BIMSTEC conference. Justice Gogoi was nominated to the Rajya Sabha following his retirement. Incidentally, Justice Gogoi was one of the four senior Supreme Court judges who held the unprecedented January 2018 press conference, spotlighting concerns over executive influence in case allocations under then Chief Justice Dipak Misra.
History shows that political friction with the judiciary carries ‘unsettling’ consequences. Following the landmark Kesavananda Bharati judgment, which established the basic structure doctrine limiting Parliament’s amending powers, Indira Gandhi’s government superseded Justices J.M. Shelat, K.S. Hegde and A.N. Grover to appoint Justice A.N. Ray as Chief Justice of India. The move triggered the immediate resignation of the three superseded judges.
Decades later, the imperative to insulate judicial appointments from executive overreach had culminated in the Collegium system and the adoption of the Bangalore Principles.

Mobile gaming studio Spill Games has raised $10.5 Mn (about ₹100 Cr) in a Series A round led by Elevation Capital, with participation from existing investors Centre Court Capital and PeerCapital. The Bengaluru-based startup said it would use the fresh capital to scale its existing games, expand its development pipeline, strengthen the AI and technology capabilities of its Compass engine, acquire users, and selectively grow its team. Founded in 2024 by Om Misra, Tapan Ranjan, and Harsh Garg, the gaming startup builds free-to-play casual, puzzle, and hybrid-casual mobile games for global audiences using an AI-led, portfolio-driven studio model. Its in-house engine, Compass, brings together tools for analytics, player retention, monetisation, and live operations. The startup said this lets it reuse infrastructure across games and shorten the time taken to develop and test new concepts. It is targeting development speeds of roughly 4X those of traditional approaches. Spill launches games quickly to test its initial assumptions, then uses player feedback and in-game data to refine them. It directs more resources towards titles that show potential to scale globally. Its portfolio now comprises six games, including Cozy Finds, Sticker by Number, Zen Math Crossword, Bird Rescue Jam, and Grill Master. The startup monetises its games through advertising and in-app purchases. The fresh funding comes months after the startup raised $3.1 Mn (around ₹28 Cr) in its seed funding round in April. At the time, it said that around 50% of its user base originated from the US, followed by Brazil (15%) and Japan (10%). The startup said then that it was aiming to test over 20 prototypes in the next 18 months and was targeting to launch 5-10 profitable new titles. Gaming Beyond Real Money Spill’s fundraise also comes amid changes in India’s gaming industry following the government’s ban on real-money gaming. Separately, in May, the Supreme Court upheld the 28% GST levy on the full face value of online gaming bets, backing tax demands on past transactions. Spill’s advertising and in-app purchase model places it in a different segment from platforms that rely on real-money wagers. Other studios building games outside RMG have also attracted investors. In August, cricketer Rohit Sharma joined LightFury Games as an investor, alongside MS Dhoni, Jasprit Bumrah, and Hardik Pandya, among others. At the time, LightFury said it planned to begin a phased closed beta rollout of its flagship eCricket game in September. The developments come against the backdrop of a large domestic gaming audience. Speaking at the India Mobile Congress last week, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said more than 50 Cr Indians are estimated to be connected to the gaming ecosystem, with growing participation among young people in Tier II and III cities. He said participation extends beyond playing games to competing in esports, creating gaming content, and building gaming businesses.

An OpenAI engineer was arrested after the company said it discovered a “sophisticated recording device” hidden in one of its offices. The employee was identified as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national. Alfozan is charged with using or endeavoring to use a device to intercept oral communications, according to a press release from the Department of Justice.
OpenAI employee arrested for allegedly planting a bug in a conference room
The recording device was apparently discovered plugged into a TV’s USB port in an executive meeting room.
OpenAI’s post about the incident says it used its AI models to “understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier.”
As noted by the DOJ, OpenAI found the device plugged into a TV’s USB port in an executive conference room, where discussions about “highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information” often take place.
Alfozan didn’t have access to this room, but CCTV footage allegedly showed him “near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery,” according to the DOJ. Footage also captured Alfozan appearing to look behind the TV where the device was installed, federal prosecutors claim.
The device was covered in toilet paper and installed on or around September 28th. Its contents were encrypted. Additionally, the DOJ claims OpenAI security discovered a bag Alfozan left in another room inside the company’s office, where they found his wallet, ID, and another recording device.
OpenAI says it fired the employee and referred the incident to the FBI. Alfozan was arrested Friday and has remained in custody since, appearing in federal court for the first time on Tuesday.
We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.
At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated.
We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.

Nineteen founders across 13 new-age tech companies earned a combined ₹52.57 Cr in fixed remuneration in FY26, up 2% from ₹51.54 Cr in FY25, according to data compiled by Inc42. Average fixed remuneration per founder increased to ₹2.76 Cr from ₹2.71 Cr. Of these, 13 founders received increases in fixed pay, four saw reductions, and two reported unchanged remuneration. Honasa Consumer cofounder Ghazal Alagh recorded the highest percentage increase, with her fixed remuneration rising 60% to ₹2.4 Cr from ₹1.5 Cr. Delhivery cofounder Sahil Barua followed with a 21.4% increase to ₹3.4 Cr from ₹2.8 Cr. Ola Electric founder Bhavish Aggarwal recorded the steepest percentage decline, with his remuneration falling 34.8% to ₹4.5 Cr from ₹6.9 Cr. Nykaa founder Falguni Nayar’s fixed pay fell 14% to ₹74 Lakh from ₹86 Lakh, while Swiggy cofounder Sriharsha Majety’s remuneration declined 12.5% to ₹1.4 Cr from ₹1.6 Cr. Lenskart cofounder Peyush Bansal drew the highest fixed remuneration among the founders tracked, despite a 1.7% decline to ₹5.7 Cr from ₹5.8 Cr. Meesho cofounders Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Kumar followed with ₹4.8 Cr each, ahead of Ola Electric’s Aggarwal at ₹4.5 Cr and Paytm founder Vijay Shekhar Sharma at ₹4 Cr. Sharma’s fixed remuneration remained unchanged from FY25. However, fixed pay tells only part of the story. Peyush Bansal received ₹12 Cr in bonuses and performance incentives – more than twice his fixed remuneration – along with perquisites and retirement benefits. Fellow Lenskart cofounder Neha Bansal received ₹6 Cr in bonuses and performance incentives, in addition to her ₹2.7 Cr fixed pay. Share-based compensation also featured prominently. Majety’s ESOP gains stood at ₹549.3 Cr, while Delhivery cofounder Kapil Bharati recorded ₹6.9 Cr in ESOP gains. Separately, the cost of stock options granted to FirstCry founder Supam Maheshwari stood at ₹31.7 Cr. He also received ₹2.1 Cr in perquisites and ₹84 Lakh in performance incentives. These components require separate treatment. Stock-option costs and ESOP-related benefits do not necessarily represent cash received by a founder during the year and should be distinguished from fixed salaries and cash incentives. Inc42 has been tracking founders’ remuneration since FY23, covering the startup ecosystem’s shift from the era of funding boom to the funding winter and now, more recently, towards profitability and IPOs. Building on the FY25 edition, the FY26 tracker examines changes in fixed pay, other compensation components, and the financial performance of the companies these founders lead. How Ukrainians are uniting behind Shakhtar in London
- Published
Artem Genne's favourite footballing memory is standing on the Donbas Arena pitch, waving the Champions League flag, before Shakhtar Donetsk faced Chelsea.
That was in 2012. Two years later, the Russian-backed capture of Donetsk led many Ukrainians to leave the city, including ardent Shakhtar supporter Genne.
A large number fled to other areas of Ukraine and beyond, with the region's football club forced to find a new home. Fourteen years later, they are still searching.
It has led Shakhtar to Kyiv, Lviv and Kharkiv in Ukraine, and Poland, Slovenia and Germany for European games.
This season they will play their home Champions League fixtures at Chelsea's Stamford Bridge, with Genne, who now lives in the West Midlands, aiming to attend all four - starting with AEK Athens on Wednesday.
"When the invasion started, lots of people left, thinking that it's all going to be over in several weeks, we'll be coming back. But unfortunately, that didn't happen," he says.
"When I meet people from my home area of Ukraine abroad, it gives you a sense of home and hope.
"Knowing that you're sharing the values and you remember the times when it was different, that's important. It gives you a bit of a soft tear because that's something you cannot touch any more.
"In the UK, people are very supportive and I want to highlight that I'm extremely grateful to this country for hosting so many of our people at the most difficult time.
"When you're walking around in a Shakhtar shirt, people are clapping their hands and giving you high fives and there is no aggression whatsoever."
Dima Prasolov, who left Donetsk for Kyiv after the war started and now lives in Kent, is another who will be supporting, with fans able to buy a four-game pass.
"I was ecstatic because it's the first time in about 15 years that I will be able to buy some sort of a season ticket for Shakhtar," says Prasolov.
"It really means everything to me because it's the club I've been supporting all my life. But since the Russian invasion, for us Donbas people, watching our team regularly is almost impossible.
"For me, it's a very emotional situation, because of how much the club means to me and how dedicated myself and my family are to the club."
Indeed, the London stadium offers a brief safe haven from the uncertainty faced in Ukraine.
Chief executive Sergei Palkin says Shakhtar have had to move their under-12 team to a safer area of Kyiv following recent attacks, while their women's side had a match disrupted by a nearby drone strike.
"Every day when our team goes to the pitch, it's much more than football because behind it we have a lot of challenges every day," says Palkin.
"It's a human question, a mental question, a family question for our players, for the academy and so on. The most difficult and important challenge is uncertainty.
"You wake up in the morning and you don't know what's going to happen today or tomorrow."
Palkin adds: "Part of our role when we play in London and other cities in Europe is to send these messages and remind people what's going on."

This week's occasion is more important than just watching Shakhtar. It will be a chance for Ukrainians to come together in London, even involving rival fans.
The dynamic of Ukrainian football support has changed for many clubs since the invasion in 2022. Shakhtar's fanbase, meanwhile, has shifted since 2014, with many ultras fighting in the war but still supporting their clubs from afar.
"My two friends are supporters of Dynamo Kyiv, but in Europe we support each other," Genne says.
"It's about representation of the country. The hooligans don't fight any more with each other because they know they have one enemy and it's not the football enemy."
The decision to play in London was met with some scepticism in Ukraine because of the difficulty for fans to visit the UK - a visa costs £135 and you must apply at least three months before entering.
One Shakhtar fan, who is speaking anonymously but attends many home and away games in Ukraine, says: "That sort of money for some Ukrainians is a monthly income. And no-one has time in Ukraine now to wait a few months for a visa.
"So the poor thing is we want to support the team, but we can't go to support because the regulation in England is crazy now."
Instead, fans will watch in pubs all over the country, with similar support from beyond Shakhtar's traditional fanbase.
The fan adds: "When Shakhtar play, it's like a big family. It's more than rivalry because they represent Ukraine. Ukraine is always the first place. Then comes football."
It is expected many fans in attendance will be travelling from within the UK to watch Shakhtar, which is a common occurrence for the Miners when they have previously played away games in England.
When tickets went on sale for the club's away leg against Crystal Palace in the Europa Conference League semi-final last season, and when they played Arsenal in the 2024-25 Champions League campaign, Shakhtar's allocation sold out in an hour.
Prasolov explains: "The club are making a big gamble on the existing Ukrainian population in London, of which in west London there is a big Ukrainian diaspora that's been there for a number of years.
"They are actually a very passionate fanbase of all things Ukraine. Any time Ukrainian teams plays in London, they always turn up.
"There will be lots of Ukrainian national songs and chants. It will be a good atmosphere for sure. I think people will enjoy it. It will be very friendly."
It is also an opportunity to celebrate Ukrainian culture, with many fundraising activities helping to fund supplies in their home country.
"There's a massive community," says Genne. "There are constantly events like concerts with Ukrainian artists and they fund-raise for med kits, for equipment, for everything.
"We're all united by the symbol to liberate our country and to do what we can. Even though we're far away, we help with what we can.
"It's great that there will be another reason for Ukrainians to get together. It'll be something positive rather than something that's not so positive, which unfortunately is happening a lot more lately."
The club want to use this opportunity to bolster relations with Ukrainians living in London.
Palkin says: "We have a very good connection with the Ukrainian diaspora in England.
"We will do activities with Ukrainian children living in London. We will come to schools, bring them to training sessions and connect them with the team.
"For Ukrainian people living here, it's a good connection to Ukraine."
London has welcomed many of the roughly 265,000 Ukrainians who took refuge in the UK, and Shakhtar hope to keep raising awareness of issues faced back home.
"For Ukraine, it's very important to be visible at this moment of our history. And for us it's very important because we are playing for our nation," says Palkin.
"At this moment 99% of news coming from Ukraine is all negative. To see Ukraine represented in a tournament like the Champions League is very important. It means one message: that we are alive, Ukraine continues to fight, continues to work, continues to live and continues to compete on this stage."
Amir, another Shakhtar fan in the UK, left Donetsk at 15 and now lives in London.
Seeing the club competing in the Champions League remains important to such supporters.
Amir says: "I think it is a beacon of hope. Seeing Ukrainian sportsmen succeeding internationally gives a lot of reassurance and a sense of power to the Ukrainian people.
"There is a sense of reconnection to their roots and the national achievements for Ukrainians living abroad.
"In a way it is quite important the club that is from Eastern Ukraine which is currently occupied by Russia is the club representing Ukraine internationally.
"It is important internationally as a reminder of the regional roots of Shakhtar and of Donetsk overall."
Wednesday's game against AEK Athens will mark an emotional moment for many Shakhtar and Ukraine fans, before Real Madrid, Sporting and Fenerbahce also visit.
Genne says: "Any sort of positive news, any positive results, are bringing people joy and making us a little bit happier.
"It doesn't make us forget about all the rest of the things that are happening, but it makes us a bit more joyful.
"Like remembering what joy of life is, in supporting your club, having fun, coming together, having the sense of community.
"It's way more than just football and analysing a player's performance and goals. It's way, way more than that."
