Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
- Published
Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.
During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."
Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.
The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.
After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.

In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.
Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.
Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.
Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.
Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join.
Within hours, he was dead.
His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans.
As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government.
"I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said.
"It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him."

Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2 hands-on: A look at the audio updates and Siri AI
Listening to Apple's new sound features with Siri as our binge-watching companion.
Apple's "Welcome home" event may have been mostly for the HomeView debut, but the company also announced updated versions of the HomePod mini speaker and Apple TV 4K. After spending some time with the main attraction this morning, I was also able to check out the HomePod mini 2's revamped home theater features and see Siri AI in action on Apple's streaming box. I also listened to a pair of the new speakers connected to an iMac as part of an enhanced desktop audio setup, and can confirm the new colors match up nicely with the company's all-in-one computer.
Apple TV 4K's Siri overhaul
Let's start with the Apple TV 4K. The main upgrades here are meant to bring Siri AI to the living room, primarily for content discovery. Thanks to the assistant's ability to pull in context from places like Messages, you can ask it to do things like "play the show Sam texted me about." The new Apple TV 4K has far field microphones built in, so the Siri experience is now hands-free, meaning you could shout at it from your couch. This worked well the demo area I was in, though I have to point out the environment was relatively quiet.
Siri AI can also answer questions about content, like whether Ted Lasso is a real person or if AFC Richmond is an actual football club. Thankfully, Siri's responses are tucked in the corner of the TV screen, so you can see them without the text blocking your movie or show. What's more, they're text only, and the assistant won't respond to you by speaking over the audio from whatever you're watching. I saw this in action a few different times, and I think it's a clean implementation of Siri on the Apple TV 4K. I really like that I won't have to hear competing sounds from Siri and a TV show, forcing me to try to decipher the info I asked for.
Another welcome upgrade for the Apple TV 4K is an overhauled remote. While it looks the same on the outside, a new feature inside will play a sound when you ask Siri for help finding it. I prefer this approach since it's much quicker to determine where something is if it's beeping than having to wave a phone around to see how close I'm getting to it. If you've ever played a sound to find your AirPods, that works the same way. I'm constantly looking for my Apple TV remote after one of my kids has stashed it somewhere, so this will all be handy at my house.
Audio updates on the HomePod mini 2
The HomePod mini 2 has also been updated for Siri AI. Right off the top, the speaker is now powered by the S10 chip, a big upgrade over the S5 that was in the 2020 model. This hardware will eventually enable Siri AI, but the next-gen — or now current-gen — assistant won't be on the HomePod mini 2 at launch. Apple says that feature is coming at a later date.
For now, the two big new features are Sound Glow and expanded surround sound functionality. Sound Glow mimics album artwork on the HomePod mini 2's back-lit touch panel. If you're listening to a soundscape, the lights will mirror things like rain drops and waves. This is a neat addition, but I wonder how often I'll actually see it since I don't tend to sit near or even look at my HomePod speakers. Next, you can now use up to four HomePod speakers with the new Apple TV 4K for home theater audio. Before, you could only use two as a stereo pair.
After hearing two different configurations at Apple's event, I'm convinced this is going to be an audio upgrade for those willing to buy four HomePods. I enjoyed the setup of two second-gen HomePods in the front and two HomePod mini 2 speakers in the back as it offered more bass and rumble during my demo. However, a quartet of HomePod mini 2 speakers holds its own, providing dimensional sound that enveloped the sofa I was sitting on. But again, this is all dependent upon you buying four HomePods and putting them all in your living room, which seems like a rare scenario.
Lastly, I got to hear a pair of HomePod mini 2 speakers being used for audio from an iMac. These new speakers can sync with any Mac over AirPlay to function as a set of desktop speakers. This setup provides an obvious upgrade over built-in iMac speakers, and the stereo pair offered solid directional sound for basic games like Angry Birds. At around $300 for two of the HomePod mini 2, this seems like a more plausible arrangement than the four-pack in the living room.

Modern medicine has never been more capable than it is today. Tests detect illness earlier, scans reveal invisible abnormalities, medicines prevent and treat diseases, and interventions and procedures can save lives within minutes. Yet, the same system that can do more is increasingly tempted to overtreat and overmedicate.
Also read |Lifestyle, not medicine, is key to good health
Overtreatment and overmedication are not simply the use of an unnecessary medicine but often a chain: a test detects an incidental abnormality, which leads to another test, a diagnosis and then a prescription that may become permanent. What begins as prevention can end in long-term medication or surgery. Then, in India, overtreatment coexists with undertreatment: unnecessary interventions are offered to some, while many others still lack essential primary care, affordable medicines and timely treatment.
Health packages and tests
The rise of overtreatment is the result of a convergence of several factors. The first driver of overtreatment is unnecessary and excessive testing — both screening and diagnostic — which creates a cascade of care. A review article in the prestigious National Medical Journal of India in 2016 found that routine health-check packages often include unwarranted tests that can lead to false-positive results, anxiety, further investigations, overdiagnosis and overtreatment. The truth is that the ability to test has expanded faster than our ability to decide who actually needs testing.
The second driver is the fragmentation of health and medical care. Its most visible manifestation in India is an excessive focus on specialist and super specialist care. A person with a common health problem often goes directly to a specialist or superspecialist. A person with chronic conditions may consult several specialists, each optimising one part of care without necessarily paying attention to the person’s other health problems. The patient is treated in parts, while the human body does not live in specialties.
This matters particularly in older adults. A systematic review and meta-analysis of Indian studies, published in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2021, reported polypharmacy in about 49% of older adults. Another study, published in Scientific Reports in 2025, found that roughly one-third of older adults were taking five or more prescribed medicines (polypharmacy), with potentially inappropriate medicines identified in 28.8% of cases.
These figures do not mean that everyone taking several medicines is being overtreated. They do, however, show why medication reviews and deprescribing must become routine.
A third force is the transformation of health care into a marketplace. Laboratory tests, radiological investigations, procedures, supplements and monitoring devices have become products to be sold — sometimes products in search of potential customers. As a result, the boundaries between those who genuinely need these interventions and those who do not can become blurred. A linked aspect is that much of health care and medical care in India operates on a fee-for-service model, which can reward activity rather than restraint. Many patients consider a medical consultation complete only when several medicines and investigations have been prescribed.
Health insurance is a proven solution for financial protection from health-related expenses, as the cost is borne by the insurer. However, it can create both ‘ex-ante’ and ‘ex-post’ moral hazards, discouraging preventive care and encouraging hospitals and patients to favour costlier interventions. What is forgotten is that while someone else may bear the financial cost, it is the patient’s body that undergoes the intervention. Paying insurance premiums for years does not mean that one must ‘recover’ the money by undergoing a relatively unnecessary procedure or surgery.
Fourth, patient beliefs and expectations arising from advances in medical care where people want certainty when they are worried and may feel that something tangible should follow a consultation. Reassurance can look like inaction; observation can feel inferior to a scan; lifestyle advice can appear less serious than medication. Doctors may respond to these expectations, particularly in crowded clinics where explanation requires time.
The fifth driver is the rise of ‘defensive medicine’, in which clinicians, fearing that they might miss a rare diagnosis, may consider ordering another test as the safer option. What is often forgotten, however, is that every test carries potential risks, both from the test itself and from the discovery of abnormalities that may never have caused harm.
Choosing wisely
India is not alone in facing this problem. Overtreatment first became widely recognised in high-income countries and is now increasingly visible across many middle-income nations. This gave rise to the global Choosing Wisely movement, which encourages people to choose health-care interventions more carefully. It is against this backdrop, between 2012 and 2023, that nearly 80 specialty societies worldwide published close to 700 recommendations identifying hundreds of tests and treatments that clinicians and patients should question. The message is that medicine requires stronger mechanisms for self-correction. The solutions are about practising better medicine. Halting and reversing overmedicalisation requires the engagement of all stakeholders, including individuals, communities, professional societies and health policymakers.
First, India needs to rebuild stronger and functional primary care and restore the family physician as the first point of contact for most non-emergency health needs. A general physician can decide which problems require specialist expertise, reconcile multiple prescriptions and recognise when treatment can safely be reduced. Initiation of care by a general physician, followed by continuity through the referral pathway, protects patients against overmedication and excess surgeries.
Second, every medical prescription should carry a review date and, where appropriate, a possible stop date. Medicines should not become lifelong simply because nobody asks whether they are still needed. Older adults and people taking five or more medicines should periodically undergo a structured medication review assessing indication, benefit, duplication, interactions and opportunities for deprescribing.
Develop India-specific lists
Third, professional medical societies and the Indian Council of Medical Research should develop Indian lists of low-value tests, treatments and procedures — similar to Choosing Wisely — and embed these principles in medical training, accreditation and quality-improvement programmes. Hospitals should measure not only whether recommended care was provided, but also whether unnecessary care was avoided.
Fourth, before starting any test or treatment, patients should note that these four questions matter: Why do I need this? What happens if I wait? What are the possible benefits and risks? What are the alternatives? These questions can substantially improve clinical conversations and outcomes.
Fifth, payment systems and health insurance must reward outcomes, clinical reasoning and continuity of care rather than volume alone. A health-care system should not make it financially easier to order a scan than to explain thoughtfully why that scan may be unnecessary.
Medical advances will continue — and they should. However, the next stage of medical progress will come not only from discovering more tests, medicines and procedures, but also from learning when not to use them. Good medicine requires action when action helps. In an age of medical abundance, it increasingly requires something more difficult — restraint.
Dr. Chandrakant Lahariya is a practising physician and the author of ‘Pill-Free: You Don’t Need Everything You Have Been Prescribed’ (2026)

MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
- Published
MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said.
Sir Ken McCallum said threats from foreign adversaries had quadrupled in the last decade, with Russia "aggressor number one" as well as increased Iran-linked aggression against Jewish sites and military bases.
At an annual speech in London, MI5's chief said Russia was waging hybrid warfare at a time when AI was "supercharging the cyber-security contest between attackers and defenders".
He also warned of rising threats from "extreme right-wing terrorism" and said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI," including by integrating the technology with drones.
He said the biggest threat from the misuse of AI was extremist groups using the technology to harness new and existing bioweapons.
However, he noted that work countering terrorism and state threats was now "pretty much of equal scale" which he described as a "huge shift" in recent years.
Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against Nato and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly".
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
Sir Ken said MI5 successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks.
"With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak, he said.
"So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding."
He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand."
His comments come as a growing number of leaders across Europe have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.
Asked after the speech about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum, Sir Ken said it was "not new news" that there had been attempts from Moscow but distinguished between "interference attempted" and "outcome achieved".
He said it was a matter of public record that there were pieces in Russian media and "so-called internet trolls and bot farms" seeking to influence the Brexit debate, but also stressed that the result of the 2016 referendum was "not in dispute".
He added that he was "worried" about the the ongoing debate on Russian interference.
"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall," he told reporters.
Meanwhile, Sir Ken warned that Iran is also expanding a hybrid campaign in the UK.
The intelligence chief said there had been 50 arrests in the last year over Iran-linked activities.
Much of this Iranian aggression has been aimed at Jewish communities, Sir Ken added, and also at "harder targets, like military sites".
Sir Ken did not mention arrests at RAF Fairford directly during his speech, but told reporters afterwards the incident was "not unique".
He added: "We have seen Iranian interest beyond RAF Fairford in the UK."
The incident at the airbase in Gloucesteshire, where three suspicious vans were seen parked nearby, has seen seven people arrested and bailed by counter-terrorism police.
Burnham has said the incident was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard".
The MI5 head said in his speech: "What I can say is that those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets - whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas - will meet an unflinching response."
Sir Ken added that the National Security Act - a 2023 law designed to target people working against UK interests for foreign powers - is in heavy use, and has been employed to tackle threats from China as well as Iran and Russia.
On the emerging threat posed by AI, Sir Ken said: "It can produce propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual.
"We've caught terrorists seeking to exploit Al to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with Al-enabled drones adding a new twist."
Sir Ken said the bioweapons threat posed by AI was "not yet realised" but warned the technology has the "potential to change the stakes".
"These risks are real. The UK Intelligence Community - MI5, GCHQ, MI6 - is working closely with the UK's globally respected AI Security Institute to take them on."
Sir Ken said AI poses unknown threats, telling Thames House: "Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are".
He announced MI5 had launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre, which he said would assess sources and "separate the bluster from the realities".
In April, the UK's terrorism threat level was raised to severe for the first time in five years, meaning an attack is highly likely.
Sir Ken said Islamist groups like Al Qaeda and so-called Islamic State both continue to direct and inspire attacks, while the increased risk was also driven "in significant part" by extreme right-wing terrorism.
He continued: "Over the last year the most marked trend has been an increase in cases where extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent."
Sir Ken said extreme right-wing terrorism tended to "skew young", driven by the internet - adding that MI5 had in recent months investigated a "radicalised extreme right-wing 13-year-old here in the UK".
He said: "That investigation generated insight that enabled one of our international partners to prevent a lethal attack on their soil."

Saka responds to Arteta's challenge with 'huge impact'
- Published
Bukayo Saka responded to the challenge set by Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta as he proved a game-changer in the 3-0 Champions League win over Lille.
The England forward has been told he should aim to score "two or three" goals per game - such was his quality and the expectation from his boss.
Saka did not achieve that tally against the French visitors, but shook off illness to come off the bench and assist Eberechi Eze's strike that made it 2-0, before rolling in his side's third goal.
The 25-year-old has now scored four goals in nine games this season and looks to be taking the next step in his evolution as Arsenal's key man.
With the majority of his side's attacking play involving him, he has always been an influential figure. But with opposition defenders doubling up on him and injury issues over the last two seasons, there were doubts over whether Saka could still do what was asked of him in attack or if he had lost a yard of pace.
Arteta has tweaked Saka's positioning this season and, prior to Lille's visit, said it has been done deliberately to get him closer to the goal.
'He delivered with real quality'
"That is where we need to get him," said the Gunners boss before the game. "And if he misses the chance, so be it. At the end, the more volume we generate, the bigger the probability of him scoring more goals."
Saka's strike against Lille was a confident one-touch finish and came after he missed a late one-on-one opportunity in Saturday's Premier League victory over Leeds.
"He has been getting in great positions, getting shots, getting one-touch finishes and tap-ins," added Arteta.
"That is the kind of unpredictability we have with that player, otherwise we know how the opponent is going to defend him. He is doing well, he could have had another four or five goals by now, easily. But if he continues like that, we know.
"When he talks about scoring a certain amount of goals, he needs to be thinking about scoring a certain amount of goals per game. If that shifts, that mentality, he will get into those positions and score more goals."
Saka has scored 20 goals in a season just once in his career, which came in the 2023-24 campaign and 16 in the Premier League.
But the winger has also been in good goalscoring form for England with five in his last four matches and scored a double in the 7-0 Nations League demolition of Croatia in the recent international break.
Saka is now on 19 goals in major European competitions for Arsenal, only behind Thierry Henry (42), while he has nine assists in the Champions League which puts him behind Henry (16) and Cesc Fabregas (14).
He has refused to disclose the targets he has set himself, but Arteta welcomed Saka's response following his message to do more in front of goal.
The Spaniard said: "I don't know if that's the case, but I am very happy.
"He wasn't feeling that good yesterday and today, as he had some sort of illness. He wasn't ready to start but he was really wanting to contribute to the team if it was needed and he came on and made a huge impact and delivered with real quality."
Arteta revealed he also spoke to Saka after telling the media about his desire for the player to have a greater impact.
"After the press conference... I said 'Bukayo, I just killed you in the press conference, good luck tomorrow'.
"He was laughing. He knows that we have discussed these kind of things and he takes it because he wants to be the best version of himself.
"In order to do that, you have to put big objectives and challenges and try to reason by working and being consistent - and when it doesn't work, keep going because he has the ability to do it."
Gyokeres struggles on mixed night for fringe players
Arteta made five changes to the team that started the win over Leeds as the Gunners looked to navigate six matches in all competitions during this month.
Noni Madueke moved to the right wing after putting in a good performance on the left at the weekend, with Mikel Merino, Eze and Viktor Gyokeres all coming into the starting XI.
Eze had started just two games in all competitions before the match with Lille and Arteta had said his attitude had been "phenomenal" despite a lack of game time.
The 28-year-old showed flashes of his undoubted quality and his finish for Arsenal's second goal - and his first of the season - will give him confidence going forward.
Madueke had a mixed night as he showed his ability to beat a defender, but questions remain over his end product - even if he provided the assist for Jurrien Timber's classy opening goal.
However, it was not a good night for Gyokeres.
The Sweden striker scored 21 goals in all competitions last season as Arsenal won the title for the first time in 22 years and displayed his willingness to run and work hard.
But Gyokeres had just 12 touches before being replaced and Kai Havertz, as he so often does, looked a much better and more natural fit for the Arsenal frontline, teeing up Saka's goal too.
Arteta brought on Saka, Havertz and Martin Odegaard after going 1-0 up and all three contributed to show why they are still the first names on the teamsheet and why the Arsenal boss will be so reliant on them if they are to achieve more honours.

For years, Chinese hardware manufacturers have carved out a market niche with an array of handheld Android gaming devices focused on retro emulation and/or more modern game-streaming capabilities. Now, though, a major game industry trade group is targeting one of those manufacturers, Anbernic, asking the US Trade Representative (USTR) to add the company to its list of “Notorious Markets” that “engage in or facilitate substantial copyright piracy or trademark counterfeiting.”
TorrentFreak was among the first to notice the request from the Entertainment Software Association (ESA), which was submitted to the USTR last week. In it, the US trade group—which represents major publishers including Nintendo, Microsoft, PlayStation, Amazon, Epic, EA, Ubisoft, and more—notes that Anbernic devices “are routinely offered or shipped with removable memory cards preloaded with hundreds or thousands of unauthorized copies of copyright-protected video games published by ESA members.”
While many online sellers do include an SD card full of ROMs alongside emulation hardware of all types, Anbernic itself does not appear to do the same when selling directly from its website. Regardless, the ESA argues that these ROM-laden Anbernic devices selling through “normal retail channels” help to “normalize hardware-based piracy by delivering illicit catalogues through a polished consumer product.” This, the ESA says, meets the threshold for a “superfake,” an ill-defined designation that applies to “high-quality counterfeit trademark goods … on a commercial scale.”
Being included on the USTR’s Notorious Market List wouldn’t bring any additional direct legal consequences for a company like Anbernic. However, the USTR says the list “encourages the responsible authorities to step up efforts to combat piracy and counterfeiting” and notes that the list itself “increase[s] public awareness and help market operators and governments prioritize intellectual property enforcement efforts that protect American businesses and their workers.” Inclusion on the list could also presage a Section 301 investigation that could lead to legal consequences or restrictive import controls on the devices.

MANSA: Supporters of anti-drug activist Parwinder Singh Jhota on Wednesday took over the demolition of a medical store owned by Ashwani Kumar, accused of killing the whistleblower, and set the shop on fire after throwing medicines out of the premises.
The protesters, who had gathered amid heavy police deployment, raised slogans of “Bole So Nihal” as they entered the shop and began removing medicines. They later set the store ablaze, with police personnel present at the spot.
One of the protesters held up strips of pregabalin capsules, claiming the drug was prohibited in Punjab. The activist showed the capsules to the gathering, which responded with applause, arguing that Jhota had been fighting against the sale of prohibited substances and had no personal enmity with the shop owner, contrary to claims by the authorities.
Locals set the accused's shop on fire
The action followed a demolition drive initiated by the district administration and police against properties belonging to Kumar. JCB machines were brought in to demolish his house on Gurdwara Road and the medical store near the railway tracks in Mansa.
After a portion of the shop was demolished by the JCB, the protesters took over and continued pulling down the structure before setting it on fire.
The protesters said they had taken matters into their own hands because the state government had failed to deliver justice. 
They described the action as “people’s justice” and accused the government of failing to act against those allegedly involved in the drug trade.
Taking a swipe at the state government's anti-drug campaign, they said it was not “Yudh Nashian Virudh” (war against drugs), but “Yudh Nasha Rokan Walian Virudh” (a war against those trying to stop drugs).
Bathinda DIG Harjit Singh said the demolition action had been carried out after completing the requisite formalities.

Surendra Singh Choudhary, known as ‘Bittu Tabahi’ for his efforts to clean rivers, has shared a troubling update on the Ajnar River in Madhya Pradesh’s Rajgarh district. In a video posted on Instagram, he showed how plastic bags and other waste had accumulated along the riverbanks again, just weeks after he had cleaned the area.

‘I never imagined that eight months…’
Sharing the video on Tuesday, Choudhary expressed his disappointment at seeing the river polluted again.
"I never imagined that eight months of my hard work would go to waste like this," Bittu wrote in the caption.
He also asked social media users to suggest ways to remove more garbage from the Ajnar River efficiently.

Lions to make history with France game in Cardiff
- Published
The British and Irish Lions will play a historic first women's fixture when they face France at Cardiff's Principality Stadium before their 2027 tour to New Zealand.
Jo Yapp's side will face the French, ranked fourth in the world, in the Welsh capital on Friday, 27 August (19:30 BST).
The Lions face a Black Ferns XV the following weekend in Whangarei before the first of three Tests with New Zealand on 11 September.
"There are moments in sport that only come around once - and this is one of them," said head coach Yapp.
"For our British and Irish Lions Women's team to step on to the field for the first time, on home soil and in front of our fans, is going to be incredibly special."

Men's Lions tours, featuring players from England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland, have taken place since 1888.
The women will travel to New Zealand for a five-match tour that features Tests in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch.
Yapp's side will hope for a send-off in front of a bumper Cardiff crowd.
"It will be a tremendous rugby match and occasion," said Carol Isherwood, chair of the Lions women's committee.
"It's a chance to grow the game and leave a legacy so that we are able to continue with the Lions team by setting the foundations and give everybody the chance to see the women's game at its very best."
A crowd of 21,186 set a record for a Wales women's home game in any sport when watching the Six Nations defeat by England at Principality Stadium in 2025.
"I've been there for some England men's games and the noise is fabulous. It'll be great if it is a sea of red for the Lions and not just Wales," said Isherwood, who captained Great Britain in 1986.
"We've got a fantastic tour in line, and we're starting off with a brilliant occasion in Cardiff.
"We looked at some different options and going abroad, like the men have previously, but the Welsh Rugby Union said that they felt they could do a great job here.
"We have the fantastic stadium, the support for rugby, tradition of the women's game having some important moments in Wales and the fact that we can get thousands under that roof to see the Lions women play.
"The visibility allows girls across England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales to dream of pulling on that red shirt one day."
It will be the second time that the Lions have faced France after the men won a friendly in Paris in 1989.
France perfect preparation for Black Ferns
The Lions will go up against a France side who were semi-finalists at the 2025 World Cup and have been runners-up to England in the last seven Six Nations championships.
Last month they beat Australia and Canada in home fixtures in the WXV Global Series.
The men's Lions teams have struggled in fixtures on home soil – they drew with Argentina in Cardiff in 2005 and lost to the Pumas in Dublin last year – and Isherwood admits it will be a test against more settled opponents.
"We're bringing the best of England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales players together and you've got a really tough job to unify them very quickly and get them on the same page," she said.
"How we build an environment where they all can compete at their best is going to be phenomenal.
"It's like bringing the Harlem Globetrotters together, but you've had no time and they'll all come from different systems.
"How do you get them ready to go as a team within a short time? There's an art to that and Jo and her coaches will be looking at how they will do that effectively, because this opening game against France will be tough."

Mumbai: Shares of public sector lender Canara Bank surged nearly 4 per cent on Wednesday after the bank reported improved financial performance for the second quarter of FY27. Strong growth in net interest income, lower bad loans and reduced provisions supported the bank's September quarter earnings.
The PSU banking stock climbed to Rs 125.17 following the announcement, even as it remained under pressure on a year-to-date basis.
Net Profit Rises 9 Percent
Canara Bank reported a net profit of Rs 5,175 crore for the September 2026 quarter, registering a 9 per cent increase compared with Rs 4,774 crore in the corresponding quarter last year.
The improvement came on the back of higher core income and lower provisions, reflecting stronger operating performance during the quarter.
Net Interest Income Jumps 20.4 Percent
The bank's net interest income (NII), representing the difference between interest earned and interest paid, increased 20.4 per cent year-on-year.
NII reached Rs 11,004 crore during the September quarter, compared with Rs 9,141 crore in the year-ago period.
The double-digit growth in core income highlighted the lender's expanding loan business and interest earnings.
Asset Quality Shows Improvement
Canara Bank reported a sequential improvement in asset quality, with its gross non-performing asset (GNPA) ratio declining to 1.33 per cent from 1.57 per cent in June.
The net NPA ratio also improved to 0.30 per cent from 0.36 per cent.
In absolute terms, gross bad loans declined to Rs 18,298.95 crore from Rs 20,354.34 crore, while net NPAs fell to Rs 4,053.19 crore from Rs 4,652.95 crore.
Provisions Decline, Slippages Rise Slightly
Provisions declined to Rs 3,583 crore from Rs 3,780 crore in the preceding quarter, providing additional support to profitability.
However, fresh slippages increased marginally to Rs 1,844 crore from Rs 1,781 crore in June.
Loan And Deposit Growth Remains Strong
The bank's loan book expanded 19.3 per cent year-on-year to Rs 13.73 lakh crore, while sequential growth stood at 6.2 per cent.
Deposits increased 13.1 per cent annually to Rs 16.97 lakh crore, reflecting continued business expansion.
Canara Bank Share Price Reaction
Following the results, Canara Bank shares gained around 4 per cent to Rs 125.17.
Despite the positive earnings reaction, the stock remained approximately 19 per cent lower so far in 2026, highlighting the gap between improving quarterly fundamentals and its broader market performance.

Amid a potential fire sale on the horizon, ecommerce unicorn DealShare’s CEO Kamaldeep Singh has stepped down from his role to join electric mobility solutions provider Indofast Energy as its CEO. Singh took to LinkedIn to make the announcement but didn’t specify the reason behind his exit. Singh had joined DealShare in December 2022 as its president, before transitioning to the role of CEO in January 2024 to spearhead the struggling startup as it revives its value-commerce business. He had a near 15 year long stint with Big Bazaar prior to DealShare, where he served as the CEO for more than a year. "After more than 25 years of building and transforming consumer businesses, I am stepping into an industry that is itself going through a fundamental transformation. Mobility is being reimagined. I believe the winners in this transformation will be those who put customer experience at the core and technology at the backbone," Singh said. For context, Indofast Energy operates a fast charging battery-as-a-service network for EVs across India. It is a joint venture between Indian Oil Corporation and SUN Mobility. The company is planning to invest over $1 Bn over the next three years to deploy more than 10,000 battery-swapping stations across 50-plus cities. Singh intends to lead Indofast Energy’s next phase of growth, accelerating business expansion, strengthening its market presence and building a scalable and sustainable energy and mobility ecosystem across India. What This Exit Means For DealShare The exit comes about a month after Inc42 reported that Singh was serving his notice period, while CFO Ashish Shah was also looking to exit the startup. As of now, the ecommerce startup is yet to announce its replacement. The CEO exit comes amid ongoing questions around DealShare’s business model and future ownership. The startup’s founding team — Sourjyendu Medda, Vineet Rao, Sankar Bora and Rajat Shikhar — all exited by 2024. DealShare, which is known for online grocery delivery catering to middle and lower income "Bharat" households in tier-II and tier-III cities, has seen mounting competition pressure in the ecommerce landscape. DealShare began scaling back its online operations in April 2026 and eventually stopped fulfilling orders from its warehouses, effectively shutting down its two-hour delivery model. While the app remains available, its online business has dwindled to “next to zero”, Inc42 reported in September. The startup continues to operate physical stores, although further offline expansion has been put on hold. Amid all this, the startup is now reportedly in advanced discussions with online pharmacy Truemeds for a potential acquisition through a share-swap transaction that could value DealShare at just over $90 Mn, a 95% drop from its peak unicorn valuation. Westbridge is a common investor in both startups, holding roughly 18.4% of DealShare. Notably, the transaction is yet to materialise, with Truemeds’ existing investors not necessarily aligned with the deal. DealShare is also in talks with other potential buyers, according to sources Inc42 spoke to earlier. It has raised nearly $400 Mn to date from investors such as WestBridge Capital, Z47, Tiger Global, and Alpha Wave Global. It reached a peak valuation of $1.7 Bn in 2022. On the financial front, DealShare’s revenue from operations fell to 13.3% YoY₹432.4 Cr in FY25 from ₹499 Cr in FY24, while its net loss narrowed 91% to ₹87.7 Cr from ₹167.7 Cr.

US federal judge Timothy Kelly on Tuesday (local time) granted relief to three news outlets by extending their access to the White House, stating that US President Donald Trump may have broken the law when he tried to bar journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the premises. In his written decision, Kelly elaborated on his 24 September emergency order restoring the journalists’ access to the White House. The news outlets and press freedom organisations have alleged that Trump violated the Constitution by retaliating against journalists whose reporting displeased him, AP reported. The federal judge went on to say that Trump’s ban impacted 78 reporters at three news organisations in total. He ordered the White House to restore the reporters’ “hard passes”. The federal judge accepted the plaintiffs’ argument that the administration had raised national security concerns only after taking action but had failed to substantiate them. Kelly wrote that without a preliminary injunction, the outlets “are likely to suffer irreparable harm, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest tip in their favor.” He further stated that the White House did not give the plaintiffs any warning that they were likely to lose their hard passes before Trump announced the decision on social media. Kelly wrote, “The revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes matters a lot as to how, whether, and to what extent they can do their jobs,” and added, “President Trump’s own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before.” In his late-night order, Kelly said, “No one should interpret the Court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.” Trump announced last month that reporters from the three news organisations would be barred, saying they “shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States.” He has since defended the restrictions, describing their coverage as “negative” or “one-sided” and citing those criticisms as grounds for denying the journalists access to the White House. Hailing the court’s ruling, Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the three media organisations, said, “When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment.” Boutrous added, “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future.” The setback for the Trump administration comes weeks before the US midterm elections, scheduled for 3 November, as Republicans struggle to retain control of Congress. - To start the An Unheard Farewell quest in Valor Mortis, players have to talk to the Adjutant Sous-Officier in the Valley of Ashes.
- The quest requires players to find the scout, who is located on the mid-level of the elevator in that area.

Valor Mortis has some really interesting side quests, and one of the first ones you get in the game is called An Unheard Farewell. Like other soulslike games, the side quests in Valor Mortis can also be a bit cryptic. Many players are already having trouble with the very first side quest. So, here is a complete guide to Valor Mortis ‘An Unheard Farewell’ quest.
How to Start Valor Mortis ‘An Unheard Farewell’ Quest
To start the An Unheard Farewell quest in Valor Mortis, players will need to make their way into the Valley of Ashes. This place unlocks after fighting General Lothaire for the first time. Once in the Valley of Ashes, make your way to the next Lantern location. Once you reach there, you will find a carriage with a voice coming from inside.
This voice belongs to an Adjutant Sous-Officier, who asks you to find the scouts he sent out. If you agree to help, the An Unheard Farewell quest will begin for you.
How to Complete Valor Mortis ‘An Unheard Farewell’ Quest
The quest is fairly straightforward. All you have to do is find the missing scout’s location and defeat him to obtain the letter. Now, the issue is that the quest diverges from the main questline in the game. So, it can become difficult for players to find the scout’s location. So, here is how you can complete the Valor Mortis ‘An Unheard Farewell’ quest:
- Go down to the carriage from the Lantern, where you will find the Pistol.
- At the very bottom, you will find another lantern. Walk along the pier and jump to the spot above.
- Shoot at the red blob at a distance to destroy it. Learn how to destroy red blob in Valor Mortis from our guide if you have any doubts.
- Now, the lift will become available for use. Jump on it and wait for it to reach the first level. When the lift becomes stuck, jump to the right side and use the fire magic to burn the barrier.
- Enter the cave and make your way up until you exit. Continue going forward until you reach the top of the elevator.
- When you reach the elevator, destroy the two red blobs on each side to remove the corruption. Now call up the elevator and use it to get back down.
- While going down, look for a new platform on the left and jump to it. Burn the blocked path there and go inside the cave.
- Inside, you will find the missing scout, who will be a mini-boss. Defeat him and read the letter on the table near the ladder.
- Now, return to the Adjutant Sous-Officier to brief him about the details. This will complete the quest.
Valor Mortis ‘An Unheard Farewell’ Quest Reward
After completing the Valor Mortis ‘An Unheard Farewell’ quest, you will get the Sleight of Hand Amber. This Amber gives the following passive effect when slotted into the Skill Tree:
- Sleight of Hand: Reduces the reload times for Firearms and speeds up weapon switching.
That’s the only reward you get for completing this quest. However, there are some chests along the way that can provide some additional items.
So, that’s it. Now you know how to complete the An Unheard Farewell quest in Valor Mortis. If you have any questions, ask us in the comments below.

Tamil Nadu has achieved the National AIDS Control Programme-Phase V (NACP-V) target of 95-95-95 during 2026-27 under which 95% of people living with HIV know their status, 95% of those diagnosed are on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and 95% of those receiving treatment achieve viral suppression, Health Minister K.G. Arunraj said on Monday.
Officials said the State achieved the target in September this year. The Minister, while participating in an event on a State-level intensified IEC campaign on HIV/AIDS, said the prevalence of HIV/AIDS was down by half in the State; it has dropped from 0.40% in 2010 to 0.19% in 2023 as a result of sustained and intensive awareness efforts by the State government and NGOs.
The aim, he said, was to increase awareness and achieve a HIV/AIDS-free Tamil Nadu by 2030. Currently, 1,63,151 people are under treatment in the State, he added. He said a total of 311 integrated counselling and testing centres (ICTC) functioned in the State with funding support from the National AIDS Control Organisation, while 403 ICTCs functioned through financial assistance from the National Health Mission. A total of 2,656 testing facilities functioned at primary health centres and government hospitals, a press release said.
Free HIV testing
Free testing for HIV, prevention, and treatment services are provided through ART centres in 58 government health facilities, including government medical college hospitals, district headquarters hospitals, and government hospitals, and 28 ART centres in private medical colleges hospitals and 172 linked ART centres. As many as 104 NGOs and social organisations have been working to bring about behavioural changes among high risk groups in the State. This includes sex workers, men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, transpersons, heavy vehicle drivers, and migrants, he added.
The Minister said eliminating mother-to-child transmission of three infections — HIV, Syphilis, and Hepatitis B — was another key priority. Babies born to HIV-positive women were given a prophylactic dose of ART soon after birth to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV, he added.
Taking into consideration the need to provide social protection for children living with HIV/AIDS through nutritious food, uninterrupted education, and continuous treatment, the State government enhanced the monthly financial assistance provided to children affected by HIV/AIDS.
The revised monthly assistance was ₹3,000 for children living with HIV who have lost both parents, ₹2,000 for children who have lost one parent, ₹1,500 for children who live with their parents, and ₹1,500 for children who have lost both parents to HIV/AIDS but are not infected. An additional ₹1.21 crore has been allocated for this scheme and the enhanced assistance will benefit children from November onward, the Minister said.
He said the intensified awareness campaign on HIV/AIDS must reach every section of the society. Through the Tamil Nadu State AIDS Control Society (TANSACS), Red Ribbon Clubs have been set up in 2,329 colleges to create awareness among students about HIV/AIDS, sexually transmitted infections, and behavioural change. To create awareness on HIV/AIDS prevention among adolescents, life skills education training is being imparted to students studying in classes VIII, IX, and XI in 9,830 schools through the State Council of Educational Research and Training, Dr. Arunraj added.
Health Secretary Darez Ahamed and Project Director of TANSACS R. Seethalakshmi were present.

How the iPhone Duo's camera is different from the iPhone 18 Pro's
Going beyond the number of cameras and megapixels.
The iPhone Duo has by far the highest starting price of any iPhone to date. Which makes sense in a way, since it's basically two devices in one. But at $1,999, it still lacks the iPhone 18 Pro's more advanced camera hardware. A telephoto lens and variable aperture are out, while tricks that take advantage of its foldable design are in. Most of the differences exist due to the limitations and benefits of any dual-screen phone, including challenges around squeezing more cameras into an already crowded device and being able to use an external display for more content. Here's exactly what your photography gives up (and gains) if you choose the Duo over the iPhone 18 Pro.
Fewer cameras, shorter range
Sensor resolution isn't where the iPhone Duo loses ground. It has two 48-megapixel rear cameras: a main camera and an ultrawide, which also handles macro shots. But camera count is another story, as Apple does not offer the telephoto camera on the Duo.
With their high resolution, both phones offer a 2x view by cropping into their 48MP main sensors. But the iPhone 18 Pro has a dedicated 4x telephoto camera, which can also crop its 48MP sensor to make a 12MP "optical quality" 8x zoomed shot. The best the Duo can do is 2x optical-quality zoom.
In practice, that means the iPhone Duo probably won't be a great choice for shooting distant subjects like a performer on a concert stage or athlete at a sporting event. Sure, you can use digital zoom to go past that "optical" limit, but quality will suffer the farther you go past 2x.
Why would Apple leave something as basic as a telephoto lens out of its first $2,000 iPhone? Well, the company hasn't said, but it may be as simple as physical constraints. Since a foldable phone opens into a bigger device, its cameras have to fit into one very thin half. Camera modules also have to compete with other hardware (especially batteries) for extremely limited internal space.
That doesn't mean future versions of the Duo won't get a dedicated zoom lens. After all, other foldable manufacturers have managed to squeeze one in. And it leaves at least one obvious place for Apple to entice upgraders with sequels.
Another big omission is variable aperture, which is one of the iPhone 18 Pro's headline features. It can physically widen or narrow its opening, adjusting how much light enters (and how much of the scene stays in focus). The Duo's aperture is fixed, just like on all previous iPhones. It still supports portrait-mode background blur, but that digital effect isn't the same.
The Duo's unique tricks
Since the Duo can stay upright and basically prop itself up when partially folded, its camera can take advantage of this faux built-in tripod. This makes it an interesting choice for things like group photos and video calls.
The Duo has a 12MP selfie camera on its outer screen, along with a separate 1080p FaceTime camera hidden beneath the inner folding display. The outer screen can also act as a viewfinder for the higher-resolution 48MP rear cameras, and if you open the Duo all the way, you can point those cameras at your face while still seeing what's in the shot. Perfect for high-res selfies.
You can also set it down somewhere and join the shot while using the outer screen to check the framing. Traditional slab-like iPhones can't do that.
A Duo-specific feature called Smart Take goes a step further: it recognizes when everyone in a group photo is ready and takes the photo automatically.
The Duo also has a trick for video calls: Duo FaceTime lets someone around you join the call using the outer display and camera, rather than crowding next to you for the inner screen. Then there's Kid Cue, which shows Peanuts animations on the outer display to get kids to look toward the phone.
So, it's not that the Duo's camera setup is without its own unique (if quirkier) perks. It's just that the iPhone 18 Pro provides the more complete and traditional camera experience.
The iPhone 18 Pro's other advantages
The two still have plenty of overlap. Both support 24MP and 48MP photos, adjustable portraits and updated Photographic Styles, including texture and grain adjustments. They can each record in 4K Dolby Vision at up to 120 fps, and both let you apply Cinematic effects after the fact.
But the Pro's advantages become clearer when you want to take over from the phone's automatic settings. Thanks to the new variable aperture, the Pro offers, well, Pro Controls, which are manual adjustments for things like shutter speed, white balance and aperture. The Duo doesn't offer that.
The Duo also lacks ProRAW photos, which preserve extra sensor data for advanced editing in apps like Lightroom. Video gets shorted, too: there's no ProRes, ProRes RAW or Apple Log 2 for more flexibility in post-production. Of course, those features will be missed by those who are into fine-tuning professional-class shots with professional-class tools. But if your photography doesn't go much farther than selfies and capturing the dog doing something funny? Well, you probably won't miss them.
Other features are also MIA. The iPhone 18 Pro has second-generation sensor-shift stabilization (the Duo uses the older version), an Adaptive True Tone flash (the Duo's isn't adaptive) and a studio-quality four-microphone array. The Duo also can't record spatial photos or videos, and it lacks Apple's new Reference Image feature, which captures signed sensor data alongside the photo to verify what the camera originally saw.
So, the iPhone 18 Pro is better if you want to shoot distant subjects, more advanced manual control or edits or the more all-around capable camera system.
With cameras that are a step down in several ways, the Duo isn't simply an iPhone 18 Pro that folds. For $2,000 and up, that might be a hard pill to swallow. If you're forking that over, it's probably because you like the folding design and have disposable income. But hey, as a bonus, at least it's also easier to prop up, join the group shot and let everyone check their framing.

The roar of plane engines and the hustle and bustle at Hong Kong International Airport’s Terminal 2 present a stark contrast to the pin-drop silence at the adjacent 11 Skies commercial complex.
A South China Morning Post reporter who travelled between the two places in early October found minimal footfall at the shopping centre, with the bright and airy environment of the airport terminal replaced by dim, stuffy and boarded-up corridors, and poor air conditioning amid the simmering outdoor heat.
Occupying a gross floor area of 3.8 million square feet, 11 Skies is a mammoth project at the airport. Seventy per cent of the space was originally earmarked for a mall with 800 stores and 120 food and drink concepts, and the rest equally divided between experiential entertainment facilities and grade A office spaces.
But only one of its three office towers currently houses some companies running businesses at the airport.

India’s supreme court has demanded accountability from the government and the senior election body over a controversial exercise that has led to the deletion of tens of millions of voters from the electoral roll and prompted mass protests.
Demonstrations have erupted across the country in recent days as opposition parties, student groups and the youth-led Cockroach movement have demanded the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the head of the Election Commission of India (ECI).
They have accused Kumar of overseeing a direct attack on India’s democracy through an exercise to verify and “purify” the electoral roll in states across the country, which so far has led to 130 million names being removed. In Delhi, hundreds of people were detained as they tried to protest over the weekend.
On Monday, the supreme court issued notices to Narendra Modi’s government, the ECI and Kumar to demand answers over concerns raised about the voter list revision, saying they expected all “to respond in a clear, transparent manner”.
The ECI has claimed the exercise is simply cleaning electoral rolls of duplicate, dead and ineligible names, as well as removing “illegal infiltrators”. However, large numbers of people in Delhi and states such as Bihar and West Bengal say they have been wrongly stripped of their vote and have struggled to get it back.
There are accusations that revision of the electoral rolls particularly targets minorities such as Muslims, who are traditionally not voters of Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The opposition alliance, led by the Congress party, have accused the ECI of being hand in glove with the government over alleged vote “chori” or cheating. Kumar was chosen to head the ECI by a panel headed by Modi.
While the exercise, known as the special intensive revision (SIR), began last year, widespread outrage only recently erupted after a report in the Indian Express newspaper revealed multiple irregularities in the process, which were flagged in more than a dozen internal objections.
The two petitions taken up by the supreme court on Monday alleged that the credibility of the ECI was now in question and called for an independent inquiry into the decisions taken by Kumar in how the SIR process was conducted.
“Deletions of voters have been made in the largest democracy,” said Menaka Guruswamy, a lawyer acting for one of the petitioners. “We have grown up with free and fair elections, that is not the case now.”
Another advocate told the supreme court judges that if action was not taken to ensure that India’s electoral rolls remained fair, “this country will burn”. Another hearing in the cases will be held next week.
The controversies over the ECI have once again driven India’s young people on to the streets in protest, amid rising frustration at the Modi government.
The Cockroach Janata party (CJP), which led massive unrest over the summer that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister, have once again mobilised and called for the resignation of Kumar. Thousands of CJP supporters took to the streets of Mumbai last Friday in protest and another demonstration was held on Saturday in Delhi.
In Delhi, police have been criticised for their heavy-handed approach to stopping any student groups protesting in the heart of the capital. Officers have been accused of sexually assaulting three journalists at the protests over the weekend and hundreds of young people were forced on to police buses. Delhi police said it was investigating the assault claims.

The Trump administration warns Ukraine it could cut off intel, Zelenskyy tells NPR
KYIV, Ukraine — The Trump administration warned it could cut off intelligence-sharing with Ukraine unless Ukrainian forces stop long-range drone strikes on oil refineries inside Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NPR.
In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, Zelenskyy said the Trump administration's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel will not bring down fuel prices. He also refuted President Trump's assertion this weekend that Ukraine was to blame for the rise in diesel fuel prices. Zelenskyy pointed out it is because of the Iran war.
"Mostly people in the world know why their prices on any kind of energy, including diesel, raised up, why they increased. Because of Hormuz. Yes. Because of blocking the Strait of Hormuz," Zelenskyy said, referring to the vital shipping chokepoint between the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman.
President Zelenskyy's sit-down with NPR comes as Russia's full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark, at a time when the White House has renewed efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war. Tensions between Zelenskyy and President Trump have also flared up again after the U.S. made a key concession to Moscow.
On Friday, Trump moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Zelenskyy said in a statement it was a "a weak decision by strong partners."
Trump lashed back hard at Zelenskyy, saying, "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," a leader who can reach a peace deal with Putin.
Then on Sunday, Trump announced on social media Russia and Ukraine had allegedly agreed to a partial ceasefire to halt attacks on each other's energy infrastructure — catching Kyiv by surprise — even as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued.
Zelenskyy told NPR he found out about Trump's assertion of an energy ceasefire agreement "through social like you" — meaning, from Trump's post on his Truth Social account.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked Sunday about the announced energy truce and told reporters that contacts were ongoing.
Zelenskyy told NPR his country is striking Russian energy and logistics sites to weaken the Kremlin's ability to wage war. Ukraine wants the war to end, he said, but will not stop these strikes unless Russia stops attacking Ukrainian energy sites.
Putin doesn't respond to diplomacy, the Ukrainian leader said, "he understands force."
Meanwhile, high fuel prices have been a major concern in the U.S. as the midterm elections approach next month. In the U.S., diesel fuel costs an average of $6.27 per gallon — more than 70% above what it was a year ago when it was a little over $3.65 a gallon, according to AAA.
Zelenskyy said said Trump's decisions to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel would not influence "the price in the United States. I'm sure … because the volume is not enough."
What it would do, he said, is provide the Kremlin with more money to spend on its war.
Last year, the Trump administration paused intelligence-sharing with Ukraine amid tensions with Zelenskyy. The White House did not comment on whether the administration has threatened to do so again, instead referring NPR to comments Trump made Tuesday. "We are helping them and we are sharing intel, we want the war to end. So, we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end," Trump told reporters.
Later, Zelenskyy described a new Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital. "A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners," he wrote on social media.
He said the target was a power plant, and added, "It is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing."

Google’s screenless Fitbit Air made a splash, but it’s been three years since the company updated its display-equipped Charge 6. That older tracker is showing its age, lacking newer automatic workout detection, deeper health metrics, and an IP68 rating. That's where the new Fitbit Edge comes in.
Announced on Monday, it is the successor fitness tracker fans with a screen preference have been waiting for. It sits in a sweet spot at $180—not as costly as a Google Pixel Watch but offering a similar experience in a slimmer, pill-shaped design. And unlike the Pixel Watch, it's compatible with Android and iPhones via the Google Health app. Preorders are available now, and it goes on sale on October 27.
The Fixable Fitbit
The Edge has a user-replaceable battery, a Fitbit first, aligning with Google’s efforts to make its Pixel Watch more repairable. (Likely also due to new battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union.) Repair options will vary by region and availability.
If you find the Pixel Watch’s round face too bulky, the Edge's capsule-shaped alternative might suit smaller wrists better. If the Charge 6’s 1.04-inch display was too small, the Edge upgrades it to a larger 1.34-inch screen. The difference is noticeable, and that extra real estate could make a real impact when glancing at your metrics mid-workout.
The Edge borrows a few more attributes from the Pixel Watch, including an altimeter that uses atmospheric pressure to measure elevation changes. That means it can record elevation gain and loss during outdoor activities, track floors climbed, and add more context to your outdoor stats. It also has a far-field skin temperature sensor, replacing the standard device temperature sensor found in other Fitbits. By bringing some of the Pixel Watch’s more advanced hardware to a fitness-first wearable, Google is giving the Edge a compelling middle-ground position in its lineup at a Fitbit-friendly price.
The Edge inherits the Fitbit Air’s improvements while restoring several Charge 6 features the screenless tracker lacks, including built-in GPS and electrical sensors that work with the electrocardiogram (ECG) app. You can also control music playback on a connected Bluetooth device, as you could with the Charge 6, and Google Maps turn-by-turn directions will arrive later this year.
Google also announced more advanced automatic activity tracking for the Edge, using Gemini Intelligence to identify up to 100 workout types. It can track more than 50 exercise modes, up from 40 on its predecessor. Google will also roll out these features to the Pixel Watch 5 and Air. If they work as promised, it means users won't have to log every activity manually.
With a Google Health Premium subscription, the Edge can track blood pressure trends without manual calibration and insulin resistance trends without requiring a blood draw. Google first announced these capabilities alongside the Pixel Watch 5's debut, but they only became available at the end of September. They’re also available on the Air, keeping Google’s screenless tracker up to date as its lineup expands.
The seven-day battery life remains unchanged, but it’s one of the Edge’s biggest advantages over the Pixel Watch. Like the Air, it takes about 90 minutes to fully charge, which is half an hour less than the Charge 6.
One odd omission is a near-field communication (NFC) sensor, which means the Edge doesn’t support contactless payments through Google Wallet. That’s a downgrade from the Charge 6 and a strange function to lose on a fitness tracker that Google is pitching as a step up from its basic Fitbits.
Dressed for Every Occasion
The Edge introduces new digital and analog clock faces, and the Canyon band color returns from the Pixel Watch 5, alongside five other band styles (Active Band, Active Sport Band, Performance Loop Band, Magnet Band, and Metal Links Band). The Stephen Curry collaboration ($220), which also appeared with the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5, is back in the same brown-orange color.
Alongside the Edge, Google is also giving the screenless Fitbit Air a visual upgrade with a new Metal Mesh band. It’s an even dressier strap than the polyurethane Elevated Modern Band. The Air may have initially been designed to disappear on your wrist, but the new band makes it a statement accessory.
If you’re all in on the screenless Fitbit Air, the Edge won’t change your mind. But if you’re not ready to give up a display, the Edge might be a compelling and affordable alternative for both iPhone and Android users. Stay tuned for our review.

And while of these factors are true, what we may not have realised is that infections could also, in some cases, lead to cancers. Journalist to be crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute
- Published
Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo I, who is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom later, has long been a familiar face in the country.
For many Ugandans, he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller, as a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster.
But Kijanangoma, 56, has now become the subject of media attention himself - his rise to the Tooro throne sparking controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country.
Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it has been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant.
Oyo became king in 1995 at the age of just three, following the death of his father. Then the world's youngest monarch, he ruled until he died last month from cancer, aged just 34.
The coronation is a day for celebration, involving traditional practices starting from midnight. The new king then walks about 4km (2.5 miles) to the official Karuziika royal palace where he is crowned.
A mock fight follows, to signify that kingship does not come easy, and he is then blessed by members of the royal Babiito clan, the Tooro kingdom's Information Minister Charles Mwanguhya told the BBC Focus on Africa podcast.
He performs other ceremonies that signifies his assumption of the throne, before he sits on the throne and an actual crown placed on his head to signify his new authority, his new position as the new Tooro king.
But the selection of Kijanangoma as king was far from straightforward.
According to tradition, a recognised son of the late king should succeed him. Close members of the royal family said Oyo had left a young son and a will with instructions that the child should be next on the throne.
But the son has never been revealed to the public and nor was he recognised by the committee of 21 Babiito clan members who choose the king and eventually selected Kijanangoma.
The late King Oyo was never publicly married, and little is known about his wife or their son.
Nonetheless his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, argued that the late king's will ought to have been respected.
However, the royal succession committee ignored her wishes, insisting their selection process was conducted in accordance with Tooro customs and traditions.
The new king has thus found himself at the centre of a succession dispute, with Kemigisa and her close relatives unhappy with the outcome.
Kemigisa referred to Kijanangoma's selection as the "announcement of a second king" being "made after the will of King Oyo was read to members of the royal family".
"As a mother, that was extraordinarily painful," she said, describing celebrations for the next king taking place "only metres from where my son's body lay".
The queen later said Oyo's son, who was in the US state of Texas, had been due to return home but that could not happen amid a "tense and polarised succession dispute".
"No child should be placed in circumstances where returning to his father's homeland could mean being drawn into hostility and conflict," Kemigisa asserted in a post on X.
But according to the Tooro kingdom's information minister, the son being talked about "hasn't been presented anywhere, which means there is a growing acceptance that sad as it may be, King Oyo didn't leave a son behind".
While King Oyo inherited the crown from his father, Mwanguhya told the BBC "the crown has moved to a different line within the ruling clan".
A king must come from the Babiito clan, specifically the lineage of King George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III, according to royal palace sources.
Kijanangoma and the late King Oyo are cousins. Both are grandsons of Rukidi III, the 11th king, or Omukama, who ruled the Tooro kingdom from 1928 to 1965.
Kijanangoma was among several people who were considered for the role, including Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, who plays football for one of the UK's best-known amateur clubs.
According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities.
After he was formally announced, Kijanangoma promised that the palace would be open to the people, while vowing to focus on unity and development.
"I ask you for one thing - they have given me this title as king but I cannot work alone, I have to work with you," he said.
Uganda's traditional kings have no formal political authority, but they retain cultural influence and command significant loyalty in the communities they lead.
The country is home to four main kingdoms, the largest and most prominent being Buganda in the central region, which encompasses the capital Kampala.
The kingdoms were abolished in 1967, but the government under President Yoweri Museveni restored them in the early 1990s.
The government said this was to promote cultural pride and national unity, but the move has also been interpreted as a way of appeasing communities and fostering political loyalty.
Amid the succession dispute, the government backed the Babiito clan's choice of Kijanangoma. Attorney General Sam Mayanja said the Tooro kingdom was cleared to go ahead with the coronation, as there had not been a formal complaint against him.
The date of the coronation was announced by the government and Museveni is scheduled to attend.
The president's son and the head of the military, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has also publicly supported Kijanangoma. "Long may he reign," he posted on X.
Kijanangoma's very name points to his royal heritage.
His father, the first Kijanangoma, was born in the year King Rukidi III became king. The king gave him the name, which means the "one who comes with the royal drum".
The drum of royalty, foretold two generations earlier, is now returning to its bearer.
Kijanangoma was born in 1970 and raised at their family home at Kidukuru village in Fort Portal, about 300 km (186 miles) from Kampala.
He left the village to pursue further studies and graduated with a mass communication degree from Uganda's prestigious Makerere University in 1999.
He worked as a broadcaster in a career spanning more than two decades, including in neighbouring Rwanda and at home, with the Uganda Broadcasting Corporation.
The years spent engaging with the public, the interactions with leaders and the exposure to national affairs in his work as a journalist may yet serve him well as he returns to the community he came from, this time as their leader.
After he was named king, Kijanangoma said he would use the connections he had built up over 21 years working as a journalist "to get good things for our people".
His mother, Assimwe Yusta Kijanangoma, is confident that he is well prepared for his new role. She says his upbringing was deeply rooted in tradition.
"I really raised him with the teachings of the old kingdom of a cane and instructions and scolding. I laugh with him, and other times I scold him," she told the BBC.
She added: "Eddy is well-mannered, he does not fight, or shout, even when wronged, he says a few words and does not go so much into it."
She feels good for her son, although she admits to having mixed emotions, especially as her son is taking over after the death of a "great man".
