I'm begging...: Man cries on camera after mother denied BJP ticket for local body polls
Vijay Meena, a former Zilla Parishad chairman broke down in tears in a viral video while appealing to the BJP to reconsider its decision to deny his mother, Manju Meena, a ticket for the upcoming Rajasthan panchayat polls.
A man broke down in tears while appealing to the BJP to reconsider its decision to deny his mother a ticket for the upcoming Rajasthan panchayat elections. A video of Vijay Meena, son of former village head Manju Meena, has gone viral on social media amid discontent over ticket distribution in Jaipur.
The BJP denied Manju Meena a ticket from Ward No 47 of the Jaipur Zilla Parishad. Vijay, a former Zilla Parishad chairman, alleged that his mother's candidature was rejected because he had raised public issues and protested against the authorities. The Rajasthan panchayat polls will be held in four phases between October 23 and November 16.
In the video, a weeping Vijay claimed he had approached a local MLA and completed the application process after being told her mother would get a ticket. However, he alleged that the party later accused him of protesting against it. He said "he was begging", while appealing to the BJP for justice.
Vijay said he had raised issues affecting residents, including the need for a trauma centre and highway lighting. He also highlighted the difficulties faced by poor families who have to travel long distances for emergency medical care.
He questioned whether fighting for people's concerns was wrong. “I am begging now. If I have fought for people, I swear on my mother, give me justice,” he said as he continued weeping.
Claiming that his activism had cost his mother the ticket, Vijay said, “I will continue to fight for the people. You can remove me from the party or the organisation, but can you stop me from fighting for them?”
“People have to run to NIMS and SMS hospitals (in Jaipur) from villages for deliveries and even snakebite cases. If my daughters fall ill, I can take them to AIIMS Delhi or Mumbai for treatment. But what about poor families who cannot afford that?” he added.
Vijay also expressed anguish that his mother's candidature had been affected by his work for the public, saying he would rather forgo a ticket than stop raising people's concerns.
The viral video has surfaced as the BJP's ticket distribution for the Rajasthan Panchayat elections triggers resentment among aspirants and their supporters.
Elections to Zila Parishads and Panchayat Samitis are scheduled for October 23, 29, November 4 and 14, while polling for Panch and Sarpanch posts will take place on October 25, 31, November 6 and 16.
The polls cover 41 Zila Parishads, 457 Panchayat Samitis and 14,403 Gram Panchayats across Rajasthan. Counting for Zila Parishad and Panchayat Samiti seats will be held on November 20.

Ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party-led protest in Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, and on the day of the protest on October 10, Hindu Rakhsha Dal (HRD) chief Pinky Chaudhary and its members posted a series of videos on social media platforms inciting violence against the demonstrators. Strikingly, several such videos were made in the presence of police.
In the clips, Chaudhary and other HRD members urged “Hindutva supporters” to “set the protesters’ minds right” while using communal and inflammatory rhetoric. He described those planning to demonstrate as “anti-national” and “anti-Hindu”.
Despite reports claiming that Chaudhary was placed under house arrest, he continued to issue calls for HRD members and other “kattar Sanatanis” to reach Jantar Mantar and confront the protesters ahead of Saturday’s protest and on the very day.
Moreover, a video posted by News Capsule on October 10, the day of the protest, showed a group of men dragging, beating and physically assaulting young protesters near Kamla Market. Alt News identified one of the alleged assailants as Ravindra Govinda, a member of Hindu Raksha Dal.
Govinda shatred a clip on his Facebook account in which he declared “support for the Delhi police in treating the protesters” while identifying himself as a member of HRD. “…As we, the Hindu Raksha Dal, had declared, we will stand with Delhi police in treating these cockroaches…,” he says, while continue to issue threats against the agitators.
Govinda was also seen in a video posted by Pinky Chaudhary, claiming that HRD members were fighting against CJP protesters to “protect Sanatanis”.
One of the goon seen beating the kid is Ravindra Govinda. Member of Hindu Raksha Dal. He was detained in the morning. Look how Police is handling the goons. https://t.co/nONEQVhY4f
— Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear) October 10, 2026
‘We Will Beat Them With Sticks’
On October 9, Chaudhary posted a video in which he stood alongside a group of men carrying batons and openly threatened physical violence against protesters expected to assemble at Jantar Mantar the following day.
Chaudhary declared in the video: “Laath bajake inke pichwade thik karne, dimag thik karne jayenge” (We will beat them with sticks and set their minds right). He added: “Jo log iss desh ko Islam meh le jane ki galat fehmi rakhte hai” (Those who are under the misconception that they can turn this country into an Islamic nation.) He said HRD members and staunch Sanatani believers will “handle” all those who have the “insect of secularism” in their head.
View this post on Instagram
Threats Continued Despite Police Intervention
A few hours later on October 9, Chaudhary uploaded another video claiming that police had arrived at his residence and placed him under house arrest. However, even as he stood in front of several police personnel, he continued to issue threats.
In this video, he declared that several members of HRD had already reached Delhi and were prepared to confront the demonstrators. Referring to Jantar Mantar as an “adda of terrorists”, he reiterated that HRD members would use their batons against those he described as opponents of Sanatan Dharma. “Jitne Sanatani virodhi hai, unke pichwade laal karke hi wapas ayenge” (We will return only after making the backsides of all those who oppose Sanatanis red), he said. He further described HRD members as warriors who are “neither afraid to die nor to kill.”
Chaudhary portrayed the outfit as pro-police and pro-nationalist, claiming that its members wanted to teach the protesters a lesson for allegedly misbehaving with police personnel. He also accused CJP supporters of insulting Hindu deities, attempting to establish an Islamic state, and acting against the nation. “India is safe till date, only because Sanatani warriors are here,” he said.
View this post on Instagram
Chaudhary’s Son Joins Calls For Violence
In another video, Harsh Chaudhary, son of Pinki Chaudhary, posted a video appearing alongside several HRD members, including Lalit Sharma. The video was accompanied by the caption: “Hindu raksha dal puri takat k saath cockroach-o ki gaand pitne pohunch raha hai” (Hindu Raksha Dal is arriving in full force to beat the asses of cockroaches).
Dismissing the need for batons, he claimed that he was physically strong enough to pick people up and pin them down himself. “We don’t need lathis; I am tough enough to pick them up and pin them down,” Harsh said.
View this post on Instagram
Threats From Inside Police Station
On October 10, Harsh and his team were detained by the Ghaziabad police. They went on to post a video after recording it while sitting inside the police station and in front of police personnel, where they urged Hindu warriors to “set the mind right” of the protesters. Even as the continued to issue these threats while in police detainment, no cops were seen preventing them from recording the videos or issuing violent threats.
View this post on Instagram
Ravindra Govinda, Other Assailants Held
Prior to his Instagram account becoming unavailable, Govinda had also uploaded several videos in which he expressed support for the Delhi police and BJP government. In these videos, he said HRD members would stand along with the police and participate in “treating” the cockroaches.
Independent journalist Pranav Pradhi, posting a video on X, questioned Delhi police officials regarding the apparent disparity in treatment of protestors and “Sanatani warriors” of HRD.
He pointed out that Govinda and other members of HRD, who had been making inflammatory statements and issuing violent threats, were not detained on October 10, while several other protesters faced prompt detention. Pradhi highlighted that there were at least six people gathered together, which violated Section 163.
Delhi Police is stopping ordinary citizens from gathering or protesting, citing Section 163 of the BNSS. But Hindutva groups are gathering openly and threatening protesters.
They claim the protesters are raising anti-India slogans. I have covered these protests and haven’t witnessed this. And frankly, this is an old tactic. Nothing new here.
So I asked Delhi Police a simple question: if ordinary citizens aren’t allowed to gather, how are these groups allowed to assemble and openly threaten protesters?
They had no answer.
— pranav pradhi (@pranavpradhi1) October 10, 2026
Govinda later uploaded a video indicating that he and his associates had been detained by the police.
On October 11, Sunday, Delhi police arrested the four men seen allegedly assaulting protesters in the video. “Taking suo motu cognizance of a video circulating on social media showing four men allegedly assaulting a male protester, Delhi Police, PS Kamla Market, acted promptly and initiated legal proceedings,” Delhi police said in a statement. The four held include Govinda (35), Raman Saini (50), Vivekanand (32), and Kapil Kumar (27).
‘We Won’t Let India Become Bangladesh’
Ahead of the protest on October 8, Sharma released a video in which he issued threats while brandishing a baton. In the video, he stated that the HRD team would go to Jantar Mantar to “treat” the “anti-nationals.” He also declared, “We won’t let this country become Bangladesh.”
On October 9, Sharma uploaded a video showcasing a baton that resembles a baseball bat. He specifically threatened Dipke and Rathee, saying, “Do not confront HRD members, or this baton will enter through your mouth and come out from your ass.”
He stated that in places where Sanatan Dharma is insulted, where Sita Mata is disrespected, and where slogans against Brahmanwad and Thakurwad are raised, they will wreak havoc at Jantar Mantar on those individuals so that seven generations of theirs will remember it. He further claimed that HRD will take revenge for the mistreatment suffered by the Delhi police.
On live video, he used inflammatory language and expletives, urging Sanatanis to gather at Jantar Mantar in large numbers to confront the protesters. Sharma also uploaded several videos issuing threats of violence at Jantar Mantar against the protesters. In a video posted in the early hours of October 10, Sharma used expletives targeting Dipke, Rathee and their mothers while reiterating that HRD members were prepared to use violence against the demonstrators.
Later, Sharma uploaded another video where several HRD members were seen gathering and raising ‘Jai Sri Ram’ slogans, and other inflammatory slogans in police presence. 
Journalist Rana Ayyub posted a video in which Sharma was identified by Alt News. The video shows Sharma making inflammatory slogans like, “Dipke, Rathee kaha milenge? Rahul k pichwade meh!” in the presence of several police officials. The police officials can be seen asking them to board their cars. In the post, Ayyub said, “They threatened to detain me when I asked if they were facilitating this hate.”
This is Delhi police in all her glory. They threatened to detain me when I asked if they were facilitating this hate https://t.co/5cmHhw3Hke
— Rana Ayyub (@RanaAyyub) October 10, 2026
Notably, there was deployment of a massive contingent of police personnel and army battalions at Jantar Mantar. The authorities invoked Section 163 and detained protesters and journalists, Opposition politicians en masse.
Meanwhile, Indian Express Hindi posted a video showing a group of men adorning saffron scarves brutally assaulting a man at Connaught Place. The assailants were seen wearing metal knuckles, due to which the victim sustained wounds on his back and tore his shirt. The protester ran ahead to safety, where a few policemen were visible standing by the roadside, but none of them came to his rescue, Indian Express reported.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Eight injured in South Korea knife attack
- Published
A man has been arrested after stabbing several people in a shopping centre in Incheon, in a rare knife attack in South Korea.
Eight people were wounded in the incident on Tuesday afternoon, according to local news reports.
The 59-year-old suspect was reported to have carried out the attack at 13:40 local time (05:40 BST) with knives strapped to both of his hands, according to Incheon Namdong Police Station.
Law enforcement is currently investigating the suspect's motives for the attack, which took place in a building housing an outlet of Homeplus, one of South Korea's largest discount supermarket chains.
The suspect reportedly started stabbing people while travelling on an escalator from the floor where Homeplus was located.
Pictures and clips carried by local media show him attacking people at a food court.
The man was subdued by bystanders who used chairs to block his path and was later detained by police officers.
All eight victims - six women and two men - were taken to the hospital.
One of them suffered from "cardiac arrest", while the others had injuries to their back and shoulders.
In response to the casualties, authorities had set up an emergency medical centre on the building's first floor.
According to local reports, the suspect was wearing an electronic monitoring ankle bracelet at the time of the attack.
Reports said he had been previously convicted for attempted murder after he stabbed his ex-wife, and had spent four years in prison.
He had also reportedly been booked by police last month on suspicion of carrying a knife while holding a one-man protest in front of an Incheon hospital over medical treatment he had received.
The attack happened in a country known for its high public safety standards.
South Korea recorded about 0.5 homicides per 100,000 people in 2024, according Statistics Korea. That is about one-tenth of the global average.
However, a series of seemingly random and violent attacks across the country in 2023, which resulted in multiple fatalities and injuries, caused widespread fear.
Such attacks were known as 'Mudjima' or 'Don't Ask Why' crimes, a term used to describe acts of violence targeting strangers conducted by people with no personal link to the victims nor had obvious motives.
In April 2025, a man in his thirties attacked random strangers at a supermarket resulting in the death of a woman in her sixties.

Russian strikes leave 600,000 without power in Ukraine, Zelensky says

At least 600,000 people across Ukraine are now without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
He said "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit in Kyiv and the capital region and also in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv - despite a claim by US President Donald Trump on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine.
In Kyiv, at least three people were killed and 21 injured, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said.
Russia's defence ministry said its "massive" strikes overnight had targeted communications and energy facilities in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions used by Ukraine's military.
The defence ministry also said 902 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight over a number of Russian regions, including the capital Moscow and Crimea - Ukraine's southern peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014.
Ukraine's air force said that overnight, Russia had launched 39 ballistic and cruise missiles and 128 drones, and that four of those missiles and 115 drones had been shot down.
On Sunday, Trump wrote in a post on social media: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
President Zelensky has since repeatedly said Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow did the same.
But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. Under any truce, he added, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons" for it to continue the war.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.
“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it’s for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”
The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.
The point of the game was to stress-test the world’s response to a group of prospective technologies known collectively as solar radiation modification. These technologies promise to reverse global warming by reflecting away a portion of the sunlight reaching Earth, for example by spraying particles of sulphur dioxide or some other manufactured substance into the atmosphere. The cooling effect of this kind of solar geoengineering is widely accepted. It would mimic the well-known impacts of large volcanic eruptions, which temporarily cool the planet by half a degree or more. But the fallout is less certain—and less equal. Some regions will suffer: Models predict drying in sub-Saharan Africa and more intense tropical storms in the Atlantic. The cooling effect would also last only as long as the geoengineering continued; after that the global temperature could shoot back up with wild and hard-to-predict effects.
Until recently, the idea of solar radiation modification was a speculative niche of climate science. That has changed fast. Private firms are exploring solar geoengineering as a commercial opportunity: Last year, a US-Israeli startup called Stardust Solutions raised $60 million, and in May it released details of a suite of new inventions it claims would give humans the ability to dial down the global temperature as desired. In August, Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX might be a candidate for delivering geoengineering interventions, threw his voice behind solar geoengineering, writing on X: “Space satellites to control temperature and massive geo-engineering will be needed or it will be game over.”
The world is going to have to make decisions about how to govern this technology much sooner than most policymakers imagine, Cynthia Scharf, a former UN advisor, told WIRED. “It’s not 15 years from now; it’s in the next decade, easily.”
It was against this backdrop that Danielle Young, an assistant professor in international relations at Leeds University, arranged the war game. Its setting was a hastily convened UN committee charged with coordinating the international response to developments in solar geoengineering. The game unfolded over simulated meetings set at three points in time: the present, September 2027, and September 2028. Each step ratcheted up the stakes, with the game creators introducing new advances in sunlight-reflecting technology. As in real life, no one knew all the facts, and players had to respond to events that were bringing the world closer to a full-scale attempt at deploying solar geoengineering tech, even when they may not have a full picture of what had truly occurred—or what any of the others were up to.
The first session set the tone. Distrust and disinformation dominated. As participants discussed rules governing outdoor experiments in an attempt to agree an international deal, players representing both the US and China told the group they could not sign a deal that constrained their pursuit of research considered to be in their “national interest.” Nor could they accept a deal that would see their superpower rival taking the lead technologically. Speaking to WIRED, Jeffrey Nielsen, a major in the US Army who played the role of a US national security attaché, summarized the position as “worse than no deal at all is any deal that favors China.”
Tensions escalated when the team running the simulation handed the Russian delegates an “intelligence report” indicating they had found a plane near the Bering Strait believed to be involved in a US geoengineering research program. The US team—which was indeed flying research missions—accused Russia of disinformation.
Meanwhile, the US became convinced China was also conducting research and developing its own program. Beijing’s representatives had tried to insert language into a mooted deal that would ensure no retroactive punishment for past experiments. Then, China approached a player representing SpaceX to float the idea of a technology-sharing program. In a private discussion away from the group, the SpaceX player immediately reported the Chinese approach to the US team. The US demanded an international investigation. The finger-pointing continued, and countries abandoned the talks. The Canadian representative called it a “humiliating defeat.”
At the end of the session, Nielsen was pumped. He’d busted China and derailed any prospect of a global deal. In the context of the game, he told WIRED, it was a “humungous victory” for the Americans. But Young, the researcher who designed the scenario, said the Chinese were not, in fact, conducting experiments in the game. Mutual suspicion meant all parties left the room believing the others were moving as quickly as possible to build their own geoengineering capability.
What played out in the first session reflected “the likelihood, in my opinion, of the geoengineering arms race,” says Nielsen, who clarified he was speaking to WIRED in a private capacity and not representing the views of the actual US government. Most experts agree it would take a superpower’s reach to ensure the safe passage of planes needed to deliver payloads of dust to the stratosphere in a geoengineering exercise. But neither the US nor China would lightly cede control over the global thermostat, says Nielsen, and distrust and poor communication are a significant risk: “Any action related to the issue by one actor can be perceived as malintent by the other.”
The threat of falling behind a rival is “a very strong driver of research and development of capability,” a former British diplomat with a background in national security told WIRED. “But that’s not at all the same thing as deployment.” There are similarities with nuclear arms dynamics—though solar radiation management, unlike nukes, has more obvious benefits as well as downsides, many of which are poorly understood. “There is an interdependence here,” says the former diplomat, who was not involved in the game and spoke on condition of anonymity to preserve relationships. “It’s not an inherently zero-sum game.”
Scharf, who represented the US government alongside Nielsen in the game, told WIRED a “scientifically transparent international collaboration” between China and the US “might be the best we can do in terms of fending off a very dangerous competition between the two. But I certainly cannot imagine that happening under the Trump administration.”
Compounding the problem is a lack of information. Geoengineering has historically been viewed with suspicion and often ignored by the scientific mainstream. One researcher told WIRED he’d experienced ostracization and barriers to academic progression owing to his interest in the technology; he no longer works in the field.
This lack of scientific interest greatly frustrated Golja, who spent much of the game watching as a bystander while political posturing dominated. Given the low level of knowledge around solar radiation modification and its side effects, she was one of very few experts who could help the participants understand the climate impacts of what they were discussing—yet she was largely ignored.“I was just so surprised about how little anyone actually cared about the science,” she says.
In the next sessions, the organizers tried in vain to nudge the talks back toward the realities of climate change. The participants received frequent notifications of climate disasters. These barely registered. Golja had prepared an “emulator,” a real-world demonstration of the best available science on how solar radiation management might affect weather patterns in different regions. It was ignored. If country representatives asked her anything, it was usually a leading question looking for data that would serve their ends or frame a rival’s proposal as reckless.
Then, during the last day, players were trying to find a way to respond to reports that a major plume of aerosols had been detected. In the game, this had been caused by a joint US-Saudi test of Stardust’s technology, though not everyone knew this. Finally, scientific advice was at a premium. Countries needed to know how to establish a monitoring network of satellites and other observational tools in order to prevent tests like this from happening in secret. A player representing an NGO called the Climate Futures Cooperative approached Golja, offering her money to fund such a scheme.
“Great. Fabulous. Why wouldn’t I do that?” she recalls thinking.
But it soon came out that the Climate Futures Cooperative was actually backed by the fossil fuel industry. The organizers had recognized that fossil fuel companies and major producing countries like the US and Saudi Arabia would have a clear interest in removing barriers from the development of a technology that could combat climate change without having to immediately stop burning coal, oil, and gas. The shadowy NGO spent the game subtly wrecking the vibe and carping about process—though mostly they just sat back and let it burn. Some players—Russia, the US, SpaceX and Stardust—figured out the CFC was not what it seemed, says Young. “But they assessed it was to their benefit and didn’t draw attention to it.” Then the CFC chose its moment to offer money to Golja, only to crater her credibility, isolating and fragmenting the voice of science in the room.
“It was a whole mess,” says Golja.
That final lesson in fossil fuel realpolitik was about all Golja could endure. By the end of the last day, she was in tears.
At no point did the countries in the game agree to a deal, despite multiple proposals being put forward. European countries and Canada tried to build support for safeguards and open scientific research, but the talks constantly got bogged down by delay tactics and veered into tense showdowns over duelling strategic interests. In their final report, the researchers running the simulation—whose work was sponsored by the UK government-funded Advanced Research and Invention Agency—concluded that “strategic competition and state sovereignty drove the simulations, not climate concerns.”
Simulations like this one are not supposed to predict the future. The outcomes depend on the design of the game and the relative personalities and experience of the players. Many of those in the room lacked first-hand diplomatic and national security experience. The UN forum, which organizers selected as the game’s setting, may also not be as effective as talks between smaller groups of major countries. But the experiment in London echoed and refracted through the real world, during and after the months it was running.
In March, two papers from conservative US think tanks urged the Trump administration to take the lead on solar radiation modification and counter China’s threat. One memorably invoked a new, MAGA-coded term: “Weather sovereignty.” This month, the Observer newspaper in London revealed that the UK Ministry of Defense had paid a deep tech security consultancy to conduct research into sunlight reflection. Then, last week, the British government released its first official policy paper on the field, backing further research but stating firmly that it did not support deployment and “does not plan to do so.” Stardust has continued its lobbying of the US and governments around the world; CEO Yanai Yedvab told WIRED its job was getting easier as, unlike before, “the majority of policymakers … are already aware of this technology.”
Stardust has always maintained that it will not conduct large-scale outdoor experiments, let alone full deployment, before global governance is in place. “We are developing a very powerful tool,” Yedvab says. “When you develop this kind of powerful technology—and you have many precedents—national interests will play out. We’re not naive about it.”
Meanwhile, drivers of the climate crisis are intensifying. During the time span of the game, efforts to curtail the use of fossil fuels were being undermined by rising energy costs and political hostility. Week after week, an incredible summer of drought and heat pounded Europe. In the final week of August, the collapse of a glacier on the Tibet-Nepal border fulfilled the prophecies of decades of climate scientists, killing more than 1,450 people.
In the months since the simulation ended, Golja has reevaluated many things. On a corkboard behind her desk, she has pinned up a note to herself, laying out a vision for life in a world ruled by narrow geopolitical self-interest rather than science, evidence, and reason. Her answer: She plans to return to the small coastal town where she grew up in Connecticut and use her expertise to help local climate groups build the seawalls and coastal erosion buffers they will need to cope with the inevitable. “To try and make a difference where it feels like I actually have traction,” she says. After what she saw, pursuing science in the hope of informing global decisions no longer held as much appeal. “Now it feels a little bit more personal.”

Grad student accused of trying to flee U.S. after police questioned her about alleged poisoning
Microbiology grad student alleged to have poisoned tea of University of Wyoming colleague
A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents, then tried to flee the U.S. after police questioned her.
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested Oct. 6 at Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were "multiple" laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police.
Investigators say Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the alleged victim, who specialized in technology for disease treatment — research similar to work Wang had done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles.
It's claimed the poison was first detected when the wife of the alleged victim and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations have left him reeling. He said he was uncertain if the alleged victim will fully recover.
"It's been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your student's life is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that," Gomelsky told The Associated Press. "That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career."
Wang has no attorney listed in court documents. The Associated Press tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.
Surveillance in shared office space
The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as K.T., began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical acrylamide in the coffee maker's water.
K.T. and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie, Wyo.
Wang allegedly was recorded Sept. 27 going through K.T.'s desk. On Oct. 1, she was recorded "taking photos and manipulating notebooks" on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer's affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
Police said Wang had asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer.
A carcinogenic byproduct of cooking starchy food and burning tobacco, acrylamide, which can be acutely toxic in high doses, is also used in microbiology research involving proteins or DNA.
During an interview by campus police on Oct. 5, Wang allegedly said she "had not used acrylamide in years."
A day later she was taken into custody in Los Angeles while in possession of "multiple laptops, multiple portable external digital storage devices, related accessories, physical records and written materials," according to a request by Wyoming prosecutors to "significantly increase" her $200,000 US bond upon extradition.
Wang had no reason to go through the desk of the other student whose federally funded, patent-pending research involved "new technology for cancer, neurological and genetic disease treatment," according to the affidavit.
Wang "was reportedly working on similar research in China before coming to the U.S.," the affidavit alleges.
Envied colleague's success, prof says
Gomelsky described the alleged victim as a highly successful student from Vietnam.
Wang failed her first attempt to defend her dissertation and became envious of her colleague's success in discovering how to deliver RNA to human cells using bacteria, Gomelsky told The Associated Press.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a conference in August, Gomelsky said.
Later that month he went to the campus health clinic with worsening finger tingling and numbness, and leg weakness.
The student also said he had noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said, and that when he washed the coffee maker the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.
The water from the coffee maker was boiled down to isolate 63 milligrams of white powder that tested positive for acrylamide, according to the affidavit. The amateur investigators turned the sample over to university police.
Unclear if alleged victim will recover
Discovery of the substance immediately made Tak Sumaya, an assistant professor who helped identify it in the coffee maker water, suspicious. Acrylamide is "not something you would find in that kind of quantity anywhere," Sumaya said.
The alleged victim was working on "a pretty promising cancer therapy method," Sumaya added.
The alleged victim continues to experience symptoms from the poisoning, including not being able to focus, tiring easily and a loss of sensation in his left hand, Gomelsky said.
"Acrylamide is a neurotoxin that cannot be neutralized so it stays in neurons and basically kills them. So it's unclear if he'll fully recover or not," the professor said.
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 US fine.
It's not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany County Circuit Court Judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors' request and raised bond to $1.5 million US, cash only.

Tyreek Hill: NFL free agent receiver found liable for two counts of battery as jury awards estranged wife $500k
Tyreek Hill found liable for two of 10 counts in battery civil trial; Hill, 32, ordered to pay estranged wife $500k in damages; former Dolphins and Chiefs player's timeline to return to NFL still unclear
Wednesday 14 October 2026 09:00, UK
A Miami jury has found Tyreek Hill liable for two counts of battery but not liable for the eight remaining claims made by Lakeeta Vaccaro, ending the high-profile civil trial involving the NFL wide receiver and his estranged wife.
Hill, who has played for the NFL's Kansas City Chiefs and Miami Dolphins, was found liable for two counts of battery - one stemming from an incident in January 2024, and another from April 2025.
The jury awarded Vaccaro $500,000 (£377,000) in compensatory damages but did not award her punitive damages.
The jury found Hill, 32, not liable for eight other counts that included battery, assault and continuing domestic violence.
The trial involved allegations of abuse made by Vaccaro, 30, who on the stand described instances in which Hill allegedly pulled her hair and "treated me like I was, just, a man."
Hill took the stand last week and mostly denied what he called "false allegations" made by Vaccaro, while saying in one instance he shoved her and "created a hole in the wall."
Hill, wearing a dark polo shirt on Tuesday, embraced one of his attorneys and shook hands with others following the verdict before leaving the courtroom by himself.
It is not immediately clear what the verdict means for Hill's return to the NFL.
He is still working his way back from a dislocated knee and torn ligaments suffered in September 2025 while he was with the Dolphins, but his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, has indicated he could be ready to play by November.

Jantar Mantar denotification as protest site based on Supreme Court orders: Delhi Police tells high court
The court issued notice on a request to reconsider a protest-permission denial and will hear the case on November 17.
The Delhi Police on Tuesday told the Delhi High Court that they denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site in the Capital following a Supreme Court order earlier this month that nudged authorities to consider alternative, better-equipped spaces where residents could exercise their democratic rights without hindering public safety.
“We denotified Jantar Mantar after Supreme Court’s order dated October 9,” the Delhi Police told the single-judge bench of justice Amit Mahajan.
The submission was made while the court was hearing a petition filed last week by Indian Youth Congress (IYC) president Uday Bhanu Chib against Delhi Police’s denial of permission for a protest at Jantar Mantar.
Deep Dive
Delhi Police was represented by additional solicitor general Chetan Sharma and standing counsels Ashish Dixit and Amit Tiwari.
Also Read | Jantar Mantar’s changing place in Delhi’s protest map
The Supreme Court on October 9 called for a rethink of Delhi’s decades-old arrangement of holding demonstrations at Jantar Mantar, recording that the Delhi Police commissioner and other competent authorities would consider designating an alternative venue with better facilities for peaceful protesters.
A bench comprising chief justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the national capital needed a larger, better-equipped space where citizens could exercise their democratic right to protest without compromising public safety, access to emergency services or the interests of other residents. “It is high time that some other place with amenities for peaceful protestors need to be identified and designated,” the bench said in its order.
Delhi Police on Monday denotified Jantar Mantar as a protest site, ending its 33-year-long designation as one of the country’s demonstration hubs. They designated three alternative venues for protests: Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground in north Delhi, and CBD Ground in east Delhi.
Also Read | Jantar Mantar gone, Delhi's 3 new protest sites come with cost, booking, distance woes
The order, titled “Guidelines for Holding Protests or Demonstrations in Delhi”, said the Union ministry of home affairs constituted a committee to “examine alternative proper venues for citizen’s right for organising protest demonstrations in place of the existing ‘designated site’”.
“Based on the committee’s recommendations, Jantar Mantar as a protest venue has been de-notified,” the order said, adding that three new venues were designated for organising protests and demonstrations.
On Tuesday, Chib’s lawyer Siddharth Luthra urged the court to issue notice in the prayers to reconsider its request by undertaking a fresh, reasoned and individualised assessment. With regard to the prayer against Delhi Police’s October 1 denial to hold a protest at Jantar Mantar, the senior counsel sought time to amend the prayer in view of Monday’s notification.
Also Read | ‘Hands off': CJP's Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka breach Jantar Mantar, detained | WATCH
The law officer opposed notice being issued, saying the petition was infructuous in view of Monday’s notification. He said that all the prayers emanated from Chib’s prayer against the denial.
However, the bench issued notice on the reconsideration prayer and will now hear the case on November 17.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

In summer and fall 2026, numerous posts claimed U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr said, "Infertility is genetic. If your parents can't have kids, neither can you."
For example, a meme of Kennedy featuring the purported quote spread widely on Facebook on Oct. 2.
Snopes readers have also reached out to us to verify the authenticity of the alleged remark.
(Facebook user "Truth and Accountability Project")
Though Kennedy has spread incorrect health information many times over the years, there is no evidence he said the above quote. Variations of this quote are on X and in humor books dating back years before he was sworn in as health secretary in 2025. As such, the remark is incorrectly attributed to Kennedy.
Entering variations of the quote in Google, Bing (archived) and DuckDuckGo uncovered no authentic video or reportage indicating that Kennedy ever made such a statement.
Earlier online examples of the quote are not attributed to him at all. One of the earliest variations of the quote on X, from Aug. 14, 2022, reads: "Infertility is genetic, if your parents couldn't have kids you also won't." Other X accounts, including one labeled as a parody account, shared the same quote days later.
Another variant of the quote appears in the 2002 book, "Science Askew: A Lighthearted Look at the Scientific World," by Donald E. Simanek. An even earlier version appears in the 1997 book of humor, "Living, Laughing, and Loving Life," by Dan Miller and Jeanne Zornes. Snopes contacted Zornes to learn if the quote originates from this book. We will update this article if we learn more.
While he didn't originate the quote in question, Kennedy has long been concerned with infertility issues. In May 2026, at a White House event, he raised the alarm on male infertility, saying:
The fertility crisis for women began in 2007; for men in 1970. Men had twice the sperm count as our teenagers do today. This is an existential crisis for our country. We had a series of presidents who were trying to discourage childbirth and motherhood in this country. We now have a president who is trying to encourage it.
In 2025, Kennedy said on Fox News: "We have fertility rates that are just spiraling. A teenager today, an American teenager, has less testosterone than a 68-year-old man. Sperm counts are down 50%." Experts debunked this particular claim, according to an NBC News report.
An analysis by The 19th, a nonprofit newsroom focused on gender and politics, found that while evidence shows sperm counts are lower than decades ago, it is not clear that factor influences the declining birth rate in the United States.
For further reading, Snopes has looked into numerous quotes rightly or wrongly attributed to Kennedy.

BBC correspondent Joe Inwood explains how Pillay's childhood in South Africa led her to become a driving force in international law and human rights, from Rwanda to Gaza.

U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. this week launched an agency-wide effort to study and document any health problems reported after vaccination, the Department of Health and Human Services said on Thursday.
The initiative is the latest step by Kennedy, who spent years questioning vaccine safety and founded an anti-vaccine group before taking office, to reshape federal immunization policy. The American Academy of Pediatrics says childhood vaccines are studied in placebo-controlled and comparison-group trials and monitored for safety after approval.
The federal Vaccine Injury Table lists 14 compensable injuries across 16 vaccine types under the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, a no-fault system in which claimants file against the government, not vaccine makers. Since 1988, it has awarded roughly $5 billion across about 12,300 injury and death claims.
The new moves, which appear to be part of Kennedy’s decades-long efforts to sow skepticism about vaccines, come as he faces legal challenges to his attempts to alter US childhood vaccination schedules and growing concern among public health experts about falling immunisation rates, particularly against measles, which has seen a resurgence in the US since last year. The effort centers on a National Institutes of Health clinic
opened on Monday to treat and study patients reporting health problems after receiving vaccines, HHS said in a statement. Other measures include a proposal by the Centers for
Medicare & Medicaid Services to reimburse physicians for reporting suspected injuries to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, or VAERS; a CDC effort to update VAERS; and HHS requiring electronic health records to capture vaccine-related adverse events.
Kennedy has said U.S. children receive too many vaccines, falsely claiming repeatedly that kids get up to 90 doses before age 18, which has been echoed by President Donald Trump. Kennedy has long argued that chemicals in vaccines are dangerous, though experts say there is no evidence of harm.
In his first year heading HHS, he fired all 17 independent expert members of the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee and selected new panelists, many of whom shared his anti-vaccine views.
In January, the CDC announced a revamped childhood vaccine schedule that reduced recommended vaccines, dropping universal recommendations for flu, rotavirus, hepatitis A, hepatitis B at birth, some forms of meningitis and respiratory syncytial virus.
A federal court issued a preliminary injunction in March blocking key parts of the proposed changes, finding that Kennedy and HHS had violated federal law in reshaping the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunisation Practices. The injunction has prevented ACIP from holding meetings to make recommendations on immunisations often needed for insurance coverage.
