The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded in disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”
Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.
Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.
“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.
“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.
Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Donald Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Monday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

On the night of Feb. 3, 1972, the prints of “Pakeezah” arrived at Bombay’s Maratha Mandir cinema in a palanquin pulled by four horses. Military bands played outside, police held back the thousands crowding the gates, and inside, the film’s star, Meena Kumari, sat beside her husband, director Kamal Amrohi, and gripped his wrist so hard through the screening that her nails drew blood.
Amrohi’s son Tajdar was in the theater that night. His father never pulled his arm away.
“He just gave a smile, and she also smiled in an embarrassment, you can say,” Tajdar Amrohi says. “And it seems that even after 54 years, I feel as if that incident took place yesterday.”
Popular on Variety
Kumari died on March 31, 1972, weeks after the film opened. Now, Film Heritage Foundation’s (FHF) 4K restoration of “Pakeezah,” carried out with the Amrohi family, is back in front of audiences. Thierry Frémaux presents its world premiere at Festival Lumière in Lyon on Wednesday. It then plays a gala at the BFI London Film Festival’s BFI Imax on Oct. 18 that Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, the foundation’s director, will introduce with Tajdar Amrohi, his sister Rukhsar Amrohi and Kamal Amrohi’s grandson Bilal Amrohi. Dungarpur says he heard the Imax screening sold out “in no time.”
The film is set in Lucknow as the age of the nawabs (Muslim nobles) fades. Kumari plays Sahibjaan, born in a graveyard to a courtesan who was spurned by her husband’s aristocratic family. Raised in a brothel, Sahibjaan grows up to be the most celebrated courtesan of her day, though she longs for love and respectability. Then Salim, a forest officer played by Raaj Kumar, wanders into her train compartment by mistake while she is asleep. Taken with her feet, he leaves her a note in verse and slips away. When they meet again, they fall in love, but the stigma attached to her profession stands between them.
Few Indian films carry a backstory as heavy as this one. Amrohi was already married, with three children, when he married Kumari. Rukhsar grew up with her mother in the family’s hometown of Amroha, in Uttar Pradesh, until she was 13, while her father lived in Bombay (now Mumbai) with Kumari, whom the children called Chhoti Ammi (little mother). Amrohi conceived “Pakeezah” in the mid-1950s around Kumari, his wife and muse, and shooting began in 1956, in black-and-white, before moving to Eastmancolor and then CinemaScope. The production stalled in 1964 when the couple separated, and Kumari’s health declined sharply over the following years. The film’s German cinematographer, Josef Wirsching, who had come with Himansu Rai and Devika Rani from Bombay Talkies, died partway through. Composer Ghulam Mohammed died in 1968 after writing the songs, leaving Naushad to complete the background score.
Through all of it, Amrohi refused to let the film go.
“His relations, his health, his wealth – he put everything into ‘Pakeezah,’” his daughter Rukhsar Amrohi says.
She remembers that every household request, from new decor to things for himself, got the same answer: after “Pakeezah.” His kurtas (tunics), which usually arrived from Lucknow a dozen at a time every six months, wore thin during the shoot. When she pressed him to reorder, he told her that people came to see him, not his clothes.
“I’ll order all of this after ‘Pakeezah’ – not 12, I’ll get 24 – but let my ‘Pakeezah’ get into theaters,” she recalls him saying.
Tajdar Amrohi says that by the time the film was ready for release, his father didn’t have a penny to keep for himself and was deep in debt. Financiers, Rukhsar says, pushed him to drop Ghulam Mohammed’s music as old-fashioned and credit Laxmikant-Pyarelal or Shankar-Jaikishan instead. He refused, whether or not that meant the film got made.
The family’s own life bent around the production. When Kumari left and the shoot stopped, Amrohi sent Rukhsar and her mother back to Amroha. He didn’t want anyone to say that his first wife and daughter had arrived and driven Kumari out. He later wrote to Rukhsar asking her to raise her small hands in prayer that he would finish the picture. He had expected to complete it in a year, and it now felt like a noose around his neck.
“Isn’t that a sacrifice?” she says.
When shooting resumed, the haveli (mansion) set on Stage 3 at Filmistan Studio in Goregaon was modeled on the Amrohis’ ancestral home in Amroha. Rukhsar went to the set every day because her father wanted her there. She also traveled with the unit to Mysore for the outdoor shoot of the song “Mausam Hai Aashiqana” and the elephant attack sequence. Her mother’s paandaan (a box for paan, or betel leaf), part of her wedding trousseau, was lent at Amrohi’s request. It appears in the Gulabi Mahal (Pink Palace) scenes beside the actor Nadira. It now sits in the drawing room of the Amroha house, which Rukhsar restored and filled with her father’s furniture, photographs and belongings. Locals, she says, began calling it Kamal Amrohi’s museum.
The siblings are protective of how their father’s marriage is remembered. Tajdar Amrohi is adamant that the couple never divorced, and says that Kumari had asked Amrohi to promise he never would, calling him Chandan, her pet name for him. He also pushes back on the widely told account that actors Sunil Dutt and Nargis and composer Khayyam persuaded Kumari to return to the film in 1969. Dutt deserves credit for going to her, he says, but many others in the industry, Ashok Kumar among them, had urged the same.
“Frankly speaking, if Meena ji herself hadn’t wanted to complete this film, she wouldn’t have,” he says.
Nor, he says, did “Pakeezah” become a hit because its star died weeks after release, a reading his sister also rejects. If that were how it worked, he argues, “Every producer-director would pray that once the film is complete, one of their main artists leaves the world, and the film will be a hit. That’s not how it is. A good thing is good, and a bad thing is bad and won’t run.”
Tajdar Amrohi was at St. Elizabeth Nursing Home on Malabar Hill when Kumari died, and says it was the first time he had ever seen tears in his father’s eyes. Amrohi died in 1993 and is buried beside her. His son sees that as a kind of divine verdict on decades of gossip about the pair.
“Just as Shah Jahan immortalized Mumtaz Mahal by building the Taj Mahal, Kamal sahab [sir] immortalized Chhoti Ammi, Meena ji, across the whole world by making ‘Pakeezah,’” he says.
For Rukhsar Amrohi, who also calls Kumari Chhoti Ammi, the film is a token of the couple’s love, made by her father out of his love for Kumari. “‘Pakeezah’ is the love child of our Baba [father] and Chhoti Ammi,” she says.
For Dungarpur, the film goes back to his own childhood. He was 3 when it was released, and his grandmother, Usha Rani, the Maharani (queen) of Dumraon in Bihar, was obsessed with it. She played its LP and later took him to see it on rerelease. He founded FHF in her memory in 2014 and had wanted to restore “Pakeezah” ever since.
“It’s one of my most beautiful memories of restoration, and the most important film in my life,” he says. “She was the driving force on seeing this restoration.”
The job turned out to be among the hardest the foundation has taken on. When the FHF team examined the film’s original camera negative at a Mumbai lab, it had melted, with no images left on the celluloid.
“Meena ji went into a coma two days before her death, and the negative of ‘Pakeezah’ had also gone into a coma,” Tajdar Amrohi says.
The team rebuilt the film from an interpositive, a CinemaScope print and a color reversal internegative held at the National Film Archive of India, which Dungarpur credits to archivist P.K. Nair. The sound negative had also survived. The two-year restoration was carried out at L’Immagine Ritrovata in Bologna, with the soundtrack remixed in 5.1.
The on-and-off shoot left its own scars. Day-for-night sequences didn’t match from one stretch of the film to the next. The opticals, meaning the fades and shot changes, drifted in and out of focus. Padma Khanna and other doubles performed some of the dances instead of Kumari, which made the continuity puzzle harder.
Color was the biggest test. The available versions had faded badly, and accounts differed on whether Kumari’s costume in “Inhi Logon Ne” was pink or red. Original color photographs were scarce, since continuity stills were usually shot in black-and-white to save money. FHF found a few, and Rukhsar Amrohi, who had been on set, came to Dungarpur’s studio to check them. She told him the lyric itself mentions a dupatta (scarf) dyed pink, so red couldn’t be right, and pushed for a deep magenta. That is what made it to the screen.
“You have to make sure that you don’t do something which he had not done, or you enhance it to that level, but keep it exactly his vision, the way he had conceived the film,” Dungarpur says.
He points viewers to the tracking shot at the end of the “Chalte Chalte” song where the camera glides over a fountain. For him it shows what the film’s camera team pulled off before zoom lenses were in common use. The film also has an anniversary this month: Dungarpur notes that Oct. 8 marked the 100th birthday of its male lead, Raaj Kumar, who replaced an aging Ashok Kumar as Salim.
FHF has run into missing negatives before. Dungarpur says the restored “Sholay” had the same problem. So did the foundation’s work on “English, August,” which was rebuilt from a single print, and Shaji N. Karun’s Cannes winner “Piravi,” for which only subtitled prints survive.
“So much money is spent on the production, so much money is spent, but there’s very little money spent on preserving these elements,” he says. “And that’s been quite a tragic story of India’s cinematic history.”
The foundation has had a busy 12 months on the festival circuit. It took “In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones” to Berlin, “Amma Ariyan” to Cannes and “English, August” to Venice, with stops including New York, Toronto, Shanghai, Singapore and the Festival of Three Continents. Dungarpur says FHF deliberately programs Indian commercial landmarks such as “Sholay,” “Pakeezah” and “Amar Akbar Anthony” next to independent titles. That way, Western audiences who would otherwise never see them get the chance. “Pakeezah” is set to travel to the Smithsonian and the Academy Museum, and its producers plan a wide release in India.
FHF’s next restorations are Shyam Benegal’s “Bhoomika” and “Mandi,” John Abraham’s “Agraharathil Kazhuthai” (“Donkey in a Brahmin Village”) and Aribam Syam Sharma’s “Imagi Ningthem” (“My Son, My Precious”). The Abraham film will be the foundation’s first Tamil-language restoration. With Criterion, FHF is restoring Bimal Roy’s “Bandini,” “Devdas” and “Madhumati” as well as Satyajit Ray’s “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne,” and it plans to take on “Piravi.”
Tajdar Amrohi still regrets that “Pakeezah” won no awards. When he once complained about it to his father, the director just smiled.
“You haven’t noticed one thing,” he told his son. “All these people who are coming to watch the picture – that is my award.”

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday, October 14, wished Pope Leo XIV a full and speedy recovery after the pontiff underwent successful lung surgery at a hospital in Rome. Modi expressed his wishes in a post on X, hoping for the Pope’s recovery and continued good health.
“Happy to learn that His Holiness Pope Leo XIV’s surgery last night was successful. Wishing him a full and speedy recovery as well as continued good health,” Modi wrote, tagging the official papal account, @Pontifex.
Pope Leo XIV Undergoes Surgery In Rome
The 71-year-old pontiff underwent a thoracic operation on Tuesday, October 13, at Rome’s Agostino Gemelli Hospital. According to the BBC, the procedure lasted approximately 90 minutes and involved removing the lower lobe of his right lung using a video-assisted surgical technique.
The surgery was performed to address a small, localised lung nodule that had been detected at an early stage. An examination during the procedure reportedly confirmed pulmonary adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, which had been suspected during preoperative testing.
The Vatican said the operation was successful, was completed as scheduled and proceeded without complications. The Pope reportedly awoke normally and returned to his room after a brief period of observation.
Public Engagements Cancelled During Recovery
Pope Leo XIV is expected to require approximately a week to recover from the procedure. All audiences and public engagements have been cancelled through October 20 as he recuperates.
The development has drawn messages of support from leaders across the world, with several expressing their wishes for the pontiff’s recovery and good health.
Among those who have conveyed their wishes are Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Pope Leo XIV Elected In May 2025
Pope Leo XIV, 71, became the first American pontiff when he was elected in May 2025. His election marked a historic moment for the Catholic Church, which is led by the Bishop of Rome.

A cluster of Shigella infections linked to a temple festival has put health authorities in Thrissur on alert, with 10 cases reported in the district in the first nine days of October. Seven of the cases, including that of a seven-month-old child, were reported from Tholur among people who had attended a festival at a temple there.
The suspected source of the infection has been traced to a well at the temple, from which water was drawn for rituals. The well has since been chlorinated, District Medical Officer M. Sujatha said.
“The seven Shigella cases reported from Tholur were among people who attended a festival at a temple in Tholur. The source of infection has been identified as the temple well from which water was taken for rituals. The well has been chlorinated,” Dr. Sujatha said.
Health teams are closely monitoring the situation, while hospitals have been instructed to respond immediately if any further cases are detected. Awareness campaigns have also been conducted in the area, with people advised to seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms, she said.
All those who tested positive for Shigella have sought treatment, and most have recovered. The remaining patients are also recovering, according to the DMO.
The other three Shigella cases reported during the nine-day period were from Wadakkanchery, Arimbur and Adat.
The Shigella cluster comes amid a wider surge in fever cases in the district. As many as 4,914 people sought treatment for fever between October 1 and 9. During the period, 39 dengue cases and four cases of leptospirosis were also confirmed.
Dengue cases have been reported from several parts of the district, including Kodakara, Mattathur, Meloor, Thrissur Corporation, Avinissery, Chalakudy municipality, Kaiparamba, Kodassery, Pananchery, Puthukkad, Adat, Alur, Puthur, Mullurkara, Pariyaram, Tholur, Orumanayur, Thalikulam and Choondal.
Leptospirosis cases were reported from Pananchery, Pazhayannur, Porkulam and Kuzhur.
Dengue cases
The DMO said a significant number of dengue cases had been detected in migrant labour camps and among their contacts. “Most of the dengue cases have been reported from migrant labour camps and their contacts. We are keeping a close watch on them and monitoring the situation,” she said.
Health authorities have stepped up surveillance and preventive measures across the district. The DMO urged people with fever to take adequate rest, drink sufficient water and consume nutritious food, while vulnerable people, particularly those with compromised immunity, should take extra precautions and seek medical care when necessary.
With Shigella cases emerging in connection with a common gathering and dengue continuing to surface across multiple locations, health officials are keeping a close watch on possible further transmission and urging the public to maintain strict hygiene and food and water safety.

Regulator would quit over Man City interference
- Published
The head of English football's independent regulator says he will resign if he encounters any political interference over the future of Manchester City.
As chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan has the power to assess the suitability of club owners and executives.
If an independent commission's findings that the club broke Premier League financial rules are upheld, the watchdog would have to decide whether to force a sale.
Last month, the Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's Abu Dhabi owners decided to sell up.
When asked about Burnham's comments, Kogan told BBC Sport: "The Prime Minister is entirely entitled to make his own observations on anything.
"We are independent. That is in the name. I am the chairman of the Independent Football Regulator and independence absolutely runs through everything we're doing.
"And no politician has tried to influence and would try to influence anything we do on that."
When asked what he would do if he did come under political pressure over the case, Kogan replied: "I would resign."
An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations. City insist they are innocent and have appealed.

Kogan on next steps on Man City
The prime minister initially told the BBC of his concerns, before later denying his reaction had "downplayed the seriousness of the findings".
However, some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by Burnham's stance that sources told BBC Sport they were "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process.
Burnham's previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City's Abu Dhabi ownership.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanded all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club are released. The government released these details on Monday.
"As far as we, as the regulator, are concerned, we have a very, very clear course of action that is governed by statute and we are going to follow that course of action and no comment by any politician or indeed any individual is going to affect what we do", said Kogan.
"Process is going to drive what we do. Process will lead us to a conclusion.
"We cannot reach any conclusion at this stage because we don't know the outcome of any appeal and once we do then we will act accordingly."
The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing - which could take months to convene - to decide the punishment.
City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving the club and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty.
City's punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or being ejected from the Premier League, to being stripped of the eight trophies they won in the affected period.
Asked how crucial it is that it was resolved as soon as possible, Kogan said: "I think it's very important."
Kogan added that the case was "raising very serious issues if Manchester City on appeal is found to be guilty of the allegations within those findings".
"We are waiting like everybody else to see what the independent panel will do… and then we will bring in a view in terms of our own investigation and statutory powers if we need to do so.
"Our powers relate to individual owners, directors and senior executives. They refer to whether people are in a position to run a club in a way that is safe, coherent and done with probity, and we will be examining those things."
An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 that led to the verdict announced last month, with City also guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation.
The commission's report said that "a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence".

Writer Yiyun Li does not talk about "grief" or the "grieving process." To her, those words make it sound that at some point you emerge from grief. Instead, Li prefers to use the word "abyss," which, she says, is where she expects to be for the remainder of her life.
Li's teenage sons both died by suicide six years apart, Vincent in 2017 at age 16, and James in 2024 at age 19. Her Pulitzer Prize-winning 2025 memoir, Things in Nature Merely Grow, chronicled the loss of her sons and her effort to go on.
"James' death taught me to suffer better," she says. "To say, 'I can do it, and I can live with my pain and sorrow without ever wanting to stop feeling.'"
Li's new novel, Music Against the Night, is set in the late 1700s and early 1800s and centers on two prodigies who are brought together by music, and drawn apart because of their aspirations. The novel focuses on music, which sits outside of words.
"I think I've had the feeling both times after my children's death that words often fall short, and falling short doesn't mean not succeeding, falling short doesn't mean failing," she says. "But when I start a new project, I would like a subject [where] words naturally fall short. So music is that choice."
Li grew up in China and served a year in the Chinese military before coming to the U.S. to study immunology. She eventually left her Ph.D. program to become a writer. Li is now a professor in the creative writing program at Princeton University.
Interview highlights
On the decision to set Music Against the Night in a different time period
I was in the middle of the novel when James died. This is a novel far from my usual interests or concerns, and the reason I think I went back to history is I would like to live again through history, through historical figures, through my characters living in the late 18th and early 19th century. ... I'm making the past into a new now for myself and possibly for my readers.
On how playing piano connects to her grief
I began my piano lessons at the end of 2023, purely to get to know how to play the piano. And James died in February 2024, so two months into my piano lessons he died, and it occurred to me that piano or music is a good way for me to count time — because music is about time. It's about counting the measure, counting the rhythm. And also music is about ... be[ing] engaged with something else. You can sit in your sadness all day long, do nothing, or crying. Or, like me, I could just sit there and just play the same drill again, and again, as a way to know I was, in a way, staying in touch with the world. ...
I'm not a concert pianist, but somehow I find it liberating and healthy to do something that you absolutely love but cannot do well. Every time I go to my piano lesson, I'm so intimidated. I'm sweating because I just can't do it. I can hear other people do it, I cannot do it myself. But I think that's, again, acknowledging the limit of my capacity.
On raising two gifted children
Both my children could be called prodigies, but James, my younger son, especially was extraordinarily odd and brilliant. ... We were greatly baffled. I remember he was 5 or 6, he said, "Mommy, you will never see the world. I see it full of dots and squiggly lines." And that again was a strange perception of the world [that] we adults did not have access to. …
What is the responsibility or the difficulty of bringing up a child [who is] very brilliant? … Some people would say, well, you really have to train him to be the next Einstein, but we did not want him to be the next Einstein, we want him to be a normal, happy boy living in an ordinary life.
On her son Vincent
He was a brilliant painter and we still have all his paintings around the house. He was an oboist and when he wanted to learn the oboe, the oboe teacher said he was a bit young, because he was 8 when he want to learn oboe, but he was certain. ... [He had] started on the piano and he could articulate that piano was not his instrument. He wanted to play the oboe. But mostly, he wrote beautiful poetry. He was a great poet. And he was a greater reader. I wouldn't call him an outlier, as James was, but he was brilliant and fun and interesting.
On struggling with suicidal ideation
Sometimes I think people have all sort of thoughts about or against people who have chosen suicide, and people who've chosen or attempted suicide are often called selfish. But my experience is oftentimes people [are] in great pain, whether it's great mental pain or great physical pain. And sometimes people in deep depression cannot tell the difference between mental pain and physical pain, because everything together is a great kind of suffering. I think it's not that people who experience that kind of suicidal urge, it's not that they want to die or they want [to] use this to hurt other people.
On becoming a writer
I was born with innate curiosity and also sensitivity to things that did not quite make sense. So I grew up in China. And for instance, when I was little, all the adults would say, since you're a child, you have no right to decide who you want to be or what you want to do. And my mother even had a saying, something along the [lines] that an adult decides and the child follows. I was quite young, you know, 4 or 5. I just couldn't make sense of all of these teachings because I thought I was as capable of thinking as the adults, and why did I have to follow them? So I think that sort of sensitivity to things that are very, very nonsensical, I think maybe that's one thing that made me into a writer.
Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez Wisler produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

Taiwan plans to buy liquefied natural gas from Alaska pipeline project
Taiwan planned to buy liquefied natural gas from a U.S. project after extraction and could invest up to $4.4 billion in it
TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan planned to buy 6 million metric tons (6.6 million U.S. tons) of liquefied natural gas annually from a U.S. project after extraction and could invest up to $4.4 billion in it, its economic affairs ministry said Wednesday, in what U.S. President Donald Trump touted as “one of the biggest deals ever made.”
The United States is Taiwan’s main informal supporter and arms provider in the face of increased military threats by China, which sees the island as its own breakaway province, to be annexed by force if necessary. The details of the natural gas purchase plan came as Taiwan awaited a $14 billion arms sales package from the U.S.
Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs said in a statement that state-owned oil and gas firm CPC Corporation signed a letter of intent in March 2025 on the natural gas project in Alaska, and the company and the U.S. side have made significant progress after more than a year of negotiations and evaluation.
Under the current plan, the annual purchase and participation in the Alaska project development, with an estimated maximum investment of $4.4 billion, are part of the cooperation areas, the ministry said. If the project proceeds smoothly as scheduled, it is expected to start supporting the island's natural gas supply in 2032 at the earliest, it said.
Approaches such as long-term energy procurement and project investment would help diversify natural gas supply, enhance flexibility and deepen Taiwan-U.S. cooperation, the ministry said.
It stressed that the cooperation would would be conducted on the principles of mutual benefit and professional, while CPC Corp would continue to coordinate with the U.S. side. The specific investment arrangements, shareholding ratios and related terms would be handled in accordance with subsequent negotiations between both sides and commercial contract procedures, it added.
At a political rally in Alaska on Tuesday, Trump hailed Taiwan's planned purchase from the proposed mega-gas project — an 807-mile (1,300-kilometer) pipeline connecting Alaska’s North Slope to a liquefied natural gas export terminal in the southern part of the state.
“Taiwan has just agreed to buy 30% of the gas coming off the pipeline for the next 20 years,” Trump said. “That guarantees success. It’s one of the biggest commitments in history for anything. It’s one of the biggest deals ever made.”
The statement from Taiwan did not specify how many years it has committed in the plan.
Trump had similarly touted a $54 billion investment from South Korea in the Alaska pipeline. But South Korean officials were more cautious, saying they needed to assess the project’s commercial viability before committing to the investment.
Maintaining a good relationship with the U.S. is important to Taiwan, which faced growing military and diplomatic pressure from Beijing.
China has been pressing Trump to halt arms sales to Taiwan. After his summit in May with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Beijing, a record-breaking $14 billion arms sales package to Taiwan was stalled. Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China.
Washington approved another $11 billion package for Taiwan in December.
China and Taiwan have been governed separately since 1949, when a civil war brought the Communist Party to power in Beijing. Defeated Nationalist Party forces fled to Taiwan. The island has operated with its own government since then.

During my 10+ years of clinical experience in various States and with numerous patient populations, I have seen that dental anxiety is a constant challenge. I have seen this phenomenon in children clutching their parents’ hands before their first cleaning and in accomplished professionals quietly cancelling appointment after appointment in the hope that the problem will somehow resolve itself.
It doesn’t.
In my experience, the longer you leave a fear unchecked, the greater the clinical and human cost becomes. Dental anxiety is not a moral failing. This is a well-documented psychological response—and one with important, measurable public health consequences.
How severe is it?
Roughly a third of people have significant dental anxiety, and roughly a tenth have a clinical phobia. That’s not a little footnote. That means a lot of the population is actively avoiding or delaying care that could prevent serious disease. The downstream consequences of this avoidance are visible daily in my clinical work: infections tolerated for months, decay advanced far beyond what early intervention would have required, and patients presenting with pain that could have been prevented years ago.
Knowing where it starts
Dental anxiety typically has a definite source. A painful or poorly done procedure in childhood can be a source of dental anxiety. A provider who was in a hurry or didn’t tell the patient what was happening. The specific sensory environment of a dental office—the sounds, the smells, and the physical vulnerability of lying back with your mouth open—can leave powerful imprints, especially in young patients. That memory is not just wiped out; it impacts behaviour for decades. For some, it’s not just one event but an accumulation. Years of avoidance layered on top of embarrassment about how their teeth look now, and a fear of judgment prevents them from asking for help. This cycle of shame avoidance is one of the hardest patterns I see clinically. When these patients do come in, they need much more intervention than if they had come in sooner, and this becomes an instance of the very fear that kept them away.
The health price of avoidance
Research literature teaches us, that oral health is not an island. Untreated dental disease is a chronic inflammatory load on the body. It has been linked to cardiovascular risk, dysregulated blood sugar, and impaired immune function. When a patient avoids dental care for years, it is not just their smile that is at risk; they are carrying a preventable health load that will rise elsewhere in time.
In addition to the system effects, the impact on quality of life is immediate and real. A toothache interferes with sleep. It impacts nutrition, concentration, and the ability to speak with confidence. These are not trivial consequences; they affect how people show up in their professional and personal lives every day.
What works in practice
The most significant change I’ve made in my practice is making communication a priority before any procedure begins. When patients feel informed and in control, it greatly reduces their dental anxiety. A stop signal—a raised hand that stops everything instantly—can alter the psychological dynamic in the room. It shifts the patient from passive recipient to active participant, and that shift matters enormously. I also allow extra time for anxious patients. The problem is not that procedures take longer, but that rushing them increases anxiety. I explain everything before it happens, check in frequently, and never minimise what a patient is feeling. These should not be luxury accommodations; they should be routine parts of effective care.
For patients with more severe anxiety, pharmacological support is appropriate. Nitrous oxide is safe, effective, and rapidly reversible. There are also oral sedation choices if needed. These are clinical tools, not last resorts, and patients should feel comfortable asking about them.
A message to patients
If fear has kept you from the dentist, remember you are not alone, and you are not too far gone to be helped. What I ask of patients in this situation is one small step—not a treatment plan, not a procedure, simply a conversation. Come in and tell us about your nervousness. A good provider is a good listener and will start there. There is no need to be afraid of the dental chair. With the right approach, it can be a place where you take difficult things and make them manageable—and where the relief on the other side is worth it.
(Dr. Sowjanya Gunukula is a U.S.-licensed dentist with international training who focuses on preventive and evidence-based oral healthcare and contributes to advancing community and public health dentistry. sowji.gunukula@gmail.com)

East Bengal FC let a promising start slip through its fingers as it squandered a twice-earned lead before going down 2-3 against Iraqi side Al-Shorta in its second Group D outing of the AFC Champions League Two at the Salt Lake Stadium here on Tuesday.
David Lalhansanga Hmar struck twice in a lively first half to put the host in the driving seat, but Al-Shorta hit back with two quick goals after the break to turn the contest on its head. Despite being reduced to 10 men in the 76th minute, the visitors held firm to leave East Bengal ruing a string of missed chances.
David opened the scoring in the seventh minute with a superb piece of opportunism. The East Bengal forward brought down Hardik Bhatt’s centre while shielding an Al-Shorta defender, swivelled sharply and fired home with a clinical left-footed finish.
The East Bengal lead lasted only seven minutes as Ahmed Yahya rose to meet a corner in the 14th minute and headed home to restore parity. East Bengal had less of the ball but looked dangerous on the counter attacks, troubling the Iraqi side with its direct attacking play. The host registered 10 shots, of which seven were on target, while Al-Shorta managed just one effort on target in the first half.
East Bengal vs Al Shorta - As it happened
The Red and Gold brigade reclaimed the lead four minutes before the break. Daniel Ramirez’s free-kick was parried by goalkeeper Jalal Hassan, but Basim Rashid kept the move alive near the goal line with a clever back-heel. David was on hand to finish from close range, completing his brace and sending the home crowd into celebration.
David had two more opportunities before half-time to complete a hat-trick, but failed to convert either. Those misses would come back to haunt East Bengal after the break.
Al-Shorta emerged with renewed purpose after the restart and levelled the scores through Hussein Al-Saedi in the 51st minute before Kingsley Kuku struck again two minutes later, heading home a corner delivered by Argentine substitute Cristian Barco.
Suddenly, East Bengal was chasing the game. The host came agonisingly close to restoring parity in the 66th minute but Hassan came in the way again as he first saved Ramirez’s effort from inside the box and reacted swiftly to deny Edmund Lalrindika on the rebound. The goalkeeper’s double intervention proved crucial as Al-Shorta clung to the slender advantage.
The visitor was reduced to 10 men in the 76th minute when defender Abdoul Magid Boubacar was sent off after receiving his second yellow card. Gaining the numerical advantage, East Bengal threw men forward in search of an equaliser. However, Al-Shorta’s defence stood its ground, frustrating the home side until the final whistle.

Surendra Singh Choudhary, the 20-year-old known online as Bittu Tabahi, who drew widespread attention for cleaning the Ajnar River in Madhya Pradesh largely on his own, shared a disappointing update about the river on his Instagram account on Tuesday. In a video, Tabahi showed the current condition of the Ajnar River in Rajgarh district, saying that his eight months of hard work had been wasted. He highlighted a disappointing contrast with its condition a few weeks ago, when the river was clean. As of Tuesday, it was once again covered with plastic bags and garbage. Tabahi, who earned recognition last month from many people, including those far beyond his town, has consistently drawn attention to the recurring problem of river pollution and the lack of responsibility among citizens. Over two days, he shared two videos highlighting the river's dire condition. These videos came weeks after he shared a video showing the clean banks of the Ajnar River. Tabahi spent almost eight months cleaning the river and pulled tonnes of garbage from it, without any support from the authorities or fancy equipment. However, after seeing the river polluted again, he resumed cleaning it and pulled out trash bags, one at a time. In his video, he highlighted that although he is not a strong swimmer, he is cautiously continuing his efforts to clean the Ajnar River. He also asked people to share suggestions that would help him remove garbage from the river more swiftly and efficiently. Following Tabahi’s video, several people praised his efforts on social media and applauded him for his courage in cleaning the river again. While one user wrote, “That's an awful amount of waste floating in the water beneath that bridge! It must be frustrating to face this every time, but please don't give up. Your hard work deserves so much appreciation,” another offered advice, suggesting that he wear appropriate clothing for this type of cleaning, including special boots and special pants. A third user highlighted the root cause of the problem: “Talk to the Municipal Corporation and get a fine imposed for dumping garbage here. Otherwise, this will keep happening.” A resident of Biaora in Madhya Pradesh’s Rajgarh district, Choudhary shares videos of his cleanup efforts on Instagram, recording how he removes plastic, algae and other waste from the Ajnar River. Reports say he began the initiative in January this year and has cleared accumulated garbage from stretches of the river. Digital content creator KR Talks claimed that Choudhary spent approximately ₹30,000 on the work. He previously received appreciation from industrialist Anand Mahindra and also received a job offer from Boyan Slat, founder and CEO of the Netherlands-based environmental organisation ‘The Ocean Cleanup’. NEW DELHI: NCP(SP) spokesperson Anish Gawande sharply criticised the arrest of CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, calling the preventive arrest 'bizarre'. Gawande also said Rahul Gandhi had asked the INDIA bloc to be ready at 24 hours’ notice for further protests, as the bloc seeks Supreme Court intervention over the arrests and other concerns related to the Election Commission.He questioned the trespassing FIR against them and asked Bihar chief minister Nitish Kumar whether he supported the action against young protesters at Jantar Mantar.
“This preventive arrest is bizarre. What is the actual complaint? Trespassing, filed by the JD(U)?” Gawande said, calling it a “sad day for the JD(U) and an even sadder day for Indian democracy”.
Das and Ranka were detained early Tuesday after allegedly breaching barricades and entering Jantar Mantar, recently denotified as a designated protest site, while raising slogans demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The police case includes charges of trespassing, violating prohibitory orders, breaching a peace bond and obstructing a public servant.Gawande invoked Nitish Kumar’s background in student politics and the JP movement, asking whether the Bihar chief minister supported the FIR against young people who, he said, were trying to wave the national flag at Jantar Mantar.
He also said the INDIA bloc had been asked by leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi to remain ready at 24 hours’ notice for further protests.
The bloc expects the Supreme Court to address what Gawande described as an illegal FIR, alleged police brutality and concerns over the functioning of the Election Commission, including Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.The arrest follows protests by CJP and other organisations over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. On October 11, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar designated Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground as venues for demonstrations, removing Jantar Mantar from the list of approved protest sites. CJP has argued that shifting protests away from the capital’s political centre reduces the visibility of dissent.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will be on a five-day visit to India and Uzbekistan from Saturday, October 17 to Wednesday, October 22. During his visit, Rubio will go to Mumbai and Jamnagar in India, and Samarkand in Uzbekistan. The White House released his travel schedule and agenda for his visit to the two countries in a statement on Tuesday. Marco Rubio will come to India after visiting Samarkand, Uzbekistan. This will be Rubio's second official visit this year. He last travelled to the country in May, when he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and participated in a Quad foreign ministers’ meeting. Quick answers to key questions Rubio is scheduled to visit India from October 17 to 22 as part of a five-day trip to India and Uzbekistan. In India, he will visit Mumbai and Jamnagar; the exact date of his arrival in India has not been confirmed. Rubio is expected to meet senior Indian government officials to discuss the strategic partnership, regional and global issues, and prospects for greater energy cooperation. He will also meet business leaders to promote commercial investment and economic cooperation. The visit comes as India and the US continue to negotiate a proposed trade agreement amid changing US tariff policies. It is also an opportunity to discuss energy cooperation and broader strategic and economic ties. The articles do not say that the visit will finalise the deal. Negotiations remain active, but the agreement has not been concluded, and changing circumstances and tariff policies have prompted further discussions. The exact date of Rubio's arrival in India is not confirmed yet. There's no comment from the Indian side so far. Rubio's visit to India holds significance in the wake of the stalled India-US trade deal, the framework of which was revealed in February this year. Since then, US President's tariff dynamics have changed; the President extended $100,000 H-1B visa fee, which would likely impact several India aspirants, and suspended US's permanent labour certification programme or PERM for several technology giants and IT outsourcing companies, including Microsoft, Infosys, Cognizant, Tata, Wipro, HCL Technologies, Capgemini and Adobe. The programme is an important step in the employment-based green-card process for many foreign workers. According to White House statement, Rubio will meet with senior government officials "to strengthen the US-India strategic partnership, exchange views on regional and global dynamics, and discuss prospects for enhanced energy cooperation." Secretary Rubio will also meet with business leaders to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation. The White House's press note came as Indian and American officials indicated earlier this month that long-running efforts to finalise a bilateral trade agreement have stalled again. Earlier, in October, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said the US and India announced in February that they had reached a framework for an interim trade agreement, but circumstances have changed, and the pact will be finalised accordingly. "USA [trade pact] February me announce hua. Thodi paristhitiyan badli hain, usko abhi madde nazar rakhte hue final hoga. [It was announced in February. Some circumstances have changed; the final decision will be made keeping that in mind]," Goyal was quoted by PTI as saying while addressing members of industry chamber PHDCCI. The minister did not elaborate about those circumstances, but the changing tariff landscape in the US has led to further negotiations about the first phase of bilateral trade agreement (BTA) between India and the US. India is seeking lower tariffs for its goods than its competitors in the American markets. The latest flashpoint with Washington comes after the suspension of some of India’s biggest IT services businesses as well as Microsoft Corp. and Adobe Inc. from a longstanding immigration initiative as part of a crackdown on alleged abuse of the H-1B worker visa system. Vice President JD Vance urged US firms to hire more US workers and to “stop importing an indentured servant to do a job that an American worker would happily do.” The Ministry of External Affairs branded the comments “deeply offensive.” Despite tensions over the US-India trade deal, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said India’s ties with the US are “very good." "Of course, it is already very good. I don’t see any problem as we speak,” Goyal was quoted by Bloomberg as saying on Wednesday at the New Economy Forum in New Delhi. He was responding to a question on whether India’s relationship with the US would improve under a different administration. “The relationship with the US that India enjoys is very substantive, is very consequential for the world, being two large democracies,” the minister said during a panel discussion. Goyal attempted to allay concerns that relations were again on a downward trajectory. “The United States and India continue to have a very close relationship, and we continue to engage with them on so many tracks,” including in defense, working toward ensuring open supply chains on technology, on goods, on services. He added, "One must bear in mind that we have, it's not only about trade, which of course they are our largest trading partner and I think will continue to be in the years to come. And by and large, I don't see any problem in any agreements also with the United States." "It's about trade, it's about defence partnership, it's our technology partnership, it's our critical minerals partnership, it's our people-to-people engagement," Goyal was quoted by PTI as saying at Bloomberg New Economy event. In Uzbekistan, Rubio will participate in the C5+1 Ministerial "to highlight how strategic cooperation through this diplomatic platform promotes a more peaceful and prosperous future for the United States and the countries of Central Asia." In Uzbekistan, Rubio will also participate in bilateral engagements with senior officials from all C5 countries – Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and the Kyrgyz Republic. PSG's Luis Enrique hopes Man City avoid sanctions
- Published
Paris St-Germain boss Luis Enrique says he was surprised to learn Manchester City had been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules and hopes the club can avoid sanctions.
City host European champions PSG in the Champions League on Wednesday (20:00 BST) - their first home match since being found guilty of the majority of 115 charges.
"There is a lot of noise around Manchester City and there is often noise around big clubs," said Enrique when asked about City's guilty verdict at a news conference at Etihad Stadium on Tuesday.
"We just have to wait and see what the final decision will be. I hope everything works out well for Manchester City because I think what they have done on the pitch has been incredible over the last few years and they certainly deserved to win on the pitch all the trophies they have won.
"Now we have to wait to see what the authorities decide or the judge is going to say."
An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.
City insist they are innocent and have appealed.
Luis Enrique added: "The first thing that you hear, it is a surprise, but we need to respect the process and wait for the final decision.
"The authorities are responsible for making these decisions. But speaking only about football, they deserved those trophies. I love their football. Beyond that, we have to wait for the decision.
"The trophies you win on the pitch remain on the pitch. They deserved to win that and I hope they can avoid the sanction. But we have to wait."

I'm petite, have a small frame, and have never had to struggle with weight issues. 
I regularly went to the gym six days a week, and have done so for years taking a combination of strength training and boot camp-style classes in addition to walking. Despite my efforts, I started adding on weight — just over 10 pounds in about 24 months.
I didn't know why or what to do about about the weight gain. I was working out almost every day, but I felt exhausted and defeated. Others suggested I turn to medication. "Don't stress, just get on a GLP-1, and if your doctor won't give it to you, just grab it online," one friend told me.
My BMI wasn't high enough for my doctor to prescribe medication, and I didn't want to override my provider's advice. But despite all of my effort, I wasn't seeing the results I wanted.
I was bored at the gym
Then, during a gym class, I realized I had become lazy. I was picking up the easiest weights and would go through the motions, never pushing myself too hard during workouts. The repetitive movements were just so boring.
After that class, I tried to think of an activity that might bring me more joy. Wasn't there something else that could be more fun? That's when I decided to take more dance classes, instead of just the one I was already taking on Saturdays.
I was hesitant to dance like I used to years ago
I was a danced into high school, but I had to leave the program because of difficulties at home.
I always felt sadness and disappointment about quitting. I had continued dancing on and off as an adult, but I had never really returned to it in a meaningful way. I thought about how much I loved to dance as a little girl, grinning ear to ear even when I forgot all the steps. Research has shown that the surprising benefits of dance extend beyond physical fitness.
Now I take four to five dance classes a week, a combination of modern, and West African.
It's fun and doesn't feel like the same drag that the gym was to me. And I finally lost those stubborn pounds I had gained. When I take classes every week, I mix up levels to keep challenging myself and track my progress. Dance has also given me a community where we hold one another accountable and empower one another as we cheer one another on.
More on workout routines
Dance was the true exercise I really needed
Returning to dance has helped me shed those few extra pounds, but it has also helped me connect to a part of me that is more accepting of myself and others. I'm happier and healthier than I've been in years, and no longer associate something I love with failure. 
I've learned that the workout that keeps me coming back is the one I enjoy, and it's never too late to try again.

Creating question papers at the last-minute can curb incentive to leak, says Nadan Nilekani
Nandan Nilekani also suggested expanding the computer-based testing (CBT) infrastructure across the country.
Generating examination papers at the last minute from a “massive question bank” will eliminate the “economic incentive” behind paper leaks, Infosys chairman and head of the high-powered task force (HPTF) on examination reforms Nandan Nilekani said on Tuesday. He also suggested expanding the computer-based testing (CBT) infrastructure across the country.
“The moment you have a question paper then that creates an economic incentive for that to be sold. So the way to do that is to really have a massive bank of questions and only at the last minute generate the question paper for that day and therefore then the question of having a question paper goes away and there is no economic incentive for that,” he said while addressing the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi.
Also Read I Government, NTA officials may not be named in CBI charge sheet over NEET-UG paper leak
To be sure, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), in its first charge sheet filed in a Delhi court in May in the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak case, said question papers for the May 3 examination were sold and purchased by the accused for amounts ranging from ₹25,000 to ₹25 lakh.
Six-member task force
Nilekani added that expanding the network of testing locations was another priority. “We have 150,000 locations (of CBT centres) where a young boy or girl can take a test that needs to be expanded. So I think these are all systemic issues, which we will address in our committee,” he said.
When asked if he could envision a future where AI spontaneously creates examination papers on the actual day of the test, Nilekani responded with affirmation. He further said that using technology and looking at the root causes of exam leaks and irregularities systematically could solve the problem. “They are solvable issues.”
The government-appointed six-member HPTF, constituted on July 27 with a three-month mandate, was set up after the cancellation of NEET-UG 2026 on May 12 by National Testing Agency (NTA). At least 120 questions in a guess paper — a compilation of suggested questions based on previous trends and patterns — were found to match the May 3 examination paper, triggering widespread protests and eventually the resignation of then education minister Dharmendra Pradhan on July 25.
An October 5 affidavit filed by the Department of Personnel and Training in the Supreme Court said the panel had held about 18 meetings and more than 40 consultations including one with Union health ministry on whose behalf NTA conducts the test for admission to UG medical courses, and remained “on track” to submit its report within the prescribed timeframe.
The debate over shifting NEET-UG from pen-and-paper testing (PPT) to CBT has, however, exposed significant infrastructure and policy hurdles.
Also Read I 'Why do we need a question paper': Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani on ways to combat exam leaks in India
More than 2.2 million candidates registered for the 2026 examination currently held in pen and paper mode, requiring question papers to be printed, packed, transported under security, stored in vaults and distributed to examination centres. The lengthy supply chain, involving printers, transporters, storage facilities, centre coordinators and invigilators, creates multiple potential vulnerabilities for paper leak.
In CBT, encrypted questions are electronically distributed to examination infrastructure under strict access controls, reducing dependence on physical transportation. The format is already used for JEE-Main, CUET and UGC-NET.

Trump’s DOJ threatens to block California votes in explosive pre-election showdown
The Justice Department on Tuesday gave California officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action

The Department of Justice has given California authorities 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action, according to a letter Reuters reviewed, marking an unprecedented attempt to find evidence of voter fraud ahead of next month's elections.
The letter, authored by acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter and sent to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, says federal officials gave Los Angeles County administrators a "password-protected thumb drive" containing the names of individuals the government "believes are likely noncitizens" who were issued mail-in ballots.
The directive requires the state to withhold ballots from those named on the list until it can verify their citizenship status. Flagged voters who have already received ballots must have their submissions "segregated" once returned, and ballots already submitted should not be counted "until citizenship has been determined," the letter dictates.
Federal authorities "will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," the letter warns, if state officials fail to follow these instructions.
"Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes," McCotter wrote in the communication.
The ultimatum reflects a heightened effort by the Trump administration to pressure states over alleged voting by non-citizens, signaling that the Justice Department may be prepared to challenge ballots in the weeks before the November 3 election, when Republicans will be defending narrow congressional majorities.
Justice Department spokeswoman Kiersten Pels confirmed the letter's existence in a statement to Reuters, stating: "The department will take all necessary legal action to protect election integrity and ensure compliance with federal law."
Spokespersons for the White House and the California secretary of state's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Under President Donald Trump, the Justice Department has repeatedly asserted that voting by noncitizens is a widespread problem, despite numerous studies demonstrating that the practice is rare.
A Reuters review in September found that while software glitches and clerical errors may have added more than 30,000 noncitizens to state voter rolls since 2000, it remained unclear how many had actually cast ballots.
Experts emphasized that these figures were far too small relative to the nation's 170 million registered voters to influence election outcomes.
In July, the Justice Department dispatched letters to chief election officials across all 50 states, warning of potential criminal prosecution if they knowingly permitted noncitizens to vote or remain on voter rolls.
The department's Civil Rights Division has requested nonpublic voter information, including birth dates and Social Security numbers, from nearly every state as part of its effort to identify noncitizens. It has filed lawsuits against 30 states led by both Democrats and Republicans that refused to release their rolls, losing 26 of those cases.
Reuters reported last month that the Department of Homeland Security was utilizing a commercial data broker to access sensitive voter details not included in public records, a practice that officials and experts warned could result in eligible citizens being mistakenly identified as illegal voters and potentially detained.
Federal prosecutors have also stepped up prosecutions against noncitizens accused of registering fraudulently or voting in previous elections, announcing 16 new criminal cases on Monday.
Officials in Democratic-led California have clashed for months with the Trump administration over federal efforts to intervene in state voting procedures based on allegations of voter fraud.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin informed California officials on July 16 that federal authorities believed noncitizens were present on the state's voting rolls, according to the letter.

Kipchoge, 41, breaks course record at Melbourne Marathon
- Published
Two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge says "his body is still peaking" after winning the Melbourne Marathon in a course record time at the age of 41.
The Kenyan crossed the line in two hours nine minutes 10 seconds for his 17th career win over the distance and first since the Berlin Marathon in 2023.
"I believe that my body is still peaking - still able to compete with the next generation," Kipchoge said.
"The oldest athlete is still competing but I am happy to run with the Gen Zs."
The course was partly raced along the Australian Formula One track at Albert Park and finished inside the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG).
"On the course, it was really wonderful, I enjoyed seeing people standing, cheering, and shouting my name," added Kipchoge, who slowed down inside the MCG to wave to the fans.
"It was actually different - running on a beautiful course, but also running on the Formula One track, and above all else, finishing on a cricket ground.
"It makes me proud to run with the younger generation and inspire the running community in Melbourne."
Australian Thomas do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35, with compatriot Reece Edwards third.
New Zealand's Camille French won the women's race in 2:28:25, followed by Australian Sinead Diver and Nichola Sheridan of Ireland.
The Melbourne Marathon was the third leg on Kipchoge's world tour, on which he hopes to complete a marathon on all seven continents, including Antarctica, over two years.
Each marathon will raise funds for the Eliud Kipchoge Foundation, which focuses on education, environmental sustainability and health.
Kipchoge is considered one of the greatest long-distance runners of all time, winning two Olympic marathon golds, plus a silver and bronze over 5000m.
His honours also include a world title, 12 World Marathon Major victories and two official world records.
In 2019 he became the first person to break the two-hour marathon barrier under special conditions in Vienna, clocking an unofficial time of one hour 59 minutes 40 seconds.

Even as the Centre informed the Supreme Court on Monday (October 12, 2026) that it had decided to cap trade margins at 30% for non-scheduled cancer drugs, the court questioned why the benefit of such price regulation should be confined to cancer drugs and not extended to other essential medicines and medical products.
The development comes after a Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta expressed concern over stark disparities between the price to retailer (PTR) and the maximum retail price (MRP) of certain medicines, particularly cancer drugs, with mark-ups in some instances soaring to 1,000%. The Bench had flagged that such exorbitant mark-ups constituted “broad daylight dacoity” and placed an enormous financial burden on patients.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, informed the Bench that the proposed 30% trade-margin cap would cover both patented and non-patented cancer medicines, with an expert committee headed by the Director General of Health Services tasked with identifying the drugs to be brought within its ambit. The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) will examine the committee’s recommendations before issuing a price notification to implement the cap.
The Bench, however, said that while the intervention was commendable, it was inadequate, and questioned why other medicines and medical devices could not also be brought within the 16% retailer margin prescribed under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013.
“This is just the tip of the iceberg... this has come around only because of the unduly hard observations we made during earlier hearings. What about other drugs,” the Bench asked.
The top court was hearing petitions filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha seeking stricter enforcement of price controls under the DPCO to curb disproportionate margins across the pharmaceutical supply chain.
Justice Mehta drew attention to steep markups on medical devices and consumables, pointing out that an India-made cardiac stent costing around ₹5,000 was being sold by hospitals for more than ₹25,000. He cited the example of a saline drip line carrying an MRP of ₹11 being sold for ₹270.
“We understand that there are transportation costs, raw material costs, R&D costs and other ancillary costs, but all these are included in the MRP. What is the logic behind allowing them to sell at 400 times the actual cost? How can you allow this? What is the benefit for the patients?” the Bench observed.
‘Balance in pricing’
Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, also appearing for the Centre, cautioned against a uniform cap across medicines, arguing that low-value products often required higher margins to remain commercially viable for retailers. Excessive regulation, she said, could discourage retailers from stocking such medicines and affect their availability, particularly in rural areas.
Ms. Bhati stressed the need to preserve some room for market forces rather than subject the entire pharmaceutical sector to price controls.
“Higher margins in such cases are important for ensuring the availability of such medicines to consumers… Our concern is that there has to be a balance in pricing. There has to be some level of market play available for drugs. We do not want to control the entire ecosystem of drugs. The policy was framed with the outlook that there should be intervention only when necessary,” she submitted.
The Bench, however, was not persuaded, observing that ensuring the availability of price-controlled medicines was the government’s responsibility.
“If the DPCO -approved medicines do not reach customers, then it is the duty of the government to ensure it reaches [sic] the patient. The actual dispute is over which medicines should be on the DPCO-controlled list and which should not,” Justice Mehta observed.
Accordingly, the Bench gave the Centre until October 27 to work out the modalities for capping medicine prices, when the matter will be heard next.
Centre’s affidavit
The Centre, in its 551-page affidavit, said the proposed trade-margin rationalisation (TMR) was expected to reduce the MRP of anti-cancer drugs by 20% to 70%, translating into estimated annual savings of around ₹2,500 crore. It said the measure would reduce patients’ out-of-pocket expenditure and improve the affordability and accessibility of cancer medicines, while retaining a 30% trade margin for the distribution chain.
The Centre cited a similar intervention by the NPPA in 2019, when a 30% trade-margin cap was imposed at the first point of sale on 42 select non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines. The margin was based on an industry-practice assumption of 10% for distributors and 20% for retailers.
The measure, it said, led to a substantial reduction in the MRP of 526 brands and annual savings of around ₹984 crore for patients, based on information furnished by pharmaceutical companies. The Centre said the 2019 exercise provided a policy and operational precedent for extending trade-margin rationalisation to a wider range of non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines.
Detailing the existing price-control mechanism, the Centre said the ceiling price of medicines listed in Schedule I of the DPCO is determined by taking the simple average of the price to retailer of brands and generic versions with a market share of at least 1%, and adding a 16% margin.
“The ceiling price so fixed becomes the MRP, i.e., the price above which the drug cannot be sold in the market. However, the manufacturer is at liberty to give an appropriate margin to the wholesaler and the retailer within the ceiling price,” it said, adding that ceiling prices had so far been fixed for 935 formulations.
For non-scheduled formulations, manufacturers are free to determine the initial launch price, subject to the NPPA’s regulation of subsequent price increases. The Centre said competition in the pharmaceutical market generally acted as a restraint against arbitrary pricing.
