For the first time in medical and legal history, a prisoner has “survived a complete execution attempt in the U.S.” According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Christa Pike’s failed execution was “the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era (since 1976). There is no precedent.” This game-changing bioethics case may even end lethal injection.
About 7,000 people were executed in the U.S. between 1900 and 1976, and 1,683 people after 1976. Ultimately, since 1900, only 0.6% (55) have been women. Pike is now the second woman on death row the U.S. Supreme Court declined to rescue from a botched execution.
On June 18, 1953, the controversial case of accused spy Ethel Rosenberg, who had two small children, also came before the Supreme Court. It overturned her stay of execution. The following day, on June 19, 1953, the electric chair execution of Rosenberg failed; the settings were not properly adjusted for a woman of Rosenberg’s size, and she did not die after the first round of electrocution.
A doctor examined her and informed the state she was not dead and that they needed to electrocute her a second time. The report from United Press International and The New York Times described the debacle and the role of two physicians involved who “ordered” more electrocution. According to Rosenberg’s biographer, “she was removed from the electric chair after three charges, only for it to be discovered her heart was still beating, so, gruesomely, she had to be strapped back into it.”
Nineteen years later, in 1972, after five more women were executed without incident in the U.S., the Supreme Court of California ruled the death penalty unconstitutional in People v. Anderson, which led to the commutation of all California death sentences to life sentences. This included three of the women involved in the brutal Manson murders — Susan Atkins, Patricia Krenwinkel, and Leslie Van Houten — all scheduled to be gassed. That same year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that capital punishment violated the Eighth Amendment in Furman v. Georgia.
In response to the Furman ruling, states began to explore more humane methods of execution, which is what led to the current lethal injection protocol, originally pioneered by Oklahoma’s state medical examiner at the time, Jay Chapman in 1977, and later adapted by Jack Kevorkian as a method of “medicide” — an early version of what we now call medical assistance in dying.
In 1976, the U.S. Supreme Court sanctioned state executions again in Gregg v. Georgia because it saw lethal injection as a “sanitized, quasi-clinical procedure” upholding the Eighth Amendment. Lethal injection became the norm when executions restarted in 1977; Ronald Reagan compared it to putting an animal to sleep. On June 11, 2001, Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh was executed using the Chapman protocol. It was even broadcast on a closed-circuit system to survivors and affected families.
But over time, due to a variety of systems issues with obtaining certain medications, the lethal injection protocol has deviated from the standard devised by Chapman.
More importantly, since the lethal injection protocol requires an intravenous line insertion, the person administering it has to be competent in IV infusion. But the people facing execution often have veins that are tricky to access. A disturbing report in 2022 found that more than a third of executions are “botched” because of unskilled personnel.
Since the American Medical Association and the American Nurses Association state that it is unethical for medical providers to participate in any way in executions, state prisons struggle to find skilled personnel to handle lethal injection, resulting in many failed attempts. The case of Lee Hamm, another failed attempt at lethal injection, raised numerous questions about the role of health care providers after a botched procedure.
Just prior to Pike’s planned execution, NPR reported that the opaque Tennessee protocol does involve health care providers, and some are willing to cross ethical lines. Physician Mark Fowler, for instance, was involved in the failed execution case of Tony Carruthers in May.
But the Carruthers case created a bioethics chasm where “dozens of Tennessee medical professionals told the governor that health care professionals shouldn’t help with executions, ever. No matter the method.” Fowler reportedly was involved in Pike’s failed execution as well.
The majority of health care providers maintain either the American Medical Association’s code of ethics or the American Nurses Association’s position. A recent Hastings Center Bioethics Forum essay concludes that lethal injection is unethical, while other bioethicists have suggested that the presence of a health care provider would not only be “lending the prestige of medicine to the execution” but also provide the false impression that lethal injection was being supervised by doctors, and therefore more acceptable.
The Pike case is novel not only because it’s the first time in legal history a prisoner has survived a completed execution procedure resulting in dizzying legal repercussions, but because of the “hot mess” clinical ethics case that has emerged.
When Pike remained alive after the failed procedure, she was rushed to the hospital for lifesaving treatment. What were the “goals of care”? To make her medically stable enough for another attempt at execution? (Tennessee’s Prison Commissioner resigned, and the state has paused executions for the remainder of the year, but not indefinitely.) Per national and local news reports on Oct. 7, Pike initially remained intubated and unconscious as her health care team planned to remove life support in the belief that Pike was progressing to brain death. Pike also remained in restraints (handcuffed and shackled to her bed), which complicated her care.
But then she awoke and spoke, raising new questions about her neurological status. Pike first inquired: “Where am I and who are you?” Her attorneys state: “There is still a lot of cognitive confusion. … She is very aware that the state tried to execute. … She is very aware up to a point.”
Any clinical ethicist would advise at this juncture that Pike may fully regain decision-making capacity and is already showing signs of understanding and appreciation. Patients who are inmates and have decision-making capacity can make all medical decisions, including end of life decisions, but the correctional institution may limit options based on costs. In general, correctional officers should not be involved with inmates’ medical decisions, but health care providers do not have the authority to remove restraints; such decisions reside with the correctional facility.
Bioethicists have been actively debating this case, with consensus that if Pike were deemed to be incapacitated, a court-appointed surrogate decision-maker (someone who makes decisions in the best medical interests of a patient who does not have autonomy) would be necessary since the state — even Tennessee’s Adult Protective Services — would have a conflict of interest. Pike’s biological family has provided insight into her childhood that would also raise questions about authentic surrogacy. Because of Ford v. Wainwright, incapacitated prisoners cannot be executed, so if Pike regains capacity, the legal road is unclear.
As of this writing, it’s impossible to predict Pike’s ultimate prognosis or fate, but the legal and medical issues in the Pike case are on a collision course. Pre-Pike, lethal injection was “passing” as a “death with dignity” medical assistance in dying procedure, which, ironically, is illegal in several death penalty states, including Tennessee. Post-Pike, lethal injection will never be the same. Its procedural flaws have been exposed; it’s the emperor with no clothes because it only “pretends to be medicine.” Of course, there are other forms of execution that actually look like one instead of medicine, as in the case of the planned execution by firing squad of the Fort Hood shooter, which may even be streamed live.
For states that want to continue lethal injection, medical expertise at various points in the process — whether it’s training prison staff, providing medical opinions on “candidacy” for lethal injection, or actually participating — will likely become a requirement that most health care providers will find ethically incompatible with clinical ethics principles of practice. If medical expertise becomes a legal requirement for lethal injection, but no reputable health care provider will participate, then the stigma of participation may effectively end lethal injection as we know it.
M. Sara Rosenthal, Ph.D., is professor and founding director of the University of Kentucky Program for Bioethics and Oncology Ethics Program and chair of the UK HealthCare Ethics Committee.

Afcon move to every four years under review by Caf
- Published
The Africa Cup of Nations could continue to be held every two years, with discussions under way to reverse its proposed switch to a four-year cycle.
Speaking on Friday at a Confederation of African Football (Caf) strategy conference in Cape Verde, president Patrice Motsepe said: "We've discussed it over the last few days.
"We are looking at everything, including having the Afcon coming back every two years. We are very clear, the matter is being reviewed."
The tournament has taken place every two years since 1968, bar a one-year gap between the 2012 and 2013 editions.
However, in December 2025 CAF announced it would shift to being staged every four years after the 2027 Afcon in East Africa and a 2028 edition.
That planned alteration to the schedule had received widespread criticism across the continent.
National associations had raised concerns about the visibility of their teams, the commercial implications and where Africa's biggest competition would sit in the international football calendar.

On October 12, 2026, hackers successfully jailbroke the PlayStation 5 and launched Overdrive, an illegal PS Store with 1,600+ free downloadable PS4 and PS5 games and DLCs. Since Sony announced it would end PS5 physical discs starting in 2028, both players and hackers have tried to get back at the company. Fast forward two days later, and Sony has reportedly taken down the storefront.
According to user Oliver Darko on X, Sony Interactive Entertainment lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter to the hackers behind the successful PS5 jailbreak and Overdrive storefront. As Overdrive appeared on mainstream channels, Sony took notice and shut down the massive storefront on October 14. To give you the bigger picture, before Sony sent the cease-and-desist letter, the company pushed multiple PS5 updates to counter jailbreaks.
Before Overdrive, developer Nathan Fargo released the Relapse public PS5 jailbreak on September 29, 2026, supporting firmware versions 7.00 through 13.60. However, Sony’s firmware 14.00, released earlier on September 16, reportedly patched the vulnerability.

The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals.
Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week.
The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries.
Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs. Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”.
The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU.
Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China.
On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.
Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints.
“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said.
Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too.
Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.”
Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin.
Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”.
The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes.
On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.

A “video recording device” was found in the cabin of a Royal Australian Navy ship in Cairns, the defence department has revealed, just hours after senator Jacqui Lambie alleged in parliament that a camera had been found concealed in a women’s shower on the vessel.
The department confirmed on Wednesday afternoon that a device had been found aboard the HMAS Leeuwin three days earlier. In a statement after Guardian Australia had contacted the department for response to Lambie’s allegations, a spokesperson said police were investigating, but did not reveal further details about where the device was located.
“On 11 October 2026, Defence became aware that a video recording device had been located in the cabin of Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin, while alongside in Cairns, Queensland,” they said.
“The incident was referred to the Joint Military Police Unit and Defence is working with civilian authorities. Defence takes this incident extremely seriously and does not tolerate unacceptable behaviour in any form.”
On Wednesday morning, Lambie – an ADF veteran and advocate for defence personnel – told the Senate that she’d been contacted by a former member of the navy with allegations about a camera being found aboard HMAS Leeuwin.
“The sender told me that concealed cameras have recently been found in the female sailors’ showers facilities on the vessel HMAS Leeuwin, based in Cairns,” she said in the Senate.
“I was also told this had occurred recently and prevented the vessel from sailing while investigations were ongoing. Even more disturbing are claims that footage from these cameras may have been uploaded online before the cameras were discovered.
“How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask Navy.”
Guardian Australia asked the department if any perpetrator had been identified, if the defence force was aware of hidden cameras being found in other navy facilities, and if any such footage from hidden cameras had been found to have been shared online.
The department did not directly answer those questions. In its statement, it said HMAS Leeuwin had “remained alongside to enable the investigation and ensure immediate support was provided to members of the ship’s crew”.
“The welfare of individuals remains Defence’s priority, and support is ongoing. As the matter is currently under investigation and to protect the privacy of the affected individuals, Defence is unable to provide further comment at this time,” it said.
Asked at a subsequent press conference about the incident, Lambie said she was unhappy with the department’s response.
“Defence needs to know this. Your people had a gutful, and if there was abuse going on, they’re now coming to me. OK, I’m right on their tail. Enough is enough. Get control of what is going on in the defence force,” she said.
“What I want to know is, have they gone around on the rest of those boats, the subs, whatever, and had a look and make sure there’s no other cameras? Because we are not sure whether it’s coming from contractors that go on them, or whether it’s come from defence members.”

Women account for 43% of the workforce in India’s Ayush services sector, with their representation crossing 50% in several organised segments, including hospitals, day-care centres, educational institutions and wellness establishments, according to a new assessment of the sector released by the Central government on Thursday (October 8, 2026).
The Ayush Services Sector Report, prepared by the Research and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS) and released on Ayurveda Day 2026, estimates that the sector supports 1.76 million livelihoods across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services.
Women’s representation is highest in spas and wellness resorts, where it exceeds 60%, followed by educational institutions at 58%, day-care centres at 57% and hospitals at 53%, says the report.
The findings come as the Ayush services economy expands beyond traditional clinical practice into wellness, education, preventive health and medical value travel.
16.91% growth
The sector, comprising Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy, was estimated at $36.92 billion in 2024-25. It has registered a compound annual growth rate of 16.91% since 2022-23.
Standalone clinics remain the largest segment, generating an estimated $16.21 billion, or 43.9% of the sector’s revenue. Day-care centres contribute another $10.13 billion. Together, the two segments account for more than 70% of the sector’s revenue.
“More than one million livelihoods are concentrated in local and standalone clinics, underlining the sector’s employment footprint across urban and rural areas,’’ says the report.
The wellness segment has recorded a 21.29% compound annual growth rate, while yoga centres registered about 75% growth in revenue over two years, according to the assessment.
Ayurveda remains the largest individual Ayush system, accounting for $17.73 billion, or about 48% of the total services revenue.
The sector is also gaining a foothold in medical value travel. Ayush-related medical value travel generated an estimated $1.77 billion in 2024-25. Although international patients account for only around 5% of patient volumes, they contribute an estimated 15-25% of hospital-segment revenue, with therapeutic programmes typically involving stays of five to 11 days.
The assessment projects that the Ayush services economy could expand to between $216 billion and $318 billion by 2047.
Job opportunities
Union Minister of State for Ayush Prataprao Jadhav said the sector’s expansion was creating employment opportunities across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services, while also opening avenues for entrepreneurship and women’s participation.
The report projects further employment opportunities in healthcare delivery, wellness, education, medical travel, research, digital health and allied services as the sector expands.

- Xbox has launched Xbox Labs to make games more accessible through emerging technologies.
- According to CEO Asha Sharma, community efforts to run games in browsers and on unsupported platforms inspired Xbox Labs.
- Sharma said Xbox Labs will build openly, measure success by player engagement and creation, and share its tools with other devs.
After unveiling the Xbox XP division last week, CEO Asha Sharma has announced Xbox Labs, a small team of “game makers, engineers, and scientists” who focus on using new game development tools and AI technology to test out new ideas, make Xbox games more accessible to players, and “turn emerging ideas” into an experience that benefits both the players and developers.
Xbox Labs Will Focus on Browser Gaming, Apple Silicon Support and Mods
According to Xbox’s latest blog, Asha Sharma has created Xbox Labs with Xbox CTO Scott Van Vliet and will apparently “build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.”
Sharma acknowledged the gaming community’s recent efforts to bring classic games to new platforms, including running games in browsers using paid browser tech such as WebAssembly and WebGPU. The GTA 5 browser port is one example, while online game remixes have also gained traction, including a crossover between Marvel’s Spider-Man and Batman: Arkham Knight.
These experiments prompted Sharma to launch Xbox Labs, which aims to revive older and some of the best Xbox games and make game creation more accessible. While she didn’t explicitly mention AI, she highlighted opportunities for players to become creators and co-creators.
Sharma then drew parallels between gaming and AI agent workloads, saying players spend over 72 billion hours playing Xbox games annually on Xbox Series X|S and Xbox Game Pass, five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide, and that combining gaming and software development could make games more accessible.
“These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models,” said Sharma. According to Gamesindustry.biz, an Xbox spokesperson has laid out what Xbox Labs will be focusing on:
- Making existing games playable in the browser
- Bringing games to Apple computers via Apple Silicon support
- Developing and supporting modders
- Expanding multiplayer experiences
This news comes during the company’s “XBOX Reset” restructuring, and Xbox Labs is likely a part of this plan. However, Asha Sharma remains committed to Xbox’s 4Cs and to making great games and hardware, potentially including the Xbox Helix.
Sharma concluded by saying Xbox Labs will explore emerging technologies in game design, potentially opening new possibilities for existing titles without abandoning their current development priorities. Xbox also confirmed it will not use AI explicitly beyond what’s necessary to implement a specific idea.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) on Wednesday filed a supplementary chargesheet in the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test-Undergraduate (NEET-UG) 2026 paper leak case, people familiar with the development said, adding that “this concludes the probe in the leak”.
An additional private individual has been named in the latest report submitted before a Delhi court. Earlier, 13 people, including three subject experts hired by the National Testing Agency (NTA), middlemen and coaching centre representatives, were named in the first charge sheet on July 28.
“No government official has been named,” said an officer.
HT had reported first that CBI has not found any evidence against any government official in the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak.
On May 12, NTA announced the cancellation of the 2026 NEET test after at least 120 questions in a guess paper – a compilation made by subject experts and teachers of suggested questions, based on previous trends and patterns – were found to be common with the NEET exam paper on May 3.
The leak was only detected a week after the exam was conducted, triggering massive protests in Parliament and eventually leading to the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan after millions of young people -- under the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) banner -- hit the streets.

Frederick G. Banting and John J.R. Macleod were awarded the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of insulin, a hormone that regulates blood glucose levels. Their work helped establish insulin as a treatment for diabetes, a disease that, in its severe forms, had often been fatal before insulin therapy became available.
The prize was shared equally. Banting and Macleod were recognised “for the discovery of insulin”. The award acknowledged research conducted at the University of Toronto in the early 1920s, when investigators developed pancreatic extracts that could lower blood sugar in diabetic animals and subsequently demonstrated their therapeutic potential in humans. Charles Best, who worked with Banting, and biochemist James Collip, who helped purify insulin for clinical use, also made important contributions to this work.
Research on pancreas and blood sugar
Diabetes had been linked to the pancreas decades before insulin was isolated. In 1889, researchers Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering demonstrated that removing the pancreas from dogs produced diabetes. Subsequent research established the importance of the islets of Langerhans, clusters of cells within the pancreas, in regulating blood sugar.
The challenge was to identify and extract the substance responsible for this effect. Several researchers attempted to prepare pancreatic extracts, but obtaining a preparation that could be used safely and consistently in patients remained difficult.
Frederick G. Banting was a Canadian physician and surgeon whose interest in diabetes led him to investigate the role of the pancreas in regulating blood glucose. After serving in the First World War, he returned to Canada and worked in medical practice before pursuing research.
John J.R. Macleod was a Scottish-born physician and physiologist who had built his career around teaching and research in physiology, including carbohydrate metabolism. By 1920, he was a professor of physiology at the University of Toronto.
Banting approached Macleod in 1921 with a proposal to isolate a substance from the pancreas that could regulate blood glucose. Macleod provided laboratory facilities, scientific guidance and access to experimental animals. Banting began the work with Charles Best, a medical student who assisted with the experiments. Their collaboration brought together Banting’s research hypothesis and Macleod’s experience in physiology, setting the stage for the experiments that led to the development of insulin as a treatment for diabetes.
The researchers tied off the pancreatic ducts of dogs, allowing the enzyme-producing tissue to degenerate while attempting to preserve the islets. They prepared extracts from the pancreas and tested them in dogs whose pancreases had been removed. The extracts lowered blood sugar and improved the animals’ clinical condition.
These experiments provided evidence that an extract from the pancreas could help compensate for the loss of its normal blood sugar-regulating function. However, the early preparations were not suitable for prolonged use in humans because they contained impurities that caused adverse reactions.
Purifying insulin for treatment
In 1922, biochemist James Collip joined the research team to improve the purity of the pancreatic extract. His work helped produce a preparation suitable for clinical testing.
In January 1922, insulin was administered to Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old boy with severe diabetes, at Toronto General Hospital. The first injection produced limited results, and an abscess developed at the injection site. After the preparation was further purified, a second course of treatment produced a marked improvement in his condition, with a substantial reduction in blood glucose and urinary glucose.
Thompson’s response demonstrated that insulin could be used to treat diabetes in humans. The development of more reliable preparations and the expansion of production subsequently allowed treatment to reach more patients.
Insulin did not cure diabetes, but it changed the outlook for people living with the disease. Before its introduction, severe diabetes was often managed through restrictive diets that could prolong life only for a limited period. Insulin enabled patients to use glucose more effectively and helped prevent the severe metabolic disturbances associated with insulin deficiency.
The role of Best and Collip
The Nobel decision remains a significant part of the history of insulin research. Although Banting and Macleod received the prize, the work involved a larger research team.
Banting was unhappy that Best had not been included among the laureates. He shared half of his prize money with Best. Macleod, in turn, shared half of his prize money with Collip, recognising his contribution to the purification of insulin.
Later historical assessments of the discovery acknowledged the importance of contributions made by researchers who were not included in the award.
Laboratory discovery,modern diabetes care
The introduction of insulin marked a turning point in the treatment of diabetes. It allowed many people living with severe insulin deficiency to survive and helped establish hormone replacement as a major approach to treating endocrine disorders.
Insulin is produced by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. It helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy or stored for later use. When the body produces insufficient insulin, or cannot use it effectively, blood glucose levels can rise.
Insulin remains essential for people with type 1 diabetes, in which the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells that produce the hormone. It is also used by some people with type 2 diabetes when other treatments do not adequately control blood glucose.
The treatment has evolved considerably since the first pancreatic extracts were administered. Modern insulin preparations are manufactured under controlled conditions, with different formulations developed to vary how quickly they begin working and how long their effects last.
The Nobel recognition
Banting and Macleod received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for 1923. Banting delivered his Nobel lecture, titled ‘Diabetes and Insulin’, on September 15, 1925, while Macleod’s lecture, ‘The Physiology of Insulin and Its Source in the Animal Body’, followed on May 26, 1925.
The discovery also has a lasting connection to World Diabetes Day, observed on November 14, the birthday of Banting, who was born in 1891. More than a century later, insulin remains a cornerstone of diabetes treatment, changing a condition that was once often fatal into one that can be managed with sustained treatment.

Bouncing back after a poor run of results, defending champion Rajputana Royals registered back-to-back wins with a classy display against high-flying Chero Archers in the Archery Premier League’s season 2 in Hyderabad on Tuesday.
The Royals, who went through a rut with three straight defeats before turning it around on Monday, were in terrific rhythm as they thrashed Chero 6-0 without dropping a set.
The result moved Royals to six points and keeps them firmly in semifinal contention, while Chero also remains on the same tally. The star of the show for Royals was compound world No. 1 Ella Gibson, who scored 60 out of a possible 60.
Chero, who went back to their recurve international archer in Casey Kaufhold ahead of Kumkum Mohod, lost the first set 73-74 after the American started with a costly 7. In the second set, Royals edged ahead 76-75 with Chero paying the price for a couple of 9s from their compound archers.
The third set was tied at 58-58 after six arrows each, after which Atanu Das, who has otherwise been in fine form when selected, hit a rare 8. For Royals, Sangeeta – who was playing her first match in place of Ankita Bhakat – responded with a sensational 10. With an 8 needed to win, Tokyo Olympic champion Mete Gazoz delivered a 9 and brought out his signature celebration and some thigh-fives with his team.
“We didn’t start well over the first four days. I guess everybody misses us because I think the APL needs more energy and more dancing and now we’re giving that,” Gazoz quipped after the win.
Mighty Marathas and Kakatiya Knights seem to be peaking at the right time as they moved clear at the top of the table with eight points each.
Marathas’ recurve star Dhiraj Bommadevara was in terrific form, repeatedly shooting clutch 10s with barely any time left on the clock as the anchor for his side. At the top, ‘Mr. Perfect’ Mike Schloesser set up the sets well and finished with 78 out of the possible 80 points as Marathas’ stunning resurgence continues. They top the table ahead of Knights with only set points difference separating the two sides.
In the final match of the day, the Knights consigned Chola Chiefs to the bottom of the table as Nico Wiener and Neeraj Chauhan were both in terrific form at the start and end of the sets – both registering 59 out of 60 – while Spain’s recurve archer Elia Canales was an able support. In Jyothi Surekha Vennam’s absence, Avneet Kaur also stepped into the lineup admirably for the home franchise.

Rajputana Royals bt Chero Archers 6-0 (74-73, 76-75, 77-75).
Mighty Marathas bt Prithviraj Yodhas 6-2 (76-74, 77-73, 70-78, 76-75).
Kakatiya Knights bt Chola Chiefs 6-0 (74-73, 79-78, 77-75).

Why Saudi Arabia has struggled to defend its airport against recent Houthi attacks
The attacks have struck Saudi airports, killed at least 14 people and forced schoolchildren and businesspeople to stay indoors

Saudi Arabia possesses one of the world’s most costly and sophisticated arsenals, packed with American warplanes, missile defences and other cutting-edge technology.
Yet in recent days, it has appeared helpless in the face of waves of missiles and drones launched by the Houthi rebel group from neighbouring Yemen. The attacks have hit Saudi airports, killed at least 14 people, and forced schoolchildren and businesspeople to remain indoors and work from home.
The Iran-backed Houthis, once regarded as little more than a ragtag militia, have transformed into a formidable fighting force. They have damaged the region’s top oil producer, threatened vital supply routes in the Red Sea, and now risk reigniting a full-scale war on the Arabian Peninsula that displaced millions and killed tens of thousands.
The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports government forces in Yemen the rebels seek to overthrow. As Saudi Arabia investigates how its air defences failed to stop the Houthis' attacks, it must also consider how to respond and what the rebels might do next.
Here’s what we know and don’t know about the Saudi and Houthi conflict:
Saudi Arabia has a vast arsenal of US weapons
Saudi Arabia is the world’s top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It says the Saudis received 12 per cent of all U.S. arms exports from 2021-2025.
Over the years, the Saudis have purchased American F-15 warplanes, Patriot air defence systems, as well as advanced radars and offensive missile systems, according to the think tank, which tracks global arms transfers.
Saudi Arabia's annual budget for 2026 listed $83 billion for military expenditures. Earlier this year, it struck a $9 billion deal with Washington for 730 Patriot missiles.
But it has a huge area to defend
The Houthis have been able to exploit Saudi Arabia's large size.
Vulnerable energy, civilian and military assets are scattered across the country's sparsely populated territory roughly three times the size of Texas. Its border with Yemen stretches more than 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) through rugged desert areas.
“Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defence can guarantee complete protection,” Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, said in a post online Monday.
At the same time, regional officials say that Saudi Arabia is running low on interceptors and has reached out to allies for help.
Saudi Arabia recently struck a joint defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey. But so far, the two countries appear to be largely staying on the sidelines or limiting their support.
President Donald Trump said this week he is evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. But he has not yet announced a decision.
Houthi weapons and tactics are battle-tested
Like their patron Iran, the Houthis have deployed asymmetric warfare for the 21st century by capitalizing on their strengths — primarily drones and missiles. For the Houthis, success on the battlefield doesn’t require toppling Saudi Arabia; disrupting the Saudi economy and sowing fear within its society may be enough to give the Houthis leverage in any possible negotiations to end the fighting.
The Houthis have a large arsenal capable of striking targets well over 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) away. Some warheads change direction during flight and pose an extra challenge to air defence.
The group has fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Israel since its war in Gaza erupted in October 2023. While most were intercepted, a handful managed to land, in one case killing an Israeli man. Another strike hit an Israeli airport last year.
Andreas Krieg, a professor at King’s College London, said this experience in challenging Israel’s cutting-edge air defenses has given the Houthis confidence and expertise as they now strike Saudi Arabia.
“They’ve learned how to over-saturate the radars,” he said.
The Houthis, working with allied militias in Iraq, have also targeted Saudi oil installations, including a vital pipeline used to export oil through the Red Sea while movement through the Strait of Hormuz is limited. The Houthis have also seized territory in Yemen near the Bab el-Mandeb, a key Red Sea waterway, putting additional pressure on Saudi oil exports.
Saudi Arabia appears to have miscalculated
Michael Ratney, a former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia, says the kingdom assumed the Houthis wouldn’t strike civilian targets like airports. Doing so marked “a paradigm shift,” he said.
Ratney, now an adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the Saudis now find themselves in a position where they have to respond while also trying to prevent the fighting from spinning out of control.
“They can’t not strike back — they were attacked in a very brutal way by their archenemies,” he said. “They need to exert military pressure on the Houthis and then find a way to kind of deescalate.”
Rather than sending troops into Yemen, the Saudis will likely launch airstrikes against the Houthis and ramp up support of nationalist forces, several analysts said.
“It will be surrogate warfare,” Krieg said.
The Houthis are now a formidable force
While the Houthis don't have the firepower of Saudi Arabia, they have grown into a fearsome force controlling roughly one-third of Yemen thanks to help from Iran.
The United Nations estimates that the Houthis by 2024 had recruited up to 350,000 fighters. That's up from just 30,000 in 2015, when Saudi Arabia intervened in the internationally recognised Yemeni government's civil war against the Houthis and imposed a naval blockade.
Ratney says the Houthis now have a “symbiotic relationship” with Iran and should not be seen as an Iranian puppet.
The strikes on Saudi airports and economic assets symbolise a sharing of lessons in asymmetric warfare between the Houthis and the Iranians: how to not just puncture expensive air defences, but also damage vulnerable energy installations and threaten global maritime routes.
“Over the course of the past few years, the Iranians have been innovating and sharing that with the Houthis and it’s gone both ways. The Houthis have been innovating, and sharing it with the Iranians,” Ratney said. “It’s no coincidence that they’ve ended up with a similar approach.”
Their recent military successes have made the Houthis feel “untouchable,” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a fellow at Chatham House focused on Yemen.
“It’s very hard to convince a man he’s going on the wrong side if he just moved forward and he has a gun in his hand,” he said. But the Houthis are now likely to suffer a brutal Saudi counterattack, he said.

Huss Valley is a battleground arena game where you play the classic game of tag. Despite sounding simple, the game has a lot of mechanics you must know before entering the arena. In this beginner’s guide, we will tell you the best tips and tricks to play Huss Valley.
How Does Huss Valley Work
Huss Valley is a classic tag game where Chasers try to catch Runners. Each class comes with unique abilities in Huss Valley. Although the rounds in Huss Valley follow a simple set of rules, things can get chaotic as more players get caught. Here is how the game works:
- One player randomly gets assigned as the Chaser.
- The remaining players become Runners.
- The Runners must run across the arena safely.
- If you get caught, you become one of the Chasers.
- The last surviving player wins.
Every round, you can earn coins and gems, which you can use to unlock different abilities, consumables, and emotes from the in-game shop. You can also earn resources by using Huss Valley codes.
Understand the Movement System
Huss Valley is all about movement. Your character accelerates once you start moving and slows down once you release the movement key. This means you cannot instantly change direction or stop whenever you want.
You can use your dash to juke the Chasers and make your way across the arena. The only drawback is that you can only dash sideways instead of classic forward/backward.
Gems and Coins in Huss Valley
Gems and Coins are the two main currencies in Huss Valley, but they serve different purposes.
You can earn Gems through match rewards and by collecting them from the arena floor while playing as a Runner. Use them to permanently unlock abilities.
Coins can be earned at the end of a match and claimed by spinning the wheel and completing quests. You can spend them on consumables, which provide temporary advantages during a match.
All Consumable Items in Huss Valley
Using the resources, you can get the following consumable items in Huss Valley:
| Consumable | Effect | Best For | 
|---|---|---|
| Banana Peel | Trips an opponent on contact. | Chasers trying to catch Runners. | 
| Rescue Kit | Revives you after being downed. | Runners who need another chance. | 
| Adrenaline | Boosts acceleration and cornering speed for 5 seconds. | Runners approaching the finish line. | 
Huss Valley Controls
Like most Roblox games, the controls for Huss Valley are pretty standard:
| Action | Keybind | 
|---|---|
| Movement | W, A, S, D | 
| Dash | Space | 
| Use Item | Left Mouse Button | 
| Use Ability | Q | 
Best Huss Valley Tips and Tricks
Just knowing the controls isn’t enough to get more wins under your belt. To reach the top of the leaderboard, you must know about utilizing all mechanics in the game. Here are the best tips and tricks to play Huss Valley:
Best Tips for Runners
If you are playing as a Runner, you need to stay unpredictable. Here are some of the best tips:
- Avoid running in a straight line for too long.
- Hold directional keys and hit space to dodge sideways.
- Pick up gems scattered around the arena.
- If another Runner gets downed nearby, revive them before the Chaser catches them again.
Best Tips for Chasers
As a Chaser, your goal is to catch every Runner before they complete their crossings.
- Predict their movements instead of simply chasing where they are.
- Focus on groups instead of targeting a single runner.
- Use abilities like Banana Peels and Bear Traps to catch the runners.
That ends our full Huss Valley beginner’s guide. If you already know the basics, make sure you use the Huss Valley tier list before equipping abilities.

Huss Valley is an Arena game where chasers must catch runners and stop them from crossing.

You can earn Gems by collecting them from the arena floor or winning the matches.

The Best Coffee Grinders for Espresso or Pour-Over
Featured in this article
coffee Is Only as good as the beans you use to make it, and the beans you use are only as good as the grinder you use to render them extractable. Beans fed into a coffee grinder right before you brew them might as well be a whole different substance from the bag of ground beans you get at the supermarket, full of aroma and flavor compounds that quickly dissipate as they oxidize in the air. (It also helps to use fresh beans from excellent roasters: Check out our Best Coffee Subscriptions guide for some of our favorites.)
Grinders have become the most active tech frontier in coffee, and over the past decade coffee geeks have become devoted to the idea that getting the right grind on your beans is every bit as important as the machine you brew with. Uneven grinds can mean uneven extraction and uneven flavor—which is why we use particle size analysis to test the character of each grind from every grinder we review. But, of course, particle size alone does not tell the whole story, which is why I use the grounds from every model for cups of drip coffee, pour-over, Aeropress, and, when applicable, espresso.
Our Reviews team has tested dozens of grinders over the past five years, and I've retested all the top burr-grinder picks this past year. And while super-high-end grinders like the wonderful Mazzer Philos ($1,595) can run into the thousands, our top pick, the Baratza Encore ESP ($200), will keep most people happy for much less. This said, the Fellow Ode Gen 2 ($400), our favorite flat-burr grinder for drip coffee, is able to wring a special sort of poetry from each cup. The five machines below are the coffee grinders we currently recommend to anyone who cares a lot about home coffee.
Be sure to check out WIRED's other coffee coverage, like the Best Drip Coffee Makers, Best Espresso Machines, Best Latte and Cappuccino Machines, and Best Cold Brew Devices.
Updated October 2026: We tested and added the Mazzer Mini-G and the Fellow Opus 2 to our top grinder picks. We’ve also updated and edited descriptions and prices, where appropriate.
Compare Our Top 5 Grinders
| Grinder | Wired | Tired | Type | Grind Settings | Espresso Rating | Drip Rating | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baratza Encore ESP ($200) | Innovative dial offers fine adjustments for espresso. Precise grinds, with clarity of flavor. Built like a tank. Admirable versatility for all coffee types. Best value proposition overall. | Not a looker, really. Neither loud nor quiet. | Conical burr | 40 | 4/5 | 4/5 | 
| Fellow Opus 2 ($200) | Versatile for all coffee types. Stepless grind system. Very precise, clear flavor on drip coffee especially. Light, compact, stylish. Very quiet. | A bit plasticky. Some inconsistency on dial tightness in early production runs. | Conical burr | 100+ | 4/5 | 4/5 | 
| Oxo Brew Conical Burr ($100) | Lowest-cost burr grinder that still offers a good grind. Slim, sturdy build. Good for drip, Aeropress, French press. | Few espresso adjustments. Not as precise as top picks. A little loud. | Conical burr | 30 | 1/5 | 3.5/5 | 
| Fellow Ode Gen 2 ($400) | Tuning-fork precision on drip and pour-over. Minimalist-pretty design. Low static. Auto-shutoff when hopper is empty. Helpful grind size guide. | Not a good pick for espresso. Odd haptics on power switch. Grind cup also weird. | Flat burr | 31 | 2/5 | 5/5 | 
| Kingrinder K6 Hand Grinder ($109) | Wild precision, at a low price. Sturdy, wholly analog machining and engineering. 180 fine adjustments. Compact. | Hand grinding is a process. Instructions are few. Best for single-serve, not batch. | Manual | 180 | 4/5 | 4.5/5 | 
| Mazzer Philos Coffee Grinder ($1,595) | Wonderful clarity, depth, and body for espresso. Fine adjustments, easy cleaning, capability for all coffee brew styles. | Quite large. Drip coffee is excellent but not as good as with the Ode. | Flat burr | 145 | 5/5 | 3/5 | 
Best Budget Coffee Grinders
As mentioned above, the best bang for your buck will always be a hand grinder like my favorite, the Kingrinder K6 manual coffee grinder ($109). A precisely machined manual coffee grinder can rival coffee grinders many hundreds of dollars more expensive, both in precision and durability. And so the best manual coffee grinder will also be the budget option that'll lead to the best coffee. I've personally come to love the routine and the control.
But I get it. You'll happily grind your pepper with the best pepper grinder, but you draw the line at grinding coffee. Mornings are hard. Electricity helps. These are the budgetiest of budget electric coffee grinder options for each style of brew, all blessedly hands-off. None of these will lead to the clarity of flavors or sweetness or delicacy of our top picks. But they're the absolute lowest-cost devices we recommend for each category of brew.
Just when you thought Oxo had already cornered the market on affordable conical burr coffee grinders, the company comes in at an even lower price with this compact model. The Oxo Brew is stacked like a wee layer cake. And so the grind cup is housed within the column of the device and can be pulled out when you're done grinding. But while this is quite clever, neither consistency of grind nor ease of use is quite on par with Oxo's $110 basic conical burr, which remains my pick for an entry-level drip coffee grinder. But it's also very easy to move from the cabinet to the counter and back, and $30 less is $30 less. This is the lowest-price electric grinder I could actually recommend for Aeropress, drip, pour-over, French press, or cold brew. I wouldn't attempt espresso, though.
The lowest-cost electric espresso-capable grinder I can recommend with a clean conscience is the Wirsh Geimori T38 Plus for $150. This portable conical-burr grinder is about the size of a Christmas nutcracker and looks alarmingly like Pinocchio's left leg. But it offers surprisingly low coffee retention, stepless grind adjustments, and far better precision than expected for a grinder of its price. It achieves this by grinding at low RPMs—meaning it grinds quite slowly and carefully for an electric grinder. This also means the T38 Plus takes more than 30 seconds to grind enough beans for a double shot of espresso. This is disqualifyingly slow for batches large enough for drip or French press, and the T38 doesn't really have the clarity you want for pour-over. Still, it might be the only electric grinder I've tested south of $150 that can make decent espresso on non-pressurized baskets. It's also wee—great for small kitchens or as a travel coffee grinder. It's the grinder I'd definitely take with me to a hotel room if I didn't feel like grinding coffee by hand.
Look, blade grinders like this KitchenAid won't offer the powdery fineness and full-bodied coffee pleasures of a great conical burr, nor the precision of WIRED's top flat-burr pick. Blade grinders chop the heck out of beans, offering an uneven grind. But this is a very affordable coffee grinder, it's simple as pancakes to use, and blade-ground fresh beans are still a little better than the stuff in the supermarket. That said, they're probably still worse than getting beans fresh-ground at a café and using them within a week. When non-bean-geek friends ask for a grinder that costs less than dinner for two at Arby's, this is the one I offer up—especially if they're using darker grinds, and favor French press or a less expressive drip coffee maker. At the very least, it's enough so you're not crippled when you get whole-bean coffee as a gift. But let's be clear. The Oxo Compact conical burr grinder above is five times as good for about $30 more.
Results of Particle Size Analysis of Coffee Grinders
I of course assessed coffee grinders by tasting the resulting coffee across a number of brew styles and beans. But I also backed up my taste buds with scientific instruments. I analyze the flavor profile and the grind consistency of each of WIRED's top burr coffee grinder picks using particle analysis by a device called the DiFluid Omni. You can read a broader discussion of that particle analysis here.
Specifically, I tested each of WIRED's top burr grinders on multiple grind settings using the same medium-grind coffee beans—at both espresso-fine grinds and medium grinds more suitable for drip or pour-over coffee. Since September 2025, I also test every grinder I review or consider as a top pick, including the Moccamaster KM5, whose results are included here. I tested at least five times for each grind sample, collating the results into a characteristic curve for that bean and grinder.
Expand the discussion below for detailed discussion, bar graphs, and such.
Particle Size Analysis of Top Coffee Grinder Picks
Particle size analysis of coffee grinds is not a cut-and-dried test: It's more a clue as to the probable character of a brew. Patterns begin to emerge that correlate to the experiences I've had tasting coffee from each grinder. Taste is the ultimate test, alongside consistency of finicky espresso pulls. But quantitative analysis helps me (and you) actually trust and maybe understand those sensory test results.
When looking at these bar graph curves below, there are also a few rules of thumb. Big boulders north of a thousand microns will often lead to muddier character. Too many fines below 100 microns might lead to bitterness. A tight particle size distribution is associated with greater clarity of flavor. Look at the standard deviation (SD) for a clue as to overall precision: Smaller numbers indicate likely greater clarity. This said, a broad distribution of coffee ground sizes can also lead to better body and more perceived sweetness.
Our top pick for most people, the Baratza Encore ESP, proved itself to have quite precise results at very fine grinds—with standard deviation below 200 microns on espresso grinds, and 30 percent of particles concentrated within a single range. At its price range, this is admirable precision matched by very few grinders.
The same wasn't as true at pour-over coffee settings for the Baratza Encore ESP (seen above at setting 22), which showed a broader and more heterogeneous particle size distribution—with both small and large particle sizes. In practice, this led to a full-bodied and rounder cup, but with a little bit less of the precise aromatics one can get from our favorite grinder for drip and pour-over, the Fellow Ode Gen 2.
The Ode showed a characteristic bell-curve shape, surrounding a single high peak, which corresponded with the precise aromatics I taste when brewing drip or pour-over coffee using the Ode.
Even greater precision was on display with the Technivorm Moccamaster KM5, a flat burr grinder that showed precise results across the board—rivaling the Encore ESP at fine grinds and the Ode Gen 2 at grinding for drip. It's not as user-friendly as some of the top-pick devices, and the resulting brews can sometimes feel clinically clean, with a thinner body. But my lord it does offer clarity.
The Kingrinder K6 hand grinder, our top manual grinder pick, also showed strong peaks at grind sizes appropriate for pour-over coffee. Shown here are analyses of two medium-fine grinds, at 60 and 70 clicks from zero, respectively. Hand grinders have a secret weapon, which is that they cause you to grind slowly—which works very well at coaxing out more clarity from conical burrs. For pour-over grinds, the Kingrinder showed a higher peak than basically any grinder I tested, meaning grinds are very concentrated in a tight range of sizes: as many as 40 percent of coffee grounds were functionally the same size, and about 70 percent were grouped tightly around this. This leads to quite pronounced, intense flavor notes.
At grind sizes suitable for espresso, the Mazzer Philos bests this precision, with more than 90 percent of coffee grounds huddled in a tight grouping while using the i200D burr set. Nonetheless, while boulders are all but nonexistent, enough coffee fines exist to give each shot an almost syrupy consistency. The result is both body and perceived sweetness, with a surprisingly delicate clarity. While I haven't tested the i189D burrs also available as an option, reports from the world say that the i189Ds lean even harder into clarity of flavors. But note that at bigger grind sizes more suitable for drip coffee, you'll get a quite broad distribution. This will lead to a well-rounded cup, but may not offer the clarity of flavor of the Fellow Ode Gen 2 or the Kingrinder K6 for drip and pour-over brews.
Frequently Asked Questions
How We Test Coffee Grinders
WIRED tests coffee grinders by grinding a lot of beans and making a lot of coffee—testing each grinder to see if it can serve well for espresso, Aeropress, drip, and pour-over coffee, and coarse-ground cold brew and French press. I tend to always grind a drip Stumptown Homestead or Single-Origin Colombia as a baseline, because each is readily available at my local supermarket with stamped roast dates, and because I know the flavor well enough that I can detect variations. But I'll also try out a number of flavors and roasts on each grinder for different brewing methods.
We assess each grinder for decibel level while grinding, ease of cleaning and operation, hopper design, the presence or absence of “popcorning” (where the beans pop around inside the hopper, often leading to more uneven results), messiness and static electrical buildup, grind retention, ease of use, value, and simple aesthetics.
Previous WIRED reviewers assessed grind uniformity visually with the aid of macro lenses or filtered coffee grounds with sieves. In more recent rounds of testing, I reassessed each top coffee grinder pick using particle grind size analysis, with the help of the DiFluid Omni roast color and particle size analyzer, as well as a data analysis app.
I tested both fine and medium grinds on each grinder, using the same beans for each grinder, roasted within a month of testing. I repeated the particle analysis at least five times for each grinder and setting, and collated the results. I assessed the uniformity of the grind and the overall distribution of particle sizes—paying particular attention to the share of coffee fines (the tiniest particles smaller than 100 microns) and boulders (big coffee bits larger than 1000 microns).
Why Grind Whole Beans Instead of Buying Pre-Ground?
The reasons are simple: flavor, freshness, and aroma.
Whenever you open a vacuum-sealed bag of beans, a little invisible clock starts. Oxidation begins to erode the character of your beans, breaking down organic compounds and degrading them, turning your lovely beans to cardboard. Aromatic flavor compounds also escape from the bean, gassing out into the air where they do no particular good.
When you grind your beans, these processes go into overdrive. Freshness for whole beans can be measured in weeks. For ground beans, freshness in the open air is a matter of hours or even minutes. That bag of pre-ground beans you got from the supermarket? It's still coffee, of course, and it'll taste like coffee. But the vibrancy is gone. As far as true freshness is concerned, that coffee's been dead for weeks. (Pre-ground beans can be kept airtight for a week or so and maintain their flavor if you get them ground fresh at a coffee roaster.)
The only reliable way to get truly excellent flavor from your coffee beans, the way you experience it at a café, is to use fresh, whole beans. This is also how you can exercise some control over extraction and dial in your brewer or espresso maker to get perfect results for each bean.
Espresso requires a fine grind, pour-over a little coarser, and electric drip coffee a little coarser than this. Each grinder should have a guide to the best adjustments for each brewing method. Lighter-roast beans will want a finer grind than dark-roast to aid in extraction: Porous dark-roast beans give up their secrets a lot easier.
It's all kinda fun to figure out if you let it be fun. But certainly, when you strike paydirt, you'll know it: Finding the right marriage of grind and bean, on a good grinder, can turn into the best cup you've ever had. It's like the magical first time you seared a perfect steak or baked a perfect layer cake. Effort meets reward. It's marvelous. The grinders in this guide will help you find that moment more often.
What Is a Conical, Flat, or Blade Grinder?
Most coffee grinders fall into three main types: Conical-burr, flat-burr, and blade grinders. Burr grinders are generally higher quality and higher cost.
Conical-burr grinders are the category occupied by our top pick, the Baratza Encore ESP, and pretty much all of the most affordable grinders that still make good coffee. And there's a reason for this: Conical tends to offer the sweet spot at the intersection of high performance, cost, and flexibility. In a conical grinder, coffee beans are crushed and ground between two rings of burrs. They deliver a finer, much more consistent grind than you’d get with a traditional blade grinder, even the nicest blade grinder you've ever met. Conicals do tend to throw off more fines than a flat burr, but many feel this leads to more body and a more rounded flavor character.
Flat-burr grinders are thought to be more precise than conical grinders (though this is by no means universal). They’re also typically more finicky and also more expensive. Burrs are laid on top of each other, and the beans pass through them as they grind. The grinder action pushes the grounds out of one end, instead of relying on gravity like a conical-burr grinder, which means the beans spend more time in contact with the burrs. This often results in a more consistent grind, and therefore more precise flavors. For this reason, flat-burr grinders are often preferred as a way to elicit clarity of tasting notes in single-origin beans for pour-over, drip, and Aeropress.
Blade grinders have a chopping blade that spins around like a food processor. But blades don't produce even results. Some of your coffee will be fine powder at the bottom, and at the top you'll have bits too large for even French press. The result is an inconsistent, unpredictable brew. These grinders are generally quite cheap. But in case you're wondering, using fresh beans in a blade grinder is still probably better than buying stale ground coffee. (You can learn how to shake the beans to even your grind just a little. Pulsing the machine often also works. See world barista champion James Hoffmann's video for some more blade grinder hacks.) Still, if you can afford it, the conical or flat-burr grinders on this list will lead to far better coffee than any blade.
What's the Difference Between a Cheap and Expensive Burr Grinder?
The machinery in a high-quality burr grinder is a bit more complicated, and it's built to withstand greater wear and tear. In cheap burr grinders, the burrs can get blunt from regular use, and flimsier motors may burn out in a matter of months.
But also, coffee grinders have undergone a revolution in technology and design in the past decade. Manufacturers have been experimenting with different shapes of burr even on conical burr grinders—pentagonal, hexagonal, heptagonal. And grinders with more precise cuts will cost more money.
Flat burrs also cost more money to manufacture, and are seen as having more precision. The true geeks are swapping out for new generations of flat burr that offer greater precision in machining, and multistage grinds. Grinder makers are experimenting with larger and smaller burrs and different materials. It's a hive of invention out there. And these precision parts cost money: Some burr sets might cost hundreds all by themselves.
The end result of all this attention is a greater range or finer adjustment of grind sizes, better and more reliable calibration, and often more precision in the resulting coffee grinds—and thus more precision in the flavor of your coffee or the brew of your espresso.
Can I Run Pre-Ground Beans Through My Burr Grinder to Get Better Coffee?
No, please don't do this.
First off, if you're trying to improve the flavor of store-bought beans, the game's already lost. One of the main reasons to use fresh-ground whole beans is to avoid oxidation, and pre-ground beans have already been cardboarded up by evil, stale air.
But also, you'll mostly just muck up your machine. Logically, it might make some sense. Your grind is too coarse, so let's just run them through again at a finer setting, and perfect coffee results! Alas, on burr grinders, pre-ground coffee will get stuck inside the burrs, gum them up, and cause you to have to take the whole thing apart and clean it with your little brush and put it back together.
What Are the Best Coffee Grinders for Espresso?
Quite simply, the best coffee grinders for espresso are the ones that offer the finest calibration at the “fine” end of the spectrum. If you want to get super specific, look for coffee grinders that offer a number of fine calibrations at the fine end of the spectrum.
Dialing in individual espresso beans can require quite fine adjustments—and so even if a grinder is technically able to grind fine enough for espresso, it should also be able to make precise enough adjustments within that range to account for different beans, roasts, and machines. (For a real-world counterexample, witness the wall WIRED reviewer Joe Ray ran into when trying to get the (excellent) Wilfa Uniform Coffee Grinder to work for espresso. Without fine adjustments, chances are you'll fail.)
Otherwise, what you're looking for is excellent build, a motor that can withstand the higher torque you'll need to grind finely even on lighter roasts, and a machine that deals well with static electricity: Finer espresso grinds can turn static into a terrible enemy, sending coffee grounds spraying wildly.
The most vaunted espresso grinders can travel upwards into the high hundreds of dollars (see the Timemore Sculptor 064S flat-burr) or the thousands of dollars (see the Zerno Z1).
The Mazzer Philos Coffee Grinder ($1,595) offered maybe the best shots of espresso I've pulled at home in the past year. This offers delicate flavor and syrupy shots like the ones you'll get from a café, even on lower-cost espresso machines. (See my full review of the Mazzer Philos.)
But in this guide, we focused mostly on the best espresso grinders for the 90-some percent of people who are trying to gain access to good coffee without spending four figures. For most people and most budgets, our top pick, the Baratza Encore ESP ($200), will be the best choice, with sturdy construction and 20 grind adjustments for espresso alone. If you don't mind a little elbow grease, you can tune your grinds even finer by using a manual coffee grinder like the Kingrinder K6 ($109).
And then there's the true budget electric option. The tiny, slow-grinding Wirsh Geimori T38 Plus ($150) is the lowest-cost electric espresso grinder I've tried that can actually make good espresso on non-presurized baskets, though I'd probably limit it to medium roasts or darker, lest you strain the machine. Torque is not a strong suit.
Honorable Mentions and Runners-Up
Baratza Encore for $150: Baratza's original Encore is the Honda of the conical burr grinder world: easy to maintain, runs great, easy to use, lasts forever, replacement parts easy to find. It's been on the market largely unchanged for more than a decade. For not much more money, though, our top-pick Encore ESP offers beautiful adjustment on espresso settings, so I tend to recommend paying an extra $50 for the added versatility. But the original Encore remains a solid entry-level choice.
Baratza Virtuoso+ for $250: The Virtuoso+ uses the same burr set as the ESP, but is not quite as optimized for espresso. The biggest upgrade against the Encore ESP is a timer. Both have similar rock-solid but compact builds (although the Virtuoso is a little more stylish with its fitted grounds bin), 40 grind settings, and burr grinders for consistent grounds. The Virtuoso’s digital timer, however, is great for those wanting consistent coffee ground dosings each morning. You’ll have to dial in on your grind time versus coffee grounds output, but once you figure that out, you can walk away from the grinder and multitask if you please. —Tyler Shane
KitchenAid Burr Grinder for $200: This KitchenAid is stylish and easy to clean, and former WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey likes that the burrs are accessible thanks to their placement directly beneath the hopper. It also features precise dose control, with grind size controlled by a dial. For espresso lovers, one excellent feature is that you can swap the little container that catches the grounds with a holder for a portafilter.
Technivorm Moccamaster KM5 Flat Burr Grinder for $349: The performance on this stepless (read: infinite adjustment) grinder is somewhere between good and damn good. The razor-thin grind size distribution in early testing makes the KM5 a credible rival to the similarly priced Fellow Ode, in fact. And like the Ode, this Moccamaster is made especially for bringing out precise flavors on drip and pour-over. Particle analysis shows this Moccamaster to potentially offer even more precise grinds, leading to an almost clinically clean brew with light body. The KM5 not overly user-friendly, mind you: It cranks at 90 decibels, you have to hold down its analog switch to grind, and its aesthetics are the same sturdy industrial chic as all Moccamasters. Indeed, it's designed to sit alongside the classic drip coffee maker that's been on our buy-it-for-life guide since we've had one. If you prefer clarity to ease of use, this gives the Ode a run for the money, for less money.
Eureka Mignon Filtro for $269: The precision on flat burrs is terrific. But usually, so is the price. This no-frills Filtro from beloved Italian coffee brand Eureka clocks in at more than $100 less than our top-pick flat-burr, and it's an absolute metal-clad tank of a machine, says former WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey. It's as robust as the higher-end models and offers excellent consistency of grind size. Sure, it's a little loud, and you have to hold the button down when you grind. But life is full of trade-offs.
Lardera Wilfa Uniform for $299: This Wilfa has long been on our list as a great flat-burr grinder for pour-overs and drip. It remains such, though the Ode springboarded it as the top pick with its Gen 2 burr update, at about the same price. Like its name suggests, the Wilfa offers a beautifully consistent grind size and will make you a lovely pour-over. That said, it's fussier to adjust and louder than the Ode.
Breville Smart Grinder Pro for $200: WIRED has recommended this Breville in the past for its accessible burrs that make it easy to clean. But it's not really optimized for lighter-roast espresso, and ever since Breville bought Baratza, they've slowly been swapping out the grinders in their top-line semi-automatic espresso machines with those excellent Baratza burrs. For a stand-alone grinder at the same price, we give the same advice to you.
Baratza Vario W+ for $600: The Encore has a bigger, beefier, flat burr cousin, the Baratza Vario-W+ (7/10, WIRED Recommends) with a built-in scale and ridiculously granular adjustment (230 settings!). But like a lot of flat burrs, it struggles on finer grinds, according to WIRED contributor Joe Ray. And static is an issue. With price in play, the Ode Gen 2 comes out on top, but Ray was still a big fan of the Vario.
VSSL Java manual grinder for $165: VSSL specializes in ultra-durable camping tools, and it applied this same durable construction to this hardy campsite-ready hand grinder that WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson attests to be rugged enough to survive the zombie apocalypse. The handle folds out to provide a lot of leverage while you grind, and you can use it as a hook to hang the device up when you're done.
Also Tested
Wirsh Geimori GU38 for $200: The GU38 grinder from Wirsh/Geimori uses an identical burr set to the T38 Plus model I recommend as a budget espresso grinder. It's also bulkier and built a little sturdier. But the angled hopper causes more coffee retention, including some coffee beans that just refuse to feed into the grinder. Performance also seems slightly less reliable than the TU38, perhaps because the GU38 grinds faster. Either way, I'd opt for the lower-cost T38 Plus over this quite similar model.
Aarke Flat-Burr Grinder for $400: This pretty, shiny, stainless steel Aarke grinder contains a unique feature when paired with Aarke's coffee brewer, detecting the water in the brewer's tank and grinding the appropriate amount of beans. But this feature wasn't as calibrated as we'd like, and there have been a lot of online reports of grinder jams. I didn't have the same problem, but at more than $300 for a grinder that hasn't been long on the market, prudence is often rewarded.
Hario Skerton Pro for $55: The Hario Skerton was the gateway hand grinder for many a coffee nerd, but it has since given ground to newer entrants. It's fast and cheap, but it'll give you a heck of a workout and isn't as consistent for coarse grinds, plus the silicone handle has a habit of falling off.
Hario Mini-Slim Plus for $39: This smaller Hario manual grinder is slower than the Skerton, but its plastic construction makes it good to throw in a travel bag. The low price is its main advertisement.
Cuisinart Burr Grinder for $75: At first, it seems like a good deal. It's Cuisinart, a known brand, and a conical burr grinder for less than $100! But former WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey found that the low price came with a cost: These things apparently burn out faster than a rock star in the late ’60s.
Bodum Bistro Electric Blade Grinder for $20: This little blade grinder is quite cheap, and the model has served WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane for years. That said, after some inconsistent reports on reliability, we favor the KitchenAid as our ultra-budget pick.
