Mumbai: Hyundai Motor Group announced on October 13, 2026, a comprehensive investment strategy for India, committing USD 15.5 billion (approximately ₹1.29 lakh crore) from 2026 through 2032.
The initiative was discussed during a meeting between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chair Euisun Chung in New Delhi on October 13, 2026.
Investment Focus
The seven-year investment will span manufacturing expansion, research and development (R&D) infrastructure, local supplier cultivation for parts localisation, and future technology innovation. This aims to foster a comprehensive automotive industry ecosystem in India.
Dedicated Investment Entity
To manage this large-scale investment, the group will establish a dedicated investment entity in India. This entity will coordinate investments across R&D infrastructure, future technologies, and the broader automotive industry ecosystem.
Executive Comments
Euisun Chung, Executive Chair, Hyundai Motor Group, said India remains one of the group’s most important markets globally. He added that the investment reaffirms the group's commitment to India for the next 30 years and beyond, expecting to create more employment opportunities and support India’s industrial development.
Manufacturing Expansion
The group plans to expand manufacturing capacity across Hyundai Motor India Limited and Kia India Pvt. Limited. This expansion aims to support volume growth and localise production to meet India’s market demands, positioning India as a global export platform.
R&D Infrastructure
A complete R&D system will be established in India, focusing on infrastructure expansion and local talent cultivation. Approximately USD 700 million (around ₹5,830 crore) is planned for the R&D centre, including a vehicle testing track, to accelerate next-generation automotive technology development.
Local Supply Chain and Future Mobility
The group will strengthen its local supply chain through investments in regional partners to enhance parts localisation and support supplier development. It will also explore opportunities in new business verticals, including specialised automotive financing, EV charging infrastructure, and end-of-life vehicle recycling.
Economic Impact
Hyundai Motor Group currently employs more than 24,000 people across India. The investment is expected to create high-quality employment opportunities in manufacturing, R&D, engineering, and supply chain sectors, stimulating employment across the broader automotive ecosystem.
Production Capacity
Hyundai Motor Group has an established production capacity of more than 1.4 million vehicles annually across India. This includes HMIL’s facilities in Chennai (824,000 units capacity), HMIL’s manufacturing facility in Pune (170,000 units capacity), and Kia India’s Anantapur plant (431,000 units capacity). Pune’s capacity is scheduled to be scaled up in phases.

What is NVIDIA DLSS and how does it work?
The company's upscaling software is truly powerful when used in the right situations.
If you own a recent NVIDIA GPU (or Nintendo Switch 2), there's a good chance you bought it partly from hearing good things about DLSS. Short for Deep Learning Super Sampling, DLSS is a proprietary upscaling technology designed to increase game performance. With DLSS enabled, your GPU will first render a game at a lower internal resolution, meaning it will need to draw fewer pixels. DLSS will then upsample the image to your monitor's native resolution using a machine learning algorithm trained by NVIDIA.
When it's implemented well in a game, DLSS allows you to effectively turn up the graphical settings higher than your GPU would normally allow at a native resolution while still getting a playable framerate. Alternatively, you run a game at lower settings and push the framerate even higher, which can be useful if own a high refresh rate monitor.
How does DLSS work?
The above gives a decent starting point for how DLSS works, but knowing a bit more can help with tweaking to get the most out of the tech and your GPU. As mentioned already, with DLSS enabled your GPU will first render a game at a lower resolution before upscaling the image it produces to whatever resolution you've set as the target. In almost every case, you'll want to configure the target resolution to match your monitor's native resolution. So if you own a 1440p monitor, set the output resolution to 1440p. In most games, you do this simply by setting the "display" resolution.
Now comes the more complicated part. DLSS can feel like magic, but ultimately it involves a compromise. The different machine learning models that underpin the tech are trained to interpret motion vectors, as well as depth and brightness information when they upscale an image. Over the years, NVIDIA's GPUs and models have gotten better at doing that, but at the end of the day, some amount of fidelity is lost any time you upscale an image. How much is lost depends on the DLSS mode you use, which determines the internal render (or starting) resolution your GPU has to upscale from:
Quality: When set to Quality mode, your GPU will render a game at 66.7 percent of your target output resolution. For a 4K monitor, that means you're starting with a 1440p image. With a 1440p monitor, your starting point is 960p. DLSS Quality offers the best image quality of the different presets, but expect only a moderate increase in frame rate.
Balanced: When set to Balanced mode, your GPU will render a game at 58 percent of your target output resolution. At 4K, that means a starting point of 1253p. At 1440p, meanwhile, you're upscaling from an 835p image. As the name suggests, Balanced mode is intended to offer a middle ground between image quality and a higher frame rate.
Performance: When set to Performance mode, your GPU will render a game at 50 percent of your target output resolution. That translate to 720p internal resolution when used in conjunction with a 1440p monitor and a 1080p internal resolution when the output is a 4K resolution.
Ultra Performance: When set to Ultra Performance, your GPU will render a game at 33.3 percent of your output resolution. This mode is intended to be used with 8K monitors. Expect a blurry image if used in conjunction with a 1440p or 4K monitor.
As a rule of thumb, if you're running a 1440p monitor, DLSS Quality is a good starting point for most games. If you're not happy with your performance or chasing an even higher frame rate, drop down to Balanced mode. Beyond that, the final image can get quite blurry. For 4K monitors, Balanced mode is a good starting, and then bump things down to Performance if you need or want more frames.
The many different features of DLSS
One of the confusing things about DLSS is that the branding has come to encompass a handful of related technologies that you can use in combination with one another.
Deep Learning Super Sampling: The initial version of DLSS arrived in 2019, following the release of NVIDIA's RTX 20 series GPUs. At launch, only a handful of games supported DLSS, namely Battlefield V and Metro Exodus, due to a limitation that meant NVIDIA had to train the algorithm specifically for the game it was meant to enhance. Since the release of DLSS 2 in 2020, that limitation no longer exists, and according to NVIDIA more than 1,000 games and apps offer DLSS support as of the start of 2025.
Following 2020, the biggest upgrade to DLSS came at the start of 2025 when NVIDIA reworked the algorithm to take advantage of a new transformer-based machine learning architecture and released DLSS 4. The new model offers better image quality, reduced ghosting and improved image stability. On older RTX GPUs, running DLSS 4 can result in worse performance relative to previous versions of DLSS due to a higher overhead. For that reason, NVIDIA gives users access to different DLSS "presets" (separate from the modes described above), which they can use to access older models.
Deep Learning Anti-Aliasing: Where DLSS is primarily designed to increase performance at the cost of image quality, Deep Learning Anti-Aliasing or DLAA does the opposite. Rather than upscaling an image, DLAA takes a native output and makes it more stable by reducing the amount of shimmer and flickering. Think of it a better version of temporal anti-aliasing or TAA. Not every game natively supports DLAA, but even in the ones that don't, you can use the NVIDIA app to add DLAA.
Frame Generation: Originally introduced as part of DLSS 3, frame generation allows NVIDIA RTX 40 series GPUs and up to generate a single interpolated frame from every two traditionally rendered frames, thereby increasing the overall framerate of a game. Frame generation is best used when your GPU can render a game at a consistent 60 FPS or more, and you have a high-refresh rate monitor that will benefit from the extra frames.
With DLSS 4, NVIDIA introduced multi frame generation, which allows RTX 50 series GPUs to generate and interpolate a greater number of frames based on a single traditionally rendered frame. As of the release DLSS 4.5 this past March, the current limit is six generated frames for every rendered frame.
Ray reconstruction: With DLSS 3.5 NVIDIA introduced ray reconstruction, a denoising algorithm designed to reduce artifacting from ray tracing effects. The algorithm works by sampling the light rays in a scene and then generating high quality pixels in between those rays. While ray reconstruction can offer performance gains, it's primarily designed to make games with ray and path tracing look better and more coherent.
What about DLSS 5?
DLSS 5 is an altogether different beast from the features described above. Rather than upscaling an image, DLSS 5 interprets a game's color and motion vectors to apply, in the words of NVIDIA, "photoreal lighting and materials that are anchored to source 3D content and consistent from frame to frame." In short, DLSS 5 is adding an AI filter to your games.
In early demos, the effect was uncanny, making it look like the tech was yassifing characters. But used more carefully, it can add more layers of realistic shows and textures to a game. Unfortunately, unlike other iterations of DLSS, DLSS 5 does not improve your framerate. It instead lowers it due to the overhead required to run the tech.
As of October 2026, DLSS 5 is officially available in just a single game: NBA 2K27. At this early stage, it's unclear if DLSS 5 will see widespread developer adoption, but that hasn't stopped modders from adding the tech to all sorts of games.

Only one person agreed to be Alex Gibney’s new Elon Musk documentary immediately: Musk’s father. “We had Errol Musk at ‘hello,’” Gibney says.
Eventually, the director would speak with scores of Musk’s associates for his film. His first wife, Justine Musk, appears, as does his ex-girlfriend Ashley St. Claire. Journalist Kara Swisher, LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, myself, and WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond also spoke to Gibney for Musk, which hits theaters nationwide on Friday. But landing Errol Musk, with whom the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has a complicated relationship, was a watershed.
“Everybody else took a lot of persuasion,” Gibney says. “It was very difficult to get people to appear because the risk profile for talking about Musk in a way that was honest was high.”
Once Gibney interviewed all of his subjects, he had enough material to make a documentary that runs nearly four hours, including a 10-minute intermission. It’s a damning portrait of the trillionaire CEO, detailing how much of his genius is based on his formidable ability to promote his own mythology—and the stock price of his public companies.
Musk never agreed to an interview with Gibney. Instead, the director’s team researched every public comment Musk ever made and created a simulated Elon Musk who appears throughout the film.
I spoke with Gibney earlier this month about his experience making the film, why he decided to make his simulated Elon attractive, and what material he had to leave on the cutting room floor.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
ZOË SCHIFFER: Alex Gibney, thank you so much for being with us today.
ALEX GIBNEY: Good to see you, Zoë.
This shouldn’t spoil anything, but in the four years that you spent making Musk, Elon Musk never agreed to sit down with you for an interview. Instead, your team looked back through the archives of everything he has said publicly, and you put together a sort of simulated interview, which appears throughout the film as a through line. Basically, it plays into Musk’s idea that we are all, in fact, living in a simulation. How did you decide on this approach for the film?
Well, what were we gonna do? He’s the main character.
I actually thought because he’d been so outspoken about this idea of a simulation, that cinematically we should lean into that. We should play in Elon’s sandbox and have a simulated interview. As we began to develop that idea, by using his real words, his actual audio recordings, but placing them in a kind of avatar which we would design, I think there became all sorts of thematic reasons to do it.
One was because he himself had said we’re living in a simulation. But two was the importance of this notion in the Elon Musk story of the shifting sands between what is real and what is unreal. Then also, because a lot of the film deals with his issues of AI, that discomfiting relationship that we’re beginning to explore, all of us on planet Earth, with these AI LLMs and how we begin to project things on these computer interfaces, it felt like this might be something interesting to do.
By the way, you’ll notice that when Elon is talking to people in a normal interview situation, he rarely looks at the interviewer or at the camera. He’s always looking this way or that way. So we designed this in a very different way, where he’s looking right down the barrel of the lens directly at the viewer, and we thought that that would be OK. We’re gonna give Elon a break, and actually, I thought our avatar made him look pretty good compared to some of the recent images of him.
I have a question about that because your simulated Elon Musk—I think it’s fair to say—looks a lot hunkier than present day Elon Musk. He’s kind of chiseled and tan, and …
It is kind of a two-day growth of beard.
Exactly. Was that an intentional choice? And if so, can you just talk about why that was?
It was. I joke about this, but he’s the star of my movie, I want my star to look good. But I think also it would’ve been a mistake to go into slop AI territory, like some of the images that Elon’s fans are posting about me right now, to sort of denigrate him visually.
Also, to some extent, the story is also about image building, too. So I thought, “OK, let’s have some fun with that as well.” Because we had a lot of choices. I mean, we started out with the design firm, like how should he look? What should he be dressed in? You know, we put him in a gamer chair, a leather jacket. There were conscious choices.
That extends to some of the comments he makes, where I don’t find like the most bumbling comments that Elon ever made.
When we have somebody speaking about something, I want a rejoinder from Elon. We looked for the best rejoinders, like how can he come back at us? Now, later on in the film, his statements become more and more fantastical, but that also is part of what happens.
I think it really worked for the film. I’ve seen it a couple times and I think there are these famous images of Elon Musk. I’m thinking of the one where he’s on the yacht and he’s shirtless. There, it seems like if you had leaned into a less flattering image, you would’ve been playing on his turf, but in a way that would undermine the message of the movie. Whereas elevating his look allowed you to hold him quite accountable in a way that comes across pretty fair.
Yeah, we were respectful. We gave him a good look. And much better by the time we go to the archive, particularly the archive of the SpaceX IPO, when he’s begun to start looking like Kim Jong Il.
I’m curious about your thoughts on ethics. It’s not putting words in someone’s mouth, because these are all statements that Elon Musk has really made, and it’s not even like you’re particularly mashing stuff together.
But your decision, for example, to have him look right at the camera, you are making decisions for him in a way that you couldn’t with a live interview subject. So I’m just curious if you could speak to the ethical implications of that.
I think that goes to the heart of what’s different about a documentary like this and maybe a podcast interview in the sense that we’re rendering that image in a kind of broader cinematic context. The imagery itself is intended to either convey meaning or to raise questions for the viewer that they should start to think about.
As you know from being interviewed for the film, we interviewed you in front of a green screen and then placed you in a background, which we sort of reveal at different times in the movie. All of this had to do with this kind of strange unreality, real unreal world we’re living in right now.
Mm-hmm.
But also by shooting him looking into the lens I sometimes do that and I sometimes don’t. There is this interesting psychological relationship that you begin to have with a subject that I think is both real and unreal at the same time, which was part of this larger conceit in terms of trying to find a way to make the movie and the formal devices in the film itself reflect some of the thematic concerns.
Right. It also makes him feel like there is a fair amount of conviction behind what he’s saying, and there’s this relationship between him and the audience.
I feel like over the course of his public life, he doesn’t appear to have had an allegiance or ideology to one coherent political identity or to even his colleagues or close friends. These things are shifting and changing. So I am curious how that kind of came up for you in the making of the film of wanting to convey an Elon Musk in the simulated interview that represented, to the best of your ability, the quote-unquote, “true Elon.”
I mean, it’s a shape-shifting image and one which is, after all, confected, which is useful, particularly when you’re using it as a vehicle to put these statements in. I agree with your point that you just made about Elon’s ideology. I think there are a lot of wise and very perceptive books that have been written that in my view sometimes make one kind of critical flaw. They try to render a coherence about Elon’s thinking that I’m not sure is there. I think he’s far more of an improviser and shape-shifter. He has an image of himself that he wants to convey, but he’ll sculpt and change that image according to conditions and evidence, like the way he acted with Obama versus the way he acted with Trump.
I mean, there was a history there, but still they’re both serving the same purpose for him, which is, “How do I cadge the most amount of resources out of the federal government?”
I’ve thought about this a fair amount as well. I think his acquisition of Twitter now acts as a very clear example where in the moment it was clearly this impulsive decision, but now that it’s become this big source of political power for him, there’s this tendency to be like, “Oh, he was playing a complicated game all along.”
My view has always been that if Elon has a superpower it’s that he has a pretty high risk tolerance, and so he’s able to make impulsive, rash decisions and then deal with the fallout in a way that a slightly more cautious person might not be able to, for better or often worse.
He’s so comfortable with risk. It’s as though he goes through life on a canoe moving down the rapids. When he sees a rock there, he goes this way. He sees another rock or a shifting current, he goes that way. In the case of Twitter, as you pointed out in your book, he kind of bought the company on a dare, and he grossly overpaid for it and also abandoned all due diligence.
From the standpoint of a businessman, it was just dumb. But he didn’t care, and he had so many resources, what did it matter? Twitter, now X, was always a vehicle for his ambitions and his ability to court retail investors.
I don’t think it occurred to him until later when he had virtually destroyed the value of the company for the rest of us, that actually this would be a good propaganda platform for me. That’s what it becomes. Then suddenly it actually has enormous political and economic utility in a way that I don’t think he thought through at the beginning.
So Musk aside, plenty of people did speak to you for this film: Musk’s first wife, Justine; his former girlfriend, the influencer Ashley St. Clair, who he has a kid with; his father; former business partners; former colleagues; people he’s fired; the former ambassador to the United Nations, Samantha Power; Kara Swisher.
Walk me through the process of getting these people to say yes, to trust you. Specifically, was there anyone who really surprised you in their immediate willingness to say yes, and anyone who really needed extra time and conversation with you in order to be able to say yes?
Almost everybody who appeared in this film needed time to be able to process and accept appearing, in part because there was a sense of risk associated with it. Only one person agreed immediately, and that was Errol Musk.
Oh my gosh.
It was almost like, what’s that line from that great film “You had me at …”
“You had me at ‘hello.’”
We had Errol Musk at hello. “Hello, Errol, would you like to appear in this documentary?” “Yes.” We quickly rushed a crew over to his house. I did a remote interview in South Africa. It was the one interview we did that was not green screen, and he was remarkably revealing, sometimes in intended and sometimes in unintended ways.
Everybody else took a lot of persuasion. I was having conversations with Justine for over a year, I think, before she agreed to sit down. Even somebody as powerful as Reid Hoffman, same thing. So it was very difficult to get people to appear because Musk’s—the risk profile for talking about Musk in a way that was honest was high.
In some cases I did talk to a lot of people, sort of powerful people in Silicon Valley, on background—some of whom had fond feelings toward Elon and some who didn’t. I found it interesting that there’s sort of like talking to people in a gentleman’s club, and one doesn’t talk about other people publicly.
While I did learn things when they were talking to me on background or off the record, I found that kind of revolting in a way. It’s like we’re dealing with a figure now who has enormous sway over all of us, and isn’t it important to weigh in on that kind of public debate?
But that wasn’t the view that they had. In fact, there’s a guy I know who is friends with Elon and treasures his friendship with Elon, and I said, “Let’s have a conversation off the record. You know, tell me what’s great about Elon and why you like him so much.” He said “I would never betray a friend like that.”
I got that for my book as well. I don’t feel as surprised. I think if we were talking about six, seven, eight, nine, 10 years ago, like, yes. But these are similar people to those who are flying to Washington, DC to pay fealty to Trump, and going directly against values that they were talking about not that long ago.
That’s right.
I do wanna talk about Errol Musk because you brought him up. There’s this very powerful interview in the film where he talks about his son. He seems to have had a very big impact on Elon Musk’s life, and not necessarily a positive one. This was kind of the central thesis of Walter Isaacson’s biography of Elon Musk.
It kind of came down to daddy issues. So I’m curious to get your perspective on Errol’s influence on Elon and how you balanced showing the hardship of his childhood without using that as an overly simplistic explanation for his behavior today.
I think that’s an important point. I do think that Errol Musk had a powerful impact on Elon, because of how Elon felt he was treated by his dad, sometimes cruelly, psychologically. We don’t know of any kind of physical abuse. But also I think, you know, by watching Errol, you grok—to use a term from the Heinlein book—the notion that the apple doesn’t fall far from the tree.
There’s an element you can see the character of Elon. We kept it in a kind of short contained section and as an element of how we can think about Elon Musk. But I think the Walter Isaacson conclusion, in a way, is a little bit too easy. There are a lot of people who’ve been bullied or abused by their parents who don’t end up becoming bullies or abusers.
And to say it’s a kind of a mechanical thing that happens is kind of letting Elon Musk off the moral hook. That was an issue I had with Walter’s book. To some extent, we’re all grateful for the fact that he was able to spend so much time with Elon. There’s an accretion of detail in the book that’s valuable.
But I think the conclusions were sort of a get out of jail free card for the performative cruelty that ultimately he engaged in. Yet you need to know about the origin story without—it can be an explanation without being an excuse, I guess is what I would say.
I would imagine that in the making of a film like this, there is an open question at the beginning in particular about whether you’re actually going to get enough access for this to work. It’s certainly a question with features that we write. I’m curious if there was a particular interview, maybe with someone close to him, where you knew like, “OK, we’re, we’re gonna be able to do this. I think we’re gonna have enough.”
Well, weirdly, it didn’t happen until very late, and I would say it was the Justine Musk interview. I mean, the Ashley St. Clair interview is powerful as it is, and it is powerful, and it gives you a front-row seat to the election of 2024. The Justine Musk interview gave me insights into his personality that were very powerful in both understanding him as a person, but also understanding some of what he did thematically.
Because I asked her—and this answer is not in the film, but it helped to guide me—“What was it that attracted you about him back in college?” They met in college in Canada. And she said it was his enormous confidence. And then the other thing she said that’s powerful that is in the film is that she learned about gaslighting from Elon Musk.
That gaslighting thing, the idea of trying to convince somebody that the truth is other than what it is, and to suggest that you’re crazy and if you don’t go along, is a super important insight into who Elon is. And confidence, of course, is what allows that to happen.
Justine’s was such a powerful interview in the film. There are multiple moments where she cries or is near tears. She comes across as just so genuine, and I think she also seems like someone who doesn’t appear to be in it for attention or power or money. Like, there’s a point in the film where I think she says, “I really wanted to have a say in how this story was told.”
I’m thinking specifically of when their first child died in a SIDS-related incident, and Elon Musk tweets that he was holding the child. The child died in his arms. And Justine says, “No, this was one of the most defining moments of my life. He died in my arms.” You really just see how Elon has hurt her over the years.
That’s right. That gets me kind of emotionally worked up even as I think about it, because of course that moment was deeply painful for Elon, which is what Walter Isaacson spent some time on in the book. But to credit-grab in the midst of a tragedy like that seems so petulant and small and, you know, talk about main character syndrome.
One of the defining things about Elon Musk is that over time, as he increased more and more power, there was only one character in all his companies, and that’s Elon Musk, and only one character in all of his marriages. That’s Elon Musk. Everyone else recedes into the background. It’s interesting.
Justine is a storyteller. She’s a talented novelist. I went deep into reading her blogs and also the article that she wrote for Marie Claire. You know, her ability to be a storyteller is actually quite profound precisely because she’s reaching for a deeper truth.
I think when Elon is a storyteller, he’s actually reaching for fiction. He’s reaching to mythologize in a way that undoes the truth, that steers us away from that kind of hard work of getting to the stuff that is really deep and painful because it’s true.
I am curious about your take on this because it’s a question that I have had about Elon Musk: Does he actually believe what he’s saying or is he knowingly lying?
I think it’s closer to the former, and I’ve dealt with a number of characters who are like this. Sam Harris in the film makes a distinction between liars and bullshitters, and liars, of course, have to assiduously keep track of the truth in order to know when and how they’re lying.
Bullshitters just say what comes to their mind. It’s a kind of—it’s on the right track, but sort of insufficient. I think for somebody like Elon Musk—or people in the past like that I’ve dealt with, like Elizabeth Holmes or the guys at Enron or even somebody like Lance Armstrong—in the moment, because you feel a kind of righteousness about your cause, you feel you’re kind of entitled to make things up, You feel over time so entitled and so corrupted by this notion that the end justifies the means, that some kind of psychological trick is played inside your own mind where in order to be forceful and confident about what it is you’re saying in the moment, you have to believe it.
I reckoned with that with Lance Armstrong, where he could look people in the eye at a press conference and say with great force, “How dare you say that I, as a cancer survivor, would ever use performance-enhancing drugs?” And then he’d get down off the podium and do a bag of blood.
But I think in the moment he did believe what he said, because that’s how you come off as being effective. You see it particularly for people who become kind of addicted to a growing power that they have, and they see that also they have an ability to convince, like Elizabeth Holmes did.
It’s a psychological quirk that kind of takes over, and it’s peculiar, but I think it’s real.
It’s so hard to remember when talking about Elon Musk that this goober in an Occupy Mars T-shirt who’s thrashing around with a chainsaw waxing poetic has had this undeniable impact on so many people’s lives and livelihoods, and a lot of that impact has been negative.
The part of your film about DOGE, Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, which is a short-lived stint in Washington, DC where he fired, I think, 300,000 federal workers to, quote-unquote, “solve the federal deficit.” Spoiler alert, he didn’t even come close. That was probably one of the hardest moments to watch.
Samantha Power, former ambassador to the UN, spoke specifically about the lives lost, thousands and thousands, and millions more projected, after he shuttered USAID. I’m curious, given all you know about Elon Musk at this point, and the reporting you did on DOGE, what do you think that period and that experiment was really about for him?
It wasn’t about waste, fraud, and abuse. There was an aspect of glee and performative cruelty that we tried to represent in the film by showing the DOGE cuts as a kind of first-person shooter game, juxtaposed of course, with the sober testimony of Samantha Power, who talks about how many children died as a result.
But I think in many ways the waste, fraud, and abuse was kind of the magician’s sleight of hand to say, “This is what we’re doing.” But what he was really doing was something very self-serving, which as a big tech baron, was literally destroying the regulatory state.
If there was a lot of collateral damage, people died, disease went up, who cared? It was the destruction of the inspectors general, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. He called everything corrupt without any evidence and so forth and so on.
The other thing, and the more controversial thing, which we’re all still chasing in a way, is the fact that the DOGE boys, who were clueless about the agencies they went into, nevertheless seemed to know an awful lot about data extraction and data access.
And they were granted, according to one head of IT at a federal agency I talked to, super admin status, which you know better than I, allows them to break through all sorts of silos that are intended to be erected to either protect classified information or protect our private data.
So the DOGE boys had access to vast amounts of data that no one has ever had access to in history. All of that didn’t go unnoticed, but it was the flash over the chainsaw all of the press conferences kind of hid a lot of what was really going on, I think.
Yeah, if you’re really worried about waste, fraud, and abuse, then there’s a certain level of care that you would take in your auditing. The DOGE boys were posting on X this kind of, quote-unquote, “wall of receipts” where they would talk about contracts that they’ve slashed, not understanding that in procurement paperwork, oftentimes you’ll put the total lifetime amount that could ever be spent on a contract, which is sometimes quite different, millions of dollars different, from the actual amount that was spent.
So they were claiming savings that were nowhere close to what had actually been saved. There was another, and this is in the film as well, moment where Elon Musk was talking about how they were finding tons of people who were getting Social Security benefits who were 150 years old, not understanding that when you don’t have a birthday for someone in the Social Security system, which is built on very arcane technology, really old code, it defaults to a birthday that shows someone as 150.
Anyone who had worked in SSA would’ve been able to tell them that, but they didn’t seem, to me, to be particularly interested in the details, which again, if you’re really worried about waste, fraud, and abuse, that’s all about details.
Correct. And indeed the detail that you mentioned about Social Security was actually posted on the Social Security website. So they could’ve read the website. But it goes to this kind of performative cruelty where it almost didn’t matter to them, you know?
One of the more chilling interviews, which I got from a deposition, was with one of the DOGE boys, a kid named Nate Cavanaugh.
Mm-hmm.
The questioner asked him, “Did you not care about the lives that were being affected by all of these mass firings and, and the kind of pain and suffering that would cause?” And he said, “Well, no, because we thought it was more important to reduce the federal deficit.” Next question: “Did you reduce the federal deficit?” “No.” But, you know, for a guy who’s supposed to be such a genius, you would think there would be some analysis done.
But that parallels what happened at Twitter, as you know better than anybody. In other words, they would fire people at Twitter who had actually critical jobs, without even knowing what they did.
Ezra Klein has talked about this. I think it’s really true. Like at Twitter, when you make a rash decision or you fire people, the feedback loop with the company or social media is pretty small. You can see the effects of that pretty quickly. The site starts to get glitchy.
In government, the feedback loop is really long. You don’t get to see immediately the impact of those decisions, and to me that appears to be a large reason why the effects were just so much more devastating, and honestly, while he has admitted publicly DOGE was a failure, it seems like there was no move made to kind of correct any errors.
I think even as a failure, it was sort of an intended failure in the sense that it was an attempt to really fire cannons at the government, particularly the regulatory state, so that the castle couldn’t be repaired.
Yeah, I guess I should say the stated goal of the budget deficit was a failure, but the implicit goal was quite successful.
That’s right. It was really successful. The other thing that is so disturbing about the DOGE moment is that in a lot of cases they were literally warned about the damage that was done, and that, that was certainly the case at USAID. You can make a decision as a country that we’re not gonna give aid to developing countries anymore, but money had already been appropriated by Congress. Indeed, food had been bought to send to starving children, and in some cases, boats were literally stopped to prevent that food from going to the children, who then subsequently died while they ended up burning the food on pallets someplace, literally wasting food that had already been bought and paid for.
So the cruelty had a kind of performative quality to it, which was meant, I think, to speak to the roiling anger that Musk is so good at fomenting on X and which the MAGA movement is so good at exploiting politically.
Toward the end of the film, Geoffrey Hinton comes on and says, quote, “It’s fairly clear to me Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections. If you want to corrupt those midterm elections and you want to use AI, what you’d need to do is get detailed information on US citizens. And what DOGE did looked to me like just what you would do if you wanted to get data on US citizens.”
Basically, he’s saying Musk appears to have already gathered up the data Trump would need to meddle in the upcoming election. We’re now less than a month out. So based on the interviews that you conducted and the information that you have coming out of this project, I’m curious what you are most worried about, and what is the concern in terms of what Musk may have been cooking up, and how do you see this playing out?
The first thing I should say is I don’t really know.
You guys are doing a lot of interesting reporting now about where the money is going and how much of it is going to focus on negative advertising versus pro-candidate stuff. But also, what kind of stories are people particularly susceptible to? We know from years of having our data mined by Facebook and X and others that it’s really useful to know what people respond to and what people think, and you have enormous data about them, then you can message certain things in order to be able to reach those soft points psychologically.
I would have to say at this moment, because it does look like we’re not far away from the election, and it looks like it’s gonna be a blue wave. We’ll see. But if it is, my bigger concern is over a disinformation campaign, aided and abetted by Elon Musk, with massive amounts of data that would try to undermine people’s confidence that the election was free and fair.
That’s what I fear most at this moment.
The documentary comes in at just under four hours.
Three hours, 45 minutes, but there’s a 10-minute intermission.
OK. The documentary comes in just under four hours, but I know from talking to you and being a little bit involved in the project that there was a ton that you left on the cutting room floor. So I’m wondering if you can speak about what parts you had to cut that were the hardest, what you wish you could’ve kept in, and how you ultimately made those decisions.
There are sections that I wish I could have kept at their expanded length. One of them is Twitter, where we had a lot more detail about the chaos of Twitter. DOGE also. There were a lot of things I would’ve liked to have expanded rather than have to condense to their essence.
The SolarCity story was one that we left out, which was a really interesting story. There was a Russian influence story that was quite powerful, though we never got to a kernel that would indicate exactly the dimensions of it.
There was a counterintelligence investigation, the whole SEC thing about the tweets, and then we got an incredible deposition. I love depositions. They show so much about people sometimes, particularly people in power who are being held to account in a deposition.
So there was a lot of wonderful detail that was left on the cutting room floor. Maybe someday for all of us geeks, we’ll release it.
We’ll get the six-hour cut.

'Unplayable' Stanway a free-scoring warrior for Lionesses
- Published
Whatever the game, whatever the result, Georgia Stanway always seems to score for England.
Manager Sarina Wiegman called the midfielder a "warrior" after her performance against Greece helped seal an impressive 5-0 victory to complete an 8-1 aggregate triumph.
Stanway scored in both matches as the Lionesses progressed to round two of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs with ease.
She opened the scoring in Crete as they won 3-1 and when Wiegman called for more ruthlessness in Leicester, Stanway delivered again.
The 27-year-old is quickly becoming one of England's most important players. So what makes her so effective in front of goal?
'She has that tenacity in her'
Stanway's strikes in the last five days capped off a season in which she finished as England's top scorer and netted 11 times in her last 11 matches.
She also ranks inside the top three for most goals scored by European players in international football since Euro 2025.
While Wiegman was frustrated by her side's lack of ruthlessness in Greece, Stanway always looked dangerous and made sure she got on the scoresheet.
It felt inevitable she would join in the fun in Leicester when Alessia Russo and Lauren James grabbed a double each.
Stanway came close to matching them when the Arsenal midfielder coolly took control of a long ball inside the box with one deft touch and, with the second, fired it powerfully into the bottom corner.
It would have been the perfect strike to mark an impressive few days but it was ruled out for offside, much to Wiegman's dismay.
"She is always so eager to go towards goal. She has that tenacity in her," said the England boss when asked about Stanway's goalscoring form.
"She is always aggressive out of possession but also in possession. She scored a great header and controlled that really good ball from Alex Greenwood.
"That was really good athleticism and composure. Unfortunately that was disallowed but it was really good!
"Football is about scoring goals, but also playing in the pockets, keeping the ball and connecting with other players - and I was happy with her [doing those]."
Former England goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis told BBC Radio 5 Live that Stanway was "unplayable at times" against Greece on Tuesday night.
She won all her tackles, had a 90% passing accuracy rate, took four shots, scored once and had another disallowed.
It was also a slightly different role for Stanway for most of the match as she played more as a right winger after changes in the midfield.
"She has something different to others," Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"She is goal-orientated, has a great shot and the disallowed goal showed her great mobility and athleticism.
"When you really need a fight, or a duel, or a counter-attack breaking up, she is there. She is a warrior who you can play a possession game with too."
Tactical tweaks offer Wiegman fresh options
Stanway was even more effective in large part to a new-look midfield which included 20-year-old debutant Lexi Potter.
The Chelsea midfielder provided cover for the experienced Stanway and Keira Walsh to push higher up, while Lauren James played in the number 10 role.
It proved to be an inspired change from Wiegman as Stanway caused problems throughout for the visitors and was able to adapt to the tweaks impressively.
"Stanway has shown how flexible she is, how exceptional she is both at the bottom end of the pitch, breaking up play, as well as at the top end," added Brown-Finnis.
"She was playing as a second striker, playing out on the right, dropping deep as a number 10. She's been absolutely brilliant."
England still have a job to do to qualify for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil with a two-legged play-off tie against Ukraine to navigate at the end of the year.
They have already beaten their opponents 9-1 on aggregate in two games of the league phase of the qualifiers.
After Wiegman's formation experiment worked so well this week, could it be an option for the future that brings out the best in Stanway, as well as others?
"I liked the balance of the midfield. There is a lot of competition going on in that area," admitted Wiegman.
"There were a few reasons. First of all, I wanted to see Lexi Potter deeper on the pitch and what that might bring.
"There was also the option to put Georgia Stanway higher up the pitch. We wanted to score more goals and we know that she can do that.
"She can play in the pocket and also deeper on the pitch so we wanted to see all of that."

Hong Kong urged to add online safety briefings, penalise no-shows at public gyms
Industry leader and lawmaker propose solutions after ombudsman probe reveals severe shortages in mandatory briefing sessions
Hong Kong should make better use of its public gyms by allowing online safety briefings and penalising no-shows, an industry leader and a lawmaker have urged after the ombudsman identified management loopholes.
The Office of the Ombudsman launched the inquiry into public gym management on Tuesday, noting that rigid mandatory training requirements combined with a severe shortage of places were creating significant barriers to public participation and leaving facilities underused.
The watchdog also flagged booking loopholes for monthly ticket holders, including late cancellations and the absence of penalties for no-shows.
Gordon Yau Yick-chung, chairman of the Hong Kong Fitness Guide, on Wednesday described the briefing and training requirements as outdated.

- U.S. President Donald Trump's claim that Russia and Ukraine agreed to a ceasefire he announced on Oct. 11 is unproven. Ukraine said it had no knowledge of such an agreement, and Russia didn't comment.
- The claim stemmed from a post on Truth Social in which Trump wrote: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Later, in response to questions about Ukraine and Russia agreeing to it, Trump said, "They agreed because I said they agreed."
- Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelenskyy told Axios the ceasefire was "news" to him but he would support it if Russia agreed to follow it. Russia didn't comment either way, saying "contacts are ongoing." However, Ukraine accused Russia of attacking its energy facilities on the very same day.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. Snopes has reached out to the Russian Foreign Ministry and will update this post accordingly.
On Oct. 11 U.S. President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that Ukraine and Russia had "agreed" to an "energy ceasefire" in their war. Such an agreement would means neither country would attack the other's energy sites. 
The ceasefire appeared to be news to Ukraine and Russia, however, with Trump unable to provide any evidence that the two countries had actually reached such an agreement.
Numerous posts claimed Trump had not actually managed to get the countries to agree. When a reporter pointed out to Trump that both sides said they had not agreed, Trump replied: "Well, they agreed. You know why? Because I said, 'You agree.' That's why."
It wasn't clear whether Russia had or hadn't agreed to a ceasefire before Trump's announcement, but news reports stated that Russia violated the ceasefire shortly after. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he didn't know about the supposed ceasefire agreement beforehand but would support it only if Russia agreed to follow it.
"Even after yesterday's messages from [Trump] … Putin attacked our gas infrastructure," Zelenskyy told Fox News. "When we speak about energy ceasefire, it means only one thing: that they don't attack our energy infrastructure and we don't respond on their energy infrastructure."
Snopes reached out to the Russian Foreign Ministry to seek comment on Trump's announcement and a response to Ukraine's accusations that Russia violated the ceasefire. We will update this story as we get more information. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told the media on Oct. 12 that "contacts are ongoing."
Snopes has covered a great deal of misinformation about the Russia-Ukraine war since Russia invaded the former Soviet republic on Feb. 22, 2022.

Epic Games is shifting to an “AI first” development strategy for its collaboration with the Walt Disney Company, letting AI models write all the code and guide all the artwork for an upcoming shooter. That’s according to a Bloomberg report, which cites unnamed people familiar with the project who commented on the significant pivot in internal development at the Unreal Engine maker.
Human developers will be tasked with managing and guiding code and art assets generated by models such as Anthropic’s Claude, according to internal Epic employee messages viewed by Bloomberg. That means “no more hand-written code” and art assets “generated with full AI workflows,” according to the report.
The $1.5 billion collaboration between Epic and Disney, announced in early 2024, was slated to release a Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter in March 2027. That project has now been delayed indefinitely amid the AI-related shakeup and understaffed, slower-than-expected development thus far, according to the report.
“We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do,” an Epic spokesperson said in a statement.
“We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Epic CEO Tim Sweeney wrote on social media shortly after the Bloomberg story was posted. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.”

Swans' Eom the target of alleged racism at Millwall
- Published
Swansea City head coach Vitor Matos says the lengthy stoppage during their 1-0 win away at Millwall was a result of racist abuse aimed at Ji-sung Eom.
The South Korea winger was among the Swansea substitutes, and had been warming up on the side of the pitch when the Championship game was brought to a halt.
Referee Edward Duckworth had lengthy discussions with both sets of coaches, during which the game was paused for around seven minutes.
Following the stoppage, an announcement was made over the speakers at The Den confirming there had been alleged chants of racism and that police were working to identify any offenders using CCTV.
Speaking after the game, Matos said it was the 24-year-old who had been the subject of the abuse.
"The situation was with Ji-sung Eom," said Matos.
"The referee followed the protocol for these sort of situations, they did the right thing. Millwall also did the right thing to get the protocol moving on.
"We all know there is no space for this, this kind of situation should not happen.
"When they do happen we are here to stand with the player, in this case it is our player."
The incident marred what was otherwise an evening of celebration for the Swans, as Ronald's late strike sealed a 1-0 win for the league leaders.
Millwall stated they were "aware of an alleged, individual incident of discriminatory abuse towards a Swansea City player during the second half" of the game.
"The club operates a zero-tolerance policy towards any form of discriminatory abuse. Any individual found to have engaged in such behaviour will face the strongest possible action," added the hosts.
"The club is working alongside the relevant authorities to establish the facts and is unable to comment further as tonight's alleged incident is the subject of an ongoing police investigation, which the club fully supports."
Victory kept Swansea two points clear at the top of the Championship, with the Welsh club putting together their best start to a season in a century.
Matos said he was saddened by the abuse aimed at Eom, but says the rest of the squad will rally around their team-mate.
"He is a smart kid, he is not happy with the situation but he knows we will stay with him and follow the situation as long as we can," added Matos.
"Millwall did the right thing by announcing there is no place for this sort of thing.
"I'm happy with how it was handled, but really sad that it happened. Now it is about evaluating the situation and we'll see what happens."

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer, according a statement by the Vatican on October 13, 2026
The 71-year-old spiritual leader of the Roman Catholic Church was in the operating room for about 3 hours, and the surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes. The lower lobe of his right lung has been removed after the diagnosis.
The surgery was successful and there were no complications.
The pontiff has lung adenocarcinoma, according to a bulletin by the Vatican.
It added that tissue tests conducted during the operation confirmed what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations.
What is lung adenocarcinoma?
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), lung cancer is a disease in which cells in the lung grow out of control.
Lung cancers are grouped into two main types called non-small cell and small cell.
The CDC website adds that “non-small cell lung cancer is the most common type of lung cancer” and “it grows more slowly and often doesn’t cause symptoms until it is advanced.”
The website adds that adenocarcinoma, the type of cancer Pope Leo XIV is suffering from, is the “most common type of non-small cell lung cancer” and “begins in cells in the alveoli, which are tiny air sacs in the lungs that make mucus.”
Current status of Pope Leo XIV’s health
The Pope regained consciousness normally after the operation and later returned to his hospital room, where he was resting, Reuters reports, while citing the Vatican’s medical bulletin.
It added that the Vatican had said earlier this week that he was expected to remain in hospital for about a week, and all his public events have been cancelled until October 20.
Pope Leo was seen waving to a supportive crowd of well-wishers before heading to Rome’s Gemelli Hospital. Several of his supporters shouted “auguri” (best wishes) to their religious leader before his surgery.
The Christian leader is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru from November 6 to 17, 2026, but it was not clear if the trip would still go ahead.

Karnataka has urged the Centre to extend price-control measures beyond cancer medicines to other high-cost, life-saving drugs used to treat cardiac and kidney diseases, following the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority’s (NPPA) in-principle approval to cap trade margins on certain non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines at 30% of their maximum retail price (MRP).
Addressing presspersons in Bengaluru, Health Minister U.T. Khader said price rationalisation should translate into direct savings for patients, and urged the Union government to extend similar measures to other essential medicines where high treatment costs place a burden on patients.
At its meeting on October 8, the NPPA gave in-principle approval to rationalise trade margins on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines identified under Paragraph 19 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013. The measure is subject to finalisation of the list of medicines to be covered.
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has been asked to constitute an expert committee under the Directorate General of Health Services to recommend the anti-cancer medicines to be brought under price control. The committee is expected to submit its report by October 14.
The Centre estimates that the measure could reduce the MRP of several anti-cancer medicines by 20% to 70%, potentially saving patients around ₹2,500 crore. “The financial strain of cancer treatment often pushes families into debt, making it inevitable for them to exhaust their savings and sell assets to meet medical expenses,” Mr. Khader said.
Citing examples, the Minister said a cancer drug/injection costing around ₹3,250 was reportedly priced at ₹23,347. Medicines with a landing cost of about ₹3,000 are being sold at a cost of ₹27,000. Under the 30% trade-margin cap, the maximum price of a medicine would depend on its applicable pricing base and can substantially reduce out-of-pocket expenditure for patients, he explained.
Also Read: Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing
Karnataka’s representation to the Centre
In a letter dated September 23 to Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda, the Karnataka government had sought national-level action after inspections in the State found substantial differences between the procurement costs of medicines and the prices charged to patients. The State identified pricing concerns involving 253 medicines and consumables with mark-ups.
Karnataka had sought the inclusion of advanced chemotherapy, targeted therapy and other expensive cancer medicines under the ambit of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, along with a comprehensive cap on trade margins for high-cost and life-saving medicines.
The State had also called for expanding the NPPA’s price-control oversight and strengthening enforcement against excessive charging and profiteering.
Disclosure of medicine costs in hospital bills
The State has also sought greater transparency in the prices charged to patients. A circular issued on October 1 asked healthcare institutions to disclose both the purchase or landing cost and the MRP of medicines in patient bills. The instructions are advisory in nature and are proposed to take effect from November 1.
Karnataka’s call follows observations by the Supreme Court questioning why the MRP of essential medicines, including cancer drugs, could not be capped at 16% above the price to retailers, as is applicable to scheduled medicines under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013.
The State said the proposed 30% trade-margin cap on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines should be followed by wider action to cover other essential, high-cost medicines, including those used in cardiac and kidney treatment, so that the benefits of price rationalisation reach patients directly.

India’s leprosy programme is falling short of several projections set for 2025-26. The country reported 91,783 new leprosy cases in 2025-26, 41.2% higher than the projected 65,000. New cases among children were 91.6% above the projection while the rate of Grade 2 Disability (G2D) among new cases was 1.34 per million, against a projected one per million.
India’s national prevalence rate was 0.56 cases per 10,000 population at the end of March 2026, below the elimination target of a prevalence rate below one case per 10,000.
But the burden remains concentrated geographically. Chhattisgarh had the highest prevalence among States/UTs at 1.66 cases per 10,000 population, followed by Jharkhand (1.51), Chandigarh (1.49), Odisha (1.25) and Maharashtra (1.14).
At the district level, 14.8% of districts had a prevalence rate above one case per 10,000 in 2025-26, down from 18.6% in 2013-14 but 114 districts still remained above the programme’s elimination target. Moreover, only 148 districts have provisionally achieved interruption of transmission, against a projected 300.
G2D was also concentrated in a few States/UTs. Chandigarh, Delhi, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Odisha together accounted for 42.5% of the 1,945 G2D cases reported in 2025-26. Chandigarh recorded the highest rate at 13.54 per million, followed by Delhi (11.53) and Chhattisgarh (7.87).
Single-Dose Rifampicin Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (SDR PEP), a preventive dose given to people who have been in contact with a leprosy patient, was administered to 91.2% of the 16.94 lakh eligible contacts in 2025-26, up from 71.4% of the 6.48 lakh in 2019-20.
Source: National Leprosy Eradication Programme (2025-26) and National Strategic Plan and Roadmap for Leprosy 2023-2027

Newly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has repeatedly described herself as an attorney.
The conservative commentator is now facing scrutiny about her legal qualifications after she was pressed to explain them following her first White House briefing with the media.
As President Donald Trump spoke to reporters after the briefing on Tuesday, one asked him where Zacharia had passed the bar exam.
"What state did she pass the bar exam in? You said she is an attorney. Where did she pass the bar exam? Which state?" the reporter asked.
Trump then turned to Zacharia, standing behind him, and asked, "Which state?"
"When I moved to China," Zacharia answered.
Her response added to the confusion over where she may be licensed to practice law in the United States. State bar exams are generally administered in person within the jurisdiction.
In a statement, Zacharia said she "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials." She did not say if she'd passed the bar in any state.
"Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team," Steven Cheung, White House communications director, said. "She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary."
Zacharia does not appear to be listed in the State Bar of California's attorney database, despite living and working in the state. She also does not appear to be listed in the D.C. Bar's member directory.
The Substack publication, Popular Information, reported earlier on Tuesday that it searched records in all 50 states and Washington, DC, and turned up no evidence that Zacharia is licensed to practice law.
Zacharia graduated from California's Pepperdine University in 2007 with a bachelor's degree in political science and government. She then received a law degree from the university's Caruso School of Law in 2011, according to the college.
The White House said that after she graduated, Zacharia moved to China with her husband for his job at an American private equity firm. She worked on international transaction law, according to the White House.
Her LinkedIn page says she served as general counsel for the California-based nonprofit Fix California from January 2024 to March 2025. More than a decade earlier, according to her LinkedIn, Zacharia worked as an associate at the Beijing-headquartered Zhong Lun Law Firm.
Trump announced Zacharia's appointment to the White House in a Truth Social post last week, saying she has an "unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning." He also referred to her as an attorney in the post.
In her own post that followed, Zacharia called serving Trump and the American people the "honor of a lifetime."
"I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work for him for a very long time," Zacharia said during Tuesday's White House press briefing.

Beneficiaries of the Public Distribution System (PDS) across Karnataka can use the ‘Anna Seve’ mobile application to complete their e-KYC process from October 14, allowing them to verify their identity without visiting fair price shops or government offices.
The app, which enables beneficiaries of schemes such as Anna Bhagya to complete e-KYC, was launched by Food, Civil Supplies and Consumer Affairs Minister Rizwan Arshad on October 1. It has so far been available on a pilot basis in eight districts.
Completed so far
According to the department, 1,60,267 beneficiaries in these districts completed e-KYC through the app between October 1 and 12. The app will now be available in the remaining districts as well.
Developed in collaboration with the National Informatics Centre and the Department of e-Governance, the app can be downloaded from the GooglePlay Store.
The facility is expected to help beneficiaries who migrate to cities and towns for work. Many had to travel to their native villages or visit government offices to complete the verification process. Others had to wait in long queues at fair price shops.
Repeat process
Of the 2,67,64,276 beneficiaries in Karnataka required to complete e-KYC, 2,06,76,278 had completed the process as on October 12. Beneficiaries who completed e-KYC more than a year ago must also repeat the process, according to a release from the department.
With October 20 set as the deadline, Mr. Arshad has urged those yet to complete the verification to use the app and finish the process at the earliest.

William Shatner wasn’t sure if the audience would approve of his new documentary or not.
When the 95-year-old star took the stage at the Regal Times Square theater for the New York premiere of The Sixty-Year Mission: How Star Trek Changed Television and the World he said “maybe you’ll like it, maybe you won’t.” But, the Captain Kirk actor declared, “you’re going to see a lovely film made by people who cared.”
Focusing on the original Star Trek series, which ran from 1966 to 1969, The Sixty-Year Mission is written and directed by Mark A. Altman, creator of the Inglorious Treksperts podcast. The documentary, which screened during New York Comic Con and hit select theaters this weekend, explores the show’s cultural impact and legacy, and also demonstrates how much it was a product of the political climate of the era in which it was made.
“I think audiences are pleasantly surprised that Sixty-Year Mission shows how the ‘60s shaped Star Trek,” Altman explains. For the film, Altman interviewed dozens of prominent fans and stars, from Shatner and Simon Pegg to Star Trek: The Next Generation stars Jonathan Frakes and Brent Spiner. The president’s niece—and Trek fan—Mary L. Trump praises the show’s pioneering representation, specifically Nichelle Nichols’ Lieutenant Uhura. George Takei, who played Sulu, gives a harrowing account of his time in an internment camp for Japanese Americans during World War II. Others discuss how characters like Spock became heroes for queer fans.
As has been well-documented, these considerations were important for Gene Roddenberry, the show’s creator, who died in 1991. He was a WWII veteran with a progressive bent despite years spent in traditionally conservative spaces like the US Army and the Los Angeles Police Department. Altman insists that “Captain Kirk was ‘JFK: Space Captain,’” and that President Kennedy’s idea of a New Frontier was the final frontier that Trek sought to explore.
Shatner, however, didn’t initially see the show that way at all. “I didn't think in those terms when they offered me the role,” says Shatner, who served as executive producer on Sixty-Year Mission. “I thought, ‘I got a regular paid job.’ Only later did the magic of Star Trek happen.”
Part of that magic, Shatner adds, is how “Star Trek had an effect on people’s lives.” Those people come from many backgrounds, and the show remained accessible because of the very special tension that existed within its politics, Altman explains. “Roddenberry was liberal on social issues but hard-nosed on defense, and that is absolutely what Star Trek is,” he says. “We need our phasers to defeat the Klingons, but we believe in a diverse crew.”
Karim Diané, who plays Jay-Den Kraag on Star Trek: Starfleet Academy, notes that as the person playing the first openly gay Klingon character in the franchise, he’s playing someone who means a lot to viewers. “I wish I could release the DMs because the love I've gotten is overwhelming,” Diané says.
Trek even had a point of view on AI that feels incredibly relevant in 2026 as Trump and Silicon Valley leaders talk about a new era of “superintelligence.” The franchise’s most recognizable AI—the android Data from Next Generation—was an ideal version of the technology. In that series Data consistently struggled to be understood, as both smarter than humans and incapable of emotional intelligence. One episode, “The Measure of a Man,” even addressed whether Data was his own being or merely property.
For Spiner, who played Data, AI’s modern incarnation is far from the thoughtful machine he portrayed. “If only AI could be what Data was: responsible, truly concerned about humanity, considering what serves humans best as opposed to what serves profit best,” he says.

For at least several decades, people have attributed the following quote as something physicist Albert Einstein once said: "Learn from yesterday, live for today, hope for tomorrow."
On social media, users' posts pairing the quote with Einstein's name have appeared, for example, on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived) and X (archived).
(@ramblingsloa via X)
However, no evidence supported the claim that Einstein ever said the words. Research into historical records found that other people expressed the exact same thought without Einstein's name as early as the 1970s. Other persons from decades prior shared the same general idea, albeit in different words, about learning from the past (yesterday), that you can only live in the now (today) and have aspirations for the future (tomorrow).
No records from the years during or immediately following Einstein's 1955 death featured the quote with his name. The authoritative compendium "The Ultimate Quotable Einstein" also did not include the quote — or similar thoughts — in its text, not even in its list of misattributions.
If Einstein had truly spoken or penned the thought, credible historical documents, such as books or newspapers, would contain that information. It would not only appear in social media posts and on quote-collecting websites — two types of sources that can lack credibility.
Some posts, for example on Facebook (archived) and Reddit (archived), featured the incorrectly attributed quote with the added line, "The important thing is not to stop questioning." Einstein truly once said that sentence while talking about pursuing curiosity in life. Life magazine printed the "not to stop questioning" quote without the "Learn from yesterday, live for today, hope for tomorrow" part in 1955.
Researching the quote
As a small part of beginning our research, we noted that searching Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo failed to locate any credible historical records documenting that Einstein said, "Learn from yesterday, live for today, hope for tomorrow."
To perform deeper and more meaningful research, we then looked to archives of literature via Google Books, as well as newspapers on Newspapers.com, where we found several interesting results — though none indicated Einstein ever said the words.
For example, in 1965, a Kentucky newspaper credited a teacher named Donna Jean Roberts as saying, "Learn from yesterday and hope for tomorrow, but live today for today."
A 1971 Indiana newspaper article reported, "HERE'S A slogan which makes sense to Mack McGinnis: 'Live for Today—Dream for Tomorrow — Learn from Yesterday."
In 1972, a newspaper in Illinois printed the earliest record we found of the exact quote that users later wrongly attributed to Einstein. The paper credited the thought as the class motto for Gardner High School in Gardner, Illinois. Some books published in the 1970s also featured the exact quote without any direct attribution.
A 2000 classified advertisement for a California mobile glass company featured possibly the earliest newspaper record of the quote containing the attribution to Einstein. According to Google Books, the 1998 edition of "The Michiganensian," the University of Michigan's annual yearbook, also showed the quote with Einstein's name.
In 2011, an author wrote a book with the quote as the title, saying in the text that he was inspired to publish the work thanks to Einstein supposedly penning the thought.
1930 article about meaning of 'Today'
In all of our searches, one California newspaper article from 1930 featured the Chicago Journal of Commerce opining in a unique way about the meaning of "Today":
We live only today. Yesterday we lived, and through all the multitude of yesterdays, each of which had its influence in making us what we are today. What we do and are today will have its effect on what we shall do and be tomorrow.
We all live in the present—not in the past, which is gone forever, nor in the future which we cannot know until time makes it the present for us. We all have aspirations as to what we shall be and do in the future, but we have only our todays in which to put in action the principles and forces by which we may make our tomorrows what we would have them be.
We may, and must, learn from our yesterdays in order to make today count in our ambitions. Our mistakes in the past are warnings. Our achievements alone can encourage us by promises for the future. We all have our settled purposes as well as our past experiences, to guide us. Thus memories have power to help us to the future we desire. The purpose is a powerful incentive, strengthened by the knowledge if what has been accomplished in the past through definite purpose.
We learn from the past that all good things come slowly, that we must earn every advance we make. That is what makes today so prodigiously important to thinking men. It is the introduction to our tomorrow. When we go to bed after having done our level best, we have the finest assurance that we can do better tomorrow.
For further reading, we previously reported that Einstein truly married his double cousin.

Pope admitted to hospital for surgery to remove lump on his lung
- Published
Pope Leo XIV has been admitted to Rome's Gemelli Hospital for surgery to remove a lump on his lung, detected during what the Vatican has described as "routine checks".
It said the operation would take place on Tuesday afternoon.
The 71-year-old pontiff was met at the hospital by a large crowd, some of whom had been waiting outside for several hours to catch a glimpse of him.
They cheered greetings and well wishes as he passed, waving and smiling back through the lowered back window of his car.
He was then met by staff on the hospital steps. "I'm sorry," one of them commiserated, to which the Pope gave a smile and a shrug. "We're here for you," he was assured.
It was Leo XIV himself who on Sunday announced news of his operation to the world, speaking from the balcony in St Peter's Square after delivering the traditional Angelus blessing.
He said the nodule, or growth, on his lung was "contained" and had been found "at a very early stage", but that doctors had advised him to have it removed.
The Vatican said the Pope would be operated on by the Gemelli's thoracic surgery team and promised an update on his condition on Tuesday evening.
His schedule has already been cleared until 20 October to give him time to recover.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous. But doctors say when a lump is removed it will usually be tested to check for any sign of the disease.
The Vatican has stressed that the pontiff, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.
Cardinal Kikuchi Tarcisio Isao of Tokyo wrote on social media that he'd had an audience with Pope Leo on Monday, and said the pontiff felt "nothing wrong" physically.
He said the Pope had decided to check in for surgery as soon as possible because he was due to travel to Latin America in early November, and was keen to stick to that plan.
The trip is particularly significant because it includes a visit to Peru, where the pontiff was a missionary and then a Bishop for many years.
Despite all the reassurances, the news has shaken Catholics all over the world.
"Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly wasn't expecting anything like this," Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Parolin told journalists on Tuesday.
He agreed that the news was like a "bolt from the blue", but said the cardinals had been struck by the Pope's "serenity" and were confident in his recovery.
Outside Gemelli Hospital, which has treated several popes and is home to a large statue of John Paul II, a few Catholics lingered after the pontiff was admitted.
Carla had come specially, wanting to be close.
"He seems calm, so we are calm too - even though illness is always unpleasant," she told the BBC. "We will wait here and pray."
"I was in St Peter's Square when he made the announcement, and I felt really awful," said Elsa, who was also present. "I was really taken aback," she said, explaining that when Pope Leo was elected she had thought he was a younger, healthier pontiff.
"It turns out he's vulnerable too. I really hope it's something superficial, that can be contained, like he told us."
