Afcon final to play out in court - when will Morocco or Senegal be crowned champions?
- Published
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes but, in its own way, the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) has been playing out for nearly nine months.
Now, finally, one team or the other - either Morocco or Senegal - willl grab the winner. Only that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.
On Thursday, Sport's highest legal authority - the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) - will hear Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they had won back in January against the hosts in Rabat.
But those hungry for a resolution have already been warned it will not arrive on the same day.
So how did we get here? And what happens next?
What happened in the Afcon final?
In front of 66,000 home fans creating an electric atmosphere inside Rabat's Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco appeared set for a date with destiny as they chased their first Afcon title since 1976.
Instead, the final descended into chaos deep into stoppage time.
With the match still goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had already blown for a Moroccan free-kick.
The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a VAR review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.
Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.
Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Real Madrid's Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the grateful arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.
Or so they thought.
- 'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Senegal's triumph 
  - Published19 January
- Senegal decries imprisonment of fans after Afcon clashes 
  - Published24 February
Why was the Afcon final result overturned?
Unsurprisingly the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing Senegal had breached competition regulations.
Article 82, contained within a chapter titled "Withdrawals", states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team… leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" they shall be "considered the loser and shall be eliminated from the current competition".
In March, a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.
While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, others, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.
The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.
- Afcon final 'deficiencies' dealt with - Motsepe 
  - Published13 May
- Denounce 'abject' Afcon decision - senior Caf member 
  - Published19 March
What is the Court of Arbitration for Sport?
Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.
For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.
More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.
The appeal will be heard by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.
In this instance, the panel will be led by 76-year-old Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
If the panel fails to come to a consensus, its president will make the final decision.
- How does Cas work and why can't Man City appeal to it? 
  - Published28 September
When will we get a verdict?
While the hearing, which will be heard in private at the request of the parties involved, is expected to end on Thursday afternoon, Cas have already warned that this is merely the starting point of the panel's deliberation.
In a statement, the court warned it "cannot state when a final decision will be rendered but it will not be on the day of the hearing".
Having already waited nearly nine months to get to this stage, the bad news is that the Cas code states that appeal verdicts should be delivered a maximum of four months after a hearing, though guidelines also say panels should aim for less than three months.
The good news is that it can be quicker.
In 2020, Manchester City appealed to Cas over Uefa's decision to ban them from European club competitions for breaching financial fair play regulations.
The hearing took place on 8 June with the verdict landing in City's favour on 13 July.
What could the long-term fallout be?
Even though Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has already been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.
Caf president Patrice Motsepe said back in March that they will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.
The Teranga Lions' walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.
"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at a referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, back in April.
"This new rule will also apply to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."
Thiaw has already been given his marching orders by Senegal, having lost his job following the team's last-32 World Cup exit, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Moroccan dugout back in January, was dismissed in March.
Both men will no doubt still view success with Cas as a moral victory.
Whatever the outcome, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.
The FMRF's senior hierarchy were furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.
The FSF and the Senegalese government have, meanwhile, leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.
Other incidents also irked them, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which eventually led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf being tackled to the ground by three ball boys when he tried to intervene.
With the next Afcon scheduled to take place in June and July next year, the chances of a high-profile rematch between Africa's best two teams is a tantalising thought.
But while the chaos of this year's final may have given birth to a new rivalry for fans to revel in, there is unanimous agreement that such encounters should be settled on the pitch and not in a courtroom.

Thundering to a crowd of thousands of far-right supporters in São Paulo on 7 September, Brazil’s Independence Day, the senator Flávio Bolsonaro focused less on his opponent in the presidential election, the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, than on someone who is not running at all.
“Whoever votes for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes,” Bolsonaro shouted, referring to the shaven-headed supreme court justice once described as “Voldemort” by Elon Musk.
Although Lula did not appoint Moraes to the court, Bolsonaro’s supporters have linked the two men ever since the judge oversaw the case in which the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting a coup.
Now, just days before the election runoff on 25 October, Moraes is once again at the centre of a presidential scandal – one that Lula believes may have helped Flávio Bolsonaro overtake him to emerge as the frontrunner. The justice once hailed as democracy’s “saviour” for containing Jair Bolsonaro may now have helped pave the way for the family’s return to power.
The scandal began with a police investigation, which found that Moraes’s wife’s law firm had a contract worth about £20m with Daniel Vorcaro, the banker accused of orchestrating Brazil’s largest banking fraud. Text messages also emerged suggesting a close relationship between Moraes and Vorcaro, though the judge denies the messages are authentic.
Investigations subsequently revealed that at least four other justices had links to the disgraced banker, meaning half of the court’s 10 current justices have been drawn into the scandal.
The crisis peaked last month with a ferocious exchange of insults between Moraes and another justice during a televised court session. A series of rulings followed in which the pair – as well as other judges aligned with each side – overruled one another, dominating public debate for weeks.
Lula, the day after losing the first round, blamed his poor result in part on having to “carry on his back … the promiscuity” of the supreme court, in what many political observers saw as an attempt by the president to distance himself from the crisis. His campaign coordinator, Edinho Silva, said that, “in the eyes of society … [Lula] paid the price for that institutional damage”.
Although analysts point to a range of reasons for the far right’s lead, from household debt to a simple preference for Flávio Bolsonaro, many agree that the supreme court crisis played a decisive role, particularly among indecisive voters who, with the electorate generally divided between two similarly sized left and right blocs, are the ones who ultimately decide the election.
“These are people who thought that, just as they see congress, the country’s highest court had become corrupt, too. That deepened apathy among some who might otherwise have voted for Lula and fuelled the anti-system sentiment that feeds the far right,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right and has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters.
“We asked people about the court crisis, and they would say: ‘Everything is very confusing, but one thing we do know is that the big villain is Alexandre de Moraes,’” she said. “Precisely the judge who jailed Jair Bolsonaro now emerges, for these people, as the big corrupt figure and the main villain.”
Conrado Hübner Mendes, a professor of constitutional law at the University of São Paulo and a leading scholar of the supreme court, said Moraes put himself in that position by “embracing the role of heroic protagonist”.
The judge blocked some of Jair Bolsonaro’s moves during his government and drew the ire of far-right figures such as Musk and Donald Trump. The US went as far as to impose sanctions on him, in a move widely seen as an attempt to interfere in Jair’s trial.
On Monday, Moraes authorised Flávio Bolsonaro to resume visiting his father after a 90-day ban imposed in July, when the senator read out a letter from his father that Moraes considered a breach of Jair Bolsonaro’s ban on using social media.
Legal scholars and some on the Brazilian left, while acknowledging Moraes’s decisive role in the coup trial, have also criticised several of his other rulings as authoritarian.
“He took on a huge responsibility, and now he has thrown that away in the most mediocre way possible, with this alleged corruption case,” said Mendes.
While acknowledging the contract between the law firm run by his wife, Viviane Barci de Moraes, and the disgraced banker – who is worth an extraordinarily large sum by Brazilian law firm standards – Moraes denied any wrongdoing. He said he had never ruled on any case involving Vorcaro and that there was therefore no conflict of interest.
Vorcaro has been behind bars since he was arrested in November as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta. He is accused of leading a scheme through his Banco Master involving aggressive fundraising, unrealistic returns and falsified balance sheets that left an estimated £9bn hole, much of it involving public money and pensioners’ savings.
Text messages extracted from Vorcaro’s phone show that, two days before his arrest, the banker asked someone whom police later identified as Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?” Moraes denies being the recipient and accuses a fellow justice, André Mendonça, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, of using the police against him for electoral reasons, allegedly to benefit Flávio’s campaign.
Mendonça is one of the four other justices suspected of having links to Vorcaro. An institute he created is said to have taken out an £800,000 loan from one of the banker’s associates, though he says it has already been repaid. In the other justices’ cases, investigators uncovered links ranging from a £64m contract to an alleged stake in a fund that received £5.2m from Vorcaro. All deny wrongdoing.
No reports had linked Lula to the scandal until Friday, when Veja magazine reported that Vorcaro allegedly said he had paid £4.5m to finance a 2024 Oliver Stone documentary about the president. The federal police and the public prosecutor’s office, however, said the banker had neither made the allegation nor provided evidence to support it in his testimony. Lula denied receiving money from the banker.
Flávio Bolsonaro is being investigated over what happened to the £20m he was caught on tape asking Vorcaro to provide for a biopic about his father. One suspicion is that the money helped cover living and travel expenses for his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, during his self-imposed exile in the US, where he lobbied the Trump administration against Lula. The senator said all the money went towards sponsoring the film, which still has no release date.
Besides Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead, the far right’s sweeping victory ensured an even more conservative congress in 2027, including the senate majority needed to impeach supreme court justices – a demand among his father’s supporters since the former president was convicted.
“With the scandal, the justices handed Bolsonarismo something it still didn’t have: an impeachable offence that could justify their removal,” said Mendes. “A court that ignores conflicts of interest and immerses itself in relationships with political and economic power is a court that has already become corrupted.”
Even if no justice is impeached, should Bolsonaro win, he could be entitled to fill four seats as justices retire during his term, leaving the court with at least six of its 11 members appointed by either him or his father.
“We can expect a court completely servile to the government,” Mendes said, adding that the separation of powers would be at risk and that the justices themselves bear part of the responsibility.
“The court ended up doing to itself the work an autocratic project needs – and brought itself down”.

A large randomised controlled trial among heart failure patients in India led by the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST) in Kerala, has found that hospitalisation episodes and all-cause mortality among heart failure patients can be significantly reduced if patients are systematically followed-up by a nurse, with the help of a mobile health application.
The two-year Telemonitoring and Integrated Multidisciplinary care for Heart Failure (TIME-HF) trial found that heart failure patients with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) who received nurse-led collaborative care had a 22% lower risk of death than those receiving usual care. They were also more likely to remain alive without hospitalisation during the two-year follow-up.
The trial results were published in the American Heart Association’s Journal, Circulation, on August 30, 2026.
What makes the trial relevant is that it addresses critical gaps in heart failure care: in Keralam, heart failure registries have reported high mortality post-discharge — 82.7% mortality over 10 years, alongside the fact fact that only 25.4% of the patients with heart failure receive guideline-based therapies. It also holds lessons for the rest of the country: with nearly 27% of all deaths in India being due to heart disease, and 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease occurring between the ages of 40 and 69 years, there is an urgent need for quality, post-discharge care.
What the trial did
The TIME-HF trial involved 1,507 adults at 22 government and private hospitals in Keralam and neighbouring States, with 755 patients assigned to the intervention and 752 to usual care. The mean age was 61.9 years; 77.6% were men, 57.3% lived in rural areas and 70% had relatively low educational attainment. Ischaemic heart disease was the predominant cause of heart failure, accounting for 77.4% of cases.
Results indicated that nurse-led intervention substantially improved prescription of the four major components of guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure — renin-angiotensin system inhibition/ARNI, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors.
“Our heart failure patients receive sub-optimal care, as most of them do not adhere to therapies or follow up with the doctor on time. There is also the issue of physician inertia. HF Registry evidence indicates that the median survival after diagnosis of heart failure is just 3.7 years. This collaborative care model is proof that survival and quality of life of these patients can be improved if we systematically address the gaps in care so that proven therapies for heart failure become part of routine care,” said lead researcher and additional professor at SCTIMST P. Jeemon.
Centring nursing care
The model put a trained nurse at the centre of the care pathway, who would closely monitor heart failure patients after discharge, educate the patient and family about heart-failure self-care, lifestyle modification and encourage medication adherence.
Nurses reviewed the patients’ medication regimen at discharge to ensure that there was no deviation from the guideline-mediated therapies. This was again reviewed at every follow-up visit with the help of a mobile-health app. The m-health app helped the nurses monitor all physical parameters of the patient real time and to identify warning signs of worsening disease, communicate and connect with patients and physicians so that timely hospitalisation was possible.
All participants underwent scheduled follow-up visits every three months for two years. Adherence to all four guideline-directed medical therapies was only 22.1% in the usual-care group, while it was 37.3% in the intervention group at two years.
“The health system engaging with the patient regularly was the key here. The m-health app gave the patient updates in real time to the nurse. Oxygen saturation levels, weight gain, weight loss, drop in blood pressure or respiratory rate comes as alerts, and then were escalated to the physician,” Dr. Jeemon points out.
The TIME-HF trial thus helped address one of the health system’s persistent weaknesses: that of proper follow-up care of patients with chronic diseases. The model is suited for strengthening chronic disease management and reducing the burden of hospitalisation and mortality in resource-limited settings across the country, experts said.

SGH head of neurosurgery under probe for failing to report patient's death to coroner
Dr Jai Prashanth Rao said that he had mistakenly believed he had the discretion to decide whether to report the case to the coroner, and wanted to show compassion to the patient's family.
SINGAPORE: The head of neurosurgery at the Singapore General Hospital (SGH) is being investigated for failing to report a patient's death to the coroner as required under the Coroners Act.
Clinical Assistant Professor Jai Prashanth Rao heads the neurosurgery department of the National Neuroscience Institute (NNI) at SGH.
The investigation came to light on Wednesday (Oct 14) during the opening of a coroner's inquiry into the death of Madam Tan Suan Lin, 75, who died six days after undergoing surgery by Dr Rao. The operation was meant to remove a brain tumour.
Complications during the surgery on Jan 3, 2024, led to brain swelling and about 3L of blood loss, prompting Dr Rao to abort the operation and close the wound.
Dr Rao testified on Wednesday that he had initially told Mdm Tan's daughter and husband that he had to report the case to the coroner.
However, he changed his mind out of compassion and a desire to give the family closure and instead issued a death certificate.
Dr Rao explained that "probably my heart overruled my brain" and said he did not push back against the family's reluctance to have the case reported to the coroner. They did not want Mdm Tan to undergo an autopsy or sustain any more cuts.
The death certificate stated the cause of death as "malignant neoplasm – brain, unspecified", which Dr Rao said was intended to indicate that Mdm Tan had died from a brain tumour.
However, a forensic pathologist from the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) indicated that a possible cause of death was instead bleeding complications during surgical intervention for the tumour.
The case was flagged to the coroner by the National Neuroscience Institute (NNI) only about a year later in February 2025, following which a police report was filed in March 2025 over Dr Rao's failure to report the death.
No autopsy was performed as a result of the delay.
THE CASE
Three witnesses took the stand for the state on Wednesday, the first of whom was investigation officer Benedict Lim Wei Sheng.
He said that Mdm Tan first had progressive vision deterioration in her left eye from early 2023.
A brain MRI scan later revealed that a large brain tumour was pressing against her optic nerve.
She was counselled by Dr Rao and agreed to undergo brain surgery to remove as much of the tumour as possible.
The surgery proceeded largely uneventfully on Jan 3, 2024, until the team encountered extreme difficulty stopping the bleeding.
There was massive surgical blood loss of about 3,000ml, the brain began to swell and would have come out of the skull cavity if the swelling had continued.
Dr Rao thus stopped the operation and closed the skin before telling Mdm Tan's husband and daughter outside the operating theatre about the complications and her poor prognosis.
The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit, but her condition later deteriorated, and she died on Jan 9, 2024.
In the interim, Dr Rao told the family that Mdm Tan's likelihood of survival was not high.
He also told them there was a possibility that an autopsy would have to be done, although he was not the one to make that decision.
Dr Rao, who testified as the second witness, said that Mdm Tan's husband was not keen on this at first, but he tried to accept the rationale with further explanation.
However, Mdm Tan's daughter said many times that she did not want her mother to go through the process, Dr Rao recounted.
He said that she wanted her mother to retain "dignity in death".
MISTAKEN IMPRESSION
Dr Rao said he had been under the mistaken impression that only deaths occurring within 24 hours of a surgery required mandatory reporting to the coroner.
He thus assumed that he had discretion over whether to report the death.
He said he told the family that he would prefer to report the death to the coroner, but was motivated by the desire to "demonstrate compassion" and provide closure, as well as prevent further distress.
State Coroner Adam Nakhoda questioned whether Dr Rao had received any training on determining when a report should be made to the coroner.
Dr Rao said that such training occurs "when we are very junior". He added that he has since refreshed his memory and knows now that he ought to have reported the case.
"I work in a specialty that, unfortunately, when complications happen, they are severe," he said. "This is the only death I've had in 12 to 13 years."
He also said he was not sure where he got the mistaken impression that he only had to report deaths that occurred within 24 hours of surgery.
Dr Rao added that there were no unexpected events during the surgery that deviated from standard operating procedures, except for the brain swelling at the end.
"I couldn't explain the cause," he said. "But from my medical expertise, it seemed like a seizure to me."
He said Mdm Tan had been given the usual medication to reduce the electrical activity that causes seizures before the surgery, but such medication is not 100 per cent effective.
When questioned about the exact wording of the cause of death on Mdm Tan's death certificate, Dr Rao explained that a junior doctor had signed it.
This is because death can happen at any time, and junior doctors are usually on site.
Dr Rao said he had given instructions to indicate the cause of death as a brain tumour, but the junior doctor then went into the electronic system and selected the relevant category.
He was not required to review the cause of death after the junior doctor selected it, Dr Rao added.
An independent expert witness, who was called by the state, told the court it was obvious to him that the case should have been reported to the coroner, but said he empathised with Dr Rao.
"Yes, the death should have been reported because that is in our training and experience from the time we started this speciality, that has been one of the things that is highlighted," the expert said.
"However, the academic knowledge of it sometimes can be marred by emotions."
He added that as a surgeon himself he understood that the main surgeon is the one who bears "the most emotional burden", and it is "entirely reasonable" that this burden can sometimes cloud one's judgment.
The coroner's findings will be delivered at a later date.
Under the Coroners Act, any person who becomes aware of a death that is, or appears to be, a reportable death, must make a report to the police as soon as reasonably practicable.
Failure to do so without reasonable excuse is an offence, punishable by up to one month's jail or a fine of up to S$1,500, or both.
The Coroners Act lists examples of reportable deaths, including an unnatural or violent death, a death that resulted directly or indirectly from medical treatment or care, and any death in Singapore where the cause or manner is unknown.
CNA has contacted NNI for more information.

Centre invites bids for two offshore mineral blocks in Andaman Sea
The ministry issued the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) to grant operating rights for the Sewell Rise-01 and West Sewell Ridge-01 blocks under a composite licence.
The Union ministry of mines on Tuesday invited prospective bidders to explore two offshore mineral blocks in the Andaman Sea, spanning a combined area of 1,632 square kilometres, as part of efforts to strengthen India’s access to critical minerals used in manufacturing, clean energy and emerging technologies.
At an outreach programme in New Delhi, the ministry officials briefed stakeholders on the geological potential of the blocks, the auction procedures, the regulatory requirements, and the financial assistance available for exploration.
The ministry issued the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) on October 1 to grant operating rights for the Sewell Rise-01 and West Sewell Ridge-01 blocks under a composite licence.
Sewell Rise-01 covers 632 square kilometres, while West Sewell Ridge-01 spans 1,000 square kilometres. Both blocks contain polymetallic nodules and crusts that can contain nickel, cobalt, copper, and manganese.
Officials highlight importance
Ministry of mines Secretary Keshav Chandra underscored the importance of strengthening domestic mineral supply chains to support economic growth, technological advancement, the energy transition and manufacturing competitiveness.
He also highlighted the potential role of a Critical Mineral Processing Park being developed on India’s eastern coast in supporting offshore mineral processing.
Additional secretary Veena Kumari Dermal said the government had undertaken policy reforms to facilitate transparent and responsible development of offshore mineral resources.
“Taking stakeholder feedback into account, the ministry has revised block configurations, including increasing the area of polymetallic nodule and crust blocks to provide greater operational flexibility for exploration,” she said.
She added that the Terms of Reference and guidelines for collecting baseline environmental data and preparing environmental management plans for offshore mineral exploration and exploitation within India’s exclusive economic zone had been circulated to concerned central ministries and departments for comments.
“These will be finalised shortly,” she said.
The Geological Survey of India (GSI) outlined the geological characteristics and mineral potential of the two blocks. SBI Capital Markets Ltd, the transaction adviser, explained the policy framework, tender conditions and bidding requirements, while MSTC demonstrated the process of purchasing tender documents and submitting bids through its electronic auction portal.
The National Mineral Exploration and Development Trust (NMEDT) also explained a scheme providing partial reimbursement of exploration expenses to composite licence holders of offshore mineral blocks.
Auction details
The auction is being conducted under the Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Act, 2002, as amended in 2023, and the Offshore Areas Mineral (Auction) Rules, 2024, as amended. The framework aims to ensure transparent allocation of offshore resources and promote systematic exploration.
Tender documents went on sale on October 1. The pre-bid conference is scheduled for November 4, while the last date for submitting queries is November 13. Prospective bidders can purchase tender documents until December 21, with bids due by December 28.
The government said systematic exploration would be essential to establish the blocks’ mineral potential and assess their prospects for future development.

Greta Thunberg joins French teens protesting over run-down schools: ‘Whole world watching with awe’
She joined and applauded hundreds of teenagers who demonstrated boisterously outside school north of Paris

Greta Thunberg on Tuesday threw her high-profile support behind high school protesters rattling the government in France, saying “the whole world is watching with awe”.
She joined and applauded hundreds of teenagers who demonstrated boisterously outside a school north of Paris under the watchful eye of police.
The surprise appearance by the 23-year-old climate activist, along with another day of marches in the French capital and elsewhere, suggested that high school students’ push for more resources for run-down schools is far from running out of steam. That’s despite mass arrests, mounting injuries and fatigue from more than three weeks of blockading schools and demonstrating.
Police used clouds of tear gas, water cannons and repeated charges to disperse protesters Tuesday when violence erupted on the fringes of the Paris marches. The Interior Ministry estimated that 161,500 people marched in demonstrations across the country, including 41,500 in Paris.
Outside the Paul Éluard high school in Saint-Denis, where staff and students have long complained of dilapidated facilities and even rat infestations, Thunberg said French pupils are “fighting back, reclaiming their future that has been taken away from them” and are inspiring young people in other countries.
“The international community sees these students and they’re leading by example,” she said to The Associated Press. “This generation is one that has been growing up with a sense of hopelessness for the future, when we can see our future and our rights taken from us,” she said.
“Of course people are going to fight back,” she added.
The students’ grievances have resonated in neighbouring Belgium, where some schools closed in Liege.
Several Italian cities have also seen student protests, though on a smaller scale than in France and focused on broader complaints. In Germany, high school students are calling for an international youth strike on Nov. 20, in solidarity with the French protests.
Some French pupils say they see parallels between their protests and the “Cockroach” youth movement challenging the government in India and youth-led demonstrations a year ago in Morocco that also demanded better schools and hospitals.
Thunberg also cited protests in Spain, gripped by demonstrations for affordable housing, and in Latin America.
“These movements are connected in one way or another. We are fighting against the same system,” she said.
“Even though these local issues are different and may vary, we have the same enemy and I definitely think that these movements are inspiring each other.”
The government of outgoing president Emmanuel Macron, whose term ends in May, argues that the movement in France is losing momentum. The Education Ministry said fewer schools were closed Tuesday although the number of staff injured since protests began in mid-September has risen to 147. The government says hundreds of police officers have also been wounded but has not detailed the severity of their injuries.
Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. The interior minister suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand.
Pupils and university students who blockaded the Maurice Ravel high school in eastern Paris on Tuesday said they feel that their complaints are being heard by supporters in France and abroad but not by the government. Some vowed to keep protesting until that changes.
“We’re certainly making noise and getting people talking, but unfortunately, our message isn’t reaching the people who should be making the changes,” said Ryan, a 20-year-old student who said he didn’t want to give his surname for fear of possible repercussions.
“That’s why the movement needs to keep going and persist.”

As Stelco rejects demand to halt layoffs, NDP leaders call on Carney to nationalize steelmaker
Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis, Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles call for Stelco to be nationalized
Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis and Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles are calling on the federal government to nationalize Hamilton-based steelmaker Stelco, amid layoffs Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says violate the company's agreement under the Investment Canada Act.
In a release Tuesday, Lewis said the federal government should take "immediate action" after Stelco's American owner Cleveland-Cliffs broke its commitment to maintain the same number of unionized workers and similar numbers of non-union workers for five years when it bought the company in 2024.
Joly has vowed to take Cleveland-Cliffs to court, saying Saturday in a post on X that "all options are on the table" as government lawyers consider next steps. But Lewis said Tuesday that going through the courts will take too long to save those whose jobs are in the crosshairs.
"Canada cannot afford to lose its steel industry," he said. "If we’re serious about saving these jobs and the Canadian steel industry, we need immediate action."
An industrial worker walks near the Stelco Hamilton Works on Oct. 9. The American steelmaker announced 300 to 350 layoffs at the plant amid the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade war. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
Lewis noted that the United Kingdom nationalized British Steel in July, saying the move protected "thousands of jobs." In September, the U.K. government announced plans for the public takeover of another steelmaker, Specialty Steel.
Lewis also jabbed at Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves, who has expressed support for the U.S. tariffs on foreign steel that led to these layoffs, saying they "are designed to deindustrialize our economy and destroy our manufacturing base."
Goncalves maintains the company is within the law to conduct layoffs because they are temporary, until Canada and the United States reach a trade deal.
"There is no provision in the contract that I have to keep employment at a certain level every single day of the five years," Goncalves told CBC's Rosemary Barton Live on Sunday.
"If that was an imposition of the Canadian government, I would not have accepted."
Ontario NDP says Ford should offer steel industry relief
Speaking at Queen's Park on Tuesday, Stiles pushed for Ontario Premier Doug Ford to "work with the federal government to push Cleveland-Cliffs to give up their ownership interest in Stelco and establish public ownership and Canadian management."
“The cost of not doing this is thousands of jobs. It’s spinoffs. It’s the whole community of Hamilton that is impacted," she said. “The industry will lose out if we let Stelco go under.”
In a release issued the same day, Stiles and her Ontario NDP colleagues from Hamilton — MPPs Sandy Shaw and Robin Lennox — also said Ford should "get back to work and deliver a tariff relief package for the steel industry," as well as a "Buy Ontario First" procurement strategy. The Ontario government remains on a 21-week summer break that ends Oct. 27.
CBC Hamilton asked Ford's office for a response to the calls for nationalization but did not hear back by the time of publication.
When asked last week whether his government would consider such an action, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he would wait to hear Cleveland-Cliffs' response to Joly's letter demanding the jobs be reinstated, and then he would "take appropriate action."
The company has since declined to reverse the layoffs.
Time now to consider public ownership, prof says
Nicolas Lamp, associate professor at the faculty of law and school of policy studies at Queen's University, told CBC Hamilton last week he thinks the government should step in and take public ownership before Canada's steel expertise is lost.
“At the moment when Canada is trying to build a lot of infrastructure, major plants, major projects, it's really a question of whether Canada should just let all that expertise kind of die," he said.
Lamp pointed to the purchase of the Trans Mountain pipeline from Kinder Morgan in 2018 as an example of the federal government taking on major infrastructure from a private company.
Mike Watt, whose career at Stelco spans 20 years, standing outside the Stelco Hamilton Works on Oct. 9 after receiving a layoff notice. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
“I'm not saying we should definitely nationalize it,” he said.
“I would say that the Canadian government really has to look very closely at what the reasons for these layoffs are and whether a company that was more sympathetic — that had the Canadian workers and also the Canadian national interest in mind — would act similarly.”
Last week, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he supports the government taking legal action against Stelco. He reiterated that Tuesday, but said the best way to fix this problem would be getting a deal to remove the tariffs.
"Our message to the prime minister is get back to the table and get a tariff-free deal," he said in Windsor on Tuesday.
"The workers at Stelco, Stellantis, Ford and every other trade-dependent company in this country are relying on the PM to keep his word and get a deal."

Pressure on Norway in play-off final - Wilkinson
- Published
Rhian Wilkinson says the pressure will be on Gemma Grainger's Norway in their Women's World Cup play-off final against Wales in December.
Wales moved a step closer to reaching the Women's World Cup for the first time as a 3-0 win over Albania in Llanelli secured a 4-0 aggregate success in their play-off semi-final.
Wales now face a step up in a class as they take on a Norway side ranked 14th in the world, but Wilkinson insists Wales can "absolutely" cause an upset as they are reunited with former boss Grainger.
"The pressure is always on the big nations and that's something I think we thrive on," said the Wales head coach.
"We're a small nation, we fight for each other. You see some of the play tonight [against Albania] any you'd be proud of [that] from any team in world.
"[There were some] fantastic levels of play and that's with probably one of the younger teams that's playing in this competition right now, so I think it's an exciting time and why not be excited about the possibility."
The play-off final first leg will be played at the Cardiff City Stadium on Tuesday, 1 December before the return leg in Norway four days later.
Norway, the 1995 world champions, have reached every Women's World Cup since the tournament began in 1991.
They will begin as firm favourites against Wales, who are ranked 17 places below them by Fifa and who have never beaten a top-20 ranked side in a competitive fixture.
But Wilkinson insists Wales, whose only previous major championship appearance was at Euro 2025, can cause Norway problems.
"They're a team that's performing well, that's doing well, as are we and we've got some fantastic players that can absolutely go toe-to-toe with them," she added.
"I've just talked to the staff I think everyone needs a few days off to rest and recover.
"Then we're going to go again, do the best we can to deliver a team that's going to fight for their country."
The complex nature of the qualifying process means that even if they were to upset Norway, Wales may not be guaranteed a place at next year's World Cup.
Depending on which other sides come through the eight European play-off finals, Wales may have to negotiate an inter-confederation play-off next February to secure their spot in Brazil.
"The World Cup is off in the distance - I'll keep saying that because we don't even know if and when we beat Norway if that's the final hurdle," Wilkinson said.
"So it is the next game in front of us - we don't get too far ahead. It's the next job and we've got a lot of work to do as a staff."
Mayzee Davies, Elise Hughes and Hannah Cain found the target as Wales eased to victory over Albania having limped over the line in the first leg last Friday.
"I think we know that the performance away wasn't one that we were particularly pleased with," Wilkinson said.
"I thought we lacked intensity, lacked teeth in our defending, we weren't connecting our passes in a way I know we can.
"Tonight was the absolute reversal of that. I thought from the first minute Angharad [James] led her team in an intense, strong performance where the team really showed what they're capable of. It was fun to watch."

After Rahul Gandhi, Asaduddin Owaisi moves SC against SIR; court agrees to hear plea on October 15
Referring to the petition, Asaduddin Owaisi's advocate told the bench that it concerned the manner in which the SIR exercise was being conducted.
Amid growing opposition to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi on Wednesday moved the Supreme Court, challenging the manner in which the exercise is being conducted. The court agreed to hear his plea alongside other petitions on Thursday.
Advocate Nizamuddin Pasha, appearing for Owaisi, urged a bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi to list the petition alongside similar matters scheduled to be heard by the top court on Thursday, news agency PTI reported.
Referring to the petition, Pasha told the bench that it concerned the manner in which the SIR exercise was being conducted. Responding to the request, the CJI-led bench indicated that it would examine the matter and the reference to similar petitions. Pasha submitted that the relevant cases had been identified in the memo accompanying his request for listing.
Deep Dive
Owaisi's petition comes amid a series of legal challenges to the SIR process and alleged voter deletions linked to the revision.

Rahul Gandhi, 10 INDIA bloc leaders also move SC
Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and 10 other INDIA bloc leaders filed a petition in the Supreme Court on Monday against the Election Commission of India (ECI), raising alleged discrepancies in voter deletions and other issues linked to the SIR process.
The petition was filed by Gandhi along with Congress president and Leader of Opposition in the Rajya Sabha Mallikarjun Kharge, Trinamool Congress MP Saugata Roy, Samajwadi Party president and MP Akhilesh Yadav, Rashtriya Janata Dal leader Tejaswi Prasad Yadav, Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut, CPI(M) general secretary MA Baby, CPI general secretary D Raja, Jharkhand Mukti Morcha MP Mahua Majhi, NCP (Sharad Pawar) MP Supriya Sule and Indian Union Muslim League MP ET Mohammed Bashir.
The petition seeks to highlight alleged discrepancies in voter deletions during the SIR exercise. It also seeks the summoning of records concerning decisions taken by the ECI and an independent probe.
Following this, the top court registry flagged 14 defects in the petition filed by Gandhi and the 10 other INDIA bloc leaders, preventing it from being heard on Tuesday.
The defects included a ₹220 shortfall in court fees, an illegible photocopy of Kharge's identity card and missing vakalatnamas for nine of the 11 petitioners.
Opposition march to Supreme Court

The Supreme Court of India agreed to intervene for Delhi’s voters deleted from the electoral roll pursuant to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), and are now effectively being asked by the Election Commission of India to misrepresent themselves as fresh applicants by filling out Form 6 to restore their names on the voter list.
A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant was informed by advocates Prashant Bhushan and Neha Rathi, appearing for petitioners Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri, that deleted voters seeking re-inclusion in the electoral roll are being compelled by the Election Commission (EC) to file a declaration that they had never voted before or face imprisonment.
Form 6, prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules of 1960, requires every applicant to affirm that they are “applying for inclusion in the electoral roll for the first time”.
“The EC should either allow them to file Form 8 [for shifted voters] or create a new form for voters deleted in the SIR,” Mr. Bhushan submitted.
He said the Delhi SIR case was listed on October 30. But that would be too late, as the last date for filing claims and objections for the ongoing SIR was the same day.
The Chief Justice advanced the date of the hearing to October 28.
“We are thinking of passing an order which will take care of this issue,” Chief Justice Kant remarked.
The application has asked the court to direct the EC to frame an appropriate mechanism for restoration/inclusion of deleted voters without forcing them to apply as first-time voters.
During the enumeration phase of the SIR in Delhi, 47,56,722 electors, that is, 32.78% of the voters who existed prior to the start of the SIR, were excluded from the draft electoral roll under the category of ASDD (Absent, Shifted, Dead or Duplicate). For any person on the ASDD list, the only mechanism for filing a claim for having their name restored in the voter list is through Form 6.

“This creates a fundamental anomaly as all these people were previously enrolled on the voter list but are now required to submit Form 6 and make a declaration that they are seeking inclusion in the electoral roll for the first time, which is factually incorrect and wholly inapplicable to their circumstances,” the application said.
Further, it said these persons would become vulnerable to punishment for giving a false declaration under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, which provides for imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine or with both.
The petition also pointed out that the additional declaration form required to be submitted along with Form 6 was without the force of law and must be struck down. The additional declaration form, published in the SIR guidelines issued in June 2026, was subsequently modified in the SIR guidelines issued in October 2025 and the May 2026 guidelines applicable for Delhi.
It said that a clarification by the EC that the additional declaration form would not be required during the non-SIR period creates a parallel mechanism for the same purpose.

A landmark survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has revealed the once endangered species is thriving.
A population of Aldabra giant tortoise lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.
The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island.
This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.
The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022.
It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.
Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.
Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve.
“This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”
The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.
In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island.
But a recovery programme meant the island became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.
Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it.
“Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.
“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”
Despite the good news, the study’s authors warn that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.
The study authors say invasive mammals remain a key threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings.
The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.
“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.
“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.
“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”

Vaccine skepticism has worked its way from the fringes of the public to the highest levels of the federal government. The Trump administration is reportedly considering changes to a critical policy, the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, that has protected domestic vaccine supply for 40 years, which could further jeopardize vaccine access and even create shortages in the United States. These attacks on vaccines could have much more far-reaching impacts than may appear at first blush: They could effectively blow up a key pillar of the industrial policy that has maintained stable vaccine access in the U.S. for four decades.
This could create a situation where Americans who want vaccines can no longer get them. But as I explain in a new paper, the Trump administration doesn’t have to have the final word. Policymakers at the state level can step in to directly produce vaccines to prevent shortages and harm to the American people.
Vaccine access in the U.S. hasn’t always been guaranteed. In the 1980s, a flood of lawsuits alleged that the vaccines for diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough caused severe seizures in children. While researchers belatedly debunked many of those claims, vaccine makers wound up on the hook for significant payouts to litigants. This led vaccine makers to increase prices, and some exited the market entirely. By 1984, only one company was left producing the whooping cough vaccine in the United States and had raised its price tenfold. This led to shortages and jeopardized supply.
In response, Congress created the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP), a program that provides reasonable compensation to patients injured by vaccines while capping the legal liability for vaccine makers. Because vaccines are exceedingly safe, VICP payouts are rare. According to the government’s own data, between 2006 and 2024, more than 5 billion doses of covered vaccines were distributed in the U.S. During that period, around 10,500 injury claims were awarded compensation under the VICP — or about one individual per 1 million administered doses. The VICP has sustained stable vaccine access while ensuring fair compensation for injured patients for 40 years.
But the Trump administration may be about to upend the VICP, and in doing so, could jeopardize the widespread access to vaccines that most Americans enjoy today.
First, reporting suggests that health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and one of his chief advisers may remove certain vaccines — such as the childhood vaccines it is attempting to render optional under federal recommendations — from the VICP, which would increase legal liability for producers of those vaccines.
Second, based on debunked claims connecting autism to vaccines, the administration may make conditions related to autism compensable “injuries” under VICP. That could quickly bankrupt the program: Such claims could produce $100 billion in awards, far eclipsing the VICP’s $4 billion balance, and approaching 20 times the amount the fund has paid out for all claims to date over its entire existence.
If the VICP is rendered a shell of itself by federal policy, private vaccine makers could retreat from the U.S. market, viewing it as too risky with too much legal exposure to do business. That could lead to vaccine shortages — and a situation where Americans who want vaccines can no longer get them — and ultimately declining immunization rates, more outbreaks of communicable diseases, and more avoidable deaths.
To avoid that outcome, states can step in to create public factories to directly produce vaccines. There is a strong tradition of public factories for vaccines in the United States. For example, in 1894, Massachusetts created a public drug manufacturer and research lab known as MassBiologics, which has produced vaccines for smallpox, tetanus, typhoid, and pertussis, among other biologic products. MassBiologics, now operated by the UMass Chan Medical School, remains the nation’s only nonprofit vaccine manufacturer, and currently produces a vaccine against tetanus and diphtheria that is distributed nationwide.
If the Trump administration persists in jeopardizing the country’s vaccine supply, Massachusetts and other states can mobilize new or existing publicly owned vaccine production facilities to produce those vaccines that would otherwise fall into shortage. Each state could use its health department or university system to establish production facilities to manufacture vaccines jeopardized by federal policy. Those states could license vaccine formulations from the private manufacturers exiting the U.S. market.
Because these production facilities are owned by states, they would be protected by the legal doctrine of sovereign immunity, which insulates states from lawsuits — allowing them to avoid the uncapped risk problem that would otherwise deter production by private manufacturers. To compensate patients with rare but legitimate vaccine-related injuries, each state could create a “mini-VICP” that provides modest, capped payouts for injuries.
These states can serve as a last line of defense against the Trump administration’s anti-vaccine policy. Moreover, states could join forces to create public factories to avoid shortages for critical vaccines.
State vaccine production could face a few conceivable roadblocks.
First, private vaccine makers may be reluctant to share proprietary information involved in vaccine formulation with state governments. States can make these companies more willing to license their vaccines by incorporating strict nondisclosure agreements and restricted use clauses in their licensing agreements.
Second, the Trump administration could try to prevent states from manufacturing vaccines. However, state-run vaccine production may be exempt from Food and Drug Administration regulation, which under the law is permitted to regulate “persons,” not states. This could limit the Trump administration’s ability to obstruct state-run factories.
There is a final impediment states could face: time. Building a new factory, outfitting it for production, and actually producing vaccine doses could require a significant amount of lead time. To expedite production, states should consider using existing facilities, such as purchasing or leasing space from public, nonprofit, or private entities.
Regardless, time is of the essence. There are few institutional barriers standing in the way of the Trump administration doing immense harm to public health by damaging vaccination in the United States. State governments should therefore begin contingency planning now. For more than 100 years, public factories have helped protect Americans’ access to vaccines — and they can meet the moment again now.
Joel Dodge is the director of industrial policy and economic security at Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator.

Rusty or something more? South Africa's concern after Australia loss
- Published
First Test, Durban (day five of five)
Australia 390 & 314-6 dec: Renshaw 82; Nortje 2-56, Maharaj 2-56
South Africa 284 & 206: Markram 75; Hazlewood 6-49
Australia won by 214 runs
South Africa's 12-match unbeaten run came to a shuddering stop with defeat against Australia in Durban, but were they simply rusty or is there more to read into a Test match in which they were outclassed across the five days?
The world champions held on until an hour into the afternoon session on the final day – Aiden Markram fought admirably for 237 deliveries – but Australia, led by Josh Hazlewood with career-best figures of 6-49, eventually broke any lingering resistance to go 1-0 up in the three-match series.
"I would like to see more fight," said Proteas coach Shukri Conrad. "I don't know if it is alarming [but] it is concerning."
So should South Africa be worried at the start of an eye-catching few months which includes the visit of England over Christmas?
Rusty batters or something more?
Much was made of South Africa's run to the 2025 World Test Championship final at Lord's.
They played only 12 Tests – no team played fewer – and qualified after drawing at home against India and losing in New Zealand, before beating West Indies, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Pakistan.
Mitigation for this latest Test also comes from the fact this is their first in almost a year and the majority of their batters played one domestic red-ball match to prepare.
Australia recently came off an eight-month break of their own and lost to Bangladesh in home conditions, as Conrad was keen to point out.
And last summer's famous win over Australia and a 2-0 success in India proves they can beat the world's top teams.
However, this Test only reinforced a worrying trend among South Africa's batters.
Tristan Stubbs and Ryan Rickelton are fine white-ball players, but Stubbs' two Test centuries have come against Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, and Rickelton's against Sri Lanka and Pakistan.
This was an obvious step up.
In the first innings, Stubbs, two overs after Wiaan Mulder had been bounced out, top-edged a pull to fine leg, and in the second he played a loose drive on one.
Opener Rickelton drove and edged at a wide ball late on day two and nicked through a pull in the fourth over on day four.
Similarly, Mulder scored 367 not out against Zimbabwe last year, but Bangladesh are the only other side he averages more than 30 against. His 110-ball stay for 29 on the final day before being strangled down the leg side was at least encouraging.
Wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne, in contrast, lasted only three balls before nudging Matt Renshaw's part-time spin to slip. His Test average of 30.14 drops to 28 against Australia and 15 against both England and India.
Conrad said that "a few of the guys need to step up".
"The real disappointment was the batting in the first dig on a really good wicket," Conrad said.
"Yes, a world-class attack, but quite a few guys getting starts and not kicking on."
Markram & Nortje the positives
Aiden Markram's defiant knock in the fourth innings, in which he batted for almost six hours for 75 runs before edging Mitchell Starc through to Alex Carey in the afternoon session, was one positive for the Proteas.
David Bedingham also looked comfortable in his new position of number three, albeit he was one of those guilty of failing to make the most of starts after reaching 49 and 46.
This defeat was not solely on the batters, either.
Bavuma, who tasted defeat as captain for the first time in this match, allowed the game to drift on day two as Australia extended their score from 124-6 to 390 not out.
Australia's Matt Renshaw played brilliantly for his 190 but was not challenged as he casually farmed the strike and protected Nathan Lyon in their ninth-wicket stand of 134.
And while judging them against Australia's fearsome attack, the most successful quartet Test cricket has seen, is hardly fair, South Africa's bowlers lacked the relentless pressure of their counterparts.
Anrich Nortje was impressive in taking four wickets in his first Test since March 2023. His last spell was quicker than his first as he brought pace and hostility, hitting Steve Smith on the helmet with a bouncer on day four.
But Mulder offered little after his new-ball spells and Marco Jansen was quiet after dismissing Nic Maddinson and Steve Smith on day one.
The return from injury of their premier quick Kagiso Rabada, who was seen bowling at lunch on day five, cannot come soon enough.
Spinners Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj did not escape Conrad's gaze either.
"Anrich's return was phenomenal and really pleasing," Conrad said.
"If we were brutally honest, our spinners were not as sharp as they normally are."
With the second Test starting in only five days' time in Gqeberha, South Africa must hope this Test has removed the rust.
The alternate takeaway would be far more concerning.

Man Utd defender Lisandro Martinez extraordinarily calls out club's hierarchy after Atletico Madrid loss in Champions League
Man Utd's Lisandro Martinez astonishingly attacks club's hierarchy after Champions League loss at Atletico Madrid; Martinez told Amazon Prime: "We expect more from the top, from upstairs, to bring in more players to compete"; he added: "I expect more from our technical director"
Wednesday 14 October 2026 00:06, UK
Manchester United's Lisandro Martinez launched an extraordinary attack on the club’s hierarchy after their 2-0 Champions League loss at Atletico Madrid.
In an astonishing post-match interview, the Argentina international criticised the lack of summer investment in the squad.
The defender said he had expected more from "upstairs", singling out technical director Jason Wilcox, in the most recent transfer window in which they failed to improve their options at left-back and up front.
Man Utd spent £155m on just four major summer signings after a third-place Premier League finish last season, which earned a return to the Champions League for the first time in three years.

"I have to control myself a lot, but sometimes it's a reflection of how our club is at the moment," Martinez told Amazon Prime.
"We had a fantastic season last season, and now we expect more from the top, from upstairs, to bring in more players to compete because many teams have brought in many players as well."
Asked whether he had expected more investment in the squad in summer, Martinez said: "Yes, 100 per cent.
"I expect more from our technical director. I have to be honest. And also, as a player, we have to do more.
"It's also important to build a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night."
Tuesday's loss in Madrid extended Man Utd's winless run to five games, piling pressure on boss Michael Carrick.
"He does his best," he said of Carrick. "But every season is different. You can't stay with what you did last season.

Carrick and Tielemans asked about Martinez comments
It was a jaw-dropping interview that Youri Tielemans, one of three outfield summer signings, refused to comment on, while Martinez's outburst dominated the post-match press conference with Carrick.
Asked if he agreed with Martinez's view, he said: "Well, I haven't seen the interview. I've half heard about it in the other interviews I've done.
"I think it's a little bit on the emotions of the game as well, coming here and being disappointed not to get something from the game.
"Straight after a game for me is not the time to talk about that interview because I haven't seen it, so I can't really comment on that.
"But I think it's important for us to move forward quickly, really. I think there's a big game on Sunday, and it's really important that we move forward and we stay focused on that.
"There's disappointment within the group. I'm bitterly disappointed in certain things, and the boys are as well as a group."
Rooney heavily criticises Martinez outburst
Manchester United's all-time leading scorer Wayne Rooney speaking to Amazon Prime:
"It's a difficult one because I always used to think I was outspoken as a player and you want to have your opinion.
"I think he has maybe gone a bit too far. That's for the manager, and that should really stay internal.
"The fans want to hear the players speak; they want to hear the players care, so you can clearly see he cares and he wants the team to invest more money, and more players, and to do that he is probably one of the players who is out the door through his performances. His performances haven't been good enough.
"But I think in some ways he is right in terms of the club needs to invest more, at the top end of the pitch and in defence as well.
"But it looks like that was a bit of an agenda; he's wanted to say that, because that doesn't mirror the performance. I thought the performance was better.
"It's a bit disrespectful to his team-mates as well. He is disrespecting his team-mates because he's saying the team isn't good enough.
"Bruno (Fernandes) is the only one who has any right to come out and say anything like that as captain. And even then it should be behind closed doors if there are issues, which does happen.
"Players have conversations with the manager, the manager has conversations with the board, but that interview is not going to help the situation the club are in at the minute.
"That's going to bring a greater noise around it; the players are not happy, they're not settled, they don't trust in their team-mates. That's not going to help at all."
Carra: It's awful from Martinez
Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher speaking to CBS Sports:
"Doesn't do anybody any good at all, and they will be the story now for the next few days, all about this.
"Now, as supporters, every set of supporters don't like the suits or the guys upstairs, so United fans will lap this up and think it's great. I think it's awful that he's come out and said that right now. I do.
"And when he's saying 'we had a fantastic season last season', they didn't. A manager got sacked last season. They finished third because they had no cup games. They weren't in Europe. They got knocked out of the cup competitions very early.
"The reason they finished third is that Liverpool and Chelsea were that bad as well. Now we're seeing the real Manchester United this season."
Analysis: Martinez unlikley to last long at Man Utd
Sky Sports' Zinny Boswell:
Everyone has heard a Manchester United fan voicing the criticisms made by Lisandro Martinez in Madrid. It is another thing entirely to see a player doing it.
Many of those fans will see Martinez's comments as a necessary intervention to address an issue which long pre-dates INEOS' involvement at Old Trafford but has certainly not been helped by Sir Jim Ratcliffe's minority investment.
Others, like Wayne Rooney, will question the player's motives. Martinez has entered the final year of his contract and cannot claim to have done enough to have earned another. Perhaps he has been told as much. Players who speak out publicly like this do not tend to last long.
Cristiano Ronaldo called out the Glazers in 2022 in his famous Piers Morgan interview and left United within a week. Martinez's compatriot Cristian Romero criticised Spurs' hierarchy in January in an Instagram post and was gone by the summer.
Irrespective of Martinez's motivation, it is hard to argue with his point. United set Carrick up for a fall by failing to sign a left-back or a striker over the summer. The midfield rebuild that was hyped up for many months before the summer has not lived up to expectation either.
It is hard to understand quite what the plan is at United looking back at the last few years. United have had three managers in that window of time. Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick. All with different approaches that bear little resemblance to the other.
Martinez's comments will not help Carrick. But given the sense of hopelessness that has engulfed the fanbase, you can understand why some will welcome his comments. Martinez is right in saying United's issues stretch far beyond the manager.
Your views on Martinez's interview...
Steve: Martinez is 100 per cent right. The board are an absolute disgrace; the biggest club in the world and yet they persist with the same defenders we've had for five years. Teams know our weaknesses; the board have once again let the manager down badly.
Jonesy: I don't agree with Martinez. They had money, but spent it on players like Andrey Santos who can't get in the Chelsea team - what makes him good enough for Utd? I saw professional players unable to execute simple passes, and lapses of concentration in defence, again. Not good enough!
Date D: You can change the manager as much as you want, but when the hierarchy stays the same, you get the same results. Well done, Martinez!
Ciara: For once, a Man Utd player coming out to call out hierarchy. What a legend.
Dantoken: I stand with him. Nothing changes until changes are made at the top of the club.
Garbs: Agree with Martinez, squad should be bigger and more quality. The main issues are with those above off the pitch.

Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of espionage, Moscow said on Tuesday.
Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it has joined western sanctions over its war in Ukraine. Russia has arrested several citizens of “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for western intelligence services.
Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, saying Imai was accredited with the ministry but was accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”.
Japan’s embassy in Moscow told news agency Kyodo that the government was trying to ascertain the journalist’s reported detention.
Russia’s FSB security agency said a Japanese national, who it did not name, was arrested on Sakhalin and alleged he had worked for Japanese intelligence to collect information about Russia’s defences.
The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him. The man was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention. It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Moscow and Tokyo have been locked in a territorial dispute for decades over the status of a string of islands in the Pacific Ocean, off the north-east coast of Japan and to the south-west of Russia’s Sakhalin region.
The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national”, and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, Russian news agencies reported, citing the agency.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December.
“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia … to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Zakharova said, alleging this was “not an isolated case”.
The Kuril islands – which Japan calls the Northern Territories – have been under Russia’s control since the end of the second world war, when they were seized by the Soviet Union.
Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an uproar in Japan. Tokyo has said it would continue implementing sanctions against Russia and supporting Ukraine.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap.
