Ryan Coogler's X-Files reboot gets a full series order from Hulu
It stars Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel as two new FBI agents that aren't named Mulder and Scully.
Hulu has officially picked up Ryan Coogler's X-Files reboot, after greenlighting a pilot back in February. Variety reports that Coogler wrote and directed the pilot, fresh off of Sinners, and will stay on as an executive producer for the rest of the episodes.
We don't know much about the plot here, though Coogler has made comments that suggest this is a sequel series of some kind and not a total reboot. He has called it a "new chapter" and that the team "wanted to honor everything that made the original series connect with so many people while also finding our own way into that world."
Both a reboot and a sequel series have their risks. X-Files was on for 11 seasons in total, with an absolutely nutty mythology that nobody in their right mind would be expected to remember. However, people tend to resent total reboots of properties that are highly beloved and aired in most peoples' living memory.
We do know that the show stars Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel as two FBI agents who are not named Mulder and Scully. Their characters have been described as "two highly decorated but vastly different FBI agents" that "form an unlikely bond when they are assigned to a long-shuttered division devoted to cases involving unexplained phenomena." That certainly sounds like X-Files to me.
Jennifer Yale is the showrunner, and not Coogler. She's written for shows like Legion, See, Dexter and Your Friends & Neighbors, among many others.
This pilot getting picked up for a full series order wasn't a given, despite the name recognition of Coogler and the X-Files IP. Hulu also greenlit a pilot for a Buffy the Vampire Slayer sequel series, which was helmed by Oscar-winning director Chloé Zhao. The platform eventually passed on that one, which is a bummer.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

A video of late actor Nana Patekar is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) amid the Cockroach Janata Party’s protest at Jantar Mantar. In the video, Patekar apologises to a man named Abhijeet before speaking in Marathi. The video is being shared with claims that Patekar was apologising to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke for not attending an event and was supposed to accompany him to the protest at Jantar Mantar. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows late actor Nana Patekar apologising to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke for not attending the protest at Jantar Mantar.
Fact: The video shows late actor Nana Patekar apologising to Marathi film producer Abhijeet Gholap for missing the NAFA Marathi Film Festival. Gholap, who produced the 2011 Marathi film Deool, shared the video on his Instagram account on 8 October 2026, stating that Patekar was unable to attend the festival. The video is unrelated to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke or the protest at Jantar Mantar. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
After reviewing the video with Google’s NotebookLM tool, we found that Nana Patekar speaks in Marathi, apologises to Abhijeet, and regrets not attending an event. Addressing Abhijeet, he says, “It was great working with you in the film Deool.”
Deool is a 2011 Marathi film in which Nana Patekar acted, and Abhijeet Gholap produced it. This suggests that Patekar was referring to Abhijeet Gholap in the video, not CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke. Patekar also praises Sonali Kulkarni, who acted in the film.
Further search revealed that Abhijeet Gholap had posted the video of Nana Patekar on his Instagram account (archived) on 08 October 2026. In the caption, he wrote, “Nana was unable to attend the NAFA Marathi Film Festival, and he promised he would definitely come this year. We will miss you very much.” In a Facebook post, he wrote, “Nana, you missed your visit. Now we will just keep waiting.”
Abhijeet Gholap is the founder of the North American Film Association (NAFA), which was established to promote Marathi films in North America. According to the organisation’s website, Gholap founded NAFA to bring together actors, directors, choreographers, singers, cinematographers and editors to create Marathi films, web series and documentaries based on local stories and subjects in North America.
To sum up, this viral video shows Nana Patekar apologising to film producer Abhijeet Gholap, not CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke.

10 dead, at least 20 missing after boat capsizes in Bihar’s Raghopur
Around 25 to 30 people were reportedly aboard the medium-sized boat, most of them travelling to attend a feast organised as part of Hindu funeral rituals.
At least 10 people have died and 20 others are missing after a boat capsized in the Ganga river near Rampur Shyamchand village in Bihar’s Vaishali district on Tuesday evening.
Around 25 to 30 people were reportedly aboard the medium-sized boat, most of them travelling to attend a feast organised as part of Hindu funeral rituals.
The boat was ferrying passengers between hamlets along the river when it overturned in the Raghopur police station area. Officials said an imbalance caused the vessel to capsize, though the exact circumstances of the accident remain unclear.
Some passengers managed to swim to safety, while others drowned. Locals rushed to help and alerted the administration after witnessing the incident.
Rescue teams, including personnel from the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), are searching the river for missing passengers. Darkness and deep water have hampered rescue efforts.
Raghopur Block Development Officer Seema Kumari confirmed the incident. A senior police official said the boat had been carrying passengers from one riverbank settlement to another.
Boat capsized in Bihar’s Samastipur
Earlier this year, at least three people died and four went missing after a boat carrying 14 passengers capsized in the Ganga near Sultanpur Diara in Bihar’s Samastipur district in May. Seven passengers were rescued safely, officials said.
The passengers, all residents of Bind Toli in Masoomganj under Patna district’s Barh police station area, had travelled to Sultanpur Diara for agricultural work. They were returning to Umanath Ghat with vegetables harvested from parwal fields when the boat overturned.
Mohiuddin Nagar circle officer Brijesh Kumar Dwivedi confirmed three deaths, saying the deceased included two men and one woman. Officials have established the identities of all three victims.
The Patna district administration said the boat departed from Bind Toli around 5.45 am with 14 people on board. The passengers regularly crossed the river to work in agricultural fields. An initial update from the administration said seven people had been rescued, two bodies recovered and five passengers were missing.
Officials cited strong winds as a possible cause of the accident, while Barh sub-divisional officer Garima Lohiya said the boat’s engine failed midstream. Rescue teams from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), along with the Patna and Samastipur district administrations, took part in the operation.
As news of the accident spread, local residents and relatives gathered at Umanath Ghat. Authorities continued the search for the missing passengers and carried out procedures related to the recovered bodies.

Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.
Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.
One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.
“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.
In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.
Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.
Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Journalists’ Syndicate, whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.
Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.
The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.
For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.
“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

The story so far: The Serum Institute of India’s indigenously developed quadrivalent human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, CERVAVAC, has received prequalification from the World Health Organization (WHO), allowing the vaccine to be procured by United Nations agencies and potentially supplied to countries running HPV immunisation programmes. The WHO lists its prequalification as effective from September 25, 2026.
The development is significant for India as well as the global effort to prevent cervical cancer. CERVAVAC is India’s first indigenously developed gender-neutral quadrivalent HPV vaccine and targets HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18. It is licensed in India for girls and boys aged 9 to 26 years.
CERVAVAC is the first Indian-made quadrivalent HPV vaccine to receive WHO prequalification. This prequalification means the vaccine has met WHO standards for quality, safety and efficacy, following evaluation of data, samples and manufacturing sites.
Globally, cervical cancer caused an estimated 604,000 new cases and 342,000 deaths in 2020. In India, where cervical cancer remains a public-health burden, the national HPV vaccination programme was launched on February 28, 2026, targeting about 1.2 crore 14-year-old girls with a free single dose; more than 80 lakh doses had been administered by September this year, according to the Union Health Ministry. India’s national HPV vaccination programme uses Merck’s Gardasil-4, a quadrivalent vaccine protecting against HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18.
India also has an indigenous quadrivalent vaccine, CERVAVAC (now WHO-prequalified) and access to other HPV vaccines, including Gardasil 9 and Cervarix, through the private market.
What exactly is WHO prequalification?
WHO prequalification’s biggest significance is access. A vaccine that has already been licensed in India can now potentially enter international procurement channels used to supply national immunisation programmes, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.
WHO prequalification is not a marketing authorisation or regulatory approval. For the prequalification, the vaccine undergoes assessment of its quality, safety and efficacy, including evaluation of data, testing of samples and inspection of manufacturing facilities. A vaccine that meets WHO standards is placed on the WHO List of Prequalified Vaccines, making it eligible for procurement by United Nations agencies and giving countries an internationally recognised assurance about the product and manufacturing standards.
What is HPV and why is this important for prevention?
HPV is an extremely common sexually transmitted infection. Most infections clear naturally, but persistent infection with high-risk HPV types can lead to cervical cancer. WHO estimates that persistent infection with high-risk HPV types causes more than 95% of cervical cancers. HPV can also cause anal, vulval, vaginal and some other cancers, as well as genital warts.
The vaccine is a cancer-prevention vaccine and not just a vaccine against an infection.
WHO’s priority target is girls aged 9–14 years, before exposure to HPV. The organisation recommends either a one- or two-dose schedule for this age group, depending on the vaccine and national programme.
The four HPV types targeted by CERVAVAC are important for different reasons. HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk types responsible for a large proportion of cervical cancers. Types 6 and 11 are responsible for most anogenital warts. The quadrivalent vaccine therefore provides protection against both cancer-associated HPV types and genital warts.
Its indication for both sexes also matters. Although cervical cancer is the largest component of the HPV disease burden, HPV can cause disease in men, including anal cancer and genital warts.
What could the WHO listing mean for India?
CERVAVAC’s WHO prequalification does not automatically mean that it will now be substituted into the Indian government programme. Vaccine selection for a national programme involves considerations including regulatory status, evidence, price, supply capacity, presentations, logistics and programme requirements.
But the new status gives India another WHO-prequalified HPV vaccine from a domestic manufacturer. It could also potentially strengthen competition and supply security if CERVAVAC is considered for future procurement.
How many other Indian vaccines have WHO prequalification?
India already has a substantial presence on the WHO prequalified-vaccine list.
Serum Institute is among the largest Indian participants. The company has WHO-prequalified vaccines covering a wide range of diseases, including BCG, diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis combinations, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b, measles, measles-rubella, measles-mumps-rubella, meningococcal disease, pneumococcal disease, polio, rabies, rotavirus, rubella and malaria, among others.
Other Indian manufacturers with WHO-prequalified vaccines include Bharat Biotech, Biological E, Zydus Lifesciences, GreenSignal Bio Pharma, Haffkine and Panacea Biotec, among others.
Bharat Biotech’s Typbar-TCV, for example, was the first typhoid conjugate vaccine to receive WHO prequalification; Zydus’s ZyVac TCV received WHO prequalification in September 2026.
What is different about CERVAVAC?
The HPV milestone is distinctive because, until now, WHO’s prequalified HPV portfolio consisted of vaccines manufactured outside India. WHO’s HPV product-choice document lists bivalent vaccines such as Cecolin, Cervarix and Walrinvax, quadrivalent Gardasil, and nonavalent Gardasil-9. CERVAVAC was previously nationally licensed but was not WHO-prequalified.
Its inclusion therefore adds an Indian-made HPV vaccine to the global WHO-prequalified pool.
For India, the larger significance is that a vaccine developed and manufactured domestically can now potentially contribute not only to India’s cervical-cancer prevention programme but also to HPV vaccination programmes elsewhere.
The WHO’s global target is to have 90% of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15, alongside screening and treatment targets for women. By the end of 2025, HPV vaccination had been introduced in 165 countries, but global first-dose coverage among girls was only about 33%, well below the 90% target.

Days after Ukrainian military drones took down several Russian data centers, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that the campaign had hurt Russia’s disinformation efforts. “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms,” Zelenskyy said Monday. “There was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations.”
Russian bot farms are still trolling, even after Ukraine’s drone strikes on Yandex
Zelenskyy celebrated ‘less division’ on social media after the strikes but the data isn’t backing that up yet.
Zelenskyy isn’t the first to assert that the drone operation, which targeted data centers belonging to the Russian technology company Yandex, has cut down on spam and disinformation campaigns fomented by Russian bot farms. Social media users have claimed they’ve noticed less traffic on posts by MAGA-affiliated accounts, as well as those associated with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. Some have even said they’ve noticed a steep drop in spam calls and messages.
But these people are wrong. The drone strikes appear to have affected Yandex’s web crawlers, not any disinformation or political operations.
In fact, the account antibot4navalny, which tracks state-sponsored troll farms, reports that bot traffic is steady as ever. On Monday, the same day Zelenskyy claimed that disinformation had died down, antibot4navalny reported that several Kremlin-aligned accounts posted videos falsely claiming that experts are demanding the European Union lift the ongoing sanctions on Russia. Danish analyst Valdemar Osted said interactions on MAGA and AfD accounts have actually increased since the strikes. And the charts purportedly showing a decline in bot activity appear to be AI-generated.
Ironically, claims that the drone strikes hindered Russian disinformation campaigns appears to be a form of disinformation itself, no matter what Zelenskyy says.

The Delhi Police crackdown on the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protest on October 10 has drawn international scrutiny, with human rights bodies and press-freedom organisations flagging police excesses, and international media outlets reporting on the severity of force used against young protesters.
Police detained over 2,000 protesters and used force to suppress the mobilisation in the national capital. In arguably the most brutal assault on press freedom in India since the Emergency, journalists from both independent and mainstream media outlets were stopped from doing their work and detained in a display of police excess that bordered on madness. Some were dragged by their clothes, pushed and manhandled, some had their phones snatched, and pressured to delete footage of police action.
‘Restrictions Violate India’s Obligations under Int’l Law’
The global human rights non-profit Amnesty International on Friday put out a statement urging Delhi police to ensure that the fundamental right to peacefully protest is guaranteed to Indian citizens. In the statement, titled, ‘Delhi police must facilitate right to peaceful protest amid lockdown-like restrictions in capital’, Amnesty highlighted that “approximately 22,000 armed personnel from across the country have reportedly been brought to Delhi, in addition to more than 10,000 Delhi police officers expected to be deployed.”
Aakar Patel, chair of board, stated: “From denying permission for a peaceful demonstration, halting all Delhi-bound trains, and sealing the city’s borders, to issuing an internet suspension order near the protest site, and pre-emptively arresting activists – India’s authorities are leaving no stone unturned in their bid to prevent this march from happening. The right to protest is protected in India’s constitution. The authorities must immediately lift all these arbitrary restrictions, which violate India’s obligations under international law.”
After reports of rapid mass detentions began to surface on Saturday, the United Nations Human Rights Commission published a press release: ‘Concerns over mass detentions before and during protests’. Spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan called for the unconditional and immediate release of all those arbitrarily detained. “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled. Restrictions on peaceful protests must meet strict tests of necessity and proportionality. The Indian authorities should also ensure law enforcement forces exercise utmost restraint in response to peaceful protesters, consistent with the country’s democratic traditions and human rights obligations,” read the statement.
Similarly, the global media watchdog Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) urged Delhi police to “immediately release all detained journalists and media workers, return their equipment, investigate reports of physical abuse, and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests…and the police response without interference.”
CPJ highlighted the detentions of Newslaundry reporters Ashwine Kumar Singh, Astha Savyasachi, and Anmol Pritam, and Scroll reporter Ayush Tiwari. “Newslaundry has also reported that police seized its reporters’ phones, while other reports indicate that journalists were physically manhandled,” the statement read.

Putting out a list of around 20 journalists detained through out the day on October 10, global journalists’ body Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said, “Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police’s actions against the press are unacceptable.”
BBC Focus on Scale of Government Pushback
The BBC published at least five reports specifically focusing on the heavy security deployment, police crackdown and mass detentions. The BBC published first on Saturday, ‘Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest’. The report highlighted the sheer scale of government pushback — it stated that the BBC saw at least five people being detained near the site as “police and paramilitary personnel [were] stationed behind barricades and ropes, preventing people from entering the protest site…and drones could be seen flying overhead.”
The report stated that 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed and that the “restrictions caused major disruption across central Delhi, with traffic diverted from several key roads.” It also mentioned the “dramatic scenes” involving Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi and other Opposition leaders since October 6, as the police vehemently prevented them from agitating.
In a second report, the BBC reported the detention of Dipke, Das, and Ranka and hundreds of other demonstrators. In ‘‘Cockroach’ group leaders among hundreds detained in Delhi protest’, BBC highlighted the way the three were detained before they could even deboard their flight, prominent protest face, All India Students’ Association (AISA) leader Neha Bora’s detention, and how more protesters were jam packed into buses than on the streets. “The large number of protesters expected to descend on Delhi were unable to get anywhere close to Jantar Mantar due to the heavy security presence and road blocks,” the report stated.
In a third report on October 11 — ‘Delhi sees more protests as freed ‘cockroach’ group’s leaders vow to fight on’ — after the detainees were released, the BBC highlighted the 7,000 protesters who were detained and released on Saturday and hundreds were also detained on Sunday. The report led with Dipke’s promise to continue fighting. BBC also posted live updates on the detentions on its website.
The New York Times also published multiple reports on the wrath the Delhi police unleashed on the protesters on Saturday. All their reportage described the scuffle between the state agents and the demonstrators with headlines reading: ‘Indian Police Round Up Protest Leaders and Lock Down Delhi’, ‘From a Sikh Sanctuary to Chaotic Streets, Protesters Brave Police in Delhi’, and ‘Blocked by Police, India’s Youth Voice Their Fury’.
‘Indian Police Round Up Protest Leaders and Lock Down Delhi’ read the headline of a report published by US-based news outlet NPR. The report described at length how “Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India’s youth…sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.”
Highlighting the elaborate measures taken by Delhi police to curtail the movement on Saturday, the report stated: “The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities’ determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilised thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi.”
The British news outlet The Guardian also extensively covered the police action on Saturday. Alongside Dipke’s video from when he was being arrested inside the aircraft, where he can be heard saying, “You can see where the nation is heading…this is dictatorship,” the outlet published a report ‘‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown’, wherein it describes the police lockdown as “severe”.
‘Modi is in Trouble’
Qatar-based Al Jazeera reported on the mass detentions on Saturday, and published a feature headlined ‘Meet the man helping India’s detained protesters get home’ and an opinion piece ‘Modi is in trouble’ on Sunday.
The former video report featured 25-year-old Rajiv Choudhary who built an AI-powered app to help the detainees get home safely after police drop them off at the city’s outskirts; the latter opined that the protests “exposed India’s hollowed-out democracy.” “These acts further erode the tenuous position Modi is in, prompting more rebuke from critics who now question his fitness to occupy the office of the prime minister. On Friday, the opposition parties, led by Rahul Gandhi, met President Draupadi Murmu and submitted to her that the government had subverted India’s democratic framework…Under Modi’s watch, problems have accumulated like barnacles on the side of the ship. Every time he has been challenged, he has gone farther away from the democratic principles on which this nation was founded,” the article read.
British news agency Reuters published at least six reports on the protest since Friday. The first report, ‘Why India’s tens of millions of voter deletions have led to widespread protests’, discussed the contentious SIR deletion which have led to the mass outrage and protests.
“The BJP and the Commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately impacted by the deletions…They say the deletions have affected the outcome of some recent state elections that the BJP won, and have cast a shadow on the electoral process in the world’s biggest democracy,” explains the report.
On the day of the protest, another report details the preemptive measures and subsequent police action. With the headline, ‘India detains thousands, locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest’, the report describes the frequent protests as a “new challenge to Modi”. “The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi…The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027,” it states.
While various other articles report on the CJP leaders’ detention and eventual release, the police excesses faced by thousands, a news feature by the agency spotlights Neha Bora’s rise “as one of the most visible faces of a protest movement in India that has mounted the most serious challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government in years.”
Germany-owned international broadcaster DW published four reports on why the protests were taking place, the dramatic detention of CJP leaders ahead of the protest, the police crackdown on Saturday, and the CJP leaders’ vow to continue protesting despite the heavy police action, respectively.
In the report, ‘Indian authorities crack down on ‘Cockroach’ protest’, which was accompanied by a 24-minute-long video carrying footage of the police excess, DW describes the crackdown as “extraordinary”. “Indian authorities launched an extraordinary security operation in Delhi on Saturday to prevent a major demonstration…Roads across India’s capital were sealed, police checkpoints established and public transport heavily disrupted before demonstrators could gather,” the report read.
UK-based Financial Times published two reports on Saturday and Sunday, ‘Police arrest leader of India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement as protesters take to streets’ and ‘India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement plans more protests after release of leaders’, respectively. Both focused on the police crackdown and the protesters’ predicament.
While the global news hub CNN published multiples features on he CJP movement through May-July, on Sunday, it reported the release of the CJP leaders and the excessive police clampdown. In ‘India’s ‘Cockroach’ movement founder and leaders released from detention after Delhi protest crackdown’, CNN stated that the movement’s “target” this time around is the “62-year-old chief of the Election Commission that holds the keys to India’s democracy – the world’s largest – and who the CJP alleges is responsible for disenfranchising tens of millions of citizens.”
CNN witnessed, the report mentioned, that “despite the capital turning into a fortress to keep out protesters and mobile internet blocked, supporters gathered Saturday — as security moved swiftly to crack down on the unrest with many people at the protest site detained by police.”

Saudi Arabia overturns death sentence for man over Facebook comment, Sri Lanka says
- Published
Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court has set aside the death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan migrant worker over a comment he made on Facebook, Colombo's Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra said.
Anojan Sivarasa, 27, was sentenced to death in September after a Saudi appellate court convicted him of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over his comment.
The case sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, spurring diplomatic efforts to seek clemency.
Saudi Arabia's top court set aside the sentence on Wednesday, Hemachandra said in a post on Facebook, where he thanked the authorities and legal teams of both nations for their efforts.
In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.
During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Sivarasa to respond in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.
Although Sivarasa promptly deleted the comment and posted an apology video, a screenshot of it was brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.
It is not clear if there will be further legal proceedings or whether Sivarasa will remain in detention, and for how long. He was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of three million Saudi riyals ($0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court.
Faizer Mustafa, a Sri Lankan lawmaker who is involved in legal negotiations with Saudi Arabia regarding Sivarasa's case, confirmed to BBC Sinhala that Saudi Arabia had overturned the death sentence, adding that they are reviewing the Supreme Court's latest ruling.
Sivarasa's family had earlier said they have had no direct contact with him since 28 September.
International rights groups had also joined calls for Saudi to spare his life.
"Saudi authorities should end their use of abusive laws to hand out extraordinary sentences for speech-related offenses, especially against migrant workers who are already in a vulnerable position with limited protections," Joey Shea, senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch, said on Tuesday.

The rise and fall of a MAGA princess
How Kimberly Guilfoyle lost her ambassadorship.

Here's why your phone's proximity sensors are so important
They do way more than you might think.
Any recent smartphone, be it an Android device or an iPhone, is chock-full of sensors. It wasn't always this way, but after the original 2007 iPhone, many sensor-reliant features quickly became standard. And of course, phone makers are constantly trying to one-up each other, sometimes in ridiculous ways. For a few years, some Google Pixel phones offered external temperature readers — no matter that even if the technology were bulletproof, a phone would still be an unreliable way to check for fever, never mind whether your chicken is done.
Particularly important are proximity sensors. These are actually a category rather than a specific kind of sensor, but they're so critical that the phone you're using has several of them. Arguably, smartphones would be impossible without them.
Here we're going to cover what constitutes a proximity sensor and how your phone uses this data. Some good news is that the data is rarely of interest to anyone but yourself. With, perhaps, a couple of major exceptions.
The main proximity sensors in your smartphone
The most basic proximity sensor in your phone is the one used to shut off the screen whenever you raise it to your ear. This relies on infrared and/or capacitive technology. It not only prevents accidental touch commands, but also extends battery life, since the display will always be one of your phone's most power-hungry components. It's pointless for it to outshine the sun while you're on a 40-minute tech support call.
Some phones rely on advanced infrared sensors to detect when you are nearby. The best example of this is Apple's Face ID, which projects a series of dots to create a facial depth map and compares that against one you saved during calibration. The main purpose of this is replacing passcode and password logins. In some cases, however, facial recognition is "attention-aware" — meaning that whether or not you're looking will determine things like screen brightness, alert volume or whether sensitive content is shown. Given the potential for abuse, companies go to extreme lengths to prevent facial recognition data from leaving your phone, including heavily encrypted authentication chips.
Another sensor connected to valuable info is your phone's NFC (near-field communication) chip. This detects a similarly equipped device and transmits data over an extremely short distance, generally just an inch or two. But because this enables things like retail payments, digital keys, device pairing and direct file transfers, it's crucial that only vetted apps have access.
The sensors you might have missed
Most touchscreens can be considered proximity sensors, actually. While pressure-sensitive screens exist, anyone who's used them can vouch for how cumbersome they are. Capacitive screens instead react to the electricity in your body, so even the slightest gesture will register. This is the source of a lot of accidental commands, as it's remarkably easy to bring your fingers close enough for the screen to register a touch without physically tapping.
At times, even your phone's Bluetooth module enters the game. Using Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), a phone can automatically detect and talk to some nearby devices, such as item trackers or "beacons" installed for things like advertising. There are more benign excuses for beacons, luckily. When entering a sports arena, a beacon might prompt your phone to display your season pass on the lock screen, saving you a few seconds.
If you want to stretch the definition of proximity, some phones use LiDAR sensors to map nearby rooms and objects or increase the camera's focusing speed in dim conditions by bouncing infrared light off of subjects. That second purpose is the main one, since, of course, a camera system has a hard time discerning objects when there's barely any contrast to work with.
Can you turn your phone's proximity sensors off?
Sort of. It's dead simple to disable things like Bluetooth or facial recognition, and Android phones should have an NFC toggle (look for options similar to Settings > Connections > NFC) if they support the technology. But you probably can't disable LiDAR or a screen's automatic shutoff sensor, at least without invoking a special developer mode that's intended only for the most tech-savvy users. iPhones are missing even that NFC toggle — the most you can do is disable features that exploit NFC, such as Bringing Devices Together under Settings > General > AirDrop.
As we've hinted, however, there's usually plenty to lose and little to gain by disabling proximity tech. A phone with Bluetooth and NFC off is potentially more secure, but hackers have to resort to extreme measures to exploit those systems. They're not directly reachable from the internet, and there's not much that can be triggered automatically in person. Facial recognition typically makes your phone more secure rather than less. It enhances your privacy in public and slows down thieves in the event that your phone is stolen. Infrared-based recognition is surprisingly difficult to fool, so they'll have to resort to brute-forcing your passcode.
Ultimately, it's just good to be aware of the sensors your phone is equipped with. That gives you a more realistic picture of its strengths and vulnerabilities. It's not magic, regardless of how Steve Jobs once pitched things. Humans engineered and tested all of this to maximize your convenience.

Home services company Urban Company is considering a fresh fundraise a little over a year after its stock market debut in September 2025, amid continued spending on its instant household services vertical InstaHelp. The company’s board will meet on Friday (October 16) to consider raising funds through equity shares or securities convertible into equity shares, in one or more tranches, it said in an exchange filing. The routes under consideration include a preferential allotment, private placement, QIP, or another legally permissible mode, or a combination of these. Urban Company is also scheduled to release its Q2 FY27 numbers on the same day. The fundraise proposal comes as the company continues to invest in InstaHelp amid intensifying competition from Snabbit and Pronto. The vertical’s expansion weighed on Urban Company’s profitability in FY26 and remained a drag in Q1 FY27. InstaHelp Weighs On Profitability Urban Company reported a consolidated net loss of ₹235 Cr in FY26, compared with a net profit of ₹240 Cr in FY25, while operating revenue grew 34% YoY to ₹1,692 Cr. In Q1 FY27, operating revenue rose 44% YoY to ₹528 Cr, while its consolidated adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to ₹65 Cr from ₹98 Cr in the preceding quarter. Excluding InstaHelp, the company reported an adjusted EBITDA profit of ₹67 Cr. InstaHelp’s revenue grew 26% QoQ to about ₹11 Cr, while its adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹132 Cr from ₹119 Cr in Q4 FY26. However, its adjusted EBITDA loss per order narrowed to ₹346 from ₹447 over the same period. Management has said spending on InstaHelp will remain elevated as the company seeks to strengthen its position in the category. During the Q1 FY27 earnings call, cofounder and CEO Abhiraj Singh Bhal said the vertical would continue to require investment for at least the next two years. He also said InstaHelp was likely to remain a low-margin business compared with Urban Company’s core India consumer services operations. Management does not expect to make money from the vertical over the next five years and is working on the assumption that it will break even by FY31. The proposed fundraise also comes while Urban Company retains a sizeable cash balance. It reported cash and treasury investments of ₹2,019 Cr as of June 30. Separately, ₹310.83 Cr of the ₹472 Cr raised through its IPO’s fresh issue remained unutilised at the end of Q1 FY27. The proceeds were allocated towards technology and cloud infrastructure, office lease payments, marketing, general corporate purposes, and issue expenses. Post-IPO Fundraising Gathers Pace Urban Company’s proposed fundraise comes at a time when publicly listed new-age tech companies are increasingly tapping equity fundraise opportunities, especially QIPs, to fund further growth soon after their IPOs. QIPs allow listed companies to offer equity shares or convertible securities directly to institutional investors like mutual funds, banks, and insurance companies. For instance, Kissht parent OnEMI Technology Solutions received shareholder approval to raise up to ₹832 Cr through a preferential issue, around four months after raising approximately ₹926 Cr through its IPO. Meanwhile, Swiggy raised ₹10,000 Cr through a QIP in December 2025, around a year after its stock market debut. Ola Electric raised ₹780 Cr through a QIP in June 2026, while Ather Energy raised ₹1,300 Cr through a QIP roughly 14 months after its IPO. Zaggle, RateGain, Nazara have also tapped institutional investors through QIPs. Travel tech company ixigo raised around $146 Mn through a preferential issue roughly 16 months after its listing. Ola Electric is now raising a further ₹1,000 Cr via rights issue that is set to open on October 22 for and close on October 30 at an issue price of ₹27 per share.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

Adam Rubin said he wasn't supposed to come into work on Tuesday.
The co-owner of Art of Play — a small Brooklyn-based shop with tarot cards, funky home decor, magic trick books, and a wooden bird named Molly — said he was supposed to get some stitches removed. Instead, he came in to answer questions about Kelly Clarkson's viral social-media complaint.
"It's like she threw a Molotov cocktail at us," Adam Rubin told Business Insider. "And we're just here to pick up the pieces."
On Saturday, Clarkson wrote on X that she had driven to Brooklyn to visit Art of Play and was treated as if she could not afford an item she wanted to buy. She compared the experience to the "Pretty Woman" scene, when Julia Roberts' character is dismissed by salespeople at a luxury store.
Art of Play has an altogether different story.
The store said Clarkson had asked to buy Molly, a one-of-a-kind bird automaton that was not for sale. Clarkson responded by calling the shop liars. On Tuesday, Rubin told USA Today the bird is now for sale for $15 million.
Internet sleuths have been attempting to sort out the drama, largely to no avail. Investigative journalist Pablo Torre is also on the case — an update Rubin declined to comment on.
The back-and-forth has pushed an otherwise sleepy block of Brooklyn into a surprisingly large online drama. Art of Play sits adjacent to a hospital and across from the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, in what Rubin called a "Robert Moses-abandoned" stretch of old buildings that had fallen into decay before businesses like his arrived.
On Tuesday, angry Clarkson fans showed up outside the shop, Rubin said.
"It's only a matter of time until a person carrying a Samurai sword and an 'American Idol' T-shirt shows up outside our store," he said.
Several nearby businesses told Business Insider they didn't see the protests. The neighborhood's older residents were largely unaware of the very online drama, they said.
The other businesses said the controversy only came up in conversations with people who worked in the area. They largely talked about the absurdity of their small neck of the woods getting national media attention.
The fight, Rubin said, has gotten ugly online — and he said Clarkson's international stardom plays a big role. Her X post, as of publication, has more than 45 million views, while Art of Play is a local retailer with 172,000 Instagram followers.
"We had no idea what would happen to us," Rubin said. "She did. She's the superstar."
Rubin said the store has received threats and a barrage of online hate. He's also gotten a ton of in-person love, he said, including from frequent customers and strangers who came to visit. A woman he doesn't recognize came by to give him a hug, he said.
The dispute is especially strange for Art of Play, Rubin said, because the business is built around in-person interaction. During Business Insider's visit, he noted that shoppers inside were talking rather than scrolling on their phones.
Rubin said he would welcome Clarkson back, but he said she should expect the same treatment as anyone else who walks in.
"We treated her like any other customer," Rubin said. "She wasn't happy because she wanted to be treated like a star."
Clarkson's representatives did not respond to a request for comment.

GTA 6 is reportedly coming to PC in early 2027
PC players might be able to dive into Jason and Lucia's story by the end of March.
PC players may not have to wait too much longer to jump into Grand Theft Auto 6. According to GamesBeat's sources, Rockstar Games' upcoming blockbuster will hit PC in the first quarter of 2027, just a few months after its debut on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on November 19.
That's a much shorter window than Grand Theft Auto 5's initial release on consoles and its arrival on PC. The previous game in the series made its debut on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 on September 17, 2013. It didn't come to PC until April 2015.
Most other developers and publishers have given GTA 6 a wide berth this fall, as it's all but guaranteed to be a massive hit that captures the attention of many players. It could well be the case that games that were supposed to arrive early next year end up being delayed to avoid competing with the PC port as well. The release slate for the first quarter of 2027 currently includes Stranger Than Heaven, Metroid Ravenous, Until Dawn 2, Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, God of War Laufey and Fable.
It's not clear when Rockstar will add the inevitable online mode (about which it's been tight-lipped) to GTA 6 either. However, Twitch CEO Dan Clancy has claimed that'll happen next year. For what it's worth, the hugely popular GTA 5 roleplaying mods are PC-only. Rockstar recently added a GTA 5 roleplaying option to its PC launcher, three years after it acquired the team behind roleplaying server company FiveM. Connecting the dots here, the company may be waiting until it releases the PC version of GTA 6 before it switches on multiplayer.

Cardiac rehabilitation, a multidisciplinary approach to recovery and risk-reduction, is an important addition to medications, interventional and surgical procedures in heart patients. A cardiac rehab programme usually includes medical assessments, supervised exercise, nutritional guidance, psychosocial counselling and health education tailored to the clinical, cultural and behavioural needs of the patient.
Cardiac rehab has been incorporated into the routine care of patients in developed countries, while it is just now gaining inroads in low- and middle- income countries like India. The primary benefits of attending a cardiac rehab programme are faster recovery from cardiac procedures, reduced risk of future complications, improvement in blood sugar, blood pressure and lipid levels, increased cardiorespiratory fitness, adherence to a heart healthy diet, better weight management, abstinence from tobacco and excessive alcohol consumption, better emotional health and health-related quality of life, and decreased mortality.
The scenario in India
There is now a growing prevalence of heart diseases in the young Indian population, both in urban and rural parts of the country. According to the Global Burden of Disease, 2021, heart disease is the most common cause of death in India, accounting for 28.6 lakh deaths. Estimates indicate that nearly 27% of all deaths in India are due to heart disease, while 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease in the country are premature, between the ages of 40 and 69 years. Among those who survive, the effects can linger for years, affecting productivity and quality of life. This has brought to the fore, the urgent need for more widespread and accessible cardiac rehab facilities. There is a wide gap in the number of heart patients requiring cardiac rehab and the actual numbers being referred for these services.
Barriers to rehab
Even among those who access and enrol in cardiac rehab programmes, not everyone completes the programme. The main barriers to completing the cardiac rehab program after enrolling include patients’ work commitments, family responsibilities, financial constraints, and medical complications. Programmes that can offer personalised solutions including flexible scheduling, return-to-work counselling, sliding scale payment options and close collaborations with the referring cardiologist to identify and treat complications early, could help decrease drop-outs. Programme facilitators must also be able to proactively identify cues for potential non-adherence and work with patients and their families to circumvent challenges and complete the programme.
What works
A ‘TRACK and CARE’ policy could help in improving patient engagement in cardiac rehab programmes. TRACK denotes establishing Trust, involving the patient’s Relatives, helping them set clear Aims for the programme, Checking on the progress made on a daily, weekly and monthly basis and finally remembering to say Kudos to every single positive behaviour change made by the patient. The CARE refers to multidisciplinary care, comorbidity care and holistic care, where various specialists work together to address the different medical and psychological needs of the patient.
Young people are increasingly contracting heart disease. Getting them back to be productive, healthy and happy members of society is vital. While prevention remains the most important goal, cardiac rehabilitation must become an important part of treatment, not just an add-on that is optional. And to do that, we have to proactively address the potential barriers to access, adherence and programme completion.
(Dr. Priya Chockalingam is the clinical director, Cardiac Wellness Institute, Chennai. drpriya@cardiacwellnessinstitute.com)

Google will let you distribute vibe-coded Android apps with just a Google account
The company is revamping the Play Store for the AI era with changes to publishing, recommendations and more.
As part of a collection of updates to the Play Store, Google has announced that it will allow anyone who vibe codes an Android app to distribute it through the Play Store with just a Google account. The company's app store has changed a lot in the last few years, both in the wake of Google's efforts to inject AI into everything and legal pressure the company has faced to open the Play Store to competitors. But this change could prove to be one of the biggest.
Users have been able to sideload APKs of Android apps to their phones or tablets for a while, with Google making the process more complex in the last year. This new publishing process will make things easier. Rolling out to users in the US and other select markets who are 18 years and up, Google will let you upload a vibe-coded Android app from Google AI Studio without a paid developer account. For those who aren't familiar, Google's AI Studio is capable of generating apps with just a written prompt to Gemini, and you can adjust your results with more prompts or directly editing the generated code yourself.
Your app will only be available on your own devices to start (including tablets and computers with access to the Play Store) in a new "personal library" section, but Google eventually plans to let you securely share your vibe-coded apps with friends and family, too. When you want to distribute your apps to a global audience, the company says it will also be possible to "graduate" to a professional developer account and submit your apps to the Play Store's normal safety reviews.
Alongside this major change to app publishing, Google is also making tweaks to app discovery and its ever-growing list of gaming-focused features. The company already introduced its biggest change, Ask Play, at I/O 2026, but now it's also bringing similar app discovery features to Gemini by allowing the AI assistant to surface direct links to Play Store apps in chats. Google will also feature more apps through its sports topic pages that appear in the Play Store during live matches. They'll now expand to cover soccer games from Premier League, Major League Soccer and more. In cars with Google built-in and Android XR, the company is also updating the Play Store's layout to better fit the size of your physical or virtual screen.
If you're specifically interested in finding games, the new Game Finder feature can recommend things to play that fit your unique taste. Google says it's able to offer these recommendations based on your Gamer DNA, a new taste profile that you can finetune with your preferences and favorite genres. In a roundtable with press, Google suggested it hopes to make the filters and genre tags increasingly granular, opening up the possibility of drilling down into, say, games that specifically offer controller support, for example. You can also find new things to play via the new game playlists feature, which lets you recommend a collection of mobile games for other people to try.
The company is updating the overall experience of playing games on Android, too. Its Sidekick overlay has a new feature that allows it to record 30-second clips of gameplay, and developers are receiving a collection of new tools they can use to increase engagement. These include Sprints, Community Posts and an expansion of the Quests feature.
Sprints are 48-hour in-game challenges that match you with players of a similar skill level to compete for the highest score. Quests, which allowed developers to reward players with Play Points, now also lets them provide in-game rewards. Finally, Community Posts adds a Q&A section to store pages so players can ask and answer questions about games in the Play Store.
The helpfulness of these new features depends a lot on your faith in AI's ability to build apps and offer recommendations. But they're a sign that Google is trying to stay competitive with third-party app stores now that they can be installed through the Play Store.

India's 'cockroach' leaders jailed after holding protest
- Published
Two top leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi.
Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka appeared before a magistrate on Wednesday after being detained at Jantar Mantar, a longstanding venue for demonstrations that police recently removed from the city's list of authorised protest sites.
The two were among a group who climbed a locked gate and crossed barricades to enter the site on Tuesday.
The GenZ-led movement has been protesting for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud - charges the poll panel denies.
Police accused Das, Ranka and their fellow activist Ajinkya Shinde of trespassing, breaching a peace bond, violating prohibitory orders and obstructing public officials - charges they deny.
Delhi's Special Executive Magistrate Court remanded Das and Ranka to five days in judicial custody, while Shinde was released on a personal bond. The two leaders can seek bail from a higher court.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who has been holding separate protests against the Election Commission, condemned the arrests, describing them as "an act of cowardice", and expressed support for peaceful demonstrations at Jantar Mantar.
"Students. Youth. Journalists. The [opposition's] INDIA bloc. Different banners, one cause. All protests are one: citizens demanding their constitutional rights," he wrote on X.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who was travelling to Delhi after the arrests, accused the government of cracking down on dissent and challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to "declare the Emergency officially", according to news agency PTI.
His comments drew parallels with India's 1970s Emergency, a period when civil liberties were curtailed under then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.
The CJP, which is a pressure group and not an official political party, has been demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
Wednesday's actions follow a weekend of protests during which Das, Ranka, Shinde, and Dipke were taken into preventive custody ahead of planned demonstrations at Jantar Mantar. They were later released by a magistrate.
Police imposed extensive security restrictions across Delhi, closing several metro stations and deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site. Thousands of people, including journalists, were detained and later released, while videos showed police forcibly dragging some protesters into buses.
Following the weekend protests, Delhi police removed Jantar Mantar from its list of authorised protest sites, instead designating three other venues - Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground.
The CJP criticised the decision, saying it would make demonstrations less visible and harder for protesters to make their voices heard.
On Tuesday, the activists returned to Jantar Mantar despite the restrictions. Videos shared by Dipke and other CJP leaders showed Das and Ranka climbing over police barricades, carrying Indian flags and chanting slogans.
"You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X.
Ratna Singh, head of the CJP's legal team, alleged that the activists were denied access to lawyers for several hours before being taken to Parliament Street Police Station in a private vehicle at about 03:00 local time (21:30 GMT on Tuesday).
She also rejected a police allegation that CJP leaders had called on others to join the protest at Jantar Mantar.
"Absolutely false! No public call was ever made," she wrote on X.
The CJP emerged from student-led demonstrations earlier this year over alleged exam irregularities and demands for education reforms.
Weeks of protests led by the movement culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The group began as an online satire movement after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May.
He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people demanding change.
Following the summer protests, the CJP developed into a wider pressure group, tapping into discontent over unemployment, examinations and government accountability.
The CJP launched its latest nationwide protests in Mumbai on 2 October, following an Indian Express report alleging that Chief Election Commissioner Kumar had ignored objections from his two fellow commissioners over changes to voter registration.
The newspaper reported that commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised concerns at least 14 times over 10 months about decisions taken without their knowledge, including changes affecting voter databases and electoral rolls. The Election Commission has denied the allegations, saying its decisions were unanimous.
The controversy has intensified scrutiny of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, a voter verification exercise that opposition parties allege has benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission and the government denies this.
Although the CJP and opposition parties have not held joint protests, their demonstrations have coincided in recent days. Gandhi is among politicians, lawyers and journalists detained during protests across several cities.
