Are Chromebooks still worth buying after the Googlebooks release?
How Google's new laptops compare to traditional Chromebooks.
Google has been working on its next generation of laptops for a while. They're now here, and they're called Googlebooks: an evolution of Chromebooks and ChromeOS. But does that mean the end of Chromebooks? Not exactly. Google will continue to support ChromeOS until 2034, and the two product lineups are aimed at different customers.
If you've been thinking about buying a Chromebook, there are still plenty of reasons to choose one over the new Googlebooks. It all depends on what you're looking for in a laptop.
What Googlebooks do that Chromebooks can't
The main difference with Googlebooks is that they run an Android-based operating system instead of ChromeOS. While ChromeOS can run Android apps, it emulates them, leading to occasional poor performance and bugs. In contrast, Googlebooks can run most Android apps natively at full performance, taking better advantage of the hardware — although some apps might run poorly on Intel-based laptops. They have access to the full Google Play Store.
Speaking of hardware, Google is pushing for better specs, with laptops starting at 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. The first Googlebooks deliver around 14 hours of battery life, which is much longer than most Chromebooks.
And because they run an Android-based system, they also integrate much better with Android phones. You can open your phone apps on your laptop and access your files without having to transfer them. Many settings can also be synced between the two, such as your passwords and notifications. The idea is similar to what Apple offers when you use both a Mac and an iPhone. That is, of course, if you have a phone running Android 17 or later — don't expect to use all these features with an iPhone or ancient Android device.
It's also worth noting that, similar to Chromebooks, the Googlebook isn't a single laptop. Instead, Google has been working with brands such as Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP and Lenovo to deliver Googlebook-certified laptops. They all must follow certain guidelines, such as using carbon-fiber chassis instead of cheap plastic, high-end processors (whether Intel or Snapdragon) and high-resolution screens. It's no surprise that they all come with Gemini built-in at the system level.
So in theory, Googlebooks are an upgrade over Chromebooks in almost every way. Why would anyone choose a Chromebook over a Googlebook, then?
Where Chromebooks still make sense
Price is the main reason to consider a Chromebook over a Googlebook. Chromebook Plus models, which come with at least 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, usually cost less than $500. If you want to go even cheaper, there are entry-level Chromebooks with 4GB of RAM for less than $300. Googlebooks, on the other hand, start at $899 and can go as high as $1,299. That's a significant price difference.
Of course, Chromebooks won't suit everyone, so it's important to think about what you need to do with your laptop. Because of their less powerful hardware, Chromebook are good for light tasks like browsing the web, streaming and editing documents. If that's the case for you, you don't need the performance of a more powerful device. But if you need a laptop for video editing and playing casual games, a Googlebook is a better option.
Another element to consider is that Googlebooks are a brand-new ecosystem, so there might be some growing pains early on. Chromebooks have been around for over a decade, and thus ChromeOS is a much more mature platform where you know what to expect. Longevity shouldn't be an issue either way, since ChromeOS will still get software updates and security patches through 2034. By then, you'll likely have already replaced your laptop. And they won't stop working overnight, either.
Chromebooks have some big downsides, which explains why some people have never liked them. ChromeOS doesn't run most of the popular desktop software you'll find on Windows or macOS. Plus, very cheap Chromebooks have poor hardware, so they feel slow and their bad displays aren't fun to look at. Still, if you only need a basic laptop, they might work for you — there are pros and cons to using a Chromebook as your PC, and we've rounded up the best Chromebooks you can buy in 2026.

30 Great Tech Books to Gift (or Keep for Yourself)
Featured in this article
It is tough to overestimate Big Tech’s influence on the modern world. But how did we get here? The best tech books unravel the rise and, occasionally, fall of some of the dominant companies and characters that created the gadgets and software we spend so much of our lives using.
You’ll find intensely detailed biographies, in-depth company histories, and plenty of drama and enlightenment in these tech tomes, and they also make great gifts for the techy folks in your life. You may also be interested in our Gifts for Book Lovers, Best Cookbooks, and Best Kindles guides.
Updated October 2026: I added five books, including Apple in China, More Everything Forever, Gouged, The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, and The Nerd Reich.
- Chip Chase The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World's Most Coveted Microchip by Stephen Witt Charting Nvidia’s rise to become one of the most valuable companies on earth, this biography of cofounder and CEO Jensen Huang is educational and entertaining. Witt explains how the company spun GPU (graphics processing unit) manufacturing for gaming into parallel processing and a marriage of hardware and software that has powered the rise of AI. It has also made Huang very rich, but he isn’t always painted in a flattering light, which helps to counterbalance the founder worship vibe. For a slightly different view on Nvidia's history, try The Nvidia Way: Jensen Huang and the Making of a Tech Giant, by Tae Kim.
- The Early Days of the Computer The Soul of a New Machine by Tracy Kidder A well-deserved winner of the Pulitzer Prize, this book should be required reading for anyone who works in technology or harbors a curiosity about how it came to dominate our lives. First published in 1981, the book reveals the inner workings of Data General in the 1970s as the company strives to design and release a successful next-generation minicomputer. Kidder captures the struggle between management and creatives and weaves a fascinating tale from an ostensibly dry subject. He explains the intense time pressure on engineers that led to a constant state of crunch, the need for recruits to feel like they are working on something important they have some stake in, and the psychology of leadership intent on realizing ambitious projects. It is positively prescient about the dangers of burnout for the unsung heroes who sacrifice so much to build new machines. Follow this up with WIRED’s article chatting with some of the subjects in the book 20 years after it was published (this article itself is now more than 20 years old).
- Evil Twin Doppelganger: A Trip Into the Mirror World by Naomi Klein This fascinating dive down the rabbit hole of Covid conspiracy is ostensibly about how people confuse Naomi Klein with Naomi Wolf. Klein is a leftist journalist and climate activist; Wolf was a third-wave feminist but is now a rabid anti-vaxxer. If you’re still puzzled over the convergence of wellness and the far-right or wondering why so many ordinary folks are swallowing the kind of misinformation that breeds racism and climate denialism, Klein has some convincing answers. This is challenging and sometimes bleak reading, but it was also the most important book of 2023. It's brutally honest, calling out the absurdities of capitalism and the role social media has played in the rise of narcissism.
- An Icon by Walter Isaacson Released just 19 days after the death of Apple cofounder Steve Jobs, this astonishing biography takes a deep dive into his life and goes some way toward explaining his enduring legacy. Isaacson was picked by Jobs himself, who granted more than 40 interviews to his biographer and reportedly exerted no control over the final edit. Jobs’ intense passion and ambition saw him successfully marry creative ideas with technological innovations and sell them to the general public. This is an accessible book that never gets too technical. It insightfully charts the rise of Apple and Pixar and the development of the Mac, iTunes, the iPhone, and the iPad. While it is flattering at times, Jobs’ ruthlessness is not sugar-coated, and anyone with more than a passing interest in the man must read this book. For a less Jobs-centric exploration of the Mac’s development, read Revolution in The Valley: The Insanely Great Story of How the Mac Was Made, by Andy Hertzfeld.
- Cancel Culture So You've Been Publicly Shamed by Jon Ronson The dark side of the internet’s hive mind is brought into sharp relief by Ronson’s cast of characters—all have been publicly shamed via the internet. From the fascinating tale of Jonah Lehrer’s plagiarism to the vilification of Justine Sacco after an ill-advised joke tweet decried as racist, Ronson digs into the stories behind the scandals and looks at the havoc relentless online shaming can wreak. The book is a fun and fascinating look at how shame, empowered by social media, is a forceful form of social control with real-life consequences. Jon Ronson is my favorite non-fiction writer, and I also highly recommend The Castle: Adventures in a World of Unraveling Men and The Psychopath Test: A Journey Through the Madness Industry.
- Made in China Apple in China: The Capture of the World's Greatest Company by Patrick McGee Who would have thought that maximizing profit at any cost might lead to problems? Apple’s pursuit of every cent led it to outsource virtually all of its gadget production to China, and now it’s grappling with the economic, political, and cultural fallout. McGee has spoken with many former Apple executives and engineers to uncover what happened, why, and what it means for Apple and the US.
- Google’s Machinings In the Plex: How Google Thinks, Works, and Shapes Our Lives by Steven Levy I could have easily included a few entries from WIRED's own Steven Levy on this list, from his hugely influential 1984 debut, Hackers: Heroes of the Computer Revolution, to his most recent release, Facebook: The Inside Story, but I’ve chosen In the Plex. Despite the impact of Google, a company whose name has become a verb, most of us know little about its internal workings. This is the best book to read if you want to change that. Levy secured unprecedented access to serve up a fascinating dive into what makes Google tick, what drove successful expansion into new areas, and how the company and its products have changed the world. If you want more, How Google Works, by Eric Schmidt and Jonathan Rosenberg, offers some insight into management at the company.
- Resisting Big Tech The Internet Con: How to Seize the Means of Computation by Cory Doctorow I remember when the internet was good, before we got trapped in walled gardens and Big Tech put the thumbscrews on us to extract every last cent. Cory Doctorow’s wonderfully evocative “theory of enshittification” is widely accepted now and increasingly common everywhere you look. He reckons that interoperability might just be the antidote, and while his sharp critiques are more fully formed than his suggested solutions, at least he’s trying to offer some hope.
- The Rise and Fall of Theranos Bad Blood: Secrets and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup by John Carreyrou Noble aims and raw ambition are lauded in the tech world, often attracting praise and investment, but what happens when a project goes wrong? Building on Wall Street Journal reporter Carreyrou’s shocking exposé of Theranos, this book follows charismatic founder Elizabeth Holmes as she tries and fails to build a blood testing machine to sweep away the need for hypodermic needles, with the promise of accurate tests done from a drop or two of blood via a pinprick on the finger. Although the company raised hundreds of millions of dollars, its technology was horribly inaccurate. Rather than admit defeat, it pressed on, which is why Holmes was put on trial for fraud and sentenced to 11 years in prison. The book highlights the dangers of the popular “fake it till you make it” approach. Theranos reached a paper valuation of $9 billion and employed more than 800 people before its spectacular fall.
- Broligarch Bashing More Everything Forever: AI Overlords, Space Empires, and Silicon Valley's Crusade to Control the Fate of Humanity by Adam Becker Silicon Valley ideology and the self-serving narratives of tech billionaires are exposed as delusional rationalizations for the crazed accumulation of wealth and power in this fascinating, reasoned, sometimes depressing, but always well-argued book. Becker does his homework thoroughly to debunk our immoral CEO overlords and the philosophies and movements they espouse.
- Generative AI You Look Like a Thing and I Love You: How Artificial Intelligence Works and Why It's Making the World a Weirder Place by Janelle Shane If you can't help but ponder about artificial intelligence these days, you'll get a kick out of this book. It delves into machine-learning algorithms and their limitations in an accessible, engaging, and often hilarious way. Shane is the research scientist behind the comical AI Weirdness blog, and she does a solid job of demystifying AI, explaining how machine learning really works, and highlighting its strengths and weaknesses. Although you’ll learn about things like generative adversarial networks, the book never gets dull, thanks to witty and moreish writing peppered with practical examples of AI attempts at creativity that are frequently laugh-out-loud funny.
- Power Shifts The New New Thing: A Silicon Valley Story by Michael Lewis Opening on a computerized superyacht, the talented Michael Lewis takes us on an adventure into the mind of billionaire Jim Clark, cofounder of Netscape and Silicon Graphics. The book charts the power shift in Silicon Valley startups from “money men” to “idea men” and engineers. Lewis also attempts to uncover what drives Clark’s endless pursuit of the next thing and his seemingly unquenchable desire for more. This modern captain of industry is restless, constantly dissatisfied, and not very likable. The voyage is an interesting frame, and there are echoes of Kidder’s book in its subject’s idiosyncrasies and the author’s earnest attempt to explore what truly motivates him.
- AI Race Supremacy: AI, ChatGPT, and the Race That Will Change the World by Parmy Olson The race to make AI mainstream is framed as a battle between CEOs, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Demis Hassabis of DeepMind, but Olson does a good job of showing how seeming idealists with good intentions can be swayed by billionaires and end up selling out. If you wonder about the forces fueling the AI arms race, how bloated valuations have led to political power, or the laundry list of ethical and legal concerns AI raises, you’ll find this book enlightening.
- Silicon Valley The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America by Margaret O'Mara If you have ever wondered how such a small suburban area came to dominate the tech world, Margaret O’Mara, a history professor at the University of Washington, has some answers. This concise and comprehensive book weaves together interviews, biographies, and countless other sources to explain how Silicon Valley has driven and dominated technological innovation. O’Mara exposes the foundations that self-mythologizing founders and businesses are built on, and the vital role the government played in their rise. Folks seeking an insider’s view might like Uncanny Valley: A Memoir, by Anna Wiener.

India 'cockroach' leaders detained after entering barricaded protest site
- Published
Leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were detained early on Tuesday after they entered a heavily-guarded protest site and chanted slogans demanding the country's election chief resign over a controversial revision of electoral rolls.
Party founder Abhijeet Dipke shared a video showing Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das being taken away by police from Jantar Mantar, a historic Delhi observatory popular for protests.
Footage showed the two - along with others - climbing over police barricades before chanting slogans while holding the Indian flag.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's opponents allege the voter list revision benefits his party, a charge it and the Election Commission reject.
There have been days of protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
Police have stepped up security across Delhi as demonstrators challenge restrictions on where protests can be held.
Early on Tuesday, Dipke, Das and Ranka all shared videos showing Das and Ranka entering Jantar Mantar.
"You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X.
Das also posted a message declaring that the site had been "reclaimed" and that they were being detained.
It was not immediately clear where police had taken the leaders.
Ranka later appeared on an Instagram live broadcast from a police bus alongside other detainees where they appeared cheerful and said they would not back down.
The detentions came a day after the federal home ministry announced that Jantar Mantar, long associated with public protests in Delhi, would no longer be a designated protest venue. Authorities instead identified three alternative locations where demonstrations can be held with permission.
Before the decision, the CJP had met Delhi Police officials to seek permission for a peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar and had warned that it would announce further demonstrations if it received no response.
"30 mins after we went to Delhi Police asking for a date when we can go to Jantar Mantar, Jantar Mantar was de-notified as a protest site," Ranka had earlier posted on X.
Most of the party's leadership has been in Delhi in recent days. Dipke, however, had travelled to his hometown in Maharashtra after the death of his grandmother. He was among several CJP leaders detained ahead of a planned demonstration on Saturday and was released the next day.
The CJP had called for a protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday, but authorities imposed extensive security restrictions across the capital to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site.
Several metro stations were closed, train services were disrupted and thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed.
Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.
Separately, opposition parties held a march in Delhi on Monday from Connaught Place - a major shopping district in the heart of the capital - to the Supreme Court.
The Congress, India's main opposition party, also petitioned the Supreme Court on Monday, challenging the Election Commission's voter revision exercise, which has resulted in tens of millions of names being removed from electoral rolls.
Critics say the exercise risks excluding eligible voters and making it harder for them to prove their eligibility.
Anger over the revision exercise intensified after The Indian Express reported that Kumar had disregarded concerns raised by the two other election commissioners over changes to voter registration. The Election Commission has said its decisions were unanimous.
The current protests follow student-led demonstrations earlier this year over exam irregularities and demands for education reforms.
The CJP led weeks of action that culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The group began as online satire after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May. He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people seeking change.
After the summer protests, the CJP evolved into a pressure group, tapping into wider anger over unemployment, exam irregularities and government accountability.

Ukraine received no intelligence from partners on incoming missile strike on Kyiv
Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about a Russian missile strike on Kyiv, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv in which five missiles hit civilian infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday in a post on X.
Zelenskyy characterized the barrage on the capital as “particularly vile,” and emphasized that receiving intelligence from Ukraine's partners on such ballistic missile attacks “helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues.”
"This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed — when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he wrote. He did not apportion blame for the lack of warning.
Russia's war in Ukraine hasn’t seen major shifts on the ground since last year, but Ukraine is struggling to fend off Moscow's intensified aerial attacks on cities that include speedy ballistic missiles and high-flying jet-powered drones.
Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 100 weapons since Monday evening. Among the damage was a residential building in the northeastern city of Kharkiv that was destroyed, killing four people despite an all-night rescue operation, he said.
Russia has increasingly used attacks on civilian infrastructure such as energy facilities to deny Ukrainians power, heat and running water during the 4 1/2-year war, hoping to wear down public support for Ukraine’s response to Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
U.S. President Donald Trump has blamed Ukraine's earlier strikes on Russian oil refineries for record U.S. diesel prices — rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran — and struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday to import diesel from Russia in an attempt to bring fuel prices down ahead of U.S. midterm elections.
Meanwhile, Trump claimed on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed on an “energy ceasefire” in which both parties would refrain from striking each other's energy infrastructure. Russia has not confirmed the existence of such a deal, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Tuesday saying only that “contacts on this matter continue.”
Zelenskyy on Tuesday said Ukraine had not struck Russian oil refineries or other energy sites in the two days since Trump announced the purported deal. He criticized Moscow for what he said were Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities and critical infrastructure in the time since Trump's announcement.
“These are absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said.
The claim that Ukraine has halted its strikes on energy sites could not be independently verified, but neither Russian officials nor media have reported Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries since the energy truce was announced.
Russian strikes across Ukraine caused injuries and deaths overnight Monday and into Tuesday, with Zelenskyy saying that in addition to the four deaths in the apartment building in Kharkiv, 41 people were wounded in the city in one evening alone.
A woman was wounded in a Russian strike on a private home in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district, the Kyiv city military administration said, while a Russian drone hit a residential building in the village of Murovane, near the western city of Lviv, during a morning attack Tuesday, Lviv Mayor Andrii Sadovyi said.
One person was killed in the Fastiv district of the Kyiv region and at least two others were hurt in a Russian attack on the area, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration.
A Russian drone struck an educational institution in the center of Rivne in northwest Ukraine, wounding 14 people, according to Oleksandr Koval, head of the Rivne regional military administration.
The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement Tuesday that its forces overnight “launched coordinated strikes using ground-based precision weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles against Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, logistics centers, railway and port infrastructure, as well as vessels involved in delivering military cargo to Ukraine.”
The ministry also said a bulk carrier headed to the port of Mykolaiv with military cargo on board was hit in the estuary of the Bug river along the Black Sea.
The Russian Defense Ministry on Tuesday said its air defenses overnight shot down 604 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions and the Sea of Azov.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 417 drones targeted the Moscow region. Most were downed far away, while 65 were intercepted as they approached the Russian capital.
A school, two private houses and a car were damaged in the attack in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow, Gov. Vladislav Shapsha said.

Ukraine's access to Starlink internet service was suddenly disrupted, interfering with military operations, sources in the country's defense ministry and a top presidential advisor said on Wednesday.
Serhii Beskrestnov, a top advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said in a social media post that Elon Musk's SpaceX had implemented speed limits for Starlink terminals overnight. He did not provide evidence to support his claim.
Beskrestnov said the restriction throttles the operation of Starshield, the company's dedicated satellite network for military services, at speeds above 100 miles per hour. He said the Ukrainian military was not notified in advance.
Sources in Ukraine's defense ministry confirmed the disruption and told Business Insider it complicates military operations, including logistics and drone strikes. They said the cause is being investigated.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Business Insider.
Starlink has become critically important to Ukraine's military, which has adopted it as a battlefield comms system and also uses it in drone warfare. Drones equipped with Starlink dishes, which can be controlled remotely by pilots hundreds of miles away and adapted to new targets mid-mission, have become one of the country's most potent weapons in the battle against Russian forces.
Ukraine's use of Starlink has made it reliant on Musk and SpaceX, however. In 2023, the world's richest man said he refused a request from Ukraine's military to activate Starlink to assist a Ukrainian assault on Crimea, and Reuters reported last year that SpaceX jeopardized a 2022 Ukrainian counteroffensive by cutting Starlink access to frontline troops.
Recently, Musk has proven to be a more reliable ally. In February, SpaceX clamped down on Russian forces' use of Starlink terminals in Ukraine after Ukraine's then-defense minister made a personal appeal to the billionaire CEO, a move that allowed Ukrainian forces to wage a successful counteroffensive.
Musk has not yet addressed reports of Starlink disruptions in Ukraine. On Saturday, he reignited his past criticisms of Zelenskyy with a post on X that the Ukrainian president had "gone too far" with his strikes on Russian refineries.
The disruption comes after a series of Russian ballistic missile attacks against Kyiv on Monday and Tuesday nights. Ukrainian officials said that in both cases, international partners did not provide an advance warning about their launch, breaking from standard practice.
Asked by reporters before the attack on Tuesday if the US would cut intelligence with Ukraine over its strikes on Russian energy sites, President Donald Trump said Washington continued to share it.
Zelenskyy's advisor suggested that the Starlink disruption could be linked to tensions between the US and Ukraine.
"It is clear that this action is not coincidental and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram, according to a translation of his statement.

Victoria’s firefighting fleet needs funding, auditor general report finds
Victoria’s auditor general has found the state’s fire authorities need $1.5bn over the next decade to replace and upgrade their firefighting fleets, but have received only a quarter of the funding required.
The report, tabled in parliament this morning, found that the Country Fire Authority, Fire Rescue Victoria and the department’s firefighting fleet - which operates through Forest Fire Management Victoria - collectively need $1.5bn to “make sure their fire trucks are fit for purpose, reliable and safe,” but have only received $390.4m in current funding and future grants.
It said the CFA needed the majority of the funds - $962.5m – to replace 1,657 fire trucks that are “beyond their estimated useful life”, while FRV needed $297.3m to replace 153 fire trucks that are more than 15 years old.
But the auditor general said neither the CFA or FRV requested the full amount of funding they needed ahead of the most recent budget. The report said this was “due to instruction from the treasurer to all ministers that agencies should limit funding requests for new initiatives in line with the government’s fiscal strategy”.
It said the FRV in particular only submitted a budget bid of $20.7m – just 7.5% of what it needs over the decade.

Together, these issues increase the risk that fire authorities will not have enough fit-for-purpose fire trucks to respond to fires and other emergencies.

An Air India flight from Frankfurt to Delhi was diverted to Jaipur on Wednesday morning after a suspected security threat prompted an emergency response, with the aircraft landing safely and security agencies launching checks following reports that the pilot had briefly transmitted the international hijack alert code.
Flight AI-2030, operated using a Boeing 787-9 aircraft, was taken to an isolation bay at Jaipur International Airport after landing. Security personnel began examining the aircraft, while passengers and crew were deplaned under supervision, according to initial reports.
The emergency response followed a distress signal received by Ahmedabad Air Traffic Control (ATC). Officials in the know told PTI that the pilot had briefly squawked transponder code 7500, the internationally recognised signal for unlawful interference with an aircraft.
The circumstances surrounding the transmission were not immediately clear.
The Frankfurt-Delhi flight was diverted after a suspected bomb threat triggered security procedures, according to sources cited by PTI.
Shiv Dayal, Assistant Commissioner of Police for Malviya Nagar, told PTI that airport authorities had informed the police about the emergency landing following a bomb threat.
Police said security personnel were checking the aircraft after it was moved to the airport's isolation bay. Further details about the threat and the events leading to the diversion were not immediately available.
Transponder code 7500 is the internationally recognised aviation code indicating unlawful interference, including a hijack situation.
According to initial information cited by a source, the pilot transmitted the code briefly while the aircraft was in the Mumbai Flight Information Region (FIR). The aircraft was subsequently diverted to Jaipur.
The transmission prompted a heightened security response, although it was not immediately established whether the brief use of the code confirmed a hijack threat or whether the incident involved another form of security concern.
A transponder code is an important communication tool between an aircraft and air traffic control. Code 7500 alerts air traffic controllers to possible unlawful interference and allows the appropriate procedures to be initiated.
Investigators will need to establish the circumstances behind the transmission and determine the nature of the reported threat.
Security agencies moved to secure the aircraft after it landed at Jaipur International Airport.
The Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS), airport security personnel and local police were involved in the response. The isolation bay was cordoned off as security teams began examining the aircraft and screening those on board.
Initial information indicated that passengers and their baggage were being subjected to security checks. The aircraft was also undergoing inspection as authorities worked to establish whether any threat remained.
The National Security Guard (NSG) was placed on standby in New Delhi in case its intervention became necessary. There was no immediate confirmation that the specialist force had been deployed to Jaipur.
The aircraft was operating an international service from Frankfurt to Delhi when it was diverted to Jaipur on Wednesday morning.
The Boeing 787-9 landed safely and was moved to an isolation bay for security checks. The reported bomb threat and the pilot's brief transmission of transponder code 7500 prompted a coordinated response involving airport authorities, police and security agencies.
The number of passengers on board had not been immediately confirmed, and the airline had not issued an official comment at the time of reporting.

The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.
Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.
The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.
On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings. In the end, he was released in the late afternoon wearing a red T-shirt to be greeted by friends, family and flowers.
Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.
His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.
The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”
Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.
The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.
The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.
His Dumbarton-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn’t dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes. The last two weeks have been torture – knowing that Jagtar had been granted bail, but the authorities were refusing to let him out. I’ll sleep well tonight, knowing that he’s not behind bars.
“Tomorrow morning, the fight continues, because he’s still on trial and facing the death penalty for something he didn’t do, trapped in a sham legal process designed to punish him for standing up for human rights”.
Reprieve’s deputy executive director, Dan Dolan, said: “While tonight is the first night in almost nine years that Jagtar Singh Johal is not caged in a prison cell, he still has the threat of a death sentence hanging over him. It should also be noted that, despite bail being ordered, the prison refused to release Jagtar until his family brought a habeas corpus petition and a judge warned the jail they’d be found in contempt of court”.
The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.

Do you remember the first smartphone you bought around 2012? Chances are, you spent more time choosing the phone than thinking about its case. Phone cases were largely an afterthought, sold by local stores and small sellers in an unorganised market dominated by inexpensive, China-sourced products and copies of established brands. That began to change as smartphone adoption accelerated. Indians were increasingly willing to spend ₹20,000, ₹30,000, ₹40,000 and even ₹50,000 on their phones. As these phones became more central to everyday life, consumers began looking beyond basic protection, even demanding accessories that reflected their personal style — an opportunity DailyObjects tapped into early on. Founded by Pankaj Garg, in 2012, as a multi-category online business, the company narrowed its focus to smartphone cases in 2014. Over time, it expanded into bags, charging products and workspace accessories, building its brand around design and quality. Today, DailyObjects revenue crossed ₹200 Cr in FY26, nearly doubling year-on-year. It is targeting ₹400 Cr in FY27 while working towards EBITDA profitability. But the more interesting part of DailyObjects’ story is not just how quickly it is growing today. It is how long it took to build a brand in a category that many consumers once barely thought about. Making Phone Cases More Than A Commodity DailyObjects had started as a multi-category online business, but by 2014, it decided to focus on smartphone cases. Rather than spread its resources across different product lines, the startup chose to focus on one category, differentiate through design and quality, and build a customer base willing to pay a premium. The category offered an opportunity to build a design-led brand in a market crowded with inexpensive, unbranded products. Consumers could walk into almost any mobile shop and find a case, while copies of products from established international brands were also widely available. DailyObjects’ answer was to make the product itself more distinctive. The startup began offering designer cases and collaborating with artists, bringing design into a category largely treated as a commodity. But differentiation was not limited to aesthetics. DailyObjects also wanted its products to compete with global brands on quality and materials. But building a better product was only half the battle. DailyObjects also had to decide how it wanted to grow. The startup had begun as a multi-category business, but it chose to drop car accessories and other retail products to concentrate on smartphone cases, which it saw as a larger and faster-growing opportunity. The idea was to build depth in one category before expanding into others. The same thinking shaped its distribution strategy. DailyObjects could have leaned on marketplaces to reach a wider audience and chase volumes. Instead, it largely stuck to its own channels, believing marketplaces could help sell a product but could not build a brand for it, even though it was a slower, more demanding route. The startup had to generate its own traffic, establish a distinct design identity and convince consumers to pay more for products they could find at a fraction of the price elsewhere. During this period, the startup raised ₹9 Cr from Ronnie Screwvala’s Unilazer Ventures. But according to Garg, the business had an important advantage: it had been profitable from its early stages. That gave it the room to grow without relying heavily on deep discounts or chasing marketplace volumes simply to keep the business running. DailyObjects stayed focused on phone cases for nearly five years before entering another major category. Its approach was to establish a foothold in one category, build distribution around it and then move to the next. By resisting the rush to scale through marketplaces, DailyObjects had more time to build a direct relationship with its customers. That strategy continues to define the business today, with nearly 70% of its sales coming through its own channels. DailyObjects’ Playbook: Making Everyday Products Desirable There was a logic to what DailyObjects added next. The startup was not looking to build a sprawling catalogue of accessories. It wanted to find products that appealed to the same customer it had won over with phone cases. The idea took DailyObjects into bags in FY21, opening up a much bigger opportunity than phone cases. However, it also brought a new challenge: manufacturers were unwilling to take on its small orders. Therefore, DailyObjects decided to make bags itself. The operation began with just two tables and eventually grew into its own factory. Today, bags account for around 40-45% of the company’s revenue. They are manufactured entirely in India at its own facility, which employs around 600 people. DailyObjects’ average order value is now around ₹26,000 and has been rising about 10% every year. The startup attributes the increase to products such as bags, power banks, and premium phone cases. Two years later, in FY23, DailyObjects entered into charging products. It was during this time that the startup bagged $10 Mn from 360 One Asset for product innovation and expanding its manufacturing capabilities. Its charging and STAC categories have grown nearly threefold since. The latest example is NODE, a modular wireless charging system around consumers carrying several devices between home, work and travel. The startup currently has around 50 core SKUs, excluding colour and size variants. Its revenue has grown from ₹ 24.1 Cr in FY21 to ₹39.2 Cr in FY22, to ₹84.4 Cr in FY24 and ₹110 Cr in FY25 . Garg said that the startup closed FY26 at over ₹200 Cr. While the founder didn’t divulge bottomline details for FY26, DailyObjects posted a loss of ₹16 Cr in FY25. The startup is yet to file its FY26 audited financials with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. The Next Challenge: Taking The Brand Beyond Metros DailyObjects spent years building its own traffic and customer base, a slower process that gave it greater control over how its products were presented and how they were priced. The payoff is beginning to show in its customer metrics. The company says its lifetime repeat purchase rate stands at around 45%. Its average order value has also risen by roughly 10% YoY to about ₹2,600, suggesting that customers are increasingly spending across its wider product range. Its customer base has also moved beyond the metros. Around 35–40% of DailyObjects’ sales now come from Tier III and IV cities, while another 20–25% comes from Tier II markets. The shift points to a broader opportunity: consumers in smaller cities are increasingly willing to spend on products that combine design with everyday utility. DailyObjects is now expanding its reach into cities such as Vizag, Patna, Ludhiana, Indore, Lucknow and Surat. But reaching more customers is only one part of the next phase. The other is making that growth more profitable. DailyObjects is currently operating close to break-even and remains on track to achieve EBITDA profitability in FY27. It expects operating margins, currently around 5%, to expand to 15-20% over the next four to five years. The improvement is expected to come from a combination of factors, including a higher-value product mix, a larger contribution from offline retail and greater supply-chain efficiencies. Recently, D2C lifestyle startup DailyObjects has raised ₹332 Cr ($34.3 Mn) in a Series C funding round co-led by Xponentia Capital Partners, Anicut Capital and Axiom Asia Private Capital. The funds will allow DailyObjects to scale its offline network, deepen its product and R&D capabilities, strengthen brand building and evaluate opportunities in international markets. DailyObjects’ Offline Push Comes With A Bigger Test For years, DailyObjects’ biggest asset was something consumers could not touch: the brand itself. Now, it is bringing that proposition into physical stores. The startup currently operates 13 exclusive brand outlets. It is opening two to three stores a month and plans to add 30-35 stores in FY27. Over the next five years, it aims to build a network of 150-160 stores. It is also present at 300 Apple premium reseller outlets. For DailyObjects, this is more than a conventional D2C brand moving offline. It is a chance to put the products at the centre of the buying experience. Consumers may discover them online, but a physical store lets them feel the materials, examine the finish and understand how a product works before paying a premium for it. According to the founder, all stores become profitable from the first month of operations. Its airport stores, in particular, are generating margins of close to 15% from the first month. Rather than limiting itself to India’s largest cities, DailyObjects is using physical retail to reach markets where it already sees significant online demand. It is also beginning to explore international markets. The startup is researching the US, where it already receives around 1,000 orders a month without dedicated marketing. But as the business grows, so will the challenge. With DailyObjects targeting ₹400 Cr in revenue in FY27, can it scale its offline and international presence while building a profitable business without losing what made its brand distinctive? A Chronicle Of Minor Things, from Indian filmmaker Tribeny Rai, picked up the APM Busan Award and the Sorfond Award at the close of this year’s Asian Project Market in Busan.
The jury said the project stood out for its original story and narrative structure, and for the director’s ability to weave a social issue subtly into the story, while the project’s distinctive landscape and themes were also recognized for their potential to appeal to international audiences.
Casparina, from Indonesian filmmaker Reza Rahadian, received the CJ ENM Award for transforming the director’s most personal story into a family drama with universal emotional resonance.
Goldfish from Indonesia’s Aditya Ahmad picked up three awards: the VIPO Award, the Kongchak Studio Award and the QCinema Special Award. VIPO recognized the project for its “fresh exploration of identity against a changing environment and the production feasibility demonstrated by the close collaboration between its director and producer”.
Watch on Deadline
E Del Mundo’s Once Upon a Time in the Philippines received the ArteKino International Award for its “original analysis of structural violence and the individual’s capacity to resist it”. Korean filmmaker Park Syeyoung’s Satellite Of Love received the Songwon Award for its original story, strong visual vision, and ability to contain the complex dimensions of love within a simple narrative.
The CathayPlay Award went to Taiwanese director Yen Hao-hsuan’s Uncle, which draws on Yen’s personal experience to explore family, shame and belonging in a rapidly changing Taiwan.
The Kantana Picture Award went to Korean filmmaker Kim Jinyeong’s Red Hunger for its strong storytelling and visual potential, while Fatimah, from Thailand’s Panu Aree, received the Kantana Virtual Production Award for its story spanning dual identities, long-buried family secrets, and a journey across both geographic and internal landscapes.
This year’s APM, which takes place as part of Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), received a record 604 submissions from 48 countries, with 30 projects from 17 countries participating as official selections. Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
- Published
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.
Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya
Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.
The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.
The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.

In early October, Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor of Ohio, went for a classic “politician on the stump” move: He picked up a kid. Or at least he tried to. Ramaswamy fumbled the boy a bit, producing a clip that quickly went viral on social media.
Why the right turned on Indian Americans
The GOP pivots to a new kind of racism.
The next day, Ramaswamy posted a picture of himself with his son in his arms on social media. It was a cute retort. But many of the responses were ugly — racist attacks against Ramaswamy that drew on anti-Indian stereotypes.
It was the latest example of a broader shift on the right, where Indian Americans and Indian immigrants have become a conspicuous target of online conservative anger.
“The people who had negative stereotypes about Indians in their mind said, ‘Hey, look, the guy can’t even pick up a kid…he can’t even act like a normal American family man,’” freelance journalist Zaid Jilani told Today, Explained co-host Noel King.
Jilani, who recently wrote about the surge in anti-Indian racism for Vox, joined the podcast for a conversation about how he sees the bigotry as rooted in status envy, how Indian Americans and Indian immigrants are responding, and his surprisingly hopeful outlook for the future.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
American racism is very interesting, always has been. And there is a type that says, immigrants are dirty, they come here, they’re uneducated, they leach off the government, they’re taking our resources.
The stereotype of Indian immigrants to America and Indian Americans is people who go to college, people who often have advanced degrees, people who often live in nice neighborhoods, make good money, are family-values people.
Why do you think these values that seem as if they mesh with what Republicans want are so triggering to people these days? Is it just yes, but they’re brown?
I think that is a component of it. I spoke to one Indian American advocate who told me that Indians and South Asians more broadly are visible minorities, right? If you think about other minorities who are highly successful, that’s not always the case.
For instance, I think that Jewish Americans have been known since the late 20th century as being a successful minority group, but they’re not necessarily highly visible. You can’t always identify someone. If [Texas Railroad Commissioner candidate] Bo French saw a bunch of white people in the stadium with the Longhorns, I’m not sure he would be picking out who’s Protestant, who’s Catholic, who’s Jewish. But with Indian Americans, they are highly visible.
That being said, I think you have to think about where Indian Americans are in society and the kind of feelings that can create among everyone else. If you look, for instance, at Silicon Valley, the major tech companies, Microsoft, Google — the head of [Microsoft’s] Xbox division is an Indian American woman now.
You have a group of people who I think are in many ways a very micro minority — we’re talking about 1 percent to 2 percent of the United States — visibly rising into so many positions that I think a lot of people have typically associated with white folks. White people generally run the Fortune 500, white folks run the universities, white folks are the most successful doctors and engineers. And that was true for the 20th century.
But when you start seeing a much larger influx of Asian immigrants, starting with liberalization of immigration laws in the ’60s, but also when there was a rapid growth of the technology sector in the early 2000s, you start to understand a little bit more where the resentment comes from because it’s more, I would say, analogically similar to antisemitism than it is to the racism that Mexican Americans face or the racism that Black Americans face.
“It’s a much larger anti-globalization backlash on the right, not only when it comes to things like immigration, but also trade and tariffs and restrictions like that.”
It’s not that Indian Americans are necessarily being stereotyped as antisocial, criminal, coming here illegally, so on and so forth. It’s more that they’re being seen as a status threat to a lot of particularly middle-class Americans, people who want their kids to rise to the top of their school, who want their kids to have the corner office. They want their kids to be able to get the most prestigious positions.
I think in the minds of a lot of these people, not only now does their kid have to compete with all the other normal white kids in their community, they have to compete against the entire world. It’s a much larger anti-globalization backlash on the right, not only when it comes to things like immigration, but also trade and tariffs and restrictions like that.
When you talked to Indian Americans for this piece, what did you hear from them that surprised you?
Probably the most surprising thing was how much pragmatism they responded to all of this with. Nine times out of 10, when you have stories about racism, the victims of racism are outraged — understandably and justifiably outraged. Nobody wants to be mistreated. Nobody wants to be denigrated. They certainly don’t want to see restrictions on the right to immigration, or other things to limit their numbers, which is the end point of a lot of this.
At the same time, I think a lot of the people I spoke to were very upfront. They’re like, “Hey, look, we have found a lot of success in America. We got the golden ticket to be able to come here, for our kids to study here, to be able to really seek these opportunities, but we understand what’s happening in the economy. We understand there’s a lot of people who are struggling and then they see us rising to the top of all these organizations. They see us with our kind of well-ensconced place in the economy. And I think it’s important for us not to flaunt our success that much.” At least a couple people said something to that respect. They almost empathize with the people who were hating on them.
It struck me as such a classic immigrant pragmatism that you see from the first or second wave of immigrants: people who realize that they are newcomers to a society or maybe their parents were newcomers to a society, and that there is a certain level of grappling they have to do with, “Hey, how can we continue to have success? How can we continue to grind and resist this racism, but also not rub it in people’s faces that we’re doing well because the more they do that, the tougher it can be?”
A number brought up Vivek Ramaswamy in the sense that Vivek happened to go on social media and talk about what he felt like were deficiencies in American culture when it comes to studying, when it comes to working hard.
I think that in bringing that up, they were saying that that wasn’t particularly helpful because whatever positive aspects there may be to Indian immigrant culture, we shouldn’t talk about them in ways that denigrate other people because that’s obviously going to rub people the wrong way.
You’re making the point that some of the surge in anti-Indian racism on the right is about status anxiety. I was listening to this podcast that Chris Rufo and Jonathan Keeperman did. These are two influential right-wing activists. They called it “The Indian Question” — a lot of people’s eyebrows shot up — and they seem to be making the argument that it is about status anxiety.
They also were making less coherent arguments about how it’s un-American to study for the spelling bee, which is what South Asian kids do, and that white kids are more American because they play football, then they go to a party and get drunk, and then they get 1,500 on the SAT.
I’m not saying any of this makes sense. I’m saying it was fascinating. I’m assuming you watched that exchange. What did you make of that?
There’s a certain level of coping mechanism being deployed there in the sense that they are trying to explain the success of Indian Americans as a deficiency: “Maybe they’re getting to the top schools, but that’s because they’re shut in all day studying.”
But it’s not really true that Indian Americans are necessarily cloistered into unhealthy habits. They’re actually finding success across society. For instance, I’ve tutored kids for five, six years. I just really enjoy working with kids. And something you’ll find with a lot of the Indian American kids, they are actually getting increasingly well-rounded.
Part of that is because you have to, to have success, to get college admissions and so on and so forth. They almost always play sports. They’re involved in extracurriculars. You’re seeing a lot more Indian Americans go into the arts, into cultural fields, into Hollywood. I think that’s actually a very normal path for immigrants.
I think the first or second wave of immigrants has to be very pragmatic. They have to keep their heads down. They have to grind, study, and their parents encourage them to do the same thing. Indian American parents are always like, “You got to be a doctor. You got to be an engineer. Don’t be foolish and try to be a journalist or go to Hollywood.”
But as they establish themselves, as they build nest eggs, they have a little more breathing room, and so they can do different things. I know that Christopher Rufo, for instance, is an Italian American, and I believe I read one time that he even speaks Italian at home because he really values that culture so much and he wants to raise his kids in that. The first wave of Italian immigrants were no different than that. They cloistered into a few sectors where they felt they could find success that was necessary for their integration into the economy and to get their footing. But now we don’t think of Italian Americans as stereotyped into just a few parts of the country or a few parts of society — we barely notice, unless maybe you notice from someone’s name that there even are Italian Americans.
What they’re describing about Indian Americans is very normal. It’s actually very normal for first waves of immigrants to cluster in a few areas and then they spread themselves out as they’re able to get that a little bit of breathing room and room to ground to stand on.

Martin Shkreli is back. The Federal Trade Commission isn’t happy.
The FTC and seven states on Tuesday asked a federal court to hold Shkreli in contempt for “flagrantly and repeatedly” violating a court order banning him from working in the pharmaceutical industry.
Shkreli, who became known nationwide as “pharma bro” in the 2010s for imperiously defending his decision to raise the price of an anti-parasitic drug called daraprim by 5,000%, was sentenced to seven years in prison for defrauding investors in 2018. Before he was released in 2022, a court banned him from ever working in the drug industry again, saying he illegally tried to prevent generic competition to daraprim.
