UPDATED, with additional comment: A federal judge prohibited the Trump administration from banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds, granting the three outlets a preliminary injunction that ensures access for the foreseeable future.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, wrote in his opinion that the news outlets “are likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two First Amendment claims.”
Kelly did caution that “no one should interpret the court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.” But when it came to the blanket ban on the three outlets, the judge was unpersuaded by the government’s justifications.
Trump announced on Sept. 18 that he was barring CNN, MS NOW and Politico from access to White House grounds, complaining that they were “‘reporting’ fake news.”. A day later, their reporters who tried to enter the security checkpoint found their hard passes deactivated.
Watch on Deadline
The news outlets sued, and Kelly issued a temporary restraining order halting Trump’s restriction on the outlets, something that forced the White House to restore the hard passes to dozens of reporters and other staffers. That TRO expired on Tuesday; the preliminary injunction means that the White House cannot enforce Trump’s ban in the long term, either until a trial or an appeal. The news outlets warned that the White House was likely to reimpose the ban absent further court intervention.
In defending the ban, the government cited national security reasons, although DOJ attorneys also argued that the news organizations did not meet “minimum requirements of professionalism.” While the DOJ pointed to stories published or aired that had to do with national security, they also cited as an example an MS NOW report that Trump aides considered an option of adding the president’s name to Ford’s Theatre. Trump later denied it.
In his 26-page opinion, Kelly cited D.C. Circuit precedents in that reporters had a right to due process before their hard pass is revoked.
“To put it mildly, [the news outlets] likely did not receive notice either of the conduct that would subject them to revocation of their hard passes, or of the magnitude of the revocation sanction itself,” the judge wrote.
The judge noted that some of the stories flagged by the White House were published earlier this year and written by reporters who later had their hard passes renewed. Then came Trump’s ban, and they were revoked. They included a CNN report from January 2026 on the top secret bunker being built beneath the East Wing, and an MS NOW story that quoted an anonymous White House official who said the president underestimated Iran’s willingness to resume the war.
The White House press office sent letters to the news organizations on September 22, informing them of the reasons and their ability to contest the action, but that was four days after the ban was implemented.
The judge also sided with the news outlets’ in their claims that Trump was engaging in retaliation and viewpoint discrimination in violation of the First Amendment.
“President Trump’s own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before. After explaining that he excluded Plaintiffs from the White House because they ‘purposely write negative news . . . to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,’ President Trump remarked that he is prepared to take ‘the ban . . . as far as you can,’ but that he would “love it” if they “could straighten themselves out.”
The judge added, “The record is clear that President Trump made the decision at issue. And his announcement of the ban and later remarks explaining the reason for it make this a straightforward conclusion: President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him.”
He also dismissed the government’s national security argument. He noted that there was “no evidence in the record” that he made the decision to revoke the passes for those reasons “from the get go, nor at any time has he directly stated that national security was the reason for his decision.”
The judge explained that because the D.C. Circuit has held that the White House press area is a “non public forum,” the government cannot limit access based on someone’s viewpoint.
The judge wrote that “it is likely that Plaintiffs were selected by President Trump for revocation of their access to the White House press area because he believes their coverage of him and his administration is generally inaccurate and biased—in other words, it was ‘an effort to suppress the speaker’s activity due to disagreement with the speaker’s view.'”
The judge also ruled that the news outlets should put up a nominal bond of $1.00 as the case moves forward.
Theodore Boutrous Jr., the lead attorney representing the news outlets, said in a statement, “When the president issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment. Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers.”
Boutrous added, “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Vietnam buries remains of 731 war dead nearly 6 decades after the Tet Offensive
The remains of 731 people believed killed during the 1968 Tet Offensive have been laid to rest in Ho Chi Minh City, nearly six decades after North Vietnamese communist forces launched coordinated surprise attacks across South Vietnam during the Lunar N...
HANOI, Vietnam -- Thousands carrying white flowers lined the roads in Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh City Wednesday as the remains of 731 people believed to have been killed during the 1968 Tet Offensive were taken for burial nearly six decades after their deaths.
Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung attended the memorial services at Le Thi Rieng Park, where the remains were recovered from mass graves after over three months of excavations. They were laid to rest at Ho Chi Minh City Martyrs’ Cemetery in the city previously known as Saigon.
Generations in Vietnam have spent decades searching for loved ones who never returned from war, hoping to recover their remains, give them a proper burial and finally find some measure of closure.
The Tet Offensive began on Jan. 31, 1968, when North Vietnamese communist forces launched coordinated surprise attacks across South Vietnam during the Lunar New Year holiday, known in Vietnam as Tet. One of the largest campaigns of the Vietnam War, it sparked fierce fighting and heavy casualties, including in the southern capital Saigon, where communist fighters attacked the U.S. Embassy, military installations and government buildings.
Although the communist forces suffered a military defeat, the offensive shocked Washington, undermined U.S. public support for the war, and became a turning point in the conflict. “The resultant conflict has changed the pattern of the war,” The Associated Press reported in February 1968.
The South Vietnamese government collected the bodies of communist fighters and civilians and buried them in mass graves during and after the fighting, according to Vietnamese government news.
The remains at Le Thi Rieng Park, which was previously the site of Do Thanh Cemetery, were discovered during excavations that began on June 23 at the park. Over weeks, excavators painstakingly unearthed bones and fragments, along with weapons, ammunition, military hammocks and personal belongings, said the Vietnamese government’s official news portal.
They discovered a wallet containing a faded military document bearing the name Huynh Van Quen, which helped authorities identify one of the dead as a soldier from the 1st Long An Battalion, a communist unit that fought a fierce seven-day battle at Saigon’s Y-shaped Bridge.
Among the mourners was Vo Huy Thinh, 70, who remembered watching bodies being buried there when he was 12. “The memory of that burial pit has stayed with me,” he told Vietnamese state media.
For years, architect Nguyen Xuan Thang pored over photographs from the Vietnam War, searching for clues to the location of the burial site.
A breakthrough came when he found a color photograph taken by an AP photographer on Feb. 12, 1968, with a caption describing three large burial trenches that each contained about 300 bodies, he told state media.
The photograph shows two men carrying a body as two others look on. Three boys stand nearby, one of them wearing shorts and a short-sleeved shirt and looking directly at the camera. A water tower is visible in the background, providing a crucial clue to the site’s location. The image was shot by a French photographer credited as Gautron.
Thang told state media that he spent months riding his motorbike through Ho Chi Minh City, comparing old military maps with present-day landmarks, including the water tower. His research was part of a nearly eight-year effort, from November 2018 to May 2026, involving his team and the military, which helped authorities narrow their search to the park.
Investigators worked with researchers, historians, journalists and witnesses to piece together the location of the mass graves. They examined other wartime photographs, satellite images, military maps and archival records from Vietnam and abroad, comparing them with field surveys and accounts from people who witnessed the burials, said the Vietnamese government’s official news portal.
The recovery is part of a nationwide 500-day campaign running through July 2027 to locate the remains of about 7,000 war dead and identify them.
More than half a century after the war ended in 1975, many Vietnamese families are still searching for relatives who never returned home. The remains of about 175,000 Vietnamese soldiers have yet to be recovered, while hundreds of thousands more lie in graves without confirmed identities, according to government figures.
Of the 731 sets of remains recovered in Ho Chi Minh City, 307 were found with personal belongings, according to state media. Most have not yet been identified.
“Due to the harsh conditions of war and the passage of time, we have been unable to identify the names, ages, or hometowns of the majority of the martyrs in this group,” said Nguyen Manh Cuong, who heads the city's war dead identification efforts.
Samples have been sent to the Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology in Hanoi for DNA testing and comparison with samples from relatives.
Similar memorial and burial ceremonies will be held Thursday in three other parts of Vietnam, with the remains of what are believed to be 93 people to be buried in Tuyen Quang province. Another 65 will be buried in Hai Phong and 120 in Can Tho.

In October, social media users spread an image of two shirtless men standing in a boat along with the claim that the subjects were former U.S. President Barack Obama and his wife, Michelle Obama. A timestamp appeared on some copies of the image purporting to date it to July 19, 1985.
For example, this X post (archived) captioned the image "Barrack Obama and Mitchelle on a boat cruise in 1985."
(X user @MavenUg)
The image was also posted elsewhere (archived) on social media with captions implying (when they didn't state it outright) that it depicted Barack and Michelle Obama. Snopes readers searched the site wondering whether the image was authentic.
It was not. In fact, it's an altered copy, likely re-edited using AI tools, of an AI-generated image we fact-checked a few weeks before of two completely different (though equally well-known) people.
Therefore, we've rated this image fake.
The older fake image purported to depict President Donald Trump posing on a boat in swimming trunks beside the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. A digital watermark on it indicated it was created using OpenAI tools. 
(X user @YvetteABonnet)
Not only are the boat and distant background identical in both pictures, but the swimsuits worn by the figures in both and the timestamp in the bottom right of some versions are exactly the same, as well. Both images feature a nonsensical pole that goes nowhere to the left of the blue swimsuit.
Regarding the appearance of the person identified as Michelle Obama in the newer edit, only the face bears even a slight resemblance to how she looked in 1985. More pointedly, she is incorrectly depicted as a young man.
Even beyond that obvious giveaway, though, the image meant to depict the Obamas simply doesn't align with the couple's history or appearance at the time.
Prior to marrying Barack Obama, Michelle was Michelle Robinson. This is confirmed by the Obama Foundation website, which also has a photo of Michelle when she was a young girl. She went to Princeton University before studying at Harvard Law School.
Below is a photo of Michelle Robinson from Page 289 of the 1985 Princeton University yearbook in which she looks quite different, to say the least, from the figure on the left of the boat image.
There don't appear to be many publicly available photos of Barack Obama from 1985, but there are images of him from when he was elected as the first Black president of the Harvard Law Review in 1990. In the AI-generated boat image, Obama's hairline appears to be slightly higher than it is in the 1990 photos of him, possibly because the AI tool based its rendition of Obama's face on more recent photos of him.
The boat picture couldn't possibly be from 1985, anyway. The Obamas didn't meet each other until 1989, when Barack Obama took a summer internship at the Chicago law firm Sidley & Austin, where was assigned to train with a young associate named Michelle Robinson. The two eventually started dating and married in 1992.
The AI image of the couple on the boat features a watermark referencing an X account on the upper left. That account, which uses the handle @iMemeDemocrats, is labeled by X as a "parody account." It has previously posted other AI-generated images of Michelle Obama with captions amplifying a false, years old, politically motivated rumor that she is trans.
The user's original account, which is suspended, used the handle @ScummyMummy511. Snopes previously fact-checked an AI-generated image depicting an ICE officer's shooting and killing of Renee Good posted by that account. The account acknowledged in another post that the image was AI-generated.

Two months after the release of an open letter on potential safety issues tied to a rare disease drug sold by Neurocrine Biosciences, patient advocates and some experts are expressing growing alarm over the perceived risks of the therapy, STAT reports. The drug, approved to treat Prader-Willi syndrome, which can cause an insatiable feeling of hunger, has been linked to the deaths of seven people and the hospitalization of nearly 100 others — all since the treatment, called Vykat XR, was approved 18 months ago. Case reports on those deaths and hospitalizations that were submitted to regulators do not prove causality; many of the Vykat cases involved complex medical issues and multiple medications. But some experts say the evidence is sufficient to conclude Vykat is causing unacceptable harm.

Black Hawk down: Trump's trade war pauses Canadian helicopter deal
Ottawa halted plans to buy 16 U.S.-made helicopters ahead of trade talks: sources
The Liberal government quietly ordered a pause on a modest, but important purchase of 16 U.S.-made UH-60M Black Hawk helicopters just before trade negotiations began last summer with the Trump administration, CBC News and Radio-Canada have learned.
The aircraft, which are intended for use by Canada's special forces, are manufactured by Sikorsky, a subsidiary of the U.S. defence giant Lockheed Martin.
The decision to suspend the acquisition is linked to trade and diplomatic tensions with the Trump administration, according to several sources within the government and defence industry.
The purchase had been signed off by the U.S. State Department agency that handles foreign military sales and was headed for congressional approval when the halt was ordered before trade negotiators met in Washington, according to two confidential sources.
- What tariffs are still in place? Tracking the Canada-U.S. trade war
- Front Burner Should Canada have taken the U.S. deal?
The decision, the sources said, was partially related to the trade talks, which ultimately failed. It was also part of a wider effort by federal officials to inventory what the Canadian military planned to purchase from the United States.
U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly questioned Canadian sovereignty since being re-elected. He has also launched a major trade war with Canada, imposing tariffs on key sectors such as steel, aluminum and automotive manufacturing.
As Canada seeks to reduce its military reliance on the United States, the government decided that the timing was not right to purchase American helicopters without a competitive bidding process, several sources said.
CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
Since being elected in the spring of 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney has made it a priority to boost domestic defence industrial production, establish partnerships with foreign firms operating in Canada and — only as a last resort — purchase directly from abroad.
The pause on the Black Hawk purchase comes as the Carney government continues to review whether it will purchase a full order of F-35 stealth fighters, which are also manufactured by Lockheed Martin.
The government ordered a review of that plan in the late winter of 2025 and has yet to decide whether it will buy all 88 fighters as originally planned.
Canada has committed to buy 16 F-35s, but has also ordered the parts for more than a dozen others.
Government 'continues to evaluate options'
Whenever Canada — or other countries — buy U.S. military gear, the purchaser is required to request permission through the U.S. Foreign Military Sales program.
Once reviewed by officials, the deal is sent to American lawmakers who have 15 days to object before it becomes official.
A spokesperson for the agency overseeing Canada's military procurement suggested options other than the Black Hawks could be considered.
"The government of Canada continues to evaluate options to meet the needs of the special operations forces," said Sofiya Sapeha, spokesperson for Stephen Fuhr, the parliamentary secretary responsible for military procurement.
"Canada remains in contact with the relevant partners and continues to review all information necessary for decision-making."
A Black Hawk helicopter is seen on display in Kielce, Poland, last month. A defence expert tells CBC News that the U.S.-made helicopter is well suited for Arctic operations. (Kacper Pempel/Reuters)
The Black Hawks are intended to replace the special forces' use of the CH-146 Griffon, which is more than three decades old and significantly inferior in terms of military operations.
One of the reasons Canada's commandos were keen on the Black Hawk was because of its range and robustness for operations over vast distances in the Arctic.
The UH-60 has a typical combat radius of about 595 kilometres, which can be extended by air-to-air refuelling. In that case, its range goes out to 2,250 kilometres. The Griffon's normal combat range is up to 656 kilometres, but can be fitted with external fuel tanks that take it up to 909 kilometres.
Special forces have been using the Griffon since their inception as a separate unit within the Canadian military in the early 1990s. The helicopter is currently flown by 427 Special Operations Aviation Squadron.
Retired major-general Denis Thompson, who commanded special operations troops, said the difference between the two helicopters is stark.
- Harper says Canada had 'no choice' but to walk away from trade talks
- Trump's top trade rep says U.S. 'comfortable' with state of relationship
"In some ways you're comparing apples and oranges because a Griffon is a small, agile helicopter better suited for temperate climates and frankly better suited for urban operations than something as large as a Black Hawk," Thompson said.
"Range is important and the fact that it's a military design, a helicopter designed expressly for the military, means that it is just more robust and it can stand up to more punishment than the Griffon."
Thompson questioned the political calculus, but said he understands the way Canadians feel about the Trump administration.
"When we buy a piece of equipment, we're not hanging on to it for the two years that are left in Mr. Trump's mandate," Thompson said. "We're hanging on to them for 20, 30 years. And so what's important is to make sure that we buy the equipment that Canadian Armed Forces need and that we look to the long-term and not short-term political gain."
Low public support for buying American
Earlier this year, Policy Magazine published the results of a poll that indicated that 62 per cent of Canadians disagree with purchasing military equipment from the United States. Similarly, Abacus Data found that 64 per cent support an immediate halt to U.S. military purchases.
"I know it's difficult to explain that to the public, but that's what needs to be done," said Thompson.
He said equipment like the Black Hawk and F-35 weren't selected "for political reasons, at least not from the military standpoint. They were selected because they are the best piece, the most suitable piece, of equipment to fulfil the task that the military believes it might have to fill."
Defence analyst Justin Massie said the government is also clearly grappling with military procurement projects that were set in motion before the trade tensions began.
"What is changing is not so much the strategy as the political discomfort of publicly announcing purchases of American military equipment." said Massie, a political science professor at Université du Québec à Montréal.
A spokesperson for Lockheed Martin highlighted the firm's willingness to continue working with the Canadian Armed Forces, without commenting on the status of the acquisition process.
"We are ready to support international customers wishing to acquire the latest-generation UH-60M Black Hawk helicopter through the Foreign Military Sales program," said the spokesperson, Amanda Hauck.
Other projects stalled
According to government and defence industry sources, Ottawa is hesitating to approve further military purchases from the United States, or even announce contracts already signed with American firms.
For instance, a recent Department of National Defence contract for specialized cloud computing services with California-based Google has not yet been announced. This contract involves storing and protecting classified information related to national security.
Another contract for a ground vehicle crew training system is reportedly slated for the U.S. firm Raytheon but has not been announced, sources say.
Earlier this year, the government waited months before confirming a contract to purchase M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS) from Lockheed Martin.

India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.
Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Thousands are expected to march to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, New Delhi, on Saturday, amid mounting anger in the world’s largest democracy.
A spokesperson for the CJP, Ashutosh Ranka, said in a post on X on Thursday that “at least 10,000” people from CJP demonstrations, student organisations, affiliated grassroots groups and political parties had been detained across the country.
Police authorities didn’t immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comments. Videos posted on social media platform X showed activists being taken away in vans.
The CJP said that among those detained was a group of students from the western city of Pune who were headed for the 10 October protest in Delhi. It said they were being taken away in a bus to an unknown location.
The nationwide voter list review, known as the special intensive revision, has been carried out in most of India’s states and federally administered territories. More than 130 million names have been removed so far, a number larger than the populations of countries like Japan and Mexico. Millions of people have appealed against the deletions.
The opposition says the removals disproportionately affect voters who support them, while voters more likely to back prime minister Narendra Modi’s party have been preserved or added to the lists.
The election commission and the government reject the allegations, saying the revision is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries.
The campaign has been led in part by the “Cockroach” movement, which began as an online youth campaign in May and has since organised street protests across the country.
The protests present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar demonstrations led by the CJP forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
In the lead up to Saturday’s planned demonstration, hundreds of supporters of the CJP youth movement protested in tech hub Bengaluru on Thursday.
Many of the protesters held posters that said, “Every name counts, Every vote matters” and “Stop the Murder of Democracy”.
“I think voting right is the most basic point of democracy … People who actually want to vote, who actually care about the future of India, they are just being (denied) voting rights,” said Khushi Shrivastava, a 22-year-old architecture student who attended the Bengaluru protest.
There were also protests over police action against congress party leaders and the voter lists revisions.
On Wednesday, the opposition Congress party accused police of using “brute force” to briefly detain party leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Vadra, and other lawmakers as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.
Delhi Police said the allegations were being used to “defame” the force.
BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia said the allegations were “being levelled by an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. The claims had “no base, not an iota of evidence”, he told reporters at a media briefing on Thursday.
Police have barricaded the area in Delhi ahead of Saturday’s planned demonstrations.

The move may be surprising. In September 2025, Disney joined others in publicly criticizing Character.AI for stealing content and harming kids. Specifically, Disney sent a strongly worded cease-and-desist letter that accused Character Technologies of weaponizing Disney characters “in a way that could damage its brand long term,” Axios reported.
“Character.AI’s infringing chatbots are known, in some cases, to be sexually exploitive and otherwise harmful and dangerous to children, offending Disney’s consumers and extraordinarily damaging Disney’s reputation and goodwill,” Disney wrote at the time.
That scandal ended with Character Technologies wiping all Disney-owned characters from its platform, but since then, Disney has hired former Character.AI chief Karandeep Anand as its first chief technology officer, Deadline reported.
Disney did not respond to Ars’ request for comment on whether the company plans to use Character.AI technology in products for kids.
It’s possible that Disney will be outbid and not acquire any Character.AI intellectual property. But ever since Disney’s potentially lucrative partnership with OpenAI fell through after Sora’s abrupt shutdown, the entertainment giant has been looking for more ways to “get in the AI game and profit from its boom,” Deadline reported. (Meanwhile, OpenAI apparently plans to revive Sora without Disney, insiders told The Information.) So, Disney may be moving early in the hopes of acquiring chatbot technology proven to resonate with its fanbase. It may possibly even take over the platform in a transition that preliminarily would be managed by Character.AI employees, the press release said.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on Wednesday that she probably spends “three or four more hours” than her male predecessors tackling household duties on top of her already packed daily schedule.
“In the morning, I bathe, fix breakfast and then wash dishes, not to mention apply makeup,” Takaichi, elected last year as Japan’s first female prime minister, told parliament.
“I feel like I’m spending three or four more hours than male prime ministers doing these things.”
A self-described workaholic, Takaichi has previously said she slept just two to four hours a night and sometimes scheduled 3 a.m. staff meetings.
Gender roles are rigid in Japan and women are chronically under-represented in politics, with just 68 female lawmakers elected out of 465 seats up for grabs at the last Lower House election in February.
Discussions about Takaichi’s time management came up when a ruling coalition member asked her about the marathon hours prime ministers customarily spend attending parliamentary sessions.
It is common for Japanese leaders to devote five to seven hours a day being grilled by opposition lawmakers or otherwise just sitting in parliament.
Citing a study, lawmaker Fumitake Fujita of the Japan Innovation Party, also known as Nippon Ishin no Kai, said that, in 2022, Japan’s prime minister attended parliamentary sessions for 72 days, versus 50 days in the United Kingdom and 13 in Germany.
While acknowledging the importance of legislative discussions, Fujita said: “The fact that our leader is confined for such long hours to parliament isn’t in line with the global standards.”
Takaichi said in a post on X in July that she was “getting consumed until dawn with poring over documents brought home from work and those related to parliamentary questioning.”
“I do enjoy reading these piles of documents at midnight that I took home,” she said on Wednesday.
“But it is difficult for me to squeeze out time to buckle down and think with a clear head” about “the future direction of this country or my grand vision for it,” she said.

The other day I whizzed past several people while running in the park, my playlist blasting at full volume. The next morning, I smiled at a barista while ordering a caramel apple-flavored matcha latte. Afterward, I sat on a park bench reading a book, called up a pal to chat about her recent trip to Prague, and then asked my Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses what meetings were coming up on my calendar. The chipper AI voice said I hadn’t connected my Google Calendar yet (I had) and asked if I would like help connecting. I sighed and then asked it to play an upbeat song. It picked Kendrick Lamar’s “Not Like Us.”
I don’t miss the camera on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses
It’s harder to be a perv in these audio-only glasses, but removing the ick does make them less ‘useful.’
These past few days, dozens of people have seen or interacted with me while wearing smart glasses. Not a single person noticed. Probably because these audio-only versions look just like normal glasses. They come in a retro Clubmaster look — like the ones pictured in this review — or a more Wayfarer-esque Burbank style. Honestly, people usually don’t notice when I wear camera glasses either. But for once, I didn’t feel like a creep.
The Good
- I don’t feel like a creep wearing these
- Long battery life
- Lightweight
- Stylish
- Good for open-ear audio
The Bad
- Expensive for what they are
- Still not convinced AI is the killer app for these
The audio-only Ray-Bans aren’t a novel concept. Seven years ago, I strutted around Manhattan taking calls and listening to tunes in the Bose Frames, which also combined Bluetooth audio with stylish sunglasses. Nobody noticed me in the Bose back then, either. What makes this pair notable is that it’s 2026, they’re made by Meta, and, well, there’s been vigorous discourse about whether smart glasses are a form of spyware.
Let’s get privacy out of the way. During setup, all the privacy and data opt-out disclosures were much more prominent than when I’ve previously tested Meta glasses. A screen explained how visual data from AI experiences is handled. (You can opt out of Meta using that data to improve AI; voice data, however, is still used.) There’s no visual data from these glasses — this is simply the new messaging for any pair of Meta glasses. You can also opt out of sharing “additional data” with Meta as well, which is enumerated in a separate document online. This is a good thing, though it doesn’t address what makes people uncomfortable about smart glasses: the uneasy feeling that someone else is recording you.
You know what sort of does, though? Removing the camera. The Bose Frames never triggered the same level of distrust because they were “just” sunglasses-shaped headphones. That applies here too. Frankly, I felt much lighter wearing these out into the world precisely because I couldn’t record footage of anyone. (Even if I feel lame saying “Hey Meta” in public.)
I can imagine people still distrusting these Ray-Bans because they have always-listening capabilities for waking up the AI assistant. However, you can disable the wake word in settings and use a customizable button on the right temple arm instead. (This automatically feels 10 percent less silly if you “must” talk to AI assistants outside the home.) There’s no native way to record a conversation directly from the glasses. Any other audio-based feature, like live translation, has to be manually started.
I’m not saying these can’t be modded or used for evil out of the box. Where there’s a perverse mind and ill will, there’s a way. I’m saying it’d take more effort because these glasses simply don’t do very much.
At least, not yet.
Meta’s Muse AI is eventually coming to the glasses, but it’s not available right now. Right now, the glasses ship with the less powerful Muse Spark model. It’s better than what was on the Ray-Bans in 2023, but it’s still meh unless you’re using it for accessibility reasons. In which case, these glasses may not be the best use of $350. A camera-equipped model is more helpful for low-vision and blind users. For hard-of-hearing users, the FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature isn’t available yet, and for deaf users, the Meta Ray-Ban Display may be more useful because they support live captioning.
For everyone else, Muse Spark is nerfed without the camera but can still come in handy. For example, granting access to your messaging apps, Google Calendar, and email lets it do some light scheduling and correspondence on your behalf. If you enable location sharing, you can send where you are to the group chat. It’s fine for these tasks, but not great. It’s adept at short queries like “What’s my next calendar event?” or “Set a reminder to update my editors at 12PM.” With more complex asks, I’ve found Muse Spark gets confused, and it’s faster to whip out my phone. I ended up mostly asking it to set reminders for to-dos I remembered while in the middle of something else.
Muse Spark can also give you local recommendations and turn-by-turn audio directions while walking. As I’ve written before, that’s great if you’re traveling. Less so if you’re familiar with your local haunts. In my neighborhood, I already know which coffee shops have the best Wi-Fi and snacks — and it wasn’t the one Muse Spark suggested. As for walking directions, they’re not something I need that often. When I did, I found using Google Maps on my phone more helpful for getting my bearings.
I’m sure Muse will open up more possibilities when it arrives later this year. Then again, I’ve seen demos, and I’m still skeptical that agentic AI will be the thing that convinces people to buy smart glasses.
So what do I like about these? They’re simply a good pair of open-ear headphones.
I said good, not great. Sound quality is decent, but you’re still dealing with all the tradeoffs that come with this form factor. They struggle at louder volumes. The trebles start to get tinny, and bass can sound distorted. There’s inevitably sound leakage. My spouse frequently reminded me that they could hear everything I was listening to, all of the AI’s responses, and my phone calls. Conversely, even at top volume, ambient noise can still drown out your content. These won’t cut it on a loud subway, for instance.
Still, it’s nice to listen to audiobooks around the house without jumping out of my skin anytime my spouse or cats want my attention. On my daily walks, I’m less afraid of my maniac neighbors mowing me down in their murder mobiles. (New Jersey drivers, man.) It’s not mind-blowing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to my day-to-day routine. And I don’t have to think too hard about it.
At 43 to 47g, these are also much comfier than every other pair of Meta glasses I’ve tried. So far, I’ve worn them for two full days, including a 30-minute run and multiple walks, with zero issues. My Clubmaster review unit also has nose pads — huzzah for anyone with a low nose bridge. That also made for a huge improvement in call quality since the mic for calls wasn’t smushed up against my schnoz. The temple tips can also be adjusted for a better fit.
I usually ding smart glasses for not supporting my -10 prescription and severe astigmatism. These support a range of -12 to +6 — I’m still waiting on a prescription pair, but at least my garbage eyeballs don’t preclude me from wearing these as my daily glasses. All in all, these glasses will fit a much broader range of faces and vision needs.
Battery life is also phenomenal. I was able to eke out two full workdays without sticking the glasses back into the case.
Okay, I lied — one more gripe. These feel expensive for headphone glasses that don’t do much yet. The Meta Glasses, for example, now start at $250 and technically do more. These are $100 more for what, exactly? The Ray-Ban branding? The privilege of not worrying about freaking out other people? If these were $150 or $200, I’d say these would be a no-brainer. Starting at $350 without prescription lenses, without the hearing assistance features, without Muse? That feels off.
But pricing complaints aside, I didn’t miss the camera. (I only ever use it to take cat videos anyway.) Muse Spark isn’t what I’d call the most compelling AI model, but it’s useful now and then. For the casual user, the headphones are the most useful part of smart glasses.
I wish I could just thrust these into the air and declare that nixing the camera solves the privacy problem. I can’t. Yes, I’m relieved that I don’t have to worry about people punching me in the face if I wear these out and about. I don’t think most people want more than this right now. Still, I’d be lying if I said I didn’t personally know several people who would miss the camera. Not because they’re perverts, but because they find them to be genuinely useful tools for candid home videos, content creation, accessibility, or multimodal AI. For those people, this type of smart glasses isn’t a real option.
Besides, who’s to say Meta won’t add more ambient listening features down the line? Then what? The lack of a camera is only a comfort for now. It doesn’t negate the need for continued, thoughtful discussion about AI wearables, the definition of recording, and what role these gadgets ought to play in our lives.

Agree to Continue: Ray-Ban Meta Audio
Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate.
To use the Ray-Ban Meta Audio smart glasses, you’ll need a Meta account and the Meta AI app downloaded onto your phone. A Meta account works across platforms like Meta, Instagram, and Quest and comes with its own terms of service and privacy policy. Should you decide to integrate with services like WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, Apple Music, Apple Health, Garmin, Strava, Amazon Music, and Spotify, you also agree to those terms and privacy policies. You may also be asked to give permissions related to Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, location services, and voice data. If you choose to get a pair of prescription lenses, you may also be asked to share that information with Ray-Ban and/or LensCrafters.
If you are concerned about privacy, you can access the Glasses Privacy menu in the glasses’ settings. There you can view the voice activity log as well as the “Share additional data” toggle. To access the visual data opt-out toggle, go to the glasses’ settings and navigate to the Meta AI menu.
The smart glasses also come with supplemental terms of service and privacy policies / notices, including:
Final tally: Two mandatory agreements, eight supplemental agreements and notices, and several optional agreements.

Kenya must be 'clean' to be credible, says Wada chief
- Published
Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain its credibility as it prepares to stage the 2029 World Athletics Championships, according to Witold Banka, president of the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), .
Banka was speaking at the end of a three-day visit to Nairobi where he held talks with President William Ruto, government and sports officials, the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya (Adak), athletes and representatives of law enforcement.
Wada said the visit was intended to build on recent progress in Kenya's anti-doping programme at a critical time following Nairobi's selection to host the 2029 World Championships.
"Kenya calls itself probably 'home of champions', but every home has to have a good host and has to be clean to be credible," Banka told the BBC.
"We absolutely need to instill the culture of clean sport."
Kenya was awarded the 2029 championships in September, making it the first African country selected to host the event.
The decision has increased scrutiny of its efforts to tackle a long-running doping problem.
More than 140 Kenyan athletes, predominantly distance runners, have been suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit since 2017.
The Polish former sports minister said he had received a clear commitment from Ruto's government to a policy of zero tolerance towards doping, but warned promises would have to be matched by results.
"Wada will monitor this situation and observe the dynamic. Action speaks louder than words," he said.
Banka said his discussions with Ruto also focused on strengthening an independent Adak, and ensuring it has sufficient government support.
- How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships 
  - Published15 September
2029 will be the real test
Nairobi 2029 could provide a global test of Kenya's ability to protect its sporting legacy.
For a country whose distance runners have helped define global athletics for generations, the stakes extend beyond staging a successful championship.
"The problem with anti-doping is not with rules and standards," Banka said. "The problem is with implementation."
Another challenge is testing infrastructure.
Africa currently has no Wada-accredited doping control laboratory following the loss of accreditation of the facility in Bloemfontein, South Africa.
Wada initially suspended the laboratory in March 2024 because of multiple failures to comply with its International Standard for Laboratories.
Its accreditation was formally revoked in May 2025 after those problems were not satisfactorily resolved.
Banka said Kenya has shown political interest in establishing its own facility, but cautioned against expecting a laboratory to be accredited in time for the 2029 championships.
The process, he said, takes years because the consequences of laboratory error can be enormous for an athlete.
That leaves Kenya facing a more immediate priority: strengthening the system around testing rather than relying on a new laboratory as a solution.
'Doping has no colours and flags'
Banka also rejected the idea that doping should be viewed as an exclusively Kenyan, or African, problem.
"Doping has no colours and flags," he said, pointing to cases across established sporting nations including the United States, Germany and his native Poland.
"The problem would be to ignore this issue, not to tackle, or to pretend that there is no doping here."
Wada, he added, can investigate sport but cannot dismantle the criminal networks supplying prohibited substances.
"We are not a superpower. We are not law enforcement," he said.
"They have tools to really go after those who are destroying the credibility of the sport and the country."
He said intelligence indicated performance-enhancing drugs were being produced in Kenya and described Africa as a significant market.
According to him, athletes are often the "weakest points in the ecosystem", arguing that anti-doping authorities need to pursue not only competitors who break the rules but also the coaches, doctors, managers and suppliers who enable doping.
Some athletes, he suggested, are being exploited by people "who have money, who have power" and see them as a route to profit.

The Russian Gymnastics Federation says former Olympic champions Angelina Melnikova and Viktoria Listunova are among three athletes denied visas to enter the Netherlands for the world championships starting on Saturday.
Melnikova would have been the defending champion in the women’s all-around in Rotterdam for the week-long worlds that are a team qualifying event for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Russian officials will ask the International Olympic Committee and World Gymnastics to strip the championships of its status as a Los Angeles qualifier, sports minister Mikhail Degtyaryov wrote on social media on Tuesday.
Melnikova and Listunova were gold medalists in the team event at the 2021 Tokyo Olympics, edging a United States team competing without Simone Biles who withdrew.
The Russians were due to travel to the Netherlands with 18-year-old Anna Kalmykova. Four other Russian gymnasts were allowed into the country, Russian media reported.
Russian gymnasts were cleared in May of restrictions to competing internationally by World Gymnastics, after years of being banned or required to pass vetting for neutral status during the full military invasion of Ukraine.
Countries hosting sports events still retain the right to deny visas for political or security reasons.
At the 2024 Paris Olympics, no Russians competed in artistic gymnastics.

Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993
- Published
Rwanda has signed a 10-year deal with Formula 1 to host races in the African country, starting "in the early 2030s".
The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali and next to the city's new international airport. It will be the first F1 race in Africa since 1993.
A statement from F1 said the project came as a result of "years of collaboration to ensure the right foundations, with the best partner, are in place to deliver a successful, sustainable and world-class grand prix for generations to come".
The circuit, designed by the former F1 driver Alex Wurz, has been "designed to work in harmony with the natural landscape, using the area's elevation changes to create a unique and challenging racing experience while delivering exceptional viewing opportunities for fans," the statement added.
F1 hopes the race will provide an opportunity for the sport to expand its profile in Africa, a relatively unexplored market compared to Europe, Asia and the Americas.
It has not yet been established where the race may best fit into the schedule during the year.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
- Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A 
  - Published7 hours ago
The sport is likely to want to avoid holding the race in the main rain season of March to May. There is a shorter, less disruptive rain season from October to November.
F1 is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.
Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: "For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement.
"Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.
"The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people."
F1 president Stefano Domenicali said the new contract was "a landmark moment for F1", which would mean the sport was racing "on every inhabited continent".
Domenicali added: "Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."
Sportswashing controversy
The race is likely to lead to opposition from human rights groups accusing Rwanda of sportswashing, as has been the case with its sponsorship of Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa.
Rwanda's east-central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
A spokesperson for F1 said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."
The track's build process will be overseen by three companies, with long-time F1 track architect Tilke and DAR working alongside WurzDesign as the creator of the circuit.
It is designed to be fast and flowing, with significant elevation change, using the natural contours of Rwanda's hilly landscape.
The first grand prix in Africa was the final round of the World Championship in Morocco in 1958.
South Africa hosted a race during the apartheid era - from 1960-66 in East London, now known as KuGompo City, before the race moved to Kyalami near Johannesburg from 1976-85.
Kyalami returned for two races in 1992 and 1993 as apartheid was coming to an end.
The country has held talks with F1 in recent years about a return at various venues, including Kyalami and Cape Town, but a deal has not proved possible.

Lena Dunham's Girls to return for limited HBO run
- Published
HBO's award-winning show Girls will return to screens for a limited run ten years after the series finale aired.
Lena Dunham – the show's creator, writer, and one of its stars – shared the announcement in a mock zoom call with members of the original cast Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Andrew Rannells.
All five actors, whose careers launched off the back of Girls, will be part of the five-episode revival with production set to begin in 2027. Judd Apatow, who helped get the show green lit with HBO, will also return as executive producer.
"We always said we would only return to 'Girls' if there was a specific story we were burning to tell," Dunham said in a statement.
"I've missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn't quite picture them in the present day," she said.
"Then, right around my 40th birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it's pretty hard to get them to stop," she said.
Girls, which ran for six seasons from 2012 to 2017, was nominated for 19 Emmys and won two, including best casting.
It follows the lives of four friends – Hannah, played by Dunham, Marnie, played by Williams, Jessa, played by Kirke and Shoshanna, played by Mamet – living in New York City during their 20s.
The show, created by Dunham when she was 23-years-old, attracted both praise and controversy during its airing. The BBC ranked it as number 30 on its 100 Greatest TV Shows of the 21st Century.
"We're thrilled to have Lena turn her gaze from the tumult of one's twenties to the milestone of turning forty," Amy Gravitt, executive vice-president of HBO programming, said.
"To say the world has changed since we last saw Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, Jessa, and Elijah is a massive understatement, but we know fans - old and new - will be happy to see how they've grown and relieved to see that they're still the 'Girls' we knew way back when."
The title of the limited run has yet to be announced, but Dunham did ask her fellow cast on the mock zoom call, "can we still call it Girls?", before joking "because we're old as".
Other cast and production members, most notably actor Adam Driver, were absent from HBO's official statement. Driver, in his breakout role, played Dunham's on-and-off again love interest in the show.
In her 2026 bestselling memoir Famesick, Dunham alleged Driver's on-set behaviour at times turned verbally aggressive and physically imposing. Driver has not publicly commented on the allegations.
In Famesick, Dunham also wrote about the breakdown of her working relationship and friendship with co-showrunner and executive producer Jenni Konner. Konner is not included in HBO's statement about the show's revival.
Dunham wrote on her Substack that "it's rare in life that you get the chance to return to something you love with new knowledge and a ... ton of gratitude.
"I love these girls (and boy) and I love all the people who have reminded us afresh why we do this, which is the joy of being together and the chance to wear yellow mesh…" she wrote.
Since Girls ended, Dunham has gone on to create the Netflix series Too Much in 2025 and indie film Sharp Stick.

Friends become foes: Vaishnaw on how India guards against geopolitical shocks
As wars upend the global order and the US's reliability as an ally comes under question, Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said India must identify economic vulnerabilities and plan 20 years ahead to withstand geopolitical shocks.
India must prepare for a world where friends can turn into foes and geopolitical shifts can upend economic calculations, Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said, making a case for reducing strategic vulnerabilities as global alliances become increasingly unpredictable.
Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, Vaishnaw said India could not afford to depend blindly on other countries for critical technologies, manufacturing inputs and economic stability. The focus, he said, must be on identifying vulnerabilities before external policy changes disrupt domestic production and growth.
"There are times when friends become foes, so it is very important to identify the factors that could make your production and economy vulnerable to someone else's policies," he said.
"Things change, politics change, and geopolitics plays a big role. So, we have to constantly calibrate our approach," Vaishnaw added.
His remarks come at a time when wars, protectionist trade policies and uncertainty over traditional partnerships, particularly with the US under a mercurial Donald Trump, are forcing governments to reassess their economic dependencies.
INDIA’S 20-YEAR GAME PLAN
Vaishnaw said India was taking a long-term approach to building economic resilience, planning decades ahead rather than reacting to each geopolitical disruption as it unfolds.
The government's planning framework divides its priorities into three horizons: short-term goals spanning three to five years, medium-term objectives covering five to 15 years, and long-term ambitions extending 20 to 25 years.
"We think along those lines, identify those vulnerabilities, and start working on them," he said, adding that India’s approach to identifying vulnerabilities and addressing them is very methodical.
US TRADE TENSIONS ADD TO UNCERTAINTY
Vaishnaw did not name any country, but his comments are reflective of India’s strategic restraint in the face of the long-pending trade agreement with the US, which has turned into a major test of bilateral ties.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said earlier this month that negotiations had reached a "plateau", leaving limited room for further concessions. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has also said a deal is not imminent, despite both sides striving to iron out differences.
India is seeking better tariff treatment for its exporters while protecting sensitive sectors. New Delhi has resisted opening up markets for products such as dairy, poultry, rice and wheat, and has sought greater clarity on US tariff measures before making concessions.
Washington, meanwhile, has pressed India to reduce its Russian oil dealings, arguing that revenue from those sales helps finance Moscow's war in Ukraine. A new US law that could pave the way for tariffs of up to 100% on Indian goods over purchases of Russian oil has thrown another spanner in the works.
During Trump’s second term, ties between India and the US have been rocky for the most part. Tariff threats and an immigration crackdown by targeting H-1B visa holders have cast a shadow on efforts to stabilise the partnership.
Against this backdrop, Vaishnaw's remarks indicate that India’s resilience will depend not only on who its partners are today, but also on how prepared the country is if their priorities change tomorrow.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the City Council speaker have agreed on legislation to end horse-drawn carriage rides in Central Park, a change animal-rights advocates have sought for more than 150 years. The City Council is due to vote on the measure on 22 October. If approved, it would phase out horse-drawn carriages by 1 June 2028, Politico reported on Tuesday. Council Speaker Julie Menin said she expected the 51-member body to approve it with enough support to override a veto. The agreement announced Tuesday (local time) includes changes to the bill proposed earlier this year, including provisions to help horse-carriage drivers find new jobs and receive compensation after the ban takes effect. Under the amended proposal, city agencies selected by the mayor would have to submit a plan by 1 April 2027 to assist drivers, owners and stable employees. The plan may include financial support, although the bill only requires the city to consider compensation for carriage owners and does not guarantee payouts. It also includes what the City Council leader's office described as stronger protections for horses, including prohibiting owners from selling or transferring licensed horses to other carriage businesses or for slaughter. Horse-carriage owners would have to inform the Health Department, along with the Mayor's Office of Animal Welfare, at least 10 days before they get rid of a horse. Additionally, anyone caught running a horse-drawn carriage after the ban could face penalties of $10,000. In a statement, Menin said, “Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City’s history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability.” She added, “Next week, the Council will take decisive action by voting on [this bill] to protect New Yorkers, visitors, and the horses themselves.” A spokeswoman for Mamdani declined to comment on whether he would sign the bill into law, but stated that “a deal had been struck” with Menin regarding the legislation. The spokeswoman added, “We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all.” In a social media post, Mamdani wrote, “The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected, and the horses are safe.” Central Park currently has 68 horse-drawn carriages, supported by about 150 drivers and more than 180 horses, industry spokesperson Christina Hansen said. The bill has 29 City Council co-sponsors, enough to secure passage in the 51-member chamber. The use of horse-drawn carriages in Central Park has been a contentious issue for a long time. Animal-rights activists have argued that forcing the animals to work in urban conditions undermines their long-term health and is unsafe. In 2013, during his campaign, former Mayor Bill de Blasio pledged to shut down the industry on his first day in office, but failed after his plan was unable to secure support from the City Council. However, calls to ban the rides escalated earlier this year after an 18-year-old Indian tourist, Romanch Mahajan, who was riding in a carriage with his family, died after falling from it. Following Mahajan's death, a poll by the Central Park Conservancy, which has advocated for the ban, revealed that roughly 68% of New Yorkers supported banning the carriages. David Saltonstall, the CPC’s vice president for government relations, said, “This is fundamentally about public safety,” and added, “It’s about mitigating a known and growing risk that we have watched build for years, which very sadly culminated in the death of Romanch Mahajan.” Carriage operators have argued that the rate of horse-related injuries is far lower than that of other activities permitted in the park, including riding e-bikes or scooters. They argue that, without carriage revenue, they will likely struggle to care for their horses and pay fees to relocate them after the ban comes into effect. A video is circulating on social media (here, here) that purportedly shows a young woman criticising the ongoing Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a young woman criticising the ongoing CJP protest demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
Fact: The video is AI-generated and does not show an authentic recording of a young woman criticising the ongoing CJP protest demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed a watermark bearing the Instagram handle @sifatsangh. A Google search for the handle led us to the same video (archived), which was uploaded to the account on 07 October 2026. We also observed that the speech patterns throughout the video resemble those commonly found in AI-generated audio.
To further verify the video, we analysed it using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive, SynthID, and Hiya. Hive and SynthID indicated that the video was AI-generated, while Hiya identified the audio as likely to be a deepfake.
We then analysed the photos and videos posted on the profile using Hive’s AI detection tool, which indicated that the content appeared to be AI-generated. This suggests that the profile may be entirely AI-generated and could be fake.
To sum up, this viral video of a young woman criticising the CJP protest demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation is AI-generated.

Greta Thunberg backs French high school protests over run-down schools
Greta Thunberg has thrown her support behind high school protesters in France
SAINT-DENIS, France -- SAINT-DENIS, France (AP) — Greta Thunberg on Tuesday threw her high-profile support behind high school protesters rattling the government in France, saying “the whole world is watching with awe."
She joined and applauded hundreds of teenagers who demonstrated boisterously outside a school north of Paris under the watchful eye of police.
The surprise appearance by the 23-year-old climate activist, along with another day of marches in the French capital and elsewhere, suggested that high school students' push for more resources for run-down schools is far from running out of steam. That's despite mass arrests, mounting injuries and fatigue from more than three weeks of blockading schools and demonstrating.
Police used clouds of tear gas, water cannons and repeated charges to disperse protesters Tuesday when violence erupted on the fringes of the Paris marches. The Interior Ministry estimated that 161,500 people marched in demonstrations across the country, including 41,500 in Paris.
Outside the Paul Éluard high school in Saint-Denis, where staff and students have long complained of dilapidated facilities and even rat infestations, Thunberg said French pupils are “fighting back, reclaiming their future that has been taken away from them" and are inspiring young people in other countries.
“The international community sees these students and they’re leading by example," she said to The Associated Press. "This generation is one that has been growing up with a sense of hopelessness for the future, when we can see our future and our rights taken from us,” she said.
“Of course people are going to fight back," she added.
The students' grievances have resonated in neighboring Belgium, where some schools closed in Liege. Several Italian cities have also seen student protests, though on a smaller scale than in France and focused on broader complaints. In Germany, high school students are calling for an international youth strike on Nov. 20, in solidarity with the French protests.
Some French pupils say they see parallels between their protests and the “Cockroach” youth movement challenging the government in India and youth-led demonstrations a year ago in Morocco that also demanded better schools and hospitals.
Thunberg also cited protests in Spain, gripped by demonstrations for affordable housing, and in Latin America.
“These movements are connected in one way or another. We are fighting against the same system," she said. "Even though these local issues are different and may vary, we have the same enemy and I definitely think that these movements are inspiring each other.”
The government of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron, whose term ends in May, argues that the movement in France is losing momentum. The Education Ministry said fewer schools were closed Tuesday although the number of staff injured since protests began in mid-September has risen to 147. The government says hundreds of police officers have also been wounded but has not detailed the severity of their injuries.
Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. The interior minister suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand.
Pupils and university students who blockaded the Maurice Ravel high school in eastern Paris on Tuesday said they feel that their complaints are being heard by supporters in France and abroad but not by the government. Some vowed to keep protesting until that changes.
“We’re certainly making noise and getting people talking, but unfortunately, our message isn’t reaching the people who should be making the changes,” said Ryan, a 20-year-old student who said he didn't want to give his surname for fear of possible repercussions.
"That’s why the movement needs to keep going and persist.”

There were days when Dr. Koyyala Ruth John Paul struggled to find food. Estranged from her family after coming out as a transgender woman, she spent years trying to make ends meet, searching for jobs while refusing to give up on her dream of becoming a doctor. When the path to postgraduate medical education was blocked by the absence of clear admission procedures for transgender candidates, she turned to the courts.
On Saturday (October 10, 2026) her perseverance culminated in a milestone. Dr. Ruth John Paul cleared all subjects in the recently announced MD/MS examination results, completing her postgraduate degree in Emergency Medicine at the ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar, Hyderabad, where she studied during the 2023-26 academic session. She has become the first transgender person in India to complete a postgraduate medical course. “I am feeling very happy. It is a matter of pride for me and my community. It is a great achievement in my life,” she said.
A childhood marked by loss
The youngest of three siblings, Dr. Ruth John Paul hails from Khammam district and grew up in a family with limited financial means. She lost her father when she was eight years old and was raised by her mother. She completed her schooling and intermediate education in her native district before clearing the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) and pursuing undergraduate medical education. She came out as a transgender woman during her undergraduate years. This led to her family rejecting her, leaving her separated from them for nearly six years.
The period that followed was marked by financial insecurity and the struggle to survive independently. “There were times when I did not even have food. I struggled to survive and looked for jobs,” she said.
In 2021, she found part-time work at Mitr Clinic (now Sabrang Clinic), which is India’s first transgender clinic. She worked there for around two years while continuing to prepare for postgraduate medical entrance examinations.
A legal battle to pursue her dream
Clearing the entrance examination was not the end of her struggle. Dr. Ruth John Paul said she encountered difficulties during postgraduate medical counselling because there were no clear protocols for accommodating transgender candidates.
With the assistance of transgender rights activist Vyjayanti Vasanta Mogli, she approached the Telangana High Court seeking relief. The legal proceedings continued for nearly two years. An interim order from the High Court eventually enabled her to proceed with admission. In 2023, she secured a seat in Emergency Medicine at ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar.
Her admission marked a turning point, but the challenges did not end there. She said she continued to encounter stigma and apprehension from people who were unfamiliar with transgender individuals.
From apprehension to acceptance
Working in a clinical environment brought its own challenges. As an emergency medicine trainee, she had to interact with patients during some of their most vulnerable moments, while also navigating the prejudices that transgender people can face. She recalled how some people were initially hesitant or uncomfortable around her. “Initially, some people were scared and did not know how to respond. But when I interacted with patients and treated them with care, they began to appreciate me. People who were initially apprehensive have now become comfortable with me,” she said.
A doctor with a larger purpose
Now that she has completed her postgraduate course, Dr. Ruth John Paul wants to use her medical training to help people in need, particularly transgender individuals who require emergency and critical care. “I want to serve everyone, especially transgender people who face critical medical emergencies. I want to provide care without discrimination based on gender identity or sexuality,” she said.

Brady Tkachuk recorded a natural hat trick during an 8:03 span of the second period, brother Matthew Tkachuk posted five assists and the visiting Florida Panthers won 7-3 over the Columbus Blue Jackets on Tuesday night.
Matthew assisted on all three of Brady’s goals, making him the first to assist on each of a brother’s natural hat trick, meaning three consecutive goals in a given game. Brady Tkachuk added one assist for four points; the point totals tied a career high for each Tkachuk.
Seth Jones had four assists, Carter Verhaeghe scored twice and Sam Reinhart posted two goals with a helper for Florida, which went 4-for-6 on the power play.
With Jacob Markstrom day-to-day due to tightness, Florida’s Akira Schmid made 24 saves.
Kent Johnson scored early, while Denton Mateychuk and Cole Sillinger each added a late goal for the Blue Jackets. Cam Talbot stopped 17 of 23 shots before being pulled in the third period for Columbus.
Johnson opened the scoring with 5:49 remaining in the first period. Off an own-zone Panthers turnover, Johnson possessed the puck, broke free and went low to beat Schmid.
Florida, though, tied it 2:27 into the second period, when Matthew Tkachuk slid the puck through the slot for Brady to record his first goal as a Panther. Less than four minutes later, and on the power play, a circle-stationed Matthew sent the puck into the slot for Brady to bury.
Tkachuk completed the natural hat trick with 9:30 left in the middle frame. Again on the power play, Brady benefited from a generous bounce off the end- board of Reinhart’s shot for a top-shelf conversion.
With 6:16 to go in the second, Columbus’ Mathieu Olivier was issued a five-minute major penalty and game misconduct for his slash between the legs of Florida’s Uvis Balinskis. And, in the waning moments of that extended power play with 2:10 remaining before the second intermission, the Tkachuk brothers set up Verhaeghe’s successful net-side one-timer.
Matthew Tkachuk’s fifth assist came 1:20 into the third, via Reinhart’s tip-in, power-play score. Verhaeghe’s wrister through traffic with 16:32 remaining in regulation made it 6-1 and ended Talbot’s night.
Columbus’ Jet Greaves stopped all four shots faced in relief.
