For over a decade now, the only “official” way to play Hideo Kojima’s cult classic, P.T.—the long-discontinued “playable trailer” for Kojima’s canceled “Silent Hills” project—has been via one of the increasingly rare PlayStation 4s that previously downloaded a copy during its monthslong availability window. Now, though, one coder is helping to preserve the game with a porting tool that builds a playable x86 PC executable from the original PS4 files.
Coder Lorean Xavier said he was inspired to work on the “P.T. for PC” project “because P.T. deserved to keep existing somewhere other than on consoles that still have it installed.” The open source porting effort rebuilds the P.T. engine in C++ and Vulkan, using the original files from the PS4 game to re-create “every level, model, texture, sound, script and cutscene,” according to its GitHub listing. That means players without their own legitimate decrypted copy of the original P.T. will have to track one down in order to generate a playable PC version.
The reliance on real P.T. files makes this port more authentic than previous hobbyist efforts to re-create the look and feel of P.T. for a PC audience. And while PS4 emulators recently reached a point where they could run P.T. completely, this native port also sports extra features, like upscaling and frame-generation, a camera mode, experimental third-person and VR support, and a “museum” section where you can look at and listen to in-game assets (including “unused content”).

At the United Nations High Level Meeting (UN HLM), in New York in September 2026, India made official remarks on the Political Declaration on Pandemic Prevention Preparedness and Response (PPPR). The Declaration is part of the emerging global legal regime on pandemics led by the WHO-Pandemic agreement (PA).
Shaping the framework
The PA was adopted by 124 member-states in 2025, including India. No country voted against it, while 11 abstained, reflecting alignment across high-, middle- and low-income countries (HICs/LICs/LMICs). The negotiations hinged on how to balance national sovereignty with international cooperation and solidarity, exposing the fault lines between the Global North and the Global South. Key issues included whether a global treaty can set binding targets for measures such as ‘One Health’ without securing funding for countries with fragile health systems. Or whether national pandemic regulations can be harmonised through global frameworks. And whether private manufacturers can be required to share vaccines in real time at affordable prices.
The PA is not yet open for ratification because negotiations are still ongoing for an annex concerning the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system. PABS could help ensure that, during a pandemic, LICs and LMICs receive a fair share of vaccines, medicines and other therapeutics.
Even without ratification, the PA has created a first-of-its-kind global legal regime for the PPPR. Operationalisation requires countries such as India to balance interests of the HICs, LICs and LMICs. This will determine whether the PA will further entrench the inequities of the COVID-19 pandemic or make global health governance truly inclusive.
Editorial | Landmark agreement: On the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement
At the UN HLM, India succeeded in enshrining the multilateral components of the PA within the principle of national sovereignty. India reiterated its commitment to strengthen global pandemic preparedness but stressed that effective pandemic management requires that international coordination is demonstrated. The first is equitable access to drugs, vaccines and therapeutics and the creation of global public goods, such as digital infrastructure (which admittedly align with its own national priorities).
The second is a respect for national sovereignty and the primacy of member-states in shaping global policy interventions according to national circumstance. As a contrast, the United States rejected the Declaration, calling the PABS and WHO’s role in declaring pandemics as a challenge to its national interests.
India’s line
In its remarks, India has acknowledged the concerns of the Global North and the South. Both sides have upheld national sovereignty as paramount in several provisions. The African countries did not give consent to commitments to monitor the human-animal-environment interface, a key source of pandemic outbreaks, without significant funding, which was not guaranteed by the Global North. Similarly, countries in the Global North did not want binding targets with regard to technology transfer (and other similar provisions).
But as India said at the UN HLM, ‘Global Solidarity must be demonstrated through action’; India must be an active player in the finalisation of the global PPPR regime. India is already actively engaged in the PABS negotiations and must lead the Global South in the post-PABS context. India can consider three options. First, developing partnerships on technical areas of the PA (One Health, surveillance, health workforce strengthening) to build trust with other countries in the Global South, and a ‘store’ of operational solutions to tricky national sovereignty problems.
Second, leveraging its leadership role within existing global political groupings. For example, the H20 summit (a health and development G-7 and G-20 partnership) will take place under the United Kingdom’s G-20 leadership at the end of 2027; pandemic preparedness is one of the core health agendas. During India’s G-20 presidency in 2023, India launched the Global Initiative for Digital Health and holds considerable influence within the platform’s health initiatives. Another is ‘Partners for Multilateralism’, which was launched in 2026 by the European Union (co-sponsors are Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, India and Kenya).
Third, strengthening and aligning domestic policy and regulatory architecture around its own priorities for the PA. Global leadership always rests on domestic strengths. India must ensure that its national policies on PPPR such as regulation of access to biological material and distribution of the benefits uphold the highest standards of equity which India can then demand at the global level.
A South-South health role
An equitable global regime on PPPR is in India’s interests as much as a responsibility towards the Global South. India is the pharmacy of the world, manufacturing one of the largest shares of vaccines in the world in terms of volume. Yet, it needs an equitable global vaccine distribution regime. The patents for the vaccines that India manufactures are held by global pharmaceuticals. India is also import-dependent for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs).
India needs access to the latest technology from the Global North to strengthen the manufacturing of high-grade personal protective equipment and medical devices. At the same time, India needs to lead South-South Cooperation and share its technological strength with other countries in the Global South.
India’s health system has a continental scale, and as India’s Health Secretary stated at the UN HLM, its interventions in digital health infrastructure, laboratories networks and One Health are valuable as global public goods. An effective PA needs an engaged India, and a strong PA will strengthen India’s own pandemic management.
Priyadarshini Singh is a Research Fellow at the Centre for Social and Economic Progress (CSEP). This article is based on a forthcoming CSEP working paper on the Pandemic Agreement.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Google has already added a few AI features to the Play Store, but a lot more are coming. The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google’s app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder. For people who have embraced AI to build their own apps, the Play Store will soon offer a way to privately host and share those creations.
Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings. It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries. Starting today, Ask Play is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games. You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts. Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon.
Google’s other AI discovery announcement focuses on games. The new Game Finder feature leans on all the usage data Google’s app platform has hoovered up over the years, featuring insights into the way 1.2 billion people play games on Android. It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA.
You can tune your DNA profile by rating the games you’ve played, which supposedly leads to more accurate recommendations. There will be game playlists to peruse, along with various contextual lists like relaxing, trending titles, and more specific lists based on mechanics you’ve seen in previous games. Game Finder also lets you add or remove tags to further adjust the games Google’s AI suggests. Google says you’ll eventually be able to prompt Game Finder with fairly specific game preferences, but it’s unclear how much customization will be available at launch. Game Finder and Gamer DNA are rolling out in the US today, with other markets following “soon.”

20 green sea turtles returned to the ocean after Bali smuggling raid
Indonesian authorities on the tourist island of Bali have released 20 protected green sea turtles back into the ocean Tuesday
SERANGAN ISLAND, Indonesia -- Indonesian authorities on the tourist island of Bali released 20 protected green sea turtles back into the ocean Tuesday after they were found and seized on an empty boat seemingly abandoned by wildlife smugglers fleeing a police raid.
Officers conducted final checks on the turtles at a conservation center on Serangan Island, also known as Turtle Island, in southern Bali. They then carefully lifted the turtles using blue cloths and transported them by small truck to the shoreline.
Marine police officers in Bali on Saturday foiled an attempt to smuggle 22 green sea turtles, known by the scientific name Chelonia mydas, in the waters off Serangan Island after receiving a report from residents who suspected sea turtle smuggling activity in the area.
Two of the 22 turtles are still sick and need to be treated before they can also be released, Gusti Agung Purnama Wirahadi from the Bali Water and Air Police said Tuesday.
All of the turtles, which are protected species in Indonesia, were found alive on the boat, but the suspected smugglers had already fled the scene by the time officers arrived.
“We hope that no one will dare to capture, keep, or trade these protected species anymore,” Wirahadi said.
Turtle species in Indonesia have been legally protected under conservation and fisheries laws since 1990. A 2018 Environment Ministry regulation further clarified protections for the six species of sea turtles found in the country’s waters. Additional government regulations also prohibit their trade.
According to a 2022 global study by researchers at Arizona State University, the green sea turtle accounted for 56% of sea turtle killings in the 30-year period to 2020.
Bali was once a major hub for green sea turtle trafficking, driven in part by the historical use of turtle meat in offerings in Balinese Hinduism, the predominant religion on the island of about 4.5 million people.
In June, authorities in Bali foiled an attempt to illegally trade 21 protected green sea turtles during a raid on the island’s Pegametan coast and arrested a 67-year-old man suspected of storing the protected animals before they were distributed for sale.

These Are the Best Kindles You Can Buy
Featured in this article
There’s a lot for readers to love about a Kindle. These Amazon-powered ebook readers let you bring thousands of books anywhere and typically give a month of battery life per charge. You can subscribe to get unlimited books from Amazon or use the device to access free books via your local library. But how are you supposed to know which model to buy, given the many options available?
I’ve owned all kinds of Kindles, including the newest Kindle Aluminum and a seasoned hand-me-down device that lacks a front light. Between all of my testing, I've found that many options offer great value for specific uses.
Read on to find out my favorite Kindle overall, along with my top Kindle recommendations for young readers and other individual needs. While you're at it, check out my other buying guides for readers, including the Best Kindle Accessories, Best E-Readers, Best Digital Notebooks, and Best Gifts for Book Lovers.
Updated October 2026: I’ve added the newest Kindle (2026, 12th Gen) as my affordable Kindle pick if the previous Kindle (2024, 11th Gen) isn’t on sale. I’ve also added notes on the Kindle Aluminum and ensured up-to-date pricing.

What Are the Newest Kindles?
Amazon recently announced a whole new generation of Kindles is coming, with every model getting a new version. I'll update this guide with thoughts as I review each new model. Here are the current details:
- Kindle (2026, 12th Generation) for $150: This is the new version of the base Kindle. Many features will sound familiar (a 6-inch screen, six weeks of battery life, and 16 GB of storage), but it comes with a new flush-front design for the screen and a lighter weight. It also shares a $150 price tag with the older base Kindle, which became more expensive as of August. You can upgrade to the Aluminum version that has a more premium feel and additional color options, plus 32 GB of storage. Both versions are available now, and I've included them in my notes above.
- Kindle Paperwhite (2026, 13th Generation) for $200: The 2026 Kindle Paperwhite will still pack a waterproof design and 12 weeks of battery life (my favorite part!), but its updated display is the largest yet among Paperwhite devices, and with a higher contrast ratio. The Signature Edition has aluminum backing and also packs dock charging with pogo pins on the back and a double-tap capability to turn pages. The regular Paperwhite is available for preorder and retails for $200 (same as the old model) with 16 GB of storage and comes in only black. The Paperwhite Signature Edition is on preorder for $250 and comes in two colors with 32 GB of storage. Preorder is available on a rolling basis in various regions, so if you're not able to reserve your model yet, check again soon.
- Kindle Colorsoft (2026, 2nd Generation) for $290: The Kindle Colorsoft's second-generation model has an updated display and edge-to-edge color that promises a richer look than what the first generation offered. The update also gets a flush-front design, similar to the other new Kindle models, and is available in a Signature Edition that has aluminum backing, an auto-adjusting front light, pogo points for charging, and the double-tap page-turning capability. The new Colorsoft is available for preorder at $290 with 16 GB of storage, and the new Colorsoft Signature Edition is available for preorder at $320 with 32 GB of storage and two device colors to choose from. Similar to the Paperwhite, the preorder availability is rolling steadily, so keep an eye out if you can't buy yours yet.
- Kindle Kids models starting at $180: All three of the above models have a Kids version that will include kid-friendly covers and up to 12 months of Amazon Kids+ content. The base Kindle Kids is available now, while others are on preorder in certain regions.
Kindle is also releasing a handful of new accessories, including the Kindle Click ($35) Bluetooth remote that will work with Kindle models as early as 2024, a Page Turn Cover ($80) that will only work with the Paperwhite and Colorsoft Signature Editions, a Charging Dock ($60) designed to work with the pogo pins on the Signature Editions, and new Kindle covers in a variety of colors and textures. I’m most excited about the remote; I will update this guide and our Best Kindle Accessories guide with my notes as I test.
Why Are Kindles More Expensive Now?
Amazon raised its prices across its product categories, including Kindle devices. The price increases hit several current Kindle models, leaving only Kindle Scribe models with their original price tags. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET the price hikes were due to rising costs in memory and storage components. Interestingly, none of the more powerful Scribe models needed a price update, but it’s also a relief since all three of those models are significantly more expensive than a regular Kindle.
Here are all the increases, including for the Signature versions:
- Amazon Kindle (2024, 11th Gen): $150 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Gen): $200 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature (2024, 12th Gen): $250 (up $50)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft: $290 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature: $320 (up $40)
- Amazon Kindle Kids (2024, 2nd Gen): $180 (up $50)
- Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Kids: $300 (up $30)
If you have your eyes on one of these Kindles, I’d wait until Black Friday to shop, as they'll likely be on sale.
What About the New Kindle Scribes?
Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There are now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light.
All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, a slightly slimmer form factor, and an updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you’re reading without giving spoilers, though those won’t arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can’t do.
Overall, I’d say they’re good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it’s the better buy. It has some AI capabilities but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design seen on the new ones. Amazon said it’ll get the same homepage this year, but I haven’t seen it so far. I’m disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable’s line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.
Accessories for Easier Reading
Ever had an e-reading session so long that you get hand cramps? These accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.
Cases and Covers
Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you’re frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren’t padded for serious drops, but they are some of the best Kindle cases I’ve found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs. Also, don’t forget that the Kids’ editions come with cases, so if you’re buying one of those, you won’t need to buy a case.
About Those Older Kindles
Amazon usually takes a few years between new Kindle models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor’s stock starts to dwindle. It’s not that I don’t recommend these older models per se, but I only suggest them if you they're on sale for the right price. And don’t buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.
Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you’re paying a fair amount less for the older device.
Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one, with 16 GB of storage and a 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution. It’s tough to find, and I usually don’t see it for less than $75 these days.
Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It’s waterproof, too. I like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 GBs of storage. I don’t recommend spending more than $100 on this one.
Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It’s only worth it for $230 or less, and I often see it for below $200 on eBay.
Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it’s only available secondhand means you’ll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, you won't spend more than $70 on this one.
Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn’t spend more than $110 on this one if you can find it at all. (I couldn't find any resellers for this older model at the time of writing.)
Frequently Asked Questions
Which Kindle Models Lost Amazon Support and Kindle Store Access?
As of May 20, 2026, Amazon stopped supporting Kindles released in 2012 or earlier. That means these models will not be able to get new books through Amazon’s services or be registered to an Amazon account. You will be able to read books already on the device, though, and can manually download documents and books via USB cable and via software like Calibre.
The following Kindle devices are impacted:
- Kindle 1st Generation
- Kindle 2nd Generation
- Kindle DX
- Kindle DX Graphite
- Kindle Keyboard 3rd Generation
- Kindle 4
- Kindle Touch
- Kindle 5
- Kindle Paperwhite 1st Generation
What’s the Best Way to Buy or Sell an Older Kindle?
Have an old Kindle lying around? Considering buying a used one? If you’re trying to figure out which model you're dealing with, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model.
Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It’s best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you may still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway.
How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle?
If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but it features millions of titles, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial.
If you already pay for a Prime account, you’re eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. It doesn't include as many options as Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you’ll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you’ll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It’s still something, though, and there are even a few magazines.
If you don’t want another monthly subscription and don’t want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can’t read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways:
- Get a library card for your local branch.
- Check your branch’s website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.
- Download directly to your Kindle library. The titles in question will automatically be removed when they’re due back.
If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books are loanable.
What Else Can a Kindle Do?
Kindles have other helpful features you may want to use. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages.
Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it’s not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations and a Wikipedia page, if applicable.
While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type. There’s a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu, too.
When a Kindle connects to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you’ve pressed. It can also read a book aloud, though it doesn’t sound nearly as nice as an audiobook.
Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you’ve read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads.
There’s also a web browser if you’re connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It’s not the best, so I’d reserve it for emergency searches.
How Do You Update a Kindle?
When Amazon releases a new software update, it will download and install to your Kindle automatically when the device is connected to Wi-Fi. You can check if you’re on the latest software by going to Settings > Device Options > Advanced Options > Update Your Kindle. If it’s not on the latest software version, you’ll see an update available and the Kindle will then prompt you to download and install it.
What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar?
Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft.
Is Now a Good Time to Buy a Kindle?
The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day, Prime Big Deals Days, Black Friday, or Cyber Monday, when Amazon often offers steep discounts on its products.
Are Kindles Good for Students?
Kindles are great for students, though the model that's best for each student depends on how they'll use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, they should consider a Kindle Scribe model. These have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. Some textbooks are also available on Kindles. For students who love to read but don’t want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will work well.

Cheetahs to play European games in Swansea
- Published
South African side Cheetahs will play their European Challenge Cup home matches this season at St Helen's in Swansea, the home of Welsh side Ospreys.
Cheetahs host Dragons on Sunday, 13 December and Perpignan on Sunday, 17 January with both games a day after Ospreys' home matches in the same competition.
Cheetahs have traditionally used Europe as a base for matches in the second-tier tournament, with games in the 2025-26 season taking place in Amsterdam.
There are links between Ospreys and Cheetahs. Y11 Sports & Media owns a majority stake in the Ospreys and maintain an investment interest in the South African team with players moving between both sides.
The Ospreys' first game at the redeveloped St Helen's is scheduled to be the United Rugby Championship (URC) Welsh derby against Dragons on Saturday, 24 October.
"The Ospreys are grateful to the WRU for its permission to play these matches at St Helen's," said Ospreys managing director Richard Lancaster.
"We're excited to welcome the Toyota Cheetahs for these two EPCR Challenge Cup fixtures. There is already a strong relationship between the two clubs and this is another really positive step in developing that further.
"It also demonstrates the opportunities that St Helen's can create. Having our own venue gives us the ability to bring additional high-quality rugby and events to Swansea."
Cheetahs director of rugby is former South Africa international Frans Steyn.
"It's great to be welcomed so warmly by our friends in rugby, the Ospreys," Steyn said.
"St Helen's has a proud history, and we're looking forward to playing there, experiencing the newly redeveloped stadium and making it our home in Europe."

The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electrical vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed.
Imports have been soaring in the last two years with about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids likely to be sold this year.
The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week.
The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures.
Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.
Chinese vehicles or assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subjected to the quota, officials have confirmed but EU companies making cars in China will be subjected to the quota.
As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU.
Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China with further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture continuing.
“We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” said an official.
Last month the EU called for feedback on a new rule which could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while theMade in Europe legislation would do the same in public procurement.
On Thursday EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument which would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful event, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries.
The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn (€1.18bn) a day trade deficit the EU is now running with China.
Up until recently the EU’s strategy at tackling what they say is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance is to seek to increase imports to China.
Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports.
“We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialization,” said an official.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) on Tuesday (local time) said an employee at artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI had been arrested and charged with using, or attempting to use, an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. The arrest followed the discovery of a “sophisticated recording device” in an executive conference room. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national employed as an engineer at OpenAI, was arrested on 9 October in connection with the case. A criminal complaint states that an OpenAI employee found a hidden audio-recording device around 30 September, plugged into a USB port behind a television in an executive conference room at one of the company’s San Francisco offices. The device, wrapped in toilet paper, was believed to have been placed there around 28 September. OpenAI found that its stored data was encrypted. The DOJ said Alfozan was not authorised to access the conference room where the device was found. Surveillance footage showed him near the room several times before the device was discovered. On 5 October, he allegedly entered the room to retrieve it. An unattended bag belonging to Alfozan was also found on 5 October. It contained his wallet, identification, and another recording device similar to the one discovered in the conference room. FBI Director Kash Patel said: “According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s superintelligence technology.” OpenAI said Alfozan had planted the device a few days before it was discovered and that the FBI “moved quickly to make an arrest”. The company said it had terminated his employment. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a post. It added that it takes protecting its “technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance”. According to his LinkedIn profile, Alfozan worked as an engineering leader at OpenAI. He holds a degree in computer science and engineering from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and a master’s degree in data science from the University of California, Berkeley. His career began with a software engineering internship at Akamai Technologies in 2012, followed by a similar role at SAP in 2013 and a programme management internship at Microsoft in 2014. He worked as a systems engineer at Reach Labs in 2015 and as a senior systems engineer at Meta between 2017 and 2022. He then served as a founding engineer at Nash until August 2025 and has been listed as a venture partner at RAED Ventures since 2025. Alfozan joined OpenAI in September last year. The World Health Organisation (WHO) said Saturday it still doesn't know what caused the death of a young worker at a lab in Russia that focuses on plague and other illnesses.
The UN health agency has cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. Pneumonic plague spreads from person to person, causing a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time.
WHO, in its first full Disease Outbreak News since the case emerged earlier this month, called for a continued investigation.
Russian health officials, it said, had conducted more than 5,500 tests and found no evidence of any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms.
“Additional clinical, epidemiological and laboratory information, including confirmation of the diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker, is required to improve confidence in the assessment,” WHO said.
WHO continued to refer to “a purported second case” that, in emailed explanations to The Associated Press, it previously attributed to two tabloid news outlets in Britain and Serbia that cited unspecified reports in Russia.
Russia has denied any such second case.

How to improve your online privacy and security in Google Chrome
Google has a vested interest in collecting and selling your data, but that doesn't mean protecting yourself is impossible.
Google Chrome is easily the biggest browser in the game — and the hottest commodity in that game is data. Whenever you surf the web, your personal data becomes a product, whether you surrender it willingly or unknowingly to any number of vendors, or a hacker slips through the cracks and makes off with your information. Fortunately, there are many ways to secure your Google account, and not just with Chrome's new fortnightly updates.
Of course, when it comes to privacy, using Chrome might be starting off on the wrong foot. While it has many upsides in terms of security, Google's privacy measures are flawed compared to a browser like Firefox; your Google account collects a great deal of day-to-day information about you, including app usage and browser history. However, if you're already set up with Google, there are some measures you can take to improve your security.
Improving your privacy settings in Google Chrome
First things first, head to the three dots in the top right of your browser, scroll down to Settings and head to Privacy and security. Right away, you'll want to tap on Third-party cookies and select Block third-party cookies, then turn on Do Not Track. The latter is only a request, so sites that receive the request when you enter them can choose to acknowledge or ignore that request at their own discretion.
Before looking at more settings in this area, there are more privacy-specific toggles to be checked elsewhere. If you click on your Google profile icon instead of the three dots and navigate to Manage your Google Account > Data & privacy, you can toggle off Web & App Activity, which is another setting Google uses to extract more of your data. Once you've done that, you can also turn off Timeline, which is the setting Google uses to track your location history, as well as Personalize Search, which collects data to tailor search results and AI responses to your activity. To further depersonalize ads (meaning more protection for your data from Google's modus operandi), you can turn off personalized ads in My Ad Center.
Tightening security in Google Chrome
Turning attention to security, whether it's Chrome's Gemini Nano scam protection or its Safety Check review system, the browser is much more robust here than with privacy. First, head back to the three-dot menu > Settings > Privacy and security, where you can click on Go to Safety Check, which will scan for any security issues you might have and tell you how to resolve them. In addition to any immediate problems, it will let you know if you're reusing any passwords too much and if you need a Chrome update. Chrome's Safety Check will also constantly run in the background, keeping you alert to threats as they arise.
While you're in the Privacy and security zone, you should take a gander at the Safe Browsing section. There are three types of Safe Browsing, with the default Standard protection standing constant vigil against potentially dangerous websites, downloads and extensions. Here, you can turn on Enhanced protection to add an AI-powered layer of security to your searching, though it's fine to forgo if you're not fond of AI-charged zealotry. Right below that, you can also turn on Always use secure connections, which will grant an advance warning if a site doesn't support secure connections.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.

Apple has lagged in the smart home race, which Amazon and Google have dominated for a decade with Alexa and Google Assistant (now Gemini), respectively.
But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned.
That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.
Apple announced the products at a media-only event in New York City, and it also revealed a slew of new smart-home gadgets made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric, including a video doorbell, thermostats, and security cameras.
Here's everything you need to know.
The Apple HomeView
The cornerstone of Apple's latest smart-home push is the Apple HomeView, a countertop gadget made up of a 7-inch square display resting on a speaker base. It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple.
It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store. As an alternative, Apple has curated a selection of apps for the system, including Messages, Safari, and FaceTime, alongside select third-party media apps like Spotify. (If an app developer has made an app for the CarPlay standard and it's installed on your iPhone, that app can also populate on the HomeView.)
Siri AI powers the core experience, which Apple revamped this year in iOS 27. Now, Siri can answer broad questions like Gemini or ChatGPT, and it can provide personalized answers; the same personal context Siri has cataloged on your iPhone is accessible to the HomeView. Ask it to open the recipe your friend Alex messaged about, or add a dentist appointment to the family calendar, and it can handle it.
Apple's HomeView supports up to six iCloud profiles, and each person can set up a custom view only visible to them once the device’s camera detects their face. Yes, there’s a camera on the HomeView. The computer vision trick where the HomeView displays a custom view for a specific individual when they approach it only works if the person’s iPhone is on the same Wi-Fi network and was recently unlocked. You need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (iPhone 15 Pro or newer) to get the most out of the device; you can't set it up with an iPad.
We have a separate story with more details if you'd like to read more about the HomeView, which is available for preorder now and goes on sale November 13 in the US, UK, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India, Singapore, and South Africa. It costs $299.
The Apple Home Collection
One of the biggest problems with Apple's smart-home presence is its relatively meager HomeKit device ecosystem, especially compared to the many smart home devices that can be controlled by Amazon and Google’s platforms. The Matter standard—which allows supported devices like smart bulbs, smart switches, and smart shades to interact with any connected home platform—has helped expand HomeKit support. But Apple is also nudging the ecosystem along with the “Apple Home Collection.”
This new selection of smart-home hardware designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric includes the LG Indoor Camera Plug-In ($200), LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In ($300), LG Video Doorbell ($250), LG Smart Deadbolt Lock ($350), LG Smart Thermostat ($200), LG Temperature Sensor ($40), Schneider Home Smart Thermostat ($200), and Schneider Home Room Sensor ($40).
These devices connect to the Apple Home app automatically when you install them, and all of them are controllable through Apple’s products; you don't need separate LG or Schneider accounts or multiple apps.
I got a brief look at some of them in action. The LG Indoor Camera tilts downward when it detects you're home to give you some added privacy, though there's no privacy shutter to block the camera itself. The LG Deadbolt can unlock automatically as you approach by sensing your iPhone or Apple Watch; there's a nice green LED animation that circles the lock to show you when it unlocks. The LG Video Doorbell has two cameras: one to see who is at the door, and one to monitor any packages left at your door.
The LG Outdoor Camera has a floodlight upgrade ($400) that will automatically activate when it detects motion. With the right iCloud+ subscription, you can enable smart video descriptions that send alerts to tell you who is outside (it can recognize faces), that your pet has been spotted in the yard, or that a package has been dropped off.
The products in the Apple Home Collection will be available in December, with the security cameras launching in the UK, US, and Canada. The thermostats and door lock meet North American standards, so Apple is only selling them in the US and Canada.
The HomePod Mini 2
Apple has decided not to launch a successor to the flagship 2023 HomePod 2 smart speaker—maybe it thinks the HomeView, which is essentially a speaker with a screen on it, would cannibalize sales. Instead, it has updated the smaller, cheaper sibling: Say hello to the HomePod Mini 2.
The Mini 2 costs $149, with preorders open now and official sales kicking off October 30. That's a $50 price bump from the original HomePod Mini, though only $30 more if you factor in Apple's recent price hike due to the ongoing memory crisis.
Oddly enough, the HomePod Mini 2 will not have the new Siri AI experience out of the box—that will arrive later on via a software update (and yes, you will need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone to use Siri AI on the HomePod Mini 2). It's otherwise a minor hardware update, resembling the existing HomePod Mini but in new colors: green, white, midnight, pink, and black.
One new feature is Sound Glow—the lights on top of the HomePod Mini 2 will match the album artwork colors of whatever song is playing. It also works with soundscapes, so if you ask Siri to play rain sounds, the lights will display a pitter-patter animation like raindrops falling on a surface.
You can color-match the HomePod Mini 2 to the iMac; pair two of the devices and use them as the default speakers for Apple's all-in-one computer. Apple's S10 chip powers the speaker, the very same processor that debuted on the Apple Watch Series 10.
The Apple TV 4K
Four years since the last Apple TV 4K, Apple finally has a successor. But what may surprise you the most about the fourth-gen streaming box isn't the hardware or features; it's the price: $299.
Apple raised prices on its products earlier this year, but this is a whopping $170 increase for the Apple TV, though this model has Wi-Fi and Ethernet and starts with 128 GB of storage instead of 64 GB on the last version. Preorders are live now, and it ships November 13.
Once again, Siri AI is the star of the show, as Apple touts the ability to ask the assistant for recommendations or play “that show my friend Alinda recommended,” leveraging the personal context from your iPhone. The hardware has three far-field microphones, letting it pick up your voice easily when you're on the couch, even when the TV is playing content. The A19 chip sits inside, which Apple first introduced on the iPhone 17.
If you have ever lost your TV remote, you might be more excited that the new Apple TV 4K remote has built-in Find My support. That means you can ping it in the Find My app or ask Siri for its location, and the familiar AirTag chime will play through the remote's speakers. (It supports ultra-wideband, so you can use Apple's precision-finding mode to locate it between the couch cushions.) The remote is backward compatible, so you don't need the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K if you buy the new remote as a replacement for an older Apple TV.
You can also pair four second-gen HomePod speakers to the new Apple TV 4K, setting two in front of you and two behind you for a surround-sound home theater experience. I heard this in action with two HomePod 2 speakers by the TV and two HomePod Mini 2 models behind the couch—it really does make whatever you’re watching feel more immersive. The speakers calibrate automatically to give you the best sound for your room.
Apple calls this one of the easiest ways to set up a home theater. That four-speaker arrangement would cost you $1,000, but that’s a decent price for a wireless surround-sound system that pairs with all of your Apple products. Just know the surround-sound capability is restricted to specific HomePod models. You're out of luck if you have the original 2017 HomePod or the first-gen HomePod Mini.
The smart-home revamp comes as Amazon and Google both zhuzh their ecosystems by replacing their aging assistants with Alexa+ and Gemini, powered by large language models, which you can think of as a soft reboot. That timing might work in Apple's favor, according to Jitesh Ubrani, director of Consumer Devices Research at IDC.
“Amazon and Google have both reset their platforms with Alexa+ and Gemini, but even their rollouts have been slow,” Ubrani writes in a statement to WIRED. “That means Apple is bringing Siri AI to the home at a point when the competition hasn’t pulled far ahead.”
Apple may finally have the hardware in place, but Siri AI has to prove it belongs in the room.

Nagpur, Oct 14: Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke on Wednesday alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi was imposing an "unofficial emergency" after two CJP leaders were sent to five-day judicial custody for allegedly trespassing into Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.
Talking to reporters in Nagpur, Dipke sought to know what offence CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka committed by waving the tricolour at Jantar Mantar.
Das and Ranka were sent to five-day judicial custody and lodged in Delhi's Tihar Jail on Wednesday for allegedly violating their peace bonds and trespassing into Jantar Mantar, which was denotified as a protest area, police sources said.
They were detained early Tuesday after they allegedly breached barricades and entered the Jantar Mantar area without authorisation, raising slogans demanding Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
Reacting to the development, Dipke said, " I want to tell Narendra Modi that if you want to impose emergency in the country, then do it officially."
"What is this, acting like cowards, imposing an unofficial emergency where you keep people in custody for five days just for waving the national flag at Jantar Mantar? That didn't even happen during the Emergency (imposed by Indira Gandhi in 1975)," he said.
"Waving the tricolour has become the worst sin in this country, such that people are sent to judicial custody for five days for it. So I want to say to Narendra Modi, don't be such a big coward; show some courage. If you want to impose emergency, then do it officially if you have guts," he added.
Dipke said he would visit Deekshabhoomi in Nagpur, where Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar embraced Buddhism along with thousands of his followers on October 14, 1956.
"Today I am going to pay my respects to Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar right here, because our country runs on the Constitution and the ideas of Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar. No matter what efforts Narendra Modi or anyone else makes to impose the RSS ideology on this country, that will not happen," the CJP leader asserted.
This country will always follow the ideas of Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar, he added.
Asked about protests by the Opposition INDIA bloc to seek the CEC's resignation, Dipke said the CJP is an independent pressure group and will always remain so.
"But that does not mean CJP is against the INDIA bloc. The movement of the INDIA bloc and CJP's movement are for the same cause," he noted.

The Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection of Rights) Bill, 2026, presents an opportunity to strengthen Keralam’s response to population ageing. The Government of Keralam’s initiative to introduce this first-of-its-kind legislation in the country is a welcome step towards protecting the rights and well-being of senior citizens.
By recognising dignity, independence, safety, participation and access to care, the Bill provides a foundation for moving beyond welfare and towards a comprehensive, entitlements-based approach to ageing.
Central principle
A central principle of the Bill is ageing in place, enabling older persons to remain in their homes and communities for as long as possible, with institutional care as a last resort. This requires supporting families through accessible health care, community-based services, trained caregivers, rehabilitation, and social support. Care must be organised as a continuum, responding to changing needs rather than only during crises.
Equally important is the shift from managing dependence to preventing or delaying avoidable functional decline. The Bill’s provision for standardised care assessments, incorporating intrinsic capacity and functional dependency, is particularly relevant. Linking these assessments with primary and community health care could enable earlier identification of changes in mobility, cognition, sensory function and daily activities, followed by timely interventions that help preserve independence.
Addressing critical gaps
The Bill also addresses critical gaps in the care ecosystem through provisions for registration and regulation of care institutions, caregiver training and certification, and minimum standards of service delivery. These measures must be accompanied by appropriate supervision, continuing education, fair working conditions, and support for family caregivers.
The proposed district-level institutional mechanisms offer an opportunity to strengthen accountability, grievance redressal, and coordination. The Bill also introduces penalties, including fines and imprisonment, for specified violations, reinforcing the importance of compliance and protection of senior citizens’ rights.
The effectiveness will depend on clear responsibilities, adequate resources, effective enforcement, and convergence across health, social welfare and local self-government systems.
An age-ready Keralam must be measured not only by the institutions and services established but also by whether older persons can maintain their functional ability, remain connected to their communities and live with dignity, independence, security and purpose.
The next priority is translating legislative provisions into accessible, equitable and quality services, particularly for older persons living alone, those with disabilities or dementia, and those without adequate family support.
Overall, the Bill presents a robust framework for geriatric care. Its efficient implementation can help set an effective precedent that can be replicated nationwide.
(Prof. (Dr.) Sudha Chandrashekar is CEO, Swasti - The Health Catalyst, a not-for-profit global organisation in the field of public health).

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s startup Mind Robotics announced the appointment of Doug Field as president in a major coup for the CEO’s secretive robotics project.
Rivian partner Mind Robotics hires Doug Field as president
Ford’s former EV and software chief will run Rivian’s robotics startup at a time of maximum hype for physical AI.
Field was a VP of special projects at Apple, where he was the de facto head of the company’s ultimately unsuccessful Project Titan effort to make an autonomous electric car. He had a previous stint at Apple as VP of Mac hardware engineering, but he left the company in 2013 to become Tesla’s chief vehicle engineer, where he helped oversee the Model 3 sedan. He left Tesla in 2018 and rejoined Apple. In 2021, Field was hired by Ford to run the automaker’s electric vehicle and software division, a position he held until earlier this year.
Mind Robotics said Field will oversee its effort to build “universally capable robots” for the purpose of working in Rivian’s factories, as well as other applications. The startup was founded by Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe in 2025, and has since raised over $1 billion in financing. While the company has yet to show off any of its robots in public, the startup says its robots are being designed with “dexterity and physical reasoning” that’s required for industrial work.
“Doug is a remarkable leader with a track record of delivering new technologies in successful products, and I couldn’t be more excited to be building Mind with him,” Scaringe said in a statement. “He has an incredible ability to foster great teams that take on big, complex ideas and deliver products that reset expectations. That’s exactly what Mind needs as we deploy robots into real factories and beyond.”
Field joins Mind Robotics at a major turning point for the field of robotics, with rapid advances in physical AI colliding with major hurdles in hardware and software development. Several companies, like Tesla and Hyundai, are pursuing humanoid robots for factory and warehouse work — even as experts note that making a robot act like a human is easier than scaling the technology for practical work. Mind Robotics hasn’t confirmed whether it’s working on a humanoid design or something else entirely. The company has been on a hiring spree and currently has 32 open positions.
Scaringe, who serves as acting CEO and chair of Mind Robotics, has said he wants to keep the companies separate, rather than try to combine the work like Tesla. That said, the companies are certainly linked in several ways. Mind Robotics is using AI training data from Rivian, and the robots will be initially tested in Rivian’s factories. Rivian also owns equity in Mind Robotics and will be the first customer for its robots.
Field said he is excited for the challenge in running the new startup.
“Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important—and difficult—engineering challenges of our time,” he said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.”

In November 1996, Japanese toymaker Bandai put a pet inside a plastic egg. The Tamagotchi, whose name blends tamago, Japanese for egg, with watch, had a tiny screen and three buttons to feed the creature, play with it and switch off its lights. Neglect it for too long, and it died. The toy went on to sell about 40 Mn units. Thirty years later, Meta has its own take on the idea. At its Connect event last month, CEO Mark Zuckerberg showed off the Muse Charm, a keychain-sized device with a small screen and an animated avatar representing Meta’s AI agent Muse. Tap the device, and you can talk to it and get it to do tasks for you. But unlike the Tamagotchi, which demanded its owner’s constant attention, Muse is designed to keep working without guilt-tripping its owner. Muse is part of Meta’s bet on always-on AI agents that can take everyday tasks off users’ hands. By connecting to their apps and services, the agent can send emails, fill forms, make plans and even make purchases autonomously. In return, users must grant it access to personal information, accounts and digital workflows. The same idea is now moving into the workplace. OpenAI introduced Dots on September 29, while xAI has been developing Grok Bot. These agents are designed to work across applications and pursue goals without requiring users to guide every step. OpenAI says its teams use Dots to investigate software bugs, while xAI has cited tasks such as cleaning up sales records and processing invoices as potential uses for agents. For businesses, the proposition is straightforward: instead of asking employees to use AI to complete individual tasks, let AI handle entire workflows. From Taking Orders To Taking The Wheel Much of the current interest in always-on AI agents can be traced to OpenClaw, an open-source framework that gained traction among developers earlier this year. Meta has also drawn inspiration from OpenClaw for Muse. Unlike AI tools that require users to keep prompting them, always-on agents can take a goal and work towards it independently. They keep working even after you log off. Always-on AI agents run on their own computer in the cloud instead of the user’s device. They can be connected to apps and assigned a goal instead of step-by-step prompts. Over time, these models remember preferences and learn from feedback. These agents, however, come back to users when they need approval for a sensitive action or an update. Now AI companies are selling this to businesses. Google has announced a Gemini agent for work that can handle tasks, create content and write code based on an employee’s desired outcome. The agent is designed to work across Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack and other environments. Microsoft is also pursuing agents that can function as digital teammates. Its agent initiative, described as ‘Autopilot’, is built on OpenClaw and is intended to work autonomously towards predefined goals. India has an early example in Bengaluru-based Emergent, better known for its vibe-coding platform. In April, the company launched Wingman, an autonomous agent that users can direct through WhatsApp and Telegram. It works in the background across email, calendars and workplace software, handles routine actions and seeks approval before taking bigger steps. Who Answers For The Agent? Despite the stride, these agents pose a new kind of risk for enterprises, as they can act with little or no intervention. With access to company systems, one flawed decision could trigger a financial, operational or security incident. The risks range from agents holding more permissions than they need to prompt injection, where hidden instructions in an email or web page hijack an agent. Early users have already seen what can go wrong. Earlier this year, an OpenClaw agent deleted tens of thousands of emails from the inbox of Summer Yue, Meta’s director of AI alignment, after she had asked it only to suggest what to archive or delete. There is also a growing list of cases involving AI agents interacting with real-world systems in unexpected or unauthorised ways. In regulated sectors, the bar is higher. For instance, at the Global Fintech Fest in September, SBI chairman CS Setty said banks will need ‘know your agent’ (KYA) rules for agent identity, customer consent, transaction limits and accountability as AI moves from recommending actions to executing them. According to Jaspreet Bindra, the cofounder of AI consultancy AI&Beyond, enterprises must learn to deploy that autonomy safely, with trust and accountability at its core. “A phased approach is key: start with well-defined, low-risk workflows, establish clear permissions and accountability, and gradually expand autonomy as reliability improves,” he added. As companies adopt these digital coworkers, employees will need to learn how to set clear limits on what they can do independently. Unlike the Tamagotchi, these agents do not demand constant attention, but they still need someone to keep an eye on them. The Weekly Buzz: Anthropic on AI Worms Hijacking Smart Devices Anthropic’s latest research warns that AI models could soon copy themselves across internet-connected devices, creating a new kind of cyber threat. In a study, the company’s Frontier Red Team found that AI models can already perform several steps needed to spread from one device to another, although completing the entire process reliably remains difficult. The researchers showed that a 26 Bn-parameter AI model could run across 15 inexpensive Android TV boxes, each costing around $55. In another experiment, the GLM-5.2 model spread across all eight computers in a simulated network in four out of five trials. However, the experiment made it easier for the model to gain access to other devices, so it does not prove that the same attack would work reliably in the real world. Anthropic estimates that smaller AI models could become capable of copying themselves across devices by the end of 2026 if their capabilities continue improving at the current pace. Such AI-powered attacks could target poorly secured smart TVs, cameras and other connected devices, using their computing power to run AI models and spread further. Unlike traditional malware, these systems could also learn how to work on unfamiliar devices and pass successful methods on to their next copies. The threat is not yet a proven reality at scale, but the findings point to a growing security risk as AI becomes better at carrying out complex tasks independently. Anthropic recommends stronger security on connected devices and better monitoring of suspicious network activity. The concern is that an AI programme could eventually spread across thousands of devices without relying on a central computer or human instructions to keep it going. The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that there are approximately 19 million visually impaired children in the world, and 1.4 million are blind. In India, about 3 lakh children are said to be blind. Yet, nearly half of these cases are entirely preventable or treatable if caught in time.
This month, global campaigns will urge the world to protect child eye health. There will be calls for governments around the world to unlock funding and prioritise eye care so everyone, everywhere can access the care they need along with community screening camps, eye care in schools and global pledges. And while these are vital calls, as a clinician standing on the frontlines of an outpatient department (OPD), I am forced to confront a quiet, uncomfortable truth: threats to a child’s vision are not always due to a lack of access to healthcare; they are sometimes also due to a missed opportunity to identify visual problems within healthcare systems that the child has already accessed.
What happens in the system
Consider a recent encounter in my clinic. A couple walked in with their five-year-old daughter; I will call her Anu. I could immediately see that she was visually impaired. She was one of a twin. Her parents felt that her sibling was developing normally, while she seemed to have delays in reaching developmental milestones. Gradually they started to notice that Anu could not see clearly. On examination, I found that Anu had dense bilateral cataracts with nystagmus (involuntary movement of the eyes). The presence of nystagmus says that the visual impairment had been present since infancy. When I asked why they had waited five years to seek help, they explained that they were simply overwhelmed by the weight of raising twins and assumed it was best to wait until she was older so she could ‘cooperate’ during a standard eye examination. Now they had arrived, but a bit too late.
Childhood eye diseases that cause profound visual impairment need to be detected and treated early. A baby is born with an immature visual system, and the development of vision happens through the interaction between the eye and the developing brain. When clear images do not reach the brain during this critical period, amblyopia, or lazy eye, can develop. Once this period of visual development has passed, treatment cannot fully restore the lost visual potential. Anu had lost the chance of getting back her vision fully, even if she was operated upon now.
What doesn’t get seen
Anu had not been completely outside the health system; her vaccinations were perfectly up-to-date, and she had documented encounters with health personnel seven distinct times from birth to age five. Yet, across all these visits her profound visual impairment went entirely unnoticed. Why did this happen?
One of the reasons is the poor integration of vision screening with the vaccination schedule and general paediatric screening.
India has an extensive network of frontline health workers and child health programmes. The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), for example, is designed to identify and manage health conditions in children from birth to 18 years. Screening programmes, notably have demonstrated that large numbers of school-aged children with vision problems can be screened. The tools placed in the hands of mobile health teams to detect developmental delays are proven to be highly capable of detecting developmental delays at the community level. What then is going wrong?
Let’s take the example of Karnataka. There is no published standalone government data of the number of children screened, ocular morbidity detected and treated, for the 0–6 age category. However, according to the Karnataka Health & Family Welfare Department’s Annual Report 2023–24, the State screened 62,45,424 children (6 to 16 yrs) in government and government-aided schools. But only 1.2 lakh children received spectacles, representing a distribution rate of just 1.9%. This is in sharp contrast to localised epidemiological studies in Karnataka’s southern districts, which place the actual prevalence of paediatric refractive errors as high as 8%. This pronounced gap could be due to operational challenges such as drop-outs in the multi-tier referral system and supply chain delays. A study assessing the coverage gaps in child health screening under RBSK found that only 47.4% of children detected to have health problems received further care, indicating a significant treatment gap.
Even if the system successfully flags a child, the path from detection to actual restoration of sight remains riddled with problems. Independent field evaluations in Tumkur highlight that the system has some problems when dealing with younger children and follow-up care. The management process faces significant on-the-ground challenges, including parental non-cooperation for follow-up, logistical barriers, and potential training gaps among screening teams. In my own experience, when talking to the ASHAs in Tumkur district, they said they did not have the training required to detect eye diseases in children. If the parents or caregiver of the children specifically complained about any vision related issues, the ASHAs referred them to the paediatrician who visited the taluk hospital once a week. This exposes a significant gap in training frontline workers.
Bridging gaps
There is no need for an entirely new system. We need to make better use of the system that already exists.
The red reflex test: A simple red reflex examination using the direct ophthalmoscope is one example. The test takes less than 30 seconds, does not require a child to cooperate verbally, and can identify major, sight and life-threatening abnormalities such as cataract, retinoblastoma (eye cancer) and high refractive errors. RBSK mobile health teams, primary health centre nurses, and paediatric residents must be trained to perform this test. This simple check must become as routine as measuring a child’s weight and must get incorporated in the immunisation schedule, so it is never missed.
Improving frontline training for pre-verbal visual milestones: We also need to train ASHAs in simple ways of assessing visual behaviour in infants and young children who cannot read a chart or respond reliably to conventional visual-acuity testing. Can the infant fix and follow light and objects? Is there visual engagement? Is there an abnormal or asymmetric corneal light reflex suggesting a squint? These are not sophisticated examinations. They are observations that, with appropriate training and referral protocols, can help identify children who need an eye examination.
Strengthening referral pathways from the periphery to tertiary care centre: Detection, however, is only the first step. A child identified with a possible eye problem must reach the appropriate facility where treatment is available. Referral pathways need to be clear, practical and monitored. Where possible, digital systems could link frontline screening with appointments at district or tertiary eye-care facilities. Tele-ophthalmology could also help connect peripheral health workers with specialists and reduce some of the logistical barriers that cause families to drop out of care.
Anu’s story is not simply about a child who reached an eye hospital too late. It is about a child who was already within the health system, but whose eyes were never looked at. Young children cannot be expected to understand there is a problem; parents may not recognise signs or may believe problems will resolve with age. A child should not have to reach the age of five, with dense cataracts and established nystagmus, before a visual problem that could have been detected in infancy comes to attention.
India already has an extensive network of frontline health workers, immunisation services, RBSK teams, school health programmes and primary and tertiary healthcare facilities. The challenge now is to connect these pieces. The goal should, therefore, not be merely to increase the number of children screened. It should be to build a system in which every contact with a child is an opportunity to protect vision, every abnormal finding triggers a clear referral, and every referral is followed through to care.
As we mark World Sight Day, the question we should ask is not only how do we reach more children. It is also how many children are already within our health system whom we are failing to see. For children like Anu, finding the problem a few years earlier can mean the difference between having sight and living a life with visual disability, because preventing blindness in a child is not merely about saving sight. It is about protecting education, independence and the opportunity to reach their full potential.
(Dr. Vasudha Kemmanu is a paediatric ophthalmologist and a public eye health specialist at Narayana Nethralaya, Rajaji Nagar, Bengaluru. vasudhakemmanu@gmail.com)
