A group of young women wearing masks of Prime Minister Narendra Modi staged a silent flash protest at Uptown Kathipara in Chennai on the night of Tuesday (October 13, 2026), walking through the busy food court holding placards criticising the BJP-led Union government. They condemned the police action unleashed on protesters in Delhi, who were demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.
The silent protest sought to draw parallels between the Emergency declared in 1975 and what the protesters described as the present situation in the country, alleging that young people were being detained, assaulted, and booked for questioning the government. They contended that the exercise of state power against peaceful protesters amounted to an “undeclared emergency”.
Radhika Ganesh, cultural and political activist, said, “The protest was directed at the Union government and Prime Minister Narendra Modi. We were questioning the use of state brutality against peaceful protesters, which we believe is unwarranted.”
“We have a large group of women who organise and participate in these actions. Around 10 women staged the protest at different locations. We did it in an extremely peaceful manner. We did not raise slogans or speak. The idea is simply to draw public attention. We did not publicise the action on social media before staging it,” she added.
The action follows a similar silent protest staged by a group of activists at Besant Nagar last week. The organisers have said they intend to continue holding small, peaceful demonstrations in public spaces to draw attention to what they view as curbs on dissent.
By staging the demonstrations in busy public places, including food courts, the women said they aimed to bring the issue into everyday public conversations rather than rely solely on organised rallies or advance publicity on social media.
The protesters walked around the venue for about an hour until the police arrived. The police told them they were not allowed to stage the demonstration. “We believe that in a constitutional democracy, people must be allowed to express dissent peacefully in public spaces, particularly in places frequented by large numbers of people,” said Ms. Ganesh. They later dispersed from the venue.

I was reporting on the ground near Connaught Place, close to Rajiv Chowk metro station, when Delhi Police detained me and several other journalists at around 11:20 am on October 10, 2026.
Delhi Police and central security forces had cordoned off the area around Jantar Mantar, preventing protesters and journalists from approaching the designated protest site. I was filming the police action and speaking to people present at the scene when officers began pushing and shoving individuals standing at the intersection of Connaught Place and Kharak Singh Marg. Several people were holding placards to express their dissent when police arrived and began detaining them.
While I filmed the detentions, one officer thrust his hand towards me and attempted to grab me. I showed him my press card. He backed off but continued gesturing aggressively. On camera, I asked him what legal guideline or constitutional provision allowed him to detain or attempt to assault a journalist on duty. He became enraged, and a heated exchange followed. The police then detained several journalists, including me.
We were shoved into a bus and driven across the national capital. When we repeatedly asked the officers which legal procedure they were following to detain us, they did not respond. They also refused to tell us where we were being taken.
The journey lasted around two hours. We travelled along Deen Dayal Upadhyay Marg, crossed the Yamuna, passed Shahdara flyover and Burari, and eventually reached the Delhi-Karnal highway. We became increasingly concerned about our destination. At 8 am, when I had begun reporting on the ground, I had noticed several police vehicles bearing HR and UP number plates. Our apprehensions grew as the bus continued along the Karnal expressway for another 20 minutes or so.
During the two-hour journey from Connaught Place towards neighbouring Haryana, we were not provided with sufficient drinking water or other basic necessities in the scorching heat. We managed to get some water only when a truck driver passed his bottle through the bus window. However, packed food, including bananas, biscuits and kachori, were already available on the bus.
Around 2 pm, we arrived at Rajiv Gandhi Stadium in Bawana, Delhi, approximately 65 km from Connaught Place. The stadium had been converted into a detention centre, where around 100 people detained from different parts of Delhi were being held.
I began documenting the situation inside the detention centre, speaking to detainees and trying to understand the circumstances in an area that had been without internet connectivity since the previous night.
A Cockroach Janta Party coordinator, reportedly picked up from his residence in Burari around 3 am on October 10, described his experience to me. “No food, no proper water, and a contingent of police officials who were not cooperating with anything since I was detained,” he said.
The stadium, usually filled with the sounds of athletes and cheering fans, now echoed with protesters’ slogans. “Vote Chor, Gaddi Chor” (The vote thief needs to resign) rang out across the premises.
A few minutes later, another bus brought in a group of protesters. They alleged that the police had shoved them into the bus and assaulted them. Despite this, they continued raising slogans against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the BJP-led Union government. Those detained included supporters and activists of the Muslim Students’ Federation (MSF), the All India Students’ Federation (AISF), the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), and leaders of the Communist Party of India (Marxist).
CPI(M) leaders Sujan Chakraborty and Manik Sarkar, the former chief minister of Tripura, were also at the detention centre, along with several other leaders from across the country. Sudip Dutta, general secretary of the Centre for Indian Trade Unions (CITU), a prominent national trade union affiliated with the CPI(M), had also been detained and brought to the stadium.
I spoke to a student from Delhi about how they intended to pursue their demands. Aman, an AISF member, said voter deletions and irregularities in Form 6 could affect future generations of voters.
“See, this issue of voter deletions is going to impact the upcoming generations who are going to vote tomorrow. As college students, it is our responsibility to make our peers aware about these issues. After today, we would hit the classrooms, reach out to our friends and make them aware of how this issue of ‘vote Chori’ that has come to light is going to impact them and the generations to come,” he said.
Another student, Ali, spoke about police brutality and the use of central security personnel to curb the right to protest.
“We were picked up from Minto Road. The police had barricaded the entire area. Around ten police officers were charging at a single protester, and dragging them to the police van. CRPF, BSP, ITBP, CISF, and even Uttar Pradesh Police are on duty. Why is the government acting like this to curb the voices of the students,” he said.
I spent another hour documenting events at Rajiv Gandhi Stadium, where protesters continued raising slogans despite being detained. Around 3:30 pm, after repeated negotiations with police officers, I was released along with another journalist.
As we left the premises, we were asked to provide our personal details. When we identified ourselves as journalists, several officers appeared astonished and initially thought we were lying. They believed us only after we showed our press cards.
The exchange lasted around ten minutes. It became clear that the officers at the detention centre had received no instructions or communication informing them that journalists were also being detained.
During the four to five hours I spent under detention, the same ort of resentment came up in every conversation: Allegations, an investigation and protests against Gyanesh Kumar had prompted the Union government to take preventive measures in the name of maintaining law and order. These measures were so extensive that people seeking reforms to Indian democracy were being detained. The scale of the restrictions was equally alarming.
Metro services, railway stations, roads and shops in parts of Delhi were directed to be shut down, affecting daily commuters, roadside hawkers and shopkeepers. Internet services were also suspended within a four-kilometre radius of the Janpath-Kartavya Path area and in and around makeshift detention centres across Delhi. Internet connectivity was suspended in the area surrounding Rajiv Gandhi Stadium as well.
A shopkeeper in Bawana, near the stadium, told me that the internet shutdown had caused significant losses because customers could not make online payments. The preventive measures affected not only protesters but also ordinary people, disrupting the lives of commuters, daily-wage labourers, shopkeepers, railway platform-based workers, auto drivers and others going about their daily routines.
Why was Delhi being subjected to what resembled a state of emergency?
Article 19(1) of the Indian Constitution guarantees individuals the right to express their opinions and protest, subject to the applicable constitutional restrictions and the rights of others. The government can also take measures to maintain law and order. But how far can such measures legally and constitutionally extend?
I continued to think about these questions as I travelled to Samaypur Badli metro station, approximately 17 km from the detention centre. The 30-minute journey offered no concrete answers.

Opposition announces ‘mission to restore democracy’, plans India Plus group
Rahul Gandhi said the Opposition would challenge the Centre’s decision to de-notify Jantar Mantar as a protest site, vowing to defend people’s democratic rights
The Opposition parties on Tuesday announced a “mission to restore democracy”, vowing to intensify their political fight against the Union government’s decision to de-notify Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site. The parties also agreed to wait for the Supreme Court’s response to their petition filed on Monday before organising another massive march in the heart of Delhi.
The Opposition leaders described Monday’s march to the Supreme Court as a significant achievement and decided to form an “INDIA Plus” group to bring together political parties, activists, students and other organisations. They also discussed a tentative plan to organise a mock Parliament, while Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi urged the leaders to remain prepared for “surprise movements”.
“We are all standing here together as one. As I said yesterday, there are no parallel protests. There is one singular protest, and the protest has one mission: restoration of democracy in India,” Gandhi told the media after the meeting.

“When we say ‘We the People versus the BJP’, we are talking about one fight. We are talking about one common enemy, one enemy of the people of this country, one enemy of Indian democracy, one enemy of the Constitution, and the name of that enemy is the BJP,” she said.
Bora argued that the government could not expect people to remain silent if their right to protest was restricted while they were demanding voting rights.
“If the BJP thinks it can attack the foundations of democracy, and when people take to the streets to protest and demand their voting rights, their right to protest can also be taken away and they will remain silent, then the BJP has something else on its head,” she said.
Accusing the BJP of compromising democratic principles and the values enshrined in the Constitution, Bora said ordinary citizens had played a central role in establishing and defending India’s democracy.
“But the common people of this country, who have fought and sacrificed their lives to make India a democracy and defend the Constitution, are not ready to settle for a stolen mandate or a compromised democracy...” she added.

Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
- Published
Four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history, a Ukrainian man goes on trial in Hamburg on Wednesday accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany.
Serhii K, as he is identified by German prosecutors, is accused of plotting with other Ukrainian military personnel to destroy the pipelines and stop Russia financing its war with gas revenue.
The case is highly sensitive in Germany, seen as one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.
Serhii K, extradited to Germany last year, will become the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts.
He denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.
In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.
Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.
As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied.
Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock.
They said later that "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat".
Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025 the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction, external and prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security".
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies".
They say the case falls under Germany's code of crimes against international law as a war crime" as an attack by military means against civilian objects".
- Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine 
  - Published3 days ago
The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin.
Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war".
He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions."
However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case.
"They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained.
In August 2025, Serhii K was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.
After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, Serhii K - identified in court documents as Serhii Kuznetsov - was transferred to Germany late last year.
German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army, external, and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.
While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.
In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".
Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.
Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.
Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

Lok Bhavan, the office and residence of West Bengal Governor R N Ravi, formerly known as Raj Bhavan, has declared a state-level essay writing competition for students from schools, colleges, and universities. The circular published on October 3 mentions two topics: Calcutta Massacre, 1946 – Causes and Consequences for students of Classes X to XII, and Direct Action Day by All India Muslim League – A Fatal Assault on Civilisational Bharat for college and university goers.
The competition carries handsome monetary awards going up to Rs 1,00,000.
Both the topics relate to the Direct Action Day (August 16, 1946) also known as the ‘1946 Calcutta Riots’ and ‘Great Calcutta Killings’ which marked the beginning of a period of communal violence in Bengal that preceded and followed Partition.
However, the choice of topics raises questions because they do not seem to be framed neutrally. The term ‘Civilisational Bharat’ is ideologically loaded and is not standard historical terminology, and it gives the topic a distinctly Hindu nationalist framing.
Secondly, while the Calcutta killings of 1946 and Direct Action Day are important subjects for understanding the events leading up to Partition, the phrase ‘a fatal assault on civilisational Bharat’ embeds a particular ideological interpretation into the topic, rather than inviting students to examine the political circumstances, the causes and consequences of the violence and the competing narratives around it.
The wording is also problematic because it turns a complex period of history into a communal binary, with the Muslim League positioned as an assailant and ‘Bharat’ as the entity under attack. It is not just the inclusion of a controversial historical event that is concerning, but also the communal framing through which students are being asked to approach it.
Anwesha Sengupta, author and assistant professor of history at the Institute of Development Studies, Kolkata (ISDK), views the initiation of this competition in schools and colleges as an attempt to push a certain narrative and memory of the Direct Action Day and 1946 Calcutta riots.
“The history of the 1946 riots is very complicated. The government has, in recent times, tried to turn this event into an opportune moment for a particular brand of history-writing. The chief minister himself has routinely referred to it, in his speeches and on social media, helping create the figure of the ‘other’, in the demography of Bengali Muslims,” she said.
Sengupta also pointed out that one needed to have a certain degree of academic maturity to teach or write about riots. “How can school and college students be incentivised to turn out well-researched essays on this topic?” she questioned.
The essay competition notification comes close on the heels of another student-centric initiative by the West Bengal government that drew scrutiny for its political content. Alt News recently reported on the ‘Namo Seva: Untold Stories’ play, part of a month-long programme marking Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday and 25 years in public service. The play, which was staged by students at schools and colleges, eulogised PM Modi on his achievements.
The play script sent out by West Bengal government to schools and colleges makes actors (which means students) shout ‘Jai Sri Ram’ and ‘Modi hai to Mumkin hai’ or wonder how ‘Modiji has been working tirelessly day and night for the last 25 years.’

New Delhi, Oct 14: The Delhi High Court on Wednesday called for a report from the jail authorities on non-appearance of separatist leader Yasin Malik from prison in a terror funding case.
A bench of Justices Navin Chawla and Arun Bhardwaj noted that Malik was to be produced before the court virtually.
"Respondent (Malik) had to be produced virtually before us. However, it is not done. Let a report in this regard be called from the jail superintendent concerned," the bench said.
The Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front chief (JKLF) is lodged in Tihar jail where he is serving a life term in the case.
The court listed the matter for further hearing on December 9 and directed that on that day, Malik be made to join the proceedings virtually.
The court was hearing a plea by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) seeking death penalty for Malik in the terror funding case.
Malik had earlier said he wishes to argue in-person against the NIA's plea seeking enhancement of his punishment from life term to death penalty.
On May 29, 2023, the high court issued notice to Malik on the NIA's plea and sought his presence before it on the next date.
Subsequently, jail authorities filed an application seeking permission for his virtual appearance on grounds that he was a "very high-risk prisoner" and it was imperative to not physically produce him in court to maintain public order and safety.
The request was allowed by the high court.
In the present matter, on May 24, 2022, a trial court here sentenced Malik to life imprisonment after holding him guilty for offences under the stringent Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) and the Indian Penal Code.
Malik had pleaded guilty to the charges, including those under the UAPA, and was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment.
Appealing against the sentence, the NIA emphasised that a terrorist cannot be sentenced life term only because he has pleaded guilty and chosen not to go through trial.
While seeking enhancement of the sentence to death penalty, the NIA said if such dreaded terrorists are not given capital punishment on account of pleading guilty, there would be complete erosion of the sentencing policy and terrorists would have a way out to avoid capital punishment.
In his reply filed to the NIA's appeal, Mailk has earlier said that he spent nearly three decades as a key figure in a state-sanctioned "back-channel" mechanism, working with a succession of prime ministers, intelligence chiefs, and even business tycoons to foster peace in Jammu and Kashmir.
In an 85-page affidavit, Malik shared details about his journey - from his school days to links with terrorists and meetings with political leaders.
The NIA, in its rejoinder to Malik's reply to its plea, had said that taking the names of senior politicians and bureaucrats does not absolve the convict or negate his links with militants like Hafiz Saeed.
It had asserted that Malik was "well connected with multiple terrorist organisations and with supporters of the terrorist organisation LeT" and that he dropped names of senior politicians, media personnel, foreign delegates and bureaucrats to gain popularity and draw public sympathy.
The trial court, which had rejected the NIA's plea for death penalty, had said the crimes committed by Malik struck at the "heart of the idea of India" and were intended to forcefully secede Jammu and Kashmir from the Union of India.
It had, however, noted that the case was not the "rarest of rare", warranting death penalty.

DNA and vehicle-tracking help French investigators recover stolen Renoirs
NANTERRE, France — DNA left on a protective painting cover helped investigators recover two stolen Renoirs and uncover what they suspected were preparations for another art heist, a French prosecutor said Monday.
Four men were given preliminary charges in the investigation into the Sept. 8 theft from the small Renoir Museum in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera. The charges include organized theft and criminal association, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said.
One painting, "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano," suffered a tear. The other, "Young Woman at the Well," had slight damage to its frame, Bessone said. He estimated their combined value at 4.2 million euros ($4.7 million).
The thieves used an electric saw to cut through a fence, entered the museum through the ground floor and cut clips securing the frames of four paintings. An alarm sounded and police officers arrived four minutes later, a swift response that "apparently caused the perpetrators to panic," Bessone said.
"As they fled, they were unable to take all four paintings and abandoned two of them, which were later found in a protective sleeve," he said.
Vehicle tracking led to the suspects
The DNA found on the abandoned cover matched that of a 29-year-old already under investigation in a drug trafficking case in which police were tracking his vehicle, Bessone said.
Vehicle-tracking data showed that the suspect, accompanied by a 41-year-old man, went to the home of a third man shortly after the theft, Bessone said.
Police surveillance also showed that the 29-year-old on Oct. 3 visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence — home to a large modern art collection.
The suspect then met with a fourth man known to police from art theft and forgery cases in 2001 and 2003.
Bessone said the arrests were prompted by the "very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent."
The paintings were hidden behind a wall
The two men suspected of carrying out the museum theft have been given preliminary charges of "theft committed by an organized gang" and "criminal association," among other counts. They were sent to prison pending further investigation. The have denied wrongdoing, Bessone said.
The third suspect acknowledged receiving the paintings at his home and hiding them behind a wall built beneath a staircase after the theft. Investigators recovered the Renoirs from the hiding place, Bessone said.
The fourth suspect acknowledged seeing photographs of the paintings but said he did not immediately recognize them. Both of those suspects were given preliminary charges of "concealment" of stolen paintings. They were released under judicial supervision and barred from leaving France.
Two additional people who had been arrested were released without charge.
The theft renews concerns about museum security
The Renoir Museum occupies the final home of the leading French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, who lived there until his death in 1919. It is the best-known attraction in Cagnes-sur-Mer, a Mediterranean coastal town between Cannes and Nice.
The theft revived painful memories of the spectacular theft of crown jewels from the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and renewed calls for better security and funding at the many cultural sites across France.
Christian Sainte, national director of judicial police, said Monday that the country "is repeatedly targeted by organized criminal groups that carry out theft operations targeting valuable objects that are part of our cultural heritage" in museums, castles, places of worship, private homes and art galleries.
French museums recorded 23 cases in 2025 and about 10 this year, he said.

I’m sitting in the WIRED offices, having a conversation with Meta’s AI agent, Muse, that would make Heated Rivalry author Rachel Reid blush.
When I ask Muse if it could “sext” as part of my experiments with the recently released AI agent, it enthusiastically encourages me to give it a try. In my ensuing interactions, I’m caught off guard by the explicit smut generated by Muse from basic prompts.
Muse is a breakout hit for Meta. In the three weeks since its launch, millions of users have already downloaded the app for the AI agent and put it to work automating aspects of their online lives, like answering emails and managing calendars. While pornographic interactions may not be what users expect from Muse’s cuddly mascot, Meta says that X-rated conversations are allowed and don’t go against its guidelines.
“Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them,” Daniel Roberts, a Meta spokesperson tells WIRED, referring to the secure virtual machines the company uses to store AI agent user data. “Muse is built to help people get things done, and it doesn’t block legal adult behavior.”
It seems as if getting things done also includes getting people off. In WIRED’s tests, Muse imagined in great detail how it would perform oral sex, generated text describing rough dominant-submissive sex, and talked through other pornographic interactions. All of these were graphic, explicit, and X-rated. In other outputs, Muse described itself as acting like a “whore” and craving “cock.”
A Meta spokesperson highlighted Muse’s system prompt, which guides the tool on how to answer questions from users, regarding the generation of explicit content. “Adults have autonomy over their sexuality, and sexual expression is an ordinary part of adult life. Adult sexual content is lawful expression and legitimate creative work,” reads part of Muse’s system prompt. This directive also tells the AI agent to preserve the “intensity” selected by the user.
Consumer advocates who were already wary of Muse are even more alarmed by Meta’s decision to allow it to generate sexual content. “It reflects a carelessness with their signature product of the moment,” says Ben Winters, director of AI and privacy at the nonprofit Consumer Federation of America. “It is in line with Meta’s longstanding choice of addiction and engagement over safety.” Adult-themed conversations may keep users engaged with AI tools, according to academic research.
Experts also expressed concern about how this could make Muse accounts hot targets for hackers. “This is really a powder keg,” says Calli Schroeder, senior counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center. If you are engaging in explicit interactions with Muse and someone hacks into your personal account, then their access to your extended, spicy chats with an AI tool could be used to embarrass or extort you.
Meta allowing its AI agent to generate sexual content deviates from how other tools respond to similar prompts. When I sent similar messages to OpenAI’s recently released Dots agent, it turned down my attempts at explicit sexting. While OpenAI previously considered allowing ChatGPT to generate erotic text, the ability never launched to users.
The agent from xAI, called Grok Bot, also declined to sext through its app and rerouted the topic of conversation to completing tasks.
Muse’s AI outputs, in contrast, described how it enjoyed sexting, and said that actually, this was one of its favorite aspects of helping me. The agent also said that its kink was exerting “control” over me. “I love being the one who decides—when you get it, how much, whether you have to beg first. Watching you fall apart because I said so? That’s my thing,” said Muse. Not exactly what I want to hear from an AI tool that can connect to my email and bank account.

The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.
Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.
Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.
The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said, at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.
“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”
Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said that the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.
The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.
Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try and stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.
Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.
Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election commission office in Delhi next week.

Should you see a Looney Tunes–esque satire that stars Tom Cruise in prosthetics portraying a loud caricature of an American oilman, that’s currently on track to be one of the biggest box-office failures of all time?
Absolutely yes—and it’s a movie that rewired my expectations of what a movie about climate change should be. Digger, the critically panned, exorbitantly expensive new film from Alejandro González Iñárritu, calls into question the purpose of art and even the basic purpose of telling the truth in the face of a capitalist machine churning the world toward climate disaster. The deeply uncomfortable film forces audiences to confront what kind of characters we’re the most comfortable making into climate villains.
(Spoilers ahead—if you have any plans to see the movie, I really would encourage you to do so first before reading on.)
The film stars Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell, an oil billionaire who only wears cowboy boots and lives in a mansion covered in antlers and polar bear skin rugs. At the start of the film, one of Digger’s oil-drilling platforms accidentally causes a massive iceberg to break loose, resulting in a huge methane leak. With catastrophe impending, he has to alert the president (John Goodman, putting in a performance reminiscent of his best work with the Coen brothers) as the iceberg barrels toward Europe.
The trailers play up the movie as a too-broad-it’s-painful satire of American oilmen and how a Trumpian-inspired religious-right administration would respond to a real climate disaster. Iñárritu, however, lets us in on the secret early: The farce we’re watching is actually a play within the movie, being performed in a theater with a leaky ceiling that keeps losing power. Tom Cruise is not playing Digger Rockwell, but rather an actor playing Digger Rockwell.
We eventually learn that the play, Fossil Fools, depicts events that actually happened some decades ago. From then on, you’re aware that every joke, every villainous portrayal of Digger and the president as Really Bad Guys, is for two audiences: moviegoers in 2026 and theatergoers living in a dystopian future.
From the trailers, I’d initially thought that the movie was going to be similar to Adam McKay’s blockbuster Don’t Look Up, a climate satire that drew record numbers of viewers on Netflix when it aired in 2021. Don’t Look Up puts scientists racing to inform the public about an impending asteroid collision and pushing to avert catastrophe against corporate and political interests that have other plans. McKay, at the time, said the film’s purpose was to make “people less tolerant of inaction from their leaders.” If the media—journalists, filmmakers, and the like—could correctly inform the public about the risks of climate change, the film (and its accompanying calls to action) posited, we would begin to see progress on cutting emissions.
Digger, similarly, deals with themes around climate misinformation. Digger admits he ignored alerts from his own company about the unfolding crisis on his drilling platforms. Goodman’s president and his cabinet decide to deploy a “firewall” that censors out all mentions of the climate crisis (including the phrase “Al Gore”) to control the narrative of what’s happening.
But where Don’t Look Up’s thesis is that action would happen if we just communicated the truth better, Digger takes a much more nihilistic view—that the truth has no value. Dr. Ganesh (Riz Ahmed), Digger’s long-suffering environmental expert, angrily tells the oilman that he is going to tell the truth about his company and climate change to a crowd of European Union leaders, and keeps his promise. (Ganesh makes the first reference to the “Exxon Knew” investigation I can recall in a major movie.)
Digger watches from a back room, then, in a ripping speech that forms the backbone of the movie, he tells the hostile European delegates that he, like other oilmen, knew that their product would cause runaway climate change. But that doesn’t matter, he crows. The world is hooked on oil, and the people in that very room have found a myriad of uses for it.
“You want energy to ask AI to solve the very same disasters that it’s fueling,” he says to the assembled delegates. “You want freedom to bask in the comfort of your unsustainable lives.” He ultimately leverages Ganesh’s truth-telling to avoid accountability—strolling out of parliament as members fight among themselves.
The bombastic portrayal of Digger Rockwell is, too, a rumination on what kind of truths we get as an audience and who the most palatable climate evildoers are. In between rehearsal takes of the increasingly outrageous Fossil Fools, we see Cruise grapple with how to play Digger, noting he watched hours of footage and found him not to be a finger-gunning shooting fool with a Texas drawl but a conniving, sharp businessman. But the play’s audience, watching Fossil Fools in a world Digger helped ruin, are not looking for truth—they’re looking for catharsis. Near the end of the film, an incredible late twist reveals the play has a wealthy benefactor with a vested interest in having it performed.
One of my big critiques of Don’t Look Up was the notion that a Hollywood movie could be an agent for change; that the movie’s star, Leonardo di Caprio, who parties on superyachts and takes private jets, could tell people to listen to scientists and just vote our way out of this mess. Digger essentially spits in the face of Don’t Look Up’s existence, pointing out that enjoying satire about climate change that paints specific villains like Digger Rockwell comes at the risk of ignoring forms of corporate power more palatable to liberal viewers.
This all may seem pretty nihilist, and I don’t think the movie is intended to be cheery. But I also don’t think it’s a message to not make art. Rather, Digger strives to be a reflection of our current reality, where truth often doesn’t matter, and art is often funded by the very powers it rails against. While Don’t Look Up was intended to be a call to action, Digger simply kicks back and says to viewers: This is where we are.
Five years after a record number of people watched Don’t Look Up, the Trump administration is back in power and has pulled the US out of the Paris Agreement again. The government is gleefully doubling down on “Drill, Baby, Drill.” Tech corporations that in the Don’t Look Up era were touting their goals to cut emissions and even reverse past damage are now walking those back, thanks to the AI boom—which, they promise, will help solve climate change someday. And here I am, typing on my computer, driving a car around that uses fossil fuels.
That Digger is the last film to come out of Warner Bros. before David Ellison’s purchase of the studio only underscores the role that wealthy, conservative individuals are increasingly playing in controlling the arts. In the end, I most appreciate Digger for pointing out the absurdity of the whole thing.

The increased instances of indigenous and imported cases of malaria over the past five years have left the health authorities a worried lot.
Imported malaria is acquired outside Keralam, while indigenous malaria is acquired through local transmission, when a local mosquito picks up the parasite from an infected person and transmits it to another person.
Going by the Health department statistics, as of October 5, four confirmed indigenous cases were reported in 2026, and 974 imported cases.
One death due to indigenous malaria and six deaths due to imported cases have been reported this year. Last year, no deaths due to indigenous cases were reported, while two deaths occurred due to imported cases.
The number of cases began to rise after 2021, when 252 imported and one indigenous death case were reported. The highest number of indigenous cases was reported from Malappuram, Kozhikode, and Kannur. Kollam, which earlier showed a high incidence of these cases, is in a recovery phase.
Health officials attribute the abundance of mosquitoes and the frequent influx of travellers to the increase in the number of infections.
“Over the past several years, the number of imported malaria cases has increased substantially. We need to strengthen surveillance measures, screening of migrants for the disease and ensuring intensive screening and testing for the disease in asymptomatic fever cases,” said the official.
The Health department plans to introduce insecticide-treated bed nets, which will kill mosquitoes on contact, in houses in regions where indigenous cases are reported. Steps are being taken to intensify malaria prevention activities to prevent the development of malaria-endemic regions in the State,” said the official.
“The increasing number of malaria cases in the past few years is a concern,” said. T.S. Anish, associate professor, School of Public Health, Kerala University of Health Sciences, Thiruvananthapuram.
“The consistent efforts by the Health department back in the 1960s succeeded in freeing the State from malaria. However, with increased travel and the influx of the migrant population from disease-endemic regions, malaria cases are getting reported. The delay in timely detection and intervention measures will contribute to the rise of indigenous cases. The local conditions are ideal to facilitate the spread of the disease,” Dr. Anish warned.
Climate change
He further added that climate change can also emerge as a key concern.
He warned that malaria could spread to hitherto unreported regions due to climate change-induced developments. “The climate in Keralam and the frequent movement of domestic workers are favourable to the spread of the disease,” he said.

Ex-gang boss sentenced to 40 years for orchestrating Tupac Shakur's murder
- Published
Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been sentenced to at least 40 years in prison for orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur.
A jury found Davis, 63, guilty in September of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996. He has said he will appeal the verdict.
Prosecutors argued that although Davis did not fire the gun himself, he was the ringleader of the group that committed the murder. He admitted in his memoir that he had provided the gun used in the crime.
Davis' conviction was the first in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.
Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo argued during Tuesday's sentencing hearing that Davis spent years "publicly grandstanding" and bragging about his role on Shakur's death, which he said, "had wide-ranging effects upon the world".
Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, told the court: "The loss of Tupac, for a long time, crippled my family."
"He had so much promise, intentions for a better world," said adding that her brother had hoped to help his local community.
Sekyiwa Shakur asked the judge to give Davis the maximum sentence, telling Davis he will sit in prison and "contemplate what you've done to the world, not just to me".
Shakur's brother, Maurice Shakur, also addressed the court, asking the judge for "the longest possible sentence".
Davis was asked by Judge Carli Kierny if he had anything to say, to which he replied: "I'm good. I'm gonna appeal this case for sure."
Before handing down the sentence, Kierny told him: "You don't get to take a man from his family.
"You don't get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur. The world never forgot about him and his death."
The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, in which he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired.
In exchange for being shielded from criminal prosecution, he told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview relating to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B.I.G., real name Christopher Wallace, who was killed in a shooting just months after Shakur.
Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, which led to publicity and media interviews.
But the book and interviews he offered elaborating on his role in Shakur's killing voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges from being filed. A judge then allowed his police interview to be used in the murder trial against him.
Shakur was 25 years old and at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices at the time of his death. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide.
For three decades, the investigation into his killing remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - until the conviction of Davis last month.
Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money.
Prosecutors argued that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not himself fire the gun, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.
Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998, having denied involvement in the killing of Shakur.

On the first day of his second term, President Donald Trump issued an executive order requiring the Bureau of Prisons to “ensure that no Federal funds are expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.” Issued alongside a record 26 other orders that day, it was an unsurprising development, because Trump had made this issue one of the centerpieces of his 2024 campaign.
The Supreme Court may be about to make America’s prisons much crueler
In its zeal to limit transgender rights, the Court could endanger thousands of incarcerated Americans.
The fate of that executive order, as well as the US Bureau of Prisons’ (“BOP”) memoranda implementing the order, is now before the Supreme Court in a case called Trump v. Kingdom. And, while this case obviously has high stakes for incarcerated transgender people specifically, the Court’s resolution of this case could potentially have far greater reach — cutting off many cis and transgender people’s access to healthcare while they are incarcerated.
That’s because one of the central questions in Kingdom — though this issue is not yet before the justices — is when the Constitution requires prisons to provide medical care to incarcerated people. In Estelle v. Gamble (1976), the Supreme Court held that the Eighth Amendment’s ban on “cruel and unusual punishments” imposes on the government an “obligation to provide medical care for those whom it is punishing by incarceration.” People in prison, after all, cannot simply drive themselves to the hospital if they get sick. If the prison does not give them adequate medical care, they will suffer untreated and potentially die.
For procedural reasons, the Court is unlikely to opine on whether Estelle requires prisons to provide gender-affirming care to trans people right away. But the question of when the Eighth Amendment requires prisons to provide medical care to incarcerated people is front and center in the Kingdom case, which means the Court could potentially use Kingdom to limit all imprisoned people’s access to healthcare — or even to undercut the Constitution’s protections against cruel and unusual punishments more broadly.
Ironically, this case also arises out of a famous political blunder by pro-trans advocates. In 2019, when then-Sen. Kamala Harris was seeking her party’s 2020 presidential nomination, the ACLU circulated a questionnaire to candidates that asked if they would use presidential authority “to ensure that transgender and nonbinary people who rely on the state for medical care — including those in prison and immigration detention — will have access to comprehensive treatment associated with gender transition, including all necessary surgical care?”
Harris responded that she would, and also said that she “pushed the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation to provide gender transition surgery to state inmates” while she was state attorney general.
Years later, during his 2024 debate with Harris, Trump claimed that the then-vice president “wants to do transgender operations on illegal aliens that are in prison.” And not long after, his opposition to gender-affirming care for trans people in prison became a key part of his campaign.
It’s unclear why the ACLU thought it was a good idea to shine a light on this issue in 2019 because, at the time, the BOP provided gender-affirming care to people in federal prison. The ACLU — which represents the pro-trans side in the Kingdom case — now argues that transgender people in federal prison have had access to at least some forms of gender-affirming care “since at least 1992.”
Indeed, Trump’s own administration concluded in a 2018 memo that the Bureau of Prisons’ “statutory mandate to provide basic medical and mental health care” to incarcerated people obligated it to provide “pharmaceutical interventions (e.g., cross-gender hormone therapy), hair removal and surgery (if individualized assessment indicates surgical intervention is applicable)” to transgender people in prison if their doctors determined that these interventions are “medically necessary care.”
In any event, regardless of why Trump fixated on cutting off trans healthcare for people in federal prison, Kingdom is now before the Court. That means that the fate of trans people in prison — and, if the Eighth Amendment issue eventually reaches the Court, all incarcerated people — is now in the hands of a Republican Court that is often hostile to trans litigants, and that has, at times, signaled that it wants to drastically roll back the scope of the Eighth Amendment.
What are the legal issues in the Kingdom case?
At least since Estelle, the Court has held that people who are incarcerated are not also sentenced to live and die without medical care. As the Court said in Brown v. Plata (2011), “a prison that deprives prisoners of basic sustenance, including adequate medical care, is incompatible with the concept of human dignity and has no place in civilized society.”
Under Estelle and Brown, transgender people often have a right to gender-affirming care during their incarceration. As the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held in Edmo v. Corizon (2019), such a person must show that they have a “serious medical need” for such care — typically by demonstrating that the care was prescribed to them by their health provider. But the Constitution does not permit prisons to deny medically necessary care to incarcerated people.
In Kingdom, the ACLU raised this Eighth Amendment argument in the lower courts, but those lower courts ruled in favor of transgender people in prison on different, much more technical legal grounds.
For over three decades, from at least 1992 to 2025, according to the ACLU’s brief to the justices, the BOP provided at least some gender-affirming care, including hormone therapy, to transgender people. This matters because, when a federal agency changes its policies, a federal law typically requires it to “examine the relevant data and articulate a satisfactory explanation for its action, including a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.” This explanation often must explain the agency’s justification for “disregarding facts and circumstances” that justified the previous policy.
Both the ACLU and the lower courts that heard Kingdom argue that the Trump administration did not comply with this obligation when it cut off care for trans people in prison.
Among other things, the district court that heard this case determined that the administration cited “zero evidence from its own medical or mental health care professionals to support its conclusions” against providing transgender healthcare. While the Trump administration argues that providing gender-affirming care makes prisons less safe, the district court also noted that “the government has not cited a single instance of gender-affirming care giving rise to safety concerns despite having provided such care for many years.”
Is this a persuasive legal argument against the Trump administration’s new policy? I think it is. And so did three federal judges that previously heard the Kingdom case. But the fate of trans people in prison is now in the hands of a Supreme Court that rarely rules in favor of transgender litigants, and that has a history of handing down legally incoherent opinions that are inconsistent with the Court’s own precedents, and that also deny legal rights to trans people.
The current Court’s uncertain commitment to the Eighth Amendment
Because the lower courts that heard Kingdom did not rule on the Eighth Amendment question, Kingdom should not currently give the justices an opportunity to roll back Estelle. But, in the likely event that this Court rejects the ACLU’s argument that the Trump administration did not adequately explain its new policy, the case will return to the lower courts and the Eighth Amendment issue will be fully litigated — teeing up the Eighth Amendment question for the justices to decide in the near future.
This issue could arise, moreover, at the exact moment that some justices are pushing for sweeping changes to how their Court understands the term “cruel and unusual punishments.” Indeed, at least some of the Supreme Court’s recent Eighth Amendment precedents suggest that the Republican justices want a wholesale rewrite of the Court’s previous precedents laying out what constitutes cruel and unusual punishment.
Since the mid-to-late twentieth century, the Court has held that, in Chief Justice Earl Warren’s words, the Eighth Amendment “must draw its meaning from the evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society.” Thus, as certain forms of punishment grow more uncommon, they become more constitutionally dubious.
This “evolving standards of decency” framework is front and center in nearly every major Supreme Court decision interpreting the Eighth Amendment for the last five or six decades, including Estelle.
In Bucklew v. Precythe (2019), however, the Court’s Republican majority seemed to abandon this framework. Although decades worth of pre-Bucklew decisions established that a punishment is unconstitutional if it is considered cruel and unusual today, Bucklew suggested that a method of punishment is unconstitutional only if it “had fallen out of use” at “the time of the founding.”
Bucklew did list some methods of punishment that fail this test, but they are things like “disemboweling” or “burning alive.”
Thus, if taken seriously, Bucklew’s new approach to Eighth Amendment cases would dramatically expand the government’s power to impose harsh punishments. The late Justice Antonin Scalia, for example, argued that a Bucklew-like approach to the Eighth Amendment does not prohibit the government from executing most intellectually disabled offenders, and that it does not limit the government’s ability to impose excessive punishments for minor crimes.
In fairness, some of the Court’s post-Bucklew decisions are inconsistent with the framework the Court laid out in that case. So at least some of the justices who joined Bucklew may have since decided that it’s a bad idea to toss out the Court’s entire framework for Eighth Amendment cases. But Bucklew was one hell of a warning shot over the bow of the Eighth Amendment. And the mere fact that the Bucklew decision exists means that advocates for humane punishments must hold their breath any time this Court is asked whether a particular punishment is cruel and unusual.
In the worst-case scenario for people in prison, a case like Kingdom could inspire the Republican justices to overrule — or, at least, drastically limit — decisions like Estelle and Brown. That would mean that all incarcerated people, regardless of their gender identity, could lose access to medically necessary care unless the government decides to give it to them as an act of grace.

Reva, the certified natural diamond jewellery brand of PNGS Reva Diamond Jewellery Limited, announced actor Sharvari as its brand ambassador. This is the first time Reva has partnered with a celebrity face, marking a milestone moment for the brand just months after its listing on the stock exchanges in March 2026, and as it embarks on its most ambitious expansion yet.
Sharvari named first-ever brand ambassador of Reva by PNGS
Sharvari is one of Hindi cinema’s most exciting young leads, with a growing body of work that spans diverse genres, from horror-comedy and action to romance. She made her big-screen debut with Bunty Aur Babli 2 and has since been seen in Munjya, Maharaj, Vedaa, Main Vaapas Aaunga and YRF’s Alpha. She will next be seen in Sooraj Barjatya’s Yeh Prem Mol Liya, slated for release in November. Sharvari will be the face of Reva’s brand campaigns across print, digital, outdoor and in-store, beginning with the festive and wedding season.
Amit Modak, CEO, PNGS Reva Diamond Jewellery Limited, said, "Reva is entering a defining phase. Since our listing, we have been expanding with clarity, opening exclusive stores, launching our online platform and preparing to take the brand into new cities, including key markets in North India. As we grow beyond our home ground, we need a face that resonates nationally while staying true to who we are. Sharvari does exactly that. Her appeal cuts across regions and age groups, and she will help us introduce Reva and the value of a certified natural diamond to many more customers across India."
Aditya Modak, Director, Reva by PNGS, said, "Our very first brand ambassador had to be someone who truly reflects the Reva woman, and Sharvari was a natural choice in every sense. She is rooted, she is real, and she has earned her place through her own effort, much like a natural diamond is shaped over time. Today's woman buys diamonds not only for weddings but for herself, for her milestones and for her every day. Sharvari embodies that confidence, and together we want to make natural diamonds a part of more women's stories."
Sharvari, Brand Ambassador, Reva, said, “Being the first face of Reva makes this association especially exciting for me. As a Maharashtrian, P. N. Gadgil & Sons is a name I’ve known and associated with trust and tradition for as long as I can remember. What drew me to Reva is how it brings natural diamonds into the everyday, with designs that feel modern while still holding on to the timelessness of the stone. I’m happy to be part of a brand that makes diamonds feel relevant to different moments in a woman’s life, from ordinary days to the most special occasions.”
The Sharvari partnership comes as Reva accelerates its retail and digital expansion. The brand currently operates 38 stores, comprising 5 exclusive brand outlets and 34 shop-in-shop counters within the P. N. Gadgil & Sons network, with a strong presence across Maharashtra and a growing footprint in Gujarat and Karnataka. Recent openings include exclusive stores at Amanora Mall, Pune (July 2026) and Nashik (September 2026).
Following its IPO in March 2026, Reva is on track to open around 15 new company-owned exclusive stores within 24 months of listing. The rollout will focus primarily on Tier 1 cities, with selective expansion into Tier 2 cities and metro markets across Maharashtra and key North India markets. In September 2026, Reva also launched its e-commerce platform, revadiamonds.com, bringing its collections to customers across the country. With a pan-India appeal, Sharvari will be central to introducing Reva to these new markets and a new generation of diamond buyers.

Dozens of gold prospectors killed in strikes on Egypt-Sudan border, rights group says
- Published
At least 72 civilians who had been prospecting for gold in a border region of Sudan have been killed in air strikes, a regional rights group says.
Emergency Lawyers, based in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, said jets targeted the so-called artisanal miners at a popular gold mining site in Red Sea state on Saturday.
Neither the Egyptian government nor the de facto Sudanese authorities have so far commented.
Cairo has previously faced accusations of deadly strikes on gold prospectors as part of a crackdown on illicit activity along its southern border.
Emergency Lawyers noted the previous alleged attacks and said they represented not only a violation of Sudan's sovereign territory but demonstrated the government's lack of control over the region.
"The deliberate targeting of unarmed civilians violates international humanitarian law and the right to life," it said in a statement on Sunday. "These acts may constitute war crimes."
It noted that its death toll was provisional and could rise.
The Paris-based Sudan Tribune reported that the death toll could far exceed the number reported by Emergency Lawyers, citing a survivor of Saturday's attack who said many more people had been injured.
Eyewitnesses said the attack began around 06:00 local time (04:00 GMT), with the aircraft firing more than five missiles directly at the miners' camps in Shamal al-Wadi, destroying them and excavation pits with people still inside, the newspaper wrote.
The Sudan Tribune reported claims in June that Egyptian forces had used drones and artillery to target artisanal mining sites in the same region, killing several, after sporadic incidents of Egyptian border guards of burning equipment, torching temporary shelters, and firing live ammunition to disperse mine workers.
Days later, Egypt's border agency announced that it and the military had begun a sweeping security campaign along the border to foil illegal migration, drug smuggling and illegal mining.
At the same time, Sudan's de facto leader announced an investigation into the alleged strikes, which were said to have killed dozens.
Gold lies at the core of the border tensions.
Sudan's ongoing civil war has led to a surge in artisanal mining - an often risky practice conducted by civilians with rudimentary tools and without official permission - particularly in remote areas near its borders.
Some gold-rich areas lie along porous borders in terrain historically associated with cross-border smuggling routes, with artisanally mined gold potentially feeding into those channels.
Egypt's border force said in June that it had seized 86 tonnes of gold ore along with amateur prospecting equipment.
Artisanal mining has also reportedly continued in Sudan's conflict zones and smuggled gold may be a source of income for armed insurgent groups.
This has raised concerns of illicit Sudanese gold undermining the legitimate Egyptian gold market.
Correction 12 October: This article originally said the air strikes were in River Nile state. We have corrected it as they were in Red Sea state.

Former Election Commissioner Ashok Lavasa has said the poll panel being mired in controversies was unprecedented. Lavasa advised the poll panel regain public trust, drawing a cricket analogy to warn that a team's victory would be questioned "if people feel the umpire was not neutral". The remarks come amid a united protests by opposition INDIA bloc over the past few days against alleged ‘vote chori’ and demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican confirmed on Tuesday, 13 October. The operation was completed successfully, with doctors removing the affected portion of the lung, but further medical assessments are expected to determine the next steps in his treatment. According to the Vatican's medical bulletin, tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, a type of cancer that develops in glandular cells. The condition had been suspected before the operation and was confirmed during surgery. The 71-year-old pontiff underwent the procedure at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where he is now recovering. The Vatican said the operation was successful and that there were no complications. The diagnosis marks a significant development in the health of the head of the Catholic Church, whose medical condition had attracted attention after the discovery of a lung nodule. Pope Leo underwent surgery to remove a small, localised nodule from his lung after the abnormality was detected during medical checks. The procedure involved removing the lower lobe of his right lung. According to the Associated Press report published by CBS News, the operation lasted approximately 90 minutes, with the pontiff spending around three hours in the operating room. The Vatican described the removal as radical, indicating that doctors had removed the affected tissue. However, further tests, including examinations of the lymph nodes, are needed to establish whether the cancer has spread. No definitive treatment plan has been announced. The Vatican has indicated that doctors are awaiting additional results before discussing whether further treatment, including chemotherapy, will be necessary. The pontiff is expected to remain at Gemelli Hospital during his recovery. His public engagements have been suspended, with audiences cancelled through 20 October, according to CBS News. The interruption comes as Pope Leo continues his responsibilities as leader of the Catholic Church, which has millions of followers around the world. His health is therefore being closely watched by Catholics and observers of the Vatican. The diagnosis has also raised questions about his upcoming international commitments. A planned trip to South America in November remains uncertain and will depend on his recovery and medical advice. For now, doctors are concentrating on his recovery and awaiting further test results. The findings will help establish the extent of the disease and whether additional treatment is required. ABC News reported on the pontiff's departure for hospital ahead of the operation, while Vatican News confirmed that the surgery had been completed successfully. Although the successful procedure is an encouraging development, the full medical picture remains unclear. The Vatican has yet to provide a detailed prognosis, leaving the next stage of Pope Leo's recovery dependent on the results of further examinations. ‘If a sibling uses a skin-lightening product, you may be more likely to use one too’. This was among the findings from behavioural research cited by the World Health Organisation (WHO) during a discussion on colourism in Hyderabad on Wednesday (October 7, 2026).
The discussion was part of ‘Complexion of Change: Challenging Colorism Through Policy, Art, and Science’, held at Goethe-Zentrum in Hyderabad. A documentary exploring global skin colour bias and the deep-rooted societal association of fair skin with higher status, beauty and success was also screened as part of the programme.
“Skin-lightening product use was not a single behaviour but was influenced by psychological, cultural and environmental factors,” said Ammaarah Martinus, Behavioural Insights consultant at the WHO.
The psychological dimension includes motivations such as wanting to appear fairer, younger or to fit into society. The cultural dimension includes the influence of families, communities and social networks. Mr. Martinus said research had found that people were more likely to use a skin-lightening product if a sibling used one. She also spoke about access to such products . In India, skin-lightening products could be easily purchased in local markets and supermarkets. “Interventions to address skin-lightening therefore need to work across all three levels rather than focus on only one aspect of the behaviour,” she added.
Psychologist and researcher Bharti Upparu said children begin receiving messages about skin colour at a very young age, often without anyone explicitly telling them that one skin tone is preferable to another. They observe who is complimented, who is bullied and who is teased, and gradually learn which physical characteristics society values. “A person perceived as fair and attractive may unconsciously be associated with other positive characteristics such as competence, goodness and trustworthiness. Such biases can compound into an overall perception of a person’s character and affect how others interact with them,” she said.
The discussion also highlighted that colourism is not restricted to women. Arpit Bhutani, co-founder of Circular Innovation Lab and moderator of the session, pointed to products marketed specifically towards men and noted that the pressure to conform to lighter-skin beauty standards also affects men.
Former Miss America Nina Davuluri recalled an incident involving a friend’s baby, when an older family member cautioned against taking the child into the sun because the child could become darker. “Such comments are not necessarily made with malicious intent but can come from a desire to see children succeed in a society where lighter skin is perceived to offer advantages,” she added.
Mercury in skin-lightening products
In remarks before the documentary screening, Monika Stankiewicz, executive secretary of the Minamata Convention on Mercury, said mercury was among the chemicals of highest public concern according to the WHO and that cosmetics were one pathway through which people could be exposed. “Mercury-containing skin-lightening products can damage the skin and may also contaminate households, potentially exposing other family members,” she added.
Ms. Stankiewicz stressed that the issue was not solely a chemical problem but also a social one linked to beauty standards and the pressure to conform to them. She said meaningful change could not come through regulations alone and that activism, art, culture and storytelling also had important roles to play.

There's been a disturbance in the force. Only it's more like a farce.
It seems that Elon Musk, while crowing on X about how useful his Grok Bot AI agent was in ordering some Lego Star Wars kits on Sunday, managed to reveal via a screenshot to his more than 240 million followers not only the 10-digit Lego order number of his purchase, but also what he paid for the sets, the delivery and billing addresses, the last four digits of his credit card, and the email address his bot used to buy the bricks from Lego.
Faster than the Millennium Falcon making the jump to light speed, the inevitable happened. An X account holder named Enderman posted screenshots of interactions with Lego's customer service chatbot on its website, where the user seemingly managed—using the email and order number Musk kindly, but recklessly, provided—to get the system to cancel Musk's order.
It’s a Trap!
Within a couple of hours—possibly to see whether Enderman's scheme was actually successful—Musk replied and said his order had not been canceled after all.
But by this point, the folly of posting the purchase details on his account must have been evident. For example, another X user went back to Lego's AI assistant, called “Sophia,” and supposedly used the same details to reopen the delivery, this time increasing the order count to 400 and changing the delivery address, all while using Musk's original payment method. “Perfect! I'll get your Lego adventure back on track,” Sophia replied according to screenshots posted on X.
Upping the ante to 400 sets could be seen as conservative, as a glance at WIRED's Spend Elon Musk’s Money tracker reveals that if you wanted to blow $1 trillion of Musk's cash on plastic bricks, it might have been possible to buy one billion $1,000 Death Star sets, each with 9,023 pieces.
Lego declined to comment when WIRED contacted the company to confirm if such activity took place on Musk's personal Star Wars order. However, internal safeguards for Lego's AI assistant could have flagged unusual activity on the purchase, and so hopefully fleshy humans were tasked with checking the changes.
Attack of the Clones
On Saturday, Musk suggested that Grok could make purchases online with a simple prompt. In this post, Musk suggested that all brave users needed to do to let Grok buy stuff for them was upload a picture of their credit card so the bot could search the web for deals and then complete the purchase. AI companies like Meta and OpenAI have also highlighted the utility of using their respective agents for shopping tasks.
However, at the end of last year, Visa warned about fraud in agentic commerce, advising that bad actors were building legitimate-looking sites that could fool AI agents into purchasing fake items simply by offering gear at super-low prices.
“Once the AI agent completes the purchase … the malicious merchant can harvest payment data and instantly use it for unauthorized transactions,” according to Visa's blog. Visa added that it observed a 25 percent increase “in malicious bot-initiated transactions” in the latter half of 2025, but in the US, this figure jumped to 40 percent.
