Apple HomePod mini 2 vs. Apple HomePod mini: What do you get for the $50 increase?
The main differences are Siri AI, a new chip and Sound Glow.
At its 'Welcome Home" event today, Apple unveiled the HomePod mini 2 — a long-awaited update to its smart speaker, which hadn't been updated since its launch in 2020. On the outside, it looks pretty much the same, but the new model comes with some cool surprises on the inside. You get Siri AI and a few other features for those living in the Apple ecosystem — but all of this comes at a price. The HomePod mini 2 costs $149, which is $50 more than the original's launch price six years ago. Are the updates are really worth the extra cost? Should owners of the first HomePod mini upgrade? Let's break down the differences to find out.
What's new on the HomePod mini 2
The main difference between the HomePod mini 2 and the original, at least from a hardware standpoint, is its processor. The new model's Apple S10 chip replaces the S5 from 2019, which was the same chip found in the Apple Watch Series 5. The S10 is more powerful and enables Siri AI for the first time on a HomePod — though the smarter assistant won't be available at launch. But how it works on the new HomePod mini 2 also depends on which phone you have.
By default, Siri AI on the HomePod can conduct natural conversations and answer general knowledge questions more accurately than its predecessor. Of course, it can also play songs and podcasts just like before, but now you can do so with more natural voice commands. For example, you could ask it to play only the surprise songs from Taylor Swift's The Eras Tour — something the old Siri can't do. But here's the catch: to get personalized context, the HomePod mini 2 needs to be paired with an iPhone or iPad with Apple Intelligence. With a compatible device, you'll get even more features with Siri AI, such as responses based on your emails, messages and calendar.
Another subtle but cool new feature is Sound Glow. Just like before, the HomePod mini 2 has a touch-sensitive surface for media controls with glowing lights. But now, the lights will sync with the music playing and react to the bass and treble, using colors from the album artwork. Sound Glow is also another feature that requires pairing the HomePod mini 2 with an iPhone or iPad running Apple Intelligence.
Apple didn't mention any new drivers or significant acoustic improvements, but it claims that the S10 chip enhances what it calls computational audio. For instance, you can now set up a surround sound system using four HomePod mini 2 units or a pair of HomePod mini 2 and another couple of HomePod 2 (the bigger one), all connected to the new Apple TV.
Is it really worth paying extra for the HomePod mini 2?
Whether the HomePod mini 2 is worth the price really depends on how you use your speakers. If you already have a bunch of HomePod minis in your home, don't rush to upgrade them all at once — especially since Siri AI won't be available until later this year. Enhancements like Sound Glow are cool, but they don't really add much to the experience you already have with the original HomePod mini, especially since there aren't real upgrades to the sound system. Of course, if you're already in the market for a new HomePod mini anyway, you should definitely get the new model.
The upgrade starts to make more sense for those planning to build their own home theater system with Apple TV and HomePods. The ability to pair two sets together to create surround sound setups seems promising, especially since the speakers detect their position in the room to automatically calibrate the audio. Also, Mac users will finally be able to use a pair of HomePod mini 2 as their default speakers, with low latency and even the ability to use the built-in microphones for FaceTime calls. If all these features strike you as appealing, the extra cost might end up being worth it.

Over the weekend, the World Health Organization released a disease outbreak report on the events surrounding the death of a Russian infectious disease researcher earlier this month, highlighting that Russia has yet to report a confirmed cause of death. With that “key uncertainty,” the United Nations health agency said it remains impossible to assess the risk of the event or whether the public health measures Russia took were adequate to prevent spread of the unknown disease.
The WHO reported that, so far, it has seen no evidence of ongoing transmission of the mystery disease. “However, confidence in the assessment remains limited by the absence of a confirmed etiological diagnosis, and the remaining uncertainty regarding the source and mode of exposure,” the agency wrote in its report.
The agency laid out the order of events as information trickled out from Russian authorities, noting that it only became aware of the death via media reports on October 2. The WHO subsequently made contact with Russian authorities and requested information on October 3, 6, 7, and 8.
Limited information released
Early media reports indicated that the lab worker had become ill on September 29, possibly following an incident at the lab, the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute (APRI) of Siberia and the Far East. Some early reports suggested that the researcher—who was identified by media as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova—died of the plague after breaking a test tube.
On October 2, the Irkutsk branch of Russian health agency Rospotrebnadzor (RPN) said in a statement that a “special sanitary-epidemiological expert commission” had already met over a suspected case of a high-threat pathogen. Sanitary and epidemic control measures were put in place, including identifying, monitoring, and testing all contacts. At the time, RPN said that all contacts had tested negative for high-threat pathogens.
On October 6, Russia’s National Focal Point for the International Health Regulations (NFP) first responded to the WHO’s information requests, saying that no case of plague had been recorded in Irkutsk Oblast. The NFP confirmed that an APRI lab worker had died from a severe case of pneumonia after developing symptoms compatible with an acute respiratory viral infection. The worker was tested for a number of high-threat pathogens, but all the tests had come back negative. Doctors categorized the cause of death as being from pneumonia of undetermined etiology.

Apple opened preorders for the HomeView smart home hub today.
The HomeView is a 7-inch smart display and speaker that aims to be a central access point for up to six members of a family to access and control Apple’s ecosystem of devices, apps, and the Siri generative AI chatbot that’s currently in beta.
Users can speak to HomeView to control smart home devices, such as, for example, telling Siri to close the smart blinds or activate smart locks. HomeView can also show a livestream for up to nine video feeds simultaneously.
“With a supported iCloud+ subscription, HomeView works with compatible cameras to deliver intelligent, end-to-end encrypted recognition of people, familiar faces, pets, packages, and vehicles, notifying the household the moment someone arrives at the front door. With video descriptions for HomeKit Secure Video footage, HomeView helps users quickly understand what happened in a video clip without even watching it,” Apple’s announcement said.
Competing with devices like the Amazon Echo Show, HomeView uses its integrated camera to identify who’s using it and show them their profile, which users can personalize with their preferred apps and widgets. Users can connect their HomeView profile to their Apple Intelligence-supporting iPhone or iPad and use the hub to access their Messages, Calendar, Reminders, and FaceTime.
“With an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, Siri AI does more for each person—taking action across apps and surfacing relevant information from Messages and Calendar, playlists on Apple Music, and more by drawing on their personal context,” Apple’s announcement says.

DGCA bans MOBIKINS model power bank on flights after IndiGo fire incident
The aviation regulator asked airlines and passengers to ensure that the specified power bank is not carried on any flight to, from or within India.
The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has directed airlines to prevent passengers from carrying the MOBIKINS MK-PB-04 power bank on flights to, from and within India, citing potential safety risks following a recent fire incident on an IndiGo flight from Delhi to Chennai.
In a circular dated September 29, the aviation regulator asked airlines and passengers to ensure that the specified power bank is not carried on any flight to, from or within India.
To be sure, the restriction specifically names the MOBIKINS MK-PB-04 model and does not announce a blanket ban on all power banks.
“In view of the recent fire incident involving the MOBIKINS MK-PB-04 power bank, and considering the potential safety risks associated with it, the travelling public and airlines are hereby advised to ensure that the MOBIKINS MK-PB-04 power bank is not carried or transported on board the aircraft, whether as passenger baggage (including checked-in and cabin baggage) or as cargo, on any flight to, from, or within India,” the circular stated.
“Airlines are further advised to take appropriate measures to identify and prevent the carriage of the aforesaid power bank and to disseminate this safety advisory to the passengers through suitable communication channels,” it added.
The circular issued by the regulator was signed by the Director General of Civil Aviation, Vir Vikram Yadav.
The most recent fire incident involving a power bank occurred on October 11, when an IndiGo flight from Delhi to Chennai had to be diverted to Hyderabad as a precaution after a power bank placed in the overhead bin caught fire mid-air.
The flight with 191 people on board landed safely at 3.15pm in Hyderabad. While there were no injuries, the aircraft had to be grounded for checks.
IndiGo had to arrange for an alternative aircraft for the passengers. The passengers then took off for Chennai at around 5.45pm and landed at around 7.20pm.

Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses review: No camera, no problem
Normal-looking glasses with solid audio and way better battery life is a win for everyone.
Meta's audio-only smart glasses couldn't have come at a more opportune time. At a moment when there's increasing backlash against the company's growing lineup of camera-enabled glasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio frames ditch the feature most associated with "creep glasses." Instead, as the name implies, the frames are all about making the most of audio.
The result is a pair of glasses that are lighter, more comfortable and have far better battery life than any other glasses from the company. They also look a lot more subtle and are the closest to "normal" glasses we've seen from Meta.
New style, better fit
Meta has two different frame styles for its $349 audio-only glasses: Burbank, which looks a bit like a thinner Wayfarer, and Clubmaster, an immediately recognizable Ray-Ban design. I opted for the latter because it comes in a wider variety of colors and I prefer thinner frames in general.
From the front, I'm not sure anyone would recognize the glasses as having any tech abilities. My frames did have the transparent arms Meta often uses to display the inner circuitry of the glasses, but it's still relatively subtle.
There isn't a camera or front-facing LED, but the setup is overall similar to Meta's other glasses. The right arm still has a touchpad for controlling volume, answering calls and other functions, and there's a small inward-facing LED for notifications. There's also a tiny action button, which you can use as a dedicated shortcut for certain features.
It might seem like Meta simply stripped down its existing glasses designs, but the company's VP of Wearables, Ming Hua, told me that the company actually had to rebuild the speaker and microphone setup to work on a smaller frame.
That work definitely paid off. The audio-only glasses are noticeably slimmer than other models. They also fit better and are far more comfortable because less of the weight sits toward the front of the frames. At 47 grams, the Clubmaster glasses are only 2 grams lighter than the Ray-Ban Meta Optics frames, but they feel significantly lighter because they put less pressure around my nose.
If you've read my past reviews of other Meta-branded glasses, you know I often struggle with getting a good fit. Most of the frame styles feel like they are meant for faces just a bit wider than my own, and the weight tends to cause them to slip around my face.
But the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses have traditional notepads that actually stay in place. You can also get the tips adjusted by an optician (Meta also provides this service at its retail stores and pop-ups as well), but these actually fit me well out of the box without any tweaks. I wore them for several long stretches and actually forgot I was wearing smart glasses because they felt so much like my typical shades.
No camera, (mostly) the same AI
Like other recent glasses from Meta, the audio-only frames have 6 mics and open-ear speakers. Music, podcasts and phone calls sounded just as good as my Gen 2 glasses. One quirk of the audio-only glasses is that the microphones are in slightly different places. There are now two mics on the front of the frames, replacing the ones that were embedded in the nosepads in previous models. The other four are on the arms. This new placement didn't seem to affect things, though. Friends and family told me I sounded clearer on calls when I was wearing the audio glasses, compared with my second-gen AirPods Pro.
The other major advantage the audio-only glasses have compared with other models is the battery life. Meta says the frames can go 12 hours on a charge with "mixed use" and up to six hours of continuous audio playback. I haven't done a full battery rundown, but I still had close to 50 percent battery after five hours of streaming audio and a one-hour phone call. If you aren't listening to hours of music or podcasts, the glasses will easily go all day without needing to recharge.
Even though there's no camera, you can still use most Meta AI features, including live translation and walking navigation. Meta is also planning to bring its AI agent, Muse, to its glasses, so the audio frames will also be a conduit to your personal agent once that update rolls out. (The company has said to expect it in the "coming months.")
One thing that did frustrate me about Meta's implementation of its assistant on the audio-only glasses is that the action button is so limited. On other frames that have the control (Meta Glasses, Oakley Meta Vanguard sunglasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Optics line, and Gen 3 Ray-Ban Meta frames), there are quite a few options for what that shortcut can trigger. Some of these are related to the camera, but many others aren't, like call muting or playing music.
But on the audio-only frames, there are only two options for what this button can do. If you select "music," it will play recommended playlists, or you can set it as a shortcut to activate Meta AI. The latter is useful if you don't enjoy saying "Hey Meta" in public, but you can't set it to trigger a specific prompt like you can on other glasses. You also can't use the button to answer or mute calls, both of which could be useful shortcuts for audio-only glasses.
It's an annoying limitation and I don't understand why Meta would limit what the only button on the glasses could do. The good news, though, is that this is likely something that can be addressed in future software updates, so I'm hopeful we might get a little more functionality out of the action button in time.
Does ditching the camera solve the privacy issues?
When I was interviewing Meta glasses users earlier this year about how the privacy backlash has affected how they use the product, a lot of people told me they loved their glasses, but were worried about how others might perceive them. Some said they would happily buy a pair without cameras if it would make them less likely to be labeled a "creep."
The Ray-Ban Meta Audio line seems to address those concerns. No one can (credibly) accuse you of covertly recording if there's no camera. It helps that the frames themselves are more subtle, too. Not having a camera also means that you don't run the risk of Meta capturing "visual data" from your surroundings to train its AI models.
But the fact that Meta has eliminated the glasses' most problematic feature doesn't address all of the concerns people may have. The company also stores audio recordings captured from its glasses, and no longer allows US users to opt-out. These audio snippets may also be heard by "trained reviewers," though it's possible to manually delete recordings from the Meta AI app.
There's also the reality that the backlash is unlikely to go away just because Meta now makes a pair of camera-free glasses. We've already seen a growing number of venues ban smart glasses. Several countries are also considering measures that would ban or limit the technology's use. And while some of these proposed actions would apply specifically to camera-enabled glasses, I think it's reasonable to worry that camera-free frames could also end up being targeted. I know I wouldn't want to end up in a situation where I'd need to explain to a security guard that "these are Meta glasses, but they're not that kind of Meta glasses."
At the same time, one of my favorite things about the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses is just how "normal" they look and feel. I was still able to enjoy the open-ear speakers and other audio features without being constantly aware that I was wearing smart glasses, or that others around me might notice them. And with a massive improvement to battery life, the frames are a compelling addition to Meta's expanding lineup of wearables.

Srinagar, Oct 13: The State Tuberculosis Cell, Kashmir, Directorate of Health Services Kashmir, organised an awareness programme under the #TBMuktBharatAbhiyan in collaboration with Amar Singh College, GogjiBagh, Srinagar, on Tuesday.
The initiative aimed to educate students and faculty members about tuberculosis prevention, elimination strategies and the role of public participation in achieving a TB-free India. Around 200 people attended the event and were given T-shirts and caps featuring the TB Mukt Bharat logo.
The programme commenced with a welcome and presentation of mementoes to the dignitaries, followed by an introductory address by Prof. (Dr.) TehminaYousuf, Principal of Amar Singh College. She said that although TB spreads easily, it is preventable and curable. She also noted that the college had implemented key infection-control measures on campus.
Dr Basra Mir, State Tuberculosis Officer, Kashmir, thanked the college administration and recalled the momentum generated on December 7, 2024, when 23 line departments came together for TB eradication. She urged students to help identify suspected cases and spread awareness that diagnostic testing and shortened treatment modules are available free of cost.
In his special address, Dr Naveed Nazir Shah, Chairman of the State Task Force Committee under the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP), J&K, stressed that early diagnosis and tackling social stigma are essential to eradicating the disease. He highlighted modern medical advances that have reduced treatment durations and explained the use of Active Case Finding (ACF) and TB Preventive Treatment (TPT) to prevent transmission. He also highlighted the government’s support system, which provides free treatment and a monthly nutritional allowance of Rs 1,000.
Delivering the keynote address, Dr Saba Wani, Deputy Director Schemes, Directorate of Health Services Kashmir, outlined progress in TB control in the Valley. She said five districts in Kashmir had achieved TB-free status, while the overall case incidence had declined to 44 per lakh, with around 3,000 active cases. She highlighted the use of handheld X-rays and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) for sputum testing, and praised the Ni-KshayMitra initiative, under which community donors provide patients with food baskets for six to eight months.
During the technical session, DrRubayaYousuf, State TB/HIV Coordinator, NTEP Kashmir, delivered a presentation on the biology of TB and the objectives and strategies of the national campaign.
Naveed Mukhtar Zargar, State ACSM Officer, NTEP Kashmir, discussed the implementation of the Ni-KshayMitra initiative, highlighting community engagement through NCC and My Bharat volunteers.
A TB-Free India pledge was administered to participants in both physical and digital modes, followed by a signature campaign to support the eradication of the disease.
The programme concluded with a vote of thanks by Dr Sabina Rasool, Convenor of the Health and Wellness Committee at Amar Singh College, who thanked the dignitaries, organisers and student participants.

Drones hit ships in Black Sea, sinking 1, prompting rescue operations, Bulgaria says
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev says drones struck two ships in the Black Sea, sinking one and prompting emergency rescue operations
SOFIA, Bulgaria -- Drones struck two ships in the Black Sea off Bulgaria on Tuesday, sinking one and prompting emergency rescue operations, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
The Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship Dignity sank after it was hit by a military strike. Five sailors were rescued, while a search for the other 11 crew members continues, Varna district governor Mario Smrkov said.
Rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members from the Ukrainian-operated coastal freighter Chelsea 3, sailing under the Maltese flag, with five receiving treatment for minor injuries, Radev said in a video posted to social media.
The crew, which included seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijan citizens, reported the ship’s deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones.
The strikes on the two ships occurred 20 miles and 21 miles (32 and 34 kilometers) from the Bulgarian coast.
During an emergency meeting of Bulgaria’s Security Council on Tuesday, Radev called the attacks “absolutely unacceptable” and said Bulgaria was seeking NATO and European Union assistance.
While authorities do not possess clear evidence on who was responsible for the drone attacks, “it makes no sense for Ukraine to destroy its own ships in the Black Sea, and the results of these strikes favor Russia's interests,” Radev told the Russian Ambassador in Sofia during a meeting on Tuesday, the government’s press office reported.
The ambassador said that she does not have any information from the Russian defense ministry related to the recent attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea but added that she did not rule out the possibility that “these attacks represent a provocation by a third party.”
Radev has said that such attacks are unacceptable and that Bulgaria will continue to investigate the attacks together with its EU and NATO allies to establish the truth.
Radev said that Bulgaria is suffering significant economic and financial damage and added that his country will initiate talks with neighboring Romania and Turkey on joint proposals to guarantee the safety of shipping in the Black Sea.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha in a post on X on Tuesday blamed Russia for the attacks.
“Russia’s latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria’s territorial waters, which injured Ukrainian and Azerbaijani citizens, once again demonstrates Moscow’s deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea,” Sybiha wrote.
“The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponize hunger and hold the world hostage. This must be met with strength,” Sybiha wrote.
“NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea,” NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte wrote on X. He added that NATO had already strengthened its posture along the eastern flank and will continue to monitor the security environment, adjusting its deterrence and defense posture as needed.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen “strongly condemned” the drone incidents and said the Black Sea “has become another front of escalation” in Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“This is unacceptable. I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast. Putting the lives of the crew in grave danger and threatening security in the Black Sea,” she said in a post on X.
“We stand with Bulgaria and thank its rescuers for their swift response. Those responsible should be held accountable.”
European Council President Antonio Costa said in a social media post that the EU stood in full solidarity with Bulgaria following the attacks.
Costa said the growing number of Russian hybrid activities would be discussed at the European Council meeting scheduled for Thursday and Friday in Brussels.
The attacks came exactly a week after sea and aerial drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. A Togo-flagged ship sank, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated the 18-member crew of a Pulau-flagged vessel.
A day earlier, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank in the Black Sea off the coast of Romania. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued, Romanian authorities said.

Pope Leo said on Sunday (October 12, 2026) that doctors had detected a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and he would be undergoing surgery this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff’s tenure.
Leo told pilgrims in St. Peter’s Square for his weekly Sunday prayer that the growth was “well-contained” and had been spotted early.
“Recently, during some medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung,” said the pontiff. “It was detected at a very early stage and is well contained.”
“The doctors believe it is advisable to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it,” he said. “The operation is already scheduled for the next few days.”
A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors.
Leo, elected pope by the world’s cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to previously have had health issues.
The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, died at age 88 and was increasingly frail in his later years.
The Vatican press office said Leo’s recovery from surgery was expected to take about a week. It did not immediately provide further details about the pope’s health.
Leo keeps a busy schedule and is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6-17.
Before mentioning his health issue in his address on Sunday, the pope referred to the trip, thanking Catholics for their prayers “for the pastoral visit I will undertake.”

Boardroom feud tests trusted Indian business empire
- Published
Before dawn breaks over Mumbai, Mansi Kadam begins preparing vada pav, a savoury snack synonymous with the western Indian city, for the day's customers. One ingredient is non-negotiable: Tata salt.
When asked whether she would ever consider switching brands, her reply is a reminder of an old Hindi ad jingle, "If it's salt, it has to be Tata."
She knows little about the developments unfolding in the boardroom of the Tata group, one of India's oldest and most influential business empires that makes everything from salt to software.
But her instinctive loyalty points to a question confronting the group: Can one of India's most trusted brands remain insulated from a public battle over power, governance and control?
A recent public disagreement between the board of Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata group and Tata Trusts, its principal shareholder, has put a spotlight on the conglomerate.
At the centre of the dispute are two issues - the proposed public listing of Tata Sons and the reappointment of chairman N Chandrasekaran. Most of the Tata Sons board, including its biggest minority shareholder SP Group, supported the decisions.
But Noel Tata, chairman of majority shareholder Tata Trusts, has opposed both resolutions. He maintains that a public listing would dilute the group's philanthropic ethos and is likely to get both decisions overturned at its annual general meeting.
"When we say this is a governance crisis, it's a misalignment of interests between the board [of Tata Sons] and the shareholders [Tata Trusts]," Shriram Subramanian, head of independent corporate governance firm InGovern Research, told the BBC.
While he does not expect the brand's image to be affected immediately, he flags concerns over the leadership's ability to navigate the challenges.
Disagreements within the Tata Group have been simmering since the death of former chairman Ratan Tata - Noel Tata's half-brother who designated him successor after his death - in 2024. For many Indians, Ratan Tata's philanthropy and leadership had become inseparable from the brand. His death triggered widespread mourning and experts say it left a leadership void in the group's image with the public.
The Tata group has topped India's most valuable brand list by valuation consultancy Brand Finance since 2018, according to the group's website.
Tata Sons, the business entity, is described by the group as the "fastener keeping the many disparate elements of the whole together".
Tata Trusts, which represents seven philanthropic trusts that own the majority stake in the group, is widely regarded as its moral compass, guiding the businesses on social impact and philanthropy.
For many Indians, both the entities together make up what most companies cannot buy - trust.
Now with these entities in rival corners, that is coming under strain.
"Once upon a time, there was a unified audience which said the Tatas are good people with good governance. Today, the opinion is divided," said Harish Bijoor, business and brand strategy consultant.
While most consumers appear unfazed, the dispute has polarised other stakeholders including business partners, investors and employees. Some view it as corporate power politics, others as a genuine governance debate, but few agree on which side is right, Bijoor said.
"This conflict has brought the Tatas into conversations everywhere, which is not good as they have always liked to be out of it," he says.
The group has traditionally preferred being low profile about philanthropy and conflict resolution.
The Tata group did not respond to BBC's email with detailed questions.
Founded by Jamsetji Tata in 1868, the Tata group expanded under JRD Tata who transformed it into a professionally managed conglomerate. Ratan Tata drove its global ambitions through acquisitions.
Tata group, which has a combined market value of more than $260bn (£195.6bn) and employs hundreds of thousands of people in more than 100 countries, is not new to controversies.
The conglomerate has faced protests over industrial projects, scrutiny of its Indian telecom business during a spectrum allocation controversy, a high-profile dispute with Japan's Docomo and, more recently, questions over Air India's performance.
Some of its business decisions have also drawn attention, particularly Tata Steel's troubled Corus acquisition, though other overseas bets such as Tetley and Jaguar Land Rover were successful and helped expand the group's global footprint.
Its biggest controversy was in 2016 when the Tata Sons board abruptly removed Cyrus Mistry as chairman and brought back Ratan Tata as interim head. Mistry, heir to the SP Group, was chosen by a team led by Ratan Tata himself. It led to a long battle which ended in 2021 with the Supreme Court ruling in the Tatas' favour.
Last month, journalist Sucheta Dalal wrote in her column for Moneylife magazine that the Tata group has "weathered serious governance storms" and enjoys "special privileges available to no other business group [referring to a tax exemption granted to Tata Trusts for holding shares in Tata Sons]" because of a reputation built over decades.
Most Tata watchers agree.
In an email interview, Morgen Witzel, a fellow at Exeter Centre of Leadership who wrote a book on the brand in 2010, cited several examples on the group's connection with people.
At Jamshedpur in Jharkhand state, where the group set up India's first integrated steel plant and an industrial city, it provides healthcare and education to people in hundreds of villages. Watchmaker Titan supports employees who want to leave and start their own businesses. Tata Motors at Pune has supported thousands of female entrepreneurs, he points out.
"It is the concatenation of all of these things that builds trust because people see that, by and large, Tata is there to serve their needs rather than just take their money," Witzel said.
But while the group has weathered other storms, this time, the divide is within.
The boardroom tussle has increasingly spilled into the public domain, with Tata Sons and Trusts clashing through legal notices and conflicting statements.
Venu Srinivasan, vice-chairman of Tata Trusts and a nominee director on Tata Sons' board, has sought a probe into alleged governance lapses at some trusts. The trusts deny the lapses.
Noel Tata has made two proposals to avoid listing the company.
First, that the Tata Sons board buy back a portion of SP Group's minority stake as a "fair and equitable solution" to the latter's demand to monetise their stake. Secondly, restructure Tata Sons by merging with itself two businesses which would change the way it is classified by India's central bank, helping the group potentially avoid a listing.
It is not clear whether he can pull this off, given that unlike Rata Tata, he had not consolidated power yet.
"Ratan Tata's larger-than-life image is, to some extent, the reason behind the current conflict. Everyone was deferential towards him and his successor was known only after his death through his will," says Subramanian.
Had Ratan Tata overseen the succession himself, the transition would have been smoother, he says.
Brand expert Bijoor calls for the Tata group to put together a "white paper" on how the conflict plays out in the end. "They stood for transparency, and they must never shed that."
How the influential group manages these tensions may offer a glimpse into its future. The outcome will be watched closely across corporate India, where Tata's governance and business practices have long been regarded as a benchmark.

Southern California coastal communities are picking up the pieces after a weekend of extreme weather brought flooding that overtook city streets and intense waves battered beachside homes.
The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel hit Mexico’s Baja California over the weekend as well as southern California and Las Vegas. While meteorologists noted that Rachel weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it approached California, it still left a trail of destruction.
Footage showed massive waves crashing into Long Beach homes, destroying a boardwalk and forcing residents to flee. The damage to homes was significant, leaving some at risk of collapse.
At least nine have been deemed unsafe to enter, the Long Beach Post reported, meaning displaced residents cannot return to retrieve personal items. The storm has cost the city more than $1m from its emergency reserves, according to the outlet.
Farther south, the city of Newport Beach declared a local emergency and briefly closed piers to “protect public safety”, citing “higher-than-normal surf” that inundated streets.
By Monday, cleanup work was under way and Newport Beach had reopened the piers, but officials advised residents to exercise caution near the water.
In Las Vegas, a raging torrent of water rushed over a street near the strip, and the city tied an all-time daily rainfall record for October with 1.08in (2.74cm) of rain into Sunday morning, according to the US National Weather Service.
The impacts are just a taste of what’s to come across southern California as a historic El Niño unfolds in the Pacific, threatening to unleash severe storms across the region this winter.
Already, the last five hurricanes in the Pacific all reached major status and saw with winds of at least 111mph (178.6 km/h), and one set a record for time spent at category 5.
“This year, just everything that forms is just lasting a long time and getting really powerful,” Phil Klotzbach, a Colorado State University researcher who forecasts and studies storm activity, told the Associated Press, adding that the last month has been “berserk”.
The El Niño climate phenomenon, characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, has the potential to supercharge extreme weather around the world. While it’s expected to strengthen through the end of this year and into next, the excess warmth already measured is climbing off the charts. Forecasters have warned its effects could become exceptionally destructive.
In California – especially in the southern part of the state – El Niños typically carry higher risks of severe storms, and with them elevated threats from landslides, debris flows and flash floods. These dangers become more pronounced around recent burn scars, adding hazards to several areas, including in the neighborhoods still recovering from the 2025 Los Angeles firestorm and swaths of Big Sur above Highway 1.
“This year’s tilt in the odds toward wet and stormy conditions in California will be profoundly unsubtle,” climate scientist Daniel Swain said in a recent analysis, adding that its unlike anything he’s observed before.
Throughout the winter months, El Niño could also add an additional foot of sea level rise in California on top of the 8in to 12in caused by the climate crisis over the last century, according to Michael Anderson, a state climatologist.
Already, El Niño has elevated sea levels up and down the California coast, from the Mexico border up to the San Francisco Bay Area. Warm waters expanding from an extreme marine heatwave combined with a coastally trapped Kelvin wave – a large underwater band of warm water – have already inundated parts of the North American shoreline. More Kelvin waves are likely and California is already bracing for unusually high king tides to hit during holiday weekends this year, arriving near Thanksgiving and Christmas.
While the impacts from heavy rains and high surf are each destructive in their own right, when they align and overlap they can cause even more calamity.
“Between November 2026 and January 2027, I would anticipate multiple significant coastal flood events that are worse in severity and also much more widespread than what we are currently seeing,” Swain said. “Even a moderate storm could bring water levels higher still, and a strong storm would likely produce widespread damaging, and probably historic, coastal flooding.”
Meanwhile, as cities across California begin preparations for intense winter weather, there are still months left before the risks from fire begin to subside. The National Weather Service issued fire weather watches for parts of southern California, including in Los Angeles, as seasonal strong, dry winds align with high temperatures. Forecasters warned that there would be “high risk for extreme fire behavior with any new fire starts Thursday through Friday”.
With the threat of fire, heat and sea level rise colliding, as the state readies for more incoming effects from El Niño, Kevin McGowan, the director of LA’s office of emergency management, urged residents to be ready. “People should continue to prepare not just for one hazard,” he said during a recent briefing, – but all hazards.”
The Associated Press contributed reporting

Topgolf’s VMware costs were going to increase by 400 percent under Broadcom. To avoid that cost, the sports entertainment company moved 12,000 virtual machines (VMs) to VergeIO’s VergeOS and has saved over $11 million so far.
Before migrating, Topgolf’s VMware connection “ran very deep,” Scott Forehand, Topgolf’s global infrastructure manager, told Ars Technica.
Topgolf has over 100 locations worldwide featuring interactive golf games with real-time shot tracking and digital analytics. The company used vSphere and ESXi for decades and started using VxRail, the hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) platform that VMware co-engineered with Dell, in 2017. Topgolf employees previously participated in numerous VMware customer councils and have been interviewed for books on how Topgolf used vSphere and Horizon (now Omnissa Horizon), per Forehand, who is a leader of the Dallas/Ft. Worth VMware User Group.
But Broadcom’s decision to stop selling VMware perpetual licenses and bundle VMware products into fewer, larger, and more expensive SKUs led Topgolf, as well as many other VMware customers, to look elsewhere. With VMware’s strategic changes complicating future planning, Topgolf decided to migrate its on-premises workloads, including those for its venues, offices, labs, and data centers.
Twenty Topgolf venues are still running VxRail with the VMware Cloud Foundation software stack. Forehand expects Topgolf to be completely off VMware by the second week of December. He added:
Overall, we reduced or eliminated over $11.3 [million] in combined infrastructure costs prior to the adjustments in hardware cost in the market. Comparatively, it’s much more now when you look at the cost of a solution similar to the configuration of the old VxRail solution we installed.
The money Topgolf saved by moving to VergeIO isn’t typical because Topgolf has larger needs than many organizations. However, saving money on software licensing and avoiding proprietary HCI appliances and separate tools for data protection, replication, and multi-site management is common for VergeOS users coming from VMware, VergeIO Chief Marketing Officer George Crump told Ars.
“Most customers who move from VMware see meaningful reductions in all three,” he said.

The island where locals say data centres are taking their water
- Published
"Water! Water!" the crowd shouted as it stormed a compound with data centres, armed with empty plastic bottles and jerry cans.
There were about 300 of them, all residents on the Indonesian island of Batam, and they were furious that the taps at home had run dry, while the data centres in the new Nongsa Digital Park seemed to have enough water to protect their machines from overheating.
"Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months... Our water supply had been reliable until the data centres came," Dewi Susanti, one of the protesters, told the BBC.
People in her village, Bakau Serip, were now depending on tanker trucks that dispensed "dirty, cloudy and smelly" water, she said.
Batam's water utility told the BBC it was working to improve supply, but did not comment on whether the disruption was linked to demand from the data centres.
But BP Batam, the agency overseeing trade and industry, blamed it on a prolonged dry spell and denied allegations from locals that water meant for homes was being channelled to data centres.
This is not the first such protest in Batam, whose shrinking reservoirs find themselves under more pressure as the island tries to transform itself into a digital hub.
Following protests in August and September, authorities told the firms opening data centres in Batam that they must build their own desalination plants instead of relying on reservoirs for freshwater.
But locals say they are increasingly concerned that they must now compete with servers for water.
"Reliable data on data centre water use in Indonesia remains scarce, partly because companies treat it as proprietary information," says Agus Hasan, a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology.
"We should build [data centres] rationally, transparently, and responsibly, and insist on seeing the numbers... [Otherwise] those kept in the dark while their taps run dry will push back, and rightly so," he adds.
A backlash has been building against data centres across the world, from the US to the UK to parts of Asia, as tech companies pour billions into AI infrastructure.
People are worried about how the huge, windowless buildings might change their neighbourhoods, the constant hum of machines, the security lights that could stay on all night, and the pressure this puts on water and energy resources.
While electricity powers the centres, the water keeps the servers from frying - engineers deploy elaborate cooling systems, which consume a lot of water.
Research in the US suggests a typical data centre consumes around 300,000 gallons of water a day, or about as much as 1,000 US households. A larger, 50MW facility could take as much water as 2,200 households per day, and enough electricity to power 22,000 homes, according to Malaysia's central bank.
It's unclear how much water or electricity the data centres in Batam are consuming.
But the island routinely faces water shortages, and the levels are worse this year, possibly because of a historic "super" El Niño.
Devoid of natural freshwater sources, Batam's 1.3 million people rely on rainwater collected in six artificial reservoirs.
Nongsa reservoir, which supplies water to Bakau Serip, where Dewi lives, would dry up over the next month with no rainfall, simulations by local environmental non-profit group Akar Bhumi Indonesia suggest.
"The water shortage is affecting our livelihoods... Money that should be used to buy rice is now spent on water drums," Dewi says. "My husband has to wait up overnight to get water, and then go straight to work the next morning."
Batam's water utility had earlier said that it would consider measures like cloud seeding should the water shortage continue. When asked about the recent protests, they pointed us to earlier statements.
Authorities in Batam have approved 10 data centres, six of which will be located in Nongsa Digital Park. Two are up and running, while a third is under construction. At least six more are currently under review for approval, BP Batam told the BBC.
Official figures put investment in data centres on the island at more than $6.7bn (£5.1bn) as of mid-2026, spurred in part by demand from Singapore, which is just an hour away by ferry.
Singapore paused construction of data centres in 2019, citing land and energy constraints. It lifted the ban in 2022 after introducing new efficiency standards, which prompted investors to look elsewhere.
Singapore has long been promoting the Riau Islands, which includes Batam, and the Malaysian state of Johor as "complementary" regions.
Quick to absorb the spillover, Johor approved data centre projects worth tens of billions. But this soon drew the ire of residents frustrated with noise, dust and water shortages. The state has since tried to regulate how much water and electricity data centres consume.
Across the strait, Batam is just as attractive to investors - from the US, China, Australia, Singapore - because of relatively low operating costs, proximity to Singapore and connections to major subsea cable routes.
Nongsa is home to a 13,000-sq-m data centre by Hong Kong-based private equity firm Gaw Capital and Indonesian developer Sinar Primera. In April, Singapore's DayOne signed a deal with an Indonesian state utility to build one of the country's largest data centres - around 450MW capacity, enough to power 350,000 average households. In June, DayOne, chip maker Nvidia and Australian AI start-up Firmus Technologies announced a 360MW "AI factory".
By 2030, power demand from data centres in Batam is expected to cross 1,100MW, which is enough to power nearly a million homes, according to the official estimates.
The BBC has contacted DayOne, Sinar Primera and Gaw Capital for comment.
Meanwhile, the spate of construction is worrying locals in Batam who urged authorities to prioritise their needs.
"Don't just sit at the top and keep approving these projects. Come down here and see for yourselves what we are wrestling with," says Marlinda, who lives in the district of Sei Beduk, which is also facing water shortages.
"We want the government to pay attention to ordinary people," another resident told the BBC.
"Don't make billion-rupiah investments while ordinary people are made to suffer... We are not asking for anything extravagant. We just want our water supply restored."

This is the story of seven older adults who live together in a shophouse in Singapore.
Uncle Chee is usually the first up. Aunty Lydia begins her day with oats and blueberries. Uncle Cheong often heads to a nearby hawker center, sometimes returning with snacks from the 7-Eleven next door.
Some days, the space fills with people beyond its residents. On the Tuesday morning I visited in September, Camino House, their assisted-living home, was a flurry of activity. Preschoolers had come for a painting session, filling the shophouse with chatter and laughter.
This was exactly the kind of interaction Mariel Chee and Bennett Lee, both 32, hoped to foster when they founded Camino House.
Rather than build a traditional care facility, they wanted to create a space where people from all walks of life could interact.
"One that's beautiful and welcoming, not clinical or institutional. Somewhere we'd want to grow old ourselves," Chee told Business Insider.
Chee, an artist with a background in early childhood development, and Lee, an engineer, were childhood friends who later married. Lee also grew up around eldercare: his parents are both doctors and founded another assisted-living provider in Singapore.
For Chee, the project was also personal. Her father was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in his mid-60s. Chee and her siblings were still in school at the time.
"It was really hard, because he was so young and none of us knew how to care for him," she said.
A middle ground between home and a nursing home
Populations are aging around the world, raising urgent questions about how older adults will live and receive care.
In 2026, Singapore became a "super-aged" society, with 21.4% of its citizens aged 65 or older. About 152,000 citizens are now 80 and above, up by 60% from 91,000 in 2016.
For older Singaporeans who can no longer live entirely independently, care has traditionally fallen to family members, sometimes supplemented by home-based services, or to nursing homes.
Camino House is part of a small but growing private sector in Singapore that serves older adults who need some daily support but not nursing care.
It was one of five providers in a 2023 Singapore initiative to test shared caregiving for groups of seniors living together — a model the country eventually formalized in late 2025.
Life at Camino House
The seven residents of Camino House range in age from 69 to 93.
Built between the 1840s and 1960s, shophouses once made up much of Singapore’s prewar urban landscape, with businesses on the ground floor and living quarters above. Public property records show this colorful two-story shophouse in Joo Chiat, a neighborhood in eastern Singapore, was bought for $3.5 million Singapore dollars in 2020.
There are six bedrooms — four singles and two twins — each with an en suite bathroom. An elevator connects the building's two floors. Three healthcare attendants work in shifts, including overnight, to provide round-the-clock support.
While there is no doctor on-site at the shophouse, there is a clinic about a five-minute walk away, Chee said.
For many families, especially those with relatives living abroad, the reassurance is not only that a loved one is safe, but that they remain connected to people who know them well.
Christine Yee, a Singaporean who has lived in the US for nearly two decades, told Business Insider that Camino House felt like a "godsend."
Her mother, Mary, 93, was its first resident. "It was like a family, so my mom didn't feel like she was being dropped off at some place," Yee said.
Bringing the neighborhood inside
A big part of what keeps residents connected to the wider community is the Joo Chiat Social Club, which hosts most of its activities on the building's ground floor.
These half-day programs include exercise, cooking, and rattan weaving, sometimes with volunteers or children from nearby preschools.
These activities are open to all the residents of Camino House. "The idea is that they get to choose what they want to do," Lee told Business Insider.
The social club also welcomes non-resident participants, with a single-session pass costing about S$100, which covers the cost of the activities, lunch, and care support during the session. Multi-session pass bundles are also available.
The three-hour sessions run three times a week, with plans to expand to daily programming next year, Chee said. There is no age limit, though pass holders tend to be between 70 and 90.
"When younger and older adults meet repeatedly over time to create and learn together, the dynamic shifts from 'doing something for seniors' to 'creating something with seniors,' with both generations participating as active partners," Vivien Wu, an assistant professor at the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine at the National University of Singapore, told Business Insider.
Engaging in shared activities can help people connect across language and cognitive barriers, ease social anxiety, and challenge assumptions about aging, she said.
Chee and Lee are not the first to try the idea. Similar intergenerational programs have paired senior care with childcare centers in the US, including Providence Mount St. Vincent in Seattle and the St. Ann Center for Intergenerational Care in Milwaukee.
Yee said she appreciated that the club's activities gave her mom regular opportunities to interact with people of different ages and backgrounds.
"The older folks get this enjoyment from the children, whether it's their antics or their energy or their innocence," she said.
The cost of care, and of community
The average cost of assisted living in the US is around $5,511 a month, though prices vary widely by location. The Boston metro area had the highest average, at $9,577 a month.
In Singapore, there is little public data on what these shared-home providers charge, in part because the space is still small and the government only made the model a standard care option in December. A high-end assisted-living development that opened in August charges between S$8,900 and S$17,000 a month, or $6,952 and $13,280.
At Camino House, monthly costs start from S$4,500, or $3,515, depending on the room type and the level of care needed. This includes meals, laundry, and daily housekeeping.
For Victor Lee, 70, living at Camino House has brought him out of his shell.
After a bad fall three years ago, Lee realized he needed more support than he could get living alone in his two-story apartment. He moved in soon afterward and pays S$5,800 a month for his single room suite.
"I think I'm the most talkative one now," he told Business Insider.
As with any family, living in proximity can bring disagreements and tensions, Chee said. But it has meant getting to know residents in ways that go far beyond their care plans.
"We know their favorite songs, their histories, even their love stories. It feels like we're walking this journey together with them, right to the end," she said.

Young men live in fear of being snatched off the streets and sold to Myanmar's army
- Published
You do not stay out after dark if you're young and able-bodied in Hpa-An, the capital of Myanmar's southern Karen state. In recent months this has become conventional wisdom.
But Zaw Min has no choice.
"I worry, but I have to go out to work," says the 26-year-old tuk tuk driver, who asked that his real name be omitted out of fear for his safety. "My family call me all the time and remind me not to drive passengers too far; to be careful who I take as a passenger... I have to be vigilant all the time.
"People are panicked and frightened," he explains. "Some people I know have been taken."
Locals say plain-clothed members and supporters of the Myanmar junta have been roaming the streets of Hpa-An, arbitrarily arresting people in their teens, 20s and 30s and forcing them into military service.
According to leaked documents seen by BBC Burmese, authorities have been ordered to aggressively fulfil the military's recruitment quotas across jurisdictions, bolstering the junta's ranks as it endures a war of attrition against ethnic militias, pro-democracy groups and civilian-led resistance movements.
Zaw Min is the only one among his siblings who is at the age of recruitment. Many other "kids" his age have fled, he says – to Thailand, or the homes of relatives further afield. Those who remain are often under strict instructions from their parents: be home before dusk.
Myanmar has been locked in a bloody civil war since February 2021, when its own military launched a coup d'etat and ousted democratically elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
Three years later, following a string of humiliating losses, plummeting morale and soaring rates of desertion, the junta enacted a mandatory conscription law that required all men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve at least two years under military command. Those who refuse face up to five years in prison.
The enactment of the law "represents one of the most severe and impactful actions taken against the entire civilian population since the military coup", according to Maj Naung Yoe, military affairs official at the Myanmar Defense and Security Institute (MDSI) and a former military officer who defected and joined the anti-coup Civil Disobedience Movement.
Hpa-An is the latest to be caught in a dragnet that's already ensnared an estimated 100,000 young recruits over the past two-and-a-half years – many of them via coercion, extortion and abductions.
"Security forces track young people's movements to arrest them, force them into service under the pretext of statutory military eligibility, extort money through threats of detention, and arrest individuals during guest-list inspections," Naung Yoe says.
The BBC contacted the Myanmar government's Central Body for Summoning People's Military Servants regarding incidents mentioned in this story, including the forced recruitment of conscripts and reports of abductions allegedly carried out in recent months.
They said they had no comment on the matter.
With the mandatory conscription law, the junta has established a human supply chain to sustain its armed forces. And it appears to have worked. Observers note that reinforcements have played a critical role in helping the regime claw back more territory. In many parts of Myanmar, the resistance is now on the back foot.
The war, though, is far from over. And as more youths evade conscription – either to join the resistance or simply avoid armed conflict against their fellow countrymen – the junta's recruitment methods have become ever more extreme.
International rights groups such as Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and Fortify Rights say Myanmar's military is abducting civilians and forcing them into military service.
In July, open-source research organisation Myanmar Witness revealed that they had analysed hundreds of missing-person advertisements collected from Facebook between 2021 and 2025.
Researchers found that missing person notices for January rose from four in 2021, pre-coup, to 82 in 2025, post-conscription law.
"In practice, much of [the Myanmar military's] recruitment appears to be carried out through detention, coercion, and disappearance rather than formal call-up, and often without notice to families," they concluded.
Men and boys constituted the majority of reported missing persons.
"They are spreading rumours all over the neighbourhood that I sold my husband."
Ma Moe San Pan sobs the words through gulps of air. She is sitting in her kitchen, at home in Yangon, where on the morning of 8 May 2025 she saw her 33-year-old husband Phyo Wai for the last time.
"We had an argument, and afterwards he left home," she recalls."I was upset and told my cousin about what had happened."
Ma Moe San Pan's cousin worked at the local ward administration office, and she asked him to bring her husband back. It was two days later that Phyo Wai called her, from a military recruitment centre on the other side of the city.
The cousin had taken him to the ward office which had sold him on to another ward for 4 million kyats ($900; £680) to fill that ward's recruitment quota, Ma Moe San Pan says. The BBC was unable to reach Ma Moe San Pan's cousin.
In a desperate attempt to bring him back, Ma Moe San Pan was then scammed out of 4.5 million kyats by strangers who falsely promised his release.
U Maung Maung Lwin, the administrator of the ward to which Phyo Wai was taken, later admitted to the BBC that he had played a role in sending him to the military recruitment authorities.
When asked about allegations that individuals were being conscripted outside their home township, he said transfers from other townships do occur when local quotas cannot be met.
But he denied that any money was involved in such cases, or in Phyo Wai's forced conscription.
"[Phyo Wai] told me they said they would help him and made him sign documents," Ma Moe San Pan recalls.
"If my husband had been legally selected for conscription through the normal process, I could have accepted that. What I cannot accept is that our own ward administration office allegedly sold him to another ward.
"I also regret placing my trust in my cousin."
In the time since Phyo Wai was taken, Ma Moe San Pan has filed police complaints relating to two matters: the sale of her husband into military service, and the 4.5 million kyats she lost to scammers.
The police accepted her complaint, she says, but refused her request to include human trafficking charges, claiming a human trafficking case could only be registered if a person had been sold abroad.
She does not know where her husband is now.
Ma Moe San Pan's case highlights a grim mutation of the junta's mandatory conscription laws: mounting pressure from the higher levels of the regime has created perverse incentives further down the chain of command.
Surging demand and dwindling supply have fuelled an illicit market for eligible recruits. And with money on the table, security officials have taken to arresting youth at road checkpoints, tracking and ambushing workers during their daily commutes, setting traps via fake job advertisements, and forcibly entering people's homes, Naung Yoe says.
"Under the guise of the conscription law, these coercive arrests and recruitment drives have effectively transformed into a modern-day slavery and human trafficking enterprise."
In late August, police in Yangon arrested a member of the Fire Services Department – a branch of the home affairs ministry – and his son-in-law for abducting four young men with the intention of selling them for military conscription.
The reserve fire brigade unit commander allegedly deceived the men with promises of employment opportunities, luring them to his house and trapping them in a series of purpose-built detention rooms. Police officers raided the residence and arrested him on 25 August. He has since been charged with kidnapping or abducting in order to wrongfully confine a person, and faces up to 7 years in prison.
BBC Burmese made several attempts to contact the police station where he is being held, but was unsuccessful.
"Lower-level administrative bodies, military personnel and local criminal gangs employ diverse tactics to press-gang and arrest young people," Naung Yoe says.
"They sell these individuals to military units and regional commands facing manpower shortages, or traffic substitute recruits on behalf of wealthier individuals seeking to buy their way out of service."
While conscription orders are indiscriminate on paper – demanding a quota of recruits from each village, ward, or township proportional to its population – wealthier conscripts can simply pay to dodge the draft and be replaced by someone more financially vulnerable.
So it is the poor who disproportionately bear the burden.
Naung Yoe, meanwhile, told the BBC that "these practices are escalating due to increasing difficulties in meeting monthly recruitment quotas and the lucrative financial profits made from recruit trading at the ground level".
But the hardening fist of forced conscription also reveals the junta's empty hand, and its desperation for manpower.
It "seems to be another step in the junta's efforts to enlist unwilling youth in a conflict that underscores its embattled position in the civil war" says Dr Sandeep Singh, a research fellow who teaches military studies at the National University of Singapore.
The climate surrounding routine abductions, he adds, has "generated further difficulties on the youth of Myanmar, already affected by years of civil war, and their families".
In addition to the daily anxiety of life in Myanmar, many would-be recruits now fear being forced to fight in a deadly conflict that they not only don't believe in, but actively oppose. This constant threat has fuelled massive internal displacement and severe labour shortages in an already flailing economy, and sent people fleeing to neighbouring countries.
Having spent more than half a decade waging war against its own population, the junta is now wielding the conscription law as yet another tool of subjugation, observers say.
As the MDSI put it in a statement published in June: "The generals have benefited by using military law to make the citizens fight against each other."

A rumor is circulating that a confrontation took place between Turning Point CEO Erika Kirk and historian Heather Cox Richardson during a panel. According to numerous Facebook posts over the past several months, Kirk insulted Richardson by poking fun at her age.
One Facebook post stated:
Erika Kirk Insults Heather Cox Richardson: "Sit down, you 63-year-old academic" — But Her Response Shocked the Entire Nation
Erika Kirk delivered the sarcastic remark with a cold, defiant stare that silenced the entire auditorium. Heather Cox Richardson did not react immediately — at least not for the first few seconds. The historian and public intellectual simply raised an eyebrow, tilted her head slightly, and offered a calm, knowing smile, as though she had grown accustomed to pressure, criticism, and high-stakes moments throughout years of service.
Slowly, Heather Cox Richardson picked up the microphone, rose to her feet, and faced Kirk directly with the steady composure of someone who has spent a lifetime studying history and engaging the public with clarity and conviction.
When Richardson finally spoke, her words were measured, confident, and deeply grounded — the voice of a woman in her 60s fully aware of her journey, her purpose, and her identity.
Rather than reacting emotionally, she transformed the moment into something far greater than the insult itself.
"I'm proud of every one of my years," she said calmly. "They represent study, teaching, service, lessons learned, and the responsibility of standing up for something bigger than yourself. Age isn't an insult — it's a record of what you've contributed."
The Facebook post also linked to an article an ad-filled blog with the headline, "A Public Insult Sparked Silence—Then Heather Cox Richardson's Response Changed Everything Forever." 
The above Facebook post and article describe an incident that never took place. The post is an example of "AI slop" — low-quality content that's easy to create thanks to artificial intelligence tools. Such content can overwhelm social media feeds, leaving users unsure of what's real and what's not. As such, we rate this claim as false.
News organizations would have covered the alleged dramatic interaction between the two public figures if it ever took place. However, our searches of Google, DuckDuckGo (archived) and Bing for any legitimate news coverage about such an interaction or panel found no results. 
The post in question notes under the poster's name that this is "AI content." It links to an article on a blog that is clearly not a legitimate news organization. 
(Facebook user "Carl Paoli")
The article does not give us a date or time of this interaction and did not even report on the exchange. When such stories spread online about controversies between public figures and without mentioning specifics of the events but encouraging readers to click on articles from unknown websites, they are often acting as "clickbait" — directing social media users to online advertising and unrelated content.
The story also closely resembled other rumors we looked into about one public figure telling another to "sit down." For example, one similar false claim involved U.S. President Donald Trump telling Pope Leo XIV, "Sit down — you're just the pope." In another, Trump's son Barron allegedly told astronaut Christina Koch, "Sit down, you're just an astronaut."
Kirk gained prominence after the assassination of her husband, conservative activist and Turning Point USA CEO Charlie Kirk, on Sept. 10, 2025. She took over as the organization's CEO after his death. A political historian, Richardson has been a vocal critic of Trump.
Snopes has debunked many AI slop rumors and written an explainer on this trend.

Missiles intercepted near Riyadh after Saudi coalition hits Yemen fuel depot
- Published
Missiles and drones have been intercepted over Riyadh after the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen struck a fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, its spokesperson says.
Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said several projectiles targeting the Saudi capital and other cities were intercepted after the coalition carried out a strike on the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility on Tuesday night.
The Houthis warned they would target the airport and Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and Aramco's headquarters in the eastern city of Dammam.
Al-Maliki later said missiles targeting cities including Dammam had been intercepted, while shrapnel had fallen in a residential area in Dhahran.
An Armaco administration building in Dhahran was also targeted, resulting in "limited fire", Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy said in a statement.
No casualties were reported, the statement said.
It came as the Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the Iran-backed group would "bear the consequences" of its recent deadly attacks on the kingdom.
Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, while another person was killed in a similar attack there the following day.
On Tuesday, the coalition said its forces had destroyed three drones north of Riyadh.
The Houthis have said they are targeting airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones in response to deadly Saudi strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces mounting an offensive on Yemen's Red Sea coast and several other front lines.
A correspondent for AFP news agency reported that queues formed at petrol stations in Sanaa on Tuesday afternoon following the coalition's warning of an impending operation against the al-Sabaha oil facility, with many residents worried about shortages.
The Yemen Petroleum Company, which is run by the Houthis, issued a statement that sought to reassure them, saying the facility "does not contain any stock of petroleum products".
The company also said it had "taken all necessary precautionary measures to address any emergency, ensuring the stability of the supply situation and the continued meeting of citizens' needs in a normal manner".
After al-Maliki confirmed the strike, first reported by Houthi media, explosions were heard over Riyadh and other Saudi cities, with al-Maliki reporting four missiles and two drones had been intercepted near the capital.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social on Tuesday the Houthis were "behaving very badly... and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices".
Speaking to reporters, he did not answer a question on whether he'd made a decision to help the Saudis retaliate against them, but said he "might" ask Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan to intervene.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed in Yemen since August. The UN's human rights office says they include at least 54 civilians, half of them children.
More than 216,000 people have also been displaced across the country, and suspected cholera cases have tripled in three weeks, rising from 217 to 647, according to the UN.
