Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary. I’m honored to be subbing for Sigal Samuel while she’s out on parental leave. I’m diving into your questions as a way to help understand human nature and our choices through multiple lenses: philosophical, psychological, and beyond. Please send in any emotional, body/brain, sociological, perceptual, or other kind of life quandaries you might have.
Your kid wants to go vegan. Should you let them?
What to do when your child’s ethics don’t match your own.
My child, age 9, has decided she’s vegan. Neither of her parents are even vegetarian — we’re “free range chicken/grass fed beef” types. She has learned about veganism from friends at school, and seems to have come to her position more or less on her own. I want to encourage her ethical choices, but her mother and I agree that children should be introduced to new foods and flavors at this age. She has no allergies or intolerances that we know of. I worry that making accommodations for her dietary restriction may lead to a lifetime of picky eating, even if hers is a reasonable and ethical approach. She seems to be uncomfortable when her mother or I cook meat for meals we share, even if we make her another option. What should I do to support my daughter?
Dear Hold the Beef,
When I was around your daughter’s age, I went to Hawaii with my parents. One night, we ate dinner on the beach, and we watched as a pig was dug up from an underground steam oven. I was horrified to see its face and nose; most of the meat I had eaten so far in my life didn’t resemble the animal it came from. A few years later, I became a vegetarian, and then in my 20s, a vegan.
Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column?
Fill out this anonymous form! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here!
I share this story to reveal my slight bias in answering your question, but also my understanding of the ethical awakening your daughter might be experiencing. As you figure out how to talk to your child about what she decides to eat, we can at least table discussing the pros and cons of veganism itself. Instead, you should think about what amount of autonomy your child should have, and whether the moral decision-making she wants to engage in matches with her current stage of development.
People don’t turn 18 and then suddenly start engaging morally with the world. As we grow up, we try to understand right and wrong in fits and spurts. Lawrence Kohlberg, a 20th-century American psychologist, is best known for attempting to track a person’s moral development throughout their life.
Kohlberg presented people with hypothetical dilemmas in order to come up with six moral stages. In one example, he asked people of different ages about a dying woman who could be cured by a drug that was cheap to make, but that a manufacturer was charging an exorbitant fee for. The woman’s husband ends up stealing the drug. Is that right or wrong?
Kohlberg observed that in answering questions like this, young children have what he called a “preconventional morality”: Their notions of right and wrong are dictated by what their parents think, and the avoidance of punishment when breaking those rules. For instance, the main reason not to throw your dinner on the ground or hit your brother was to avoid consequences from parents, not a feeling that there’s something wrong about that action.
Kohlberg thought this stage lasted until around age 9, and in the next period, children began to understand that there isn’t just one correct action, but that people could have different moral ideas based on their social context. To sum up the rest of the stages quickly, each one progresses to encompass more views — like the moral agreements necessary to make a society function — and more complexity — like the realization that a seemingly immoral action can ultimately be moral, like stealing medicine for one’s wife.
It’s useful to pinpoint where your daughter finds herself on Kohlberg’s timeline. It sounds like she’s in the shift from the first stage and into the later ones. What you’ve decided — that it’s okay to eat meat if it’s free-range or grass-fed — is no longer sufficient for your daughter in terms of guiding her own actions. That can be a jarring moment for a parent, but at least, according to Kohlberg, it’s a sign of maturation. Your child should, at this age, start to consider her friends, as well as the experiences she’s had without you, when making an ethical choice.
But I’m her parent, you may protest. That doesn’t necessarily mean that your job is to exclusively provide black-and-white directives.
Alison Gopnik, a psychologist and philosopher at the University of California Berkeley, has written about the unique perspective and personhood of children (including babies). In her book The Gardener and the Carpenter, she questions how people have come to define the act of parenting as having specific goals in mind for their children. This approach is like being a carpenter, she writes, who follows instructions to assemble a predetermined piece of furniture. She argues that parenting is more like gardening: You cultivate the soil and the environment and realize that you could produce any number of different flowers, fruits, or vegetables. Growth is the point, not a by-the-book final product.
I see Gopnik in alignment with Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the 18th-century philosopher whose novel Émile, or On Education surprised its readers by advocating for a freer and child-centered approach to teaching. Émile, a young wealthy boy, is tutored — in high contrast to the expectations of the day — without strict rules. Rousseau thought you couldn’t make a child turn into an adult any faster, and it was foolish to try. He also thought that children had to learn by having their own experiences out in the world, and learning from those, rather than just overly didactic lessons.
As your daughter dips her toe into the morality of eating meat, Rousseau would also remind you not to expect her to have the most mature ideas about veganism or her meal plan. She is still young, and may just have come across an idea that feels ethically important to her. Your role as her parent is to help her develop her nuanced morality, a process Kohlberg suggests will continue, and not steer her towards one way of eating over another. Be Gopnik’s dietary gardener, not carpenter.
Of course, parents do have rights over their children, and an obligation to keep them safe. When we’re young, we’re not always equipped to make the right choice (some would argue this continues into adulthood, too). If your daughter decided to take up smoking cigarettes, for instance, you would step in because her choice would negatively affect her health. As her parent, you should still guide her to build healthy habits.
You say you’re worried about your daughter becoming too picky, or not being exposed to enough foods if she becomes a vegan. But rather than push back on the choice itself, you can explain what else her choice entails. You can do so in an age-appropriate way. Talk about the nutrients that she might be missing out on if she stops eating meat, dairy, and eggs, and find books or videos about what foods might be a good substitute.
For me, becoming vegan actually exposed me to all kinds of foods that I might not have eaten otherwise: from Asian and Indian cuisines that are very veggie-friendly to many other protein- and iron-rich plant-based foods. You could collaborate with your daughter to cook vegan meals for the whole family; no challenge sparks a budding home cook more than making delectable tofu.
I should add that I’m no longer a vegan. I learned a lot from committing to a diet that wasn’t always convenient or tasty, in support of my values. Then, after more than a decade, I incorporated eggs and fish back into my diet. It’s likely that your daughter will continue to change the choices she makes as she tries to align her actions with her maturing moral views about the world.
Whether or not she eats grass-fed beef with you in her teens, you should be glad that she seems to care about what impact she’s having in the world. It means you’re raising a person whose ethics are developing strongly, even as what’s on your dinner plate may change while she figures it all out.
Bonus: What I’m reading
- Speaking of tofu, I revisited an essay that George Stiffman (a self-proclaimed “tofu guy”) wrote for Asterisk Magazine about how soybean curds are prepared in China. Warning: This article will make you hungry! He dives into all the creative culinary preparations of tofu that are tragically absent in the West.
- Several years ago, I bought a plant-based cooking book especially for children, The Vegan Cookbook for Kids: Easy Plant-Based Recipes for Young Chefs. It was a present for a non-vegan family, but the kid in question was interested in learning how to cook, and when kids cook vegan, parents don’t have to worry about them handling raw meat! Looking over these snacks and meals again, I see several tasty things that I wouldn’t mind making for myself, even as a non-vegan, and non-child.
- When I was a vegan in New York City in the 2010s, I wasn’t constrained to sad tofu and sprout sandwiches. It seemed like every week a brand-new vegan restaurant opened up, covering every cuisine, and with star chefs at the helm. But lately, all my favorite vegan restaurants have been closing. Turns out I’m not imagining it, as Vox’s Marina Bolotnikova wrote in her article: “Where did all the vegan restaurants go?” She investigates why these establishments have become rarer, and what we’ll miss out on if they completely disappear.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says it’s evaluating allegations that Tesla’s 1,000 or so robotaxis using its automated driving system are exceeding “posted speed limits in active school zones.” Waymo’s robotaxis have also faced similar inquiries, including for illegally passing school buses and hitting a child near a California elementary school.
The feds are looking into reports of Tesla’s robotaxis speeding through school zones
NHTSA has received a petition requesting an investigation into Model Y and Cybercab vehicles exceeding active school zone speed limits.
NHTSA:
The Office of Defects Investigation (ODI) received a DP on September 23, 2026, requesting an investigation into model year (MY) 2026 Tesla Robotaxis (Model Y and Cybercab) with the Automated Driving System (ADS) engaged. The Petitioner alleges that the ADS exceeds posted speed limits in active school zones.
The Cybercab launched earlier this year, and is already under investigation for its lack of side mirrors, pedals, and a steering wheel. NHTSA has also opened an investigation into Tesla’s Full Self-Driving system for traffic violations, like blowing past red lights and driving on the wrong side of the street.

Formula 1’s lengthy 2026 season is entering its final stretch. The sport took to the floodlit streets of Singapore on Sunday night, but Saturday saw action, too; this Grand Prix weekend was also the final of six sprints this year. The night race might be one of modern F1’s greatest spectacles. From overhead shots, the track becomes a bright, illuminated ribbon among the looming darkness of the city-state’s overpasses and skyscrapers. At ground level, the cars shower glittering sparks from their titanium skid blocks as the drivers flirt with how close they can get to the walls. As tracks go, the 90-degree turns and concrete barrier-lined streets were a world away from the abrasive tarmac and ample runoff of Malaysia last time out. But the tropical heat and humidity were a constant given both locations’ proximity to the equator.
Showers for the sprint
In Malaysia (which was still technically the Bahrain GP), a pre-race downpour disrupted things mightily. On Saturday morning in Singapore, shortly before the start of the sprint, it seemed history was about to rhyme when the skies opened. With standing water in places on the track, the sprint was delayed by 30 minutes. The sprint format, where a short extra race replaces a practice session a day before the main event, is unloved by the drivers and teams. For one thing there’s little prestige in winning Saturday’s sprint. And with qualifying just a few hours later, risk-taking is discouraged lest one wreck the car and ruin Sunday’s race a day early.
Oh no, not again!
Credit:
Mark Thompson/Getty Images
Oh no, not again!
Credit:
Mark Thompson/Getty Images
And in Singapore, like most street circuits, the proximity of the unyielding barriers that line the track mean there are real, punishing consequences for getting it even a little wrong.
Which is what happened to George Russell. The Mercedes driver went into this season as the title favorite, only to see those hopes evaporated by a combination of car unreliability and a young teammate, Kimi Antonelli, who really does appear to be a generational talent. A win in Azerbaijan in September was a chance for Russell to get back on terms with Antonelli, but he failed to finish in Malaysia, and his sprint didn’t last much longer.
It started well. The track was still far too wet for slick tires, so the entire field lined up on intermediate treaded tires. Russell’s Mercedes made a much better start from second on the grid than polesitter Max Verstappen’s Red Bull, and he stole the lead. A lap later, Russell’s sprint was over, and his car bent and broken after he misjudged the final corner. On a wet race track, any painted sections become very slippery, something that goes double for street circuits. “I went a little bit wide, and then I touched the white line. The No. 1 rule in the rain is don’t touch the white line. It’s a very silly mistake–overly confident. I think it’s my first crash of the year. It’s annoying to happen from that position,” Russell said after the fact.
This is where Saturday’s sprint went awry for George Russell.
Credit:
Lillian SUWANRUMPHA / AFP
This is where Saturday’s sprint went awry for George Russell.
Credit:
Lillian SUWANRUMPHA / AFP
Cross that one off the list finally
Verstappen benefited from Russell’s mistake, inheriting the lead. For a while, Lewis Hamilton’s Ferrari appeared to be a threat. But intermediate tires will begin to overheat as the track dries, something that affected Hamilton and the other Ferrari of Charles Leclerc before long. At the end of 20 laps, he crossed the finish line first. Surprisingly, this was Verstappen’s first victory in Singapore. Although, as mentioned, he didn’t exactly see it as such.
“I want to win tomorrow,” Verstappen said after the race. “I don’t see this as a win in terms of actually winning a Grand Prix, you know. So we need to have a good qualifying. It will be very close with a lot of cars, I think, and we just need to try and make sure, of course, we are the best one out of them. But it will be, yeah, hopefully a good battle.”
His Red Bull was recently updated, and in combination with a power unit that has the strongest V6 in the field (if perhaps not the best hybrid system) it may well be the fastest car on the grid, at least in Verstappen’s capable hands. A few hours later, he secured pole position in qualifying for Sunday’s race. Like the sprint finishing order, he would have the two Ferraris behind him, albeit with Leclerc ahead of Hamilton.
The number of tracks that Verstappen has never won at was already small.
Credit:
David Davies/PA Images via Getty Images
The number of tracks that Verstappen has never won at was already small.
Credit:
David Davies/PA Images via Getty Images
It was a lights-to-flag victory for Verstappen, even with the added complication of radio troubles—he could hear his engineer, but his replies were unintelligible. Such was his pace and tire management that he was able to stop for tires and leave the pits without giving up the lead. “The car was really good on the tires. I could really manage them well. But to be honest, I think it was one of the first times that I’ve driven in clean air here in Singapore in the race, so I guess that’s also nice. And yeah, it’s been just a fantastic weekend for us,” Verstappen said.
The last three races have seen two wins and a second for Verstappen. “I really think, of course, that our car has taken a really nice step forward. But at the end of the day, yeah, it’s just been more driveable and more predictable. That’s what I wanted and needed from the car to find that last step to fight up front,” he said.
A newly resurgent Verstappen, currently in fourth place, could be a threat for second place in the standings by season’s end. Not that he really cares. “I hope that we can carry that momentum forward. We don’t really have anything to win in the championship, right? I think Kimi is miles ahead. For me personally, I don’t care if I’m second, third, or fourth. Like, yeah, it doesn’t do anything. But I just want to have fun till the end, you know, try to go for a day’s success,” he said.
Once again, the Red Bull driven by Max Verstappen might be faster than any other car/driver combination on the grid.
Credit:
Mark Sutton – Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images
Once again, the Red Bull driven by Max Verstappen might be faster than any other car/driver combination on the grid.
Credit:
Mark Sutton – Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images
With both sprint and race poles, and sprint and race victories, it was almost a perfect weekend for Verstappen, who only missed out on fastest lap to Leclerc, who came home second. It should have been a double podium for Ferrari. Hamilton did not have as much speed as Leclerc and started the race on an alternate strategy, using the medium tires instead of the softs.
These didn’t last long though, and Hamilton stopped on lap 17, switching to the softs. With most of the 62-lap race left to run, that set up the potential for a very long afternoon. And when Lance Stroll’s Aston Martin broke down as usual and caused a virtual safety car period, inexplicably Hamilton overrode the team’s instructions to follow Leclerc into the pits to solve the problem by making a cheap stop. Staying out on increasingly ruined tires left the seven-time champion a sitting duck to cars behind, and he turned third into sixth, apologizing to his team on the radio afterward.
More teammate fights
As we have discussed more than once this season, perhaps the cardinal rule as an F1 driver is “don’t hit your teammate.” That we’ve seen teammates battling a lot isn’t entirely unsurprising—if the cars are stratified by pace, and a team has two drivers of about the same caliber, then if they both perform well, they should qualify in similar positions and therefore find themselves racing together. Haas’ Oliver Bearman showed the right way to do that, going side by side with his teammate Esteban Ocon for several corners on lap 3, a battle that was sadly relegated to a small Picture in Picture window on the broadcast. (A couple of laps later, Bearman followed it with a late move on Carlos Sainz’ Williams, too.)
Ocon and Bearman’s battle was breathtaking to watch.
Credit:
Mark Thompson/Getty Images
Ocon and Bearman’s battle was breathtaking to watch.
Credit:
Mark Thompson/Getty Images
Sometimes, we see situations like Ferrari has faced in recent races, including this one, splitting strategies between two cars but with the car on newer, faster tires stuck behind the car on older, slower rubber. Sometimes the driver in front does what’s best for the team and lets them by without a fight—Hamilton did just this late in the race when a much faster Leclerc on much newer tires needed to get by.
What no fan—or team boss—wants to see are both their cars trying to take the same piece of tarmac. Which is exactly what happened with McLaren’s pair during Saturday’s sprint. The orange cars were in fourth (Piastri) and fifth (Norris) on the last lap of the race when Norris decided to try to invert that order. The pair made contact, Piastri’s car broke, and Norris finished eighth. Nine points for the team turned into one point, and Norris had given the team extra work to do to repair the other car in time for qualifying.
McLaren’s team principal, Andrea Stella, called the incident “unacceptable” and presumably read the riot act to his driver. Norris was suitably chastened the following day, both offering to help Piastri in the race if he could, and telling journalists after the race that “I can’t attempt what I did. I should never have attempted it in the first place, even if the move was on. I’ve simply got to think more of the team that I represent rather than myself. It was a mistake on my part, and I let down the team,” Norris said.
More cars pointing the wrong way.
Credit:
Then Chih Wey/Xinhua via Getty Images
More cars pointing the wrong way.
Credit:
Then Chih Wey/Xinhua via Getty Images
A title in Texas
With this Asian leg complete, the F1 circus now relocates to the Americas, starting with the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas. There’s a chance Antonelli could clinch the title if he leaves Texas 125 points ahead of his closest rival. Currently, that’s George Russell, who trails by 102 points, with Hamilton in third at 111 behind, and Verstappen 119 points behind Antonelli in fourth.
A win is worth 25 points, so it’s possible, but it would require yet more bad luck from Russell; by my admittedly terrible arithmetic, if Russell finishes ninth and only scores two points to an Antonelli win, his title hopes are over. But if he finishes eighth and scores four points, or does better, his hopes stay alive at least until the following round in Mexico.
Similar elimination calculations exist to rule out Hamilton and Verstappen, with higher finishing positions required to stay in it due to their greater points deficits to the leader. Given Verstappen’s form recently, and Mercedes’ inability to make its own upgrade work quite so well, there’s every prospect of a third consecutive Red Bull win in a couple of weeks. And Lewis Hamilton has finished on the podium at COTA nine times now, so he knows how to find a result there, even if a Ferrari victory seems unlikely.
Ars will be on the ground in Austin, where I’m hoping to learn more about how the teams program these fiendishly complicated power units and see who’s prepared to talk about those carbon-neutral synthetic fuels the sport was so keen to tell me about just a few short years ago.
Jonathan is the Automotive Editor at Ars Technica. He has a BSc and PhD in Pharmacology. In 2014 he decided to indulge his lifelong passion for the car by leaving the National Human Genome Research Institute and launching Ars Technica's automotive coverage. He lives in Washington, DC.

Indian drama “Kidney,” the second feature from filmmaking siblings Aakarsh and Agrim Sansanwal, has been boarded by Shiladitya Bora’s Platoon One Films, which joins as co-producer ahead of the film’s slot in the Critics’ Picks Competition at Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF).
The film is produced by Enfant Terrible Productions, the Mumbai outfit the brothers set up. Set in an isolated Indian village, it follows a young man and woman from feuding families who fall in love. When a quarrel over an inheritance revives old hostilities, their relationship comes under pressure from greed and treachery in a conflict not of their making.
“We made the film with very little money and a seemingly inexhaustible supply of spirit,” said Aakarsh Sansanwal. “When the budget ran out, the entire village, its farming community, stood behind us. They helped us through the hurdles and, in their own way, became part of the film’s journey. This film carries the hands and hearts of the people who helped bring it into the world.”
Popular on Variety
“Kidney” adds to a Platoon One slate that counts “Bayaan,” “Toh Ti Ani Fuji,” “Bhagwan Bharose,” “Minimum,” “Ghaath,” “Picasso” and “Yours Truly” among its titles.
The director said Platoon One was among the first to spot that spirit in the film and back what the brothers were attempting. “Their support gave the film a chance to travel beyond the world in which it was made and reach audiences we could only have hoped for. To see it now receive recognition and find its way into the light is deeply moving. My thanks to the Tallinn Black Nights team for discovering our film and giving it a place to shine.”
Tallinn’s Critics’ Picks strand spotlights films with a clear artistic point of view and a fresh take on storytelling, including work that wrestles with genre, cinema’s past and the social issues of the moment. Earlier selections include Arati Kadav’s “Mrs.,” starring Sanya Malhotra, as well as “The Brothers Kitaura,” “About Us But Not About Us” and “The Bone Breakers.”
Bora, who founded Platoon One, said that when he first watched “Kidney” he knew he was “looking at something different, something that hadn’t been attempted in quite this way.” He also pointed to the Sansanwals’ “strong and distinct voice.”
“It would be easy to dismiss a film like ‘Kidney’ as esoteric, but what struck me was the depth of emotion underneath its craft and form,” Bora said. “There is a dense, deeply felt emotional layer running through the film, and the film’s unique style becomes a way of expressing that emotion rather than an end in itself. That is exactly the kind of cinema Platoon One wants to stand behind: original, distinctive and deeply rooted voices. I couldn’t let go of this film after I saw it.”
The brothers divide their time between Mumbai and Delhi. Aakarsh has worked as an assistant director to Reema Kagti, Abhinay Deo and Pushpendra Misra, while Agrim trained as a filmmaker with a focus on editing and assisted editor Deepa Bhatia on “Skater Girl.”
The pair co-wrote and co-directed their first feature, the experimental “To Caterpillar, From Butterfly,” which debuted at the Dharamshala International Film Festival.

'I reduced my running because of urine leaks' – Commonwealth finalist Korir
- Published
Naomi Korir's career on the track reached a high point in August when she finished fifth in the final of the mile at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
But things could have been very different for the Kenyan middle-distance runner.
The 28-year-old was born with fistula, a medical condition in which abnormal openings develop between organs and can lead to uncontrolled leakage of urine or faeces.
While Korir loved athletics as a child, it initially forced her to rethink any plans to be a runner.
"I played most of the sports activities: football, netball, athletics, even rugby," she said.
"But it was difficult because [of] the training, and the urine is flowing continuously. It's bad.
"I reduced my running to shorter distances to reduce the leaking.
"I began doing 100m hurdles."
Despite the challenges, Korir's love of sport also offered a form of escape and belonging.
"I could do it because I loved it," she explained.
"Because most of the people could avoid me, I did a lot of activities just to pass time and not to feel that I'm excluded."
Three surgeries and a second chance
The charity Doctors Without Borders estimates that 500,000 women live with fistula globally.
Some develop a fistula after childbirth while for others, like Korir, it is congenital.
Access to good obstetrics, or to simple surgery, means that the condition has all but disappeared in some countries, but it remains a problem in sub-Saharan Africa, where high quality medical care can be hard to access.
Korir was born with genitourinary tract fistula - an opening between bladder and vagina which caused her urine leakage.
Surgery was required, but her first two operations failed to solve the problem.
In August 2013, a third operation finally brought relief for the then 13-year-old.
The procedure was carried out in her home town Eldoret by the Gynocare Hospital, which specialises in fistula, obstetrics and reproductive health.
"It's a difficult condition to live with every day," Gynocare director Caroline Mabeya told BBC Sport Africa when discussing the stigma and isolation women with the condition suffer.
"They are ostracised in the society. That's the psychological torture that they face with the fistula."
The hospital has treated patients from across East Africa since opening its doors in 2011. Its work extends beyond surgery, with a post-operation programme designed to help women rebuild their confidence.
"We offer free treatment for these women at Gynocare because most of them are very poor," Mabeya explained.
"When they come into the facility, they are crushed, they have low esteem. So, there's a huge amount of effort that is put in to make them at least be strong enough to be reintegrated and get back into the community."
'A champion in sport'
For Korir, successful surgery offered a second chance, both on the track and in the classroom.
As well as allowing her to run properly again, she continued her education through Gynocare's Beyond Fistula programme.
"I have a family in GynoCare, a fistula home," she said.
"That is where I schooled after my surgery until I finished my secondary level."
In 2019, Korir began competing professionally and two years later was part of the Kenyan duo which claimed a silver medal in the 2x2x400m mixed relay alongside her partner Ferguson Rotich at the World Relays in Poland.
A year later she went one better, bagging gold as part of Kenya's 4x400m relay team at the African Championships in Mauritius.
The mile at this year's Commonwealth Games was her first appearance in major global final.
"I'm giving hope to young women maybe who have lost hope," she said of her achievements.
"They need to come back again in living and enjoying life."
Mabeya says Korir's transformation makes her a powerful example to the women currently receiving support at Gynocare.
"She makes them realise that you can actually pull yourself out of these struggles and still make it in life and succeed.
"Naomi actually is one of those patients that inspires us to continue working very hard, because we struggle with this condition and these women. The work is not easy."
As a young girl, Korir sang in church and played the keyboard, convinced that music was a more likely career than athletics.
"But now I'm in different career and I'm so happy," she beamed.
And with the World Championships in Beijing next year and the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, Korir believes there is another chapter to write.
"I know I'm a champion in life, because conquering fistula alone is being a champion.
"Now I'm looking forward to be a champion in sport."

Is AppleCare actually worth it for the Apple Watch SE?
The affordable coverage is worth a look, but it isn’t for everyone.
AppleCare+ is relatively inexpensive for the Apple Watch SE 3: $2.99 a month or $29.99 a year for the Theft and Loss plan. That's much less than the average streaming subscription. The plan includes unlimited accidental damage incidents, along with battery service and up to two theft or loss claims per year.
But AppleCare+ is not a complete coverage option because there are stipulations and additional costs. Whether it's worth the cost depends on your typical day-to-day. There's a big difference between wearing an Apple Watch while working from home and welding for a living. Service for accidental damage to the SE 3 will still cost you $69 per incident, and a theft or loss replacement comes with a $119 deductible. There's no additional charge for battery service, but that's only if your battery retains less than 80 percent of its original capacity.
For additional context, an Apple Watch comes with a one-year warranty that covers manufacturer defects, so AppleCare+ is an addition to that standard warranty. For theft or loss, AppleCare+ will only cover you if Find My is enabled when the watch is stolen or lost, and it has to remain enabled throughout the entire claims process.
When AppleCare makes sense, and when to skip it
If you're in a trade, work in construction, play sports or regularly wear your watch in other situations that could cause substantial damage to it, it's much easier to justify coverage. If you're an adrenaline minimalist and the most dangerous part of your day is a run to the convenience store, not so much. Just remember that coverage is protection against a potential expense and far from a guarantee that you'll save money over the long term.
If you can comfortably replace the watch and prefer to set aside the cash, AppleCare+ is not essential. At Apple's current annual rate, three years of premiums come just under $90. If you add a single accidental damage claim, you're at $159. With one theft or loss claim, you've spent $209. Either way, it's a significant portion of the Apple Watch SE's $249 starting cost. And depending on how far into the device's life the damage happens, you might prefer to put the cash toward the next generation instead of repairing an older unit.
Getting a new battery is another reason for potential coverage, but only if you plan on owning and using the same Apple Watch for years. It's basically pointless if you upgrade annually or every two years, as the battery isn't likely to degrade that quickly. If the device is sitting above 80 percent health when you decide to replace the watch's battery, it's not covered.
It's also worth having non-AppleCare repair prices in mind. For the GPS model of the Apple Watch SE 3, you'll pay $99 for battery service and $199 for other damage (there's no theft option without coverage). If you have the cellular model, the damage repair jumps to $229. Your tolerance for these prices affects AppleCare's value.
AppleCare payment plan options
AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss for a single Apple Watch SE 3 is the lowest-cost option among Apple's current Apple Watch models, at $2.99 a month or $29.99 a year. Coverage renews until canceled, and annual billing costs a little less than the $35.88 total you'll pay if you opt for monthly. At three years, the difference amounts to $107.64 total for monthly payments versus $89.97 for annual payments.
AppleCare One is a potential alternative for those with several Apple devices because it lumps them all into a single payment plan, starting at $19.99 monthly for an individual with up to three devices. Add $5.99 per month for each additional device. If you already have three Apple devices, adding an SE 3 will cost more than its standalone $2.99 per month. This only makes sense if you're already paying for AppleCare One and don't have a higher-cost device to protect.
Finally, AppleCare One Family is the newest option. It costs $49.99 for up to six family members and covers all their eligible devices. New Apple products are automatically added to the plan when purchased.
For the base plan, you'll need to enroll in AppleCare+ within 60 days of buying your watch. With the other two plans, you can usually add any devices that are less than four years old to an active plan, though they'll likely require a check to make sure they're in good condition.

More AI agents will soon be able to browse and purchase from Shopify listings, marking an expansion of the company’s agentic commerce ambitions.
Shopify opens its catalog up to more AI agents
Shopify previously announced a partnership with Meta’s Muse for AI-powered shopping and checkout.
Shopify announced Tuesday it will let shoppers configure their AI agents to purchase products on their behalf, giving more agents access to over a billion listings in Shopify’s catalog. (The catalog consists of both items on and off Shopify storefronts.) In September, Shopify announced it was partnering with Meta to allow its Muse agent to browse and purchase items on a human’s behalf; now, shoppers can use any agent without a partnership integration.
To set up the feature, customers connect an agent with their account on Shop, a Shopify-owned platform that consolidates orders, tracks packages, and recommends products. Like the Muse partnership, customers use the one-click Shop Pay feature to check out within the conversation with the agent. Orders placed through the agent are funneled back to the Shop app. Shopify is marketing the feature as a “personal shopper” that humans can give rules to, like setting budget guardrails or only displaying products with fast shipping. Buyers must approve each purchase.
E-commerce has become one of the battlegrounds in the era of AI — it’s no coincidence that many demos of agentic tools end with a transaction, whether it’s buying clothing, booking a flight, or ordering takeout on a human’s behalf. The tech industry, including big commerce players like Google and Amazon, are investing in AI-driven shopping tools where the end goal is an “agent” purchasing things for a human user. It’s also the basis of an ongoing fight between Amazon and AI companies like Perplexity — and more recently, Meta’s Muse — over whether agents should be able to shop on a customer’s behalf.

Don't be scared: Being afraid is outright fun, and maybe useful
It's October and that can only mean one thing – the spooky season is in full swing.
Americans are expected to spend more than $13 billion dollars on celebrating this season, whether that's on horror films, costumes, candy or attractions, according to the National Retail Federation.
As much as $300 - $500 million of that spending comes from attending a haunt, where people willingly give up their hard-earned cash to be frightened. And tens of millions of people take part in this kind of activity every year.
But why do people like getting scared? The search for that answer starts with one of the largest haunted attractions in the country, Markoff's Haunted Forest in Dickerson, Maryland. Markoff's has more than a mile of haunted trails and dozens of themed haunted houses. It employs hundreds of engineers, retail attendants, makeup artists and actors.
Open since 1992, the attraction starts with towering skull-emblazoned wooden gates reminiscent of folk horror movies like "The Wicker Man."
Just inside, director of operations Paul Brubacher stands in between two huge bonfires.
"Some of our designers, including myself, have done some music festivals before. So yeah, that's the inspiration… from kind-of [a] Van Helsing vampire village aspect of things," Brubacher says.
There is hardly a thing that happens in this haunt without him knowing.
"This is an emergency radio that we have in each one of our scenes. In case an actor has a problem or somebody falls down and needs to be evacuated," Brubacher says. Before hitting the trail, he takes us behind the scenes to a barn where scare-actors are getting finishing touches of makeup.
Art director and makeup manager Chris Knowles and his team are using a bevy of pressurized airbrushes to quickly creep-ify all kinds of ghouls, vampires and aliens.
"It's great because you can get color on really finely or cover areas. [It] swaps colors really quickly as well, which is essential because we've only got like about seven minutes to do the makeup because we got like 100 odd people and two hours to do it," Knowles says.
Robert Doyle, 38, is in Knowles' chair at the moment.
"I love Halloween. I love going out and interacting with people, entertaining them, making them laugh. Giving them a good scare, you know, giving them a good dopamine rush," Doyle says.
Doyle has played all kinds of frightening characters in his five years at Markoff's. He's been a killer clown, a demon and tonight he's a Nosferatu-style vampire with sharp fangs, a bloody mouth and pupils as dark as coal.
Doyle thinks people keep coming back to places like Markoff's to face down their fears safely.
"People want to challenge themselves and they can say they accomplished something," Doyle says.
Another scare-actor, wearing a black top hat and looking like a cross between a straw and hair covered zombie, and hoodoo shaman is ready for his opening night.
His day-walker name is Jermaine Hoes.
"I am something that you see when you wake up at 3 o'clock in the morning," Hoes says.
Hoes has been a scare actor at different haunts around Maryland for years, and he says his reason for moonlighting as a horrific beast is pretty simple.
"I like scaring people. I like to make you run and scream and holler everywhere," Hoes says.
Leaving the actors so they can get into character, it's time to take to the trail, which begins with an ominous, steady heartbeat pumping through hidden speakers.
The trail is dark, foggy and winding. It's constructed in such a way that you can't escape the scares. Even trying to escape signals to the actors that you're ripe for a fright.
There are snakes, zombified pumpkin heads, ghosts, vampires, ghouls, aliens and even cannibals.
The trail is barely a mile, but between the terrain and its twists, it can take more than an hour to get through.
Voices cry out in pain and shriek in fear. Many seem menacing.
"You can join us," one voice in the shadows snickers.
"Don't you want your face on one of these pumpkins?," another cackles. "It just takes a little bit of a beating!"
Anything that could scare you is here, and it didn't take much in this secluded, murky environment.
The science of screams
"Fear is extremely fast," says Harvard Medical School associate professor of radiology Nouchine Hadjikhani.
For much of her career, Hadjikhani has studied what happens in the brain when someone is afraid. She uses computer screens and brain monitoring equipment to show subjects frightening images and measure their brain's reaction.
"If I show you very briefly, so for, you know, 30 milliseconds or something, snakes and spiders, I will see that your amygdala gets activated," Hadjikhani says.
She says it's this activation that makes a jump scare so effective.
"Your heart goes faster. You go a little further back and you start sweating. Your pupils get high for a stupid image on the screen," she says.
According to Hadjikhani, we get scared when something – usually visual – sets off the fear center of the brain. And she says she can elicit that same brain reaction in people just by showing them pictures of other folks who are scared. But she says it's difficult to know why some people derive pleasure from fear.
You have to talk to them.
Fear is fun
For that we need the scientists at the Recreational Fear Lab at Aarhaus University in Denmark.
Co-directors Matthias Clausen and Marc Andersen have created all kinds of studies into what keeps people coming back for frights.
Over the years, what they've found is that there is more than one type of recreational fear.
"We did an early study where we tried to see if we could identify the personality profile of the horror fan and what we found was a god-forsaken mess," Clausen says.
A rollercoaster enthusiast, for example, may detest horror films. And a scary movie scream queen might lose her lunch at a theme park.
But Clausen says survey after survey at the Fear Lab shows fear-for-fun is surprisingly universal.
"When you engage in recreational activities, you're essentially administering a fear vaccine," Clausen says. Seeking out fear is our way of preparing our bodies for the sometimes scary real world.
And this vaccine is actually fun for most people. "It doesn't hurt," Clausen says.
The duo has called this a "fear inoculation."
Co-director Marc Anderssen has also interviewed subjects who say they treat their own psychological disorders using fear.
"We have a ton of anecdotal stories about horror fans that we meet that tell us that they deal with their clinical anxiety by popping in a horror movie," Andersen says.
"The first time we heard it, we almost fell off of our chairs because it sounds so counterintuitive."
Playing with fear is also incredibly social, says Matthias Clausen. After going through a haunt for example, groups have told him they've experienced a sense of bonding.
"That's something that characterizes in fact most kinds of recreational experiences," Clausen says.
Back at Markoff's Haunted Forest, scare-actor Jermaine Hoes says his coworkers and the people he's scaring are like a family.
"The people, man. The vibes are great. You know, you meet a lot of people here. They have a ball. You get to mix and mingle with them," Hoes says.
Nothing brings people together like a good scare. Next week, find out how monsters, ghouls and slashers can also mean big bucks.

Update | October 13, 20:00 IST Adani Group’s flagship business Adani Enterprises and US-based manufacturing company Jabil Inc have signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding (MoU) to establish a 50:50 joint venture for manufacturing and assembling AI and data centre equipment in India. The proposed partnership aims to produce AI racks, servers, storage, networking equipment, and power and cooling systems to cater to India’s rapidly growing data centre capacity. It targets the expanding domestic market as well as international exports. “At Adani, our vision is to expand up the AI value chain evolving from powering and hosting AI infrastructure to engineering and manufacturing the critical systems that will define the next generation of computing. Our proposed joint venture with Jabil marks a strategic step towards this future, combining Jabil’s world-class engineering and manufacturing capabilities with Adani’s integrated strengths in energy, infrastructure and data centres to help build the physical backbone of the global AI economy,” said Adani Group chairman Gautam Adani. With this MoU, the earlier agreement between Adani and Jabil has now taken a more concrete form, although its realisation remains subject to regulatory approvals and the execution of definitive agreements. Original | June 15, 22:12 IST Indian conglomerate Adani Group has partnered with US-based manufacturing company Jabil Inc to build vertically-integrated AI and data centre infrastructure in India. The two companies intend to set up multi-gigawatt manufacturing capacity in India for high-density AI racks. They will produce AI-ready hardware such as liquid-cooled AI racks, servers, storage units, and networking systems to serve the needs of global hyperscalers and enterprise data centers. Beyond computing hardware, the platform plans to manufacture supporting infrastructure components, including power distribution units, coolant distribution units, transformers, switchgears, and advanced thermal management systems. The companies are currently finalising operational frameworks and formal documentation to execute the manufacturing roadmap, with no definitive timeline announced. The partnership with Jabil is in line with Adani Group’s bid to double down on AI. In February, Adani announced one of the world’s largest integrated energy-compute commitments with a direct investment of $100 Bn to develop renewable-energy-powered, hyperscale AI-ready data centres by 2035. Later, the Adani Group was said to be exploring partnerships with Meta, Google among others, to set up data centres in the country. To note, the conglomerate has also tied up with Uber to set up its first data centre in India, which would become operational later this year. The Adani-Jabil partnership comes at a time when the global market opportunity for AI compute infrastructure is projected to zoom past the $3 Tn mark over the next seven years. India’s data centre capacity is projected to reach 5-8 GW by 2030, driven by growing AI demand, cloud expansion, and data localisation requirements. Notably, India’s technology supply chains are increasingly shifting toward domestic manufacturing, given the focus on data sovereignty and the requirements of the DPDP Act. Along with the Adani Group, companies like Reliance Industries and Amazon are also betting on capturing this momentum. For instance, Reliance announced a partnership with Meta last week that would see the oil-to-telecom conglomerate set up a 168 MW AI-enabled data centre in Gujarat’s Jamnagar, powered by sustainable energy, within two years. Amazon has committed an investment of $12.7 Bn towards cloud infrastructure in India by 2030, while OpenAI is planning to set up a 1 GW data centre in India in partnership with TCS.

How many ways can the Trump administration clamp down on international researchers?
In the span of two days last week, the Trump administration issued two sweeping announcements meant to crack down on international students and scholars, who make up a sizable portion of the nation’s biomedical research workforce. On Wednesday, the Department of Homeland Security announced a proposed $70,000 fee for a work authorization program that many foreign students use to gain professional experience. The next day, the Labor Department revealed that it is investigating nine universities — including Harvard, Stanford, and Yale — for alleged fraud related to visas awarded to postdoctoral researchers.
This is all playing out while DHS is fighting in court to impose a four-year cap on stays in the U.S. by graduate students and postdocs. The department is also attempting to revive administration plans to impose $100,000 fees for h2-B visas, which are used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as biotech.
None of these changes have taken effect, but experts warn that the administration’s repeated attempts are already deterring students. A survey by the Association of American Universities found that, while domestic student applications for U.S. Ph.D. programs went up by 3% this year, international applications dipped 21%.
“This is an incredible series of self-owns,” said Elizabeth Goss, an immigration attorney based in Boston. “The government also knows that none of this will stand up in court. They just want to send a message: Don’t come here.” — Jonathan Wosen
What $250 million in free lunches buys you
You know the saying, “there’s no such thing as a free lunch?” Turns out, that applies to doctors too. Except in this case, the cost of the free lunch is being borne by patients and the health care system, according to a new study.
A new Cochrane review of dozens of previous studies found that gifts (including meals) and payments doctors receive from drugmakers increase inappropriate prescribing, which in turn increases health care costs. One of my favorite details from STAT’s Ed Silverman: “The research found a clear relationship between meals and inappropriate prescriptions. The more meals a doctor received from a company, the more of the company’s drug they prescribed.” Another: pharmaceutical companies spent upwards of $250 million on meals alone in 2022.
Read more about the pernicious influence of lobbying on medicine. And please — if you’ve received particularly lavish or unusual gifts from drug companies, let me know. I’d love to hear more about what this experience looks like on the ground.
DEA suggests new limits for two kratom derivatives
Proponents of natural kratom leaf products have notched another win after the DEA made changes Friday to its proposed temporary order that would place some kratom derivatives — but not natural leaf products — in Schedule I, the federal category for drugs that carry the most risk without any medical benefit.
Originally, federal agencies had planned to temporarily designate 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) above a certain potency threshold as Schedule I, in addition to three synthetic kratom derivatives at any level, including mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI). But a notice of intent issued Friday laid out new thresholds that apply to both 7-OH and MGPI individually or in combination. The new threshold focuses more on the concentration of these compounds within a product rather than the total amount.
The American Kratom Association, which lobbies for natural leaf products, celebrated the change as a resolution to its lawsuit against the original MGPI scheduling, which it argues could have inadvertently criminalized natural leaf products found to contain trace amounts of the compound. But some drug policy advocates and lawmakers want more limits around all kratom products, including natural ones.
It’s unclear when exactly the scheduling will be finalized. Experts agree that some sort of regulation needs to be enacted around kratom-related products, but they aren’t all sure that scheduling is the best approach long-term. Meanwhile, it’s worth remembering that a government watchdog report recently concluded that both DEA and HHS lack adequate policies and procedures on drug scheduling. — Theresa Gaffney
How Americans feel about science, as told in charts
It can sometimes seem like Americans’ relationship to science is uniquely fraught, weighed down by the Trump administration’s deep cuts to research funds, the ever-present battle over vaccines, and our byzantine health care system.
Given all that, new data from the Wellcome Global Monitor surprised me. Those pollsters found that 52 percent of Americans report having “a lot” of trust in science. Across the globe, that number is 26 percent. Americans, in aggregate, are also more eager to get vaccines compared to peer nations; 45 percent of Americans say they would want to get vaccines recommended by a nurse or doctor “right away.” In Germany only 28 percent say the same.
To unpack what these numbers might mean, check out Nick Florko’s story.
Doctors are trained to be deferential. That follows them their whole careers
By the time doctors reach their residency programs, they have completed college and medical school, passing several rigorous exams. Many will be nearing 30, or older. And yet residents often have to ask permission to even use the restroom.
This infantilizing treatment is creating “something plaguing medicine: learned helplessness, a psychological state wherein a person stops trying to change an unfavorable or unsavory situation because they believe that they have no control over the outcome,” writes Frances Mei Hardin, a former ear, nose, and throat surgeon, in the debut of her new column Chief Complaint.
Hardin writes that today’s doctors inherit a sense of powerlessness that’s reinforced by “increasing layers of bureaucracy, hierarchy, metrics, and threats of retaliation or lawsuits that leave physicians with less and less control. And we don’t question it.” Read more about the problems that’s creating — and the possible solutions — here.

Late last month, the state of Tennessee attempted to execute Christa Pike, a woman who has been on death row for decades after killing a classmate as a teenager.
Florida’s uniquely horrifying death penalty system
Can the death penalty ever be fair?
The execution failed: Pike survived two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital, making her the first person ever to do so.
The botched execution comes at a strange moment for capital punishment in America. Support for the death penalty has been declining for decades. And for a long time, the number of executions was falling, too. But since 2021, executions have been increasing again. The recent surge has been driven largely by one state: Florida.
According to Pamela Colloff, who covers the criminal justice system for ProPublica and wrote about Florida’s use of the death penalty for New York Times Magazine this summer, 40 percent of the executions conducted in the US last year were in Florida.
“There are so many things that make the administration of the death penalty interesting and unique in Florida,” Colloff explained on a recent episode of Vox’s The Gray Area podcast. “Among active death penalty states right now, Florida is unique in that one person determines, from the hundreds of men on death row, who will receive an execution date, and what that execution date is.”
I spoke with Colloff earlier this month following Pike’s failed execution about what happened in Tennessee, what’s driving Florida’s recent zeal for executions, and why victims’ families are often unsatisfied by the death penalty process.
Below is an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to The Gray Area wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify. (This interview also appeared more recently on Vox’s Today, Explained podcast.)
We’re taping shortly after news came out that a woman in Tennessee who was on death row, authorities attempted to put her to death. They gave her two doses of lethal injection medication, and she survived.
How much of the decline in the use of the death penalty has to do with, in your estimation, people feeling like there’s no way to do it that’s humane?
This is the second botched execution in Tennessee this year, just to give you a sense of things. This is more common there than in other states. They’ve changed their drug protocols and we don’t know a lot about what went wrong with Christa Pike. In May, it was an issue with accessing veins, which can be an issue with lethal injection.
I think it’s also important for people to remember that we had the electric chair as the method of execution through the ’80s and into the ’90s in some places. While [lethal injection] is considered a far more humane, quote-unquote, way to do this, we can see that nothing is perfect.
I will say that while the issues of botched executions are very important, and I think there are some other ones coming up to be concerned about, I am more interested in how it is that other errors are made, that other people end up with the ultimate punishment when that perhaps was not the right punishment for what occurred.
You’ve also written that death penalty convictions are just expensive, right? And on top of that, DNA evidence has made it clear that many of the people who were being convicted were not guilty, or there wasn’t strong enough evidence to convict them. How do you think about that mix of factors?
Florida, which I’ve spent a lot of time writing about, is the leading place in America by a mile in terms of the number of executions, and has a very large death row. Florida’s also the leader in wrongful death row convictions. Just to give you a sense of things, Florida holds the distinction of 30 death row exonerations.
What that means is in the modern era — the past roughly 50 years — there have been 30 men who were given dates of execution who now walk free. And for anyone who pays any attention to how the criminal justice system works and how incredibly difficult it is to overturn a wrongful conviction, if we have 30 people in Florida who have that distinction, we know that there are many more.
What’s going on in Florida? When did you realize that something was different there?
It really ramped up last year. Last year, Florida executed 40 percent of the people who were executed in the US in the last calendar year. In this year, there have been 16 men who’ve been executed in Florida so far.
Just to give you a comparison, Texas is the next state with the highest number of executions, and they’ve executed six men in that time. We already have outlier states, primarily southern states, and then we have Florida being the ultimate outlier.
There are so many things that make the administration of the death penalty interesting and unique in Florida. The thing that fascinated me the most is, among active death penalty states right now, Florida is unique in that one person determines, from the hundreds of men on death row, who will receive an execution date, and what that execution date is.
Who is it?
Gov. Ron DeSantis. I went back and looked at what were the patterns here, what were the things guiding Gov. DeSantis’s thinking in setting these dates, and was fascinated to see and very troubled to see that there are a number of men who’ve been there so long.
They’ve been there since the 1970s. These are men who were convicted when Gerald Ford was president, just to make this real to people. But the dates are not being set among the men who are what are called death-eligible, meaning that they’ve gone through all their appeals. They aren’t being done chronologically.
There’s no rhyme or reason to the process. And so there’s this speculation game among victims’ families, prisoners, their advocates about who will be next. And men can sit there on death row for decades with that hanging over them, and that is a Florida phenomenon.
You wrote about Florida’s death row turning from something like a purgatory where people stay for a long time into something closer to an assembly line, right?
I was so struck by the fact that in Florida, in order to have this pace of executions, there were people who were receiving their dates 30 days, sometimes fewer, from their execution dates.
Just to give people a sense of why that is unusual, there are so many things that kick into gear when a death warrant is written. There are numerous legal maneuvers and next steps that happen in the courts. To give you a quick example, there was one defendant in Florida this spring who, five days before he was scheduled to be executed, was finally granted the ability to test DNA evidence in his case that had gone untested.
He had great lawyers who didn’t sleep to make that happen, but that it came as close as five days to his execution date. I think that should give us all pause about how fast this is moving.
You have multiple people in the queue at the same time. There’s a place — a different unit than Florida’s death row — that you’re taken to once you get your date, called death watch.
Tell me about death watch. What does it look like and what does it feel like?
Death watch is roughly 30 feet from the execution chamber. There are three cells. When you receive your date, you are taken from death row to death watch where you’re put — I don’t want to say solitary because if there are one or two other men who are held there — but you’re in a far different situation than you would be on death row where there are guards and other people you know.
From that point forward, there are roughly 30 days where you are held within steps of where this will take place. To me, it was chilling that when I was doing my reporting in the spring on the story that I published this summer, all three cells were filled, and as soon as one person was executed, the pattern was that often the next day a new death warrant would be signed, and there would be a new person in place.
Why do they do that? Why do they put these people next to the place where they’ll die?
That’s one of the many questions I had about that. We talk about not wanting to have cruel and unusual punishment. Our Constitution does not uphold that. But it’s such a unique kind of mental torture, I think, to be 30 feet from where you’ll be put to death.
The other thing I was struck by was the waiting aspect. If you’re on death row, again, you always have this hanging over you. I talked about the way in which, when you’re in that kind of sensory deprivation, you become highly attuned to sounds and smells and things like that.
I interviewed someone who’s not on death row anymore, whose sentence was commuted, who talked to me about recognizing that jangle of keys and the steps that this group of people who come to deliver the death warrant take, and knowing that someone is about to be served with a death warrant, but not knowing, “Is it me? Is it the guy next to me? Is it someone down the hall?”
I just want to say, I understand that there’s a counterargument to all of this, which is that these are people who most often committed terrible crimes. Their victims did not know when they were going to be killed.
I do think, however, as a state that administers this thing, there has to be a rhyme or reason to this. Otherwise, you have total chaos, including for victims’ families, who never know. Are they going to wait one month? Are they going to wait 15 years? They don’t know.

Google revealed Gemini 4 Argon a few weeks ago, saying that it needed to move cautiously toward a full release because of the potential for nefarious use. Google seems to have worked all that out pretty quickly, though. Argon is beginning its wide rollout today, but it’s only coming to paying users at this time, and even those on lower-tier plans won’t have full access.
Nothing about Gemini 4 Argon’s capabilities has changed. Google still points to the benchmarks it published late last month as evidence of the model’s advanced reasoning and agentic coding capabilities. The model is supposedly trained to refuse malicious instructions, and an automated misalignment monitor can stop processing if it detects an unintended workflow. Google claims Argon needs that because it’s so capable.
The company has a few new examples of how Argon has helped inside Google, where it has been used by thousands of Googlers. Argon has reportedly been instrumental in making YouTube’s comment system more efficient. Argon identified redundant emoji rendering that, when eliminated, dropped server load by 45 percent. Engineers also turned Gemini 4 loose on the proprietary drone physics simulator used in Project Wing, and the AI found critical bugs that had been in the codebase since 2018. Google also notes that Argon has advanced its robotics program, showing a measurable step increase in embodied reasoning.

China’s trade surplus hits $938 billion for Jan-Sep as pressure ramps up to rebalance trade
China’s customs agency says the country's exports surged 36.3% in September from a year earlier
HONG KONG -- China’s exports surged 36.3% in September from a year earlier, its customs agency said Wednesday, bringing it on track to exceed last year's record trade surplus as pressure ramped up from its trading partners, including the European Union, to rebalance trade.
The exports data, which was better than what economists had expected, accelerated from the 25% growth in August. High-tech goods such as semiconductors and autos have helped fuel its rising shipments overseas.
Imports climbed 31% in September year-on-year, also accelerating from August’s 28.2% rise.
That resulted in a $133.5 billion trade surplus for China last month, widening from $119.1 billion in August.
For the first nine months, China’s trade surplus reached $938 billion, with expectations growing that it could surpass last year’s full-year $1.2 trillion record.
Strong exports have helped drive China’s overall economic growth this year, at a time when domestic consumption and investment remained sluggish, weighed on by a yearslong real estate sector downturn.
However, China’s export resilience is now faced with mounting challenges, said Ecaterina Bigos, a senior market strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management.
“While U.S.-China trade tensions have eased somewhat, the EU’s push to rebalance directly targets high-value exports,” she said.
The U.S. has launched an ongoing probe against China and other trading partners this year on their excess industrial capacity, although Washington and Beijing last month reached an agreement to extend their trade truce and cut tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods.
The 27-nation EU has particularly been struggling to rebalance a trade deficit exceeding $1.1 billion a day with China. EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič, following his visit to Beijing where he met his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao last week, said a deal has been reached with Beijing, including halving Chinese hybrid car imports into the EU over the next few years.
Many of China’s trading partners are facing weak growth prospects and are fearful of their manufacturing industries being overrun by exports from China, said Eswar Prasad, a professor of economics and trade policy at Cornell University.
Policymakers have also pointed to a weakened yuan, China’s currency, versus the U.S. dollar and other currencies contributing to Chinese exports being cheaper overseas when compared with goods from other countries, adding to trade imbalances.
China has said it has “no need or intent” to gain competitive advantages through currency devaluation and that its trade growth has been driven by its industrial competitiveness in the global market.
China’s trade surplus and its high-tech export model depend on open markets, Bigos said, and while diversifying its exports into markets such as Southeast Asia and Latin America can help, it cannot fully substitute for Western demand.
The country’s reliance on high-tech exports, meanwhile, could face challenges as some U.S. technology industry leaders called for a global slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence over safety reasons.
“A slowdown in the global AI investment cycle could pose a greater threat to China’s export growth than trade restrictions imposed by other countries,” said Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board.
Chinese leaders have set an annual economic expansion target of 4.5%-5% for 2026. It is set to release its July-September quarterly economic growth figures next week.
This week, the International Monetary Fund lowered its forecast for China’s 2026 economic growth to 4.5%, down 0.1 percentage point from its previous projection, as it warned that the country's robust exports were unable to fully offset domestic weaknesses.
While Chinese officials have highlighted the need to bolster domestic demand, analysts believe that has yet to become a priority for this year even after authorities recently rolled out new measures to help lift its economy, including subsidies for homebuyers’ mortgage interest payments.
