The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners.
“Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.
As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together, in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”
The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi university, by three men who posed as police officers.
Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood, after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year old were also reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by the bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.
Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.
Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say that nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic underreporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and they could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.
Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi university, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.
While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country requires a deep societal shift where men no longer feel they have ownership over women’s bodies.
“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,’ she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”
Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.
“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”
Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women; as one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.
Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old a graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender-equality initiative, said she has experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.
She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”
The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before – but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.
“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago, but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe.’”
Many of the Delhi university students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.
“Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades,” said Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for her masters in English at Delhi University. “It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”
Many on the marches said that it was no coincidence the protests took place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, which saw hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians take to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has raised concerns over unequal market conditions for Indian businesses in China while expressing optimism about ongoing trade negotiations between India and the United States.
Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, Jaishankar said India did not enjoy a level playing field in China, highlighting persistent economic challenges in bilateral relations.
His remarks come as New Delhi considers easing certain restrictions on Chinese investments while continuing discussions with Washington over a trade agreement.
India-US Trade Deal Moving Towards Resolution
Jaishankar indicated that negotiations between India and the US were progressing, with officials working to resolve outstanding differences.
He said the discussions appeared to be approaching a possible conclusion, although no agreement had been finalised.
Representatives from the US Trade Representative's office and India's Commerce and Industry Ministry are involved in the negotiations.
Jaishankar explained that Washington was seeking to rebuild its industrial base and revise the conditions governing access to the American market.
Tariffs, he said, formed an important part of this policy shift.
He added that India would need to assess its eventual trade arrangements against the terms offered to competing economies.
However, uncertainty remains because several countries have yet to finalise their agreements with Washington.
China Market Access Concerns
Beyond trade negotiations, Jaishankar said countries must reconsider their relationships with the US as Washington changes its approach to international engagement.
During a conversation with Bloomberg News Editor-in-Chief John Micklethwait, he outlined India's broader foreign policy priorities.
These included engaging America, managing China, cultivating Europe and reassuring Russia, alongside maintaining relations with Japan.
Jaishankar said he developed this framework in 2020 against the backdrop of Brexit, Donald Trump's election and growing opposition to globalisation.
He also noted that the US was reassessing its alliances and treaty commitments.
Unlike formal American allies, India maintains a strategic partnership with Washington rather than a treaty-based alliance.
On China, Jaishankar reiterated concerns about market access and competitive conditions affecting Indian businesses.

Britain has appealed to Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a large oil project off the Falkland Islands.
With tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory reaching levels not seen since the war with Argentina in 1982, UK officials have sought urgent assurances from the international organisation.
A letter has been sent to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon arguing that “red notice” requests from Argentina for the arrest of such individuals, including British nationals, should be seen as politically motivated.
It is understood that the UK government is concerned by what sources suggested was an attempt to bully people and companies out of working in the Falklands.
An oil project known as Sea Lion in the north Falklands basin in the south Atlantic has the potential to triple the Falklands’ GDP but Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has vowed to block it. Argentina’s strategy includes attempts to criminalise those involved in Sea Lion and deter other investors.
In its letter, the UK government has urged Interpol to be cautious in its handling of Argentinian requests for detentions, it is understood.
Andrea Clausen, the chief executive of the Falklands government, confirmed that the use of Interpol by Argentina was a threat but added: “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action.”
She said: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.”
It is understood that a response from Interpol to the UK government’s correspondence stated that it would respect article 3 of its constitution, which forbids it from undertaking any intervention or activities of a political character.
Interpol screens red notices, which are requests to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. If circulated to the enforcement agencies, individual member countries then decide whether to act on the requests. Nearly 20,000 were issued last year.
The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.
The intensity of the Argentinian menace relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by Argentina’s dictator Gen Leopoldo Galtieri.
The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.
Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the 700 islands that make up the Falklands and has dismissed a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands’ 3,600 residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.
Despite Interpol’s reassurance about its screening of red notice requests, concerns remain that Argentina could convince the organisation’s member states that its requests are not political but rooted in domestic legislation.
Milei has initiated criminal proceedings against the Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration, which are the core companies in the offshore Sea Lion project.
A draft national sovereignty introduced to Argentina’s congress would further expand the scope of sanctions to affiliates of those companies, financial intermediaries, shareholders and suppliers.
The bill additionally contains clauses that could target those involved in the fishing industry in the Falklands, which makes up a large part of the islands’ economy. The archipelago is 300 miles (500km) east of the southern Patagonian coast of Argentina.
Workers in the oil and fisheries sectors on the Falklands – known in Argentina as Las Malvinas – are understood to be concerned that they could be targeted should they travel, particularly to South America where there is support for Buenos Aires’s sovereignty claim.
In a tandem move to kill off Sea Lion, Argentina is expected within 24 hours to escalate further its dispute with the UK by requesting arbitration under annexe VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (Unclos) over the oil project.
On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline to stop the project or face such a legal action. The deadline passed on Monday and Argentinian newspapers said an application for arbitration would follow.
Under it, Buenos Aires will claim that the UK is in breach of a UN resolution inviting the parties to negotiate over the sovereignty dispute and refrain from “unilateral modifications” to the situation. It will be seeking a binding ruling that the UK must stop the drilling. However, UK government sources are confident that Unclos will not wade into a sovereignty dispute.
At a public meeting on Monday evening, one of the Falkland Islands’ assembly members, Dean Dent, told constituents that the UK government was working hard on a tough response to the Argentinian Unclos threat.
“The UK government has assembled quite an in-depth team of legal advisers, KCs – that is the first step,” he said. “There have been four recent similar cases where a case of sovereignty has been taken to Unclos and all four were disregarded by the tribunal as all four cases were a sovereignty issue, not a maritime issue.”
The UK government is expected to be increasingly muscular in its approach to Argentina in the coming days. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Monday that he had raised the issue and “the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British” with the US president, Donald Trump.

Millennials are getting older and “Girls” is coming back to see how that’s going.
HBO announced Tuesday that Lena Dunham’s comedy will return for a limited five-episode run, with its four leading women and Andrew Rannells reprising their roles.
The original series followed aspiring writer Hannah Horvath and her friends through the jobs, relationships, and financial uncertainty of their 20s in New York. It ran for six seasons from 2012 to 2017, becoming a lightning rod for debates about millennial life, feminism, and who gets to speak for a generation.
Now, Dunham is returning to the characters with another decade of perspective.
Here’s everything we know about the “Girls” revival.
Lena Dunham, Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet, and Andrew Rannells are returning
According to HBO's announcement, Dunham will reprise her role as Hannah Horvath, alongside Williams as Marnie Michaels, Kirke as Jessa Johansson, and Mamet as Shoshanna Shapiro.
Rannells is also returning as Elijah, Hannah’s ex-boyfriend and friend. All four of Dunham’s returning castmates will serve as co-executive producers.
The revival will trade the chaos of their 20s for the milestone of turning 40
HBO hasn’t revealed a plot synopsis, but its comedy chief, Amy Gravitt, offered a hint about the new episodes’ focus.
“We’re thrilled to have Lena turn her gaze from the tumult of one’s twenties to the milestone of turning forty,” Gravitt said in a statement.
“To say the world has changed since we last saw Hannah, Marnie, Shoshanna, Jessa, and Elijah is a massive understatement," Gravitt added, "but we know fans — old and new — will be happy to see how they’ve grown and relieved to see that they’re still the ‘Girls’ we knew way back when.”
Details about their careers, relationships, and where they’re living remain under wraps.
Dunham said the idea came to her around her 40th birthday
The creator said nostalgia alone wasn’t enough to bring the series back.
“We always said we would only return to 'Girls' if there was a specific story we were burning to tell,” Dunham said in a statement. “I’ve missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn’t quite picture them in the present day. Then, right around my 40th birthday, they started talking to me in the shower.”
“And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it’s pretty hard to get them to stop,” Dunham said.
Adam Driver’s return hasn’t been confirmed
Driver, who played Hannah’s on-and-off boyfriend Adam Sackler, wasn’t included in HBO’s cast announcement.
That leaves his involvement an open question. His absence from the announcement doesn’t establish whether Adam will appear in the new episodes.
Driver has several film projects on his slate. He is set to star opposite Anne Hathaway in Ron Howard’s military drama “Alone at Dawn,” scheduled for theatrical release on Christmas Day 2027. He’s also been cast as the villain Mr. Sinister in Marvel’s “X-Men” reboot, due in May 2028.
Judd Apatow is returning, but former co-showrunner Jenni Konner isn’t confirmed
Dunham will write, direct, and executive produce the revival. Apatow, an executive producer on the original series, is also returning, alongside executive producers Ilene S. Landress and Michael P. Cohen.
Konner, who ran the original series with Dunham, was not listed in HBO's announcement. The pair previously announced the end of their producing partnership in 2018.
Dunham offered a more personal account of the separation in her memoir “Famesick,” published this year, describing the breakdown of a relationship that mixed close friendship with creative collaboration.
Production begins in 2027, but there’s no premiere date yet
According to the HBO announcement, filming is scheduled to begin next year, a decade after the original series finale.
“Latching,” which aired on April 16, 2017, left Hannah adjusting to motherhood in upstate New York, with Marnie helping her raise her son, Grover. Jessa and Shoshanna didn’t appear in the final episode.
HBO has ordered five episodes. HBO has not announced a premiere date or release schedule.

Colombia's peace tribunal says former rebel leaders committed war crimes against Indigenous groups
Colombia’s transitional justice system has charged 10 former members of the rebel Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia with war crimes and crimes against humanity
BOGOTA, Colombia -- BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — Colombia’s transitional justice system Tuesday charged 10 former members of the rebel Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia with multiple war crimes and crimes against humanity, which it said were committed against five Indigenous groups.
In a news conference the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, or JEP, said that between 1996 and 2016 the suspects oversaw the torture, murder and forced displacement of Indigenous leaders. It said they also ordered their subordinates to place landmines in Indigenous territory and destroy ecosystems that tribes rely on for their survival.
“Today we are delivering justice to the most forgotten peoples of a segregated Colombia,” JEP magistrate Catalina Diaz said Tuesday. “These people have had their basic right to exist compromised.”
Three former members of the FARC’s last secretariat are among those charged with waging systematic attacks against tribes living in a remote area of southeast Colombia that is covered by rainforests and savannahs and where the FARC often exerted strict territorial control.
One of the suspects, Julian Gallo, served as a senator for eight years after the rebel group made a peace deal with Colombia’s government that gave its leadership 10 seats in Colombia’s congress.
Yhon Jairo Figueroa, a leader of the Koreguaje tribe attended Tuesday’s press conference and said he was thankful to the JEP for taking on the case.
“For the first time the Colombian state recognizes that (armed groups) did not just kill individuals,” he said. “But they attempted to kill the knowledge, the language, the territory” of Indigenous groups.
The special tribunal was established during the 2016 peace deal between the Colombian government and the FARC rebels with the aim of investigating crimes committed by both sides during decades of internal strife, and helping victims seek reparation and truth.
An independent truth commission that was also part of the 2016 peace agreement, found that at least 450,000 people were killed in the conflict, and 7 million were forced to leave their homes.
The former FARC leaders have 30 days to respond to the charges filed by the JEP.
The tribunal’s statutes indicate that if suspects accept charges and collaborate with investigations, they will not face time in prison. Instead they will have to provide reparations to victims and participate in truth and reconciliation schemes.
Suspects who do not accept charges and are found guilty of committing war crimes face up to 20 years in prison.

NEW DELHI: An Air India flight from Frankfurt to Delhi was diverted to Jaipur on Wednesday following a security alert triggered by a suspected hijack threat.The flight, AI-2030, landed safely and was immediately escorted to a designated isolation bay, adhering strictly to standard operating procedures for aviation security emergencies.Assistant Commissioner of Police (Malviya Nagar) Shiv Dayal said airport authorities had alerted the police about the emergency landing following the threat, news agency PTI reported.Police and security personnel were checking the aircraft in the isolation bay, he added.Pilot reportedly used hijack alert codeAccording to preliminary information, the pilot activated Squawk Code 7500, the internationally recognised transponder code indicating hijacking or unlawful interference, while the aircraft was in the Mumbai Flight Information Region (FIR).
The aircraft was subsequently diverted to Jaipur, the source said. The number of passengers on board was not immediately known.Following the aircraft's safe landing, the pilots and passengers were deboarded in a phased manner under security supervision, according to the information available. Passengers and their baggage were undergoing security screening.
Ground teams from the Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS), airport security agencies and local police cordoned off the isolation bay and began checking the aircraft.
The National Security Guard (NSG) was also placed on standby in New Delhi, according to the information provided. Further details about the security alert and the ongoing investigation were awaited.In a similar incident in August, an Air India Express flight from Dammam, Saudi Arabia, to Delhi made an emergency landing at Ahmedabad airport after a tissue paper bearing the word “bomb” was found in the aircraft’s lavatory.All 32 passengers on board were safely deboarded at Terminal 2, according to Ahmedabad Police.

Singapore’s AI-led economic growth set to continue in 2027: MAS
Activity in technology-related sectors is expected to moderate next year, but should remain a principal driver of economic growth, said the central bank on Wednesday (Oct 14).
SINGAPORE: Artificial intelligence-driven expansion of Singapore’s economy is projected to continue next year, though the pace of growth may slow down, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said on Wednesday (Oct 14).
Growth should be supported by strong order backlogs and capacity expansions in AI-related production, the central bank said in its latest quarterly macroeconomic review.
While activity may moderate compared with the “exceptional pace” in 2026, it should remain a “principal driver” of growth, said MAS.
Singapore’s economy grew 5.4 per cent in the third quarter of the year, after expanding 6.2 per cent in the second quarter, said the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry in its advance estimates on Wednesday.
“The technology-related sectors continued to expand robustly, accounting for around 75 per cent of overall (year-on-year) growth,” MAS said, describing the growth as “relatively concentrated”.
Tech-related sectors experienced “outsized expansion”, while non-tech and non-oil sectors saw “mixed” growth, the report said.
CAN AI-LED GROWTH CONTINUE?
The durability of the current economic expansion hinges on three key considerations, said MAS.
The first is the sustainability of the AI-driven global investment cycle. On this point, indicators constructed by the central bank’s economic policy group suggest that strong semiconductor production growth has persisted despite financial pressure on hyperscalers.
“While this points to rising downside risks, current strains remain short of levels that would suggest an imminent retrenchment in AI investment,” said MAS.
Even if capital expenditure is affected by financial vulnerabilities, there are substantial order backlogs and capacity expansions that have been committed to, which would cushion the near-term impact on production.
Industry forecasts for chip sales growth, together with increases in new orders, suggest that the AI-led semiconductor cycle is more likely to remain in a phase of expansion, said MAS.
The second consideration affecting the durability of Singapore’s current economic expansion is whether capacity constraints in the technology-related sectors will constrain the pace of further growth.
The central bank noted that significant additions are expected to come online in 2027 and 2028.
For example, Micron has embarked on multi-year investments, while GlobalFoundries and UMC are ramping up capacity.
“As additional production capacity comes onstream, firms could ramp up output further,” said MAS.
Thirdly, MAS said the sustained strength and the positive impact on overall business confidence and investment sentiment could support other parts of the economy.
“Sanguine business and investor sentiments would sustain robust financial intermediation and trading activity, contributing to firm growth within the financial sector,” it said, though it acknowledged that higher global interest rates could temper credit demand.
Overall, MAS believes that AI-led expansion will continue into 2027.
LABOUR MARKET OUTLOOK
Labour demand is expected to be supported by construction and domestic-oriented services next year, said MAS in the report.
Ongoing major infrastructure and building projects will support demand for workers in construction and in segments of professional services such as architectural and engineering services.
Employment in public administration and education is also expected to increase as plans to expand pre-school services take shape, while demand for financial investment activity, insurance and healthcare should boost hiring as well.
However, nominal wage growth is expected to moderate to levels broadly in line with the historical norm.
Despite firms planning to hire more, the share of companies that intend to raise wages edged down in the Manpower Ministry’s latest survey.
“Cyclically low resignation rates indicate limited job-to-job mobility, reducing pressure on firms to raise wages to retain workers,” the report said.
INFLATION TO EASE IN 2027
Despite the re-escalation of the Middle East conflict, MAS said oil and non-oil imported inflation are forecast to ease gradually over 2027 after remaining elevated in the near term.
Fuel prices are expected to remain high in the immediate months ahead, but as oil and gas flows normalise, prices of energy products are expected to moderate.
Similarly, weather-related disruptions could lift prices further, but food inventories in major producing countries should temper the extent of the increases.
“In the latter part of 2027, as the temporary weather-related shocks to agricultural production dissipate, the inflation impact on Singapore’s food prices is expected to fade progressively,” said MAS.

UP merchant navy sailor missing after oil tanker attacked off coast of Oman
The missing sailor, Veer Bahadur Yadav, hails from Badka Gaon village under Barhaj tehsil in Deoria district.
Uncertainty has gripped a family in Deoria after its sole earning member, a 26-year-old merchant navy sailor, went missing following a drone attack on an oil tanker off the coast of Oman on October 11.
The family has appealed to the Centre to intervene and ensure his safe return.
Nine Indian crew members were rescued following the attack on the Nicaragua-flagged oil tanker MT Petro Dolphin near Sohar port in Oman, while two crew members, including Veer Bahadur Yadav, a resident of Deoria district, remain missing.
Search and rescue operations are underway to locate them. According to officials, the attack took place on October 11 when the tanker, carrying 11 Indian seafarers, was targeted by a drone.

Chinese companies aren't winning overseas just because they're cheaper, according to Goldman Sachs, challenging one of the biggest assumptions behind China's export boom.
"Intuitively, I think we would all associate with the Chinese product, with price deflation, price cuts," Trina Chen, co-head of Greater China equity research at Goldman Sachs, said on the bank's "Exchanges" podcast published Tuesday.
But Goldman found Chinese products often become more expensive after entering foreign markets, partly as their quality improves, while price cuts tend to come later as established rivals fight to defend market share.
The finding challenges the view that Chinese firms win foreign markets by relentlessly undercutting rivals on price.
It comes as policymakers from Washington to Brussels grapple with a surge in Chinese exports, part of what someeconomists have dubbed "China shock 2.0."
China's weak domestic demand and years of deflationary pressure have also fueled concerns that its exporters could push down prices overseas.
More than a race to the bottom
Goldman analyzed 11 sectors and 40 Chinese and global companies to study where Chinese firms are gaining market share.
Chinese products typically enter new markets at about a 30% discount to incumbent rivals, but prices often rise in subsequent years.
Chen said higher prices could reflect factors including inflation, economic cycles, and improvements in product quality.
Chinese companies often raise prices as their products improve without losing their price advantage over competitors. Chen said the discount versus competitors generally remained stable.
Chinese electric vehicles are one example. They sell at roughly a 20% discount to comparable global models, a gap Chen said has remained stable over the past three to four years.
Robot vacuum cleaners show an even more dramatic shift. Chen said Chinese products in the category entered the US market at around a 40% discount but now command a roughly 60% premium as manufacturers continue innovating and adding new functions.
"I think it's fair to say the entry of the Chinese product does not necessarily create additional pricing pressure for many years post the initial entry," Chen said.
Instead, price cuts often come later, when established competitors struggle to defend their positions.
"These price cuts typically are initiated by companies who have been losing market share and trying to defend their market share in a very challenging situation and competition," Chen said.
Chen said Chinese companies tend to gain market share fastest in modular, consumer-facing, high-growth products.
Progress has been slower in mature, interconnected business-to-business markets, where customer trust, servicing networks, local distribution channels, and long operating track records make it harder for Chinese companies to gain market share.

Trump pick Zacharia gets off to bumpy start in unusual first press briefing: ‘My president, I mean my husband’
Newly-minted press secretary lasts less than 15 minutes in awkward debut before the White House press corps

White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia beat an abrupt retreat from the James Brady Briefing Room after just 14 minutes Tuesday morning, capping off an awkward appearance in which she mixed up the man who hired her with the man to whom she is married and spent the majority of her debut on prepared remarks filled with praise for the president.
Zacharia, whom President Donald Trump named Friday as successor to Karoline Leavitt appeared in the briefing room for the first time on just her second day on the job. She opened by telling reporters she was “so honored” to be working for Trump and noted that she’d “wanted to work for him for a very long time.” She spent the next six minutes reading haltingly from prepared remarks replete with praise for Trump and boasts about purported successes dating back months, including what she called a “historic one-day war” against Venezuela as the actual war Trump started with Iran approaches its ninth month.
When it came time to take questions, Zacharia first called on a reporter from the right-wing Breitbart News, who was in a seat normally used by White House staff that her predecessor repurposed for “new media” outlets that are generally friendly to the administration.
She then turned to Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy, who asked her if the U.S. has halted sharing intelligence with Ukraine amid Trump’s blow-up at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Zacharia was unable to answer and told him she’d “have to get back to [him] on that.”
Next up on what appeared to be a prepared list of reporters was a correspondent from the Daily Mail, who first asked about whether Trump was still considering firing Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a spate of embarrassing headlines about her conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
Here she made some news, telling reporters that Trump had indeed asked the ex-Fox News presenter (and ex-fiancee to his eldest son) to quit her post.
But it was a softball follow-up from the Mail that left Zacharias sputtering and led her to flee the room.
She was asked about how she will handle the notoriously tough press secretary role while juggling being a mother to four children given how her predecessor chose to resign over the burdens of balancing the job with caring for just two children.
That’s when things truly went off the rails.
“The idea of not spending evenings with my kid kids are is completely unacceptable,” she said, before confusing her spouse with her boss.
“So my president — excuse me, my husband — is out here,” she said.
She attempted to recover from the laughter in the room by pivoting to more praise for Trump, who she called “ the most family-friendly president we've ever had.”
“He has hired more women with families, and the fact that he knew I had four kids and he knew that this job would be demanding, and still placed his trust in me, shows that I know I'm capable of being able to step up to that,” she said.
At that point, she declared an end to the briefing because Trump was “heading out to Marine One for our historic trip to Alaska, and we can ask him all of the questions out there.”
The president was not scheduled to depart for Alaska for several hours.
Her brief performance left journalists stunned and MAGA insiders decidedly unimpressed.
One former Trump administration official who remains close to people serving in the administration texted The Independent to declare Zacharia’s debut “a train wreck” after previously describing her as a “joke hire” who’d likely be “gone in six months.”
Separately, a current administration official told MS NOW that Zacharia had “got off on the wrong foot” and needed to “get much better, fast” lest she lose her job faster than the 11-day record held by one of Trump’s ex-communications directors, hedge fund manager Anthony Scaramucci.
But the White House, at least publicly, is standing by the new press secretary, with White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung writing on X that Zacharias’ debut was “a tremendous start.”
“She commanded the room and effectively reminded the American people of all the great work President Trump and his Administration has done thus far,” Cheung added.

A 39-year-old unvaccinated woman in Franklin County, Pennsylvania, has become the sixth person to die of the highly infectious virus amid a state outbreak that has stricken over a thousand people since it began in April.
The woman died on Saturday, October 10. She had several underlying health conditions and had recently tested positive for measles, according to an advisory posted on social media by Franklin County Coroner Jordan Conner. The advisory noted that the woman’s death meets the definition of a measles death set by the state’s health department.
In an emailed statement to The Washington Post, the coroner’s office said the primary cause of death was listed as “probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles.”
The previous five deaths amid the state’s measles outbreak included a newborn, a 6-week-old, an 18-year-old, a 20-year-old, and a 40-year-old. All the deceased were unvaccinated; the two infants were too young to have been vaccinated.
As of the latest measles update from Pennsylvania’s health department on Friday, October 9, there have been 1,136 cases in the state since the start of the year—1,124 of which are from the current outbreak. Overall, 218 people have been hospitalized. The outbreak, which now spans 41 of the state’s 67 counties, shows no signs of slowing. There had been 157 new cases reported just in the previous week.

- The claim that Ukrainian strikes on Russian bot farms caused right-wing or MAGA social media activity to decrease is unproven.
- On Oct. 12, after the Russian technology giant Yandex reported that drone strikes damaged its servers in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had seen "less hate, less division, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots" online after the strikes.
- However, Snopes found no credible evidence that Ukrainian strikes on Yandex servers starting on Oct. 8 took Russian propaganda bots offline. Social media posts that attributed changes in online activity on certain topics such as MAGA, the far-right German political party Alternative für Deutschland or various health-related topics failed to directly connect those changes to Russian bots.
- Zelenskyy's office reportedly told the BBC on Oct. 13 that he was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity when he made the remarks about the effect of Ukrainian strikes.
- Darren Linvill, an expert on the effects of foreign information manipulation and interference, told Snopes that Ukraine's strikes had likely mainly affected legitimate, automated Yandex traffic rather than propaganda operations, which Russia often runs from overseas.
In early October, a claim (archived) circulated that Ukrainian strikes on Russian bot farms caused right-wing or MAGA social media activity to decrease.
Yandex, a Russian technology giant that provides search engine, email and cloud services and facilitates payments, ride hailing and food deliveries, confirmed on Telegram and to local media that drone strikes damaged its servers in Sasovo, Kaluga (archived) and Vladimir from Oct. 7 to 11. Work to restore services affected by the strikes continued on Oct. 13.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Oct. 12 that Ukraine had struck "Yandex data centers" and that "a lot of people" had seen fewer Russian bots on social media platforms as a result.
The Facebook page Occupy Democrats, which spread the claim about the consequences of Ukrainian strikes against Russian bots, wrote:
Zelenskyy might just have saved our democracy. The genius is brilliantly bombing Russian data centers linked to FAKE NEWS pro-MAGA bot farms in Moscow. Without them, Putin's midterm influence will accidentally fall from a 30th floor window.
MAGA, an acronym for Make America Great Again, is a political movement supportive of U.S. President Donald Trump. The U.S. has previously accused Russia of using "bot farms" to create false social media accounts that spread disinformation in the U.S.
On Oct. 11, Tomáš Zdechovský, a member of the European Parliament, shared data (archived) he claimed showed a drastic decrease in online activity around Germany's far-right Alternative für Deutschland political party in the days following the strikes. Other social media users claimed searches for various health-related topics (archived) and the number of social media accounts advocating for Alberta to seek independence from Canada (archived) also fell after Ukraine's strikes.
Whether Ukrainian strikes on Yandex servers had indeed taken Russian bots that spread propaganda or misinformation offline was unproven at the time of this writing. As we will lay out below, social media users claiming a direct connection between Ukraine's strikes and falling web traffic generated by Russian propaganda bots tended to identify correlation rather than causation.
Darren Linvill, who studies the tactics, strategies, and impacts of foreign information manipulations and interference at Clemson University, told Snopes via email on Oct. 13 that the Russian propaganda campaigns he studies do not use physical infrastructure within Russia for their efforts, meaning they would be unaffected by Ukraine's strikes. Linvill, along with U.S. and international media, also said that a lot of the traffic that was affected by the strikes was likely legitimate, automated traffic, such as web crawlers that index Yandex's search engine.
Data from the global internet infrastructure company Cloudflare shared by some accounts (archived, archived) as proof of Russian "bot traffic" decreasing after Ukraine's strikes showed graphs accounting for all automated traffic, not propaganda bot accounts specifically. Linvill described measuring a drop only in Russian propaganda bot accounts as "exceedingly difficult."
Lacking credible proof that Ukrainian strikes on Yandex servers starting on Oct. 8 took Russian propaganda bots offline, we leave this claim unrated.
On Oct. 13, Zelenskyy's office appeared to redefine his statement from the previous day that there was "less hate, less division, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots" online after Ukraine's strikes. The office reportedly told the BBC that Zelenskyy was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a fall in bot activity.
Snopes has contacted Zelenskyy's office to verify this statement to the BBC.
Parsing the 'evidence' of falling Russian bot activity
Some social media users shared data from the global internet infrastructure company Cloudflare that they suggested showed that Russian bot traffic "dropped to nearly zero" after Ukraine's strikes.
The data in question, called "Bot vs. Human Traffic," tracked HTTP requests, which are messages that a client (this could be a browser or a mobile app) sends to a server. Cloudflare assesses HTTP requests a given client sends and scores them according to whether it thinks a human or a bot sent the request.
Cloudflare's data showed that HTTP requests from Yandex bots dropped on Oct. 8 and again on Oct. 10, dipping to 0.3% of maximum levels. Bot requests had been at 88.2% of maximum levels the week before. Cloudflare's data also showed that almost all (99.6%) of the HTTP requests sent by Yandex clients were automated, which Cloudflare described as being from bots.
It is important to note that "bot" in Cloudflare's terminology is not just propaganda bots but any requests that the company classifies as automated. The technology publication Mashable and Euronews reported that Yandex's automated traffic likely included web crawlers, which are tools that search engines use to keep their database of websites up to date. Mashable reported that damage to a Yandex's data centers or servers would bring traffic such as web crawlers to a halt.
Linvill also credited the fall in "bot" traffic from Yandex to legitimate, automated traffic such as web crawlers not operating from damaged servers. He wrote that Cloudflare's data did not suggest there was "a particular reason to believe the strikes would have a significant impact on social bot activity from Russia."
Other claims about a decrease in Russian bot traffic failed to directly connect Russian bots to any perceived changes in online activity. For example, Zdechovský's post presented a graph with no source that did not specify what it measured. Another post that claimed a decrease in Google searches for various health-related topics compared data across only two weekends, which was unlikely to be enough to establish and analyze a trend.
An account that claimed accounts calling for Alberta to seek independence from Canada "fell off the face of the earth" after Ukraine's strikes provided no supporting evidence for the claim that linked it to Russian propaganda bots.
We contacted Zdechovský to ask for the source of his graph and await a reply.
Russian propaganda campaigns hard to track
According to Linvill, actually documenting a fall in Russian propaganda bot activity would not be straightforward. He wrote:
It would be exceedingly difficult to measure. You would first have to figure out what it was, exactly, you were measuring? There is no one path to influence and no one way malign propaganda is conducted. These efforts are run on global systems across a multitude of platforms and emanating from multiple actors even within the same country. They make it hard on purpose.
Linvill added that the Russian campaigns he followed did not use bots they ran themselves, instead paying for services run from outside Russia. He wrote: "It has clearly become important for Russia to outsource these services than to run them in house. It's likely cheaper and easier, but also more secure and decentralized."
In sum, readers should be cautious of blanket claims that Ukraine's strikes on Yandex's servers heavily affected Russia's propaganda operation. While that may be the case, there was no credible evidence at the time of this writing directly linking strikes on servers to a fall in Russian propaganda activity online. Linvall suggested that Russian propaganda campaigns could come from overseas, meaning domestic strikes would not be effective against them, a point that Mashable's reporting also made.
For further reading, Snopes previously published a guide to spotting bots on social media.
DeepL.com provided translations from Russian to English.

Ukraine's defense ministry said on Tuesday that its forces are about to start using a jointly NATO-developed artificial intelligence model to predict where and when Russia's drone strikes will land.
Dubbed "Model No. 13," the tool analyzes past combat data, weather conditions, and battlefield conditions to determine, with "high probability," how Russian troops will use drones on the front lines, the ministry said in a statement.
The model can forecast the strike's time, location, intensity, and type of drone used, the ministry said.
"The solution has already been validated using real-world datasets. It has been refined and is ready for integration into the Armed Forces of Ukraine's situational awareness systems," its statement read.
The ministry said Model No. 13 was developed by its armed forces and NATO's Allied Command Transformation, with support from the Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center, an organization the alliance created in late 2024 to help it innovate based on lessons learned in the war.
ACT and JATEC did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent outside regular business hours by Business Insider.
Another AI model that plans artillery deployments, No. 32, is also being jointly created, Ukraine's defense ministry said. However, Ukrainian troops are still testing a prototype of the model, it added.
The announcement comes after Ukrainian officials said in February that their forces had been working with AI and machine learning models since last year to process combat data from the war for "threat forecasting."
Model No. 13 is likely to run on Ukraine's DELTA battlefield management system, a digital app that combines intelligence from drones, cameras, and battlefield reports to give commanders an overview of the frontline from their tablets or phones.
The system already uses an AI module called Vezha that Ukraine says can automatically detect and flag Russian equipment in seconds by analyzing satellite imagery, drone camera feeds, and radio signals.
DELTA reached over 200,000 users in November, Ukraine's defense ministry has said.

The European Union on Wednesday called on Russia to "share timely and transparent reporting" about the death of a plague laboratory technician in Siberia.
"We think that it's necessary to have reliable epidemiological and microbiological findings," European Commission spokeswoman Eva Hrncirova said.
The EU is in contact with experts from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control on the matter, she said, adding "we follow the situation very closely".
Russian news outlet People of Baikal reported Friday that a 28-year-old woman employed at a plague research institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region had died of the disease -- possibly after contracting it from a broken test tube.
Russian authorities have played down the reports, saying the cause of the woman's death was not confirmed and denying they are imposing anti-plague measures.

Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced, deepening a public schism with Google DeepMind and Meta, both of which declined to back new legislation.
The Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee, comprising a cross-party panel of MPs, held an evidence session on Tuesday with appearances from four frontier AI firms, four former staff of the firms turned whistleblowers and senior British civil servants.
“The rules should be binding,” Anthropic’s head of Europe Liam Booth-Smith told the committee, when asked if the company’s view was that AI safety now needs a statutory framework. The company, he said, has “consistently believed that there should be binding rules on companies and that voluntary commitments are not enough.”
OpenAI vice president Tom Duff Gordon was more cautious but still supportive, backing a statutory framework and an international convention. Duff Gordon said “there should be some elements that should be mandatory,” starting with incident reporting. “We don’t think basing everything on voluntary commitments for frontier risk is a good long-term plan,” he said.
However, their rivals would not follow. Asked directly whether he supported a statutory framework, Google DeepMind’s Owen Larter said: “Focus on the standards is what we would be doing.” Meta’s Rob Sherman pointed to Britain’s existing regulators, telling MPs they were “not writing on a blank page.”
The hearing exposed an existing divide on the subject of regulation, putting the conflicting approaches of AI leaders on the British parliamentary record. Exposing this divide in a second jurisdiction was the point, according to select committee chair Liam Byrne. The committee set out “to light up the wide differences in opinions between some of the wealthiest firms on Earth,” he told WIRED after the hearing, and to show “that you couldn’t rely on voluntary self-regulation.”
While the four executives gave evidence to the committee on AI safety, only a few hundred meters away, Britain’s security service director issued a warning about the dangers of AI.
MI5 director Ken McCallum used his annual threat update to warn of bioweapon misuse as a significant threat from AI. “Not yet realized, but the misuse case to which I’d attach greatest weight, is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons,” McCallum said.
Responding to this comment, Byrne told WIRED: “The fact that the head of MI5 is warning about incredibly dangerous capability uplifts for bioterrorists in one part of Whitehall, and then in another part of Whitehall the permanent secretary of the Cabinet Office is basically admitting that our regulatory regime for AI is voluntary, tells you everything you need to know.”
In the final part of the evidence session, civil servants conceded to the committee how little the current system compels. Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI) tests frontier models before release, but only when companies choose to hand them over.
Henry de Zoete, director of AISI, acknowledged that the institute was entirely reliant on the cooperation of the companies and foreign governments in order to gain access. Cat Little, the top civil servant at the Cabinet Office, which houses AISI, was pressed on whether the whole regime was voluntary. “At the moment, yes, it is,” she said.
When asked what would happen if AISI judged a model to be too dangerous, but it was released by a company anyway, de Zoete acknowledged AISI had no ability to prevent them from doing so.
“What we’re not doing is kite marking,” de Zoete said, using the British term for a safety certification. “We’re not saying yes or no to any sort of model.” He added: “These companies are either American or Chinese who are building at the frontier … There’s only so much we, as the UK, can do in that kind of context.”
The frontier executives also made plain that British access runs through Washington. “We provide our models predeployment to CAISI,” OpenAI’s Duff Gordon said, referring to AISI’s US counterpart. “We will continue to provide our models pre-deployment to AISI in the UK … and as long as we’re able to do that under the US government, we will continue to do it.”
The tension of the existing arrangement was made clear to British officials by Anthropic’s Booth-Smith. “We unfortunately were not able to provide full unrestricted access to [Mythos 5.1] to UK AISI at that time ... That’s a question for the US government,” he said before adding that AISI now had access.
The session also heard from four former lab researchers, among them ex-OpenAI staffer Daniel Kokotajlo. “I don’t think the companies can be trusted to self-regulate,” he told MPs. Steven Adler, who left OpenAI in late 2024, said he was “not confident in the safety culture across the industry.” Geoffrey Irving said the labs believe they are locked in a race that governments will not interrupt and that they cannot leave. “Both of those are false,” he said. “They could just stop.”
Following the hearing Byrne told WIRED that his committee would now dedicate a lot of time examining the UK’s path forward as a middle power on AI. He wants ministers to use Britain’s coming G20 presidency, alongside South Korea, which follows it in the chair, to broker an international convention that does not depend on the current White House. “The G20 presidency will outlive the US presidency of Trump,” he said.
“The risks,” he added, “are multiplying faster than our safety regime can control.”

Manufacturing startup ThinkMetal has raised ₹27 Cr (around $2.8 Mn) in a funding round led by India Angel Network’s VC fund IAN Alpha Fund. Other investors, including deeptech focused VC 3i Partners, among others, also participated in the round. The fresh funding will help ThinkMetal in developing its product stack, expand the type of materials it utilises as well as strengthening its R&D capabilities. The Chennai-based metal additive manufacturing startup is also looking to fuel its hiring with the fresh capital. “This investment is an important step in ThinkMetal’s journey from technology development towards commercialisation. We’ll use this capital to strengthen our product development, expand our team and materials capabilities and accelerate adoption across industrial applications,” cofounder and CEO Sabyasachi Ghosh said. Founded in 2021 by Ghosh and Arushi Sharma (CTO),ThinkMetal is a Chennai-based metal additive manufacturing startup that builds industrial printing systems that can manufacture tools such as moulds, dies, jigs and fixtures. Its SistemT1 machine uses metal fused additive manufacturing to build components layer by layer from wound metal feedstock. The process is followed by debinding and sintering to achieve the required strength. The hardware works alongside the startup’s proprietary FuseX materials and Thinkware software. ThinkMetal claims its system can produce metal parts up to 10X faster and at half the cost of conventional manufacturing methods. Its customers include Ants Ceramics, ZeQube Technologies and Hosur CNC, while its components serve applications across the automotive, aerospace and defence sectors. Prior to this round, ThinkMetal raised around $1.1 Mn from YourNest Venture Capital to scale production of its first-generation system. The startup operates in India’s additive manufacturing market, which is projected to grow from $677.4 Mn in 2023 to $3.75 Bn by 2030. The funding comes at a time when the need for deeptech-focus manufacturing firms is rapidly escalating, with the sector attracting a significant interest from institutional investors in recent times. As per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals, a 2.8X jump from $105 Mn across 29 deals in Q3 2025. Hence, startups in the deeptech manufacturing domain are emerging and also getting significant traction from VCs. For instance, Ethereal Machines recently raised $28.5 Mn in its Series B funding round led by Avataar Ventures to build a 3 Lakh sq ft mega-factory near Bengaluru. Similarly, companies like Fledgetec System also develop custom-built components, assemblies, and engineering solutions for the aerospace, defence, industrial, and specialised technology sectors.

A Republican super PAC, not the Republican National Committee, paid for the ad. A spokesperson for the super PAC, Defending Main Street Superpac, said media vendor Cross Screen Media had made the mistake. We await confirmation from the vendor and its parent company.
In October 2026, a rumor spread that Republicans had inadvertently paid for a campaign ad targeting Troy Jackson, Maine's Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate and incumbent Susan Collins' opponent, to air in Portland, Oregon, instead of Portland, Maine.
Posts multiplied on social media making the claim, including on Facebook and X. One X post by the betting platform Polymarket said "Anti-Troy Jackson ads intended for Maine voters are reportedly appearing in Oregon, sparking speculation that advertisers confused Portland, Maine, with Portland, Oregon" (archived):
The post included maps of the states of Oregon, on the West Coast, and Maine, on the East Coast.
The claim is true, although some social media users were imprecise about who paid for the ads, saying it was "the GOP" or "Republicans" as a whole. A review of Google's Ads Transparency Center revealed the anti-Jackson ad, paid for by Republican super PAC Defending Main Street Superpac Inc, aired not only in Portland, Oregon, but also Washington state, between Oct. 8 and Oct. 12.
A spokesperson for Defending Main Street Superpac acknowledged the mistake in an email to Snopes, saying it had originated with the super PAC's media vendor, Cross Screen Media, whose parent company is 1903 Group.
"During a recent independent expenditure, our media vendor mistakenly placed approximately $25,000 in digital advertising in the Portland, Oregon, media market instead of Portland, Maine," the email read. The spokesperson added Cross Screen Media was refunding the ad buy.
We reached out both to Cross Screen Media and to 1903 Group to confirm and we will update this report should we receive a response.
Ad buys and social media chatter
The ad in question attacked Jackson for seeking to raise taxes in Maine:
The super PAC is an independent political advocacy group that supports Collins, who is seeking her sixth term in the Senate (she was first elected in 1996). Collins' campaign had no say in the ad's content, nor where it aired. Polls revealed that Collins and Jackson were in a tight race.
Data from Google's Ads Transparency Center showed that the ad ran in Oregon for four days and was seen between 1 million and 1.25 million times there. The buyer spent between $15,000 ad $20,000. The ad also ran in the state of Washington during that time, and cost between $5,000 and $6,000, for 350,000 and 400,000 views.
"The error was identified, the ads were immediately stopped and corrected, and the vendor is refunding Defending Main Street the full amount of the misplaced spend. No donor funds will be lost as a result of the vendor's error," the super PAC's spokesperson told Snopes in the email.
Meanwhile, internet chatter indicated that people in Oregon had seen the anti-Jackson ad. On Oct. 11, an account on X named Lillian Belle, whose bio reads "Obsessed with Oregon Politics. Ask me about Oregon and the Judiciary," said (archived) "I've gotten 5 anti-Troy Jackson ads in the last 24 hours. I choose to believe they mixed up Portlands."
Someone responded to this post, saying (archived) "Ive gotten so many this week," to which Belle responded "Interesting that it's not just me."
Asked if the ads were "digital or cable," Belle said (archived) "Digital which isn't that precise but still a lol [laugh out loud]"
For further reading, Snopes has covered several rumors about the 2026 U.S. elections, including a false claim that voting ballots are disqualified with poll workers mark them.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has brought the promotion of doctors and hospitals and how they attract patients online under the ambit of medical ethics, prohibiting paid rankings, fake reviews, referral fees, misleading claims and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to create or manipulate patient testimonials.
The Ethics and Medical Registration Board’s Guidelines on Ethical Advertising and Public Communication by Hospitals/Medical Institutions and Registered Medical Practitioners, issued on October 6, apply to communication through websites, social media, messaging platforms, podcasts, sponsored content, influencers and online platforms. The guidelines have come into effect immediately.
The guidelines prohibit registered medical practitioners (RMPs) and hospitals from making claims such as “best”, “No. 1”, “leading”, “most trusted”, “top” or “unmatched”, unless these can be objectively verified through a transparent and independently ascertainable methodology. Any ranking or award used in advertising must also be independently verifiable, with relevant details disclosed where necessary to prevent the public from being misled.
Online promotion targeted
The NMC has specifically addressed online promotion. RMPs and hospitals cannot procure or manipulate fake followers, likes, reviews, ratings, testimonials, comments, views or other digital engagement. They cannot manipulate search rankings, visibility or algorithms to create a misleading impression of their professional standing.
The guidelines also target financial incentives for bringing in patients. An RMP cannot offer, pay, solicit or receive a commission, rebate, bonus, gift, gratuity, referral fee, lead-generation fee or other consideration connected with the referral, recommendation or procurement of patients, specimens or materials for diagnosis or treatment.
Advertising agencies, digital marketing agencies, influencers and online platforms cannot be engaged in a manner in which payment is linked to the procurement or referral of individual patients.
On patient testimonials
Patient testimonials have also come under specific restrictions. An RMP cannot use or permit a celebrity, influencer, patient, employee or other third party to promote professional services through prohibited testimonials, endorsements or recommendations. The guidelines also prohibit RMPs from requesting or sharing patient testimonials, recommendations, endorsements or reviews for professional promotion on social media.
The guidelines prohibit the use of AI to create or manipulate patient testimonials and other promotional material in a manner that misrepresents treatment, outcomes or professional standing. The provisions also cover manipulation of patient images or voices and synthetic endorsements presented as though they came from actual patients or professionals.
The NMC has also specified what doctors and hospitals can communicate. “Hospitals can provide factual information about their location, departments, facilities, equipment, emergency services, accreditation, services and fees. Doctors can provide factual professional information and participate in public-health and educational communication, provided it does not become prohibited promotion,” it said.
Discounts, limited-period offers, contests, coupons, gifts, cashbacks, referral benefits and free procedures are also prohibited where they are likely to encourage unnecessary consultation, diagnostic investigation or treatment. Lawful disclosure of fees and packages can be made if it is factual, transparent and not misleading.
The guidelines prescribe graded disciplinary action against RMPs. A first violation can attract a warning and mandatory ethics training; a second can result in censure and a monetary penalty; and a third can lead to suspension of registration for three to six months. Serious violations can attract suspension for six to 12 months, while repeated violations can result in removal from the medical register for one to three years.
For hospitals and medical institutions, the applicable penalty and appellate mechanism under the Clinical Establishments Act or the relevant State law will apply. Where an RMP has authorised, participated in or endorsed prohibited communication, the doctor’s professional conduct can separately be examined by the appropriate medical regulatory authority.
The guidelines have been issued in the context of a writ petition before the Supreme Court and the existing framework governing professional conduct.

Saudi Ministry of Energy reports limited fire in building at Aramco compound targeted in attack
The Saudi Ministry of Energy says a limited fire broke out in an administrative building in Aramco, one of the world’s largest oil facilities, that was targeted in the country's Eastern Province
CAIRO -- A limited fire broke out Tuesday in an administrative building at Aramco, one of the world’s largest oil facilities, that was targeted in an attack in the country’s Eastern Province, Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy said. The ministry said no injuries were reported.
The attack came as the Iranian-backed Houthis and the Saudi coalition fighting them exchanged attacks Tuesday night. The fighting marked a fresh escalation in the widening Middle East crisis and came shortly after the Saudi coalition reported a series of alerts for incoming missiles heading for the Eastern Province, a major oil-producing region, and the capital Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense said debris from two intercepted Houthi missiles fell on residential areas in Riyadh, injuring four people and damaging 15 homes.
The coalition of forces in Yemen led by Saudi Arabia carried out new airstrikes Tuesday on the Houthi rebel-held Yemeni capital, the Houthi-run broadcaster Al Masirah and residents said.
The strikes came shortly after a coalition spokesman urged residents to evacuate the area for their safety. Witnesses reported hearing strong explosions in Sanaa hours after the coalition struck the Subaha fuel facility west of the city.
In a rare statement earlier, the coalition had urged civilians in the Houthi-controlled capital to leave the Yemeni Oil Company site, on a hill overlooking the capital, and nearby storage areas ahead of a possible strike.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki accused the Houthis of using the facility and its underground fuel depots for their arsenal of missiles and drones.
Houthi officials appeared to have anticipated the attack. The oil company said its storage facilities were empty and that a Saudi strike would not affect oil reserves or supplies for residents. Still, witnesses in the city said lines of cars formed at some gas stations amid fears of a shortage.
Shortly after the warning, Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on Telegram that any Saudi attack on Sanaa would be met with a “firm and painful” response in the Saudi capital, Riyadh.
Hours later, Saudi Arabia issued alerts for incoming missiles heading for Riyadh and the Eastern Province but quickly said the danger had passed. The coalition said it had intercepted a series of Houthi-launched ballistic missiles, drones and cruise missiles in multiple areas in the country, including Riyadh and the southern province of Wadi al-Dawasir. Riyadh residents reported hearing loud explosions.
Airlines moved a number of their planes out of Riyadh on Tuesday on the advice of insurers and government officials because of the threat of additional attacks. They needed to transfer the planes to other airports in the country so they can keep flying passengers to their destinations, said Osprey Flight Solutions Chief Intelligence Officer Matthew Borie, whose company advises airlines, insurers and countries on flight threats.
“It’s not abnormal for this to occur especially in this day and age with the types of conflict zone situations that have occurred in the region,” Borie said.
More than 3,120 flights scheduled to depart from airports across Saudi Arabia since Oct. 8 have been canceled or listed as not operating, representing about 41% of scheduled departures, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. That includes more than 300 flights that had been scheduled to depart Wednesday.
Several airlines have suspended service to the kingdom because of the Houthi attacks on airports.
It was unclear whether the Tuesday strike in Yemen was a signal of military escalation or a carefully measured response to recent deadly attacks on the Riyadh airport.
The warning and the attack show “the Saudis’ aims of upping the ante and striking deep in the heart of Houthi-controlled territory while attempting to control the narrative by presenting themselves as more careful and humanitarian actors than the Houthis,” said Adam Baron, a fellow at the Washington-based New America institute.
“It may be a warning — or it may be a sign of things to come," he said.
Saudi Arabia is still scrambling to determine how its air defenses failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by the Houthis, including an attack on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday that killed at least 13 people and wounded over 300.
The latest conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis began last month after the rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical waterway for the transport of Gulf oil and other goods at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen.
The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, has been trying to retake them.
Saudi Arabia’s Cabinet on Tuesday warned the Houthis they would “face consequences” for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.
“The Kingdom will not allow any threat to its security or to freedom of maritime navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait,” the Cabinet said in a statement carried by Saudi state-owned Al-Ekhbariya television. The Bab el-Mandeb is another area key to the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf.
On Tuesday, Yemen’s interior ministry said in a statement on X that Houthi strikes over the past day on Taiz, a major city in the country's southwest, had killed six people and injured 18 amid ongoing battles in the region.
A commander with the Saudi-backed forces said rebels had fought through fierce resistance to reach the edges of Taiz, and some had entered the city. The fight was now critical for Taiz, which has long been a sought-after prize, he said.
The commander, speaking on condition of anonymity to describe battlefield details, said rebel forces were surprisingly large, and bolstered by medium and short-range ballistic missiles.
That fighting is leading to the large-scale displacement of people and growing shortages of food and other supplies, U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric said Tuesday, with cooking gas largely unavailable and food prices that have reportedly risen about 50%.
Saudi Arabia has been pushing for the U.S. military to provide more direct support in the fight against the Houthis.
The U.S. has provided intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for a Saudi-led offensive, but has held off on carrying out strikes against the Houthis.
A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to try to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb.

The death of a laboratory worker in Siberia on October 2, 2026, and the subsequent quarantine of dozens of people have sparked concerns about a pneumonic plague epidemic, with Russia revealing little information publicly. The incident has revived memories of the COVID-19 pandemic and allegations that the coronavirus may have emerged at a Chinese lab.
What happened at the Siberia lab?
The 28-year-old woman, Darya Shipilova, employed at a research institute in Siberia, fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of people and dispatch the head of Russia’s health watchdog to the Irkutsk region.
The woman worked at the anti-plague research institute in the city of Irkutsk, where the plague occurs naturally in wild animals. She died at a hospital in nearby Shelekhov that the mayor said had been placed under quarantine. Following the incident, top Russian health officials have travelled to the region.
Russian authorities say the lab worker died of what initially presented as a “typical” acute respiratory viral infection.
Russia dismisses epidemic concerns
Meanwhile, Russia’s health regulator insists there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after the plague institute worker’s death.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said on October 7 that it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic.
No cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, it said, while adding that 90% of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens.
When asked about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution against using media reports as a reference for what was happening.
‘Causative agent behind death not known’
A top official with the World Health Organisation (WHO) said it doesn’t know how the lab worker in Siberia died. Maria Van Kerkhove, WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said the UN health agency doesn’t know what the “causative agent’ was behind the woman’s October 2 death.
She has urged Russia to provide more information about the incident that prompted global concerns about suspected pneumonic plague. The WHO initially said it estimated the risk of the Russia case to the public as low, but told a press conference on October 7 it could not make a fuller risk assessment due to insufficient information from the Russian authorities.
What is pneumonic plague, symptoms
Reports blamed the woman’s death on pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.
Pneumonic plague causes a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time. The severe disease is less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages.
Pneumonic plague and bubonic plague are caused by the same bacteria. The former is spread by respiratory particles while the latter is spread through bites from fleas that have jumped from infected rodents.
Symptoms of pneumonic plague include shortness of breath and coughing-up blood, and they can occur in as little as 24 hours after exposure, according to the WHO. If untreated, the illness can be fatal.
Not linked to a biological weapon
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday (October 8) that the death of the Russian plague laboratory worker did not appear to be linked to a biological weapon.
Mr. Trump said Russia insisted it had the situation under control, but added that not much information was coming out. He, however, said that the United States will help Russia over the incident.
The European Union has also called on Russia to “share timely and transparent reporting” about the death of the plague laboratory technician.
