“Little Princess,” the British pre-school animation classic, is heading to Sky UK, in a deal struck with Banijay Kids & Family which sees the pay TV buying its complete catalog.
Further new distribution deals on “Little Princess,” a four-time BAFTA nominee, have been struck with Nordisk Film, RTV Slovenia and Italy’s TIM.
Based on the best-selling children’s books by award-winning author and illustrator Tony Ross, “Little Princess” launched on the U.K.’s Channel 4 “Milkshake” children’s TV block in 2006 and ran through four seasons of a total 135 episodes, the last ending in 2020.
First time round, when on linear TV, “Little Princess” was released in 140 territories. The deal announced by Banijay Kids & Family on Wednesday at Mipcom o underscore that what the market is looking for is evergreen brands, not necessarily brand new linear TV shows.
Popular on Variety
“Little Princess” has, however, cultivated from 2008 to a fandom base on YouTube and other platforms, underscoring its resilient appeal.
Sky U.K. has acquired all series and specials. Nordisk Film has acquired Seasons 1-3 and the series’ specials for SVOD across the Nordics; RTV Slovenia has Seasons 1-2, and Telecom Italia’s TIM for its Italian streaming platform aggregator, TIMVision.
“Little Princess” is produced by The Illuminated Film Company, also behind Eric Carle’s “The Very Hungry Caterpillar and Other Stories” and the RTS Award winning “The Rubbish World of Dave Spud.”
Set in a comfy world of gentle blocked colors, an ever blue sky, lovely grass low hills stretching to the horizon, and a purple-bricked castle, “Little Princess” turns on the antics of the bubbly, ever inquisitive and endearing titular character.
Sporting a permanent yellow crown teeth and craggy mild teeth who confronts every day problems – such as getting a scratch after a very minor accident on “I Need a Plaster. Coddled by her parents and the cast service, she learns, however, that she might be a princess but won’t always get her own way. Each episode, as Banijay Friends & Family notes, is told with a warm blend of humor and surprise.
“Across the industry, we’re seeing continued demand for trusted, established IP that can cut through in an increasingly crowded landscape. With a new U.K. home on Sky and partners across Europe, ‘Little Princess’ demonstrates the enduring value of distinctive characters and storytelling that audiences know and love,” said Julia Rowlands, SVP Sales, Co-Productions and Acquisitions, Banijay Kids & Family.Led by CEO Benoît Di Sabatino, Banijay Kids & Family brings together leading production companies – Monello Productions, Movimenti Production, Procidis, Tiger Aspect Kids & Family, Zodiak Kids & Family France, and Zodiak Productions UK – spanning France, Italy, and the U.K.
It is behind preeminent kids’ brands including “Totally Spies!,” “Mr Bean,” “Once Upon a Time…, LoliRock,” “Super Happy Magic Forest,” “Street Football” and “MiniHeroes of the Forest.”

BBC FM radio transmissions suspended in Afghanistan
- Published
Afghanistan's Taliban government has suspended the transmission of BBC broadcasts from FM radio sites across the country.
A Taliban government spokesman said the BBC had been suspended because of "repeated violations" but did not elaborate.
The BBC has been the only international news organisation to broadcast inside Afghanistan since two US outlets were banned from operating in the country in 2022.
"Millions of people across Afghanistan rely on the BBC for accurate news and information and we are working with the authorities to address the situation," the broadcaster said in a statement.
The BBC said it was "continuing to report fairly and independently in Pashto, Dari and English to our audiences in Afghanistan, on shortwave and medium wave radio, online and via satellite".
It reaches more than 20% of the adult population in Afghanistan each week with news and other output, including educational programming aimed at girls who have been banned from secondary schools.
Taliban Ministry of Information and Culture spokesman Khubaib Ghufran told local media: "Due to some repeated violations by the BBC media outlet, it is decided that for time being its activity is suspended across the country."
The Taliban government has a tight grip on media operating in the country.
Music is not broadcast and women are less visible on screen than before the Taliban retook power in 2021. Women no longer appear on air together with men.
People can still use some social media platforms, but a lack of electricity in large parts of the country, high costs and low literacy rates remain major barriers.
The BBC's Afghan service has been operating since 1981.

Americans have more trust in science than most of the rest of the world, according to a new survey of people in 140 countries, a finding that may seem difficult to explain in a country deeply divided by issues such as the benefits and harms of vaccines.
According to the newest edition of the Wellcome Global Monitor, 52 percent of Americans report having “a lot” of trust in science. Across the globe, that number is a mere 26 percent.
Americans, in aggregate, are also more eager to get vaccines compared to peer nations; 45 percent of Americans say they would want to get vaccines recommended by a nurse or doctor “right away.” In Germany only 28 percent say the same.
And while the share of people globally who agree that science benefits most people in their society has dropped from 42 percent in 2018 to 37 percent in 2025, the share of Americans who agree with that statement has actually increased from 48 percent to 57 percent.
But the aggregate statistics don’t tell the whole story. STAT’s analysis of the Wellcome data demonstrates that while America may, in general, appreciate and trust science, it is also far more divided than peer nations.
Take the religious divide: According to STAT’s analysis there was, on average, a 5 percentage point gap between the percentage of religious and non-religious people in high-income nations who said science benefits most people in their country. In the United States that gap was 24 percentage points.
A similar divide — 19 percentage points — separates urban and rural Americans on the question of science’s benefits. The divide across other high-income nations is just three points. Education level divides Americans as well — just 47 percent of Americans without four-year degrees reported believing that science benefits most people, compared to 71 percent of college grads.
Wellcome, a British foundation focused on scientific research, funded the survey in 2018, 2020 and 2025. The most recent version was administered as part of the Gallup World Poll through a combination of in-person, telephone and online surveys of more than 140,000 adults. The global findings were weighted “to ensure that global estimates accurately reflect the relative populations of countries in the survey.”
The survey does not offer an explanation for why the United States appears to be outpacing its peers on trust. But at least some of Americans’ seeming polarization may be explained by Americans’ tendency toward extremes.
Americans are “more extreme responders to public opinion surveys,” said Matthew Motta, an associate professor at Boston University School of Public Health who is an expert on public opinion research.
For example, a smaller proportion of Germans than Americans said they would “not get vaccines at all.” Only 8 percent of Germans were completely anti-vaccine, compared to 13 percent of Americans. Instead, the vast majority of Germans said they would “prefer to think about it for some time.”
The survey also showed that Americans who historically have been less trusting are not necessarily souring on science and its benefits. STAT’s analysis finds that the proportion of Americans who identify as religious and who believe science benefits most people increased by four percentage points, from 46 percent in 2018 to 50 percent in 2025. Self-reported religious Americans are also more likely to report an eagerness to be vaccinated when compared to peer countries.
A similar pattern plays out with Americans without four-year degrees. The percentage of non-college grads who say science benefits most people increased by three percentage points over that seven-year period, and they too are more likely than residents of peer nations with similar education to want vaccines right away.
So what is causing America’s growing divide over trust in science? The poll shows it is growing enthusiasm for science among highly educated, secular Americans. Both reported substantial increases in their appreciation of the benefits of science: 13 percentage points for college grads, and 15 percentage points for secular Americans over seven years, the Wellcome survey found.
In short, America is divided not because certain groups are souring on science, but because others are becoming more appreciative of its benefits.
That might seem like good news. But the divide nonetheless underscores that the benefits of science are not reaching a large swath of Americans in ways they can see and feel.
“People are feeling left behind, they are not understanding how this benefits me,” said Brian Castrucci, president and CEO of the de Beaumont Foundation, which focuses on strengthening public health.
Some divisions facing Americans will be difficult to combat in a country as large and diverse as the United States. City dwellers with cancer who can access care at a top-rated university medical center will inevitably see science’s impact on their lives more than people in a rural area who might have to travel a great distance for even the most basic hospital care.
Wellcome found that trust in science is closely associated with confidence in a nation’s health care systems, which presents a problem for the United States as well. Just 40 percent of Americans reported a lot of confidence in U.S. hospitals and health clinics, the same proportion as in Portugal and Uruguay.
Anti-science sentiment coming from America’s top political officials is likely playing a role too, several experts said. Diverging views on science among America’s political parties became apparent during the Tea Party movement of the 2010s and was amplified during Trump’s presidency, said Yotam Ophir, an associate professor of communication at the University at Buffalo.
But experts STAT spoke to underscored that this new data doesn’t just indicate the need for the sorts of systemic changes that can take decades to fulfill. Scientists need to hone their ability to discuss the benefits of science in people’s everyday lives, and to stop expecting the public to blindly trust them, several experts told STAT.
“What we need to do is be better communicators, not better debaters. We are not going to be able to lecture people into trusting us,” Castrucci said.
Mark Henderson, Wellcome’s executive director of corporate affairs and engagement, said scientists who wish to take steps based on the report’s findings should “meet people where they are.”
“Approach people on a level with understanding and engagement and respect, and you’re going to get a better outcome,” Henderson added. “It’s not rocket science, but it often surprises me how hard people in the scientific community find it to do that.”

Global crude oil prices rebounded on Wednesday after a brief decline in the previous session, as escalating attacks in the Middle East renewed concerns over disruptions to international energy supplies.
Brent crude, the global benchmark, climbed 1.25% to $107 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) gained more than 1% to $95.34.
The increase followed reports of intensified Iranian attacks on commercial vessels and oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz late on Tuesday. Houthi rebels have also been reported to attack an office of Saudi Aramco in Dhahran. Aramco is the world's biggest oil company of the world.
The developments raised concerns about safe maritime passage through the strategic waterway, which is crucial for Gulf oil exports.
Regional security risks intensified after a ballistic missile reportedly struck a Saudi Arabian headquarters complex in Dhahran on Tuesday.
The incident caused a small fire but no injuries, according to the supplied reports.
Saudi authorities also reported intercepting additional missiles launched by Iran-backed Houthi militants.
The escalating conflict has highlighted the vulnerability of energy infrastructure, including facilities associated with Saudi Arabia's oil industry.
Reports of missile attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport have further heightened regional tensions.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for the airport strike, which reportedly caused casualties and widespread injuries.
Saudi-backed forces subsequently launched operations against Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen.
Meanwhile, security threats near the Strait of Hormuz have reportedly prompted several oil supertankers to avoid entering the Persian Gulf.
Brent prices have risen more than 70% this year amid the conflict involving the United States and Iran.
Ukraine Conflict Adds To Uncertainty
Oil traders are also assessing whether additional Russian diesel supplies could ease global fuel shortages.
A reported arrangement involving US President Donald Trump and Russia could release 4.8 million metric tonnes, equivalent to approximately 36 million barrels, of diesel.
However, the proposed volume would offer only temporary relief relative to global demand.
Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire.
The reported strikes have raised questions about the effectiveness of the proposed agreement.
Ukraine has also indicated that it would continue operations against Russia.
Together, the Middle East conflict and uncertainty surrounding Russian energy supplies are keeping crude markets sensitive to geopolitical developments.

The Union Health Ministry has asked all States and Union Territories to ensure the prominent display of rates charged for services and facilities offered by clinical establishments.
In a move aimed at strengthening transparency, accountability and patient-centric healthcare delivery, Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava, in a letter to the Chief Secretaries of all States and Union Territories, called for compliance with regulatory provisions, and ensuring information on service charges was clearly visible to patients and their attendants.
“Display of rates would help patients and their families understand the likely cost of treatment, make informed healthcare decisions, and plan their medical expenditure,’’ Ms. Srivastava said, adding that greater transparency would also help minimise avoidable confusion and billing-related disputes.
The letter refers to the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 and the Clinical Establishments (Central Government) Rules, 2012.
Under the Rules, clinical establishments in States and Union Territories where the Act is applicable are required to display the rates charged for each type of service provided, along with facilities available, at a conspicuous place, in the local language as well as in English.
Since health is a State subject, in States and Union Territories where clinical establishments are regulated by their own respective frameworks, several of which also contain provisions relating to the display of rates, the Health Secretary has called upon Chief Secretaries to ensure effective compliance.
The letter also places particular emphasis on transparency in healthcare pricing for international patients.
States and UTs have been requested to encourage the prominent display, wherever applicable, of package rates offered to foreign patients travelling to India on medical or Ayush visas.
“This would enable international patients to make informed choices, help minimise pricing and billing-related grievances and further strengthen India’s position as a trusted destination for medical and Ayush care,’’ the Ministry said.

The government has proposed a draft bill to introduce criminal penalties for the unauthorized transactions of land around important facilities, including Self-Defense Forces bases and on uninhabited border islands.
The bill to revise the law to regulate such land use and conduct related land surveys was presented to the ruling Liberal Democratic Party on Tuesday ahead of its planned submission to the current parliamentary session.
The draft says that areas within about 1,000 meters of SDF and Japan Coast Guard facilities considered vulnerable to drone attacks, along with uninhabited border islands, would be designated as regulated areas.
Land transactions in those areas would require prior approval from the central government. Violators could face up to three years in prison or a fine of up to ¥3 million.
The government is expected to approve the bill at a Cabinet meeting on Oct. 23.
The proposed revision would also add the Imperial Palace, the parliamentary building, the Prime Minister’s Office and government buildings for crisis management organizations to the list of important facilities around which regulated areas subject to land use surveys are designated.
Currently, the list mainly includes facilities related to the SDF, U.S. forces in Japan and the Japan Coast Guard.

Everstone Capital-backed EV startup GreenCell Mobility has raised ₹330 Cr ($34.6 Mn) in an equity funding round led by Impact Fund Denmark to support the rollout of about 4,500 electric buses currently under deployment. The Mumbai-based startup is eyeing expanding its fleet to more than 5,000 e-buses across 105 cities across India. “Our focus is on executing our order book with rigour, strengthening service delivery and ensuring that the organisation keeps pace with the size and complexity of our operations. This equity investment gives us greater headroom to accelerate our plans while maintaining the standards of reliability, efficiency and customer experience that are fundamental to our business,” GreenCell Mobility managing director and chief executive Devndra Chawla said. Founded in 2019, GreenCell Mobility focuses on deploying and operating electric buses for public transportation. It acquires electric buses via contract manufacturing arrangements with vendors and then deploys them for both intercity and intracity travel. Backed by Eversource Capital, a joint venture between Everstone Capital and Lightsource, GreenCell primarily operates under the brand NueGo. It claims to operate more than 1,200 electric buses in India, including 900 on intra-city routes, 300 under its NueGo brand for inter-city travel, and 50 for MSRTC. The startup also runs over 270 charging stations to support its fleet. The startup previously raised $37 Mn from World Bank’s International Finance Corporation and also counts Eversource Capital, British International Investment and Tata Capital among its backers. India’s electric bus segment has so far drawn strong interest from development finance institutions and lenders backing vehicle deployments under long-term public transport contracts. GreenCell’s latest round suggested that investors are also beginning to back the operating platform layer in the category, not just asset financing. The investment highlights the role of institutional capital in expanding electric public transportation infrastructure in India. Large-scale electric bus deployments require funding not only for vehicles but also for the operational capabilities and charging infrastructure needed to support them. Earlier in March, electric bus manufacturer PMI Electro Mobility, along with its electric bus platform Allfleet, has signed a definitive agreement with private equity giant KKR for an investment commitment of up to $310 Mn, to help scale the electric bus platform and focus on expanding its presence across India. PMI subsequently filed for an IPO via the confidential route last month.

Russian strikes kill at least 3 in Ukraine, damage dozens of power facilities
Attack left more than 600,000 without power, says Ukraine president
Russian strikes killed three people in Kyiv and plunged hundreds of thousands into darkness overnight, authorities said on Wednesday, in an attack President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called "ostentatious disrespect" to Donald Trump's peace effort.
The hours-long missile and drone attack primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, and damaged 30 energy facilities, Zelenskyy said. At least 600,000 people were left without power, he added.
U.S. President Trump, who lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last week in a bid to lower politically sensitive fuel prices, has said that both sides agreed to halt strikes on energy infrastructure, though neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed it.
"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Zelenskiy wrote on X.
"Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong."
Russia's defence ministry said on Wednesday it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets.
Ukraine reported downing just four out of 39 missiles, reflecting Kyiv's weakened air-defences against fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones amid a shortage of weapons.
Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian cities ahead of winter as it struggles on the battlefield, sparking fears of widespread power and heating outages across the country.

Ukraine, for its part, has increasingly been attacking Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs in recent months, in what it views as one of the few ways it can respond to more than four and a half years of Russian bombardment.
Railway facilities also hit
Wednesday's Russian attacks also targeted state railway facilities in five regions across Ukraine, said Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi.
Trump blames Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries for the rise in fuel costs, especially of diesel, which has hit record prices since his war against Iran disrupted global oil supplies.
Sources have told Reuters and other news organizations that the U.S. threatened to cut off intelligence used for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine unless Kyiv stops attacking Russian oil refineries.
Zelenskyy had earlier said Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a previous overnight attack on the capital. Trump said on Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence.

'No excuses' - but is Villa's stadium rebuild affecting team?
- Published
"No excuses," said Unai Emery.
The Aston Villa head coach was talking about his team's form amid Villa Park's rebuild.
He had already turned the air blue when describing their defeat to Nottingham Forest last month.
It was a rare moment of candour from the Spaniard with Villa yet to win at home this season after Saturday's 2-2 draw with Brentford.
The North Stand is a shell and currently closed for building work as the club increases the stadium's capacity to over 50,000.
It is part of the club's plan to help Villa bridge the financial gap in the Premier League, but they may have to endure some short-term pain for long-term gain.
Fenerbahce visit on Wednesday as Champions League football returns to Villa Park.
With them is Marcos Asensio, who scored eight goals for Emery's men during a successful loan from Paris St-Germain in 2025 - and a reminder of the swagger Villa used to have at home.
He scored in Saturday's 3-0 win over Rizespor, with Fenerbahce netting 11 goals in their last two games, including an 8-0 victory against Turkish Super Lig strugglers Eyupspor.
That could present a problem for a Villa defence that has kept just one clean sheet this season and been increasingly fallible at home, something Emery knows must improve regardless of the rebuild.
"Our handicap is less supporters for the situation, but the club decided it. It is something to improve us for the future," said the Spaniard.
"We must try to be together and without 7,000 supporters we must push everyone. We must play better football, compete better, be more focused. Those are more important than the stand.
"We are realistic with how we are working, improving. The things are not [good] enough yet, a lot of conversations with the team, meetings, video, practising and each match trying to show and improve."
Villa, though, have lost just once at home in Europe under Emery - against Olympiacos in the Europa Conference League semi final in 2024 - and he ended their wait for silverware by lifting the Europa League in May.
"Over the last few years our home form has been amazing, especially in Europe," said defender Matty Cash. "We need to get back to that.
"I don't want to sound like I am making excuses, because obviously we have to deal with the circumstances and it is really good to make the stand bigger and the stadium bigger, but it is obviously different.
"I am not going to sit here and lie and say it isn't but you have to deal with the circumstances. You can't make excuses. You have to play what is in front of you. When it is done it will be amazing but yeah, at the moment it is a bit different."
From invincible to insecure
Champions Arsenal and Forest have already claimed three points at Villa Park this season, with unbeaten Brentford taking a point.
Nicolas Jackson's equalising goal against the Bees was the first Villa had scored in front of the skeleton that was their North Stand this season.
Yet Villa's home struggles are not new. Since the turn of the year they have lost the aura of invincibility which Emery has brought since his arrival almost four years ago.
Between November 2022 and January 2026, they lost just eight of 61 home Premier League games, winning 44 of them.
That included 15 straight wins between March 2023 and December 2023.
They also went 12 months unbeaten in the top flight between August 2024 and August 2025, but since the turn of the year Villa have been fragile at home in comparison.
Defeats by Everton, Brentford, Chelsea and Tottenham threatened their top-four place last season, with Villa needing late goals to earn a draw against Leeds and claim victories against Brighton and Sunderland.
That has continued this season with Villa Park's capacity down to around 37,000 in the void left by the North Stand, something Brentford boss Keith Andrews picked up on, saying he hated playing when one stand was missing.
Villa could still make light of it in Europe, though, with Viking also travelling to Birmingham in the league phase on 21 October.
After an opening win at Club Brugge, successive victories would put them on course for qualification before November, despite their home issues.
"It is a massive test against a good team but we need to be winning these games," added Cash.
"That is the bar we have set for ourselves. Hopefully we can make it loud - three-stand loud."

Qantas flight grounded after bedbug outbreak
- Published
A Qantas flight from Italy to Australia was cancelled on Saturday, after an outbreak of bedbugs on the plane.
During the previous flight on Friday - a nearly 17-hour journey from Perth to Rome - some passengers had complained that they were being bitten by bugs, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.
They were reportedly given antihistamines to help ease the itch of the bites, but supplies ran out.
The Boeing 787 Dreamliner had to be grounded for "a deep clean", a Qantas spokesperson told the BBC.
"We sincerely apologise to customers for the cancellation of Saturday's Rome to Perth service, which allowed our engineers and maintenance teams to carry out a deep clean of the aircraft after an issue was identified on a small number of economy seats," the spokesperson said.
All affected customers were provided with accommodation and were rebooked on alternative flights within 48 hours of their original departure, the carrier said.
Bedbugs are small, wingless parasites that can live on clothes, furniture and bedding. Their bites can be itchy but they do not usually cause more serious health problems, the NHS website says, external.
But they can be difficult and expensive to get rid of. Treatment includes washing all bedding, clothing, and household materials like curtains on a hot wash and tumble dry, or they can be put in plastic bags in a freezer for three or four days.
Bedbugs causing travel chaos is not unusual - less than two weeks ago, several Southeastern train services in England were cancelled after drivers discovered the creepy-crawlies in their cabs.
In 2017, British Airways apologised to a family travelling from Vancouver to London, after they were left covered in bug bites from an overnight flight.
And Turkish Airlines faced with a PR nightmare last year after the New York Times reported, external of several instances of bedbug infestations on its planes - and allegations at the time that the airline did nothing about it.

The Sentinelese, living on North Sentinel Island in the Bay of Bengal, are one of the most isolated peoples on earth.
Part of an archipelago governed by India, it is prohibited by law to venture within 5km of their island. And when a missionary did manage to land on the beach in 2018, he was killed by bow and arrow.
Yet none of that was to deter influencer Mykhailo Polyakov, who last year filmed himself arriving on North Sentinel Island, and leaving a can of coke on the beach.
Features writer Elle Hunt documents the rise of a new breed of influencer, travelling around the world, and streaming to millions their attempts to contact the uncontacted – despite the warnings of indigenous rights groups that the consequences could be fatal, both for the social media stars and the communities they risk exposing to disease.
Helen Pidd also speaks to Ecuadorian indigenous rights activist María José Andrade Cerda about the rights and wrongs of this new world.

A woman who claimed to be a niece of former chief minister Mamata Banerjee allegedly tried to enter her security cordon with a knife in an intoxicated state on Tuesday evening, the Mamata All India Trinamool Congress claimed.
Party MP Dola Sen sent a written complaint to the Kalighat police station in Kolkata stating that the incident took place around 6 pm near Banerjee’s residence in Kalighat.
“This is to inform you that around 6 pm on Tuesday, a lady named Tannishtha Saha, reportedly known as a civic volunteer and a drug addict, came with a violent mode and attacked Mamata Banerjee with a knife and furthermore claimed herself as her niece,” Sen stated in her letter to the officer-in-charge of Kalighat police station.
Banerjee had come out of her house to inaugurate a Durga Puja pandal near her residence when the woman tried to enter the security cordon from behind.
“When I asked her identity, she said that Banerjee was her paternal aunt. I refused to let her in. She then tried to sneak into the security cordon from the front. When she failed, she lay down on the road and started hurling abuses. It was then that we saw that she had a knife,” Sen said.
A TMC leader said that the woman was overpowered by TMC workers around Banerjee and later handed over to the police.
No senior police officials, including Rahul De, deputy commissioner of police (south), responded to calls and messages.

In October, rumors circulated that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration did not extend an invitation to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, an international body that aims to preserve democracy and human rights across the globe, to observe the 2026 midterm elections.
The OSCE explains that its goal in observing elections is to "assess the extent to which fundamental freedoms are respected in the campaign and if the elections are characterized by equality, universality, political pluralism, confidence, transparency and accountability."
Social media users who shared the claim noted that it was the first time since 2002, when the OSCE first started observing U.S. elections, that the group had not received an invitation. One post featured an image of Trump with text reading, "Trump demands 'secure' elections, yet rejects independent scrutiny and offers no explanation. Perhaps security was never the point."
The rumor circulated after Trump's Department of Justice said it would deploy its own election monitors, sparking concerns from Trump's opponents.
The claim was true.
In a statement posted to its website Sept. 23. the OSCE confirmed that the U.S. had not invited it to observe the 2026 midterm elections.
"The decision not to invite the OSCE to observe the 2026 midterm congressional elections in the United States is regrettable, particularly given the long-standing co-operation with the country in the field of election observation," the organization said.
They wrote that the decision was "not in line with the 1990 Copenhagen Document," which the group describes as an outline of basic human rights and freedoms that "broadens the scope of human rights matters to include election commitments" and "recognizes that the presence of international observers can enhance the electoral process."
The OSCE confirmed in its statement that the 2026 midterms marked the first time it was not invited to observe a federal U.S. election since the group first began observing elections in the country in 2002. That year, the OSCE sent representatives to the Florida gubernatorial election. 
The 2002 observation occurred after the contentious 2000 presidential election between George W. Bush and Al Gore that resulted in a recount in Florida. The matter ultimately ended up with the Supreme Court, and the United States didn't see a president-elect officially declared until that December.
According to a 2004 article by the Commission on Security and Cooperation in Europe about the history of the U.S. inviting OSCE to observe elections, following its 2002 observation in Florida, OSCE observed the 2003 California gubernatorial recall election that actor Arnold Schwarzenegger won. 
OSCE said it has observed 12 federal elections, including six midterms, since 2002.
The CSCE wrote in 2004 that the U.S. had formally invited observers to its elections in 1996, 1998, 2000 and 2002, noting that 2002 was the first election that OSCE had observed. 
In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections in November, Trump continued his attempts to implement voting restrictions and pitched giving Americans $5,000 each if Republicans won, sparking opposition from critics.
A White House official told Snopes via email that "no other nation has done more to advance the cause of human freedom and representative government" than the United States and added, "American elections will be administered, participated in, and observed by American citizens."
The White House did not deny that it had declined an invite to OSCE observers and provided no explanation for departing from decades of precedent.
We reached out to the OSCE and the Justice Department for further comment and will update this article if we receive responses.
For further reading, we fact-checked a claim that Trump thanked billionaire Elon Musk for artificially increasing votes for Republicans ahead of the 2026 midterms.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.
Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.
The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.
In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.
Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.
The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.
In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

FIFA will propose to its members a $6.35 billion development fund for the next four-year cycle, including a boosted amount of $25 million for each national association, two people with knowledge of the plan and a letter reviewed by The Associated Press confirmed Tuesday.
Football’s world governing body planned to use the financial success of the latest World Cup to enhance investment in the sport’s development across 211 FIFA member associations, confederations and other stakeholders. Originally, each association was to receive $10 million for the four-year period.
FIFA planned to distribute more than $3.5 billion from its financial reserves which were boosted with the success of its 48-team World Cup, said two officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the proposal had not been announced.
FIFA estimates approximately $15 billion in revenue in the 2022-26 cycle, including the men’s World Cup hosted by the United States, Canada and Mexico, significantly above projections, both people told AP.
The proposal comes as European football leaders seek a candidate to try to oust Gianni Infantino as FIFA president. Infantino’s divisive World Cup private investment plan — that was scrapped within days of being revealed in July — prompted UEFA to act.
Also read | With FIFA World Cup 2027 looming large, US women hold world champion Spain to draw
Infantino, who became FIFA president in 2016, is seeking reelection next year.
On Sept. 28, the leaders of football’s six continental confederations received a letter from Infantino with the plan, which is expected to be finalised at the upcoming FIFA council meeting and approved at its congress in March. The AP has reviewed the letter.
“Taken together, your submissions confirm broad agreement on the central objective: FIFA’s financial success must serve football and all FIFA’s 211 member associations,” Infantino said in the letter.
“I am confident that together we can reach a sustainable and properly supported outcome for FIFA’s member associations and for football in every part of the world.”
One of the people with knowledge of the proposal said continental confederations made the suggestion for FIFA to use its reserves in the plan, which now offers $99 million for each of the six confederations.
UEFA announced in August it was preparing a criminal complaint against Infantino in Switzerland for possible financial mismanagement in the World Cup sell-off deal and has asked courts in the United States to authorise discovery of evidence.
UEFA’s 55 members account for more than a quarter of FIFA’s 211 member federations who can vote in the election on March 18 in Rabat, Morocco.
Any candidate to challenge Infantino must enter the race by a Nov. 18 deadline.
Infantino indicated last month he would be open to an independent review of FIFA’s governance system and signaled a willingness to consider reforms.

Kelly made these remarks during the Oct. 5 episode of "The Megyn Kelly Show." She called her thoughts "the narrative that is likely to have occurred here, in my opinion." She did not identify Jane Doe by name, nor did she provide any evidence credibly confirming the woman's identity.
Last week, Snopes readers searched our site and sent us emails asking whether political podcaster and former Fox News host Megyn Kelly made remarks critical of the Jane Doe in the Cornell University rape case.
That Jane Doe, a former female Cornell student not identified by name in court documents or elsewhere to protect her identity, has accused seven current or former male Cornell students of sexually assaulting and raping her in an on-campus fraternity house between Oct. 19 and 20, 2024. Snopes has produced numerous reports examining claims regarding the case.
In this instance, one reader sent an image purportedly showing a text transcript of Kelly's comments, asking, "Did Megyn Kelly say [this] on Oct. 5?" Another reader asked whether someone created video of the remarks with an artificial intelligence tool. The email read, in part:
I saw a horrific video of Megyn Kelly victim blaming Jane Doe who has accused seven Cornell University fraternity members of raping her. It was so offensive I was in disbelief that even Megan Kelly would stoop so low.
And it wasn't just me, because others in the thread following the post also wondered if what we saw was real or AI.
The text transcript image, or quotes from it, also appeared on Facebook, Instagram, Threads and X.
(@girlsreallyrule via X)
According to the transcript users shared, Kelly said she believes Jane Doe "made a decision to get it on" with four of the seven accused male students and "enjoyed it," and made negative remarks about the alleged Jane Doe's physical appearance.
In sum, Kelly authentically made these statements during Monday's episode of "The Megyn Kelly Show." SiriusXM and YouTube broadcast the show live. The relevant moments begin at around the 15-minute mark in this YouTube video.
During the episode, Kelly does not identify Jane Doe by name, nor does she provide any evidence credibly confirming the woman's identity.
Snopes contacted Kelly's Devil May Care Media company to ask if she wished to provide further comment, seeing as users were sharing her words and questioning whether she actually made the remarks. We will update this article if we receive further details.
More of what Kelly said
Just before the transcript shared on social media begins, Kelly says, "How is this progress? The absolute freak-out by all women. Not all of them are freaking out, but the ones who are, over this, accounts for zero agency for women whatsoever."
The transcript begins immediately after that, with Kelly saying, "No one will even consider the possibility that this woman made a decision to get it on with four men total, not seven, and enjoyed it because, I'm just going to be honest, she's not the most attractive gal." She then criticizes the physical appearance of the woman she asserts is Jane Doe.
Kelly describes her thoughts as "the narrative that is likely to have occurred here, in my opinion."
Her mention of "four men total, not seven" referenced reporting appearing to come from The New York Times, saying that only four of the accused men acknowledged having sexual contact with Jane Doe. The Times reported:
But in hours of interviews and a statement collected during Cornell's administrative investigation over the winter of 2024, all the men denied any wrongdoing. Four acknowledged having sexual contact with the woman but said that their interactions had been consensual. The others denied participating in sexual encounters.

How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?
- Published
Imagine a world where Manchester City had not used "sham contracts" to build a team capable of winning three Premier League titles, one FA Cup and three EFL Cups.
If City were the winners, then there had to be losers.
Not just those teams who finished runners-up or lost cup finals.
The potential impact runs much deeper and includes missed Champions League qualification, relegation and Premier League prize money.
Thirty-five other teams played in the English top flight between 2009 and 2018.
And every one could in some way claim to have been left financially out of pocket.
City, of course, continue to deny any wrongdoing and they have appealed. But as it stands they are guilty of all charges related to inflating their sponsorship income to the tune of £830m, plus another £90m in expenses.
Strip that money out and it changes the whole complexion of the competition.
BBC Sport has crunched the numbers to assess the potential financial impact on the top flight.
How the figures are worked out
When Sheikh Mansour bought Manchester City in 2008 they were far removed from the club you see today.
Since finishing fifth in 1991-92, the last season before the formation of the Premier League, City's highest placing had been eighth in 2004-05.
The Abu Dhabi money poured in via what the Premier League's independent commission described as a "disguised funding scheme". It took the club's sponsorship revenues from being on a par with Stoke City in 2008-09 to eventually overtaking those of Manchester United.
City finished fifth in 2009-10. Since then, not once have they finished outside the top four in the Premier League.
Did this money deny other clubs a place in the competition, and other kinds of success?
This article is not trying to set out how much compensation a team might be able to claim.
Nor is it saying any one team would definitely have avoided relegation or reached the Champions League.
It is about chance, the possibility that a very different City team would have taken to the field without the hundreds of millions pumped in by the club's Abu Dhabi owners.
It has not considered potential future earnings from success, including sponsors' bonuses and further prize money.
Nor has it factored in players who may feel they have missed out on salary increases, or triggered payments, for how their club might have performed.
This is purely about domestic impact:
- Lost prize money by league placing
- Missed potential Champions League earnings
- Europa League payments
- Loss of Premier League status
- Impact of cup final defeats
- What Manchester's 'super-profit' deal with City owners has paid out so far 
  - Published8 hours ago
- Were any current Man City players signed during charges period? 
  - Published3 hours ago
How City gained £1.17bn, and others may have lost £844m
The full impact of City's behaviour on other clubs could be calculated at £844m.
- £188.2m in Premier League placing money
- £349.7m in relegation costs
- £217.8m in missed Champions League prize money
- £88.3m related to domestic cup competitions and the Europa League
We calculated these figures by taking published prize money from the relevant seasons.
For Premier League place money, each team that finished below City is considered to have potentially missed a payment for one place.
For relegation, this is the minimum value of being in the Premier League for the next season, minus the received parachute payment.
For the Champions League, we took City's earnings from the following seasons and deducted the impacted teams' Europa League prize money.
But City also earned prize money themselves during this period.
Across the competitions, City were paid £1.17bn:
- £812.3m from the Premier League - total income from prize money and broadcast revenues
- £363.4m via the Champions League
- £900,000 from the FA Cup victory
- £300,000 from the three EFL Cup victories
The most impacted: How Spurs could have missed out on £120m
"We have lived through a period of deception," former Tottenham Hotspur boss Mauricio Pochettino said last month.
"No type of punishment will make it possible to repair what was done."
You can see his point. Spurs finished one place outside the Champions League positions in four (although one only was under Pochettino) of the eight seasons in which City qualified for Europe's elite competition.
BBC Sport took City's earnings from the Champions League in the following season, and deducted Tottenham's Europa League prize money.
Over the four seasons Spurs missed out, Manchester City earned £148.2m from the Champions League, with Tottenham taking £29.9m from the Europa League.
The 2014-15 campaign led to the biggest deficit, as City finished second in the Premier League and Tottenham came fifth. City received £71.2m for reaching the Champions League semi-finals in the following season, but Spurs were only paid £17.7m from the Europa League - a difference of £53.5m.
Spurs also finished behind City in the Premier League table six times, with the cumulative prize money difference worth £6.6m.
The north Londoners did benefit in the 2013-14 season, as they only qualified for Europe because City beat Sunderland in the final of the EFL Cup.
Spurs gained £5.1m from their 2014-15 Europa League campaign which would not have been possible without City's success.
Taking into account all competitions, that produced a net financial loss for Spurs of £119.9m.
Did City's EFL Cup win cost Liverpool £37.8m?
The 2015-16 EFL Cup final proved to be decisive for Liverpool's hopes of European football.
Jurgen Klopp's men lost to City on penalties following a 1-1 draw. The Europa League place transferred to the league, and went to West Ham United.
Liverpool only finished eighth, which was not enough to qualify for Europe.
Had Liverpool won the final, they would have entered the Europa League, and this provides a key financial comparison.
Manchester United won the Europa League in 2016-17, receiving prize money of £37.8m. As part of that amount, the Red Devils' market pool payment, which is based upon the value of the television rights, was £26.6m.
While we cannot say for certain that Liverpool would have won the Europa League, they were a club of similar stature to Manchester United, which provides a comparison.
The market pool share may also have been slightly lower with both Liverpool and Manchester United involved.
Together with Premier League place money of £10.6m - Liverpool finished below City in all nine relevant seasons - the total financial impact on the Merseyside club was £52.3m.
As for the FA Cup, City won it just once in the period they were scrutinised over, beating Stoke in 2010-11. The difference in prize money was £900,000, with the runners-up going into the Europa League.
Everton were denied Europe five times
Everton missed out on the Champions League once, in 2013-14, and on four other occasions they finished one place below the final Europa League spot.
The Champions League place is calculated to be worth £32.6m - the £39m earned by Manchester City minus the Toffees' £6.4m winnings from the Europa League they competed in instead.
The combined impact on missing out on the Europa League four times is £23.2m.
Add on the £10.6m from Premier League prize money, and the total financial effect is £66.4m - making Everton the third-most impacted club.
Did two relegations cost Hull City £99m?
While parachute payments provide something of a cushion, relegation from the Premier League is still a considerable financial hit.
Could the teams who finished in 18th place, one spot from safety, argue that they might have stayed up but for City?
There are a couple of ways of looking at this.
Firstly, the results against City who took at least four points off every 18th-placed team other than Birmingham.
Secondly, the mere fact that City were able to assemble a squad far better than their finances should have allowed. Could they otherwise have been involved in relegation battles?
Again, this is not to say City would have been relegated. It is about chance.
BBC Sport has taken the total prize money earned by the team finishing in 20th in the following season. That suggests a minimum return for having stayed in the top flight.
Deducted from that is the first season of parachute payments to give a net amount.
Hull were relegated twice in the period, costing the Tigers £93.78m.
The Tigers finished below City in the table four times, adding £5.2m in place money to the sum.
It leaves the East Yorkshire club as the second-most impacted on £99m.
Swansea are fourth in the table with £63.1m. Of that total, £54m is from relegation and £9.1m in place money from the seven seasons the Swans were in the top flight.
Newcastle suffered relegation by finishing 18th in 2015-16, costing them a projected £60.4m, of which £7.9m was place money.
Norwich (£43.8m), Wigan (£39.6m), Burnley (£31.1m), Bolton (£26.4m) and Birmingham (£25.1m) also suffered relegations in 18th place.
The loss of Champions League money
Alongside Tottenham, four other teams missed out on Champions League football by one place across the eight seasons when City qualified.
The biggest impact was on Chelsea, who finished fifth in 2017-18.
City earned £79.2m from reaching the quarter-finals of the Champions League, with Chelsea getting £39.4m from winning the Europa League. That left Chelsea with a deficit of £39.8m.
Also just missing out on the Champions League were Everton (5th in 2013-14, £32.6m deficit), and Arsenal (5th in 2016-17, £22.1m deficit).
The only team not to experience much of a financial impact were Manchester United, who were fifth in 2015-16.
City got no further than the round of 16 in the Champions League, earning £42.6m, while United won the Europa League that season, receiving £37.8m. It left the Red Devils with a deficit of £4.8m.
The cumulative cost of league places
In the Premier League there is no specific prize pot for being crowned champions.
Broadcast revenue is allocated on a merit basis by final league position.
It is a 1+1 system, so the club in 20th get the base payment. Then the team in 19th get the base payment two times. For 18th, it is that base amount three times, and so on.
It means that the only financial difference, in prize money at least, for the team finishing runners-up in one of Manchester City's three title-winning seasons is one base payment.
Could any team claim they might have finished one place higher?
The value of a Premier League place rose sharply in line with the broadcast deals over the period of City's offences.
In 2010-11 it was £755,881 per place, and by 2016-17 it was up to £1.94m.
If any compensation were to be considered, Everton, Liverpool and Stoke City would have the biggest claim of £10.7m, having finished below City in all nine seasons.
West Brom and West Ham's total is £9.9m, with Swansea on £9.1m.
At the other end of the scale are the seven clubs who spent one season in the Premier League, including Blackpool (£756,756), Portsmouth (£800,424) and Huddersfield (£1.93m).

When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.
“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it's for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”
The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.
The point of the game was to stress-test the world’s response to a group of prospective technologies known collectively as solar radiation modification. These technologies promise to reverse global warming by reflecting away a portion of the sunlight reaching Earth, for example by spraying particles of sulphur dioxide or some other manufactured substance into the atmosphere. The cooling effect of this kind of solar geoengineering is widely accepted. It would mimic the well-known impacts of large volcanic eruptions, which temporarily cool the planet by half a degree or more. But the fallout is less certain—and less equal. Some regions will suffer: Models predict drying in sub-Saharan Africa and more intense tropical storms in the Atlantic. The cooling effect would also last only as long as the geoengineering continued; after that the global temperature could shoot back up with wild and hard-to-predict effects.
Until recently, the idea of solar radiation modification was a speculative niche of climate science. That has changed fast. Private firms are exploring solar geoengineering as a commercial opportunity: Last year, a US-Israeli startup called Stardust Solutions raised $60 million, and in May it released details of a suite of new inventions it claims would give humans the ability to dial down the global temperature as desired. In August, Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX might be a candidate for delivering geoengineering interventions, threw his voice behind solar geoengineering, writing on X: “Space satellites to control temperature and massive geo-engineering will be needed or it will be game over.”
The world is going to have to make decisions about how to govern this technology much sooner than most policymakers imagine, Cynthia Scharf, a former UN advisor, told WIRED. “It's not 15 years from now; it's in the next decade, easily.”
It was against this backdrop that Danielle Young, an assistant professor in international relations at Leeds University, arranged the war game. Its setting was a hastily convened UN committee charged with coordinating the international response to developments in solar geoengineering. The game unfolded over simulated meetings set at three points in time: the present, September 2027, and September 2028. Each step ratcheted up the stakes, with the game creators introducing new advances in sunlight-reflecting technology. As in real life, no one knew all the facts, and players had to respond to events that were bringing the world closer to a full-scale attempt at deploying solar geoengineering tech, even when they may not have a full picture of what had truly occurred—or what any of the others were up to.
The first session set the tone. Distrust and disinformation dominated. As participants discussed rules governing outdoor experiments in an attempt to agree an international deal, players representing both the US and China told the group they could not sign a deal that constrained their pursuit of research considered to be in their “national interest.” Nor could they accept a deal that would see their superpower rival taking the lead technologically. Speaking to WIRED, Jeffrey Nielsen, a major in the US Army who played the role of a US national security attaché, summarized the position as “worse than no deal at all is any deal that favors China.”
Tensions escalated when the team running the simulation handed the Russian delegates an “intelligence report” indicating they had found a plane near the Bering Strait believed to be involved in a US geoengineering research program. The US team—which was indeed flying research missions—accused Russia of disinformation.
Meanwhile, the US became convinced China was also conducting research and developing its own program. Beijing’s representatives had tried to insert language into a mooted deal that would ensure no retroactive punishment for past experiments. Then, China approached a player representing SpaceX to float the idea of a technology-sharing program. In a private discussion away from the group, the SpaceX player immediately reported the Chinese approach to the US team. The US demanded an international investigation. The finger-pointing continued, and countries abandoned the talks. The Canadian representative called it a “humiliating defeat.”
At the end of the session, Nielsen was pumped. He’d busted China and derailed any prospect of a global deal. In the context of the game, he told WIRED, it was a “humungous victory” for the Americans. But Young, the researcher who designed the scenario, said the Chinese were not, in fact, conducting experiments in the game. Mutual suspicion meant all parties left the room believing the others were moving as quickly as possible to build their own geoengineering capability.
What played out in the first session reflected “the likelihood, in my opinion, of the geoengineering arms race,” says Nielsen, who clarified he was speaking to WIRED in a private capacity and not representing the views of the actual US government. Most experts agree it would take a superpower’s reach to ensure the safe passage of planes needed to deliver payloads of dust to the stratosphere in a geoengineering exercise. But neither the US nor China would lightly cede control over the global thermostat, says Nielsen, and distrust and poor communication are a significant risk: “Any action related to the issue by one actor can be perceived as malintent by the other.”
The threat of falling behind a rival is “a very strong driver of research and development of capability,” a former British diplomat with a background in national security told WIRED. “But that's not at all the same thing as deployment.” There are similarities with nuclear arms dynamics—though solar radiation management, unlike nukes, has more obvious benefits as well as downsides, many of which are poorly understood. “There is an interdependence here,” says the former diplomat, who was not involved in the game and spoke on condition of anonymity to preserve relationships. “It's not an inherently zero-sum game.”
Scharf, who represented the US government alongside Nielsen in the game, told WIRED a “scientifically transparent international collaboration” between China and the US “might be the best we can do in terms of fending off a very dangerous competition between the two. But I certainly cannot imagine that happening under the Trump administration.”
Compounding the problem is a lack of information. Geoengineering has historically been viewed with suspicion and often ignored by the scientific mainstream. One researcher told WIRED he’d experienced ostracization and barriers to academic progression owing to his interest in the technology; he no longer works in the field.
This lack of scientific interest greatly frustrated Golja, who spent much of the game watching as a bystander while political posturing dominated. Given the low level of knowledge around solar radiation modification and its side effects, she was one of very few experts who could help the participants understand the climate impacts of what they were discussing—yet she was largely ignored.“I was just so surprised about how little anyone actually cared about the science,” she says.
In the next sessions, the organizers tried in vain to nudge the talks back toward the realities of climate change. The participants received frequent notifications of climate disasters. These barely registered. Golja had prepared an “emulator,” a real-world demonstration of the best available science on how solar radiation management might affect weather patterns in different regions. It was ignored. If country representatives asked her anything, it was usually a leading question looking for data that would serve their ends or frame a rival’s proposal as reckless.
Then, during the last day, players were trying to find a way to respond to reports that a major plume of aerosols had been detected. In the game, this had been caused by a joint US-Saudi test of Stardust’s technology, though not everyone knew this. Finally, scientific advice was at a premium. Countries needed to know how to establish a monitoring network of satellites and other observational tools in order to prevent tests like this from happening in secret. A player representing an NGO called the Climate Futures Cooperative approached Golja, offering her money to fund such a scheme.
“Great. Fabulous. Why wouldn't I do that?” she recalls thinking.
But it soon came out that the Climate Futures Cooperative was actually backed by the fossil fuel industry. The organizers had recognized that fossil fuel companies and major producing countries like the US and Saudi Arabia would have a clear interest in removing barriers from the development of a technology that could combat climate change without having to immediately stop burning coal, oil, and gas. The shadowy NGO spent the game subtly wrecking the vibe and carping about process—though mostly they just sat back and let it burn. Some players—Russia, the US, SpaceX and Stardust—figured out the CFC was not what it seemed, says Young. “But they assessed it was to their benefit and didn’t draw attention to it.” Then the CFC chose its moment to offer money to Golja, only to crater her credibility, isolating and fragmenting the voice of science in the room.
“It was a whole mess,” says Golja.
That final lesson in fossil fuel realpolitik was about all Golja could endure. By the end of the last day, she was in tears.
At no point did the countries in the game agree to a deal, despite multiple proposals being put forward. European countries and Canada tried to build support for safeguards and open scientific research, but the talks constantly got bogged down by delay tactics and veered into tense showdowns over duelling strategic interests. In their final report, the researchers running the simulation—whose work was sponsored by the UK government-funded Advanced Research and Invention Agency—concluded that “strategic competition and state sovereignty drove the simulations, not climate concerns.”
Simulations like this one are not supposed to predict the future. The outcomes depend on the design of the game and the relative personalities and experience of the players. Many of those in the room lacked first-hand diplomatic and national security experience. The UN forum, which organizers selected as the game’s setting, may also not be as effective as talks between smaller groups of major countries. But the experiment in London echoed and refracted through the real world, during and after the months it was running.
In March, two papers from conservative US think tanks urged the Trump administration to take the lead on solar radiation modification and counter China’s threat. One memorably invoked a new, MAGA-coded term: “Weather sovereignty.” This month, the Observer newspaper in London revealed that the UK Ministry of Defense had paid a deep tech security consultancy to conduct research into sunlight reflection. Then, last week, the British government released its first official policy paper on the field, backing further research but stating firmly that it did not support deployment and “does not plan to do so.” Stardust has continued its lobbying of the US and governments around the world; CEO Yanai Yedvab told WIRED its job was getting easier as, unlike before, “the majority of policymakers … are already aware of this technology.”
Stardust has always maintained that it will not conduct large-scale outdoor experiments, let alone full deployment, before global governance is in place. “We are developing a very powerful tool,” Yedvab says. “When you develop this kind of powerful technology—and you have many precedents—national interests will play out. We're not naive about it.”
Meanwhile, drivers of the climate crisis are intensifying. During the time span of the game, efforts to curtail the use of fossil fuels were being undermined by rising energy costs and political hostility. Week after week, an incredible summer of drought and heat pounded Europe. In the final week of August, the collapse of a glacier on the Tibet-Nepal border fulfilled the prophecies of decades of climate scientists, killing more than 1,450 people.
In the months since the simulation ended, Golja has reevaluated many things. On a corkboard behind her desk, she has pinned up a note to herself, laying out a vision for life in a world ruled by narrow geopolitical self-interest rather than science, evidence, and reason. Her answer: She plans to return to the small coastal town where she grew up in Connecticut and use her expertise to help local climate groups build the seawalls and coastal erosion buffers they will need to cope with the inevitable. “To try and make a difference where it feels like I actually have traction,” she says. After what she saw, pursuing science in the hope of informing global decisions no longer held as much appeal. “Now it feels a little bit more personal.”
