Minecraft Dungeons 2 is a substantial step forward for Mojang’s action-packed RPG. Surely it traded the original game’s disconnected missions for a sprawling world packed with dungeons, dangerous mobs, and mountains of loot. But that is precisely why I enjoyed taking on my own adventure through the Overworld and the vivid Sift dimension.
I had an absolute blast completing the main campaign, and I’m dying to try out the future DLCs planned for the game. So, before you purchase it, here’s a Minecraft Dungeons 2 review to help you.
Bye-Bye Menu Hopping: The Overworld Finally Grows Up
The original Minecraft Dungeons had a pretty straightforward structure: you select a mission, clear its objectives, collect loot, and return to the hub. While it worked, the world often felt more like a collection of disconnected dioramas. Thankfully, Minecraft Dungeons 2 finally gives the adventure aspect some room to breathe.
Although I had just visited the prequel recently to brush up on the lore and obtain the Hero Cape in Minecraft, the interconnected world is one of my favorite improvements. Instead of hopping between missions through a menu, you travel across distinct regions, stumbling into unexpected side quests, unearthing hidden dungeons, and crossing paths with some eccentric-looking NPCs.
While Brave Haven acts as the central operational hub, you can still explore other major biomes and perform all your enchanting, upgrading actions, purchasing new gear, or even teleporting elsewhere.
As you explore, rewards obtained from defeating the Minecraft Dungeons 2 enemies roaming all around feel organic. The side quests give you a legitimate reason to revisit the places even after the main story content.
Most importantly, the world feels alive, especially when an impromptu ambush completely derails your planned itinerary. Say I’m chasing a quest marker, but I get horribly sidetracked defeating a bunch of Royal Guards and Illagers. Although I could’ve used the fast travel stations to reach the nearest checkpoint, that’s exactly the chaos I’m looking for in a Minecraft ARPG game.
Welcome to Mojang’s Trippiest Dimension Yet – The Sift
If the Overworld sets up the structural bread and butter, The Sift is where Mojang brings out their fine China and shows what they’re capable of. The Sift in Minecraft Dungeons 2 is a surreal dimension, flexing wild biomes, bizarre alien fauna, and some lethal encounters.
I genuinely enjoyed exploring the aesthetic palette that broke away from the usual grass and stony blocks, giving the region its own charm. Discovering new enemies and bosses also makes discovering the hidden areas exciting, as it triggers that classic, “What on earth wrecked my health bar?” excitement.
It is also a massive narrative lore drop for the broader franchise, as Mojang has confirmed The Sift comes to Minecraft in 2027.
My main gripe? The game pulls you out far too soon. The Sift teases astronomical potential, and I just hoped that the main story was a bit more connected to exploring the secrets of this dimension.
Easy to Pick Up, Hard to Put Down, Buildcrafting Comes to Dungeons
On the surface, combat retains its signature pick-up-and-play grace. Light attacks, ranged shots, dodge rolls, jump smashes, Talisman passives, and a handful of Artifact abilities clear hordes of enemies before they turn your light-hearted adventure into a respawn speedrun.
The secret sauce is in the overhauled equipment system. While the original forces you into rigid, single-slot armor archetypes, the sequel throws open the workshop doors, allowing you to mix-and-match individual pieces with unique passive effects.
Whether you love to transform into a tanky build, become a self-healing wizard, wipe out the entire mob, or one-shot bosses with your ranged weapons, there are a ton of options for the best builds in Minecraft Dungeons 2.
Apart from buildcrafting, enchanting offers endless tinkering while an equipment upgrade system ensures that your prized Special and Unique weapons don’t turn out to be a paperweight. That feature eliminates the worst crime in loot games: watching your favorite weapon immediately become useless after five minutes of finding it.
The Story is Fun, but the Real Magic Happens in Co-Op
The Minecraft Dungeons 2 lore is a reliable excuse to start smashing things because the Illagers are up to no good. The narrative momentum moves at a solid pace, and the cinematic set-pieces pack in plenty of visual punch.
Minecraft Dungeons 2 probably will not win awards for the best storytelling, but I can assure you that you’ll definitely not rest until you’ve taken a hit at one of the High Council members.
The core gameplay loop rarely misses a beat. You cleave through enemy ambushes, chart through the unknown map of Minecraft Dungeons 2, and gradually turn your unarmored hero into a walking menace.
It shines the brightest when you play co-op in Minecraft Dungeons 2. If you’re not like me, having a ton of people around to try out the game, you’ll never want to head out on a solo adventure here. Whether your friends are seasoned dungeon crawlers or you’re introducing someone to the ARPG genre for the first time, the smooth mechanics and accessibility make it an effortless recommendation.
Performance: Stumbling Launch, Yet Smooth Sailing FPS
I tested Minecraft Dungeons 2 on a mid-range gaming laptop via Xbox Game Pass, and my personal run was smooth sailing. I managed to avoid the stability hiccups, FPS drops, and instant crashes reported by fellow community members on Steam. But if you know someone facing the same network problem, the Minecraft Dungeons 2 error code guide will surely help them out.
My Setup:
CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 7435HS
Motherboard: LA-N591P Laptop Motherboard
GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060
RAM: 24 GB (2x12GB) 4800MHz DDR5
SSD: M.2 PCIe Gen 4×4 NVMe SSD
Although the launch week wasn’t quite as smooth across the broader community, Mojang moved fast and rolled out a hotfix update within days of launch. The patch targeted several client-side server crashes and bugs that would otherwise cause the bosses to show some unexpected behavior.
Verdict: Mojang Struck Diamond, but the Endgame Needs More Ore
Minecraft Dungeons 2 is a fantastic sequel that suffers from a bit of an identity crisis when the credits roll. If you’ve played the original Dungeons extensively, you should know how massive the replayability of the game was with each DLC.
I think that Minecraft Dungeons 2 falls short in that aspect, but it doesn’t necessarily mean you should not have a go at it. It’s quite the opposite.
You see, when the feeling of wanting more of Minecraft Dungeons 2 strikes right at the moment you have reached the highest level, completed the main story, side quests, and run through the dungeons more than once, then it’s pretty obvious that Mojang Studios and Double Eleven have done a fantastic job in producing this sequel.
It leapfrogs the original in almost every measurable way, and is a must for all die-hard Minecraft fans. It’s a casual ARPG made for people of a wide age range. Whether you’re in school, you’re a teenager, or a parent, Minecraft Dungeons 2 is just as easy to pick up for someone who has never held a controller before, as it has enough intricate build-crafting options for a veteran dungeon crawler.

A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1?
- Published
Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the new deal to take the sport back to Africa - ending an absence of nearly 40 years - as a "landmark" achievement.
Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time.
But the sport's bosses already recognised the importance of the project. And this deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since it bought the sport at the start of 2017.
Rwanda, which has signed a 10-year deal to host an African Grand Prix from the "early 2030s", has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed.
That's because the east-central African country has managed to put together a single plan with the requisite financial backing and ambition to make the project work.
Morocco never found the requisite finances and South Africa has up to four separate projects ongoing with different promoters in three different locations, two in Cape Town.
For F1, with other countries also interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with.
The new Rwandan circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, is part of a wider development near a new international airport, currently under construction, that also includes facilities in sectors such as entertainment, residential, hotels, spas and sports science, as well as an innovation hub.
At the moment it is a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
But for Domenicali the deal marks a key moment in the sport's development under his leadership.
"It is the legacy of all of us to be in this very special moment," he said as he took the stage at the announcement in Kigali with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.
He added that he was "very proud", and that F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision".
"Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories," he said. "A nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past.
"It is a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination. A nation that has become a destination for international investment, innovation and opportunity."
- Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A 
  - Published8 hours ago
From a purely sporting point of view, it's easy to see why Domenicali is so chuffed.
He has brought F1 back to Africa, where the last grand prix was held in 1993 in South Africa, and opened up a potential market of 100 million people that is largely untapped.
And the track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, promises a great deal.
Wurz is passionate about creating circuits with natural flow that challenge drivers, and he has envisaged this one in the style of the classic Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello tracks, with its own unique character - and the renders released do bear some obvious similarities to the first part of Suzuka.
The track is not completely finalised - there will be further consultation with teams and drivers - but is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long, with 17 corners, and will use the undulating Rwandan landscape to help create a dramatic layout. It has nearly 200m of elevation change.
President Kagame has backed this project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa.
Kagame said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent", and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return.
"We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate. We have had many other big events."
Why is Rwanda a controversial choice?
Rwanda is fighting off any allegations that money that would be better directed elsewhere, in a country that receives international aid, by emphasising that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.
Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment to accelerate Rwanda's economic transformation and expansion.
The grand prix is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment, bringing more prospects to the country and further growing the overall GDP of the nation.
But Rwanda is not the first country to want to use F1 in this way. And the use of sport to build a country's image can, depending on context, be viewed in a less positive light, as sportswashing - the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.
The F1 calendar already contains a number of countries that fall into this category, not least Saudi Arabia.
Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
F1 is far from the only sport to face such accusations. They have been levelled at Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa as a consequence of sponsorship deals with Rwanda.
Saudi Arabia will host the Fifa World Cup in 2034. Boxing has become heavily reliant on Saudi Arabian finance. Golf came close to being torn apart by Saudi money and the establishment of the rival LIV tour.
F1 is not blind to such issues. Its own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders to address any issues that arise.
It also says it focuses its efforts "in relation to those areas which are within our own direct influence".
A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."

Liverpool's Wirtz problem - does he need to be dropped?
- Published
At the end of the 2024-25 season, Liverpool head coach Arne Slot flew to the south of France to honour talks with Rayan Cherki.
Cherki was on Liverpool's shortlist in their hunt for an attacking midfielder but the main target was Florian Wirtz - who was also wanted by Bayern Munich and Manchester City.
Once Wirtz said his preference was to move to Anfield and join the then-Premier League champions, the £116m deal became a formality.
At the time, his arrival felt like a quality acquisition for Liverpool, but more than a year on things are still not clicking.
The German has scored seven goals and provided 11 assists over 56 Reds appearances, but had no goal involvements against any of the top-10 teams in the Premier League last season.
This term, Wirtz has started every game in the league and Champions League so far - managing just one assist across seven matches.
Those struggles were summed up on Sunday against Manchester City when new Reds boss Andoni Iraola - who succeeded Slot in the summer - replaced Wirtz with Trey Nyoni in the 66th minute, shortly after Ryan Gravenberch was sent off and Erling Haaland broke the deadlock.
Wirtz is only 23 but so is Cherki, who put the icing on the cake in City's 3-0 win at Anfield with an exquisite goal - the kind we have become used to seeing since his £30m move from Lyon in June 2025.
Cherki cost less than a third of what Liverpool paid for Wirtz, but has already scored 16 goals and provided 18 assists in 65 City appearances.
The France attacker has also shown an ability to provide crucial game-changing moments. Liverpool fans haven't seen anywhere near enough of that from Wirtz yet.
"Wirtz has so much ability. I wish I had that ability because he just glides. He makes it look effortless - but he doesn't hurt teams," former Liverpool defender Steven Warnock told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"He doesn't impact the game enough. He drifts in and out of games. He's here for 10 or 20 seconds and then he disappears for five or 10 minutes and you think where is he now?"
After Liverpool's defeat by Man City, Jamie Carragher said it was time for Iraola to drop Wirtz.
"I think he needs to come out of the team, I said that last time out and I'm going to say it again," Carragher told Sky Sports.
"Liverpool played well [against Man City] for a lot of the game before the Gravenberch red card but they didn't create a chance, so they have a real problem with scoring goals and creating chances and that's what you got Wirtz for.
"He's not giving you anything defensively and he's not giving you anything going the other way. I don't want anyone to pile in on the lad but I think we're justified in saying we need more and we can't wait."
'Anyone who loves football can see Wirtz is outstanding'
Given that Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai are all currently sidelined, it would be a big call to drop Wirtz - but Liverpool have two games every week between now and the November international break.
With Gravenberch suspended for Saturday's trip to Brentford, Iraola will likely keep the Dutch midfielder in for Wednesday's Champions League game against LASK in Austria and give a start to Nyoni. More changes are expected from Sunday's defeat.
When it comes to the intensity of the top flight, Wirtz is still finding his feet, but his best performance this season came in the Champions League against Atletico Madrid and he was unlucky not to get an assist when Bradley Barcola fired wide.
Asked on Tuesday if Wirtz needed more time, Iraola defended his player and said: "The other day, he probably he didn't have his best game but he has had good games with us this season.
"Everyone starts looking for answers. He had some good performances in the national team - he scored one goal and he will have better or worse games.
"But I would like to look at it more collectively and more how they help us play and get results and after that I don't care who scores. I think it's a more collective thing."
Seeing Wirtz excel for Germany under Jurgen Klopp is proof - if it was needed - as to why he was seen as one of the hottest talents in world football when he joined Liverpool.
"Attacking players always need a functioning team that works well around them. Anyone who loves football can still see how outstanding Florian is as a player," Klopp said recently.
That is also a view shared by Steven Gerrard.
"I can just picture him beating himself up on how his Liverpool thing has started. This kid is a major talent in my opinion. I've seen enough to believe and give him a chance. I think he needs help and support now," Gerrard told The Overlap.
Wirtz created 95 chances from open play in all competitions last season - at least 27 more than any other Liverpool player - and his fizzing pass for Victor Munoz's equaliser against Nottingham Forest in August showed a glimpse of his class, but those moments have been few and far in between.
Against City at the weekend there was a moment at 0-0 when Wirtz hit an effort wide despite having Barcola and Milos Kerkez in space on his left. It was a poor decision from a man desperate for a big moment.
Back in August, Wirtz spoke candidly about how he felt "more ready" for his second season at Anfield. The physicality was a key aspect, with bulking up a big focus of his first campaign.
"I definitely learned a lot. I just learned how Premier League football is played and I think I am more ready for my second season because I know how it is now. I am really excited for my next season," Wirtz said then.
He impressed in pre-season but two months into the new campaign, Wirtz needs to start delivering sooner rather than later.
If not, then Iraola will be left with a tough decision to make.

In yet another setback for immigrants amid US President Donald Trump's wider immigration crackdown, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on Tuesday (local time) issued a rule ending a grace period that previously permitted immigrants to keep working after their work authorisation expired while their renewal applications remained pending. According to Bloomberg Law, the rule permanently puts an end to the automatic 540-day extension period that allowed eligible immigrants to keep working in the country while their permit renewals were pending. The extension, which was introduced under former President Joe Biden's administration, was ended temporarily last year by DHS. The latest measure will affect asylum seekers and spouses of H-1B workers, including Indians. The federal department said the move would allow officials to conduct background checks on applicants more frequently. According to the report, the grace period was designed to provide security to immigrant workers who were at risk of being pushed out of work due to processing delays at US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). However, under the Trump administration, the agency has made it harder for immigrants to retain or renew their work permits. By 30 June 2026, the number of work permit renewal applications pending at USCIS for six months had surpassed 432,000. This included over 91,000 permit renewals that had been pending for over 18 months. Foreign workers can apply to renew their documents only within 180 days of expiry. In January, a group of H-4 visa holders sued the federal agency, arguing that the policy change violated the Administrative Procedure Act. In September, a California judge blocked the interim final rule from applying to those plaintiffs, finding that the agency had failed to meet procedural requirements or account for their reliance on the previous policy. The final rule takes effect upon publication in the Federal Register on 14 October. Continuing with its crackdown on immigrants, the Trump administration announced another policy change, under which the time refugees have to contest the termination of their status has been cut to 10 days from the previous 30 days, AP reported. The change takes effect on Wednesday (local time). Refugee advocates warned that the shorter deadline could make it difficult for those affected to find a lawyer and obtain the documents needed to challenge the decision, according to the report. The document stresses that the goal of the policy change is to “mitigate potential risks” associated with people who have been admitted to the country as refugees but were not eligible for refugee status. While the policy did not specify how many people are expected to be affected, it singled out refugees admitted under the Biden administration, alleging an “alarming erosion of the integrity” of the refugee programme during his tenure. The Trump administration is reportedly reassessing the cases of at least 185,000 refugees admitted during Biden’s presidency whose green card applications remain pending. Trump, who returned to the White House for a second term in January last year, made it clear that his administration would pursue a broader crackdown on immigration as part of his “Make America Great Again” and “America First” agenda. Other measures he announced include suspending refugee admissions, restricting entry from certain countries, and introducing a $100,000 payment requirement for certain new H-1B petitions. On 10 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) organised a major protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which protesters claim led to arbitrary voter deletions. In response to the demonstrations, authorities imposed a security crackdown, shutting down dozens of metro stations, cancelling trains, and enforcing prohibitory orders across the capital. Police have detained thousands of individuals, including political figures like Arvind Kejriwal, Pinarayi Vijayan and Mamata Banerjee, as well as CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who were later released.
Against this backdrop, a video (here & here) is being shared on social media with the claim that it shows protesters at Jantar Mantar demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing the October 10 CJP protest at Jantar Mantar, demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
Fact: The video was uploaded on 20 July 2026 and shows an earlier protest demanding Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation. It is unrelated to the October 10 CJP protest. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the same video (archive), uploaded to the Facebook page of Samar Moto Vlog on 20 July 2026. According to the post, the video shows a protest at Jantar Mantar on 20 July 2026, demanding the resignation of then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
This indicates that the video is unrelated to the CJP protest held at Jantar Mantar on 10 October 2026. Delhi Police also stated that the video was an old one from July 2026 and urged users to refrain from spreading misinformation. We have previously debunked several old and unrelated visuals falsely linked to the October 10 protest.
To sum it up, a video from July 2026 is being falsely shared as footage of the October 10 CJP protest at Jantar Mantar.

In 2020, the police department of picturesque Covington, Georgia, paid Flock Safety, the surveillance technology company, $40,000 to maintain 20 cameras around the city. The next year, it paid the same amount.
In 2022, that cost went up to $81,250. Fifteen new “Falcon” cameras, which Flock says have more sophisticated technology for reading license plates, accounted for $37,500. Another $3,750 went toward installing the new cameras, and the rest was spent maintaining the initial fleet.
Then, in 2024, the department paid Flock $113,225. Of that, $87,500 was to maintain its existing 35 cameras, a rate it agreed to pay for the next five years, and the remainder went toward eight new Falcon cameras. The next year, Covington paid Flock $159,000 for a combination of camera maintenance and enrollment in its Drone as First Responder program, which uses drones to fly to emergency scenes and stream footage back to the police station.
It’s unclear how much Covington will wind up paying Flock in 2026, but through August, it has paid $201,000—$100,000 to maintain its existing cameras, $800 to replace one, and another $100,200 for new software products. The Covington Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Overall, Flock is a small fraction of the Covington police department’s $12,488,733 budget for June 2025 to July 2026. But amid fierce blowback about Flock’s surveillance practices, contracts with the company are now being scrutinized in cities across the country. Flock did not provide a comment for this story.
WIRED obtained documents via public record request from a dozen Flock customers across the country and compared them to publicly available information from more than a dozen others. The documents shed light on how much Flock can actually cost communities, the way many of those deals are structured, and how the deals can expand over several years—leaving taxpayers on the hook year after year, with no end in sight.
“Once you let police officers try a tool,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, “it becomes really hard to get the political will and motivation to take that tool away from them.”
How Flock Gets in the Door
When Flock was founded in 2017, it originally sold its license plate readers to private homeowner associations (HOAs). By the time the company decided to sell to police departments in 2019, it had an in: Rather than starting a camera network from scratch, police could start by accessing the cameras that HOAs were already using.
A version of this story played out in Alpharetta, Georgia. In 2020, the city’s police department paid Flock $17,680 for five Falcon cameras and logins for Flock software called Wing, which can extract vehicle and license plate data from off-brand camera footage. The next year, when Alpharetta bought a few more Flock cameras, a payment justification noted that “several” local private homeowner associations had already purchased Flock and granted them camera access.
“We are looking to add more city cameras into the Flock system,” the justification read. According to the city, “other vendors” would “not integrate with our existing Flock system.”
Over the next several years, Alpharetta expanded its work with the company significantly. By 2025, the city’s annual Flock bill had ballooned to $381,000.
As in other industries, companies that sell technology to police often use financial incentives to get customers in the door. Clearview AI, Ring, and Taser have all ponied up enticing offers to agencies around the country.
“A lot of these police surveillance vendors have learned the lessons of general old salesmanship,” Guariglia tells WIRED. In other words, deals and discounts work.
In some cases, this looks like new and increasingly expansive Flock products. In 2025, for instance, Alpharetta paid for an upgrade to the Elite Package of FlockOS, which Flock describes as a real-time crime-center platform. Other products are first offered with a free trial; Alpharetta took advantage of one 90-day window last year to try a new product dubbed Nova.
Flock also expands its contracts by offering discounts if departments sign a multiyear contract. In 2024, Alpharetta locked into a five-year contract with Flock that would cost $254,250 the first year and $238,000 for each successive year. The agreement was $232,500 less than five one-year agreements, which could be subject to higher rates.
The Alpharetta Police Department declined to comment.
Five-year agreements are common among Flock customers, which the company has sometimes marketed as a “price-lock promotion.” In a November 2023 email, Flock customer success manager Gwen Saltal used this framing to offer a five-year deal to New York’s Albany County Sheriff’s Office.
“As you may be aware, on April 1st, the cost of new Falcons went from $2,500 to $3,000, which will apply for future renewal terms on existing cameras as well,” Saltal wrote. “If you would like to lock in your current camera rates, Flock is offering a 5-year contract to hold that pricing.” The Albany County Sheriff’s Office did not respond to a request for comment.
In other cities, Flock won long-term contracts because it offered a convenient product bundle. (This is far from exclusive to Flock; Motorola, for instance, recently inked a $54 million agreement with Louisiana for a slate of policing technology.)
Guillermo Mixer, the police chief of the central California city of Greenfield, reported in a January city council meeting that the annual cost of the city’s surveillance system was $112,900, spread across five contracts with three companies: Flock, the surveillance camera company SurveillanceGrid, and the drone company Paladin.

Mixer proposed ditching SurveillanceGrid and Paladin and instead locking into a five-year contract with Flock. The annual cost would be $136,940—about $24,000 more than its level of spending at the time. He noted, however, that the price included three new cameras and access to Flock911, which transmits 911 call data to responding officers, as well as drones from Aerodrome, a company Flock acquired in 2024.
A proposed order form listed dozens of other Flock products and services included in the contract, though it’s unclear how many of those were new additions.
In the end, Greenfield’s city council unanimously approved Mixer’s repackaged Flock contract. Mixer and the Greenfield Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.
What Your Money Gets You
WIRED reviewed a July 2022 “Public Sector Price Sheet” for Flock products for the Fort Lauderdale Police Department in Florida. Though it was generated for one specific agency, it reflects the approximate price ranges WIRED observed in Flock purchase orders around that time from around the country.
Historically, Flock has placed agencies into one of 14 pricing “buckets” for its software, depending on their size. Agencies in “Bucket 1” have one to 15 sworn officers and could pay as little as $2,000 or as much as $115,500 for Flock software, depending on whether they get a basic package or select multiple add-ons. The costs by bucket incrementally increase until Bucket 14—which is for state and federal agencies, or local forces with more than 3,000 officers—which the sheet says gets “custom” rates.
Hardware, meanwhile, tends to be sold at flat annual rates. According to the pricing sheet, individual license plate readers and surveillance cameras cost $3,000 to $5,200 per year, not including the cost of initial installation—which can run between $150 and $2,750 upfront.
The pricing sheet puts Flock’s individual gunshot detectors at $8,500 to $35,000 annually, depending on their range. The cost for its individual drones, meanwhile, is $50,000 to $150,000 per year, and Flock’s two “mobile security trailer” offerings cost $20,000 and $25,000 annually. Fort Lauderdale police did not respond to a request for comment.
Though prices vary depending on the size of a purchase and individual negotiations with a city, Flock’s pricing appears to be comparable to its competitors. Axon recently quoted Denver $150,000 to install 50 cameras across the city and maintain them for one year, while Motorola recently charged Manti, Utah, $4,704 for a single license plate reader.
Flock also has a pricing plan for replacing damaged or stolen products—a particularly relevant concern amid a national wave of vandalism targeting Flock cameras. Per Flock contract conditions, the company retains ownership of the products it sells to cities. This means that when people damage or destroy cameras, cities are on the hook for the cost. (It also means that if a city decides to end their Flock contract, they have to give the equipment back.)
According to Flock’s website and invoices reviewed by WIRED, the company has flat rates for replacing damaged or stolen products: $800 for cameras, $500 for poles, and $1,300 for both. (This is up from its 2021 pricing, according to documents from Anderson County, South Carolina, when its replacement cost was $500 for cameras and $150 for poles.)
Some cities have gone out of their way to draw attention to the fiscal toll of replacing damaged Flock equipment—sometimes overstating the cost in the process.
Police from Winona, Minnesota, and Rutherfordton, North Carolina, have said that camera replacements cost $3,000 and $3,500 each, respectively—or $2,200 and $2,700 higher than the listed cost. And in Derby, Kansas, after a man damaged 10 Flock cameras, local police claimed that he caused $26,000 in damages. But depending on whether he damaged the poles, replacements likely would have cost $8,000 to $13,000. Police from Winona, Rutherfordton, and Derby did not respond to a request for comment.
Flock’s pricing, ultimately, is much lower than other department expenses—like police helicopters, which can cost tens of millions of dollars annually, or hiring more police officers.
Still, when compared to other technology-related expenses, Flock spending can stand out.
In Pasadena, Texas, which has a population of about 148,500, the 2026 police budget allotted $427,133 for Flock, $500,842 for body camera software, and $500,000 for "Motorola maintenance." These were, by far, the most expensive technology purchases. Most of the other purchases had budgets of less than $100,000. The Pasadena Police Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Why Some Customers Are Ditching Flock
Across the country, cities big and small have chosen to increase their Flock spending significantly over just a few years.
Savannah, Georgia, for instance, paid $33,000 for Flock in 2020 and $193,500 in 2025. Snellville, Georgia, paid Flock $5,000 in 2021 and 2022; in 2025, it paid $163,275. This year, as of August, the city has paid Flock $138,934.94. The Savannah and Snellville Police Departments did not respond to requests for comment.
However, in some cases, Flock’s pricing eventually proved to be prohibitive.
Jack Hall—the sheriff of Lorain County, Ohio—recently announced that the county would be canceling its Flock contract. Hall said that Flock planned to raise Lorain County’s two-year rate for 15 cameras by 17 percent. For him, it was too much.
Hall and the Lorain County Sheriff’s Office did not respond for comment.
Killingworth, Connecticut, also decided to end its relationship with Flock. The town paid $14,600 last year for four cameras. Killingworth first selectman Eric Couture noted “privacy concerns” related to Flock and said that it didn’t provide much to police relative to its cost.
Couture told WIRED that Flock’s cost wasn’t entirely prohibitive. But, he added, the cameras “did not add any utility” for the town’s “resident state trooper.”

Is Mini DisplayPort becoming obsolete?
How Thunderbolt and USB-C replaced the need for a dedicated video port.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
For a while, Mini DisplayPort was one of the main options for video output on smaller devices. Apple announced it in 2008 to replace interfaces like VGA and DVI with a single, slimmer connector. While it was seen on most Mac models for several years, it's since become difficult to find computers with Mini DisplayPort — even Apple has removed the port from Macs.
But does that mean it's obsolete? Not exactly, although you won't see it as often as you used to. The DisplayPort standard remains popular, especially among workstations and gaming monitors, so it's not as if the technology itself has become obsolete. But we now have another small port that's favored.
Why Mini DisplayPort faded out
Mini DisplayPort is called "mini" for a reason. The full-size version (simply called DisplayPort) supports the same core specifications, but with a larger connector. Apple always opted for the tiny version because it fits better on smaller computers like MacBooks and the Mac mini.
It doesn't matter whether you use DisplayPort (DP) or Mini DisplayPort — both can transmit video and audio through a single cable. Compared to older connectors like DVI and VGA, one of the main advantages of DisplayPort is that it offers much higher bandwidth. Depending on the generation, DP can handle resolutions up to 8K and beyond, at high frame rates (144+Hz) depending on the resolution. Meanwhile, older connectors struggle with anything above 1080p.
When the Thunderbolt standard emerged, its first two iterations used the Mini DisplayPort connector. While a standard Mini DP port only carries video and audio, Thunderbolt also supports high-speed data transfers. That meant the same connector could be used for video, audio and data — perfect for accessories like Apple's Cinema Display.
In late 2015 and 2016, the Thunderbolt 3 standard arrived and switched to the USB-C connector. Apple and other PC manufacturers quickly moved to USB-C or HDMI, leaving the Mini DisplayPort connector behind. These days, USB-C has become the standard for nearly everything. Not only can it support high-speed data transfer, but it can also handle video, audio and even the Thunderbolt protocol — all in a single, small reversible connector. Not every USB-C port can handle the same tasks, but you'll see some version of it on almost every device.
To further push Mini DisplayPort down, USB-C also supports DisplayPort Alternate Mode, meaning a compatible USB-C cable and ports can carry the same DisplayPort signal through the more modern cable. PC makers have no reason to have people buy a Mini DP-to-DP cable when they can simply buy a USB-C-to-DP cable.
Where DisplayPort still makes sense
That doesn't mean DisplayPort is gone. Of course, you may still find older hardware with Mini DisplayPort, like past laptops and graphics cards. If you still have one of these, you can buy a Mini DP-to-DP cable to connect them to a modern monitor. Since the protocol is the same, they'll communicate with each other just fine. New hardware also continues to use full-sized version of DisplayPort. It's still the standard for many high-end monitors and graphics cards.
HDMI has come a long way in recent years and can now transmit video at incredibly high resolutions. Still, DisplayPort remains the gold standard for absurdly high resolutions and refresh rates, such as 4K at 240Hz. For comparison, while HDMI 2.1 offers up to 48 Gbps of bandwidth, DisplayPort 2.1 can reach 80 Gbps. This makes a difference for those looking to get the most out of the hardware they have. HDMI 2.2 offers 96 Gbps bandwidth, which may even the field a bit once compatible devices are widely available.
Of course, when using older hardware, not everything may work as expected. VR headsets, for example, can be picky about their video signal, and they don't always play nice with Mini DisplayPort when you use an adapter. The same goes for the old Apple Cinema Display — Apple makes it clear that it doesn't work through a Thunderbolt adapter. Still, it doesn't hurt to try if you have the right cables on hand.

The Rejinagar and Nandigram by-elections in West Bengal concluded on October 9, Friday, with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) clinching victory in both seats. BJP’s Shankharavh Sarkar won in Rejinagar and Hasirani Rath won the Nandigram seat.
Polling in both the assemblies were, however, marred by allegations of electoral malpractices, with the Congress demanding repolling.
Amid these allegations, digital censorship emerged as another flashpoint, with social media content documenting alleged electoral malpractice and vote rigging being restricted in India. The restrictions also added to concerns over the growing suppression of online criticism of the ruling party. For the past couple of months, Alt News has reported extensively on this social media censorship frenzy in India.
On October 7, the Facebook page of the Murshidabad district wing of the West Bengal Pradesh Congress (@DCCMurshidabad) was restricted under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules. The page remains unavailable at the tome of this article being written.
ALSO READ: Bengal bypolls: Facebook restricts local news pages covering Opposition campaign in Rejinagar
On the same day, prominent local news outlet NBTV Bangla’s (@nbtvbngla) Facebook page was also restricted in India for seven days following the same notification. With over five lakh followers, the outlet reported critically on issues of the government or law enforcement in the context of the Nandigram and Rejinagar bypolls.
Alt News learnt that the two videos uploaded by the Facebook page of NBTV which were restricted in India directly addressed allegations of voting malpractices in the Rejinagar by-election.
The first of the two videos — both of which are still accessible on Instagram — shows a woman claiming that voters in Rejinagar were being intimidated away from the polling booths. A man also appears in this video, alleging that not even 10 voters had been able to cast their votes.
View this post on Instagram
Another video shows allegations being levelled by voters of the Mirzapur Gram Panchayat area in Rejinagar. “Who I choose to vote for is entirely my own decision. They marked our fingers with ink and sent us home, even though we had not yet cast our votes,” a man appearing in the video claims.
View this post on Instagram
“It is not the first time this has happened. Several of our social media posts have been restricted in the past,” Zeba Noshin, a reporter at NBTV, told Alt News.
Notably, the notices received by Congress’ Murshidabad district page and NBTV Bangla state that the account had been restricted pursuant to legal requirements. This indicates that the restrictions followed a legal request or official complaint concerning the content on these pages, rather than being flagged by Meta’s own content-moderation process.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
A video uploaded on Facebook by Bengali digital media outlet Inscript.me was restricted in India under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000 on the day of the polls, October 6. A representative of the platform told Alt News that the banned video was regarding allegations of rigging in Rejinagar.
The title of the video visible on the notice sent by Meta reads, “People of Rejinagar allege rigging in byelection”.
On October 9, another Facebook post by Inscript.me, a report on Rahul Gandhi’s detainment by Delhi Police during the protests demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, was also restricted.
A Facebook user named Diya Maity also alleged that her page with close to 2.5 lakh followers had been restricted for seven days. She was also posting content on the alleged election rigging in the Rejinagar constituency.
Rigging, Malpractices & Intimidation: Opposition
The October 6 bypolls were necessitated in Murshidabad’s Rejinagar and East Medinipur’s Nandigram, after AJUP chief Humayun Kabir and Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari chose to vacate these two seats respectively, having secured victory in two constituencies apiece.
Suvendu Adhikari’s home constituency, Nandigram has a Muslim population of around 27 per cent. He vacated this seat, and retained Bhabanipur, where he defeated former chief minister Mamata Banerjee.
The demography is entirely different in Rejinagar, with Muslims accounting for around 69 per cent of its electorate. Kabir won both Nowda and Rejinagar and subsequently vacated the latter, where his victory margin was more than 58,000 votes. His son, Golam Nabi Azad, was contesting the seat vacated by him.
Opposition leaders repeatedly alleged that the BJP was manipulating votes and applying pressure tactics in the lead up to the polls. On the day of polling, the AJUP chief was taken into custody by the police after a heated altercation. He was released from the Rejinagar police station after spending 12 hours in custody.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

Retro gaming is going through a wild time at the moment, thanks to decompilations and recompilations that are letting gamers port classic titles to new devices, or merge code from two different games into a single new experience. Microsoft has witnessed skateboarding being modded into Call of Duty and Halo being played in a web browser, and the company is now officially embracing the chaos of this new AI-powered era of game modding.
Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports
Microsoft has created a new Xbox Labs group to experiment with decompiling and recompiling games.
Microsoft is putting together a new Xbox Labs group to explore the rapid emergence of these mods, many of which use AI models to help modders remix games in ways we’ve rarely seen before. Xbox Labs will be a “small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience,” says Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. “We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.”
Sharma thinks the experiments we’ve seen in recent weeks, where Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside browsers, “challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games.”
“While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators,” says Sharma. “These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.“
Modders are now doing the type of work that Microsoft has been doing for decades with its Xbox backward compatibility program, letting old games run on modern hardware. But they’re doing it without the business model restrictions that Microsoft is tied to. It’s starting to feel like we’re just a model or two away from even more breakthroughs that decouple more modern games from their intended hardware.
Sharma clearly sees an opportunity here, particularly for AI agent use at Xbox. “I think Xbox has an important role to play here,” says Sharma. “Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide.”
Xbox Labs is clearly a way for Microsoft to experiment with how AI will shape where games are played, and Xbox will share any tools and learnings with developers. The bigger question is how Microsoft will respond to decompiles and recompiles of games where modders take its precious IP and make it freely available. Modding is fun, but I can’t see Microsoft and other publishers seeing the fun side if modern console games start to appear where they shouldn’t.
I asked Microsoft to comment about unauthorized IP use, but the company didn’t respond in time for publication.
Here’s Sharma’s full memo:
Team,
The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to play them, and best of all, more people than ever playing. That growth helped make XBOX what it is today, and we’ve helped shape the industry in return, from bringing hard drives to consoles and online gaming through Xbox Live to Game Pass and cloud gaming, alongside franchises that have brought millions of people together.
In recent weeks, we’ve seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. Perhaps more surprisingly, we’ve seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another.
These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games. While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models. To explore these possibilities, I’ve asked Scott to stand-up XBOX LABS, a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience. We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.
I think XBOX has an important role to play here. Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. We’ve spent 25 years learning how to make great games, and I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible. As we learn, we’ll share the tools we build with developers across the industry, just as we always have.
Our priorities aren’t changing. We remain committed to the 4Cs, to making great games, to our hardware and to being responsible stewards of IP and the communities built around it. LABS gives us a way to explore new technology without abandoning the work already underway.
Asha
